sent: Three Thousand Years in Brief: Israel, Judah, Rome and the Name "Palestine"
One says that Jews were absent from it for two thousand years.
The other says that Palestinians appeared only in the twentieth century.
It shows Jewish kingdoms in the first millennium BCE and a Jewish presence that survived Rome's suppression of two revolts.
It also shows centuries in which the majority of the land's people became Arabic-speaking Muslims and Christians, the ancestors of today's Palestinians.
This section traces that record from the first inscriptions to the end of Ottoman rule, follows the history of the two names, "Israel" and "Palestine," and sets out where scholars disagree.
Israel in the stones.
The earliest known mention of Israel outside the Bible is on a victory stele of the Egyptian pharaoh Merneptah, dated about 1207 BCE.
Flinders Petrie found it in 1896 in the first courtyard of Merneptah's mortuary temple at Thebes; it is now in the Cairo Museum.
The line that names Israel uses a stock phrase for a conquered place, rendered "Israel is wasted, its grain (or seed) is not."
Egyptian scribes added to names an unpronounced sign, called a determinative, that told the reader what kind of thing was named.
Names such as Ashkelon and Gezer carry the sign for a place.
"Israel" carries the sign for a people or ethnic group.
At the end of the thirteenth century BCE, then, an Egyptian royal scribe knew of a people called Israel.

The Tel Dan stele, an inscription in Old Aramaic dated about 840 BCE from its script, was found in 1993 at Tel Dan in northern Israel during excavations led by Avraham Biran; two smaller fragments followed the next year.
It is held at the Skirball Museum in Jerusalem.
On it an Aramaean king, most likely Hazael of Damascus, boasts of victories over the king of Israel and over the "House of David."
Line 9 is the earliest known mention of David's dynasty outside the Bible.
From the other side of the Jordan comes the Mesha Stele, also called the Moabite Stone, of about the same date and written in Moabite.
The missionary F. A. Klein saw it in 1868 near Dibon in Transjordan.
It states that "Omri was the king of Israel, and he oppressed Moab for many days."
Two inscriptions from neighboring peoples, written in their own languages to celebrate their own victories, named the kingdom of Israel and the dynasty of David.
These are the outside witnesses to the Jewish kingdoms of Israel and Judah that existed in the first millennium BCE.
Where the name "Palestine" comes from.
The earliest surviving text to use the name Palestine is the Histories of the Greek writer Herodotus, from the second half of the fifth century BCE.
He speaks of "Syria Palaistine" for the coast between Phoenicia and Egypt.

According to one secondary account, Herodotus also mentions "Syrians who are in Palestine" who practice circumcision (Histories 2.104.3), and both Philo of Alexandria, who died about 50 CE, and Josephus, writing about 93–94 CE, used "Palestine" when writing about Jews.
The Greek name is generally linked to the Philistines, in Hebrew peleshet, an Aegean people who settled the southern coastal plain in the twelfth century BCE.
The scholar G. W. Bowersock calls the older variant forms, such as Peleset and Phlishtu, etymologically obscure.
The name was in Greek use, then, more than five centuries before Rome attached it to a province.
Rome, the revolts and the renaming.
Rome conquered the region in 63 BCE and in 6 CE created a province of Judaea whose population was predominantly Jewish.
Two great revolts against Roman rule failed.
The first ended with the destruction of the Second Temple in Jerusalem in 70 CE.
The second, led by Bar Kokhba, is dated 132–135 in some accounts and 132–136 in others, the end date being uncertain.
After it Rome killed, enslaved or expelled much of Judea's Jewish population.
It rebuilt Jerusalem as a pagan colony, Aelia Capitolina, and barred Jews from the city.
Roman inscriptions show that around the time of this revolt Judaea was merged with Galilee into a province called Syria Palaestina.
Reference summaries describe the renaming as one that most scholars see as aimed at severing the Jewish connection to the land, and many historians link it to the punishment of the Jewish rebels.
Its strongest scholarly statement is Louis Feldman's, from 1990: the emperor Hadrian was the likely author, given his decrees against Jewish national and religious life.
Feldman conceded that only circumstantial evidence links Hadrian to the change.
It had been in Greek and Latin use for centuries, including by Jewish writers.

Ronald Syme suggested that the change may have come in 130 CE, before the revolt began, and David Jacobson, writing in 1999, and others have read it as an administrative or Hellenizing step rather than a punishment.
Both cases agree on the facts that matter most: Rome did rename the province after, or around, a revolt it crushed, and the name it chose was not new.
Rome's victory did not end Jewish life in the land.
A continuous, smaller Jewish presence remained, and Galilee became its religious center.
Much of classical Jewish literature was produced there.
In the sixteenth century Jewish communities took root in the four holy cities of Jerusalem, Hebron, Tiberias and Safed, forming what came to be called the Old Yishuv, the pre-Zionist community.
Its numbers, institutions and place in Ottoman Jerusalem are the subject of .
Byzantium, the caliphate and the empires that followed.
The land passed next to Byzantine Christian rule.
Under Byzantium the region was divided into First, Second and Third Palestine.
After the Muslim conquest in the seventh century, First Palestine became Filastin and Second Palestine became al-Urdunn.
Under the Umayyad caliph 'Abd al-Malik, in the late seventh century, Palestine existed as a province of the caliphate, Jund Filastin.
The Arabic form of the name was used for the region from the early Islamic period onward.
Crusader kingdoms followed, then the Mamluks in the thirteenth century, and from 1516 the Ottoman Empire, which ruled for four centuries until 1917.
Over these centuries the majority of the population became Arabic-speaking Muslims and Christians.
Under the Ottomans, "Palestine" was an informal term rather than the name of a province; how the land was in fact administered is told in .
The word "Palestinian" for Arabic speakers of the land is attested from 1898, in the writing of Khalil Baydas, and in 1913 Ruhi al-Khalidi wrote of "the Palestinian race" in the newspaper Filastin.
Both dates come from Zachary Foster, as cited by the Jewish Virtual Library.
Four thousand years of Palestine?
Nur Masalha, in Palestine: A Four Thousand Year History (2018), argues that Palestinian place-names and identity persisted through Roman, Byzantine and Islamic rule.
Reviewing the book, Bowersock called the four-thousand-year title indefensible.
The documented name, he pointed out, begins with Herodotus, and its location and meaning kept changing from one empire to the next.
The Jewish Virtual Library takes a further position: that the name was imposed by Rome, and that Palestinian nationalism dates from the 1910s and 1920s, as a reaction to Zionism.
The persistence of the name itself, through the Byzantine provinces and Jund Filastin, is also documented.
"Stolen from Rome."

One form of the argument circulates widely in comment threads: that every Palestinian symbol was stolen from someone else, the keffiyeh, the flag and the name itself, the last taken from Rome to erase Judea.
The keffiyeh is a traditional headdress worn across the Arab world; its black-and-white pattern became associated with Palestinian nationalism during the revolt of 1936–39.
The Palestinian flag derives from the flag of the 1916 Arab Revolt, as do the flags of Jordan and other Arab states.

Rome did rename the province after the Bar Kokhba revolt, as told above, but the name was already more than 500 years old, and the Arabic Filastin was in use for the region for centuries from the early Islamic period.
A related line, that Arafat was born in Cairo, is largely accurate, as the opening section on method noted, and says nothing about a people's history.

Why Rome renamed Judaea, and exactly when, is not stated in any ancient source; the punitive reading is the more widely held, and the administrative reading has serious scholarly support, but neither can be proven from the surviving texts.
The end date of the Bar Kokhba revolt is given as 135 in some sources and 136 in others.

How much continuity of identity, as opposed to continuity of residence and of place-names, ran from the Byzantine and early Islamic provinces to modern Palestinians is the substance of the Masalha–Bowersock exchange, and the record of names alone cannot decide it.
The size of the Jewish population that remained at any given point between Rome and the Ottomans is described in the sources here only as smaller, and fluctuating.
A people called Israel is named in an Egyptian inscription of about 1207 BCE, and the kingdom of Israel and the House of David by its enemies about 840 BCE; Jews remained in the land after Rome.
Arabic-speaking Muslims and Christians formed its majority across many centuries of residence, under a name that Greek writers used before Rome and Arab rulers used after it.
Language and Ancestry: Two Different Questions
People sometimes ask which Jews are "Semitic Jews" and which are not.
"Semitic" is the name of a family of languages, as  sets out.
The answers to the two questions do not line up, and neither answers a third question: who is Jewish.
Jewish law answers that one.
A Jew is someone born to a Jewish mother or someone who has converted, and the movements differ on the details.
Hebrew was the language of prayer and study, and for many centuries almost no Jewish community spoke it at home; everyday speech followed the region.
Some of those everyday languages were Semitic.
The Jews of Baghdad spoke Judeo-Arabic, Yemen's Jews spoke Judeo-Yemeni Arabic, Kurdish Jews spoke a Neo-Aramaic language, and Morocco's older Jewish communities spoke Judeo-Arabic or Judeo-Berber.
The Beta Israel of Ethiopia mostly spoke Amharic, or Tigrinya in Tigray, both of them Semitic languages, and they prayed in Ge'ez, another.
Many more of the languages were not Semitic.
Ashkenazi Jews spoke Yiddish, a Germanic language, and Sephardi Jews spoke Judeo-Spanish, a Romance one.
The Jews of Iran, Bukhara and the eastern Caucasus spoke Iranian languages: Judeo-Persian, Bukhori and Juhuri.
Georgia's Jews spoke a Jewish form of Georgian and Greece's Romaniote Jews a Jewish Greek.
The Bene Israel spoke Marathi and the Jews of Kerala spoke Jewish Malayalam.
Ancestry is a separate question, and the most complete answer comes from a genome-wide study published in Nature in 2010 by Doron Behar and colleagues.
They genotyped 121 people from 14 Jewish communities.
Most of the Jewish samples formed a tight cluster lying over the Druze and Cypriot samples, and the authors traced the origins of most diaspora communities to the Levant.
One held the Ashkenazi, Moroccan and Sephardi Jews.
The other held the Middle Eastern communities, Iranian and Iraqi Jews, and the Caucasus communities of Georgia and Azerbaijan.
Yemenite Jews formed a compact cluster of their own, closest to Bedouin and Saudi samples.
The ancestry component typical of Europeans was larger in Ashkenazi, Moroccan and Sephardi Jews than in the Middle Eastern communities.

The Beta Israel of Ethiopia and the Jews of India, both the Bene Israel and the Cochin Jews, clustered with the non-Jewish populations living around them, although the Bene Israel showed a clear link to the Levant on the male line.
A 2016 study of the Bene Israel alone found both substantial Jewish and substantial Indian ancestry.
The mixing happened within the last thousand years, the Jewish side came mostly through men, and the local side mostly through women.
Put side by side, the two answers show why the word "Semitic" cannot sort Jews by descent.
The Beta Israel spoke Semitic languages, yet their genomes sit closest to their Ethiopian neighbours.
More precisely, they sit closest to the Semitic-speaking Ethiopians rather than the Cushitic-speaking ones.
Ashkenazi Jews spoke a Germanic language, yet they carry Middle Eastern ancestry.
The grid below places each community twice: down the side, by what the record shows about its ancestry; across the top, by whether its everyday language was Semitic.
The Jews of Kaifeng in China most likely descend from Persian Jews who arrived in the twelfth century, and Israel requires their descendants to convert formally.

The Abayudaya of Uganda began practising Judaism in 1919 as a religious movement; they do not claim descent from ancient Israel, and since 2002 their conversions have been overseen by the Conservative movement.
The Bnei Menashe of northeast India and the Lemba of southern Africa claim descent from ancient Israel.
For the Bnei Menashe the claim is not established: one test was never published, and a second was not peer-reviewed.
Studies of the Lemba from 1996 and 2000 reported Middle Eastern markers on the male line.
A 2014 reassessment found that such markers do not reliably predict Jewish ancestry, and most Lemba today are Christian.

Communities drawn with an outline (Syrian, Kurdish, Bukharan, Italian and Romaniote Jews among them) are placed by their documented history alone, because no genome study of them was consulted for this book.

The origins of the Beta Israel are still argued among historians: one view holds that they emerged as a group in Ethiopia between the fourteenth and sixteenth centuries, another that they arrived far earlier.
It does not rank Jewish communities, and it does not make any of them more or less Jewish.
Every community on it includes converts and their descendants, and under Jewish law a convert is fully Jewish.
Israel's own institutions recognised the Beta Israel as Jews in 1973 and 1975, and declared the Bene Israel "Jews in every respect" in 1964.
The same genetic research finds that Palestinians and Jews of the Levant share substantial common ancestry, a point taken up in .
Whether people speak a Semitic language, where a community's ancestors came from, and who is Jewish are three separate questions, and each has its own answer.
Arguments about Israel's character often come down to a question that can be answered from statute: who may become a citizen, and on what terms?
One opened the door to every Jew in the world.
The other decided which of the Arabs who had remained inside the new state in 1948 would be counted as its citizens.
Half a century later a third measure, presented as temporary, closed a route by which Palestinians from the occupied territories could join spouses who held Israeli citizenship.
The Knesset passed the Law of Return on 5 July 1950.
Its first section reads: "Every Jew has the right to come to this country as an oleh."

The second section obliges the state to grant the immigrant's visa, with only three exceptions: the minister may refuse an applicant found to be acting against the Jewish people, or likely to endanger public health, or likely to endanger the security of the state.

On 23 August 1954 the Knesset added a fourth ground for refusal, a criminal past likely to endanger the public welfare, and moved the power to decide from the Minister of Immigration to the Minister of the Interior.
Amendment No. 2 extended the law's rights to the child and the grandchild of a Jew, to the spouse of a Jew, and to the spouses of that child and grandchild.
It excluded a person who had been a Jew and had voluntarily changed religion (Section 4A).
For the first time the law also said who counted as a Jew: a person born of a Jewish mother, or converted to Judaism, and not a member of another religion (Section 4B).
The grandchild clause in 4A reached well beyond it, to people with a single Jewish grandparent who were not Jews under that definition at all.
According to Christian Joppke and Zeev Rosenhek, people who were not Jews under the religious definition made up nearly 20% of immigrants in 1990–94, 45% in 1997 and 53% in 1998.
On these figures, by 1998 a majority of the law's immigrants were not Jews under the religious definition.
The same study reports that 64% of Jewish Israelis surveyed at the time supported the Law of Return.
The Nationality Law, 1952.
That was settled by the Nationality Law, which came into force on 14 July 1952.
Citizenship by return went automatically to every oleh under the Law of Return.

Citizenship by residence went to a former citizen of Mandate Palestine only if three conditions were all met: he had been registered as an inhabitant on 1 March 1952; he was an inhabitant on the day the law took effect; and he had been in Israel continuously from the establishment of the state, or had entered legally.
The residence route was the one that decided the citizenship of Arabs who remained.
The scale of what was at stake appears in Joppke and Rosenhek's figures: of the 700,000–900,000 Palestinians they count, about 170,000 remained after 1948–49.
At the 1948 census, 65% of Israel's Jewish population had been born abroad, and from 1948 to 1995 net migration supplied nearly half of Jewish population growth.
The dispute over the Law of Return turns on whom it admits and whom it does not.

The strongest form of the defense was put by Alex Stein in 2013: the law restores Jewish access to a homeland lost since 70 CE, and it provides a refuge, because states with non-Jewish majorities did not reliably protect their Jews.
On that reading the law is a response to a documented history of persecution, and its preference for Jews is its purpose, not a flaw.
Palestinian refugees and their descendants cannot return, while any Jew, anywhere, may immigrate.
Critics, including Palestinian advocates, make that point, as Stein's article itself records.
Adalah, the Arab-Israeli legal center, lists the Law of Return in its database of discriminatory laws; the English text used in this section comes from that database.
A third reading treats the law as neither unique nor simply explained by Jewish nationhood.
Joppke and Rosenhek, writing in 2001, set Israel beside West Germany, which admitted ethnic Germans as "resettlers."
Germany then changed course: a 1993 law ended the status for anyone born after 1 January 1993 and capped arrivals.
Israel's equivalent law survived.
The authors explain that survival not by ethnic nationhood alone but by two particular pressures: the demographic rivalry with the Palestinians, and the memory of the Holocaust.
Ethnic-priority immigration was not unique to Israel.
But the one comparable democracy they study wound its scheme down, and Israel did not.
The Citizenship and Entry into Israel Law was passed in 2003, during the Second Intifada, as a one-year temporary measure.
It generally barred residence permits for Palestinians from the occupied territories who were married to Israelis, and was later extended to citizens of Iran, Lebanon, Syria and Iraq.
Its critics argue that it discriminates against Arab citizens of Israel, who are more likely than other Israelis to marry Palestinians from the territories.
In 2006 Israel's Supreme Court upheld the law by six votes to five in HCJ 7052/03, even though a majority of the justices found that it harmed family life and equality disproportionately.
In July 2021 the Knesset failed to extend it and it lapsed.
On 10 March 2022, the Times of Israel reported, it was re-enacted by 45 votes to 15, passing with votes from the right-wing opposition.
The new version states that its aim includes protecting Israel's Jewish majority.
After the vote, according to the Times of Israel, Interior Minister Ayelet Shaked called the result a victory for a "Jewish and democratic state" over "a state of all its citizens."
Its explanatory notes, and the State Attorney in court, argued that status gained through marriage could be exploited for terror.
Shin Bet testimony cited about 48 such cases in 2001–2021.

Interior Ministry data for 2020, as summarized by the Israel Democracy Institute, give the scale around those cases: about 800–1,000 family-unification applications a year, and about 13,000 Palestinians living in Israel on permits or temporary status.

Some supporters told the Knesset that the aim was to prevent large-scale Palestinian settlement in Israel; the 2022 text names the Jewish majority as part of its purpose; and, as noted above, critics argue that it discriminates against Arab citizens.

The two counts of terror cases, 45 for 2001–2020 from Interior Ministry data and about 48 for 2001–2021 from Shin Bet testimony, cover different periods and come from different bodies; this book has not reconciled them case by case.

The terms of the 2022 law beyond its vote and its stated aim, including any quota and how long it runs, have not been verified here, so this section does not say whether an Arab citizen's spouse from the West Bank can obtain residence today, or on what terms.

Nor does the record here document any route by which a Palestinian refugee from 1948 who was outside the state in 1952 could become a citizen; the residence route was closed by its own dates, and naturalization required a right to permanent residence, which the record here does not show such a refugee could obtain.
Whether the Law of Return is best understood as refuge or as preference is a judgment the texts cannot make for the reader.

They show only that it extends a right to every Jew, that the critics' objection rests on the refugees of 1948 having no equivalent right, and that the people who defend it and the people who oppose it are describing the same law.
The Land's Other Communities
A common shorthand presents the conflict as Jews against Muslims, and Palestinians as uniformly Muslim.

Alongside its Jewish and Muslim Arab majorities it holds Druze, whose faith took shape in the Middle Ages and accepts no converts; Bedouin, whose relationship with the state turns on land; Circassians, Muslims from the Caucasus who serve in Israel's army; Samaritans, a community of a few hundred who trace their descent to ancient Israel; and Palestinian Christians, members of some of the oldest Christian communities on earth.
Each stands in a different relationship to the State of Israel, and those differences are documented in law, in census figures and in the record of demolitions and conscription.
The legal situations of Palestinians in general, and the numbers of Arab citizens of Israel as a whole, are set out earlier in this volume .
The Druze.
The Druze faith took shape in the Middle Ages and has accepted no converts since the eleventh century .
According to Minority Rights Group, about 150,000 Druze live in Israel proper, in eighteen villages, and about 24,000 to 25,000 more in the Golan Heights .

Central Bureau of Statistics figures reported in April 2024 give a slightly higher total for Israel, about 152,000, against 14,500 in 1949; the largest Druze localities at the end of 2022 were Daliyat al-Karmel and Yarka, each with more than 17,000 people .
The Druze relationship with the state was set early.
Druze in Galilee and on Mount Carmel fought alongside the Jewish forces in 1948.
In 1956 Druze men were included in military conscription, and in 1961 separate Druze religious courts were established  .
The Golan Druze followed a different course.
After Israel captured the Golan Heights in 1967 it offered citizenship to the Druze living there, and, according to the same April 2024 report, most refused .
The sources used here do not say how many have since accepted, or whether Golan Druze who did not take citizenship are subject to the draft.
The Circassians.
Israel's Circassians are Muslims whose origins lie in the Caucasus.
They live mainly in two Galilee villages: Kfar Kama, with about 2,000 people of the Shapsug group, and Rehaniya, with about 1,000 of the Abadzakh group.
According to a community-sourced account, they were settled there at the Ottoman Sultan's request in the late nineteenth century, and Circassian men serve in the army and the police .
That account rests on a single source drawn from a Circassian foundation, and it does not settle when and why the families left the Caucasus; this book does not go beyond what it states.
The largest of these communities, and the one whose position is most contested, is the Bedouin of the Negev.
About 92,000 Bedouin lived in the Negev before 1948.
After the war about 11,000 remained inside Israel, from 19 of the original 95 tribes, according to Minority Rights Group and the Israeli-Arab legal center Adalah  .
Those who stayed were concentrated in an area known as the siyag, Arabic for "fence," of about 1.5 million dunams, against some 13 million dunams they had used before .
The Land Acquisition Law of 1953 and the Planning and Building Law of 1965 registered much of the Bedouin's land as state land .
