sent: From the 1960s the state built seven planned townships, beginning with Tel Sheva, Rahat and Kseifa .
Israel does not recognize the Bedouin as an indigenous people .
Just over 300,000 Bedouin live in Israel today, about 3% of the population .
Recognition has moved slowly.
The Association for Civil Rights in Israel counted 46 unrecognized Bedouin villages in the Negev, of which the state had recognized 11 by about 2011, leaving 35.

In May 2024 Israeli authorities demolished about 47 to 50 homes in the unrecognized village of Wadi al-Khalil; National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir called the buildings illegal constructions and the demolition "an important step"  .
Minority Rights Group puts the population of the unrecognized villages at about 100,000 people in roughly 35 villages .
Adalah, as reported by Al-Monitor in May 2024, puts it at about half of some 300,000 Negev Bedouin, which is about 150,000 .
Note also that Adalah's base of some 300,000 refers to the Negev Bedouin, while Minority Rights Group's figure of just over 300,000 refers to the Bedouin of Israel as a whole.

The state and its ministers treat construction in unrecognized villages as illegal building on state land, which is the basis on which demolition orders are issued and on which Ben-Gvir defended Wadi al-Khalil  .

Bedouin and rights groups answer that the villages either predate the state or were placed where they stand by the state itself, and that 35 of them meet every Central Bureau of Statistics test for a settlement except the minister's declaration  .
On that view, the Bedouin are a dispossessed indigenous people rather than squatters.
The Samaritans hold that they descend from Israelites who escaped the Assyrian deportation after 722/721 BCE.
They keep their own version of the Pentateuch and hold Mount Gerizim sacred; their temple there was destroyed by John Hyrcanus in 128 BCE .
In January 2003 it numbered 654: 349 in Holon, inside Israel, and 305 at Kiryat Luza on Mount Gerizim near Nablus .

The Oslo arrangements placed the Nablus community under Palestinian administration, so that a single community of a few hundred people now lives on both sides of the lines described at the start of this volume .
Palestinian Christians.
Palestinians include one of the world's oldest Christian communities.
In the early twentieth century Christians were about 12% of Palestine's population.

According to the 2017 census, fewer than 50,000 live in the West Bank and East Jerusalem today, between 47,000 and 50,000, or about 1% of the population; most are concentrated in Bethlehem, Ramallah and East Jerusalem  .
Gaza's Christians fell from about 3,000 in the early 2000s to about 1,000 before October 2023, and to a few hundred since  .
On 17 July 2025 Israeli fire struck the compound of the Holy Family Church, Gaza's only Catholic parish, where about 600 Christians and Muslims had taken shelter.
Pope Leo XIV said he was deeply saddened and called for a ceasefire.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said that Israel "deeply regrets" that "stray ammunition" had hit the church, and that the incident was being investigated  .
The same month, in the West Bank, arsonists targeted the area of the ancient church of St George in Taybeh, the last all-Christian town there, in what the reporting describes as settler arson .
Munther Isaac, the Lutheran pastor in Bethlehem, has warned that Palestinian Christians risk disappearing from the Holy Land .

Palestinian Christians live under the same occupation and the same war as their Muslim neighbors, and their presence alone is enough to show that "Jews against Muslims" does not describe the conflict.
How many people live in the Negev's unrecognized villages is disputed, with estimates from about 70,000 to about 150,000, and no source explains the gap.

Whether those villages are illegal construction on state land or the homes of a dispossessed indigenous people is a question of how the land was allocated after 1948, on which the state and the Bedouin and their advocates disagree.
The Druze figures differ slightly between Minority Rights Group's 150,000 and the Central Bureau of Statistics' 152,000.
The Circassian account rests on one community-derived source and does not establish when or why the families left the Caucasus.
And the figures for Palestinian Christians are drawn from news reporting that cites the 2017 census rather than from the census itself.
Country by Country: How the Jews of the Arab World Left
The departure of the Jews of the Arab world is usually told as one event with one number attached.
The previous section followed Iraq, the largest single case, and the arrival camps in Israel .
One says that Israel's ties to Yemen began with the Houthis and that its ties to Morocco began with the agreements of 2020.
The other shortcut makes every departure an expulsion, or every departure a voluntary emigration organized from Israel.
Libya.
Libya had about 21,000 Jews in 1911, about 4% of a population of 550,000, and 30,387 on the eve of the Second World War.
Italy's racial laws of 1938 were enforced in Libya from 1940.
By June 1942 some 2,584 Jews had been deported to the camp at Giado, where 562 of them died.
More violence came after the war, under British military administration.
In November 1945 a three-day attack on the Jews of Tripoli killed 120 Jews and destroyed at least five synagogues.
According to Yad Vashem, 30,972 Libyan Jews emigrated to Israel in the wake of the violence around 1948.
Those who stayed were pushed to the margins by law: a 1961 law denied nearly all Jews proof of citizenship.
After riots in 1967 about 6,000 were airlifted to Rome, and by 2004 no Jews remained in Libya.
In Libya, then, the sequence ran from a fascist camp to a postwar pogrom under a European administration, then a mass departure to Israel, and finally legal exclusion.
The Tripoli killings of 1945 came before the partition vote and before Israel existed.
Egypt.
Egypt's community numbered an estimated 75,000–80,000 at its height in 1948.
That figure is an Israeli Foreign Ministry estimate, cited by the University of Washington's Stroum Center.
Bombs in Cairo's Jewish quarter between June and November 1948 killed more than 70 Jews, according to the same essay.
A second break came with the Suez war.
From 29 October 1956 the Egyptian government treated Jews as enemies of the state.
About 1,000 were arrested in Cairo and 450 Jewish-owned businesses were confiscated.
From 15 November, Jews leaving the country had to sign forms renouncing their property and their Egyptian citizenship.
These details rest on the historian Joel Beinin and on an American Jewish Committee factsheet of March 1957.
According to figures cited by the Stroum Center, about 25,000 Jews left Egypt in 1956, leaving roughly 15,000 in the country in 1957.
Egypt's departures therefore came in at least two waves, eight years apart, with different triggers: the violence of 1948, and state measures taken during the Suez war.
A third episode belongs to Egypt's story, the 1954 Israeli sabotage operation in which Egyptian Jews were recruited; it is told in the previous section.
Aleppo, Aden and Bahrain: the partition vote.
The United Nations voted to partition Palestine on 29 November 1947.
Within a week, Jewish communities far from Palestine were attacked.
According to the Center for Israel Education, rioters in Aleppo on 30 November damaged the Great Synagogue and the Aleppo Codex, a manuscript of the tenth century.
They destroyed some 150 Jewish homes, 50 shops, five schools and 18 synagogues.
In Aden, then under British rule, rioting from 2 December 1947 killed 82 Jews and wounded 76.
In Manama, Bahrain, on 5 December, the synagogue was destroyed and one Jewish woman was killed, according to the same source.
The sources available for this book do not record how many Jews left each of these places afterwards, or where they went.
Yemen.
Yemen's Jews were among the oldest Jewish communities in the world and had lived there for well over a thousand years.
Between June 1949 and September 1950 Operation Magic Carpet, also called "On Wings of Eagles", airlifted about 49,000 of them to Israel.
It was organized with the American Jewish Joint Distribution Committee and flown by Alaska Airlines and other carriers.
Many of the emigrants first walked for weeks to reach the British colony of Aden, where the flights began.
In Israel many were placed in transit camps, where hundreds of children were reported dead or missing.
This became the Yemenite Children Affair, for which Israel expressed "regret" and paid compensation in 2021 .
So Israel's first tie to Yemen was a people moved by airlift, some seventy years before the missiles.
Morocco.
Morocco's Jewish community had been rooted there for two millennia and was among the largest in the Arab world, numbering in the hundreds of thousands in the 1940s.
Most emigrated after 1948, the majority to Israel.
Between 1961 and 1964 a secret operation, Operation Yachin, brought about 97,000 Moroccan Jews to Israel with the Moroccan government's quiet consent.
Historians record that Israel, together with American Jewish organizations, made payments to the Moroccan government to allow the departures.
The money chain here ran in the opposite direction from Egypt's confiscations.
Israelis of Moroccan descent became one of Israel's largest communities.

The two states' official ties came much later and did not last at first: Morocco and Israel opened low-level liaison offices in 1994, after the Oslo agreements, and closed them in 2000 during the second intifada.
Algeria.
Algeria shows how much the map depended on which empire held a country.
The Crémieux Decree of 24 October 1870 made Algeria's Jews French citizens.
The Vichy regime withdrew that citizenship on 7 October 1940, and it was restored on 20 October 1943.
Rioting in Constantine in 1934 killed 25 Jews.
According to the Jewish Virtual Library, Algeria had about 140,000 Jews in the mid-1950s, and almost 130,000 of them moved to France when Algeria became independent in 1962.
Over the whole period from 1948, 25,681 Algerian Jews immigrated to Israel.
Most of Algeria's Jews went to the country whose citizens they already were, at independence, more than a decade after 1948.
The first was violence by crowds, sometimes in places under British rule, as in Tripoli in 1945 and Aden in 1947.
The second was the action of states: Egypt's renunciation forms in 1956, Libya's citizenship law of 1961 and, in Iraq, the denaturalization law told in the previous section.
The third was organized emigration arranged from outside: airlifts by Israel and Jewish organizations in Yemen, and a paid, secret agreement in Morocco.
In Morocco and Iraq governments negotiated the terms of exit.
In Egypt in 1956 the government set them alone.
In Algeria the decisive fact was a French citizenship that dated from 1870.
The account of the exodus in this book uses roughly 850,000 Jews leaving Arab and Muslim countries between 1948 and 1972.
A survey of the regional aftermath gives estimates "commonly in the range of 800,000–900,000" for Arab countries and Iran from 1948 to the 1970s.
Avi Beker, writing in the Jewish Political Studies Review, gives about 900,000 Jews "forced out" of Arab countries, of whom about 650,000 went to Israel.
Beker writes as an advocate of one side of the argument that follows, and his figure is a position in that argument, not a settled count.
The figures also differ in scope: one includes Iran, their end years differ, and Beker's counts those he describes as forced out.
One position holds that these Jews were refugees in the same sense as the Palestinians of 1948.
Beker sets out this "dual refugee problem" case, which the United States House of Representatives took up in H. Con.
Res. 311 in October 2003.
In this view about 900,000 Jews were forced out of Arab countries, and their case has been forgotten through international indifference and Israel's own reluctance to call it expulsion.

The strongest form of the case rests on records like those above: the Giado camp, Tripoli, the partition-vote riots, the Egyptian renunciation forms, and laws that stripped people of citizenship and property.

The Israeli sociologist Yehouda Shenhav argued in Haaretz in 2006 that Palestinians did not leave of their own volition, while Arab Jews moved to Israel under initiatives by the state and Jewish organizations, some willingly and some not.
The Palestinian writer Khalid Amayreh, in an opinion piece in Ahram Online in 2012 that quotes Shenhav, called the equation propaganda meant to offset the Nakba.
The strongest form of this case also rests on the record: the organized airlift from Yemen, the payments to Morocco, and the recruitment operations described in the previous section.
The Stroum Center essay treats the Egyptian departures of 1956 as an expulsion.

It also warns, citing the historian Eyal Bizawe, against using Mizrahi history to cast Arab societies as permanent enemies, and asks that the history of coexistence be taught alongside the history of the expulsions.
Whether the Jewish departures and the Palestinian displacement of 1948 can be set side by side as an "exchange" is a separate question, taken up in .
For Aleppo, Aden and Bahrain this book has the violence but not the departures that followed.
For Egypt it has neither the destinations nor a full count of the 1948 wave.
The amount paid to Morocco under Operation Yachin is not given.
Four Words: Hebrew, Jewish, Israeli, Zionist
Four words are often used as if they meant the same thing: Hebrew, Jewish, Israeli and Zionist.
The word first appears in the Bible at Genesis 14:13, which calls Abram "Abram the Hebrew," ha-ʿIvri.

The rabbis of the early commentary Genesis Rabbah already offered several explanations: that Abram stood on one side and the whole world on the other, that he descended from an ancestor named Eber, or that he came from across the river.
Britannica notes that it may come from ʿever, "the other side."
Many scholars have also linked the word to the Ḥabiru or ʿApiru, a marginal social class named in Near Eastern texts of the second millennium BCE, but there is no consensus on that link.

In the Hebrew Bible itself, "Hebrew" is mostly the name that other peoples use for the Israelites, or that Israelites use of themselves when speaking to foreigners; it is rarely their everyday name for themselves.
Reference books follow a rough convention, "Hebrews" for the earliest period, then "Israelites," then "Jews" after the exile in Babylon, though the ancient texts do not follow it strictly.
Hebrew is a Semitic language of the Northwest branch, alongside Aramaic.

Hebrew stopped being anyone's everyday spoken language over several centuries; scholars usually put the end somewhere between about 200 and 400 CE, with Aramaic taking its place in daily speech, and Britannica dates the start of the decline as early as the third century BCE.
Through the Middle Ages it remained a working written language for poetry, both religious and secular, for some legal contracts, for philosophy and science, and for grammar and dictionaries.

Eliezer Ben-Yehuda moved to Jerusalem in 1881 and raised a son described as the first child to grow up speaking modern Hebrew; teachers who made Hebrew the language of their schools played a large part.
In 2018 the Knesset's Nation-State Law named Hebrew "the state's language" and gave Arabic a "special status"; NPR reported that this removed Arabic's earlier standing as an official language.
Jewish: a people and a religion.

To be Jewish is understood both as belonging to a people and as belonging to a religion, and Pew found that American Jews weigh the two differently: some see it mainly as religion, others as culture or ancestry.
Under traditional Jewish law, a Jew is anyone born to a Jewish mother or converted according to that law.

In 1983 the American Reform rabbinate added that the child of a Jewish father may also be presumed Jewish, a presumption to be confirmed by public acts of Jewish identification such as a Hebrew name or a Bar or Bat Mitzvah.
Israel's Chief Rabbinate, which controls Jewish marriage in Israel, does not accept every definition the movements use.
In Pew's 2020 survey of American Jews, 27 percent described themselves religiously as atheist, agnostic or "nothing in particular" while still considering themselves Jewish by ancestry or culture.
Nor is there one Jewish appearance.
The Beta Israel of Ethiopia were recognized as Jews by Israel's Sephardi Chief Rabbi in 1973, and Operation Solomon in 1991 flew more than 14,000 of them to Israel.
Israel's statistics bureau counted 168,800 residents of Ethiopian origin at the end of 2022.
India had three historic Jewish communities, the Bene Israel near Mumbai, the Cochin Jews of Kerala and the Baghdadi Jews who came in the British era; most have since emigrated, chiefly to Israel.

In Kaifeng, China, a Jewish community is recorded from the Middle Ages, and several hundred people there still claim that descent, though Israel and Orthodox authorities require them to convert formally.

In the United States, Pew found that 8 percent of Jewish adults identify as Hispanic, Black, Asian, multiracial or another race, and 15 percent of those under thirty; the Jews of Color Initiative, counting differently, estimates at least 12 to 15 percent.

Israel's statistics bureau put the world's Jewish population at nearly 15.9 million on 1 January 2026, about 46 percent of them in Israel, as reported by i24NEWS; the Jewish Agency's estimate for the start of 2024 was 15.8 million.
Most of the world's Jews live outside Israel.
Israeli: a citizenship.
An Israeli is a citizen of the State of Israel, whatever his or her religion or ancestry.

In its release of 9 September 2026, Israel's Central Bureau of Statistics put the population at about 10.3 million: about 7.83 million "Jews and others," about 2.17 million Arabs, and about 304,000 foreign nationals.
Arabs are therefore about a fifth of the population.
Most are Muslims, about 1.85 million at the end of 2025; Christians number about 184,000, most of them Arabs; and the Druze about 150,000 (at the end of 2022).
The bureau's "others" are mostly immigrants who came under the Law of Return, which since 1970 admits the children, grandchildren and spouses of Jews, but who are not registered as Jews themselves.
Recent releases no longer report Jews as a separate headline figure; the last separate count was 7.2 million in 2023, about 73 percent.
Its figures include East Jerusalem since 1967 and the Golan since 1982, and most Palestinians in East Jerusalem hold permanent residency rather than citizenship, as many Golan Druze long did.
Second, Israel's own records keep citizenship apart from a second entry called le'om, usually translated "nationality," which records a person as Jewish, Arab and so on.
In 2013 Israel's Supreme Court refused to let a group of citizens register their nationality as "Israeli," holding that no distinct Israeli nationality had been shown to exist.
In Israeli law, then, "Israeli" is a citizenship and not a nationality, which is one reason the words are so easily confused.
Zionist: a political movement.
Zionism is the movement that sought a Jewish national home, and later a state, in the Land of Israel, and that has supported that state since 1948.
It is a political position, not a birthright: a person can be Jewish without being a Zionist, and a Zionist without being Jewish.
It also did not begin with Theodor Herzl, though he gave it its organization.
In 1843 Yehuda Alkalai, a Sephardi rabbi near Belgrade, called for organized settlement in the land, and later settled there himself.

In 1862 Rabbi Zvi Hirsch Kalischer argued that redemption could begin by human effort, and the socialist Moses Hess argued that the Jews would remain a homeless people until they had a country of their own.

After the pogroms of 1881 Leon Pinsker published Auto-Emanzipation anonymously in 1882 and became a leader of the "Lovers of Zion" societies; the first Bilu pioneers landed at Jaffa in July 1882, and Baron Edmond de Rothschild began funding the new colonies in late 1882.
Nathan Birnbaum coined the word "Zionism" in 1890.
What Herzl added was the organization.
His book Der Judenstaat appeared in February 1896, and it treated Argentina as well as Palestine as possible territories.
In August 1897 the First Zionist Congress in Basel founded the Zionist Organization, elected Herzl its president, and adopted a program seeking "a publicly and legally assured home in Palestine."
Even then the destination was argued over: in 1903 the movement voted to study a British offer of land in East Africa, in present-day Kenya, before rejecting it in 1905.
Jews who are not Zionists, and Zionists who are not Jews.
Opposition to Zionism has come from Jews from the beginning.
In 1885 American Reform rabbis declared that Jews were "no longer a nation, but a religious community" and rejected a return to Palestine, a position the movement revised in 1937.
The socialist Bund, founded in Vilna weeks after the Basel Congress, opposed Zionism and argued for Jewish life where Jews already lived.

Within Orthodoxy, the Satmar rabbi Joel Teitelbaum argued in 1961 that Zionism is incompatible with Judaism, and Neturei Karta, founded in Jerusalem in 1938 (some accounts say 1937), rejects the State of Israel outright; it numbers in the low thousands, and other Haredi bodies have disavowed its activities.
In January 2019 the American group Jewish Voice for Peace declared itself opposed to Zionism.
Zionism has also had non-Jewish supporters.

Christian Zionism grew out of English Puritan "restorationism" in the seventeenth century and later out of dispensationalist theology, which reads Jewish return to the land as part of a prophetic sequence.
In 1891 the American evangelist William Blackstone petitioned President Benjamin Harrison to "give Palestine back" to the Jews.
Christians United for Israel, founded in 2006, announced in December 2020 that it had passed 10 million members, a figure it counts itself and has not defined.
How many Jews call themselves Zionists depends heavily on how the question is asked.

Recent American surveys range from 37 percent, in a survey for the Jewish Federations, to about 80 percent "Zionist or slightly Zionist," in an opt-in panel run by the Jewish People Policy Institute, and federation leaders put part of the gap down to disagreement over what the word means.

A person can be Jewish, Israeli and Zionist at once; or Jewish and Zionist but not Israeli; or Jewish, living in Israel, and opposed to Zionism, as Neturei Karta, founded in Jerusalem, is; or Jewish and neither, the position of the Satmar movement's founding text and of the organization Jewish Voice for Peace.
About a fifth of Israel's residents are Arab, and some of the bureau's "others" are not registered as Jewish.
And there are Zionists who are neither Jewish nor Israeli, the Christian Zionists among them.

Hebrew is a language and an ancient name; Jewish is a people and a religion, entered by birth or conversion and held by believers and non-believers alike; Israeli is a citizenship shared by Jews, Arabs and others; and Zionism is a political movement whose ideas go back to the 1840s and whose organization dates from 1897.
Not all Jews are Zionists, not all Israelis are Jews, and not all Zionists are Jews.

The origin of the word "Hebrew" is debated; no single date marks the end of spoken Hebrew; the share of Jews who are Zionists depends on how the word is defined and how the question is asked; and Israel's headline statistics now combine Jews with "others," so the exact Jewish share of the population in 2026 is not published as a single figure.

Arguments over the word, and over where legitimate criticism of a state ends, can make it easy to lose sight of the thing itself: a long, documented history of accusation, legal exclusion, expulsion and killing directed at Jews as Jews.
The oldest of these accusations is the blood libel: the charge that Jews kill Christians in order to use their blood.
Earlier references to the idea occur in the writings of Apion.
Its first medieval case came at Norwich, in England, in 1144, after the body of a boy named William was found in the woods.
Ritual-murder accusations followed at Gloucester in 1168, Blois in 1171, Saragossa in 1182, Bristol in 1183, Fulda in 1235, Lincoln in 1255 and Munich in 1286.
In the fourteenth century the accusation was joined to another, that Jews had poisoned wells, during the Black Death.
In 1475 a two-year-old named Simon disappeared.
The town's Jews were tortured until they confessed, and they were burned.
Simon was later counted among the saints.
In 1965 the Catholic Church removed him from the list of saints and repudiated the charge.
The confession that had condemned the Jews of Trent was a product of torture, and the institution that had honored the supposed victim formally withdrew the accusation.
In 1215 the Fourth Lateran Council decreed that Jews must wear distinguishing dress and barred them from public office.
England, according to reporting on the Church of England's later reckoning with these decrees and to the historian Geraldine Heng, was the first country to require Jews to wear a badge, in 1218.
In 1222 church leaders meeting at Osney Abbey, near Oxford, adopted a badge decree of their own; about 3,000 Jews are thought to have lived in England at the time.
England's Statute of Jewry of 1275 barred Jews from living among Christians.
In 1290 Edward I expelled the Jews of England, the first such expulsion in Christendom.
Jews were permitted to return only in 1656, under Cromwell.
The badge made Jews legible as a separate category in public.
The Statute of Jewry separated them physically from their neighbors, and the expulsion of 1290 removed the community altogether.
The blood libel did not stay in medieval Europe.
On 5 February 1840 a Capuchin friar named Thomas and his servant disappeared in Damascus.
The Capuchins accused the city's Jews of ritual murder, and the French consul, Ratti-Menton, backed the investigation.
Sixty-three Jewish children were seized to put pressure on their mothers.
On 25 April 1840 Muhammad Ali ordered the torture stopped.

After a mission by Moses Montefiore and Adolphe Crémieux, the surviving prisoners were freed on 28 August 1840, without any declaration of their innocence, and the Ottoman Sultan issued a firman repudiating the ritual-murder charge.

The Damascus affair is instructive for the way power ran through it: the charge came from a religious order, a European consul lent it official weight, the torture was halted by a ruler's order, and the release came only after Montefiore and Crémieux's mission.
The record cited here does not give the date of the Sultan's firman.
In the Russian Empire the twentieth century brought a pogrom and a new ritual-murder trial.
The Kishinev pogrom began on Easter Sunday, 19 April 1903, after articles in an antisemitic newspaper; over three days, almost 50 Jews were killed.
Between 1911 and 1913 Menachem Mendel Beilis was tried in Kiev on a ritual-murder charge, and acquitted.

By then the word "antisemitism" had existed for a generation, coined in Germany to make this same hostility sound modern and scientific; its history, and the Jewish name for the hatred, "Judeophobia," are traced in .
The same year as Kishinev saw the first appearance of a forgery that would outlast every exposure.
The Protocols of the Elders of Zion, a fabricated plan for Jewish world domination, was first serialized in the St Petersburg newspaper Znamya in the autumn of 1903.
In 1905 Sergei Nilus appended it to a book of his own.
It did not remain a Russian text.
In 1920 Henry Ford's newspaper, the Dearborn Independent, ran a 91-part series based on it.
In August 1921 The Times of London showed that the text was largely copied from Maurice Joly's satire of 1864 and called it a forgery.
Ford apologized in 1927.
Hitler cited the Protocols in Mein Kampf in 1925, the same year the first Arabic translation appeared in Damascus.
In 1935 a Swiss court in Bern ruled against its publishers.
In 1943 Hajj Amin al-Husseini, the former Mufti of Jerusalem, echoed the Protocols' themes in Arabic broadcasts from Berlin.

The text kept circulating after the war: an Iranian English edition appeared in 1985; Article 32 of the Hamas charter of 1988 drew on it; an Egyptian television series of 41 parts drew on it in 2002, and a series on Hezbollah's Al-Manar channel in 2003.
A Russian court ruled it a forgery in 1993.

Taken together, the record shows a hatred with a recognizable structure that long predates any modern dispute over Zionism or Israel: accusations of ritual murder, confessions extracted under torture, legal markers of separation, expulsion, and, in the twentieth century, a forged document that kept circulating after a newspaper, a court in Bern and later a Russian court had all exposed or ruled against it.
That history reached its documented extreme in the Holocaust, told in .
They do not give casualty figures for most of the medieval cases, nor the numbers of Jews expelled in 1290.
They do not name the newspaper whose articles preceded the Kishinev pogrom, or record the date of the Sultan's firman after Damascus.

What they do establish, case by case and date by date, is that this was a real hatred, aimed at Jews, enacted through named institutions and documents, and that it existed long before its modern name.
The Holocaust in the World's Classrooms
The previous section asked what American schools teach about the Holocaust, who supplies the material and what young Americans actually know.
A familiar assumption holds that the Holocaust is a fixed lesson taught alike wherever history is taught.
The fullest global picture is a mapping for UNESCO by the Georg Eckert Institute, published in 2015.

Its summary reports that the Holocaust appears in the history curricula of approximately half of the countries investigated, and that about a quarter of all curricula do not name the Holocaust but refer to its context, such as the Second World War or National Socialism.

A report on the study in The Conversation gave the count differently: 57 curricula directly stipulate the Holocaust with words such as "Holocaust" or "Shoah," eight countries address it only partially, and 46 provide only the context of the war or National Socialism.
Most curricula, the summary found, do not specify which victim groups to cover; where groups are named, Jews are usually the only ones explicitly listed.
Which curricula leave the Holocaust out entirely is one point on which the two summaries diverge.

The UNESCO summary gives Brunei Darussalam, Iceland and Thailand as examples of curricula with no reference to it; the Conversation report on the same study names Egypt, Palestine, Iraq, New Zealand and Thailand.
Only Thailand appears on both; the full list that would reconcile them has not been published in these summaries.

The summary also lists Argentina, Belize, Colombia, Ecuador, Mexico and Slovenia as countries whose curricula refer to the Holocaust only partially, framing it as a violation of human rights; in Mexico it appears as one aspect among others of human-rights education.
In the textbooks the study examined, the Holocaust was generally located in "Europe" and "Germany," while Russian and Indian textbooks cast it in transcontinental terms, setting Europe against Asia.
Rwandan textbooks apply Holocaust vocabulary to the genocide of 1994.
Chinese textbooks use the terms "genocide" (datusha) and "kinds of crimes" (zhongzhong zuixing) rather than "Holocaust" or "Shoah," and apply such language to the Nanjing massacres of 1937.
The authors drew the conclusion in a single sentence: "educational media provide a foundation not for education about the Holocaust, but for education about the Holocausts."
In Germany the requirement is set out officially.

The Conference of Education Ministers of the sixteen Länder, the KMK, states that the Holocaust and National Socialism are firmly anchored in the History curricula, or history-heavy social-science curricula, of all 16 Länder: a mandatory topic in grade 9 or 10 of lower secondary school, occasionally grade 8, and a mandatory, more in-depth topic in upper secondary.
The instrument is a series of KMK recommendations.
The first dates from 20 April 1978, "Behandlung des Nationalsozialismus
im Unterricht," on the treatment of National Socialism in teaching.

The "Erinnern für die Zukunft" recommendations on memory culture followed on 11 December 2014, and in October 2013 the KMK signed a declaration of intent with Yad Vashem and Israel's education ministry.
The live German argument is whether students should be made to visit a former camp.

In May 2025 Bavaria announced, according to the education site News4teachers, that from the 2025/26 school year students at all secondary schools must visit a concentration-camp memorial at least once during their schooling; before that the requirement applied only to Gymnasium and Realschule students.
The same month the Federal Education Minister, Karin Prien, called for compulsory memorial visits for school students.

In April 2024 the directors of Buchenwald, Sachsenhausen, Dachau, Bergen-Belsen and Neuengamme were reported as opposing or doubting compulsory school visits, arguing that voluntariness is essential and that coercion can reinforce rejection; the director of the Flossenbürg memorial reported very good experience with obligatory visits.
The International Auschwitz Committee answered Prien that funding for school trips and teacher training mattered more than compulsion.
Israel built remembrance into law early.

On 4 March 1959 the Knesset passed a law requiring public observances in tribute to Holocaust victims on Holocaust Remembrance Day, and a 1961 amendment required places of entertainment to close on the eve of the day.

In October 2013, according to the Times of Israel, Education Minister Shai Piron announced a programme designed by Yad Vashem with Holocaust lessons in each of the 12 years of compulsory schooling, starting in first grade; at the time, students began in-depth Holocaust study only in 11th grade.
Israeli Holocaust education also took place abroad, on school trips to Poland.
According to Notes from Poland, tens of thousands of Israeli youths visited Poland each year before the pandemic.
Israel suspended the trips in June 2022 amid a dispute in which, according to the same outlet, the Polish government was reportedly trying to dictate what could be taught.

Polish officials argued that the trips focused narrowly on the war, strengthened false and negative stereotypes of Poles, and relied on armed Israeli security guards, and that they should include Polish history and Jewish heritage.
The agreement to resume them, signed on 22 March 2023, added exactly that: Polish history and Jewish heritage, meetings with Polish youth, and responsibility for security placed on the host country.
In April 2023 Yad Vashem criticised the agreement, according to the Associated Press.

It said the recommended site list included sites that should not be visited in an educational context, that it had had no input into the list, and that the trips must keep complete historical accuracy, including Poles' roles both in persecuting and in rescuing Jews.
The United Kingdom differs by nation.
The genocide of European Jews has been a mandatory subject in the Key Stage 3 National Curriculum for History in England since 1991, in the description of University College London.
ents: the Key Stage 3 National Curriculum for History

sent: The current statutory programme of study for England, published on 11 September 2013, lists "In addition to studying the Holocaust" under Key Stage 3, within its content on challenges for Britain.
The requirement has limits that the Holocaust Educational Trust sets out: academies need not follow the National Curriculum, and Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland have no formal requirement.
England is also the one country in this record with a large study of what school students know.

The UCL Centre for Holocaust Education's October 2016 study of more than 8,000 students aged 11 to 18 found that only 37% knew what "antisemitism" means; that 8.8% correctly identified the pre-war German Jewish population as under 1%; and that only 7% understood that the invasion of the Soviet Union in June 1941 triggered organised mass killing.
ents: The UCL Centre for Holocaust Education's

sent: Fifty-five percent thought the mass murder took place in Germany.
Seventy-one percent associated Auschwitz with the Holocaust, against 15% each for Treblinka and Bergen-Belsen, and fewer than 10% suggested that the German people bore any responsibility.
France begins in primary school.

In an answer to a parliamentary question, published on 16 April 2019, the education ministry stated that the genocides of the Jews and the Roma are taught for the first time in CM2, the final year of primary school; that two parts of the troisième programme, for students aged 14 to 15, address antisemitism and the genocide of the Jews; and that the genocide is studied in the vocational-track première programme.
Among the curricula described here, it is the only one documented as naming the Roma alongside the Jews.
Poland legislated on how the war may be described.

In February 2018 an amendment to the law on the Institute of National Remembrance, signed by President Andrzej Duda, provided prison sentences of up to three years for accusing Poland of complicity in the Holocaust, according to NPR.

A joint statement by the Polish and Israeli prime ministers accompanying the change said they "acknowledge and condemn every single case of cruelty against Jews perpetrated by Poles during the World War II."

The Polish government, through Prime Minister Morawiecki, held that those who say Poland may be responsible for wartime crimes deserve penalties, and presented the law as a defence of the country's reputation.
Critics in Israel, the United States and Europe, the World Jewish Congress among them, said it whitewashed history and stifled discussion of local complicity.
The research does not record what Polish curricula require.
For Russia the record runs from the Soviet period to the present.

The historian Ilya Altman of Russia's Holocaust Center told a Yad Vashem conference in 1999 that the Holocaust was omitted from Soviet school and university textbooks from the mid-1940s to the late 1980s, that wartime reports replaced "Jews" with "peaceful Soviet citizens," and that post-Soviet textbooks mentioned the six million only in passing.

In 2008, according to the World Jewish Congress, a joint study by the Russian Academy of Sciences and the Russian Jewish Congress found that many Russian school history textbooks completely avoid the subject.

The current state textbooks for grades 10 and 11, by Medinsky and Torkunov, published in 2023, frame the war as the Great Patriotic War; a 2024 study of them by Aleksander Wawrzyńczak found no discussion of the Holocaust, and the only Jewish reference it noted was Tsezar Kunikov, listed among Soviet heroes.

In April 2025, according to the Moldovan news agency IPN, Russia promulgated a law defining "genocide against the Soviet people" during the Second World War, due to enter into force on 1 January 2026; the report on it does not mention Jews or the Holocaust.
Iran is documented here through a state act rather than a curriculum.

On 11 December 2006, according to an AFP report, a government-sponsored conference questioning the Holocaust opened at the Foreign Ministry's Institute for Political and International Studies in Tehran.
ents: the Foreign Ministry's Institute for Political and International Studies

sent: Foreign Minister Manouchehr Mottaki said its aim was "not to deny or confirm the Holocaust," and participants included David Duke.
The research holds no study of what Iranian schools teach.
For the Arab governments, the evidence is of uneven kinds.

For the Palestinian Authority, Samira Alayan's peer-reviewed study of 2016 in the Comparative Education Review found no mention of the Holocaust in its history textbooks, and compared them with Arab-Israeli curricula.

The EU-commissioned Georg Eckert Institute study of Palestinian textbooks, published in June 2021, examined 156 of 309 volumes and found UNESCO-style human-rights content alongside "anti-Semitic narratives and glorifications of violence"; its published FAQ does not address the Holocaust.
The Conversation summary of the UNESCO mapping names Egypt, Palestine and Iraq among curricula with no reference.
For Saudi Arabia the only finding comes from an advocacy group: IMPACT-se reported on 1 May 2024 that in Saudi textbooks "The Holocaust is absent from the curriculum."

In January 2023 the embassy of the United Arab Emirates in Washington said the UAE would include the Holocaust in the curriculum for primary and secondary schools, with its education ministry consulting Yad Vashem and IMPACT-se; Yad Vashem said at the time, according to Al-Monitor, that the initiative was still being developed.

In September 2018, according to Ynetnews, Morocco's Education Minister, Said Amzazi, announced at a round table at the UN General Assembly that King Mohammed VI had decided to integrate the study of the Holocaust into the national curriculum.
Latin America appears in the UNESCO summary chiefly as a region of partial, human-rights framing, and Argentina is on that list.
The Priority Learning Cores, the NAP, approved by the Federal Council of Education Ministers in 2004, list the Holocaust as a topic.
ents: the Federal Council of Education Ministers

sent: Argentina has been a full member of the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance since 2002, and its foreign ministry describes it as the only full member in Latin America.

The province of Córdoba has had a law on teaching the Shoah since about 2008, under which more than 2,000 teachers have been trained, according to the Córdoba paper Hoy Día, and in 2026 (as reported in July 2026)
The research does not explain how the UNESCO classification relates to Argentina's own documents.

In Africa, South Africa's national History curricula for Grades 9 and 11 have included the study of Nazi Germany and the Holocaust since 2007, according to the South African Jewish Board of Deputies' report on the SA Holocaust & Genocide Foundation.
Rwanda, as noted above, applies the Holocaust's vocabulary to 1994; for East, South and Southeast Asia the record holds only the UNESCO findings on China, India, Thailand and Brunei.
In this record, what publics know worldwide comes from two surveys by the Anti-Defamation League.
Only 54% worldwide had ever heard of the Holocaust, against 94% in Western Europe.

According to NBC News' report on that survey, 32% of respondents believed the Holocaust was a myth or greatly exaggerated, and only 38% in the Middle East and North Africa had heard of it, of whom 63% doubted it or considered it exaggerated.

It found that 20% worldwide had not heard of the Holocaust and that 48% recognised its historical accuracy; the share was 39% among those aged 18 to 34, 16% in the Middle East and North Africa and 23% in Sub-Saharan Africa.

A narrower survey by the Claims Conference covered eight countries, with 1,000 adults each in the United States, the United Kingdom, France, Austria, Germany, Poland, Hungary and Romania; fieldwork ran from 15 to 28 November 2023, and the results were released in January 2025.
Across the European countries, 93.5% had heard the word "Holocaust," 44% knew that about six million Jews were killed, and 81% could name a camp or ghetto.

In France, 46% of those aged 18 to 29 had not heard of the Holocaust or were unsure, against 15% in Romania, 14% in Austria and 12% in Germany, and 53% of young Romanians said the number killed had been greatly exaggerated, according to San Diego Jewish World's report on the release.

In the Netherlands, a Claims Conference survey of 2,000 adults in January 2023 found that 23% of those born after 1980 believed the Holocaust was a myth or that the number of victims was greatly exaggerated, according to an AFP report.

The International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance was founded in 1998 on the Stockholm Declaration, which pledges to promote Holocaust education in schools and universities; it states that it has 35 Member Countries and 8 Observer Countries.
The United Nations General Assembly adopted resolution 60/7 on 1 November 2005.

It designated 27 January as an annual International Day of Commemoration, urged Member States to develop educational programmes on the Holocaust's lessons, and "Rejects any denial of the Holocaust as an historical event, either in full or part."
Resolution 76/250, on Holocaust denial, was sponsored by Israel and co-sponsored by 114 nations; it was adopted by consensus without a vote on 20 January 2022, and Iran disassociated itself from it.
Sixty of the world's 195 countries were outside the UNESCO mapping, and its data are from 2013–2014, before many of the changes described here.

For Iran, Poland and most of the Arab world, no study of current school curricula is in the record at all; for Saudi Arabia the only finding is an advocacy group's; and for the UAE and Morocco the record holds announcements, not evidence of what classrooms now teach.
Whether Israel's twelve-year programme was carried out as announced, and how Russia's 2025 law has been applied in schools since January 2026, are not documented here.
Nor does any study here measure how classrooms outside the United States connect the Holocaust to the State of Israel.
The question this library puts to the story of Israel, what is taught, who writes it and through what instrument, can be put to the Holocaust in the same terms.

A ministers' conference in Germany, a minister and a state memorial authority in Israel, a statutory programme in England, a speech law in Poland, a state textbook in Russia, a foreign ministry's conference in Iran, an advocacy group's review and an embassy's announcement in the Gulf: each is an identifiable author, and the versions they produce differ.
How the story of Israel itself reaches students is told in .
Where the Lineages Lived: A Map of Jewish Communities
The previous section followed three broad Jewish lineages, Ashkenazi, Sephardi and Mizrahi, through the genetic record.
Ashkenaz is a name in Genesis, and medieval rabbis used it for Germany; Sepharad appears in the book of Obadiah, and by the ninth century it meant the Iberian Peninsula.
Both words also name prayer rites, so a Jew of Iraqi or Moroccan family may be counted as Sephardi in synagogue.
"Mizrahi," meaning "Eastern," is a modern umbrella term for Jews from Arab and Muslim lands.

Sources date it to the 1940s or the 1950s; writers including Ella Shohat have criticised it as a construction, many people prefer to name their own community, and grouping North African Jews, historically called "Westerners," under "Eastern" is itself contested.
Ashkenazi.
By the tenth century there were centres of rabbinic learning at Mainz and Worms on the Rhine, and the name Ashkenaz came to mean the Jews of that region.
After the Crusades of the eleventh to thirteenth centuries they moved east into Slavic lands.
ents: the Crusades of the eleventh to thirteenth centuries

sent: Royal charters in Poland, from 1264 and 1334, opened the way to real settlement in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries; by the early sixteenth century the centre of Ashkenazi life had shifted to Poland, Lithuania, Bohemia and Moravia, and a tax inquiry of 1764 found that about seven percent of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth was Jewish.
Their common language was Yiddish.
Estimates of their share of world Jewry vary: the Jewish Virtual Library puts it at 90 percent before the Second World War, and Britannica at more than 80 percent today.
According to the Jewish Virtual Library, the United States later became the main Ashkenazi centre.
Sephardi.
The Jewish Virtual Library dates a Jewish "Golden Age" in Spain from the Muslim conquest of 711.
In 1492 Spain gave Jews who refused baptism four months to leave; about 100,000 went, by that source's estimate, and in 1497 Portugal forced almost all of its Jews to convert.
Large numbers of exiles settled across the Ottoman Empire and in North Africa, and Sephardi communities also formed in Venice, Livorno, Bordeaux, Hamburg and London.
Salonica, today's Thessaloniki, became their great city, with about 35,000 Jews in the sixteenth century and about 80,000 around 1900.
In 1943 the Germans deported more than 45,000 of its Jews to Auschwitz-Birkenau.
Their language, Judeo-Spanish, also called Judezmo or Ladino, flourished in the Ottoman lands.

A second branch, the Western Sephardim, grew from Portuguese "New Christians" who returned to Judaism in Amsterdam from the late sixteenth century, and in London where a petition to Oliver Cromwell in 1656 led to open Jewish life in England for the first time since the expulsion of 1290.
The map above shows the communities of Europe, North Africa and the Middle East.
Mizrahi and North African.
Iraq's community traces its start to the Babylonian exile of about 586 BCE, and the Babylonian Talmud was compiled there.
By 1900 Baghdad's roughly 50,000 Jews were more than a quarter of the city.
After the Farhud riots of 1941 and an Iraqi law of March 1950 that let Jews leave if they gave up their citizenship, Operation Ezra and Nehemiah flew more than 120,000 of them to Israel.

Iran's community traces its roots to the sixth century BCE and wrote in Judeo-Persian; about 80,000 Jews lived there in 1978 by unofficial statistics, and a community of several thousand remains, with a reserved seat in parliament.
Jews are recorded in Yemen from the third century CE; Operation Magic Carpet airlifted about 49,000 Jews, most of them from Yemen, in 1949 and 1950.

Syria's community, in Aleppo and Damascus, dates its presence to the Seleucid period; after the government allowed emigration in 1992, thousands left, mainly for Brooklyn and New Jersey; others settled in Israel and Mexico.

In Egypt, Jews probably settled in Old Cairo soon after its founding in 641, and the famous Cairo Genizah was found in its Ben Ezra Synagogue; the community numbered about 75,000 at its peak; about 25,000 were expelled or forced out after the Suez war of 1956, and nearly all had left by the early 1970s.

Further east and north, the Jews of Kurdistan spoke a Neo-Aramaic language; the Bukharan Jews of Central Asia spoke Bukhori, a language close to Tajik, and now live mostly in Israel and in Queens, New York; the Mountain Jews of the eastern Caucasus spoke Juhuri; and the Jews of Georgia, by a tradition not confirmed by contemporary records, arrived after 586 BCE.
In North Africa, sources distinguished the toshavim, the Jews already living there, from the megorashim, the Iberian exiles who arrived after 1391 and 1492.
Morocco's community is documented from the second century CE; more than 90,000 left for Israel in Operation Yakhin between 1961 and 1964, and many others settled in France and Canada.
France made Algeria's Jews French citizens in 1870, and almost 130,000 moved to France after Algerian independence in 1962.
Tunisia had about 105,000 Jews in 1946, including the old community of the island of Djerba.

The Romaniotes of Greece, in Ioannina, Arta and Chalkida, are documented from the Byzantine period and spoke Yevanic, a Jewish Greek; the language declined as Romaniotes merged into the Sephardi communities of Greece, and the Holocaust nearly destroyed it.

Rome's community, which the Jewish Virtual Library dates to 161 BCE and calls the oldest in Europe, kept its own Italian rite; it was confined to a ghetto by papal order in 1555, and on 16 October 1943 the Nazis rounded up Jews in Rome and deported them to Auschwitz; by the Jewish Virtual Library's count, only a dozen of those deported survived.

The Karaites, a movement that accepts the Hebrew Bible but not the Talmud as binding, grew from the followers of Anan ben David in Babylonia about 760 CE, with later centres in Cairo, Crimea and Lithuania.
The Beta Israel of Ethiopia prayed in Ge'ez and spoke Amharic or Tigrinya.

Their origins are disputed: the historian Steven Kaplan argues that they formed as a group in Ethiopia between the fourteenth and sixteenth centuries, while other accounts place their arrival in the first to sixth centuries.
Israel's Sephardi Chief Rabbi ruled them Jews in 1973; Operations Moses in 1984–85 and Solomon in 1991 brought about 7,700 and 14,400 of them to Israel, by one historian's count.

India had three communities: the Bene Israel of the Konkan coast, who spoke Marathi; the Cochin Jews of Kerala, documented by copper plates of about 1000 CE, who spoke Jewish Malayalam; and the Baghdadi Jews, Arabic-speaking merchants who came in the late eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.

In Kaifeng, China, a community that most scholars think came from Persia in the twelfth century kept a synagogue until the nineteenth century; between 500 and 1,000 people there are estimated to claim descent today.
The Abayudaya of Uganda began practising Judaism in 1919 as a religious movement, and do not claim continuous descent from ancient Israel in the sources consulted.

The Bnei Menashe of northeastern India say they descend from the tribe of Manasseh; a Chief Rabbi recognised that claim in 2005, but formal conversion was still required, and no peer-reviewed genetic study has confirmed it.

The Lemba of South Africa and Zimbabwe have an oral tradition of origin in a place called "Sena"; early genetic studies were read as support, but a 2014 reassessment found the markers used to be unreliable predictors of Jewish ancestry.
On the map the Bnei Menashe and the Lemba are marked as claims of descent, not settled facts, and the Abayudaya as a twentieth-century movement.

The record shows Jewish communities spread from the Atlantic to China and from the Baltic to southern Africa, each with its own documented history, language and turning points, and most of them reshaped in the twentieth century by genocide in Europe or by mass emigration from the Middle East and North Africa, much of it to Israel.

The record does not settle the origins of every community: the dates for the Beta Israel, the Kaifeng Jews and the Georgian Jews are disputed, and the descent claims of the Bnei Menashe and the Lemba are not established.
"Never Again" and the Classroom
A sentence many readers have heard runs roughly as follows: Israel was the world's answer to the Holocaust, the place created so that it could never happen again.

This section takes the order of events first, then what American schools actually teach about the Holocaust and who supplies the material, and finally the history of the phrase "Never Again" itself, which has carried two different meanings for most of its life.
The political program for a Jewish state was in print long before the Holocaust.
Theodor Herzl's Der Judenstaat of 1896 weighed Palestine against Argentina as the territory for a political answer to European antisemitism, thirty-seven years before Hitler took power in Germany.

The Sixth Zionist Congress voted in 1903 to investigate British East Africa, and the Seventh formally rejected it in 1905, so Palestine was confirmed by the movement's own choice against a real alternative.
In November 1917 Britain committed in writing to "the establishment in Palestine of a national home for the Jewish people."
At San Remo in 1920 the Allied powers assigned Britain the Mandate for Palestine and carried the Balfour language into an international agreement.

The League of Nations approved the Mandate in July 1922, and it took legal force in September 1923; its Article 6 bound Britain to facilitate Jewish immigration and "close settlement by Jews on the land."
The program, the pledge and the Mandate predate Hitler's rise by between eleven and thirty-seven years.  sets out each date in full.

The Biltmore Program of May 1942 called openly for a "Jewish Commonwealth," the movement's first explicit, public statehood demand; it is best read as the culmination of the forty-six years of institution-building before it, not as their origin.
Reading it that way does not minimize the Holocaust's effect, which was real: the catastrophe reshaped the world's willingness to act.

The historian Raul Hilberg's demographic breakdown produced an estimate of 5.1 million Jewish deaths; Lucy Dawidowicz's 1975 research in the birth and death records of prewar European cities produced 5,933,900.
Yad Vashem's Book of Names project, still under way, has identified about 4.8 million victims individually through testimony and archives.

Auschwitz alone, operating from May 1940 to January 1945, received at least 1.3 million people, of whom at least 1.1 million were murdered there, the largest toll at any single site among more than 44,000 camps and places of incarceration.

Soviet troops liberated it on 27 January 1945, after the SS had driven most of the remaining prisoners onto death marches; the date has been marked since 2005 as International Holocaust Remembrance Day.

The United States Holocaust Memorial Museum describes the Holocaust as the best-documented genocide in history, and it lists the core claims of denial: that the six million deaths never occurred, that Nazi Germany had no official extermination policy, and that the gas chambers of Auschwitz-Birkenau never existed.
The years 1945 to 1948 are where the Holocaust and Palestine actually met, and they met through the survivors.
In 1945 Earl G. Harrison's team visited 30 displaced-persons camps in Germany and Austria.
They found Jewish survivors held under armed guard behind barbed wire.
Harrison wrote:
"we appear to be treating the Jews as the Nazis treated them, except that we do not exterminate them."
He delivered the report to President Truman on 24 August 1945, and the White House released it on 29 September.
Harrison reported that most Jewish displaced persons wanted to go to Palestine, and he cited the Jewish Agency's petition for 100,000 additional immigration certificates.
Truman asked Prime Minister Clement Attlee to admit 100,000.
Attlee refused.
The decision over entry to Palestine sat with Britain as the Mandatory power, and Truman's request was refused.
Truman's own lever was American immigration law.
His directive of 22 December 1945 gave displaced persons preference within the existing quotas, and about 22,950 entered the United States over two years, roughly two-thirds of them Jewish.
The directive worked inside the existing quotas, so the 100,000 Truman asked Britain to admit stood against some 22,950 admitted by his own country over two years.
That refuge argument became the core of how support for the new state was presented to Americans.
In 1948 the case rested on humanitarian grounds, with some 250,000 Jewish displaced persons in Europe, on Christian restorationist belief, and on the new state's presentation as a democracy.
The national-security establishment argued the reverse: the State Department, the Joint Chiefs, the Defense Secretary and the CIA warned that American backing would harm American interests.

Hostile framing of Arabs in pro-Zionist publicity drew heavily on the Grand Mufti's documented wartime collaboration with Hitler, a real episode used as a broad brush; the organized, well-funded anti-Islam network in the United States is documented mainly from the 2000s.
The "strategic asset" argument came later, growing after 1967 and formalized under President Reagan in 1981.
Among the founding narratives this library checks, "born of the Holocaust" fails in the same way: the Holocaust accelerated support; it did not create the program.
Turn now to the American classroom.
The federal instrument is the Never Again Education Act, H.R. 943, signed on Friday, 29 May 2020.

It requires the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum to develop and disseminate resources that improve awareness and understanding of the Holocaust, and it authorizes Holocaust education programs for prospective and current teachers and educational leaders.

The fullest account of what the states do is a report by the Government Accountability Office, delivered on 7 July 2026 to the House and Senate appropriations subcommittees for Labor, Health and Human Services and Education: GAO-26-108023, K–12 Education: How States and the U.S. Holocaust Museum Support Holocaust Education, prepared under a provision in Senate Report 118-84.
ents: the U.S. Holocaust Museum Support Holocaust Education

sent: GAO counted 51 jurisdictions, the District of Columbia among them.
Forty-three have academic standards that explicitly mention the Holocaust or laws that require it to be taught: 35 include it in their standards and 25 require it by law.
Eight have neither: Kansas, Montana, Nevada, North Dakota, Pennsylvania, Vermont, Washington and Wyoming.
Arizona's law requires at least three class periods, or the equivalent, on at least two occasions between the seventh and twelfth grades.
Florida's standards run from fifth through twelfth grade.
New Hampshire's mention the Holocaust in a single world-history standard.
Michigan's law covers grades 8 to 12 and names both the Holocaust and the Armenian Genocide.
GAO gives no typical number of hours; state officials told it that teachers "had to choose which parts of the Holocaust to cover."

According to Echoes & Reflections, which tracks them, the earliest were California's in 1985, for grades 7 to 12; Illinois in 1990, expanded in 2005; New Jersey in March 1994; and New York in 1996, amended in 2022.
