The main gap GAO found was teacher preparation.
The Claims Conference commissioned it, and Schoen Cooperman Research compiled it, from 1,350 Americans aged 18 to 39.
According to J. Weekly's account of it, 63% did not know that six million Jews were murdered: 37% chose six million and 15% chose two million.
Thirty-six percent could not name a camp, 12% said the number who died had been "greatly exaggerated," 90% said the Holocaust happened, and 49% had seen Holocaust denial online.

The Berkeley sociologist Samuel Lucas cautioned that "not sure" answers and the wording of questions are hard to interpret, and that social-desirability bias could make denial look smaller than it really is.
One curriculum GAO names is Echoes & Reflections, which it identifies as a partnership of the Anti-Defamation League, the USC Shoah Foundation and Yad Vashem.

According to J. Weekly's report of its launch in 2005, it was announced by the ADL, the Shoah Visual History Foundation and Yad Vashem, which the paper described as "Israel's Holocaust Remembrance Authority."
It offered ten lessons with maps, photographs, timelines and primary sources, and 51 video testimonies drawn from the Shoah Foundation's 52,000 interviews.
Yad Vashem supplied the historical expertise; the ADL handled outreach to schools and state officials.
Yad Vashem's own status is set by law.
The Yad Vashem Law was brought to the Knesset on 18 May 1953 and passed on 19 August 1953, making it a body of the State of Israel.

Its mandate includes representing the State at national and international commemorations, and the Knesset limited it to the Holocaust and the destroyed communities, not the rebuilding of the homeland.
A body of the Israeli state is therefore one of three partners in an American curriculum, and its legal remit is the Holocaust and the destroyed communities, not the rebuilding of the homeland.

The program's lesson "Antisemitism after the Holocaust," for middle and high school, lists this learning objective: "Identify current features of antisemitism including Holocaust denial and distortion, and demonization of Israel."

On 5 July delegates at the National Education Association's Representative Assembly narrowly adopted a new business item, NBI 39, saying the union would not use, endorse or publicize ADL materials or programs.

The ADL lesson treats demonization of Israel as one current feature of antisemitism, alongside denial and distortion, and the NEA's leadership kept the ADL as a partner; its president, Becky Pringle, said the boycott "would not further NEA's commitment to academic freedom, our membership, or our goals."

The item's sponsor, Judy Greenspan, and the teachers behind it argued that the ADL's definition of antisemitism folds criticism of Israel into antisemitism and has made real antisemitism harder to track and fight.
According to the Jewish Telegraphic Agency, its first use is murky.
JTA traced it most likely to postwar Israel: it appeared in secular kibbutzim in the late 1940s and in a Swedish Holocaust documentary in 1961.
Some trace it further back, to Isaac Lamdan's 1926 Hebrew poem "Masada," with its line "Never shall Masada fall again!"
Its English currency, by JTA's account, came from Meir Kahane, who founded the Jewish Defense League in 1968 and titled his 1972 manifesto Never Again.
For Kahane it meant "that if it happens again, it won't happen in the same way," and he used it to justify acts of terror against antisemitism.
After his assassination in November 1990, Sholom Comay, president of the American Jewish Committee, said Kahane "must always be remembered for the slogan Never Again."
Barack Obama said in 2011 that it should be "not just a phrase but a principled cause."
The United States Holocaust Memorial Museum made it the theme of its 2013 Days of Remembrance.
Elie Wiesel wrote in 2012 that it "becomes more than a slogan: It's a prayer, a promise, a vow."
In 2010 Benjamin Netanyahu used both senses.
At Auschwitz he said, "never again will we allow the hand of evil to sever the life of our people"; in the guestbook of the Rwanda genocide memorial he wrote, simply, "Never again."

On the particular reading, set out by the scholar Shaul Magid, Kahane's "Never Again" was a call to militancy as the only act of prevention, and leaders have used the phrase to mean the protection of the Jewish people specifically.

On the universal reading, Holocaust museums, Wiesel and others use it as a vow against genocide anywhere, and it has been taken up for refugees, for Japanese-American internment and for other causes; the historian Hasia Diner argues that objecting to such uses is not, by itself, reasonable.
Netanyahu's two uses in one year show that the same speaker can mean both.
GAO's report, the most complete federal account of Holocaust education, does not mention Israel at all.

No national study measures how classrooms connect the Holocaust to Israel, whether through the Echoes & Reflections lesson objective or otherwise, so any claim that American schools teach the Holocaust as the reason for Israel, or that they do not, goes beyond what is documented.
The survey of young adults measured knowledge of the Holocaust, not beliefs about Israel, and its own critic questioned how far even its knowledge figures can be read.
Before Zionism: The Old Yishuv and the Count of Jerusalem
Political Zionism did not bring the first Jews to the land.
When the movement's first settlers arrived from 1881, they found a Jewish community already there, long settled and organized on entirely different lines.
Historians call it the Old Yishuv, to distinguish it from the New Yishuv that began with the First Aliyah, the wave of immigration from 1881 onward.
It grew in the eighteenth century mainly through Orthodox groups, among them Hasidim and the disciples of the Vilna Gaon.
Its life centered on four cities that Jewish tradition held holy: Jerusalem, Hebron, Safed and Tiberias.
In the nineteenth century most of its members lived in Jerusalem.

The previous section described the Ottoman province around them, a land most of whose people were Arabic-speaking Muslims and Christians; the Jewish communities of these four cities were long established within it, as Ottoman subjects or as foreign nationals living under Ottoman rule.
Jews abroad sent donations, and the money was handed out in the land by kollels, bodies organized by country of origin or by Hasidic affiliation.
Politically, the community had a recognized place inside the Ottoman order.
The Sephardi leadership, headed by a chief rabbi, the Hakham Bashi, a title later rendered Rishon LeZion, was officially recognized by the Ottoman authorities and represented the Jews before them.
The Ashkenazi kollels, which had grown up separately, united at the end of the nineteenth century under a General Committee of Knesset Israel.
By the National Library of Israel's count, the Jewish population of the land was about 7,000 in 1800 and about 27,000 in 1880.
Most researchers put the 1880 figure somewhat lower, at 23,000 to 26,000, and agree that about half of them lived in Jerusalem.
The community roughly tripled or quadrupled between 1800 and 1880, before political Zionism existed.
Roughly 60,000 Jews arrived between 1881 and 1914.
The First World War then reversed much of it.
By the summer of 1918, after wartime expulsions, hunger and disease, 56,000 Jews remained in the land, little more than half the number of 1914.
The historian Justin McCarthy reconstructed Palestine's population from the Ottoman registers.
His counts of Ottoman-citizen Jews are about 13,000 of 369,000 people in 1860, 13,942 of 440,850 in 1878, 17,991 of 516,131 in 1890, and 38,754 of 722,143 in 1914.
They recorded Ottoman citizens, and they did not include foreign nationals, among whom were many Jewish immigrants.
Jews who lived in the land as foreign nationals do not appear in them.
They answer different questions: how many Jews lived in the land, and how many Jews the empire counted as its own citizens.

McCarthy's register totals, 516,131 in 1890 and 722,143 in 1914, are counts of Ottoman citizens; the approximate figure of 600,000 for the late nineteenth century given in the previous section comes from a different source.
In the second half of the nineteenth century Jerusalem's Jews began to build beyond the Old City.
The first neighborhoods outside the city walls are associated with Moses Montefiore, Yoel Moshe Salomon and Yehoshua Yellin.
The Old Yishuv did not last as the land's leading Jewish community.
The decline of the Ottoman Empire and the successive Zionist immigration waves cost it that place.
The most argued-over question about this community concerns Jerusalem itself.
Did Jews form the majority of the city before Zionism?
On 22 February of that year, Jordan and the United Arab Republic wrote to the UN Secretary-General in a letter circulated as document S/10130.
On 1 March 1971, Israel's ambassador to the United Nations, Yosef Tekoah, replied in a letter to the Secretary-General, document S/10138.

The Israeli letter set out a series of figures for the city of Jerusalem: 28,000 Jews among 43,000 people in 1887, citing Baedeker's guide of 1894; 40,000 of 60,000 in 1905, citing the thirteenth edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica; 33,971 of 62,578 at the British census of 1922; 51,222 of 90,503 in 1931; and 97,000 of 157,080 in 1944, citing the Survey of Palestine.

Its argument was that Jews had been the majority of the city itself in 1922, 1931 and 1944 and for decades before the Mandate, and that the Arab figures in S/10130 described the whole Jerusalem sub-district, a wider area in which Arabs were the majority, rather than the city.

The figures that Jordan and the United Arab Republic used are not reproduced in the sources available for this book, so their side of the exchange is known here only through Israel's description of it.

The same Israeli letter states that in 1948 Jordan destroyed the Jewish Quarter of the Old City, including 39 synagogues and places of learning, expelled its Jews, and barred Jewish access to the holy places from 1948 to 1967.
These are statements in an official Israeli document addressed to the United Nations, made in the course of a diplomatic dispute, and they are reported here as such.

Figures gathered by the Jewish Virtual Library, drawing on Oesterreicher and Sinai (1974), give Jerusalem 7,120 Jews of 15,510 people in 1844, 12,000 of 25,030 in 1876, and 28,112 of 45,420 in 1896, and 33,971 Jews at the British census of 1922.
By these figures Jews were a little under half of the city's people in 1844 and 1876 and a majority by 1896.
The two compilations agree on the Jewish figure for 1922, 33,971, but not on the city's total.
Israel's letter gives the 1922 census total as 62,578; the Jewish Virtual Library table gives 52,081.
The sources do not explain the difference, and it changes the Jewish share of the city in that year considerably.

Making the case for a long Jewish claim to the city, the columnist Stephen Flatow, writing in the Jerusalem Post in 2023, cited visitors' calculations showing a Jewish plurality from the mid-1800s and the 1922 census showing Jews as the majority of the city.

The strongest form of this case rests on the series of figures Israel put before the United Nations, which a separate compilation broadly matches: by both, Jews were the city's largest group by the late nineteenth century.

The nineteenth-century figures come from visitors' estimates and secondary compilations, not from a systematic census, and many Jewish residents were foreign subjects outside the Ottoman registers, so the Ottoman state's own counts cannot confirm them.
The analyst Seth Frantzman, writing in 2016, stressed who those Jews were: the Jews of nineteenth-century Jerusalem were largely Sephardi and religious, and the city was a Middle Eastern one.
A Jewish plurality, and later a majority, in the city of Jerusalem is supported by several compilations, though the earliest of them rest on estimates.

An Arab majority in the land as a whole is supported by every count here; an Arab majority in the wider sub-district is stated in Israel's own letter, though the figures behind it are not in these sources.
Under British rule the Jewish share of the whole country rose quickly from a low base.
Britain's census of 1922 counted 757,182 people in Palestine, of whom about 11% were Jews.
The census of 1931 put the Jewish share at about 17%, and the estimate of the United Nations Special Committee on Palestine for late 1946, a population of about 1.85 million, put it at about 33%.
The growth that the Old Yishuv's 7,000 of 1800 began, and the First Aliyah accelerated, continued at a far greater pace under the Mandate.
How many Jews lived in the land as foreign nationals, outside the Ottoman registers, at any given date is not established by these sources.
The difference between the two 1922 totals for Jerusalem is unresolved.
And the Arab side of the 1971 exchange at the United Nations is known here only from Israel's reply.

What the record does establish is that a Jewish community lived in the land, chiefly in its four holy cities, before Zionism, that it was sustained from abroad and represented to the Ottomans through its Sephardi chief rabbi, and that by the figures available it was the largest group in the city of Jerusalem by the late nineteenth century while remaining a small minority in the land as a whole.
The version of this history an American reader learned is one of several.

Governments and publics elsewhere read the same events through their own pasts: a debt of guilt, a memory of colonial rule or apartheid, a diaspora with family in the region, an alliance with Washington.
Germany reads the conflict through the Holocaust, and its commitment began as reparation.

In 1952 Chancellor Konrad Adenauer signed the Luxembourg Agreement, committing West Germany to pay 3 billion Deutsche Marks to Israel and 450 million to Jewish organizations; total German reparation payments reached about €82 billion by 2022.
On 18 March 2008 Angela Merkel told the Knesset that Germany's historic responsibility is part of its Staatsräson, its reason of state, a moral and political compact rather than a legal doctrine.

Per SIPRI, Germany supplied about a third of Israel's arms imports in 2020–2024, second only to the United States, and it approved €485.1 million in military equipment between 7 October 2023 and 13 May 2025.
Nicaragua's 2024 case against Germany at the International Court of Justice continued after the Court declined emergency measures in April 2024, by the latest report in this record.
On 8 August 2025 Chancellor Merz halted exports "that could be used in the Gaza Strip," leaving missile-defense and naval exports open; its status since has not been re-verified for this edition.

At home, the Bundestag declared on 17 May 2019, in a non-binding motion, that "the arguments and methods of the BDS movement are antisemitic," and at least 99 Palestine solidarity protests were banned between 7 October and 19 November 2023, according to the Transnational Institute, some later overturned in court; officials cited a sharp rise in antisemitic incidents against German Jews.
By April 2026 polling showed that only a relatively small share of Germans still saw Israel's security as reason of state.
Spain carries two histories.
In 1492 the Catholic monarchs ordered Spain's Jews, at least 200,000 by historians' estimate, to convert or leave.

Ben-Gurion rejected Franco's reported 1948 overture over his Nazi ties, and Spain opened relations only on 17 January 1986, the last Western European state to do so, as a condition of joining the European Community.
Its 2015 law offering citizenship to descendants of the expelled Sephardim drew 132,226 applications by the 2019 deadline, about 20,000 from Mexico alone.
On 28 May 2024 Spain, with Ireland and Norway, recognized the State of Palestine on the pre-1967 lines; Israel recalled its ambassador and said the three were rewarding Hamas.
Pro-Israel commentators see hostility with historical echoes; the government cites two states and international law.
South Africa reads the conflict through apartheid, and the record runs in an unexpected direction.
Drawing on more than 7,000 pages of declassified South African documents, Sasha Polakow-Suransky documented a secret security agreement signed on 3 April 1975 by Shimon Peres and P.W. Botha.
South Africa became Israel's largest arms buyer, about 35% of its military exports, while Israel publicly condemned apartheid.
Minutes record Peres saying a "correct payload" was available "in three sizes"; the Guardian read this as an offer of nuclear warheads, and Peres denied it.

On 4 December 1997 Nelson Mandela said that "our freedom is incomplete without the freedom of the Palestinians," in a sentence that also named East Timor and Sudan; South Africa's Jewish Report argues the line is often quoted without that context.
In January 2024 South Africa brought its genocide case against Israel to the ICJ.
Latin America holds a large Palestinian diaspora, much of it Christian.

Chile's community is estimated at 300,000 to 500,000, the largest outside the Middle East, and El Salvador's at about 100,000; its president, Nayib Bukele, of Palestinian descent, has been publicly pro-Israel, which divided the community.
The region also remembers Israeli arms.

Declassified Israeli and US cables show that after the Carter administration halted military aid to Guatemala in 1977 over human-rights abuses, Israel supplied rifles, aircraft, armored vehicles and counterinsurgency training; a Guatemalan ambassador said "Israel saved Guatemala."
In 1981 El Salvador received $21 million in Israeli arms credits at the US request.
Brazil split between its president and its public.

In February 2024 President Lula called Gaza "a genocide" and compared it to Hitler's extermination of Jews; Israel's foreign minister, Israel Katz, summoned Brazil's ambassador to Yad Vashem and declared Lula persona non grata, and Brazil recalled its ambassador.
A CNN Brasil poll found 83% of Brazilians disagreed with the comparison.
In August 2024 Lula suspended a $210 million contract for 36 Elbit howitzers and Brazil joined South Africa's ICJ case.

His predecessor, Jair Bolsonaro, had pledged in 2018 to move the embassy to Jerusalem, but opened only a trade office there in December 2019, after the farm lobby warned that Arab meat markets were at risk.
France is home to Europe's largest Jewish community, about 440,000 to 500,000, and to its largest Muslim population, an estimate because the census does not record religion.

Recorded antisemitic acts rose from 436 in 2022 to 1,676 in 2023, the highest since tracking began in 2012, then 1,570 in 2024 and 1,320 in 2025; in 2024 more than 30% referenced Palestine and 192 occurred in schools.
Anti-Muslim discrimination is also documented, and protest restrictions in October 2023 drew civil-liberties criticism.
On 22 September 2025 President Macron recognized the State of Palestine at the UN, calling it a defeat for Hamas.
The United Kingdom, once the Mandate power, took partial measures.

On 2 September 2024 it suspended about 30 of roughly 350 arms export licences to Israel over a "clear risk" of serious violations of international humanitarian law, but exempted F-35 components; the High Court refused permission for a judicial review on 30 June 2025, and by 2026 more than 80 licences had been suspended or refused.
On 21 September 2025 Prime Minister Keir Starmer recognized the State of Palestine.
Canada and Australia recognized Palestine the same day; Canada and the UK became the first G7 members to do so.

Canada stopped approving new arms permits on 8 January 2024, but earlier permits stayed valid: 164 were used in 2024, and reporting found at least C$28.5 million approved in the war's first months; the government says no lethal weapons have been approved since January 2024.

When the International Criminal Court issued warrants for Netanyahu and Yoav Gallant on 21 November 2024, Justin Trudeau said Canada would "abide by all the regulations and rulings of the international courts," though his foreign minister would not say whether Canada would make an arrest; Netanyahu's office called the warrants "an antisemitic decision."

In Australia the war became personal on 1 April 2024, when Israeli drone strikes on three marked World Central Kitchen vehicles killed seven aid workers, among them the Australian Zomi Frankcom; Israel called it unintentional and dismissed two officers.
Muslim-majority Asia did not take one path.

In July 2025 Indonesia, the most populous Muslim-majority country, and Malaysia joined a 12-country "Hague Group," with South Africa, Colombia, Bolivia and others, committed to halting arms transfers to Israel.
Both have long tied any normalization to a Palestinian state, while the UAE, Bahrain and Morocco normalized relations in 2020.
Ethiopian Jews are a case readers often ask about, as a test of how Israel treats its Black citizens.
Operation Moses flew about 8,000 from Sudanese camps in 1984–85, after an estimated 4,000 died on the trek; Operation Solomon carried 14,325 people to Israel in 36 hours on 24–25 May 1991.
In 1996 Maariv revealed that Magen David Adom had secretly discarded blood donated by Ethiopian immigrants since about 1991 over HIV fears.
Reports of disproportionate Depo-Provera injections led to a 2013 Health Ministry directive; the ministry denied wrongdoing, and investigations were inconclusive.

Set side by side, these readings follow the histories of the countries doing the reading: guilt in Germany, expulsion and late recognition in Spain, apartheid in South Africa, diaspora and civil war in Latin America, two large communities in France, alliance and its limits in Britain, Canada and Australia.

What the record does not settle is how far each government's policy reflects its public; in Germany and Brazil the documented polling and the policy point in different directions, and for most countries here no comparable measure exists in this record.
One Verse, Two Readings: Christians and the Promise to Abraham
Two opposite claims are often made about the Bible and the modern State of Israel.
One holds that scripture requires Christians to support the state.
Neither describes the actual situation, which is a long-running argument among Christians themselves over what one set of verses means and to whom they now apply.
The verse at the center of it is Genesis 12:3, the text Christian Zionists cite most.
It was spoken to Abram, later Abraham: "I will bless those who bless you, and whoever curses you I will curse; and all peoples on earth will be blessed through you."
The promise of land follows in the same narrative, at Genesis 12:7, 15:18 and 17:8.
One answer identifies it with the Jewish people and, since 1948, with the State of Israel, a secular state.
Another holds that the promise was fulfilled in Christ and the church and does not pass to any modern government.
The Christian Zionist reading treats the verse as a standing instruction.
Groups such as the International Christian Embassy Jerusalem describe it as the biblical mandate for standing with Israel  .
On this reading the blessing and the curse attach to how nations and individuals treat the Jewish people and their state now, and the land promise of Genesis 12:7, 15:18 and 17:8 remains in force.
Many believers in dispensationalism, a system of reading biblical prophecy, go further and regard Israel's restoration as a precondition of Christ's return.
That framework was popularized by the notes of the Scofield Reference Bible, whose history is told in .
The older British and American Protestant campaign for a Jewish restoration to Palestine is told in .
It holds that the promise to Abraham is fulfilled in Christ and in the church, citing Paul's letter to the Galatians (3:16 and 3:29), and that it does not transfer to a modern government  .

The strongest form of this reading is that it takes its key from within the Christian scriptures themselves, in Paul's own reading of the promise, and gives full weight to the verse's last clause: "all peoples on earth will be blessed through you."
Senator Ted Cruz cited Genesis 12:3 in an exchange with Tucker Carlson, and Carlson asked whether the political state led by Benjamin Netanyahu is the same "Israel" as the one in scripture .
Cruz's position rests on the identification of the biblical Israel with the modern state.
Carlson's question rests on the distinction between them.
The first reading is the theology behind the largest pro-Israel constituency in the United States.
How an annotated Bible became a political force, from the dispensationalist pulpit to organized lobbying in Washington, is drawn in the map below.
A frequent question about the dispensationalist reading is why the Roman Catholic Church never campaigned against it.
Rome never ran a public campaign.

In the 1940s the Holy Office, the Vatican's doctrinal authority and the predecessor of today's Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith, judged that premillennialism, the prophetic framework at the core of Scofield's system, "cannot safely be taught" .
Paragraph 676 of the Catechism of the Catholic Church rejects millenarianism as "the intrinsic perversity" of a falsely secularized understanding of the Kingdom of God .
Catholic doctrinal statements are addressed to Catholics, through the Church's own teaching, not issued as public rebuttals of particular Protestant authors or their reference Bibles.

Rulings against specific Protestant theological systems routinely remain inside Church documents and catechetical teaching rather than becoming public campaigns, and the Church generally does not campaign against the doctrines of Protestant denominations with which it is not in active dialogue.
Rome also had no authority over Protestant publishing in the first place.
Its doctrinal jurisdiction runs over Catholic teaching, and the Reformation had ended any mechanism by which it could approve or block a Protestant publisher's Bible centuries before Scofield.
What the ruling records is the Church's own position on the theology, not an attempt or an ability to control what Protestant publishers printed.
Whether individual Catholics or parishes ever hear of paragraph 676 is a different matter, and the record here does not measure it.
Rome's diplomatic record shows what a church that did not read the promise in dispensationalist terms actually did when Zionism came to it.
In January 1904 Theodor Herzl sought an audience with Pope Pius X to ask for Vatican support for a Jewish homeland in Palestine.
The Pope refused.
His documented answer was that the Church could not support Jewish restoration to a land central to its own theology while denying Christ .
That refusal held as Vatican policy for 89 years.

In 1949, a year after Israel's founding, the Vatican worked behind the scenes at the United Nations to make Israel's admission conditional on two commitments: allowing the return of Palestinian refugees, and formal guarantees for Christian and Muslim holy sites, particularly in Jerusalem.
Ben-Gurion said that year: "There is a major religion in the world, which has to settle with us a historical reckoning."
Israel was admitted to the United Nations in May 1949 without the guarantees the Holy See had sought.
What changed the Church's course was a change in its doctrine.
The Second Vatican Council's declaration Nostra Aetate of 1965 revised Catholic teaching on Judaism, stating that God "holds the Jews most dear for the sake of their Fathers."
On 30 December 1993 the Holy See and Israel signed the Fundamental Agreement in Jerusalem, establishing diplomatic relations, 45 years after Israel's founding, and ambassadors were exchanged in 1994.
Even then, property rights, tax exemptions and the status of Jerusalem were left for continuing negotiation under the agreement's own terms .

The documented reasons for the long delay were three: the Church's theology of the Jewish people's role in salvation history, the unresolved status of Jerusalem's holy sites, and concern for the Palestinian Christian and Muslim communities under the new state .

After the UN General Assembly's vote of November 2012, the Vatican formally recognized the State of Palestine, and in 2015 it signed an accord governing the Church's activity in Palestinian-controlled territory, which drew a formal Israeli protest .
Within Judaism, too, views of the state's religious meaning differ: early Zionism was largely secular, and some Haredi Jews oppose a Jewish state before the coming of the Messiah.
And Palestinian Christians, about 1% of the population today, are part of this story too, as a community with its own history in the land and not only as a subject of other Christians' theology.
The record settles what the verse says, which traditions read it which way, what Rome ruled and when, and how long it took the Holy See to recognize Israel.

It does not settle the theological question, which is not a historical one: whether a promise made to Abraham applies to a state founded in 1948 depends on a reader's prior commitments about how scripture is to be read.
Nor does the material here say how many Christians hold each reading.
What it does show is that "the Bible requires it" and "the Bible is irrelevant" are both wrong as descriptions.
The verse matters a great deal to many Christians, and they draw opposite conclusions from it.
The first division is over events and intent: what happened to the Palestinian Arabs who left or were driven from their homes, and how far it was planned.
The second is over framing: what kind of movement Zionism was in the first place.
Until the 1980s the dominant Israeli account held that the Palestinians had largely left on their own, or at the urging of Arab leaders.

In the 1980s Israel began to declassify its state and military archives, and a group of scholars who came to be called the "new historians," Benny Morris and Ilan Pappé among them, went into those files.
What they documented was expulsions, massacres and the deliberate prevention of Palestinian return.
Morris and Pappé, working with the same newly opened material, came to sharply different judgments about how far the expulsions were planned.
The historian Walid Khalidi, writing on Deir Yassin, argued that the Haganah, a Jewish armed force of the period, was involved there at every stage.
Historians such as Efraim Karsh reject the expulsion-centered account altogether.

In their reading, the decisive facts of 1948 are the choices of Arab leaders and the Arab rejection of partition; the departure of the Palestinian population follows from those choices rather than from a design on the Jewish side.

The strongest form of the new historians' case is that the expulsions, massacres and the barring of return are recorded in Israel's own state and military files, and that no account of the war's causes removes what those files show was done.
Scholars such as Joseph Massad describe Zionism as a settler-colonial project.
Their evidence is, in part, the movement's own vocabulary: Zionist leaders used the word "colonization" of their own work, including Vladimir Jabotinsky in his 1923 essay "The Iron Wall."
Others describe Zionism as a national liberation movement, and as a refugee movement: the effort of a people with ancient roots in the land to find safety after centuries of persecution.
For further reading across these positions, the works include Shlaim's The Iron Wall,  Masalha's Palestine: A Four Thousand Year History  and Said's work on the question of Palestine.
Material in Israeli military archives on some events, including Deir Yassin, remains classified.
The Map: Israel, the West Bank, Gaza and East Jerusalem
Four names recur through every volume of this book: Israel, the West Bank, Gaza and East Jerusalem.

When later chapters say "the West Bank," "Area C," "Gaza" or "East Jerusalem," they mean a particular piece of ground under a particular rule, and most of the conflict's arguments turn out to be arguments about where these lines run and who governs on either side of them.
Israel, in the sense used throughout this book, is the state within the 1949 armistice lines, the boundary commonly called the "Green Line."
The West Bank is the territory east of that line.
Jordan held it from 1948 to 1967, and Israel has occupied it since 1967.
The internal map of the West Bank was drawn in 1995, by the interim agreement known as Oslo II.
Area A, about 18 percent of the West Bank, was placed under Palestinian Authority civil and security control.
Ramallah, Bethlehem, Nablus, Jenin, Tulkarem, Qalqilya, Jericho and most of Hebron.
Area B, about 22 percent, came under Palestinian civil control with joint security control.
Area C, about 61 percent, remained under full Israeli control.
Areas A and B together hold some 2.8 million Palestinians.

The accord divided authority by function, not only by territory: in Area A the Palestinian Authority held both civil and security powers; in Area B it held civil powers while security was shared; in Area C Israel held both.
The zones were meant to be a stage, with the divisions transferred gradually to the Palestinians.
Since 2002 the Israeli army has entered Area A routinely, so that even the zone of fullest Palestinian control is not closed to Israeli forces.
Every Israeli settlement outside East Jerusalem lies within it.
About 60 percent of Area C is designated as firing zones, military land, state land or nature reserves, and Palestinian building permits there are rarely granted.

The result is a territory in which the 2.8 million Palestinians of Areas A and B live in the two smaller zones, while all of the settlements outside East Jerusalem sit in the largest zone, under Israeli control.
When later chapters discuss settlement growth or the prospects of a Palestinian state, the ground at stake is mostly Area C.
In all, about 737,000 Israeli settlers live in East Jerusalem and the West Bank.
Gaza is a strip of land on the Mediterranean coast with a different history.
Egypt held it from 1948 to 1967, and Israel occupied it from 1967.
In 2005 Israel withdrew its settlers from Gaza but kept control of its borders, airspace and coast.

The distinction between removing settlers and removing control runs through every later argument about Gaza's legal status, and the record supports both halves of it: the settlers left, and the borders, airspace and coast stayed under Israeli control.
East Jerusalem is the fourth place, and the one whose status is most directly disputed between Israeli and international law.
Israel occupied it in 1967 and then annexed it, a step that has not been recognized internationally.
Roughly 360,000 Palestinians live there.
How East Jerusalem's status came to be set in two contradictory ways is a story of three dates.
A familiar claim holds that everyone recognizes Jerusalem as Israel's capital; its mirror image holds that no one should.
In July 1980 the Knesset passed a Basic Law declaring "Jerusalem, complete and united," the capital of Israel.
The law covered East Jerusalem, captured in 1967.
In Israeli law, that is where the matter has stood since.
On 20 August 1980 the United Nations Security Council adopted Resolution 478 by 14 votes to none, with the United States abstaining.

The resolution censured the Israeli law "in the strongest terms," declared measures altering Jerusalem's status "null and void," and called on states that had diplomatic missions in the city to withdraw them.
After Costa Rica and El Salvador moved their embassies out in 2006, no country kept one in Jerusalem.
The change came from Washington.
Following President Trump's announcement in December 2017, the United States opened its embassy in Jerusalem on 14 May 2018, the first embassy in the city since 2006.
Most countries still keep their embassies in Tel Aviv.
Under the Oslo Accords, the city's final status was designated as a matter for negotiation between the parties.
Israel holds that Jerusalem is its capital under its own law, and the talking point that Jerusalem is Israel's undivided capital describes that law correctly.
The Security Council declared that law null and void, and most of the world does not recognize the annexation.

What the record does not contain is a single legal answer accepted by both systems, and the Oslo framework, by leaving the city's final status to negotiation, put off that answer rather than giving it.
Who Are "the Palestinians"?
One People, Several Legal Situations
When a sentence in this book, or in a newspaper, refers to "the Palestinians," it may mean any of several groups whose rights and daily lives differ sharply.

The record shows something else: one people spread across several territories and several legal systems, so that which laws apply to a given Palestinian depends on where that person was born and where he or she now lives.
The Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics estimated about 14.8 million Palestinians worldwide in 2024.

From 1949 to 1966 most of Israel's Arab citizens lived under a military government: a separate administration that required permits to travel outside their localities, imposed curfews, and designated closed areas.
Its worst single event came on 29 October 1956, the eve of the Sinai War.
Brigadier Issachar Shadmi moved up a dusk curfew on villages near the Jordanian border without adequate notice.
When Major Shmuel Malinki asked how to treat villagers returning from work who did not know of it, Shadmi's answer, according to the court record, was that anyone who left his house would be shot.

The claim that Arab citizens have enjoyed equal civil rights since 1948 does not survive these eighteen years.
On 19 July 2018 the Knesset passed Basic Law: Israel, the Nation-State of the Jewish People, by 62 votes to 55, with two abstentions.
Its eleven articles state that "the exercise of the right to national self-determination in the State of Israel is unique to the Jewish people."
They declare the state open to Jewish immigration, and they state that "the development of Jewish settlement" is "a national value" that the state will encourage.
The law contains no equality clause; a draft clause that would have permitted Jewish-only communities was dropped.
Because Israel has no written constitution, its Basic Laws carry constitutional weight, which makes this text the closest thing Israel has to a defining clause on nationhood.
On 8 July 2021 the Supreme Court rejected the petitions against the law by 10 to 1.
The majority held that it does not negate Israel's democratic character and that individual rights are protected by other laws.
The lone dissenter was Justice George Karra, the court's only Arab member.
Its defenders say it merely enshrines what Israel already is, codifying the state's Jewish character.
Its critics, among them Arab citizens' rights groups and some Jewish organizations, say it relegates Arab citizens, about a fifth of the population, to a lesser standing.
A familiar claim holds that Israel's founding commitment to equality is written into its constitution.
The second situation is East Jerusalem.
Roughly 360,000 Palestinians live in the part of the city Israel annexed after 1967, most of them holding Israeli residency rather than Israeli citizenship.
They live under Israeli rule, but most without Israeli citizenship.
At the end of that year the city had 266,300 residents: 197,700, or 74.2 percent, counted as Jews and others, and 68,600, or 25.8 percent, as Arabs.
At the end of 2023 Jerusalem had 980,700 residents: 589,300, or 60.1 percent, Jews and others, and 391,400, or 39.9 percent, Arabs.
Between the end of 1967 and the end of 2023, the Arab share of the city's population rose from about a quarter to about two-fifths.
The third situation is the West Bank, where about 3.4 million Palestinians lived in mid-2025.
The Palestinian Authority governs them in Areas A and B, and the territory as a whole is under Israeli military rule.
Israeli settlers in the same territory live under Israeli civil law.
The fourth situation is Gaza, home to about 2.1 million people in mid-2025.

About 40 percent of them are in Jordan, and the others are in Lebanon, Syria, the West Bank and Gaza.
About 6.6 million Palestinians live in Arab countries overall.

Registration as a refugee is a status in its own right, and it overlaps with the others: a registered refugee may live in Gaza or the West Bank, under one of the regimes above, or in Jordan, Lebanon or Syria.
Say that Palestinians vote and sit in the Knesset, and the record shows it of citizens of Israel, not of residents of East Jerusalem, who mostly hold residency rather than citizenship.
Say that they live under Israeli military rule, and the record shows it of the West Bank, not of Israel's Arab citizens since 1966.
A refugee in Jordan, a resident of Gaza, a villager in the West Bank, a resident of East Jerusalem and an Arab citizen of Israel share a national identity; they do not share a legal status.
That is why so much of the legal argument over Israel's conduct, including the argument over whether its policies amount to apartheid, turns on these distinctions.
What courts, United Nations bodies, human rights organizations and governments have actually found on that question, and Israel's rejection of those findings, is the subject of .
The population tables count groups, not citizenship, so they do not say exactly how many Arabs in Israel are citizens and how many are residents.

Occupation, Apartheid, Genocide: What the Words Mean in Law, and Who Has Found What
Occupation, apartheid and genocide run through almost every public argument about Israel and the Palestinians.
Each has been applied to Israel by bodies of very different standing: a court, a United Nations commission, human-rights organizations, an association of scholars.
And each finding has been rejected by Israel.
A court's opinion, a UN commission's conclusion, a non-governmental report and a government's denial are different kinds of statement, and each is named here for what it is.
On 19 July 2024 the International Court of Justice, the UN's highest court, gave its answer for the territory Israel holds.
The court was responding to a request from the UN General Assembly.
It found that Israel's continued presence in the Occupied Palestinian Territory, meaning the West Bank, East Jerusalem and Gaza, is unlawful.
It said that Israel must bring that presence to an end as rapidly as possible, cease all new settlement activity immediately, evacuate all settlers, and make reparation.

What did were Israel's policies and its assertion of sovereignty: the court reaffirmed its 2004 opinion that the settlements and the regime attached to them violate international law, held that the prolonged occupation breaches the Palestinian people's right to self-determination, and found that the policies amount to annexation.
The court left it to the General Assembly and the Security Council to decide how to act on it.
The day before the opinion was delivered, the Knesset passed a resolution calling Palestinian statehood an "existential danger."
Apartheid.
Apartheid is a crime under international law, defined in the 1973 Apartheid Convention and in the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court.

Because the definition describes a structure of domination, the argument over the word turns on the different legal situations of the people Israel governs: citizens, residents of East Jerusalem, and Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza, set out in .
Three human-rights organizations have concluded that Israel commits apartheid: Human Rights Watch in 2021, the Israeli group B'Tselem in 2021, and Amnesty International in February 2022.
The nearest a court has come is the ICJ's 2024 finding that Israeli policies breach the prohibition on racial segregation and apartheid.
Israel rejects the apartheid label.
Under the 1948 Genocide Convention, genocide means specified acts committed with intent to destroy a group, in whole or in part.
Since late 2024 a series of bodies has concluded that genocide, or acts of genocide, have been committed in Gaza.
Amnesty International did so in December 2024.
Human Rights Watch, also in December 2024, concluded that Israel had committed acts of genocide through the deprivation of water.
In July 2025 two Israeli organizations, B'Tselem and Physicians for Human Rights–Israel, reached the same conclusion.

In August 2025 the International Association of Genocide Scholars passed a resolution to that effect, and in September 2025 a UN Commission of Inquiry concluded that acts of genocide had been committed.

What a reader can take away is a way of reading the next headline: ask which word is being used, which body used it, and whether that body was a court, a UN commission, a human-rights organization or a government.
Most Americans meet this history long before they meet its documents.
Four publishers, Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, Pearson, McGraw-Hill and Holt McDougal, reach the great majority of American world-history students in grades 6 through 12.

How their books cover Israel and Palestine has been studied in the peer-reviewed literature: Sean Yom examined the framing of American world-history textbooks in 2013, and Nurit Peled-Elhanan published a mirror study of Israeli school textbooks in 2012.
Some events are named: the Holocaust, the 1948 declaration, the 1967 war.
Others are compressed: the Nakba, the 1953 CIA coup in Iran that reshaped the region, the Sabra and Shatila massacre of 1982.

A textbook can say, accurately and in one clean sentence, that Jewish settlers purchased land in Palestine.
The Ottoman government passed a Palestine-specific law in 1881–82 barring land purchase by foreign Jews.
In 1892 it required imperial approval even for purchases by Ottoman Jewish citizens.

Buyers worked around these rules through Ottoman-citizen intermediaries and through the consular protections known as the "capitulations," and in the 1890s the United States State Department found itself in a dispute over Russian Jewish emigrants who had naturalized as Americans in order to claim consular protection for land purchases in Palestine.
It appears in Wikipedia's article on Jewish land purchase in Palestine and in the United States government's own published diplomatic archive.
Jews are not one lineage.

The documented traditions include the Ashkenazi of Central and Eastern Europe, the Sephardi of Iberia and the diaspora after 1492, the Mizrahi of the Middle East and North Africa (including Iraq, Yemen, Morocco, Iran, Syria and Egypt), the Beta Israel of Ethiopia, the Bene Israel of India, the Jews of Kaifeng in China, the Bukharan Jews of Central Asia, and Georgian, Yemenite and Karaite communities.

Robert Maxwell was born Jan Ludvik Hoch in Czechoslovakia in 1923.
He survived the Holocaust, which killed most of his family, served in the British Army and anglicized his name after the war.

Between 1984 and 1991 he assembled Mirror Group Newspapers, publisher of the Daily Mirror, one of Britain's highest-circulation tabloids, which reached millions of readers a day; the academic publisher Pergamon Press; the language-education company Berlitz; and Macmillan Publishing, one of the largest textbook and reference publishers used in American schools, which he acquired in 1988 for $2.6 billion.
His relationship with Israeli intelligence is described in Seymour Hersh's The Samson Option,  in the work of Tom Bower, whose biography Maxwell:
The Outsider appeared in 1988,  and in Gordon Thomas and Martin Dillon's Robert Maxwell, Israel's Superspy of 2002; the name Bergman also appears among the sources on the point.

The biographies, working from different sources, describe a relationship with Mossad that reportedly included helping to sell software from Israeli technology firms to intelligence services around the world.

The broader pattern, a well-connected publisher with intelligence relationships on several sides, including British ties and alleged Soviet-era contacts through Pergamon's dealings with Eastern Bloc academic publishing, appears in more than one of these books rather than resting on any single one.
Maxwell died on 5 November 1991, found floating near his yacht, the Lady Ghislaine, off the Canary Islands.
The official Spanish autopsy and a later Israeli examination both concluded that he fell overboard, with drowning the probable cause.
He received an Israeli state funeral on the Mount of Olives, with six intelligence chiefs in attendance.
His daughter Ghislaine was convicted in 2021 of sex trafficking with Jeffrey Epstein, a later turn the record captures but does not explain.
What the Maxwell case shows must be stated as carefully as what it does not.
It shows that a man who owned major British media and a major American textbook publisher is described, in independently researched biographies, as having ties to Israeli intelligence.
It does not show that any Daily Mirror story about Israel or Zionism was ordered by an intelligence service, and it does not show that Maxwell altered any Macmillan textbook.

It was formalized as Zionist institutional policy before the Second World War, a step credited to Nahum Sokolow, and it has served continuously since as Israel's own name for its public diplomacy and propaganda.

"Semitic": A Family of Languages
A common claim folds two statements into one sentence: that "antisemitic" means anti-Jewish, and that criticism of Israel is therefore antisemitic.
The root is Shem, in Hebrew שֵׁם, one of the three sons of Noah in the genealogy of Genesis 10.
In 1781 the German scholar August Ludwig von Schlözer coined the term "Semitic" (semitisch) for the family of related languages that the biblical genealogy traced to Shem.
Schlözer was working as a linguist, sorting languages by their relationships.
Schlözer's framework grouped together the languages now called Hebrew, Aramaic, Arabic, Ge'ez, Akkadian and Phoenician.
He coined it more than a century before Zionism existed as a political movement, and long before the word became politically loaded in either direction.
That name, taken from Rome, covers French, Spanish, Italian, Portuguese and Romanian, and nobody takes it to mean that the French and the Romanians are one ethnicity or share one religion.
"Semitic" names a language family after a figure in Genesis in the same way.

Through most of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries it stayed a term of the comparative philology classroom, used as uncontroversially as "Indo-European" or "Sino-Tibetan" to group related tongues.
The family as linguists describe it today includes Hebrew, Aramaic, Arabic, Amharic (spoken in Ethiopia), Tigrinya, Maltese, Ge'ez, Syriac and Mehri, as well as Akkadian, which is extinct.
Their speakers include Arabs, Jews, Ethiopians, Assyrians, Chaldeans and Maltese, and by the word's original meaning all of them are Semitic peoples.
It is the definition an introductory course in Semitic linguistics teaches in its first week.
In that original sense the word applies equally to a Hebrew speaker, an Arabic speaker and an Amharic speaker.
Seen on a map, the family was spoken mainly in Mesopotamia, the Levant, Arabia and the Horn of Africa, and later across North Africa and on Malta.
Semitic is one branch of the larger Afroasiatic family, alongside Egyptian, Berber, Cushitic, Chadic and Omotic, and it is described as the only branch with members that originated outside Africa.
Its oldest written members are Akkadian, the language of Babylon and Assyria, and Eblaite, from the archives of Ebla in Syria, both of the third millennium BCE.

On the Levantine coast and inland, the Canaanite languages included Phoenician, Hebrew, Moabite, Ammonite and Edomite, the earliest of which, Phoenician, was written from at least the eleventh century BCE; Hebrew is the only one still spoken.

Aramaic, first the language of the Aramaeans, became by the seventh and sixth centuries BCE the common language of the Middle East, largely replacing Akkadian, and parts of Daniel and Ezra and both Talmuds are written in it.

In the south, Old South Arabian was written in Yemen from the eighth century BCE, and Ge'ez, the classical language of Aksum, remains the liturgical language of the Ethiopian church; Amharic, written in an adapted Ge'ez script, and Tigrinya are spoken in Ethiopia and Eritrea today.
How the branches subdivide is debated: scholars place Eblaite, Arabic and Old South Arabian differently.

Proposals include the Levant, northern Arabia and the Syro-Arabian desert; a 2009 statistical study by Kitchen and colleagues placed the common ancestor of the known Semitic languages in the Levant about 5,750 years ago, an estimate its own authors call uncertain, and most scholars put the older Afroasiatic homeland in Africa.
None of the proposals lies in Europe.

The one Semitic language native to Europe, Maltese, descends from a medieval Arabic dialect of Sicily brought to Malta by Arabic-speaking settlers, and is the only Semitic language written in the Latin alphabet.

The map above places each language at the approximate centre of where it was spoken, coloured by branch, with dotted arrows for documented spreads: Phoenician to Carthage, traditionally founded from Tyre in 814 or 813 BCE; Aramaic across the Middle East and into the Persian empire; and Arabic, after the conquests of the seventh century, through the Levant, Egypt and North Africa, where it took the place of Aramaic and Coptic over several generations.
One arrow, from southern Arabia to Ethiopia, shows a disputed proposal and is labelled so.
Careful modern usage keeps "Semitic" for languages.

By the mid-nineteenth century the word had been stretched into a supposed race;   Ernest Renan's history of the Semitic languages, published in 1855, read differences between languages as differences between peoples and called a "Semitic race" inferior to the Indo-European.

Modern scholarship rejects these theories: the historian Shmuel Almog calls the racial label a misnomer, and the US Holocaust Memorial Museum notes that there is no scientific evidence for distinct biological races.

The speakers of Semitic languages, past and present, include Akkadians, Phoenicians, Arameans, Jews, Arabs, speakers of Amharic, Tigrinya and other Ethiopian Semitic languages, Maltese and Assyrians; they share a language family, not a single ethnicity.
Nor are all Jewish languages Semitic: Yiddish is a Germanic language written in Hebrew letters, and Judeo-Spanish is a Romance language.
The everyday language of Palestinians is Palestinian Arabic, a South Levantine dialect of Arabic.
Palestinian Arabs belong to this family on two separate grounds.
The first is language: Palestinians speak Arabic, a Semitic language in the same family as Hebrew, Aramaic and Amharic.

Peer-reviewed population genetics, including the Y-chromosome study of Nebel and colleagues (2000) and the genome-wide study of Behar and colleagues published in Nature in 2010, documents that Palestinian and Jewish populations in the Levant share substantial common ancestry, consistent with descent from populations that have lived in the region continuously since antiquity.
Haber and colleagues' 2013 work on ancient Canaanite DNA points in the same direction.
On this evidence, Palestinians and Israeli Jews share more common ancestry with each other than either does with populations elsewhere.

The same body of genetic research is used in this book to trace the Ashkenazi, Sephardi and Mizrahi Jewish lineages ; here it is applied to the other population that draws on the same regional ancestral pool.
Palestinian Muslims and Palestinian Christians alike are, in the word's own sense, a Semitic people.
This is a linguistic and genetic fact, not an argument built to win a political point, and it does not by itself resolve any policy dispute between Israelis and Palestinians.

Actions against Palestinians cannot coherently be described as "pro-Semitic," and a political conflict between two Semitic-speaking populations cannot be described as a contest between Semites and anti-Semites.
The compound "antisemitism" took on its own meaning in the 1870s and 1880s, and that meaning, set by use rather than by the parts of the word, is hatred of Jews.
In 1879 the German agitator Wilhelm Marr made "antisemitism" the name of his movement against Jews, a euphemism for Judenhass, Jew-hatred.
In its original meaning, antisemitism meant hostility toward Jewish people.
It did not describe hostility toward Arabic speakers, and it never did.

The International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance's working definition of antisemitism, adopted in 2016, carries 11 attached examples, 7 of which describe criticism of Israel or Zionism as antisemitic under certain conditions.

On 25 March 2021 the Jerusalem Declaration on Antisemitism, signed by more than 200 scholars including Omer Bartov, Christopher Browning, Michael Rothberg and Noah Feldman, kept the core definition but named exceptions: boycott of Israel (BDS), criticism of settlements and criticism of Zionism as an ideology are not antisemitic.
It holds that opposing or criticizing Israel denies Jews their right to national self-determination, and is therefore discriminatory, keeping a charge close to antisemitism without using the word.

The formula appears in pro-Israel commentary, where a 2019 formulation by Bari Weiss is among the most widely cited, in the materials of hasbara (public-diplomacy) organizations, and in critiques of those materials alike.

Dr. Dana Barnett, a researcher at Israel's Begin-Sadat Center for Strategic Studies, and analysts writing for NGO Monitor have argued in print that the Declaration's explicit exceptions do less to clarify than to shelter.

In their reading, permitting comparisons of Israeli policy to settler colonialism or apartheid, and classifying BDS as ordinary non-violent protest, creates cover for anti-Zionist advocacy that can, in specific instances, cross into real antisemitism.

If "Semitic" names a language family and all its speakers, and Palestinians are Semitic-language speakers descended from the region's continuous population, then the conflict cannot be framed as Semites against anti-Semites.
It is a documented political dispute between a state, a political movement, and a displaced population native to the land, all of whom are Semitic in the word's original sense.
It does not show that a given criticism of Israeli policy is legitimate, or that it is not; that depends on what is said and at whom it is aimed.
"Antisemitism": A Word Named by the Haters
It is often said that "anti-Semitism" is a precise term: that the Semites are a people, and that the word names hatred of them.
A Jewish scholar first wrote "antisemitic" in 1860, to attack that race theory.
Then, in 1879, a German agitator who was not Jewish made "antisemitism" the name of his own movement against Jews.

The first step, told in , was a classification of grammar: in 1781 the Göttingen historian August Ludwig von Schlözer coined "Semitic" (semitisch) for a family of languages that today includes Hebrew, Aramaic, Arabic, Amharic, Tigrinya and Maltese.
The French scholar Ernest Renan's comparative history of the Semitic languages, published in 1855, treated their speakers, Hebrews and Arabs alike, as a "Semitic race" inferior to the "Aryans."
Historians now regard "Semitic race" as a discredited category, which is why the word still causes confusion.
The adjective came next, and it came from a Jewish scholar.
In 1860 the bibliographer Moritz Steinschneider wrote of "antisemitic prejudices" (antisemitische Vorurteile) to rebut Renan's claim that Semitic peoples were inferior.
In that first use the target of the prejudice was the whole invented "Semitic race," Hebrews and Arabs alike.
Within twenty years, men who hated Jews in Germany would take the word over and narrow it to one people.
The man most associated with that narrowing was Wilhelm Marr (1819–1904), a German journalist and political agitator.
He was a Lutheran, not a Jew as is sometimes claimed.
In the 1840s he had been involved in radical left politics; later in life he turned to German nationalist and anti-Jewish politics.

In 1879 he published a pamphlet, Der Sieg des Judenthums über das Germanenthum ("The Victory of Judaism over Germandom"), which argued that Jews held a disproportionate and threatening influence over German cultural and economic life.
The same year he founded the League of Antisemites (Antisemiten-Liga), the first German organization devoted to the alleged Jewish threat and one of the first to use the term as a self-description.
It called for forcing Jews out of Germany.
"Antisemitism" was a euphemism for Judenhass, Jew-hatred.

Historians of the period, including Moshe Zimmermann in his biography Wilhelm Marr: The Patriarch of Anti-Semitism (1986), show that Marr borrowed the scientific-sounding "Semitic" from contemporary linguistics to give an old religious and cultural hatred a modern, secular, pseudo-scientific surface, at a time when openly religious Jew-hatred was becoming less acceptable in educated German circles.
If Jews were a foreign "Semitic race," then neither conversion nor centuries of life in Germany could make them German.
Nothing in Marr's own writing, or in the founding activity of his League, shows any concern with Arabic speakers, Ethiopian Christians, Assyrian communities or any other Semitic-language population.
Zimmermann also reports a turn at the end of Marr's life: Marr renounced antisemitism in a text he never published.
Jews had their own name for the hatred, and it said plainly who the target was.
In 1882, after pogroms in the Russian Empire, the Odessa physician Leon Pinsker published Auto-Emancipation.
He called the hatred "Judeophobia": an irrational fear of Jews, which he described as an inherited disease.
Pinsker concluded that Jews needed a homeland of their own, which makes the pamphlet one of the founding texts of Zionism.
The pogroms, the blood libel and the older history of the hatred that Marr renamed are set out in .
In April 2015 the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance recommended writing "antisemitism" without a hyphen.
Its reason was that the hyphen "allows for the possibility of something called Semitism," lending weight to a discredited racial classification.
Style guides followed, and The New York Times dropped the hyphen in 2021.
The root is a misnomer: "Semitic" describes languages, Palestinians who speak Arabic are as Semitic as anyone, and many Jews have never spoken a Semitic language at home.
And the meaning is settled by use: since the 1880s "antisemitism" has meant hostility to Jews, and nothing broader.
The claim "Arabs are Semites too, so I cannot be antisemitic" does not hold, because words mean what they are used to mean, not what their parts suggest.
Knowing that Marr chose the word to dignify Jew-hatred does not make criticism of Israeli state policy automatically legitimate, and it does not make such criticism automatically illegitimate.
The Word as a Shield
Hatred of Jewish people is antisemitism, and nothing in this book says otherwise.
A question about what a government does is a question about a government, whether the government is Canada's, Mexico's or Israel's.
The difficulty is that a widely repeated claim, that questioning Israel is itself antisemitic, merges these two things.
The meaning of the word has not changed: antisemitism means hatred of Jews.

This section sets out the definitions in competition, the definition's own drafter's warning, the path by which a guideline became law, and what is also true on the other side: antisemitism is real, and in the United States it stands at a record level.
The most widely cited definition is the working definition of the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA), adopted in 2016.
Beyond its core sentence, it attaches eleven examples, and seven of them concern Israel.

Among them are "denying the Jewish people their right to self-determination, e.g., by claiming that the existence of a State of Israel is a racist endeavor," applying double standards to Israel, and comparing Israeli policy to that of the Nazis.
The definition was adopted by the United States government and, as of August 2024, by 35 states and the District of Columbia.
Its own text says that criticism of Israel similar to that leveled against any other country cannot be regarded as antisemitic.
That is the standard the definition sets for itself: the questions a person may ask of Canada or Mexico may be asked of Israel.
What is disputed is the territory the attached examples cover, the point at which criticism of Israel crosses into hostility to Jews.

Some hostility to Jews does express itself through talk about Israel: holding Jews collectively responsible for a state, singling Israel out by standards applied to no other country, or comparing Jews to their Nazi persecutors.
And on this view the main alternative goes too far the other way: Britain's Community Security Trust argues that the Jerusalem Declaration legitimizes calls for Israel's elimination.

That alternative, the Jerusalem Declaration on Antisemitism, was presented in March 2021 by scholars working with the Van Leer Jerusalem Institute and signed by more than 200 scholars of Jewish history and the Holocaust.
Its signatories and drafters are specialists in antisemitism, in Holocaust and genocide studies, and in Jewish history.

By its own framing they are not activists opposed to fighting antisemitism, but scholars who judged that IHRA's examples conflate two distinct things: hatred of Jews, and disagreement with a state's policies or the ideology behind it.
Its definition of antisemitism, discrimination, prejudice, hostility or violence against Jews as Jews, or against Jewish institutions as Jewish, is close in spirit to IHRA's core sentence.

Guideline 5 states that opposing Zionism as a form of nationalism, or arguing for constitutional arrangements other than a Jewish-majority state for everyone between the Jordan River and the Mediterranean (a binational state, a unitary democratic state, a federal state or a confederation), is not, on the face of it, antisemitic.
The Declaration treats Zionism as one variety of national ideology, and holds that criticizing or opposing it does not on its own constitute antisemitism.
But it also lists examples of speech about Israel that are antisemitic.
The Declaration has its own critics, who argue that it understates the antisemitism present in some anti-Zionist discourse.
Further named critics are set out in the section on "Semitic."
Between the two documents sits a third, the Nexus Document, produced by a task force linked to the University of Southern California and Bard College, which takes an intermediate position.
The question "is anti-Zionism antisemitism?" therefore has no single answer, because the three definitions give three different answers.
Kenneth Stern was the American Jewish Committee's expert on antisemitism and the definition's lead drafter.
In December 2019 he published an op-ed in the Guardian under the headline "I drafted the definition of antisemitism.

Rightwing Jews are weaponizing it," calling the executive order that applied the definition to campuses an attack on academic freedom that would harm pro-Palestinian advocates and Jewish students alike.
In 2024 he told NPR that weaponizing the definition makes students less safe.
Americans for Peace Now makes a parallel argument: that IHRA chills speech by treating anti-Zionist views as antisemitic.
The executive order Stern objected to marked the definition's move from guideline into law.
In December 2019 it directed federal agencies, including the Education Department's civil rights office, to consider the definition when enforcing Title VI of the Civil Rights Act.

sent: By August 2024, 35 states and the District of Columbia had adopted the definition in some form.

On 1 May 2024 the House of Representatives passed the Antisemitism Awareness Act, which would write the definition into federal civil rights enforcement, by 320 votes to 91, with members of both parties voting no.
The American Civil Liberties Union urged a no vote, warning that the bill would likely chill student speech by wrongly equating criticism of the Israeli government with antisemitism.

the bill is not law, and its Senate version, S.558, stalled in committee in 2025.
In July 2024, after an advocacy campaign, Meta began treating the word "Zionist" as a stand-in for Jews in narrowly defined hate-speech cases.

The argument against it is that the mechanism it applies, treating the name of a political ideology as a proxy for a protected ethnic or religious identity, is exactly the conflation the Jerusalem Declaration had been written three years earlier to name and reject.
The stated objective of Cotler-Wunsh, one of those who pressed for the change, was protected-characteristic status for Zionism: the precise claim the Declaration's Guideline 5 runs against.
The full record of the Meta decision, including who pressed for it and who objected, is in .
In 2025 Columbia University lost $400 million in federal funding within four days of a notice from a federal task force, and about 60 more universities received warning letters.
Five days after that notice Mahmoud Khalil, a recent Columbia graduate who had negotiated on behalf of the campus protesters, was detained for deportation.

Each case has its own record, and that record includes real failures at Columbia: federal investigators found that the university had no reporting system until the summer of 2024, and that swastika vandalism had gone uninvestigated.
This is the chilling effect that the ACLU and the definition's own drafter warned about.
The Anti-Defamation League counted 9,354 antisemitic incidents in the United States in 2024, the most since it began counting in 1979, with incidents on campuses up 84 percent.
Some speech that calls itself anti-Zionist does cross into hatred of Jews, and even the Jerusalem Declaration, written to defend criticism of Israel, lists examples of it.
At the same time, many of the strongest critics of Israeli policy are themselves Jewish.
Misusing the charge and ignoring real antisemitism both do damage, to Jews and to everyone asking honest questions.

Jewish organizations such as Jewish Voice for Peace campaign for Palestinian rights;  Orthodox anti-Zionist traditions predate the state; and Israeli human-rights groups such as B'Tselem document the occupation.
The first: is the speech aimed at Jewish people, or at what a government does?
If it concerns a government's actions, and the same would be said of Canada or Mexico, it is a political question, and asking it is not hatred.
If it concerns Jews as a people, holds them responsible for a state, or recycles old tropes, it is antisemitism, whatever it calls itself.

The record does not decide which of the three definitions is correct; that is a live dispute among credentialed scholars, and the answer to "is anti-Zionism antisemitic?" depends on which one is adopted.
Whether the Antisemitism Awareness Act, or a successor, will become law is open as of October 2026.
And the sources used here do not record how Mahmoud Khalil's case was resolved.
The Jewish Lineages: Ashkenazi, Sephardi, Mizrahi
No one seriously disputes that Ashkenazi Jews are Jewish.
The first holds that Ashkenazi Jews descend from Central Asian Khazar converts and carry no real Middle Eastern ancestry, and therefore no ancestral connection to the land.

The second, less often stated but just as often assumed, treats all Jewish communities as genetically and historically identical, as if two thousand years spent in different countries had left no trace.
The word "Semitic" already names a family larger than any one people.

The genealogy of Genesis 10, 11 and 25 runs from Shem through many generations to Abraham, and then divides: Ishmael, traditionally associated with Arab peoples, and, through Isaac, both Esau, traditionally associated with Edom, and Jacob, later renamed Israel.
By the text's own family tree, Jacob's line is one branch of Shem's descendants, not the whole of it, a point taken up with the history of the word itself in .
The same structure, a shared category holding real internal variety, applies to the Jewish communities themselves.
Three broad lineages make up most of world Jewry.
Mizrahi Jews, the Jewish communities of Iraq, Yemen, Egypt, Iran, Syria and elsewhere, never left the Middle East.
Their presence there goes back millennia; in Iraq it is traced to the Babylonian Exile of 586 BCE, and as late as 1945 Baghdad alone held roughly 140,000 Jews, about a third of the city.
The Jews of Iran, one of the oldest of these communities, are treated in their own chapter of this library, .
Sephardi Jews trace to Iberia, Spain and Portugal, where their roots predate the Muslim conquest.

Ferdinand and Isabella expelled them in 1492, and most resettled across the Ottoman Empire and North Africa, regions that already held related Middle Eastern Jewish populations; Salonika became a majority-Sephardic city for centuries under Ottoman rule.
Ashkenazi communities formed in the Rhineland, in Central Europe, in the early medieval period, and later moved east into Poland, Lithuania, Russia and Ukraine.
By the nineteenth century Ashkenazi Jews were the demographic majority of world Jewry, and they produced most of the Jewish immigration to the United States.
The question of what each community carries in its genes is a separate one, and it was answered most thoroughly by a study published in Nature in 2010.

Behar, Yunusbayev, Metspalu and eighteen co-authors compared genome-wide data from 14 Jewish communities spanning Europe, the Middle East, North Africa and Central Asia against 69 non-Jewish populations.

Its core finding was that most of the Jewish populations examined, Ashkenazi, Sephardi and North African among them, cluster together genetically and share their closest non-Jewish relationships with Middle Eastern populations, more so than with the European or other populations among whom they lived.
The authors' own framing was that the data support common origins in the Middle East, followed by migrations into the diaspora.
The Jewish samples divided into three groups: an Ashkenazi, North African and Sephardi cluster; a Caucasus and Middle Eastern cluster; and a distinct Yemenite cluster.
The result is therefore not that every Jewish community is genetically identical.
The Khazar hypothesis is a different claim, and it deserves to be stated precisely before it is tested.
The Khazars were a Turkic people of the Caucasus and southern Russia whose ruling elite, according to the historical record, converted to Judaism around the eighth or ninth century CE.
As a fact about one medieval kingdom's ruling class, that conversion is a real and separately documented event.
The hypothesis takes it much further: it proposes that the Ashkenazi population as a whole descends substantially from the Khazars rather than from the ancient Levant.
In its modern scientific form the claim was argued in a 2012 paper by the geneticist Eran Elhaik in Genome Biology and Evolution, which proposed a Khazar component in European Jewish ancestry.
Critics faulted the paper for its method: Elhaik used modern Armenians and Georgians as proxies for the Khazars.

Behar and colleagues, more than twenty co-authors in all, published a study in Human Biology that analyzed 1,774 samples from 106 Jewish and non-Jewish populations, including populations native to the region of the former Khazar Khaganate.
They found no particular similarity between Ashkenazi Jews and the populations of the Caucasus, and in their own words "no indication" of a Khazar genetic contribution.
Ashkenazi ancestry, they concluded, derives primarily from the Middle East and Europe.
Genome-wide and ancient-DNA studies since then have modeled Ashkenazi Jews as a mixture of Levantine and European ancestry.
How large each share is remains open; one researcher, cited in a published fact-check, puts the Middle Eastern share at between 15 and 50 percent.
What is European in Ashkenazi ancestry is real, documented and partial.
The European contribution is substantial, and it shows most clearly on the maternal line, reflecting some two thousand years of intermarriage and conversion within European societies.

The same studies document a shared ancient Levantine origin on the paternal line, and the two findings sit side by side: the European layer is part of the history, not a replacement for the older one.
The Khazar theory is addressed directly here because of what it has been used to do.

Since the nineteenth century it has served antisemitic arguments that portray Jews as alien impostors with no genuine connection to the Land of Israel, and so as not "really" Jewish or Semitic at all.
Viral claims built on it continue to appear and continue to fail.

One widely shared post asserted that a study had proved 97.5 percent of Israeli Jews have no ties to the land; fact-checkers rated it false, noting that the study in question included no Israeli Jews.
The finding that the Ashkenazi population as a whole is not primarily of Khazar descent does not deny that the Khazar elite converted, and it does not settle every question about European admixture.

On 19 and 20 February, Tucker Carlson interviewed the United States Ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, and asked: "Why don't we do genetic testing on everybody in the land and find out who Abram's descendants are?
He went on to single out Netanyahu, citing his family's Polish origin.
Huckabee, a committed Christian Zionist rather than a reflexive critic, pushed back in the room, calling the idea a "dangerous conspiracy theory" from "some of the darkest realms of the internet."

Reporters at JTA, the Times of Israel, the Jerusalem Post and the Forward identified the underlying claim as the Khazar theory: the premise that Eastern European ancestry among some Israeli Jews would undo their connection to the land.
Ancestry percentages have never been the legal or historical basis on which such claims rest: treaties, borders and citizenship laws do not run on DNA, for Israel or for any other state.
Many people are taught that "Jewish" and "Semitic" are simple synonyms, and few are taught that Jewish identity itself contains several lineages with different histories.
A Salvadoran, a Mexican and a Peruvian are all Latino, while each carries a different mix of Indigenous American, Spanish colonial and other ancestry, varying by country and family.
In the same structural sense, Mizrahi Jews carry concentrated, continuous Levantine ancestry, and Ashkenazi Jews carry that same documented root together with substantial European admixture.
The comparison borrows one idea, that a shared category can hold real internal variety, and nothing more; Jewish and Latino identities have entirely different histories, religious and genetic.
The Beta Israel of Ethiopia show that the question of who counts as a Jew has also been settled, in practice, by institutions rather than by genes.
The Beta Israel, the "House of Israel," lived for centuries in the Gondar and Tigray regions of northern Ethiopia and practiced a Judaism distinct from rabbinic tradition.
The familiar account holds that Israel always welcomed them as Jews.
