Their status was disputed by Israel's religious authorities until 1973, when the Sephardi Chief Rabbi, Ovadia Yosef, ruled that they were Jews.
The government applied the Law of Return to them in 1975, which made them eligible to immigrate.
By the end of 2019 about 155,300 Ethiopian Jews lived in Israel.

A religious ruling by one chief rabbi opened the door; a government decision under the Law of Return turned that ruling into a right to immigrate; and the chief rabbinate still imposed a further condition of its own twelve years after the ruling.
The terms of the Law of Return itself are set out in .
Genetics does not determine anyone's political rights, Jewish, Palestinian or any other.
Claims about the ancestry of Jews or of Palestinians add nothing to it, and in the Khazar case they are also false.
The size and timing of particular admixture events in Ashkenazi ancestry are still being refined, and estimates of the Middle Eastern share vary widely.
The genetic studies measure ancestry; they do not decide identity, which in the case of the Beta Israel was decided by a rabbinic ruling and a government decision.

What is settled is that the Jewish lineages share a detectable Middle Eastern origin, that each also carries its own regional history, and that the claim of wholesale Khazar descent was tested and did not hold.
A common account of Jewish opinion about Zionism runs in one of two directions.
In the first, Jewish opposition to the Zionist project is a small and marginal position, held by a handful of eccentrics.
In the second, it belongs to one particular community, usually imagined as the Jews of the Middle East set against the Jews of Europe.

Organized opposition to political Zionism, and organized critique of the state it produced, appears on the record in Ashkenazi religious tradition, in Ashkenazi secular socialism, in Ashkenazi-founded Reform theology, among the cultural Zionists who rejected partition, and in the scholarship of Mizrahi Jews living inside Israel itself.
The earlier section on  set out the distinction between a political movement founded at Basel in 1897 and a religion far older than it.
Some rejected the Zionist project outright.
Some accepted a Jewish national life in Palestine but rejected a Jewish sovereign state and partition.
One critiques the state's treatment of its own Jewish citizens.
Folding all of these into a single category called "Jewish opposition to Zionism" would flatten a real spectrum, and the record is clearer when they are kept apart.
The first is the Bund, whose founding in Vilna in 1897 the previous section described.
It organized Jewish workers across the Russian Empire's Pale of Settlement, the region of the 1880s pogroms and the mass emigration that followed them.

It was an overwhelmingly Ashkenazi, Eastern European, socialist movement, and it explicitly rejected emigration to Palestine in favor of Jewish cultural and political autonomy where Jewish communities already lived .
Its position was not indifference to antisemitism: its members lived through the same pogroms that gave the Zionist movement its urgency.
The Bund was a serious, organized mass movement, not a fringe dissent.
When the Bolsheviks took power in October 1917, the Bund split.
A majority faction, believing it was joining a genuine ally on workers' rights, merged into the Communist Party.
A minority led by Vladimir Medem rejected Bolshevik rule as undemocratic and hostile to Jewish national rights.
Bundists disagreed among themselves over whether the Bolsheviks could be trusted, and decided the question differently.
In 1921 the Bolsheviks formally dissolved the Bund, merger or no merger.
Its remaining members were imprisoned or fled abroad, under a government now hostile to independent Jewish political organizing of any kind, socialist or not.
Mark Liber, one of the Bund's leading figures and its representative on the Executive Committee of the Petrograd Soviet during the revolution itself, was executed during the Stalinist purges in 1937.
The Polish Bund took a different path.
It survived independently through the interwar years and into the Holocaust, and its members fought alongside Zionists and Communists in the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising.
Survivors tried to regroup in Poland after the war and were suppressed again, this time by Poland's new Communist government.
It does not show that the Bund's argument against Zionism was refuted by it.

Its Pittsburgh Platform of 1885, quoted in the previous section, defined Jewish identity as a religious community rather than a nation awaiting territorial restoration, and the movement that adopted it was founded and led by Ashkenazi Jewish immigrants and their American-born successors .
Coming twelve years before Basel, it was not a reaction against Zionism but a Jewish religious position that existed first, on its own terms.
It was also not permanent: Reform's institutional position shifted considerably over the twentieth century.
Neturei Karta is today the most publicly visible Haredi Jewish community that opposes Zionism, and it is Ashkenazi in origin and practice.
Rabbi Joel Teitelbaum, the Satmar Rebbe, set out the argument in VaYoel Moshe in 1958.

In this reading, Jewish tradition holds that the ingathering of the exiles and the restoration of sovereignty are to come through divine action in the Messianic era, not through human political and military effort beforehand.
The rabbinic sources behind it, the Three Oaths of the Talmud, have their own history in .
ents: the Three Oaths of the Talmud

sent: It takes the scriptural promises of restoration seriously enough to conclude that a state built by human political action violates them, the opposite of what many outsiders assume religious Jews believe.
Neturei Karta continues to hold it as a current practice and appears at public demonstrations .
The record is equally clear about its scale: Neturei Karta is a specific and relatively small community, and most Haredi and Orthodox institutions today hold other positions.
What is documented is that a serious, theologically grounded opposition from within Orthodox tradition exists and is active, not that it speaks for Orthodox Judaism as a whole.
Martin Buber and Judah Magnes, with colleagues including Gershom Scholem and Henrietta Szold, founded Brit Shalom in 1925.
It advocated a binational state with full civic equality between Jews and Arabs, rather than a Jewish-majority sovereign state  .
Brit Shalom was never a mass movement.
It drew fierce, documented hostility from the dominant Labor and Revisionist Zionist currents, some of whose members called its members traitors.
It also had notable public support: Albert Einstein backed it publicly, a fact seldom mentioned alongside his name.
Brit Shalom dissolved around 1933, roughly eight years after its founding  .
The violence at Hebron in 1929 and the Arab Revolt of 1936–39 undermined Brit Shalom's founding premise, that the Arab political leadership would accept binational equality.
In 1942 Buber and Magnes founded Ihud as a direct response to the Biltmore Conference's demand for a Jewish Commonwealth, again advocating a binational state with full civic equality .
In 1947 the two men testified in person against partition before the United Nations Special Committee on Palestine (UNSCOP), to David Ben-Gurion's documented fury.

Buber told the commission that it was "ethically and politically incumbent" on a regenerated Jewish people to live not merely alongside the Arabs but genuinely with them, developing the country for equal benefit.
He called the treatment of the Arab population "the moral acid test of Zionism"  .
Hannah Arendt reached a related conclusion separately, from outside the Brit Shalom circle.

Her 1944 essay "Zionism Reconsidered" warned that pursuing an exclusively Jewish sovereign state, rather than a binational arrangement, risked permanent regional conflict and long-term dependence on a great-power patron for security.
The founding of Israel in May 1948 made binationalism moot, and Magnes's position changed with events.
He began advocating a confederation between the new Jewish state and a future Palestinian Arab state, a documented development in his thinking cut short by his death that October.
The following year Buber wrote that "our cause has lost its footing, its face has been sullied, but it has not been overcome."
Its publication, Ner, continued until 1964, sixteen years after the state it had argued against creating in that form already existed  .
Buber and Magnes are best described as cultural and binational Zionists who rejected the model of sovereignty and partition, not as anti-Zionists in the sense of the Bund or Neturei Karta.
It shows that the argument was never only between Zionists and their opponents, but also among Zionists over what form Jewish national life in Palestine should take.
The Bund, Reform Judaism and Neturei Karta argued, in their different ways, against the Zionist project itself, before the state existed or regardless of it.
The Mizrahi critique comes from people who did move to Israel, live there and are its citizens.

Scholars including Ella Shohat, Sami Shalom Chetrit and Yehouda Shenhav documented specific patterns in how the Ashkenazi-dominated Israeli establishment treated Mizrahi Jewish immigrants after 1948: placement in peripheral development towns, discrimination in employment, and the cultural marginalization of Middle Eastern Jewish identity in favor of an Ashkenazi-coded national culture .
This is a Middle Eastern-lineage critique of the state's conduct, running alongside the Ashkenazi traditions rather than standing in for them.
It does not show that all Mizrahi Israelis share it, or that Mizrahi communities are anti-Zionist as a whole.
Many Mizrahi Israelis identify strongly with the state.
Reform's platform of 1885 and Teitelbaum's book of 1958 stand 73 years apart, and none of these currents waited for the others to reach the same conclusion.
The historical traditions say nothing about how many Jews hold any view today.
For that, the evidence is polling, and the most detailed recent survey is of American Jews only.
The Washington Post surveyed 815 American Jews between 2 and 9 September 2025, with a margin of error of 4.7 points.
Sixty-one percent said Israel had committed war crimes against Palestinians .
Thirty-nine percent said Israel had committed genocide and 51% said it had not; among respondents aged 18 to 34, half said genocide .
Forty-six percent approved of Israel's military conduct and 48% disapproved, and 68% disapproved of Benjamin Netanyahu.
Seventy-six percent said Israel's existence is vital to the Jewish future, 94% said Hamas had committed war crimes, and 91% blamed Hamas for prolonging the war .
For comparison, in February 2024 Pew had found that 62% of American Jews said Israel's conduct was acceptable.
Jewish Federations data show that about 90% of American Jews support Israel's existence as a Jewish and democratic state, while only 37% call themselves "Zionist" .

Organized opinion spans a wide range: J Street, pro-Israel and pro-two-state; Jewish Voice for Peace, which is anti-Zionist; and Haredi groups such as Neturei Karta, which oppose a Jewish state on religious grounds .
Most American Jews are attached to Israel and critical of the war at the same time.
Neturei Karta is a small community.
Brit Shalom was a study circle that lasted about eight years, and Ihud never grew into a mass constituency.
Many Mizrahi Israelis identify strongly with the state.
In the 2025 poll, three in four American Jews called Israel vital to the Jewish future, and about nine in ten support its existence as a Jewish and democratic state.
On this reading the dissenters were real, but the main current of Jewish life moved the other way.
The Bund was a mass movement, not a fringe, and it ended because two governments crushed it, not because its members changed their minds.
The binationalists came from the intellectual center of Zionism itself and testified against partition before the United Nations in 1947.
And the gap between the roughly 90% who support Israel's existence and the 37% who call themselves Zionist suggests that the word and the attachment are not the same thing for many American Jews.
Some of the earliest, most organized and most theologically serious Jewish opposition to Zionism was Ashkenazi, and one of the most developed critiques of the Israeli state's conduct was Mizrahi.
To frame opposition as something only Middle Eastern Jews do, while European Jews uniformly support Zionism, would invert the evidence.
The line runs through every lineage, between those who hold the specific political position of Zionism and those who contest or reject it.
It contains no current polling on what share of Ashkenazi, Sephardi or Mizrahi Jews support or oppose Zionism, and it cannot say how any lineage divides today.
It documents no distinctly Sephardi tradition of dissent alongside the Ashkenazi and Mizrahi ones.
The detailed polling is of American Jews alone, and it measures views of Israel's conduct in a war, which is not the same question as support for Zionism.
The record establishes something narrower and firmer: that support and opposition have both had serious, long-standing representation within Jewish life, across every lineage it documents.
Zionism and Judaism: A Movement and a Religion
Judaism is a religion and a set of ethnic and cultural lineages thousands of years old.
Zionism is a political movement.

Its ideas were argued from the 1840s, but as an organized movement it has a place and a date of birth: Basel, Switzerland, in August 1897, convened by Theodor Herzl, a secular journalist from Vienna .

The line between the religion and the movement was drawn by Jews themselves: by the movement's founder in his own diary, by the largest American Jewish denomination twelve years before the movement existed, by a mass Jewish labor party founded the same year, by a cultural Zionist who warned against the political version, and by the largest Hasidic dynasty in the world, which still teaches its position today.
Many Jews, religious and secular, have understood and still understand their support for Zionism as part of their Jewish identity, and nothing in this record shows them wrong to do so.
It was argued inside Jewish life from the start.
Herzl's founding.
Herzl was not a rabbi or a religious scholar.

He was an assimilated Viennese Jew, secular in outlook, a correspondent for the Neue Freie Presse, whose turn to politics was a response to the antisemitism he witnessed while covering the Dreyfus Affair.
He set out his program in Der Judenstaat in 1896 and convened the First Zionist Congress in Basel from 29 to 31 August 1897  .
Afterward he wrote in his diary: "At Basel I founded the Jewish State."
The verb was his, written privately rather than for public consumption, and on this reading it describes a beginning: a political project that had not existed as such before Basel .
Herzl gave serious consideration to Argentina and to Uganda as candidate territories before Palestine was settled on .
At its founding, political Zionism treated location as an open, practical question rather than a foregone theological conclusion.
And it does not mean that Palestine was arbitrary to the movement's members, only that its founder weighed alternatives in writing.
The rabbinic argument over whether Jews may return to the land by political means at all is a separate and older debate, told elsewhere in this library , and the Congress itself has its own section .
Twelve years before Basel, in November 1885, American Reform Judaism adopted the Pittsburgh Platform.

We consider ourselves no longer a nation, but a religious community, and therefore expect neither a return to Palestine, nor a sacrificial worship under the sons of Aaron, nor the restoration of any of the laws concerning the Jewish state.
This was not a reply to Zionism, which did not yet exist as an organized movement.

It was an independent religious position, adopted publicly as the founding statement of what was then the largest Jewish denomination in America, that already disagreed with what would be proposed more than a decade later .
It is difficult to reconcile with the simpler story in which Judaism naturally wanted a return to Zion and Zionism merely organized that existing desire.

The platform remained mainstream American Reform's position for over half a century, until the Columbus Platform of 1937 softened it, and substantial Reform opposition to political Zionism continued after that.
On this evidence, American Jewish institutional support for the political Zionist state is a development of the period after the Holocaust, not an ancient religious commitment .
To declare that "we consider ourselves no longer a nation" is to acknowledge that the idea of Jewish nationhood had been there to set aside.
On that reading, the question that divided the 1880s and 1890s was less whether Jews were a people than what that peoplehood required.
Ahad Ha'am, 1891.
That question was argued most sharply from inside the Zionist camp.
Asher Zvi Hirsch Ginsberg (1856–1927), who wrote as Ahad Ha'am, "One of the People," was a committed Zionist in the cultural sense: he wanted a Jewish spiritual and cultural center in Palestine .
In 1891, six years before Basel, he published "Truth from Eretz Israel," a firsthand report on the country.
"We are used to believing abroad that Palestine is nowadays almost totally desolate," he wrote, "but in fact this is not the case.
He recorded the existing Arab population and warned that a political approach that did not account for it would produce conflict.
His opposition was to the political, state-building version of Zionism that Herzl went on to champion, and to its handling of the people already there, not to Jewish attachment to the land.
The Bund, October 1897.
Two months after Basel, in Vilna, Jewish workers founded the Algemeyner Yidisher Arbeter Bund, the General Jewish Labor Bund in Lithuania, Poland and Russia .
It organized across the Russian Pale of Settlement on socialist and Yiddishist lines and rejected the Zionist proposal of national return to Palestine.

Its watchword was doikayt, "hereness": Jewish cultural and political life was to be built where Jews already lived, with Yiddish as its vernacular and national-cultural autonomy inside the existing states as its goal.
The Bund, too, spoke of Jews as a nation.
It disagreed with the Zionists about where that nation's future lay.
The Bund was not a debating society.

The historian Henry Tobias, in The Jewish Bund in Russia: From Its Origins to 1905, documents it as a genuine mass movement with real weight in the wider Russian and Polish socialist and labor movements; for a significant stretch of the early twentieth century, more organized Jewish political energy in Eastern Europe ran through the Bund than through the Zionist movement .

One account gives a membership of more than 400,000 across the Russian Empire by 1917, larger than the Zionist movement in Eastern Europe and the largest Jewish political organization in the Empire in the decade before the Balfour Declaration; another describes it in the early twentieth century as having tens of thousands of members .
Its eclipse came from outside, not from losing an open argument with Zionism.

Its membership and infrastructure were devastated by the Holocaust, and its remaining structures in the Soviet sphere were suppressed as Stalin moved against independent Jewish political organizations .
Most of its members, or their children, died in the Holocaust before the State of Israel was declared; their opposition to Zionism did not save them.
The earlier fate of the Bund in Soviet Russia, dissolved by its Bolshevik allies, is told in the next section .
What the Bund's existence settles is specific.
It does not show that the Bund's position was the authentic Jewish position any more than Zionism's was; both were real, competing currents in Jewish political life.

It does show that equating "Jewish" with "Zionist" was contested by Jews, at scale, from the movement's first year, and it means the record cannot support the statement that "the Jewish people wanted Israel" as a description of that era.
Satmar, 1958.
The religious case against political Zionism received its most substantial modern statement ten years after the state was founded.
In 1958 Rabbi Joel Teitelbaum, the Satmar Rebbe, published VaYoel Moshe, the central Haredi (ultra-Orthodox) theological argument against political Zionism .

It rests on the Three Oaths of the Babylonian Talmud, tractate Ketubot 111a, a rabbinic tradition holding that the Jewish people swore not to reclaim the land by force or rebel against the nations before the messianic era.
ents: the Three Oaths of the Babylonian Talmud

sent: In this reading, a state established by human political and military effort is not the fulfillment of Jewish religious hope but a violation of a specific religious commitment.
Satmar numbers roughly 130,000 people in the United States alone, concentrated in Williamsburg, Kiryas Joel and Monsey, with further communities in Israel, London, Antwerp and Montreal.
It is the largest single Hasidic dynasty in the world, and it still teaches this position .
It is not the majority position of Orthodox or Haredi Judaism in general, and it should not be generalized into one.
Read fairly, these documents also contain the materials of the Zionist argument.

Jewish peoplehood was not a Zionist invention: the Bund organized Jews as a nation seeking cultural autonomy, the Reform rabbis of 1885 had to declare that they were "no longer a nation," and Ahad Ha'am, whose quarrel was with Herzl's methods, still placed the Jewish cultural center in Palestine.
Satmar's objection is to the timing and the means of a return.
And Herzl's turn to politics was a response to antisemitism he witnessed at first hand.

On this reading, Zionism was one answer among several to a question that Jews widely shared, and one that drew religious and secular support from its early years; in America, the institutional support it later won came after the Holocaust.
What the record contradicts is the stronger claim that Zionism and Judaism are the same thing, so that the one cannot be opposed without opposing the other.

The line between a political movement founded in 1897 and a religion and set of lineages far older is one that the founders themselves recognized, that Reform recorded in 1885, that the Bund built a mass movement on in 1897, and that Satmar still teaches in 2026    .
It continues in contemporary Jewish life in Judith Butler's Parting Ways, in Peter Beinart's The Crisis of Zionism and in the organization Jewish Voice for Peace   .
That conversion is the slide the section on the word "Semitic" first examines.
The Jewish critique of Zionism is not an attack from outside; it is a Jewish tradition older than the state.
One argument this book offers takes Herzl's alternatives as a thought experiment.
Had the state been built in Uganda or Argentina, could criticism of it plausibly have been called "antisemitic"?
The historically dominant local languages of Uganda are Bantu languages, Luganda among them; Argentina's are Spanish and Indigenous American languages such as Quechua, Guaraní and Mapudungun.
Neither population speaks a Semitic language.
Palestine's population spoke Arabic, which is one   .

Since "Semitic" was coined in 1781 as a term for a language family that includes Hebrew, Arabic and Amharic together, and was never a synonym for "Jewish," the argument holds that the conflation is no more valid in Palestine than it would have been anywhere else; it simply found a surface hook there, through a coincidence of geography.
Nor does it address whether some criticism of Israeli policy is antisemitic in the settled sense of the word, which is hostility to Jews and which the following sections treat on its own terms.

The correct point that Palestinians speak a Semitic language, and share substantial ancestral overlap with Levantine Jewish populations according to the genetic studies of Nebel (2000) and Behar (2010), is often deployed to argue that criticism of Israeli policy cannot coherently be called antisemitic  .

But the same breadth of the word rarely appears when the subject is the displacement of some 700,000 to 750,000 Palestinians in 1948, or the conditions in Gaza documented later in this library, including a formally confirmed famine.
The argument does not propose that "antisemitism" be applied to harm done to Palestinians.
Its position is that the word has always meant hatred of Jews specifically and never fit that harm in either direction.
Its point is that Palestinian displacement and casualties are documented on their own terms and deserve the same seriousness, whichever way the "Semitic" argument is being pointed.
They do not show that any one of these positions was the authentic Jewish one, or how Jews outside these organizations and platforms would have answered the national question.

The sources differ on the Bund's size, and the record does not show how the Bund and the Zionist movement would have fared against each other had the Holocaust and Soviet repression not destroyed one of them.
Reform's 1885 position shows where a major denomination stood in that year, not where it stands now.
And the existence of a Jewish tradition of dissent does not show that Zionism's supporters are wrong to experience their support as Jewish.
Most people who see the flag of Israel take its six-pointed star to be the ancient sign of the Jewish people, carried onto the flag as it has always been.
Two symbols have a claim to represent Jewish tradition, and they are of very different ages.
The older one, the seven-branched lampstand called the menorah, reaches back to the Temple.
The younger one, the six-pointed star called the Magen David, or Shield of David, became a distinctively Jewish emblem in the Middle Ages.
That choice was made by a political congress in 1897 and confirmed by the new state in 1948, and both decisions are on the record.
Exodus 25:31–40 describes it as the lampstand of the Tabernacle, the portable sanctuary of the wilderness narrative; it later stood in the Temple in Jerusalem.
It is the oldest continuous Jewish symbol.
Its oldest visual record is in stone, in Rome: the Arch of Titus, completed in 81 CE, shows the lampstand carried off in the sack of the Second Temple.
The image that survives is a Roman one, carved to record the sack of the Temple that had housed the lampstand.
As a shape it is old and widespread, appearing in Hindu and Mayan settings and in decorative art across many centuries, in contexts that have nothing to do with Judaism.
As a distinctively Jewish symbol it is medieval, not ancient, and it is absent from the Jewish iconography of antiquity.
Its first documented official Jewish use comes from fourteenth-century Prague.
The sources describe that use in two ways: as the seal of Prague's Jewish community, and as a flag.
In 1354, the Holy Roman Emperor Charles IV granted the Jewish community of Prague the right to bear its own flag, red with a yellow Star of David.
Even then the star was not yet the Jewish symbol.
It carried Kabbalistic associations in some traditions, but it did not become widely recognized as the Jewish symbol until the modern period.
The spread came between the seventeenth and nineteenth centuries, driven by European Jewish communities that wanted a graphic emblem to stand alongside the Christian cross and the Islamic crescent.

The standard scholarly account is Gershom Scholem's 1949 monograph, Magen David: The History of a Symbol, which documents the specifically modern, and specifically Zionist, role in fixing the hexagram as the Jewish symbol.
On that account, a Jew asked before the seventeenth century to name the symbol of the Jewish people would have pointed to the menorah, not the star.
By the late nineteenth century the star was spreading across Ashkenazi Europe as a practical emblem, a modern graphic answer to a modern need rather than a recovered ancient sign.
Theodor Herzl himself, according to several historians, called it around this time a "meaningless symbol of Judaism."
The flag itself began before the state, and before the Zionist Congress.
In 1885 David Wolffsohn created a blue-and-white banner with a central Magen David for the Bnei Zion association in Boston, taking its colors from the tallit, the Jewish prayer shawl.
When the First Zionist Congress met in Basel in August 1897, Wolffsohn is credited with proposing that this design serve as the movement's banner.
Herzl's own Der Judenstaat, published the year before, had proposed a white flag with seven gold stars, standing for a seven-hour working day.
Herzl's idea never gained traction.
What flew in the Congress hall was the Wolffsohn design: two horizontal blue stripes on white, with a blue Magen David between them.
Wolffsohn later succeeded Herzl as president of the World Zionist Organization.

It was "available" for a secular political project: the movement needed a Jewish symbol, but one that did not tie its politics to rabbinic authority, and the star fit where the Temple's lampstand would not have.
By the 1890s the Magen David had become the closest thing to a widely recognized, non-sectarian Jewish emblem, and the Zionist movement drew members from many religious and secular backgrounds.
In the weeks that followed, the Provisional Council of State had to adopt a flag as a matter of administrative necessity.
The Basel banner, by then fifty-one years old and already the recognized symbol of the Zionist movement worldwide, was the obvious default.
Before simply taking over the movement's flag, the Provisional Council tried to create a distinct state flag.

Its stated reason was a concern about Jews abroad: Diaspora communities already flew the Zionist flag at their own events, and officials worried that once the same banner became a foreign state's official flag, those communities would face accusations of dual loyalty.
A government-preferred alternative, a seven-stars design by Otto Wassisch, was considered and rejected.
In July 1948 the Foreign Minister, Moshe Sharett, cabled Jewish leaders across the Diaspora to ask their view.
The answer came back overwhelmingly in favor of keeping the existing Zionist flag rather than adopting a new one.
It became the state's emblem, placed on the state seal by the Provisional Council of State in 1949, a year after the flag decision.

The winning design, by the Shamir brothers, was sent back for revision twice: once to add the word "Israel," and once to replace their own modern rendering of the menorah with the specific historical version carved on the Arch of Titus.
The emblem was made, in the end, to copy the lampstand as Rome had recorded it in 81 CE.
Nearly 1,300 years separate the menorah's oldest surviving image and the star's first documented Jewish use, and the newer symbol took the flag.
Both are genuine Jewish symbols with genuine histories, and a symbol can become deeply meaningful regardless of its age.
Nor was anything hidden: the Zionist movement never concealed that the state flag was its own 1897 banner, and the flag's history is public and uncontested.
The flag's lineage runs through a nineteenth-century political movement, not through the Temple period.

On this reading the flag signals that the state understands itself to continue the political project of Herzl and the Basel Congress, rather than the ancient Temple cult, which is consistent with a founding that was political, secular and modern.

Displayed in synagogues, schools and community centers, a flag that joins the movement's emblem to Jewish religious life may reinforce, through repetition rather than argument, the idea that the political project of 1897 and a religious tradition of millennia are one thing.
That is the distinction between Zionism and Judaism examined in , made here through an image instead of a claim.
Most people who display the flag do so out of a real connection to Israel or to Jewish identity, not as part of any messaging effort, and this reading assumes nothing about any individual's intent.
Many Israelis and Jews abroad experience the flag as holding both the political founding and the older tradition at once, which is an equally defensible way to read it.
They do not show that the choice was made to diminish the menorah or the Temple tradition.
Scholem's argument about the star's secular availability and the narrower argument from practical legibility both remain on the table, and the record available here does not decide between them.
Jews in the Muslim World: Coexistence Without Utopia
For more than a thousand years, Jewish communities lived across the Muslim-majority Middle East and North Africa: in Baghdad, Cairo, Damascus, Aleppo, Sana'a, Fez, Tunis and Casablanca.
A common claim holds that Jews and Arabs never lived together in peace, and that an ancient, irreconcilable hatred is the natural and permanent state between them.

What the record shows is a long, uneven coexistence: real violence, and real legal inequality, alongside intellectual, commercial and civic collaboration on a scale that, in the judgment of the historians cited below, Christian Europe of the same period did not match.
The oldest of these communities is older than Islam, older than Arab rule in the region and older than either modern state that now claims part of its story.
In 586 BCE Babylon destroyed the First Temple in Jerusalem, conquered Judah and deported its population to Mesopotamia, the land that is now Iraq.

Over the following centuries the community became one of the great centers of Jewish religious and intellectual life, and between roughly the third and sixth centuries CE its scholars compiled the Babylonian Talmud, a foundational work of Jewish law that is still the primary text of rabbinic study, nearly 1,500 years after it was compiled in what is now Iraq.
One of the two foundational texts of rabbinic Judaism was produced there, not in the land of Israel.

Historical and religious sources agree, without dispute, on continuous Jewish presence in Mesopotamia from the sixth century BCE, more than a thousand years before the Muslim conquest of the region, and long before the Iraqi state of 1932 or the Israeli state of 1948.
Sasson Somekh, born a Jew in Baghdad and later a professor of Arabic literature at Tel Aviv University, documents its scale in his memoir Baghdad, Yesterday (2007).

One account gives 140,000 Jews in 1917, about 40 percent of Baghdad's civilian population; another gives roughly 140,000 in 1945, about a third of the city; a more cautious reckoning puts the mid-century community at 90,000 to 140,000, depending on the year and the source, in that reckoning close to a third of the city.
Jews formed much of the commercial, banking and professional life of modern Iraq.
Trading families such as the Sassoons, the Kadoories and the Basris built networks that reached across the region, into British India and across the British Empire.
Iraq's first finance minister, Sassoon Heskel, was Jewish, and the community's chief rabbis served as advisers to the government.
In 1917 the community welcomed the arriving British forces.
It was a city community as old as Jewish life in Europe, integrated into the economy and the state.
Its place in the new kingdom under Faisal is told in .
The best-known chapter of this history is al-Andalus, Muslim Iberia, home to what is called the Jewish Golden Age of the tenth to twelfth centuries.
Its figures include Maimonides (born in Córdoba, 1135–1204), Judah Halevi (of Toledo and Córdoba), Solomon ibn Gabirol and Samuel HaNagid.
Jewish scholars wrote philosophy in Arabic, held the office of vizier and produced foundational works of rabbinic literature.
In 1066 a pogrom struck the Jews of Granada.
The historians on whom this account relies, María Rosa Menocal, David Nirenberg and Mark Cohen, do not deny such violence.
Their work nonetheless documents a substantial period of Jewish and Muslim intellectual and civic collaboration that, they argue, had no parallel in Christian Europe of the same period.
The Iberian story ended in Christian hands.
In 1492 the Catholic monarchs, Ferdinand and Isabella, ordered Spain's Jews to convert or leave; historians estimate that at least 200,000 people were affected.
The Ottoman sultan, Bayezid II, opened his territories to receive the exiles, and Salonika became a majority-Sephardic city for centuries.

Spain established diplomatic relations with Israel only on 17 January 1986, the last Western European state to do so, as a condition of joining the European Community, while pledging continued "friendship and solidarity" with the Arab world; in 1948, according to reports, Franco had sought relations and Ben-Gurion had refused because of Franco's ties to Nazi Germany.
Spain hosted the Madrid peace conference of 1991.
In 2015 the Spanish parliament passed a law offering citizenship to descendants of the expelled Sephardim, to repair what it called a "historical mistake."
By the 2019 deadline 132,226 people had applied, most of them from Latin America: about 20,000 from Mexico, the largest single group, followed by applicants from Venezuela and Colombia.
Less than a decade later, on 28 May 2024, Spain, with Ireland and Norway, recognized the State of Palestine on the pre-1967 lines with East Jerusalem as its capital.
Israel recalled its ambassador, and its foreign minister said the three states were rewarding Hamas.
Pro-Israel commentators read Spain's position as hostility with historical echoes; the Spanish government presents it as support for a two-state solution and for international law.
The Ottoman Empire, which lasted from 1299 to 1922, a span of 623 years, gave this coexistence its most durable legal form.
It organized its non-Muslim subjects through the millet system, under which each religious community governed itself under its own leaders in matters of law, education and religion.
The Chief Rabbi of Istanbul was responsible for all Ottoman Jews.
Jewish communities lived under this arrangement in Istanbul, İzmir, Salonika, Damascus, Aleppo, Baghdad, Cairo and Jerusalem.
The system was not one of equality: Jews held the status of dhimmi, protected non-Muslims, paid the jizya tax and lived under legal restrictions that did not apply to Muslims.
It was also not the persecution of the Nazi regime or of imperial Russia.
For four centuries after 1492 it framed daily civic life, and it produced Sephardi and Mizrahi literature and the mystical school of Safed, the Kabbalah associated with Isaac Luria and Joseph Caro.
Norman Stillman's The Jews of Arab Lands is the standard documentary sourcebook for this history.

Under the millet, a Jewish community could run its own courts, schools and religious life; it could not stand as an equal of Muslims before the state, and it paid for its protection through a special tax.

The first, sometimes called the "golden age" reading, stresses the length and depth of the collaboration: Jewish philosophers writing in Arabic, Jewish viziers in Muslim courts, the Talmud compiled in Mesopotamia, the Ottoman welcome of 1492, and Baghdad's community still a third of the city in the twentieth century.

In its strongest form it argues, with Menocal, Nirenberg and Cohen, that nothing comparable existed in Christian Europe at the same time, and that a hatred described as ancient and permanent cannot explain a millennium of shared life.
The second reading stresses the limits and the ruptures: dhimmi status as a permanent legal subordination, the jizya, the restrictions, and violence such as the Granada pogrom of 1066.

In Baghdad in June 1941, seven years before Israel's founding, a pogrom known as the Farhud killed 150 to 180 Jews by the count of the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, and more by some other estimates.
Nazi-inspired, it came during the political turmoil of a short-lived pro-Axis coup, during the Anglo-Iraqi War, and was encouraged by pro-Axis Iraqi elements.
After 1948 came further legal restrictions, confiscations of property and violence; at the same time, the Israeli state and the Jewish Agency actively encouraged and organized emigration.
The same holds across the region, where roughly 850,000 Jews left Arab and Muslim countries between 1948 and 1972, for several reasons operating at once.
In Iraq the mass departure came in 1950–51, and within a decade a presence of some twenty-five centuries had all but ended.
The full account, including its disputed episodes and its sequel in Israel, belongs to the section on the exodus.
One point should be recorded here: the scholar Ella Shohat has documented the second-class treatment of Iraqi Jews after their arrival, a displacement upon a displacement.

The figures for Baghdad's Jewish population differ by source and by year, and the record here cannot reconcile 40 percent of the city in 1917 with a third in 1945 beyond noting that the counts and their bases differ.
The toll of the Granada pogrom of 1066 is not given in the sources used here.
The comparison with Christian Europe is a judgment by named historians, well supported, but a judgment all the same.
And the balance between persecution and recruitment in the Iraqi exodus remains a matter of genuine dispute.

What the record does establish is narrower and firmer: Jewish life in the Muslim world was long, large and productive; it was never free of inequality or violence; and the frame of an ancient, irreconcilable hatred does not describe it.
The Exodus of 1941–1972 and Its Aftermath
Between 1948 and 1972, roughly 850,000 Jews left Arab and Muslim countries, from about two dozen states over some 24 years.
The usual way of telling it is short: Jews were persecuted throughout Arab lands until Israel gave them refuge.

The documents show several causes working at once, each recorded on its own: violence and legal persecution by Arab governments, organized and named recruitment operations run by Israel and the Jewish Agency, and, in one specific and well-documented Egyptian case, sabotage carried out by Israeli military intelligence.
They also show that arrival in Israel was not the end of the story.

What happened to many of the newcomers in their first years is a second, separate story, in places a grave one, and Israel's own state commissions and independent researchers have investigated it without reaching full agreement.

This section follows that record in order: Iraq first, because its documentation is richest and its turning point came earliest; then the other airlifts and the Egyptian operation, briefly; then the transit camps, the disappearance of children from Yemenite and other Mizrahi families, and the mass irradiation of immigrant children for ringworm.
Baghdad, June 1941.
The turning point in Iraqi Jewish memory came seven years before Israel existed.
Rashid Ali al-Gailani led a pro-Axis coup in Iraq.
The British defeated it, and his government collapsed days before the violence began.
Its fall left a vacuum in the capital and inflamed the nationalist and pro-Axis feeling it had stirred.
On 1–2 June 1941, during the Jewish festival of Shavuot, crowds in Baghdad turned on the city's Jews.
Iraqi soldiers and police who had backed the coup, together with the pro-Axis youth militias known as the Futuwwa, incited and led two days of killing, rape and looting.
Civilian mobs and Bedouin from the city's outskirts joined them.
British forces, victorious just outside the city, did not intervene.
The event is known as the Farhud.

The United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, the most authoritative single source on the event, gives 150 to 180 Jews killed, 600 injured, an undetermined number of women raped, and roughly 1,500 stores and homes looted.

An official commission of inquiry appointed by the Iraqi government recorded 128 killed by its own count, with independent estimates running as high as 180; the same account gives more than 1,000 injured and roughly 900 Jewish homes and more than 1,500 businesses looted or destroyed.
On any of these counts, the event marked the point after which Iraq's ancient Jewish community began its decline toward near-total emigration within a decade.
The Farhud took place in June 1941.
Israel was declared in May 1948.
Whatever role the pogrom later played in hastening departures, it cannot have been a reaction to the 1948 war or to the Nakba, the Palestinian displacement of that war.
It does not show, on the other hand, that every later departure from Iraq was driven by the same forces.
Iraq at war, 1947–1949.
After the United Nations voted for partition in November 1947, anti-Jewish measures in Iraq escalated.
On 15 May 1948, the day after Israel declared its independence, Iraq joined the Arab invasion.
When the fighting ended, Iraq was the only Arab combatant that refused to sign an armistice with Israel, so that a formal state of war between the two has, technically, never ended.
For Iraq's Jews it meant that their state remained formally at war with the state that most of them would soon enter.
On 19 July 1948, Iraq made "Zionism" a crime punishable by up to seven years in prison.
Because every Jew was presumed to be a Zionist, the law worked as a blanket criminalization of the whole community.
The testimony of two Muslim witnesses was enough to convict, and there was little avenue for appeal.
On 23 September 1948, Shafiq Ades, a prominent and well-connected Jewish businessman, was publicly hanged in Basra on charges of selling weapons to Israel and to the Iraqi Communist Party.
On 2 March 1950, Iraq's parliament passed a law permitting Jews to leave on condition that they surrender their Iraqi citizenship.

It worked, once people registered, as a mechanism for stripping them of nationality and then of property: a subsequent law required departing Jews to sell their property and liquidate their businesses before leaving, and the state denaturalized those who registered and stripped them of their assets.
Israel and the Jewish Agency organized the airlift that followed, Operation Ezra and Nehemiah.
It was named for the biblical leaders of the return from the Babylonian exile, a deliberate echo of the community's own origins.

Shlomo Hillel, an Iraqi-born agent of Mossad LeAliyah Bet, negotiated personally with the Iraqi authorities and helped organize the operation; he later described it from the inside in a memoir, Operation Babylon.
The aircraft were provided by the Near East Transport Company and El Al.
One account gives the route as through Cyprus and Iran; another gives it as through Cyprus at first and later by direct flights from Baghdad to Lod.
The cost was largely met by the American Jewish Joint Distribution Committee, at about $4 million.
Israeli immigration authorities had prepared to receive about 300 people a day; at the peak, 1,400 arrived daily.
By the end of 1951 more than 107,000 Iraqi Jews had been airlifted, and about 16,000 more had left by other routes.
Israeli government sources put its size before the airlift at about 135,000; another account gives roughly 130,000.
These facts establish a real, organized, named Israeli operation and a real Iraqi legal mechanism that made departure conditional on giving up citizenship and property.
They do not, by themselves, say why so many Iraqi Jews chose to go.
The Farhud, the criminal law of 1948, the hanging in Basra, the conditions of the 1950 law and the airlift's own active recruitment are all documented as contributing causes.
The Baghdad bombings, 1950–1951.
Between April 1950 and June 1951, at least five bombing incidents struck Jewish institutions and gathering places in Baghdad, among them the Masuda Shemtov synagogue.
At least four Jews were killed and others injured.
Iraq tried men for the bombings, and two of them, Basri and Shalom, were hanged in January 1952.
The Iraqi government of the time, and later some historians, attributed the bombings to Zionist underground agents seeking to panic the community into leaving faster.

Israeli officials have consistently and firmly denied any involvement, and have called the accusation an antisemitic fabrication meant to shift blame for a persecution the Iraqi state had itself created through years of pogroms, denaturalization and criminalization.

A review of newly released Israeli, British and American archives, published by the Middle East Forum, found insufficient evidence to confirm Israeli involvement, while not closing the question entirely.
The executions do not settle it either: the fairness and evidentiary basis of the trials, held amid intense anti-Zionist feeling, are themselves disputed.
What the record shows is real bombings, real deaths, and a real Iraqi prosecution that ended in executions.
Both the contemporary Iraqi accusation and the Israeli denial are documented positions.
Yemen, Morocco and Egypt.
Iraq's was one of three major named operations, each in a different country on a different timetable.
Operation Magic Carpet airlifted approximately 48,000 to 49,000 Yemenite Jews to Israel in 1949–50.
Operation Yachin, conducted in secret from 1961 to 1964, brought Moroccan Jews, later than the other two because Morocco's political timeline was different.

Both, like Ezra and Nehemiah, were organized operations of the Israeli state and the Jewish Agency, not spontaneous flight, though the hardships in the countries of origin were also real and documented.

Conditions and causes were not the same in all three countries, and they are not treated here as one undifferentiated movement; Yemen's and Morocco's own circumstances, including the payments made for Moroccan departures, are set out country by country in the next section.
Egypt supplies the one documented case of sabotage, and it touches this story because of whom it used.
In July 1954, Israeli military intelligence, known as Aman, activated Unit 131, a cell of Egyptian Jews it had recruited and trained for the purpose.
The cell placed incendiary devices at a post office, at American information-agency libraries in Cairo and Alexandria, and at British-owned cinemas.
The intention was that the attacks would be blamed on Egyptian nationalists or communists and would persuade Britain to keep its troops in the Suez Canal Zone.
Another summary of the same operation gives the intended scapegoats as Egyptian nationalists or the Muslim Brotherhood, and the aim as damaging Western confidence in Nasser's government.
The plan unraveled when a device ignited prematurely in an operative's pocket in Alexandria, and the cell was arrested.
At the Egyptian trial Moshe Marzouk and Shmuel Azar were sentenced to death and executed in January 1955.
Max Bennett, an Israeli officer, took his own life in prison.
Israel did not acknowledge the operatives for decades, and publicly honored the survivors in 2005.
The operation, later called Operation Susannah, is the earliest documented case of the Israeli state attacking a close ally's facilities under a false attribution.
Defense Minister Pinhas Lavon denied giving the order; the head of military intelligence, Binyamin Gibli, claimed that he had.
Lavon resigned in 1955; one account describes him as forced out.
The question was reopened in 1960 amid evidence that documents had been forged, split the ruling Mapai party, and contributed to Ben-Gurion's resignation in 1963.
The record documents this pattern for Egypt only; it does not establish it for any other country in this account.
The rescue reading holds that these were communities in danger, and that Israel brought them out.

Its evidence is strong and specific: a pogrom in 1941 with soldiers and police among the killers, a 1948 law that made every Jew in Iraq a presumed criminal, a public hanging meant to be seen, an exit law that took citizenship and property together.

The recruitment-and-sabotage reading holds that the Israeli state did not only receive these communities but actively worked to bring them, and in one place used local Jews in an operation that endangered them.

Its evidence is also specific: named operations, a named agent negotiating with the Iraqi government, organized airlifts at a pace the reception system could not absorb, and the documented operation in Egypt.
The disputed Baghdad bombings sit between the two readings, and the record cannot assign them to either.
New arrivals, disproportionately Mizrahi, were housed in crowded transit camps called ma'abarot, at first in tents and later in basic shacks.
Ashkenazi immigrants arriving in the same period tended to be better educated on arrival and more likely to assimilate into the existing, largely Ashkenazi-run secular establishment.
They also qualified for German war-reparations payments, which Mizrahi immigrants, who had never lived under Nazi occupation, could not receive.
The Yemenite Children Affair.
Between 1948 and 1954, hundreds of infants and small children of Yemenite and other Mizrahi immigrant families disappeared from Israeli state hospitals and transit camps.
A state inquiry, the Cohen-Kedmi Commission, investigated for nearly seven years, from 1995 to 2001.

The researcher Shoshana Madmoni-Gerber and hundreds of collected family testimonies support the argument that the disappearances reflect a real, coordinated pattern rather than isolated administrative failures.
The activist Uzi Meshulam campaigned prominently for a fuller inquiry and was imprisoned in connection with his campaign, which is itself a disputed chapter in how the authorities handled the issue.
Through the 1950s, Israeli medical authorities treated scalp ringworm, a common condition at the time, by irradiating immigrant children with X-rays.
The children treated were disproportionately Mizrahi and North African.

Ringworm was grounds for exclusion under the immigration rules of the United States and other countries, which put direct institutional pressure on the authorities to treat and clear affected children so that their resettlement could proceed.
What it does show is the scale, the disproportionate effect on Mizrahi and North African children, and the immigration-driven pressure behind it.
A 2003 Israeli documentary, The Ringworm Children, presented the episode as a serious, state-linked medical scandal, and used language as strong as "holocaust" to describe it.
It is not the same claim as the end of Jewish life in the Middle East.

It was a minority of the total Jewish population that had lived across the Muslim-majority world for more than a thousand years, in cities where Jewish communities were sometimes a third of the population or more.
The presence thinned, in some cities dramatically: one account describes Baghdad's community of 140,000 as functionally gone today.
It does not establish who planted the bombs in Baghdad in 1950 and 1951.
It does not establish who gave the order for the Egyptian operation of 1954.
And it does not establish what became of the children of Yemenite and other Mizrahi families whose fates even the state's own commission could not account for.
Two great displacements followed the end of British rule in Palestine.
In the war of 1947–1949 roughly 700,000 to 750,000 Palestinians were displaced, the event Palestinians call the Nakba.
Over the next quarter-century most of the Jewish communities of the Arab world left the countries where they lived.
In this telling the two were a clean and roughly equal population exchange: Jews out of Arab countries, Arabs out of Palestine, the one canceling the other.
Start with the Palestinian displacement.
Direct military and paramilitary action substantially drove it, including massacres at named places, Deir Yassin, Lydda, Ramla and al-Dawayima.
It was carried out by an identifiable set of forces: the Haganah, the Irgun and Lehi, and after independence the Israel Defense Forces.
The dashboard panel above gives the round number most often used, about 700,000 Palestinians displaced in 1948, beside a United Nations estimate of about 711,000.
The Jewish departures had a different shape.
Iraq's community left largely in an airlift of 1950–51.
Egypt's Jews left in two waves, in 1948 and again after the Suez Crisis of 1956.
Algeria's exodus came during that country's war of independence in the early 1960s, more than a decade after 1948.

The causes ranged from persecution and violence, including the Farhud in Baghdad in 1941 and the riots that followed the partition vote, to organized emigration operations run by Israel and Jewish organizations.
A survey of the regional aftermath puts the figure for Arab countries and Iran, from 1948 into the 1970s, "commonly in the range of 800,000–900,000".
The 1947–49 war ended with about 700,000 Palestinians displaced.

In the following years the large Jewish communities of Iraq, Yemen, Libya, Egypt, Syria and North Africa shrank sharply through emigration, pressure, expulsion and state persecution, in proportions that varied by country.
The defeat discredited the Arab governments that had fought the war.
Syria's government fell to a military coup in March 1949, Egypt's monarchy in 1952 and Iraq's in 1958.
The departure of Arab Jews belongs to that upheaval, but it was spread across years and governments that the war of 1948 did not itself control.
Israel's government granted citizenship to the Jewish arrivals and absorbed roughly 600,000 immigrants over four years, doubling the country's Jewish population.
Most Arab host states did not extend citizenship to Palestinian refugees or their descendants, even after more than seven decades.
The continuing work of UNRWA, a refugee agency dedicated to Palestinians alone, reflects that difference.
The common question "why don't Arab countries just take the refugees?" has a different answer in each country.
Jordan is the main exception.
Under its nationality law of 1954 it gave citizenship to most of the Palestinians who arrived after 1948.
It hosts more than 2 million registered Palestinian refugees, most of them citizens, although Human Rights Watch has documented arbitrary revocations of that citizenship.
Lebanon hosts about 400,000 registered refugees, roughly 10% of its population.
Palestinians there were barred from dozens of professions outside the camps and, under a property law of 2001, from owning real estate.
Lebanon justified these measures as preventing tawteen, permanent settlement, and they are linked to the country's sectarian balance.
Egypt and the Gulf states offered residency without a path to citizenship.
The Arab states' stated reason is that the Arab League instructed its members not to grant citizenship, "to avoid dissolution of their identity and protect their right of return".
Critics, including Israeli and pro-Israel analysts, argue that the policy kept refugees in limbo as a political tool.
Both readings describe the same outcome: Jordan absorbed refugees, while other states restricted them in order to keep a claim of return alive.
Egypt's President el-Sisi and Jordan's King Abdullah refused to take in people from Gaza.
Analysts noted that Palestinians forced to leave had historically not been allowed to return, and Egypt warned of militants in Sinai.
The position was summed up in reporting as "no refugees in Jordan, no refugees in Egypt": a fear that any exit would be a one-way door.
Sources sympathetic to the Palestinian narrative call the comparison "profoundly unfounded", given the different mechanisms involved.
Some sources sympathetic to the Israeli narrative reject it for the opposite reason.
They argue that the Jewish displacement, sometimes cited as the larger in raw numbers, has been ignored in international discourse.

The strongest version of the Palestinian objection is that a war-driven displacement by one set of forces, with return then barred, cannot be offset by departures from other countries that unfolded over decades, often through organized emigration.

The strongest version of the opposing objection is that hundreds of thousands of Jews lost homes, property and citizenship and have received little recognition, while Palestinian refugees have a dedicated international agency of their own.
The Jewish total remains a range, and the Palestinian figure is itself a range of estimates.
The sources here also do not give each Arab host state's full reasons for withholding citizenship, beyond the Arab League's stated rationale and Lebanon's stated fear of permanent settlement.
Jacob Becomes Israel: What Genesis 32 Says
Before the word "Israel" named a people, a land or a state, it named one man.
Its first appearance in the Hebrew Bible is a renaming, given at the end of a night of wrestling, in the thirty-second chapter of Genesis.
The story runs through Genesis 32:22–32.
Jacob is alone at the ford of the Jabbok river, on the night before he is to meet, and be reconciled with, the twin brother he had deceived years earlier.
The text calls that figure a man and an angel, and Jacob, afterward, in his own words, calls it God, seen face to face.
He names the place Peniel, "face of God," because, in his words, "I saw God face to face, and yet my life was spared."

Genesis 32:28 reads, in the rendering consistent across the major translations: "Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel; for you have struggled with God and with men, and have prevailed."
The Hebrew of the final clause, כִּי־שָׂרִיתָ עִם־אֱלֹהִים וְעִם־אֲנָשִׁים וַתּוּכָל, says "for you have striven with God and with men, and have prevailed."
ents: The Hebrew of the final clause

sent: The word Israel appears 2,362 times across the Hebrew and Christian scriptures, 2,284 times in the Hebrew Bible and 78 times in the New Testament, and every one of those uses comes after this one.
The later biblical authors themselves treated Genesis 32 as the name's point of origin.

The prophet Hosea, writing centuries afterward, recapitulates the same story in Hosea 12:3–4, which shows that the episode was understood within the tradition as the source of the name, not as one story among many that happened to use it.

One is El (אֵל), the ancient Semitic word for God, which was shared across Canaanite, Ugaritic and other Northwest Semitic languages and was not exclusive to Hebrew; it is the same shared root that appears in .
The other is a root connected to sarah (שָׂרָה), "to strive, contend, or prevail."
It is the root that also gives Sarah, Abraham's wife, her name, with connotations of "princess," or of one who contends with authority.
It is the consistent reading of the standard Hebrew lexicons, Brown-Driver-Briggs among them, of rabbinic commentary and of Christian biblical scholarship alike.
With El as the subject, it means "God strives," that is, God contending on Jacob's behalf or through him.
Jacob's birth name, Ya'akov, is related to akev, "heel": he was born grasping the heel of his twin, Esau, and the root carries connotations of crookedness and of following from behind.
The letters of Yisra'el can also evoke yashar, "straight" or "upright."

Several Hebrew-language sources read this as a deliberate contrast built into the text: the grasping, deceptive Jacob against the upright, prevailing Israel, one person before and after a transformation.
Sarah, "to strive," is the derivation the lexicons give; yashar, "upright," is an echo the letters allow, a play on sound and sense rather than a second etymology.
The common assumption is that "Israel" has always simply meant the Jewish nation, or the Promised Land.

At the moment the name is given, it belongs to exactly one person: Jacob, who had deceived his brother and fled his own family, and who wrestles through a night and comes out of it renamed as one who has struggled and prevailed.
Outside the Bible, the name's history runs on a different track, through inscriptions rather than scripture.
Its earliest mention outside the biblical text, on the Merneptah stele, where Israel already appears as a people, is set out in .
As a primary source, the verse establishes that the word's first appearance names one individual after one event, and the lexicons establish the derivation from El and sarah with high confidence.
What the verse does not establish is how later biblical authors, ancient Israelite communities or modern political movements would extend the word.
Nor does the documented etymology support any connection to Egyptian deities.
A symbolic reading that breaks the name into IS, RA and EL works on the English transliteration rather than the Hebrew, and it is kept apart, and labeled as a reading, in .

It does not claim that ancient Hebrew scribes built the names of Egyptian gods into the word Israel, and it does not replace the Hebrew derivation from El and sarah, "to strive," which remains the scholarly record.

IS evokes Isis, the Egyptian goddess associated in Hermetic and other inner-tradition frameworks with the receptive, magnetic, lunar principle, the polarity later traditions would call the divine feminine.
RA evokes the Egyptian solar deity: radiant and generative, the polarity later traditions call the divine masculine.
It is not a symbolic borrowing but the actual ancient Semitic word for God, the same root the documented etymology identifies.
Read this way, "Israel" names neither a place nor a people but a state of being: the integration of feminine and masculine under the divine.
One symbolic reading holds that this is what Genesis 32 describes happening to one man in a single night.
The IS and RA readings are a modern esoteric reading of the English transliteration of the name.
They do not work on the Hebrew original, Yisra'el, whose elements are El and the root sarah.
The single piece of the reading that is real etymology is EL.

What the reading proposes is a resonance rather than a derivation: that consciousness-transformation traditions across the ancient Near East and Egypt shared a common structural language of polarity, integration and ascent, and that the Jacob and Israel story reads coherently within that shared framework whether or not the etymology is literal.
Jacob as anyone.
Under this lens, Genesis 32 is less a genealogical account of where one group's name came from than a template.

Jacob is any person who confronts honestly the crookedness the text itself names in him, the grasping, deceptive "heel" of his birth name, and who wrestles with both the human and the divine and comes through transformed into the state the name describes: upright, prevailing, in direct relation to God.

Rabbi Jonathan Sacks, a mainstream and widely respected Orthodox authority, wrote of Jacob and Israel as two aspects of the same person, and asked his readers: "Are we Jacob, embarrassed by who we are?
Or are we Israel, with the courage to stand upright?"
The reading of the story as an inner transformation has real roots in traditional Jewish commentary.
The layer that is not part of mainstream Jewish or Christian commentary is the specifically esoteric one, IS–RA–EL as Isis, Ra and El, with its Hermetic vocabulary of polarity.
The IS and RA syllables, as shown above, have no basis in the Hebrew.
Both Judaism and Islam built it into their own formal scholarship and gave it names.
Rabbinic Judaism has PaRDeS, a structured four-level exegesis.

Peshat is the plain, literal sense; Remez, the hint, is the allegorical or symbolic layer; Derash is the comparative and homiletical meaning drawn out through study; and Sod, the secret, is the mystical layer, the root from which the word "Kabbalah" itself grows.
One documented framing of the method puts the idea of ascent at its center: the Torah descends from above, and the reader ascends through the four levels from below.

Islamic scholarship developed a parallel and equally formal distinction between tafsir, conventional exoteric exegesis, and ta'wil, esoteric or mystical interpretation, practiced across Shia, Sufi and Sunni traditions since at least the eighth century CE.
The Quran itself points to an inner meaning, in the account of Khidr, whose actions require their own ta'wil, an inner explanation distinct from how they appear on the surface.
Christian scholarship held a similar standard.

Origen, the third-century Church Father, was highly influential in establishing allegorical interpretation as a serious and legitimate mode of reading scripture within early Christianity, and the practice shaped the centuries of exegesis that followed.

In the words of documented scholarship on medieval exegesis, "High Medieval Catholic scripture commentary was only thought perfect if it contained both elements, both literal and allegorical interpretation."
The founders of the Zionist movement weighed territories other than Palestine, Argentina and Uganda among them, before Palestine was chosen; that record is set out in .

Whichever territory had been chosen, naming the resulting state "Israel," rather than "Zion" alone or a geographic name, would have carried the same layered scriptural weight, because that weight travels with the word and not with a particular stretch of land.

It does not establish, and cannot, that Herzl, the Basel Congress, Israel's founders in 1948 or any other historical actor intended an Egyptian or Hermetic meaning when the state was named; it rests on no documented evidence of any of them discussing such symbolism.

It does not establish what ancient Israelite communities understood the word to mean as the name of a tribe or nation, and it does not displace the word's later, documented use as the name of a people and a place.
Ottoman Palestine: Named, Counted and Governed
From 1516 to 1917 the Ottoman Empire governed most of the Arab Middle East as provinces of a single state.
Damascus, Baghdad, Jerusalem and Beirut were provincial cities of the same empire, and people and goods moved between them without passports.
There were no international borders between what are now Syria, Iraq, Lebanon, Jordan and Israel and the Palestinian territories, because none of those states yet existed.
Iran stood outside this order altogether: it was never Ottoman, and it kept its own dynasty, its own language and a Shia majority.

Under what is called the millet system, recognized religious communities, Muslims, Christians of several churches and Jews, administered their own religious law, their own courts and their own schooling, and governed marriage and inheritance under their own leaders.
Non-Muslims paid special taxes and held a lesser legal status; the empire taxed heavily, conscripted men, and put down revolts by force, and periodic violence was part of its record.
Almost every border that matters in today's conflicts was drawn in a six-year window, between 1916 and 1922, by two European powers, Britain and France.

The first holds that before Zionism "Palestine" was an empty, undifferentiated stretch of Ottoman desert with no population or administrative identity of its own, and that the place became real only when the British Mandate invented it.
The second holds that the Ottomans occupied Palestine much as settlers later would.
The Ottomans generally named their provinces after their capital cities.
No single Ottoman administrative unit was ever officially called "Palestine" on a map.
It is the strongest form of the claim that Palestine "never existed," and it deserves a precise answer rather than a denial.
The regional name was far older than the Ottomans.
Rome designated its province Syria Palaestina in the second century CE, and the name persisted through Byzantine, Crusader and Mamluk rule.
Throughout the Ottoman centuries it stayed in standing use in European maps, in travel writing, in religious texts and in Arabic geographic writing, including local Arabic-language sources.
An American comparison helps.
There was never a colonial charter for a place officially named "New England" in the way there was a Massachusetts Bay Colony.
Massachusetts, Connecticut and Rhode Island were nonetheless real, governed and populated, and "New England" was the regional name in continuous use for the whole of them.
It lets a speaker correct a listener, "Palestine wasn't an official Ottoman province," while implying something much larger: that the place, its people and its government were not real.
What the Ottomans did create was an administrative status for this region that was higher than that of most districts in the empire.
Ordinarily an Ottoman district, a sanjak, sat inside a larger province, a vilayet, and reported upward through the provincial governor.
Jerusalem was taken out of that chain.

After an initial separation in 1864, the district of Jerusalem was raised in 1872 to the status of a mutasarrifate: it was governed by a mutasarrif who answered directly to Constantinople, bypassing the provincial governor altogether.

That arrangement was reserved for a small number of especially significant districts across the empire, and Jerusalem held it because of the region's religious and strategic importance, both to the Ottomans themselves and to the Western powers.
It ran without interruption until the British occupation in 1917, a span of 45 years.
In plain terms, Jerusalem was one of the places important enough that the capital insisted on governing it directly, with no regional manager in between.
It reflected religious and strategic significance inside an Ottoman imperial framework.
It does not show that the Ottomans thought of the territory in the national categories of the twentieth century, Arab, Palestinian or Zionist, and it anticipated none of the politics that came later.
By 1887–88 the territory that later became Mandate Palestine was organized in three units.
In the south lay the independent Sanjak of Jerusalem, the mutasarrifate.
In the north lay the Sanjaks of Nablus and Acre, both attached administratively to the larger Vilayet of Beirut.
Taken together, these three districts map closely onto the later boundary of the British Mandate.

Across the whole Ottoman period, Palestine is described as having been governed chiefly as the district of Jerusalem together with parts of the provinces of Beirut and Damascus, and from 1831 to 1840 it passed out of Ottoman hands into Egyptian rule before returning.
The continuity that matters is that a bounded, governed region existed, and that its outline was not an arbitrary line drawn later by the British.
Their combined population was approximately 600,000 by the late nineteenth century, roughly a decade before political Zionism existed as an organized movement.
Other counts from the period give lower totals: a census of 1871–72, discussed in , and the reconstructions from Ottoman registers set out in the next section, which left out foreign nationals.
The counting continued across the transition from Ottoman to British administration between 1917 and 1922, which relabeled one continuous population rather than introducing a new one.
The administrative record itself names the towns governed under this system, among them Jerusalem, Gaza, Jaffa, Hebron, Nablus, Haifa, Acre, Safed and Nazareth.

An 1885 British encyclopedia entry on the region gives a more granular count from the same period: 753 distinct named places, with more than 54,000 houses, meaning families, across the Ottoman districts.
Populations and settlements shifted over four centuries of Ottoman rule, as they do everywhere.
Most were Arabic-speaking Muslims and Christians.
Alongside them lived long-established Jewish communities in Jerusalem, Hebron, Safed and Tiberias, whose life is the subject of the next section.
Most were Ottoman subjects, though many Jewish immigrants were foreign nationals.
This bears on the second claim, that the Ottomans occupied Palestine in the way later settlers did.
The precise term for Ottoman rule is imperial administration.
That is the distinction between an empire and a settler project, and the Ottoman record falls on the imperial side of it.
The Ottoman Land Code of 1858 is told in the next volume, in .
Ottoman rule ended in war.
British forces captured Jerusalem in December 1917, and the Mutasarrifate's long run ended with the occupation.
The Republic of Turkey, founded in 1923, renounced all rights over the former Arab provinces in the Treaty of Lausanne that year.
Modern Turkey is therefore the empire's successor state, not a claimant to the land.
The Arab majority that the Ottomans governed was still the majority when British rule ended.
British Mandate figures for 1947 counted about 1.3 million Arabs and 630,000 Jews in Palestine.

On 29 November 1947 the United Nations adopted Resolution 181, which proposed a Jewish state on 56% of the land and an Arab state on 44%, with Jerusalem under international administration, at a time when Jewish ownership amounted to approximately 7% of the land.
The Jewish Agency accepted the plan and the Arab League rejected it.
In the war of 1948 approximately 700,000 Palestinian Arabs fled or were expelled, the event Palestinians call the Nakba, "the catastrophe."

From the 1980s, Israeli scholars working in newly declassified military archives, among them Benny Morris, Ilan Pappé, Avi Shlaim and Simha Flapan, documented both flight from war and systematic expulsions, against the earlier official account that the refugees left voluntarily.
The administrative lines of the three districts moved over the decades, and how closely they matched the Mandate's border at any given date is a matter of degree.
And the Mutasarrifate's elevated status tells us how Constantinople valued Jerusalem, not how the people who lived in the district understood themselves.
Two Real Histories: Presence, Continuity and National Identity
The first holds that one people is indigenous and the other a recent colonizer: Jews native and Arabs latecomers, or the reverse.
The second holds that there is no distinct Palestinian people at all, only Arabs in general, and that a Palestinian national identity was invented recently.
The first question: ancient Jewish presence.

Ancient Jewish kingdoms existed in parts of the land, and Jewish religious, cultural and historical connections to the region are documented in archaeological, textual and religious sources over more than three thousand years.
The second question: a counted Arab population.
The Ottoman census of 1871–72 counted 381,954 residents of Palestine, excluding the Bedouin, of whom roughly 85 percent were Muslim, 11 percent Christian and 4 percent Jewish.

This Arabic-speaking population's presence under Ottoman rule is documented continuously for centuries, and modern genetic and archaeological studies find strong Levantine biogeographical continuity in it, consistent with long-term local ancestry.
The census left out the Bedouin, so the true population was larger than 381,954.
The most authoritative statement that Palestinian national identity is modern comes not from a hostile source but from the field's leading Palestinian historian.

Rashid Khalidi, Edward Said Professor of Arab Studies at Columbia University and a past president of the Middle East Studies Association, set out the finding in his foundational study Palestinian Identity: The Construction of Modern National Consciousness.

Formal Palestinian national identity, he documents, has its roots in the nationalist discourses that emerged among the Ottoman Empire's peoples in the late nineteenth century, and it sharpened through what he identifies as the critical years of 1917 to 1923.
Khalidi is explicit that this modern political consciousness drew on a much older regional history and a real population presence.
