Formal Zionist national identity was founded at the First Zionist Congress in Basel in 1897, as a modern political movement built on older religious and cultural material rather than as an ancient ethnogenesis; the movement's founding is told in .
The sharpest popular form of the second claim says there was no Palestinian people before the Palestine Liberation Organization.
The PLO was founded in 1964.
A newspaper named Filastin, "Palestine," began publishing in Jaffa in 1911 and campaigned as a Palestinian voice; its story is told in .
Palestinian Arab congresses met from 1919 and petitioned the Paris Peace Conference.
Britain's census of 1922 counted 757,182 people in Palestine.

Historians date the emergence of Palestinian national identity to the late Ottoman and British Mandate periods, the same century in which the region's other national identities formed, Jordanian, Syrian and Israeli among them.
Its kernel of truth is the one Khalidi himself documents: the national identity is modern.
Its error is to treat a modern identity as a fake one, a standard that would disqualify most of the region's nations, Israel included.
The best-known slogan of the first claim has a documented origin, and it is not Zionist.

Its earliest published version appeared in 1843 in a book by Alexander Keith, a Church of Scotland clergyman and an advocate of Jewish "restoration" who had traveled to Palestine in 1839 and had seen that it was inhabited.
The first use by a Zionist came in 1901, when Israel Zangwill wrote that Palestine was "a country without a people."
Whatever its users intended, every Ottoman and British census shows a populated country.
A companion claim holds that Jews and Muslims have been fighting over this land for two millennia.
Jews, Muslims and Christians lived together under Ottoman rule, as  sets out.

The national conflict is roughly a century old: it began with modern political Zionism in 1897 and with the British Mandate, and the first Palestinian national movement was organized jointly by Muslims and Christians: a national alignment, not a religious one.
A third slogan of the same family, that the Arabs "rejected every offer," compresses a record that runs in both directions.

Arab leaders rejected the Peel plan of 1937 and the partition plan of 1947; Israel's refugee offer at Lausanne in 1949 was made only within a full peace and later withdrawn; and the offer at Camp David in 2000 is disputed by participants on the American side, who say it was never written down.
The panel below gathers the figures the British authorities and the United Nations recorded in the decades after the Ottoman census.
Britain's 1922 census counted 757,182 people.
Britain recorded 376,415 Jewish immigrants between 1920 and 1946.
The United Nations Special Committee on Palestine (UNSCOP) estimated the population at about 1.85 million in late 1946.
They show a substantial population on the land when the Mandate began, which disposes of "a land without a people" for the twentieth century as the 1871–72 census does for the nineteenth.

The counts come from different authorities using different methods, and the Ottoman figure excluded the Bedouin, so the growth from 381,954 to about 1.85 million cannot be read off as a single like-for-like series.

Put at its strongest, the Jewish claim to indigeneity rests on what is not in dispute: ancient kingdoms in the land, and a religious, cultural and historical connection to it documented across more than three thousand years in archaeology and text.

Put at its strongest, the Palestinian claim rests on what is equally documented: a substantial Arabic-speaking population, counted by the Ottoman state itself, present continuously for centuries, with genetic evidence of long-term local ancestry, and forming the great majority of the land's people when the modern contest began.

It settles the facts: an ancient Jewish connection, a counted and continuous Arab population, and a modern national identity on both sides that took shape through comparable nineteenth- and twentieth-century political processes.
Egypt built a wall.
Rome renamed a province.
Arafat was born in Cairo, which the record shows to be largely accurate, though some sources dispute it.
The Roman renaming is real, but the name it imposed was centuries older than Rome's use of it, a point taken up in .
A claim that flatters Israel and a claim that flatters the Palestinians are held to the same test, and a false claim aimed at either people is treated the same way.
This volume opens not in Palestine, and not in any ministry or synagogue, but in a financial district of roughly one square mile in the middle of London.
It is run by the oldest municipal corporation in Britain, the City of London Corporation.
The Corporation governs through a Lord Mayor and a Court of Common Council, and it keeps its own police force.
Its privileges predate Magna Carta, and when Parliament has legislated since, it has routinely preserved them by express exception written into the later Acts.

A claim widely repeated online holds that the City is a sovereign city-state, beyond the authority of Parliament and the Crown, and that the monarch must ask the Lord Mayor's permission before entering it.
In Corporation elections, businesses are allocated votes alongside the people who live there.
Those figures come from the Green Party, which campaigns to end the arrangement, and they should be read as a campaigner's figures.
The same Green Party statement cited a Bloomberg survey that questioned how far the business vote represented the workers it is supposed to speak for.
The arrangement is unique in the United Kingdom.
The second privilege places the Corporation inside Parliament itself.
The City Remembrancer is a Corporation official who may watch the House of Commons from the visitors' under-gallery, near the Serjeant at Arms, by the Speaker's permission rather than by right.
A claim often repeated, that he is the only outsider allowed on the floor of the House, is not supported: he has no access beyond the bar.
The office reviews parliamentary legislation in order to protect the Corporation's interests, and it does so with a budget reported at about £6 million and a team of in-house lawyers.
The author Nicholas Shaxson has called the office "the world's oldest institutional lobbyist."
In 2013 the Green MP Caroline Lucas formally asked the Speaker to remove the Remembrancer from the floor of the House.
Read together, the business vote and the Remembrancer can be seen to reinforce each other: the firms help choose the Corporation, and the Corporation keeps watch on the law that governs them.
When the monarch enters the City on a state occasion, the Lord Mayor meets the sovereign at Temple Bar and presents the City's sword.

The sovereign's carriage has passed Temple Bar without stopping, as the BBC's Huw Edwards noted on air during a Jubilee, and Parliament's authority over the City is a matter of statute, not of the Lord Mayor's leave.
Laid side by side, the claim and the record separate cleanly.
The test that matters is whether the City's privileges amount to sovereignty, and they do not.
The Corporation is a local authority, not a state.
It has less autonomy than the Crown Dependencies of Jersey, Guernsey and the Isle of Man, each of which has its own legislature.
Parliament can legislate for the City, and does.
The privileges survive because Parliament keeps choosing to preserve them, which is the opposite of standing above Parliament.
The Corporation's own description of itself is more revealing than the legend.
A trade body for finance with its own electorate of firms and an official seated in the Commons is a working arrangement of influence, open to examination, and examined here on those terms.
The vote figures come from a party that wants the business vote abolished, and the Remembrancer's budget is a reported figure, not one drawn from published accounts in the sources used here.
Nor do these sources measure how often the Remembrancer's work changed the text of a bill.
That is why the story starts in the Square Mile.
N M Rothschild & Sons: The London House and Its Legend
The British state whose fleets returned Palestine to the Sultan in 1840 borrowed through the City of London, and one of its lenders was the house Nathan Mayer Rothschild had founded there.
Nathan Rothschild, it says, watched the Battle of Waterloo, raced the news to London, and made the family fortune by buying up British bonds before anyone else knew the result.

The documented record of the London house is a different kind of history, slower and more ordinary: a merchant bank that lent to a foreign state on new terms, supplied the Bank of England in a panic, sent the first Jewish member to the House of Commons, and found the money for Britain's Suez Canal shares while Parliament was not sitting.
The legend can be traced to a pamphlet published in 1846, ten years after Nathan's death, and written to stir hostility toward Jews.
Mayer Amschel Rothschild of Frankfurt placed five sons in five European financial centers: Frankfurt, London, Paris, Vienna and Naples.
The London house was founded by Nathan Mayer Rothschild, who lived from 1777 to 1836.
One account dates N M Rothschild & Sons to 1809, and places Nathan in London from that year.
This Nathan, the founder, should not be confused with a later namesake, Nathan Mayer Rothschild, 1st Baron, the father of the Walter Rothschild to whom the Balfour Declaration was addressed in 1917.
It arranged a £5 million loan for Prussia, denominated in sterling, with interest payable in London.
Until then, the currency risk of foreign bonds had kept British investors out of them.
A loan written in sterling and paid in London removed that risk.
The Rothschild Archive describes the Prussian loan as "the true precursor of the public borrowing which transformed the international capital market in the nineteenth century."
In 1825, during a banking panic, the house supplied the Bank of England with specie, that is, hard coin.
The institution that had been chartered in 1694 to lend to the Crown  now drew on a private house in a crisis.
On this book's reading, the two were not rivals but parts of the same London system of state credit.
The London house's political ties to the state came through Nathan's son, Lionel de Rothschild.
Lionel was elected to the House of Commons repeatedly from 1847, but he could not take his seat, because members were required to swear an oath as Christians.
When the Jews Relief Act ended that requirement, he took his seat in 1858 as the first Jewish member of the House of Commons.
Lionel was also head of the house when it carried out its most famous transaction with the British state.
The Suez Canal had opened in 1869.
It was owned by French financiers and by the Khedive of Egypt, but by 1874 four-fifths of its trade was British.
On 15 November 1875, Benjamin Disraeli learned that the Khedive meant to sell his shares.
Ten days later, on 25 November 1875, the purchase was concluded: Britain acquired 44% of the company's shares for £4,000,000.
Parliament was not sitting, so the government could not vote the money.
N M Rothschild & Sons, under Lionel de Rothschild, advanced it.
The Rothschild Archive calls it a "technically unsecured loan" and says it was repaid within five months.
An executive that wanted to act before the legislature could meet borrowed from a private house in the City, and asked Parliament to approve the act after it was done.
William Gladstone attacked it for its "lack of reference or consent from Parliament."
The purchase also left France as the majority shareholder.
Disraeli answered his critics in the House of Commons on 14 and 21 February 1876, and his own words, preserved in Hansard, state the government's reason without ambiguity.
He defended the purchase "as a political transaction, and one which I believe is calculated to strengthen the Empire," and said it "secures to us a highway to our Indian Empire."
He also described what the advance had to meet: after the first £1,000,000, he told the House, a further £2,000,000 "might be demanded in gold the next day."
Parliament approved the purchase on 21 February 1876.
What the house earned is the one point in the Suez story that the sources leave open.
Critics in Parliament said the Rothschild commission amounted to 15 percent interest.
Disraeli rejected that reading, and denied that the commission had "anything to do with the interest on the advance."
The critics' case, as Disraeli's speech reports it, was that the commission amounted to 15 percent interest; Disraeli's was that the commission was not interest at all.
Disraeli's stated aim, the route to India, belongs to the story of why Britain wanted the region at all, which is taken up in .
Set against that record, the Waterloo story belongs to a different category.
It first appears in 1846, in a pamphlet by Georges Dairnvaell, published under the name "Satan."
Dairnvaell wrote it after a railway accident on a line the Rothschilds had financed, and he wrote it explicitly to inflame hostility toward Jews.
Nathan had died in 1836.
According to the Rothschild Archive, nothing in the record suggests that Nathan was the first in London to know of the victory.
Niall Ferguson, author of the family's authorized history, estimates that any quick profit Nathan could have made on British bonds after the battle could not have exceeded about £7,000.
The archive's verdict, as quoted in this book's sources, is short: "The legend of Nathan Rothschild and Waterloo is just that: a legend."

A summary of the Frankfurt dynasty's history, drawing on volume 1 of Ferguson's The House of Rothschild (1998), credits him with a different verdict: that the tale is partly documented and partly embellished, that Nathan's information advantage was real, that the market timing was more complex than the mythology, and that the version in which Nathan "cornered the market" was a nineteenth-century antisemitic caricature by Édouard Drumont, later amplified.
They differ on its origin, Dairnvaell in 1846 or Drumont, and on whether Nathan had any advantage in news at all.

Both accounts invoke Ferguson, and this section cannot settle between them: the archive's statement and the £7,000 ceiling point toward the narrower reading, but the archive's words reach this book secondhand, and neither summary could be checked here against Ferguson's own text.
The family's own archive, Ferguson's authorized history and the journalist Mike Rothschild's 2023 study each take those claims apart.
The Waterloo legend is antisemitic in origin, and naming it as such is part of the record.
Its relationships with the British government were contracts: sovereign loans, a central bank supplied in a panic, the Suez advance, and a seat in Parliament won by election and delayed by an oath.
All of them operated inside the City of London that the chapter began with.
The Suez purchase was Disraeli's to make, Parliament's to approve and Gladstone's to attack.
Disraeli's own justification for it was the empire, not the bank.
The founding year of the London house is recorded two ways.
The size of the Suez commission, and so the real cost of the advance to the Treasury, is not stated in any source consulted.
The Rothschild Archive's verdict on Waterloo is known here only secondhand, and published summaries of Ferguson describe his findings differently.
The record of the London house is a record of public, contractual business with states, and the legend that replaced it in popular memory was made, from its first printing, as an attack on Jews.
The Pope's Bankers: Torlonia, the Rothschilds and the Papal Loans, 1794–1870
London was not the only sovereign borrower the Rothschild houses served.
Before 1870 the Pope was also the ruler of a territorial state, the Papal States, and like other rulers of his time he borrowed.
One lender was a Roman banker whom the papacy ennobled.
Then came the Rothschild houses.
The arrangement between them, and the hostility it drew, are a small but revealing part of the European board on which Palestine's future would later be decided.

Almost every detail of the papal loans below reaches this book through a single reference article on the Rothschild loans to the Holy See, which in turn relies on Niall Ferguson's history of the house of Rothschild.
The story begins with Giovanni Torlonia, who lived from 1754 to 1829.

According to the account summarized here, he was born to modest circumstances in the Auvergne region of France and built one of the largest banking fortunes in Rome through cloth trading, money-lending and papal patronage.
He opened his banking house in Rome in 1780.
By the 1790s he had become the Holy See's principal banker, providing loans, managing financial transactions and handling the papacy's increasingly complex needs during the Napoleonic period.
Pope Pius VI made him a noble in 1794, on 9 March according to the date the account gives from the Archivio di Stato, as Don Giovanni Torlonia, 1st Prince of Civitella Cesi.
The account describes the exchange as mutually reinforcing: the Torlonia house became the papacy's main financial institution and gained the social legitimacy of papal nobility at the same time.
The French Revolutionary period enlarged its role.

When French forces occupied Rome in 1798 and 1799 and papal finances were thrown into disorder, the account says, Torlonia's house managed the transfer of papal funds and lent the money that kept the papacy's operations going through the occupation and the restoration that followed.
By Napoleon's final defeat in 1814, the family was established as the papacy's principal financial manager.
The papacy also stood at the center of an older Roman aristocracy.
The Orsini and the Colonna, two of its oldest families, had held the ceremonial office of Prince Assistant to the Papal Throne in alternation since 1735.
The Orsini had produced three popes: Celestine III in 1191, Nicholas III in 1277 and Benedict XIII in 1724.
In 1823 the new banking family married into this old one, when Giovanni's son Alessandro Torlonia married an Orsini.
The bride's name is itself recorded two ways in the same account: once as Maria Luisa Orsini, and once as Teresa Orsini.

The account cites the evidence of the marriage as Rome diocesan records, the Orsini family genealogies held in the Archivio Segreto Vaticano and in private family archives, and Pompeo Litta's Famiglie celebri d'Italia (1819–83), a record of the great Italian noble lineages.

It goes on to interpret the match: Alessandro needed the legitimacy that only centuries-old noble blood could provide, while the Orsini needed to keep their finances afloat after the disruptions of the Napoleonic years, and the marriage was arranged, as such marriages were, with both families' positions in mind.
In this telling, the timing of the Rothschild connection eight years later was "not accidental."
The Rothschilds entered Roman finance in 1831.
After the Napoleonic wars and the Restoration, the Papal States were in fiscal distress.
The Torlonia house lacked the capital to meet the papacy's needs at the scale now required.
And the Rothschild houses were, by 1830, the dominant private banking operation in Europe.
On 30 November 1831, according to the account, Alessandro Torlonia co-signed a contract in Rome with James Mayer de Rothschild of the Paris house.
The account's short summary describes the contract as giving the Rothschilds an exclusive right of first refusal on all papal sovereign debt, by a clause kept secret.

Its more detailed description, drawn from Ferguson, describes the terms differently, as exclusive management of papal loan issues and key papal financial operations through the London house of Nathan Mayer Rothschild and the Paris house of James Mayer de Rothschild, with the Torlonia house as local intermediary.
In 1832 the Rothschilds lent £400,000 to Pope Gregory XVI.
The loan was negotiated through Carl Mayer von Rothschild, with James acting as the official papal banker.
According to the account, a letter from Gregory XVI dated 15 January 1832 acknowledges the Rothschilds' help in terms that confirm the relationship.
Nor do they say from what revenues of the Papal States it was serviced.
A cardinal named Tosti tried to refinance the papal debt with six other banks, and Carl Mayer de Rothschild traveled to Rome, produced the original contract and blocked him.
In the other, Antonio Tosti was not a cardinal refinancing the debt but the papal treasurer (elsewhere, the papal envoy), and he had embezzled papal funds.

The Rothschild houses' records of their dealings with the papacy could be compared against the papacy's own accounts, the discrepancies revealed the embezzlement, and the Rothschild correspondence, as Ferguson describes it, refers to the affair and to the banking relationship's role in uncovering it.

The second version comes with an interpretation: that the papacy's own financial management could not detect fraud by its own treasurer, that the external auditor, however informal, was the Rothschild house, and that the papacy's finances before any internal institution existed, before the Vatican bank, the IOR, was founded in 1942, depended on this outside relationship.
The question of which Rothschild house was the counterparty is itself unsettled.
The account's summary names James Mayer de Rothschild of the Paris house as the signatory in 1831.
Its detailed description names the London and Paris houses together.

A separate explanatory treatment in this book's research names the Paris house and the Naples house of the Rothschilds as the lenders, and in another version names the London house, N M Rothschild & Sons.
What the account does show is that Carl Mayer and James both appear in the record of the 1832 loan.

The Jewish Encyclopedia, published by Funk & Wagnalls between 1901 and 1906, and compiled, according to the account, by about 400 Jewish and non-Jewish scholars, describes the Rothschilds in its "Rothschild" entry as "guardians of the papal treasure."

The account reads the phrase in strong terms: as proof that the connection was publicly known by 1906, was not treated as secret by the parties, and was understood as a custodial relationship in which the Rothschilds managed papal assets rather than simply lending.
The loans drew hostility from Catholic critics, and the record is clear about its character.
Catholic criticism at the time, as a remark by Alfred de Vigny shows, centered on the Rothschilds' Jewishness.
Objection to a lender because he is a Jew is antisemitism, and this book names it as such.
The territorial state that did the borrowing ended in 1870, with the fall of the Papal States.

The Roman families who stayed loyal to the Pope afterwards, the Black Nobility, including the Orsini and the Colonna, distanced themselves from the new Italian monarchy in a specific act of protest: they kept the doors of their palaces closed in mourning.
The settlement that later compensated it for the lost territory, and what it did to the Black Nobility's court positions, belong to 1929 and are told in .

It runs from the 1831 arrangement through the Torlonia family's rental of their Roman villa to Mussolini (from 1923 in one account and from 1925 in another, until 1943) to the appointment in 2026 of François Pauly, a former chief executive of the Edmond de Rothschild group, as president of the supervisory board of the Vatican bank, dated 25 March 2026 in one account and 28 April 2026 in another.

The discipline that applies to them applies here too: each is separately documented, nothing in the record shows that they form one continuous project, and the 2026 appointment is an institutional adjacency, a former executive of a bank that bears the Rothschild name, not a family tie.
The documented core is modest and real: the 1832 loan of £400,000 to Gregory XVI, and the religious hostility it drew.
Edmond de Rothschild's Colonies, and His Refusal of Herzl
The colonies that grew through the gaps in the Ottoman rules had a patron in Paris.
A durable story holds that the Rothschilds funded Zionism from the beginning, and that Herzl's movement was their project.

One member of the family, Baron Edmond de Rothschild of the Paris house, paid for and ran Jewish agricultural colonies in Ottoman Palestine for some fifteen years before Herzl wrote a word about a Jewish state.
When Herzl came to him in 1896 asking for backing for a political movement, Edmond refused.
The First Zionist Congress met in Basel the following year without him .

Edmond's money came from the Paris branch of the family bank, de Rothschild Frères, which his father, James Mayer Rothschild (1792–1868), the youngest of Mayer Amschel Rothschild's five sons, had built into the largest private bank in France, as  describes.
When James died in 1868 the bank passed principally to his sons Alphonse and Gustave.
Edmond, the youngest, was 23.
Edmond was born in 1845 at Boulogne-Billancourt and trained in mining engineering and art collecting rather than banking .
His turn to Palestine came out of the crisis of 1881–82.
After the assassination of Alexander II in 1881, pogroms in the Russian Empire sent thousands of Jewish refugees westward; some reached Palestine and met agricultural failure and disease.
In 1882 Rishon LeZion, a new settlement south of Jaffa, was collapsing within months of its founding for want of water and of agricultural knowledge.
Rabbi Samuel Mohilever appealed to Edmond, and Edmond accepted the appeal and began to fund the colony .
In 1883, according to a reference summary, the settlers' central committee transferred Zikhron Ya'akov's assets to him .

Over the following years he financed and administered roughly thirty Jewish agricultural colonies, including Rishon LeZion, Zikhron Ya'akov and Rosh Pinna, and earned the Hebrew title HaNadiv HaYadua, "the known benefactor"  .
The principal settlements are documented in Ran Aaronsohn's Rothschild and Early Jewish Colonization in Palestine (2000) and Simon Schama's Two Rothschilds and the Land of Israel (1978).
Zikhron Ya'akov, "in memory of Jacob," was named for Edmond's father James, whose Hebrew name was Jacob; Mazkeret Batya was named for his mother, Betty, in Hebrew Batya .
The colonies were run on Edmond's terms, through an administrative system of his own, and the colonists complained of his administrators .
It flowed from a private fortune in Paris to officials employed by the donor, who managed the colonies on his behalf.

One detailed account gives approximately $5–6 million in period dollars, roughly $200 million in modern terms, and estimates it at about 40 percent of all early capital invested in the Jewish settlements, calling Edmond the single largest private funder of pre-state Jewish settlement.

Its table of every documented money stream opens with Edmond's colonies, from 1882 to 1924, and records the amount as "Not totaled in the record," with what the money bought given as "~30 settlements, later handed to PICA (1924)."
Every later stream in that table, from the Jewish Colonial Trust of 1899 to the Export-Import Bank loan of 1949, begins after Herzl's movement was founded; Edmond's is the only one that predates it.
In 1896 Edmond instructed the Jewish Colonization Association, the society founded by Baron Maurice de Hirsch in 1891 and described in the next section, to begin lending to colonists .

Another account dates the decisive step to 1899, when, frustrated by the cost of directly managing some thirty settlements, he transferred their formal administration to the Association, whose Palestine operations became a subsidiary .
Hirsch was a separate philanthropist and no relation.
Into this world Herzl came in the summer of 1896, months after publishing Der Judenstaat.
He was asking for something different in kind from what Edmond had been doing: a state secured by charter, not colonies secured by purchase.
Edmond declined.

Herzl's diary for 22–26 July 1896 records his "rude telegram to Edmond Rothschild" and his resolve that "from Rothschild's negative attitude I must salvage everything"; he turned instead to organizing the Basel Congress of 1897 .

In it Edmond first refused to receive Herzl in Paris; then, in July 1896, the two met through an intermediary, and Edmond told Herzl to his face that he opposed political Zionism and would not fund it, an exchange this account also places in Herzl's diary .

Edmond preferred quiet philanthropic settlement to political statehood, believing that Jewish safety could be advanced by slow agricultural facts on the ground without a statehood project that would attract international opposition.

And he thought that political and diplomatic Zionism, with its public meetings with the Sultan and its talk of territorial concessions, would alienate the Ottoman rulers whose consent his settlements needed, and so poison arrangements that were working .
The second reason fits what the Ottoman government was doing in the same years, when it was restricting Jewish immigration and land purchase in Palestine, as described in .
Edmond did not attend the Basel Congress in 1897 and continued to fund settlement through his own channels, not through the Zionist Organization Herzl founded there.
Herzl died in 1904; Edmond went on funding settlement for another thirty years without changing his position on political Zionism .

Edmond's philanthropic colonization and Herzl's political Zionism, which produced the Congress, the Organization and eventually the state, were separate projects, and the second was launched after the first's patron had refused it .

In 1924 Edmond transferred them to the Palestine Jewish Colonization Association, PICA, which after his death in 1934 was presided over by his son James, and which continued land purchase and settlement through the British Mandate .

The detailed account credits PICA with approximately 500,000 dunams (125,000 acres) by the 1930s and offices in Paris, London and Jerusalem, and says that in 1957 PICA transferred its remaining holdings and functions to the Jewish Agency for Israel .
Another source names Yad Hanadiv as PICA's successor, still acting in Israel for Rothschild family trusts, and records that James and Dorothy de Rothschild later funded the Knesset building .
Edmond was buried first in Paris; in 1954 his remains were moved to Ramat HaNadiv, "the Hill of the Benefactor," a memorial site in Israel he had funded in his lifetime .
David Ben-Gurion called him "the builder of the Jewish Yishuv" .
Walter Rothschild of the London branch was the addressee of the Balfour letter in 1917, a document drafted by others; Edmond of the Paris branch funded colonies and opposed Herzl .
Neither, on this record, set the course of political Zionism.
The two branches did converge later, through Walter's receipt of the 1917 letter and through PICA's land work under the Mandate .

The story that "the Rothschilds paid for it all" is examined elsewhere in this library against the whole record of pre-state funding, which shows money coming overwhelmingly from mass small-donor giving, with over a million American contributors in 1948 alone, and records that the Paris Rothschild who funded the early colonies opposed Herzl; see .
Rothschild money did build much of the physical foundation of the early settlements, and that is documented and substantial.

The idea that "the Rothschilds" as a family engineered Zionism collapses one man's philanthropy, another man's ceremonial role and a political movement that one of them refused into a single hidden hand, which is the shape of an old antisemitic story, not of the record.

It holds that without Edmond's money the First Aliyah would probably have collapsed at Rishon LeZion; that his combination of capital, agricultural assistance and management of relations with the Ottoman authorities produced the first lasting colonies and a template for later waves of immigration, the Second Aliyah of 1904–1914 and the Third of 1919–1923; and that the Ottoman restrictions of the period were a reaction to what his colonies made possible.

It traces a line from those colonies, through the Jewish population and territorial position of 1917, to the state of 1948 and to the displacement of Palestinians in that year, while stating that Edmond, who died in 1934, took no part in the events of 1948 and was not their sole cause.

This reading is a counterfactual, and parts of it rest on dates that the diplomatic documents of the period complicate: it places the first Ottoman land restrictions in 1892, a date that is itself disputed.

The same account lists what survives of his work today, without sources: the settlements as Israeli towns and cities, Rishon LeZion among the country's largest, with more than 300,000 people; Ramat HaNadiv, where he and his wife Adelheid are buried; an Edmond de Rothschild Foundation in Israel working in education, the arts and science rather than political advocacy; his portrait on a 500-shekel note of the 1982–1985 series; and streets named for the family in several cities.
It concludes that the family has no significant role in present-day political lobbying for Israel.
The total Edmond spent is not documented in any cited source, and the much-repeated figures for it are estimates without citation.
Whether he met Herzl in July 1896 or only exchanged messages depends on which account of the diary is followed.

The dates of his handover to the Jewish Colonization Association (1896 or 1899) and the relation between that step and PICA's creation in 1924 are reported differently, as is PICA's end (a transfer to the Jewish Agency in 1957, or succession by Yad Hanadiv).
His reasons for refusing Herzl are attributed to his correspondence, which is not quoted in the material available.
Catholic Rome borrowed from Jewish bankers, and its critics attacked the lenders for their religion.
In Protestant Britain, in the same decade, Jews entered politics by another door, as the subject of a prophecy.
A common assumption holds that Christian political support for a Jewish state was a product of the twentieth century: a response to the Holocaust and to the founding of Israel in 1948.

Before any Jewish political movement for a state existed, a Protestant current in Britain and the United States had already put the idea of a Jewish "restoration" to Palestine before a Foreign Secretary and a President.
Restorationism, the belief that a Jewish return to Palestine would fulfil biblical prophecy, was an organized political current decades before Theodor Herzl.
The British story begins inside a family.
Anthony Ashley-Cooper, Lord Shaftesbury, was an evangelical peer and reformer.
He was also Palmerston's stepson-in-law: the Foreign Secretary, Lord Palmerston, was his wife's stepfather.
In 1839 Shaftesbury pressed Palmerston to sponsor Jewish settlement in Palestine under British protection.
Shaftesbury's request needed a government to carry it, and the Ottoman sultan, who ruled Palestine, answered to no British minister.
What Shaftesbury had was the ear of the Foreign Secretary, whose instructions reached Constantinople.
Palmerston acted.
In 1840 he instructed his ambassador at Constantinople to urge the Ottoman sultan to encourage Jewish settlement, and Britain's new consulate in Jerusalem was given a brief to protect Jews.
Those were the two instruments Britain used: diplomatic pressure on the sultan's government, and a consul on the ground who could take named people under his protection.
The decision to admit or encourage settlers lay with the Porte, and the instruction asked the sultan to use a power that only he held.
Shaftesbury and Palmerston saw a protected Jewish presence as a British foothold in Ottoman Syria; American evangelicals read the same prospect as prophecy.
What neither reading drew on was Jewish opinion.
Most Jewish communal bodies of the period opposed restorationism or ignored it.
The idea was advanced on behalf of Jews, by Christians, for reasons of prophecy and empire.

The earliest published version of "a land without a people for a people without a land" appeared in an 1843 book by Alexander Keith, a Church of Scotland clergyman and an advocate of Jewish "restoration" who had traveled to Palestine in 1839.
His own phrase for Palestine was a country without a nation for a nation without a country.
The first use by a Zionist came only in 1901, when Israel Zangwill wrote that Palestine was "a country without a people."
The phrase was first published by a Christian restorationist more than half a century before the first recorded Zionist use.
Against the first, the counts are plain: every Ottoman and British census shows a populated country.
Keith, the man who first published the phrase, had visited Palestine and knew it was populated.
Whichever reading is preferred, the phrase described a country that had people in it.

The same set of checks examines two other claims that are often paired with this one, that Arab leaders "rejected every offer" and that the conflict is a religious war two thousand years old; both concern later periods and are taken up in .
The American counterpart came half a century after Shaftesbury.
In March 1891 the Chicago evangelist William E. Blackstone presented President Benjamin Harrison with a petition urging American support for a Jewish homeland in Palestine.
The Blackstone Memorial, as it became known, was signed by more than four hundred prominent Americans, among them John D. Rockefeller, J. P. Morgan and the Chief Justice.
It preceded Herzl's Der Judenstaat by five years and the first Zionist Congress at Basel by six.
The instrument was different from Palmerston's.
Shaftesbury had worked through a minister who could instruct an ambassador; Blackstone worked through public petition, using the names of men of finance and law to press a head of state.
The familiar order runs from a Jewish political movement to Christian sympathy for it.
The documents run the other way: Christian political support for a Jewish return came first, and Jewish political Zionism came second.

By the time the Zionist movement had an organization, a Christian political base for a Jewish state already existed in Britain and the United States, at a time when most Jewish communal bodies still opposed or ignored the idea.
That ordering helps explain why the Balfour Declaration of 1917 found a ready constituency in Britain's governing class.
In 1909 the Scofield Reference Bible gave it a theology: its dispensationalist reading made support for a Jewish state a mass Protestant doctrine.
Balfour, whose name the 1917 declaration bears, was himself a Christian restorationist.
Later still, Christians United for Israel in the Hagee era stands at the twentieth-century end of a lineage that begins in 1839, not in 1948.
The Scofield Bible and its public belong to the next part of this book, in .

Before the Zionist Congress, and before Rothschild money built colonies in Palestine, Protestant restorationism had already made a Jewish return a live question in British and American politics, for reasons of prophecy and empire that had little to do with Jewish opinion.
That constituency, not any single family, was the pre-existing structure into which the Zionist project would later connect.

It does not follow that restorationists created Zionism, which had its own Jewish sources in prayer, persecution and nationalism, nor that they could deliver Palestine: in 1840 and in 1891 the land was the sultan's, and neither a Foreign Secretary nor a President could do more than ask.
The text of Palmerston's 1840 instruction is not quoted in these sources, and neither the sultan's response nor any settlement it produced is recorded.
The consulate's brief to protect Jews is documented; what the consuls did with it in these decades is not described here.
The record does not say how Harrison answered Blackstone, or whether the memorial changed anything in American policy.
And the statement that most Jewish communal bodies opposed or ignored restorationism is made in general terms, without naming the bodies or their statements.
The City of London is often bundled with two other capitals into a single story.
In its most common form, the City of London, Vatican City and Washington, DC are three sovereign city-states that together and in secret govern the world's finance, its religion and its military.
As the previous section showed, the City of London Corporation is a local authority whose privileges are preserved by express exception in Acts of Parliament.
It has an electorate that includes businesses, and an official lobbyist, the Remembrancer, who watches the Commons from its under-gallery.
Parliament legislates for it, and the Crown Dependencies have more autonomy than it does.
Vatican City.
Vatican City became sovereign on 11 February 1929, through the Lateran Treaty with Mussolini's Italy.
The treaty recognized papal sovereignty over an enclave of 44 hectares, and Italy paid the Holy See compensation for the Papal States it had lost in 1870.
Before 1929 there was no Vatican state in this sense, so the enclave cannot have been a sovereign partner in any arrangement reaching back into the period this volume covers.
Its financial bodies, the IOR, APSA and the Governorate, publish no statements equivalent to those of a comparable secular institution, and they sit outside EU banking regulation.
The District of Columbia.
Washington, DC is a federal district under the exclusive legislative authority of Congress, under Article I, Section 8 of the United States Constitution.

sent: Its residents have elected a mayor and council only since the District of Columbia Home Rule Act of 1973, and Congress keeps a veto over the District's legislation.
Its roughly 700,000 residents have no voting member in either house of Congress.
The 1973 Act, like the Lateran Treaty, belongs to a later period; it appears here only to fix what kind of place the District legally is.
The "empire of three cities" assigns each enclave a portfolio: finance to London, religion to Rome, the military to Washington.
One is a medieval corporation kept alive by Parliament's exceptions.
One is a sovereign created by a twentieth-century treaty with Italy.
One is a federal district that its own Congress governs.
Where a later section of this volume meets real antisemitic material, such as hostility to the papal loans framed around the lenders' Jewishness, it names it as what it is.

Each is a genuine carve-out from ordinary accountability: a franchise for business inside a national legislature, a sovereign's financial bodies outside EU banking regulation, a capital whose residents have no vote in the body that governs them.
When the First Zionist Congress met at Basel in August 1897, it did not build the structures that would later fund, permit, bless or block a Jewish state.
A common assumption, reading backward from the twentieth century, holds that the Zionist movement created the international power structures that later supported Israel.

By 1896 a sovereign state in Istanbul governed Palestine and had already written rules against Jewish settlement there; European powers held rights inside that state that let those rules leak; a British Parliament seated a lobby for finance; banking houses had long lent to governments and to the Pope; Protestant restorationists had wanted a Jewish Palestine for sixty years; a Vatican would refuse one; a Rothschild had already said no to Herzl; and in Palestine itself Arab notables and Jewish communities had their own institutions and quarrels.
The state piece: Britain and the City.

The British state that would issue the Balfour Declaration in 1917 governed through a Parliament in which the Corporation of the City of London held a business franchise and kept its Remembrancer, a Corporation official seated in the Commons and reviewing legislation for the City's interests.
ents: the Corporation of the City of London

sent: Since 1694 the British Crown had borrowed from private subscribers through a chartered company in the City, the Bank of England, created to finance William III's war against France.
Finance had both a seat inside the legislature and a standing channel into the Treasury.
Parliament legislated for it, and its own description of its role, "rather like a trade body", is the documented finding.
The Rothschild houses were documented creditors to Britain and Prussia, and from 1832 to the Holy See.

The London house arranged a £5 million sterling loan for Prussia in 1818 and in November 1875 advanced the £4,000,000 with which Disraeli's government bought 44% of the Suez Canal shares, a purchase Disraeli defended as "a highway to our Indian Empire".
The 1832 papal loan of £400,000 is documented, though the sources differ on whether the London or the Paris house was the counterparty.
From 1882 the Paris house, through Baron Edmond de Rothschild, financed agricultural colonies in Palestine, roughly thirty of them by one count, on his own philanthropic terms.
In July 1896 Edmond refused to back Herzl's political project.
Edmond's money built settlements and refused the movement.
Baron Maurice de Hirsch's money, £2,000,000 of authorized capital in the Jewish Colonization Association from 1891, chose Argentina and sought no state.
Herzl in 1896 had a program; the sources here record no fortune behind it.
The two great philanthropic fortunes this chapter documents were therefore committed to resettlement on terms other than those of political Zionism, a year before its Congress met.
The church piece: a Protestant yes, a Catholic no.
Protestant restorationists in Britain and the United States had pressed for a Jewish Palestine since 1839, when Lord Shaftesbury urged Palmerston to sponsor it.
In March 1891 the Blackstone Memorial, signed by more than four hundred prominent Americans, asked President Benjamin Harrison to support a Jewish homeland in Palestine.
Their motives were prophecy and empire, and most Jewish communal bodies of the period opposed or ignored them.
The papacy had lost the Papal States in 1870 and held a different theology.

When Herzl went to Rome, in January 1904 by one source's date (another places the meeting between 1901 and 1903), Pope Pius X refused him on the ground that the Church could not support a Jewish restoration to a land central to its own theology while the Jews denied Christ.
The Holy See did not recognize Israel until 30 December 1993, forty-five years after its founding.
The sovereign piece: the Ottoman state.
None of the pieces above held power in Palestine.
The Ottoman Empire did, and it had already acted.
In June 1882 it forbade the entry of foreign Jews and their purchase of land; in July 1882 it allowed Jews to settle anywhere in the empire except Palestine, provided they took Ottoman nationality.
Through the late 1880s foreign Jews were admitted to Jerusalem only as pilgrims, for one month and later three.

An Ottoman note of 27 March 1894 barred Jewish immigrants from acquiring property in Palestine "for political reasons", for "the prevention of the permanent establishment in Palestine of Jewish immigrants".
When Herzl sought a charter in 1896, his diary records the Sultan's message that he could not sell even a foot of the land, because it belonged to his people.

Under the Capitulations and the protégé system, foreign Jews could live under European consular protection, and Britain had declared in 1847 that its consulates would protect Jews whose own states did not.

Britain and the United States protested the restrictions on grounds of religious equality, Britain citing Article 62 of the Treaty of Berlin (1878), which declared that "in no part of the Ottoman Empire shall difference of religion be alleged against any person".

From Prayer to Program: The Thinkers and Groups Before Herzl, 1840–1890
The debate over the Three Oaths turned on whether people might bring about the return themselves.
A common account has Zionism springing fully formed from the mind of Theodor Herzl in 1896.
Herzl came last.

That distinction matters for everything that follows, because the religious argument over the Three Oaths, set out in the previous section, turns on exactly this question: whether the return is something people may bring about, or something they must wait for.
Yehuda Alkalai, a Sephardi rabbi in Semlin, urged practical settlement in the land as a step toward redemption.
He did so after the Damascus affair of 1840, a blood-libel case.
Zvi Hirsch Kalischer, a rabbi in Thorn, made a parallel case in a book of 1862: redemption, he argued, could begin by natural means, through settling and farming the land.
In the same year as Kalischer's book, 1862, the secular socialist Moses Hess published Rome and Jerusalem.
Twenty years later, after the pogroms of 1881, the Odessa physician Leon Pinsker published Auto-Emancipation (1882), which argued that Jews needed a territory of their own, not necessarily Palestine.
Ideas became groups in the 1880s.
Local societies calling themselves Hovevei Zion, "Lovers of Zion", spread across the Russian Empire.
In 1884 they met in conference at Kattowitz, under Pinsker's leadership.
Pinsker's own pamphlet had not insisted on Palestine, and he and other early organizers discussed several territories before the movement settled on it.
Two years earlier, in 1882, a student group called BILU had sent its first pioneers to the land.
Finally, in 1890, Nathan Birnbaum coined the word "Zionism".
The motives recorded across these writers are four: persecution and pogroms; the failure of emancipation to end antisemitism; the age of European nationalism; and religious longing.
A fifth current pushed from outside the Jewish world altogether: Christian restorationism in Britain and America.
Alkalai and Kalischer argued from redemption; Hess from nationalism and socialism; Pinsker from physical safety.
Herzl's role was real and decisive in one respect: he did not invent the idea, but he gave a scattered movement an organization, a diplomacy and a bank, beginning in 1897.

Does Scripture Forbid a Jewish State?
Jeremiah, the Three Oaths, and a Debate Older Than Zionism
While Ottoman law was turning the land of Palestine into registered deeds, an older argument about the land ran inside Judaism.
Two confident answers circulate about what Jewish tradition says on a Jewish state.
One holds that Judaism commands it.
The other holds that Judaism forbids it.
The texts tell a different story: the question was argued inside Judaism long before anyone founded a political movement, and it is still argued now.
The oldest text in the debate comes from the book of Jeremiah.
The Babylonian Talmud, in tractate Ketubot (110b–111a), derives from the Song of Songs three oaths.
Israel was not to go up to the land "as a wall", meaning en masse and by force.
Israel was not to rebel against the nations.
And the nations, in turn, were not to oppress Israel excessively.
Two of the three oaths bind Israel; the third binds the nations.
For many Orthodox authorities, the oaths settle the matter.

On this reading, a sovereign Jewish state established before the coming of the Messiah violates them: a return to the land could come only through divine redemption, not human political action, and to force it is a transgression.
Rabbi Joel Teitelbaum, the rebbe of Satmar, built his work Vayoel Moshe, published in 1959, on the three oaths, and Neturei Karta holds the same view today.
Earlier, in 1912, Orthodox opposition to secular Zionism took organized form with the founding of Agudat Israel, whose story belongs to a later part of this library, including .
They cite as well Rabbi Abraham Isaac Kook, who would become the first Ashkenazi chief rabbi of Mandate Palestine and who saw even secular Zionism as part of the process of redemption.
Rav Kook's office, like Agudat Israel, lies beyond 1896; he enters this account as the clearest named voice of the reading that would answer the oaths.
Against the oaths themselves, religious Zionists have made two further arguments.
Others argue that the Balfour Declaration and the League of Nations supplied the nations' consent.
Both arguments are recorded as positions some religious Zionists hold, not as the view of every authority on that side.
The anti-Zionist reading can point to a Talmudic text that speaks directly to a mass return by force, and to the many Orthodox authorities who read it as barring a state before the Messiah.

The religious-Zionist reading can point to Nachmanides, a classical authority who treated settlement of the land as a commandment, and to the argument that the conditions the oaths assumed no longer held.
In 1885 American Reform Judaism, in its Pittsburgh Platform, rejected a return to Palestine altogether, on the ground that its members were "no longer a nation, but a religious community".
Most Orthodox Jews in Israel accept or support the state.
Anti-Zionist Haredi groups, Neturei Karta among them, remain a minority.
Zionism is a political movement; Judaism is a religion whose authorities have argued over that movement from its beginning.

The Land Code of 1858: How the Deeds Became Sellable
The Tanzimat's promise of secure property and a regular revenue took its most lasting form in land law.
A familiar account of the early Zionist land purchases holds that Jewish buyers acquired empty or unused land in Palestine from willing local owners.
The legal history begins earlier, in a set of Ottoman laws of 1856 to 1867 that decided who could hold a deed, whose name went on it, and who could buy it.
Those laws did not concern Zionism, which did not yet exist.

But they produced the documents through which land in Palestine would later change hands, and they explain how a sale could be perfectly lawful between owner and buyer and still pass over the heads of the people who farmed the land.
According to a reference summary drawing on work by Ruth Kark published in 1984, foreigners were officially barred from buying land in Palestine from 1856, and the ban held in practice until 1867.
In 1858, as part of the reforms known as the Tanzimat, the Ottoman state issued a Land Code, the Arazi Kanunnamesi.
The same year brought the Tabu law, the law of title deeds.

The two can be read as giving practical form to promises made in the Edict of Gülhane of 1839, which had pledged security of property, a regular tax system and regular conscription, as the  describes.
In Palestine the register opened a gap between who owned land on paper and who worked it.
A reference summary, citing Nasser Abufarha, gives the reason: registration brought taxes and conscription, and cultivators resisted it for that reason.
Title was frequently recorded instead in other names: village heads, urban merchants or notables, and absentee families living in Beirut and Damascus.

The same reference summary quotes Yehoshua Porath, writing in 1977, that the 1858 code "brought about the appropriation by the influential and rich families of Beirut, Damascus" and other cities of vast tracts.
Kark, in a study published in 2017, finds that land came to be concentrated in "families of urban effendis (absentee landlords)" who lived in cities in Lebanon, Syria, Egypt and Palestine.
In 1867 the Ottoman state issued a law allowing foreigners to acquire real property.

Its Article II, as quoted by the United States minister at Constantinople in a dispatch of 5 January 1898, placed foreign landowners "upon terms of equality with Ottoman subjects in all things that concern their landed property."
The United States accepted the law by protocol in 1874.
The barrier of 1856 was gone, and a foreign buyer stood, on paper, where an Ottoman subject stood.

Kark treats the three measures, the 1858 Land Code, the 1858 Tabu law and the 1867 law on foreigners, as one process of privatization, the process that began land survey, registration and mapping in nineteenth-century Palestine.
In her account, effendi ownership made it easier for Jewish immigrants to buy part of this land.
According to Kark, more than 52 estate buildings became the first core of Jewish agricultural settlements, and at least 15 became the core of German Christian settlements or religious institutions.
They were properties with buildings on them, held by owners who could sell, and they were bought by more than one kind of newcomer: German Christians as well as Jews.
The deeds did not wait for the British Mandate to become saleable.
By Kark's count, estates bought under Ottoman rule were already the cores of the first Jewish agricultural settlements.
The settlements of the First Aliyah, described in , were built on land that this legal sequence had made purchasable.

A thesis written at Marmara University in Turkey on land ownership by foreigners and Jews in late Ottoman Palestine calls the 1867 law, the "Safer Kanunu," an attempt to bring foreigners' purchases under legal control.
On that reading the law was meant to regulate, and Jews used gaps in it to buy fertile, strategic land on which the first settlements were later built.
The strongest form of this case is that the Ottoman state did try to keep control of land sales to outsiders, and that the purchases succeeded where the law fell short.
Kark's reading is structural.
The 1858–1867 laws together concentrated land in effendi hands, and that concentration made both Jewish and German Christian purchases easier.
Under the British Mandate the registered titles were the instruments that could be sold.
The largest single transfer to Zionist purchasing companies was the sale of the Beirut-based Sursock family's holdings in the Jezreel Valley in the early 1920s.
The 1858 code did not cause the Zionist project.
The sources here give no figure for how much land in Palestine went unregistered or was recorded in absentee names, and none for how many cultivators stood in the gap between title and tillage.
Kark's counts of more than 52 and at least 15 estate buildings are not broken down here by date or place.
The Marmara thesis is known only through its abstract, and the 1856 ban and the Porath and Abufarha passages only through a reference summary.
The Jews of Palestine before Herzl
The small share of Russia's emigrants who chose Palestine did not arrive in a country without Jews.
When Theodor Herzl published his case for a Jewish state in 1896, Jews had been living in Palestine, and arriving there, for the whole of the century.
They are easy to lose from view, because the story of political Zionism is usually told from Vienna, Odessa and Basel.

The record allows a rough count of them, and it shows that two quite different Jewish communities stood in the country by the 1890s: an older one centered on the holy cities, and a newer one of agricultural colonies founded from 1878 onward.
The older community, known as the Old Yishuv, had grown steadily through immigration well before any political program existed.
Büşra Barın, in a 2014 study of Ottoman policy toward Jewish immigration, estimates that about 5,000 Jews came to Palestine between 1800 and 1840 and roughly 25,000 between 1850 and 1880.
She puts the Old Yishuv at about 24,000 people in 1880, of whom 13,900 lived in Jerusalem .
A reference summary, citing Mordecai Elia (1971), gives a slightly lower figure for the same year, 23,000 .
On the eve of the first organized settlement movement, more than half of the country's Jews lived in one city, and Jerusalem's Jewish population was already counted in the thousands.
The strongest form of the Zionist case rested partly on continuity: Jews were not strangers to the country, and Jerusalem had a large Jewish population before any Zionist organization existed.
The Ottoman state that governed this community also permitted at least one Jewish institution from abroad to operate in it.
On 5 April 1870 an Ottoman firman, an imperial decree, permitted the Alliance Israélite Universelle to establish an agricultural school in Jaffa.
A copy of the firman is held by the Israel State Archives under the reference JM-ISA/AEB/83/32 .

It records an Ottoman grant of permission, through the regular instrument of imperial decree, to a foreign Jewish body to open an agricultural school in Palestine, eleven years before the pogroms in the Russian Empire set off the larger movement.
The First Aliyah, the first wave of Jewish immigration organized around settlement on the land, is conventionally dated 1881–1903.

According to a reference summary, Petah Tikva was first settled in 1878 and then re-established in 1882 after that first attempt failed; Gei Oni was also founded in 1878, and was taken over in 1882 by the settlers of Rosh Pinna.
Rishon LeZion and Zikhron Ya'akov also date from 1882, Ness Ziona from 1883, Gedera from 1884, Rehovot from 1890 and Hadera from 1891 .
The violence of 1881–84 in the Russian Empire and the laws that followed it form the background to this wave, told in .

In 1883 the settlers' central committee transferred Zikhron Ya'akov's assets to Baron Edmond de Rothschild of the Paris banking house , the first step in a patronage that is the subject of the section .
The First Aliyah was not only European.
Emigration from Yemen began in early 1881.
A reference summary states that a few hundred Jews left Sanaa and nearby towns for Palestine in 1881–82, part of a movement that continued almost without break until 1914 .

The arrivals are nonetheless the point at which the Jews of the Arab world enter this story as participants rather than as background: their migration began in the same years as the Russian one, from a different country and under a different government, and the record does not show that the two movements were organized together.
How many Jews came in the First Aliyah as a whole, and how many stayed, is disputed, and the range is wide.
Barın estimates about 20,000 to 30,000 arrivals .

A reference summary reports estimates running from 25,000, a Jewish Agency figure, to 60,000 in total, the latter from the historian Anita Shapira (2012), who also estimates that between 50 and 70 percent of those who came later left .
If Shapira's estimate of departures is right, a large share of the newcomers did not remain.

Barın puts the Jewish population of Palestine at about 50,000 by 1903; a reference summary gives about 55,000 at the period's close, without a source; and Elia, as cited in the same summary, gives 80,000 for 1907  .
Read together with the 1880 figure, they suggest that the Jewish population roughly doubled, or more than tripled, in a generation, depending on whose estimate is used.
That growth was what the Ottoman government was trying to limit in the same years, as  shows.
The newcomers also met opposition from Jews.

According to a reference timeline citing an edited scholarly volume (Sobel and Beit-Hallahmi, eds., Tradition, Innovation, Conflict, 2012), in the 1880s the Orthodox community of Jerusalem regarded emerging Zionism as a threat and reported Zionist newcomers to the Ottoman authorities .
That is a striking act: Jews in Jerusalem turning to the Ottoman state against other Jews over the new movement.
In Europe the objection was made on other grounds.
Adolf Jellinek, the preacher of Vienna's Jewish community, answered Leon Pinsker's Auto-Emancipation by denying that Jews had national characteristics as such.
"We are at home in Europe," he answered, as the historian Robert Wistrich is cited quoting him .
His objection went to the premise of Pinsker's pamphlet: that the Jews were a nation.
The record therefore shows a Jewish Palestine in 1896 that was older, more varied and more divided than the later national story usually allows.

It held a long-established religious community concentrated in Jerusalem; a scattering of colonies, several of them already dependent on one Paris donor; a small migration from Yemen; and Jewish critics of the national idea both in Jerusalem and in Europe.
The material used here does not describe how the Old Yishuv supported itself, how it was divided internally, or how its institutions worked, and this section does not attempt it.
The size of the Yemenite migration rests on an unsourced figure.

Whether Jerusalem's reports to the Ottoman authorities in the 1880s were the act of the community's leadership or of particular individuals is not stated in the source available, and the matter needs the underlying study to settle it.
The Bank, the War and the Debt
The City's privileges reach back past Magna Carta.
The institution through which the British state learned to borrow is younger, and this volume's clock starts with it, in 1694, because of a loan.
In that year a group of private subscribers lent the English Crown £1.2 million through a newly chartered company, and the company that held the loan became the Bank of England.
On 2 January 1672 the government of Charles II began what became known as the Stop of the Exchequer.
It suspended repayment of Exchequer orders and warrants, the instruments through which the Crown had borrowed.
The obligations were later estimated at £1,211,065 by the historian Horsefield, and the principal was assessed at £1,328,526 at the end of 1676; both figures come here through a reference summary.
The lenders who bore the loss were the goldsmith-bankers of London, and several were ruined.
Edward Backwell and Robert Vyner were among those who went bankrupt.
The Bank of England's own museum draws the line from that default to its founding.
Because Charles II had failed to repay the goldsmiths, they were unwilling to lend to the Crown again.
When William III needed money for his war against France, he had to find another lender.
This is the Bank's explanation of its own origins, offered by its museum, and it should be read as such.

The Bank's 1970 booklet The Bank of England: History and Functions states the purpose in the same terms: the Bank was "incorporated by Act of Parliament and Charter in 1694" to help "finance the war being fought by William III against Louis XIV of France."
The scheme came from a Scottish merchant, William Paterson.
He proposed that members of the public lend the government £1.2 million, a sum the Bank itself puts at about £200 million in today's money.
The Bank was formally established by Royal Charter on 27 July 1694.

According to a reference summary of the national debt's history, which draws on H. Roseveare's The Financial Revolution 1660–1760 (1991), the charter was granted through the Tonnage Act 1694, and Sir John Houblon became the first governor.
The new institution first did business in the Hall of the Mercers' Company in Cheapside.

Instead of individual goldsmiths exposed to a royal default, as in 1672, the creditor was now a chartered corporation established by Act of Parliament and Charter, whose shares were held by its 1,268 subscribers.
The Crown gained what it had lost in 1672: access to credit for war, at well under half the rates the goldsmiths had typically charged.
What the Bank became is better documented than its founders' intentions.
It dates two later turning points: the Bank Act of 1844, which centralized the issue of banknotes in the Bank, and the Bank of England Act of 1946, which brought the Bank into public ownership.
Until 1946, then, the institution through which the British state borrowed and managed its debt was a privately owned company.
The debt that the Bank managed grew with each war.
At the end of the Napoleonic Wars, British government debt reached a peak of about £1 billion, more than 200% of GDP.
That figure is given by the reference summary, which takes it from the website ukpublicspending.co.uk, and it should be read as an estimate.

The Napoleonic Wars, which pushed the debt to its peak, were also the years in which one Frankfurt family placed its sons in five capitals and became the most reliable creditor to governments that kept falling, as  shows.
The London house that family founded would later lend to the British state directly, as  sets out.

The privileges of  and the borrowing machinery of the Bank are separate institutions in the sources used here, and this book keeps them separate.

On 27 September 1810 Mayer Amschel Rothschild and three of his sons, Amschel, Salomon and Carl, signed the first agreement, under the name Mayer Amschel Rothschild & Sons.
James, still under age, was to join when he came of age.
Nathan, already established in London, was not a party to it.
The capital was set out in gulden: 370,000 from the father, 185,000 each from Amschel and Salomon, and 30,000 each from Carl and James, James's share held without interest until he came of age.
Profits were divided in fifty parts, twenty-five to Mayer Amschel and twelve each to Amschel and Salomon.
Balance sheets themselves were to be drawn up, in the Archive's summary, only as soon as business allowed.
No partner could trade on the Stock Exchange without the others knowing first.

Disputes did not go to a court: they went to Mayer Amschel as arbitrator, and after his death to two arbitrators and a chairman, with a penalty of 20,000 thalers for any breach, payable within twenty-four hours.

A 2022 review of Natalie Livingstone's history of the family's women says the will explicitly barred female descendants, daughters and the wives of male descendants alike, from holding shares or having a say.

The Porte Says No, and the Arabs of Palestine Object, 1882–1896
A familiar account holds that the Ottoman Empire welcomed Jewish settlement in Palestine, or even sold the country to the Zionist movement.

From 1882, within months of the first colonies, the Ottoman government in Constantinople, known to diplomats as the Porte, issued a series of rules meant to keep foreign Jews from settling in Palestine and from buying land there.
In the same years Arab notables in Jerusalem began to petition the government to enforce them.
According to Büşra Barın's study of Ottoman policy (Middle East Technical University, 2014), in June 1882 the entry of foreign Jews into Ottoman territory, and their purchase of land, were forbidden.
In July 1882 the rule was refined: Jews were allowed to settle anywhere in the empire except Palestine, provided they took Ottoman nationality .

A reference summary drawing on Neville Mandel's 1974 study dates the government's recognition of the new wave to November 1882, and records that restrictions were imposed despite a Sultan's permit issued in May of that year.
It adds that in 1882 the American minister in Constantinople, Lew Wallace, was told that Jews would be welcome anywhere in the empire except Palestine  .
Jews could become Ottoman subjects and live elsewhere in the empire.
On this reading, what the Porte would not accept was a concentration of foreign Jews in one district.

Barın writes that from 1882 only pilgrims were admitted to Palestine; from 1884 Jewish visitors needed visas from Ottoman consulates in their home countries; and pilgrim stays were limited to one month, later extended to three for Jews under foreign protection, whose passports were held against a red permit card .

Barın's own footnote says the card system was implemented from 1900, and the British and American diplomatic correspondence of 1887–88 documents the one-month and three-month limits without mentioning a card at all   .
On 5 March 1887 the British consul in Jerusalem, Noel Temple Moore, reported to his ambassador that foreign Jews were "only allowed to come on a pilgrimage to Jerusalem for one month."
The governor of Jerusalem gave three reasons: poverty, the overcrowding of the Jewish quarter, and public health.

The ambassador, Sir William White, replied on 19 October 1887 that the rule was "ipso facto null and void" for persons under British protection, citing the Capitulations, the treaty privileges of foreigners in the Ottoman Empire .
Britain had already protested to the Porte in September 1887 .
The American record adds the Porte's own explanation.
On 28 January 1888 the United States minister, Oscar Straus, reported that the Porte had limited the stay of foreign Jews at Jerusalem to one month and planned to extend it to three.
The Grand Vizier gave him two reasons: tensions with Christians at Easter, and a rumor that Jews meant to re-establish a Jewish kingdom around Jerusalem.
The American consul reported that a shipload of Russian Jews had been refused landing at Jaffa about two years earlier .
An Ottoman note of 2 March 1888 then set the rule in writing: foreign Jews would be admitted only on passports stating a pilgrimage, and for at most three months.
On 19 May 1888 Straus told the State Department that the United States could not accept passport rules tied to religion, which he called "utterly repugnant" to the American Constitution .
The Porte framed its rule as public order and public health, and, to the Grand Vizier, as a guard against a political project.
The Western governments did not argue for Jewish settlement in Palestine.
Britain and the United States reached the same position from their own legal commitments; these papers show no sign of a shared plan, only a shared principle.

On 14 June 1893 the Foreign Office instructed its ambassador on petitions from British Jews in Jerusalem against regulations, in the Office's words, "Prohibiting Jews from buying & selling real Estate in Palestine."
It held that rules aimed at Jews for their religion were inconsistent with Article 62 of the Treaty of Berlin .

An Ottoman note of 27 March 1894, quoted by the American minister in a dispatch of 1898, forbade Jewish immigrants to acquire real property in Palestine "for political reasons."
Its stated object was "the prevention of the permanent establishment in Palestine of Jewish immigrants."
The rule applied to native and foreign Jews alike, but a purchase could go ahead on a consular certificate stating that the buyer was not in a barred class .
The note is the clearest single statement of Ottoman purpose in this period.
A reference summary, citing the historians Ocak (2002) and Porath (1977), dates it to 1892 and says it applied even to Ottoman Jewish subjects .
Barın describes a decree of 1893 for Jewish immigrants in Jerusalem, extended the following April to all Jews .
The text that American diplomats treated as operative is the note of 27 March 1894, and in July 1893 the Grand Vizier had said that earlier restrictions were already modified  .

Barın finds that enforcement was undermined by the Capitulations and the protégé system, which let foreign Jews live in Palestine under European consular protection; Britain had declared in 1847 that its consulates would protect Jews whose own states did not.
Despite the bans, she concludes, more than 50,000 Jews settled .
The Porte could issue notes.
Local officials could refuse a landing at Jaffa or block a sale.
But a Jew who held a British, American or other foreign passport could appeal to a consul, the consul could appeal to an ambassador, and the ambassador could invoke treaties the Porte had signed.
On this record, a Jew without a foreign protector was the most exposed to the rules and a protected foreigner the least, and the settlements grew through the gaps.
The same years saw the first organized response from the Arab population of Palestine.
Emanuel Beška, in a 2007 study of Arab responses to Zionism before 1908, dates modern Jewish immigration and colonization to the 1880s and finds that Arab opposition took time to form.

According to a reference timeline citing Neville Mandel's The Arabs and Zionism before World War I, on 24 June 1891 Arab notables in Jerusalem petitioned the Grand Vizier to prohibit Russian Jews from entering Palestine and from buying land there .

A 1978 review of Mandel's book in The Detroit Jewish News describes the same action differently, as a protest telegram from Arab leaders in Jerusalem and Jaffa calling for an end to Jewish immigration and land purchase, sent "barely a decade after the arrival of the Bilu'im," the BILU pioneers .
A Jewish Agency historical overview agrees that Jerusalem notables made the request in 1891 and says it was "repeated time and again" .
Whether it was a petition or a telegram, and whether Jaffa's leaders joined it, the sources leave open.
The most persistent opponent in the record was the mufti of Jerusalem, Muhammad Tahir al-Husayni.
Beška finds that he followed Jewish immigration "since the 1880s" and took an active stance against it .
He should not be confused with an earlier mufti of the city, Tahir Afandi al-Husayni, who acted as a mediator in the revolt of 1834 and was later exiled ; the sources name them separately.
On 15 March 1893 the firm J. Frutiger & Co. complained to the German consul that the governor of Jerusalem and a "Commission for Sale" chaired by al-Husayni were blocking land sales to Jews.
The firm said the ban had been "abolished some time ago"; the mufti held that it remained in force under new regulations.
On 12 May 1893 the consul complained to his ambassador of a campaign to prompt Muslim petitions for a comprehensive ban .

Here the Ottoman rules and the Arab response meet in a single office: a local religious official sat on a commission that applied the state's land policy, read that policy strictly, while a European consul complained of a campaign to prompt petitions that would make it stricter still.
In 1895 Najib al-Hajj, editor of the Cairo paper Abu al-Hol, accused Jewish colonists of taking the means of livelihood of Arabs, according to a related paper excerpted with Beška's article .
Just after the period of this chapter, in 1897, a committee chaired by al-Husayni put land sales to Jews in the Jerusalem district on hold for several years .
The Jewish Agency overview describes the earlier local opposition as sporadic attacks and disputes over land and says it is "doubtful whether this opposition had any political connotations" .

The other side, drawing on Mandel as cited and on Beška, holds that the opposition was directed at the state from the start: the 1891 approach to the Grand Vizier and the mufti's campaign of 1893 over land sales were acts aimed at changing Ottoman policy, made by notables through the government's own channels   .
The Jewish Agency overview itself records the 1891 request and its repetition; the dispute is over whether the earlier peasant clashes carried political meaning, not over whether the notables acted.
On the evidence here, by 1891 at the latest Jerusalem notables were making a demand of their government about immigration and land; whether to call it political is the point in dispute.
