The text, signatories and authors of the 1891 protest have not been found, so its form and whether Jaffa joined remain uncertain.
There is no count here of how many Jews were turned away under the rules, as against Barın's estimate of more than 50,000 who settled regardless.
Palestine in the Ottoman Order, 1799–1840
Of the powers on the board of 1815, the one that actually governed Palestine was the Ottoman Empire.
Two opposite misconceptions are often told about Palestine before the twentieth century.
One holds that the Middle East has always been a set of hostile nations locked in permanent war.
The other comes in two forms that contradict each other: that the Ottomans "occupied" Palestine the way later settlers did, or that Palestine was an empty Ottoman backwater.
From 1516 to 1917 the Ottoman Empire governed most of the Arab Middle East as provinces of a single state, without international borders between them.
Damascus, Baghdad, Jerusalem and Beirut were provincial cities of the same state, and people and goods moved among them without passports.
The states that define the region's later conflicts, Syria, Iraq, Lebanon, Jordan and Israel, did not exist.
Iran stood apart: it was never Ottoman, and it had its own dynasty, its own language and a Shia majority.
Almost every border that matters in today's conflicts was drawn later, in a six-year window between 1916 and 1922, by two European powers, Britain and France.

Under the millet system, recognized religious communities (Muslims, Christians of several churches, and Jews) administered their own religious law, courts and schooling, and governed marriage, inheritance and education under their own leaders.
Its costs were real: heavy taxation, conscription, periodic violence, and a second-class status for non-Muslims, who paid special taxes and held lesser standing.
Palestine sat inside this order as a set of administrative units rather than as a country with its own frontier.

Apart from a period of Egyptian rule from 1831 to 1840, it was administered as Ottoman provinces, chiefly the district of Jerusalem and parts of the provinces of Beirut and Damascus, with no border separating it from what are now Syria, Lebanon or Jordan.

Governors, garrisons and tax collectors ruled over a population that remained largely Arabic-speaking Muslims and Christians, with long-established Jewish communities in Jerusalem, Hebron, Safed and Tiberias.

It ended when British forces captured Jerusalem in December 1917, and the Republic of Turkey, founded in 1923, formally renounced all rights over the former Arab provinces in the Treaty of Lausanne that year.
Modern Turkey is the empire's successor state, not a claimant to the land.
It is mentioned here only to mark where the Ottoman story ends.
In the first, the Ottoman order of 1516 to 1917, with no internal borders, is the root from which the later layers of the region grow, beginning with the Anglo-French carve-up of 1916 to 1922.
In the second, Ottoman rule is the first station in the long relationship between Turkey and Israel, and the next is the 1923 renunciation at Lausanne.
Within a single generation, a French army, an Egyptian army, a peasant revolt and a coalition of European fleets all fought over the coast and hills of Palestine.
On this section's reading, the decisive choices were made each time in Paris, Cairo, Istanbul or London.
The first pressure came from France.
During his Egyptian and Syrian campaign, Napoleon Bonaparte besieged Acre in 1799, and the campaign was defeated by combined British and Ottoman forces.
He never reached Jerusalem.
The Jewish Virtual Library's account dates his retreat from Acre to 22 May 1799.
That is also the date given for a French newspaper report about him.

A reference summary of the scholarship records that the Gazette nationale of 3 Prairial, Year VII (22 May 1799) printed a short report that Bonaparte had invited the Jews of Asia and Africa to gather under his flag.
That newspaper item stands beside one of the most contested documents in the prehistory of Zionism.
A much fuller text, a "Letter to the Jewish Nation," headed "General Headquarters, Jerusalem,
[Year VII], April 20th, 1799" and addressed to the "rightful heirs of Palestine," was first published only in 1940, when Franz Kobler announced a German translation in The New Judaea.
The letter is dated and placed in Jerusalem, a city its supposed author never reached.
Historians have divided sharply over what, if anything, Napoleon proclaimed.
Simon Schwarzfuchs (1979), Henry Laurens, Ronald Schechter and Jeremy Popkin regard the German text as forged.
Schechter goes further and reads even the 1799 newspaper report as a rumor.
A French Jewish educational site calls the forgery "almost certainly established" and attributes it to Frankist circles.
The strongest form of this case rests on the document's history: it surfaces only in 1940, in translation, with no original, and its heading places Napoleon where he never was.
Mordechai Gichon argues that Napoleon did conceive of a Jewish national home in the Land of Israel.
Nathan Schur reads the 1799 report as propaganda aimed at local Jews.
The Jewish Virtual Library prints the letter and says only that its authenticity "has been debated ever since."

The strongest form of this side's case is that a contemporary French newspaper did print a report of an appeal to Jews in May 1799, so that something was said or rumoured at the time, whatever became of the text.
What the record does not settle is whether Bonaparte himself issued any appeal, what it said, and who composed the letter that appeared in 1940.
The second pressure came from Egypt, whose ruler, Muhammad Ali, fielded his own army against the Sultan.
Ibrahim Pasha, son of Egypt's ruler Muhammad Ali, invaded Ottoman Syria on 31 October 1831 and made Haifa his main base from December 1831.
According to a reference summary, Palestine remained under Egyptian rule until 1840.
Ibrahim's conscription order of 25 April 1834 required one Muslim man in five, beginning with 200 from Jerusalem, and conscripts were to serve for life.
He also disarmed Nablus and the Hebron district and imposed new taxes, including one on the Muslim administrative class.
Judith Mendelsohn Rood reconstructed it from the records of Jerusalem's Islamic court.

In her account, the revolt was led from Nablus by Qasim al-Ahmad, with 'Isa Amar leading the Hebron district, while the mufti of Jerusalem, Tahir Afandi al-Husayni, acted as mediator and was later exiled.
He should not be assumed to be the Muhammad Tahir al-Husayni who appears later in the ; the sources name the two muftis separately and do not connect them.
On 19 and 20 May 1834, about 36 rebels entered Jerusalem through an abandoned sewer near the Dung Gate and opened the gate to the rest.
Rood reports that Ibrahim lost 1,500 of his 9,000 soldiers in rebel ambushes.
The violence did not run along a single line: 33 Christian men and women of Bayt Jala were killed on suspicion of looting.
The sources differ on Hebron, and both versions are given here.
In Rood's account, Hebron was besieged on 24 July, and 630 young men were afterwards sent to Egypt for the army.
A reference summary instead dates Hebron's defeat to 4 August and gives about 500 killed and 750 men conscripted.
Rood's study rests on the Jerusalem court records, but neither figure can be confirmed against the other with the material in hand.
Qasim al-Ahmad was captured in Transjordan in August 1834 and beheaded in Damascus.
His sons were beheaded in Acre.
It states that some 10,000 peasants were deported to Egypt, and that deportation, conscription and flight together reduced Palestine's male population by about one-fifth.
The same source records the rebels' stated aim: to expel the Egyptians and restore Ottoman rule.
The question is whether 1834 was an early moment of Palestinian national identity.

Baruch Kimmerling and Joel Migdal, in The Palestinian People (2003), treat the revolt as formative, because it joined disparate groups against a common enemy, and those groups later re-emerged as the Palestinian people.

The strongest form of their case, as this section reads it, rests on the shape of the revolt itself: peasants and townspeople from Nablus, Jerusalem and the Hebron hills, with the city's religious leadership as intermediary, acting together against one ruler.
Benny Morris argues the opposite.
The rebels demanded no independence, they likely saw themselves as Ottoman subjects, Arabs or Syrians, and they left no lasting national tradition.
The reference summary that reports his view adds that the revolt is largely absent from Palestinian collective memory, and that its declared purpose was to restore the Ottomans, not to replace them.
Shimon Shamir sees the Egyptian period as the first application of the territorial state in Palestine.
Adel Manna argues that the way twentieth-century writers felt about the Ottomans and about Muhammad Ali shaped how the revolt was later written about.
On Manna's point, the debate over 1834 is partly a debate about the twentieth century carried back into the nineteenth.
The third pressure came from Europe, and it ended the Egyptian interlude.
On 15 July 1840, in the Convention of London, Britain, Austria, Prussia and Russia backed Sultan Abdülmecid I against Muhammad Ali.
They offered him hereditary rule of Egypt if he withdrew from Syria.
British and allied ships then shelled Beirut and Sidon on 11 September 1840 and bombarded Acre on 3 November 1840.
On 27 November 1840 Muhammad Ali accepted terms.
He withdrew from Syria and the Holy Land in return for hereditary rule of Egypt and Sudan.
Acre, where a French campaign had been defeated in 1799, was bombarded by European ships in 1840.
Britain's reason for acting was stated plainly, and it was not about Palestine as such.
In William Erich Ellison's 2024 analysis of the crisis, Britain sought to "preserve Turkey" as a route to India and as a bulwark against Russian expansion.
The same years saw a separate, religious current in British policy toward Jerusalem, which is told in .
In the same years, Istanbul began its own program of reform, the subject of .

The power to decide who ruled Palestine lay with the Sultan in Istanbul, with the ruler of Egypt in Cairo, who could raise his own army, and, by 1840, with a concert of European powers that could settle the question by treaty and enforce it with ships.
They could make Egyptian rule costly, at the price of deportations, executions and a lost fifth of the male population, if the reference figure is right.
That was settled in London in July 1840 and enforced off Acre in November, and the settlement returned the land to the empire that the rebels of 1834 had said they wanted back.
No original of Napoleon's supposed letter has been found, and the scholars who have studied it disagree about whether even the 1799 report reflects anything he said.
The Hebron figures differ between the court-record study and the reference summary.

And whether the revolt of 1834 was the first stirring of a Palestinian national identity, a provincial rising for the old order, or both at once remains a matter of interpretation on which the historians named here continue to disagree.
Reform from Istanbul: Edicts, a Constitution and Jerusalem's Deputy, 1839–1878
Palmerston's instruction of 1840 reached a sultan who had, the year before, begun to reform his empire from the center.

A claim met earlier in this chapter, in the sketch of the Ottoman Empire on the board of 1789–1815, holds that the Ottoman parliamentary reforms of 1876 gave Palestine representation and that "Palestinian delegates sat in the Ottoman parliament."
The record supports one named deputy for the district of Jerusalem in the parliament of 1877, a man who used his seat to oppose the sultan and lost it within a year.
To see what that seat was, and what it was not, the story has to begin almost four decades earlier, with a series of promises issued from Istanbul to all the sultan's subjects.
The reform era the Ottomans called the Tanzimat opened on 3 November 1839.
On that day Sultan Abdülmecid I proclaimed the Edict of Gülhane, at the urging of his Grand Vizier, Mustafa Reşid Pasha.

According to a reference account, which draws on Cleveland and Bunton and on Liebesny, the edict promised three things: security of life, honor and property; a regular system of taxation in place of tax farming; and regular conscription.
The mechanism matters for Palestine.
On this section's reading, the two practical promises of Gülhane, regular taxation and regular conscription, required the state to know who its subjects were and what they held.

That need is the thread that runs from this edict to the registration of land under the Land Code of 1858, the subject of the next section, where many cultivators avoided the register precisely because it brought taxes and conscription with it.
The Reform Edict of 18 February 1856 was issued as the Crimean War ended.

According to the reference account, it promised equality in education, government appointments and justice regardless of creed, freedom of worship, and mixed tribunals for cases between Muslims and non-Muslims.
Among its provisions was military service for non-Muslims, which proved unpopular.
On 23 December 1876 an Ottoman constitution was promulgated, and on 19 March 1877 the first Ottoman parliament opened at Dolmabahçe Palace.
The Institute for Palestine Studies' PalQuest counts 120 deputies, fourteen of them Arab.
The reference account of the First Constitutional Era gives 115 members, and for the second elections a split of 69 Muslim and 46 non-Muslim deputies.
Jerusalem's deputy in that chamber was Yusuf Diya al-Khalidi.
Born in Jerusalem in 1842, he was educated well beyond the city's own schools.
He studied at the al-Fakhriyya school, at the British Diocesan Boys' School in Jerusalem, at a Protestant college in Malta, and in Istanbul.
In 1875, two years before he took his seat, The Jewish Chronicle published two of his letters on the Jews of Palestine.
He had also served as head of Jerusalem's municipality, though the sources date that service differently.
PalQuest gives his mayoralty as 1870–1874, with two later terms.
Jerusalem Story says he was appointed in September 1865, at the age of 23, and headed the municipality for nine years.
In 1877 al-Khalidi was elected as the sole deputy for the Jerusalem mutasarrifate, and by PalQuest's count he was one of fourteen Arab deputies among 120.
Both biographical sources describe him as a prominent opponent of Sultan Abdul Hamid II in the chamber.
Abdul Hamid II suspended both the parliament and the constitution in February 1878, on 14 February in one account and on 13 February in another.
When the chamber was dissolved, al-Khalidi was one of ten opposition deputies ordered out of Istanbul.
Jerusalem's representation in the imperial parliament had lasted less than a year.

It is documented that the 1876 constitution produced a parliament in which the Jerusalem district had an elected deputy, and that this deputy, al-Khalidi, was a native of Jerusalem, a former head of the city's municipality and an outspoken member of the opposition.
It names one deputy for Jerusalem.
Fourteen Arab deputies sat by PalQuest's count, but the sources used here do not say which, if any, of the others sat for districts that lay in what would later be Palestine.
"Palestinian delegates" should therefore read, on present evidence, "Jerusalem's deputy."
In the same year the parliament closed, religious equality in the Ottoman lands was written into an international treaty.
Article 62 of the Treaty of Berlin of 1878 declared that "in no part of the Ottoman Empire shall difference of religion be alleged against any person."

Al-Khalidi's part in this book does not end in 1878.

On 1 March 1899, through Zadok Kahn, Chief Rabbi of France, he wrote to Theodor Herzl urging that Palestine be left in peace, and on 19 March Herzl replied that Jewish immigration would benefit the country.

The reference accounts of the two edicts say what was promised and that Gülhane was never fully implemented, but they do not measure how far either edict was carried out in the district of Jerusalem, or how the people of Palestine received them.
Al-Khalidi's years as head of the municipality are dated from 1865 in one biography and from 1870 in the other.

The Board Before the Game, 1789–1815
The Bank of England had given a state at war a way to borrow on a regular footing.
The wars against revolutionary and Napoleonic France would test that machinery, and they would make the fortune of the lenders who could serve it.
A common way of telling Israel's story begins with the Holocaust, as though nothing before it mattered.

The dynasties, states and religious institutions that would later fund the Zionist project, permit it or shape the ground it worked on were all in place by 1789, a full century before the political movement was founded.
Between 1789 and 1815 the Napoleonic wars redrew the map of Europe.
In those same years one Frankfurt family placed five sons in five capitals and, by 1815, had become the most reliable creditor to regimes that kept collapsing.
The Rothschild dynasty is real, and its banking history is one of the best-studied cases of dynastic finance in modern European history.
Mayer Amschel Rothschild.
The founder, Mayer Amschel Rothschild (1744–1812), was born in the Frankfurt Judengasse, the walled Jewish quarter where the law of the Holy Roman Empire required Frankfurt's Jews to live.
That trade was his entry into the economy of the German courts; he was not yet a banker.
In 1769 he was appointed Hoffaktor, court factor, to Landgrave Wilhelm IX of Hesse-Kassel.
The post was a regulated intermediary role: Jews were barred by law from most professions but could serve as financial agents to particular nobles.
In 1770 he married Gutle Schnapper.
They had ten surviving children, five sons and five daughters, and under German succession law only the sons could inherit and manage the business.
In the Napoleonic Wars, Landgrave Wilhelm fled the French and entrusted his fortune to Mayer Amschel.
Mayer Amschel died in 1812.

His will, held in the Rothschild Archive in London, instructed his five sons to work only among themselves, to share information across borders, and to arrange marriages within the extended family so as to hold the capital together.
At his death he was not the wealthiest man in Europe.
Between 1798 and 1812 Mayer Amschel placed his sons in five European cities.
Amschel stayed in Frankfurt and ran the original house.
Salomon went to Vienna and the Austrian court, Nathan to London, Carl to Naples and the Italian states, and James to Paris.
One dates N M Rothschild & Sons in London to 1811 and another to 1809.
The Paris house, de Rothschild Frères, is dated to 1817 in one account and to 1812 in others; the detailed account used here has James arrive in Paris in 1812 and dates the firm to 1817.
The Barings in Britain, the Fuggers in an earlier Germany, the Warburgs in Hamburg, the Bleichröders in Berlin and later the Morgans in America all worked on similar dynastic, cross-border lines.
The London house and the wars.
Nathan Mayer Rothschild (1777–1836) established the London house.
Through the nineteenth century it was a principal underwriter of British government bonds, and in 1875 it financed Britain's purchase of shares in the Suez Canal.
In the last campaign against Napoleon, Nathan financed the payment of British subsidies to Britain's allies, and Wellington's army was partly paid through Rothschild couriers carrying gold to Spain.

On this book's reading, this is where the family's business met the state borrowing that the Bank of England had organized a century earlier: a government at war needed lenders who could move money quickly across a continent, and the five houses could.

The most famous story about Nathan, that he learned of Wellington's victory at Waterloo a day early, by carrier pigeon, and made a fortune on the London Stock Exchange, is the one the sources handle least consistently.
They agree that its popular form is antisemitic in origin and disagree on where it began and whether Nathan had any real advantage; both versions, and the evidence for each, are set out in .
The Paris house.
James Mayer Rothschild (1792–1868), the youngest son, was sent to Paris at about nineteen, following his father's death and his father's testamentary instruction.
Between 1817 and 1848 he built de Rothschild Frères into the largest private bank in France, underwriting French government loans under both the Bourbon Restoration and the July Monarchy.

From the 1830s to the 1850s he financed the Chemin de Fer du Nord, the northern French railway and one of the largest infrastructure projects of the age, where much of the Paris fortune came to be concentrated.

sent: When he died in 1868 his was the largest single Rothschild branch by capital.
His youngest son, Edmond, was 23, and inherited substantial capital but not the management of the bank.
Between 1815 and 1875 the Rothschild banks were arguably the largest private-capital institution in the world.
They underwrote sovereign loans for Britain, France, Austria and several Italian states.
The Vienna, Paris and Italian branches financed early railway building across Europe.
From the 1830s, under Pope Gregory XVI, the papacy borrowed from the Rothschilds more than once; the papal loans are told in full in a later section.
On Niall Ferguson's figures, as reviews of his history report them, the combined capital of the houses was £9.5 million in 1852 and £34 million in 1874, after which it grew little.
The Rothschilds were the largest private bankers of the period, not the only ones, and significant rather than dominant.
The Frankfurt house, the mother house of the dynasty, closed in 1901, because Amschel's line had produced no male heirs to carry it on.
By the time of the Balfour Declaration in 1917, the original branch had been closed for sixteen years.

The account used here traces the decline to four causes: the spreading of capital among dozens of cousins of uneven talent by the third and fourth generations; the rise of joint-stock banking, which outcompeted private family banks; the rise of American banking, which moved the center of world finance to New York; and the two world wars.
In 1938 the Nazis expropriated the property of the Austrian branch, which the same account says is documented in exhibits at the Nuremberg trials.
In the words of that account, the Rothschilds were victims of the Holocaust, not its orchestrators.
Descendants today run separate businesses, among them Rothschild & Co in Paris, RIT Capital in London and various family offices, none of them near the dynasty's nineteenth-century scale.
The family's later role in the history of Palestine runs through particular people, and the record keeps them distinct.

The Paris branch produced Edmond de Rothschild (1845–1934), who from the 1880s used a large personal fortune to fund agricultural settlements of the First Aliyah in Ottoman Palestine, among them Rishon LeZion, Zikhron Ya'akov and Rosh Pinna, while personally opposing Theodor Herzl and the political Zionist Congress.
His colonies, his administrators and his refusal of Herzl are told in .
The London branch later produced Walter Rothschild (1868–1937), a zoologist who founded a natural-history museum at Tring and in 1917 was chosen as the addressee of the Balfour Declaration.
He did not draft it: the letter was drafted by Weizmann, Sokolow and Sykes and signed by Balfour, the Foreign Secretary, as  sets out.
One Rothschild funded settlements and opposed Herzl; another received a letter he had not written.
Antisemitic conspiracy writing merges the two into a single "Rothschilds."
Britain, financed at scale by Nathan's house through the nineteenth century, would issue the Balfour Declaration in November 1917.
It did so as an imperial and strategic move that served three British interests at once: securing the approaches to Suez, keeping Russia in the First World War, and bringing America into it.
France, post-revolutionary and then Napoleonic, was financed at scale by James Mayer's Paris house.
It was also, in 1791, the first European state to grant Jews full legal citizenship, the model of nineteenth-century emancipation that Zionism would later argue had failed.

In 1894 the same France produced the Dreyfus Affair, the false conviction of a Jewish army captain, Alfred Dreyfus, which persuaded the Viennese journalist Theodor Herzl that legal emancipation had not made Jews safe even in the most enlightened states of Europe.

The record does not show any causal link between the Paris bank and the Dreyfus Affair, which had its own military and political causes, or that French antisemitism in 1894 was a reaction to Jewish banking.
Imperial Russia was home to the largest Jewish population in Europe.
The Pale of Settlement, created by Catherine the Great in 1791, confined most Russian Jews to the empire's western provinces.
After Tsar Alexander II was assassinated in March 1881, waves of pogroms swept Ukraine and southern Russia.
About two million Jewish emigrants left the Russian Empire between 1881 and 1914 (one account extends the window to 1924), and the great majority went to America, not Palestine.
Some did go to Palestine, and their settlements are part of this volume's story.
But the main current of the emigration ran elsewhere, which complicates any account that treats the flight from the pogroms and Zionist settlement as one movement.
Palestine itself was Ottoman, as it had been since 1516 and would remain until 1917, more than four centuries.
Under the millet system, Christian, Muslim and Jewish communities had substantial internal self-government.
The source behind this point adds that the Ottoman parliamentary reforms of 1876 brought Palestinian representation, and that Palestinian delegates sat in the Ottoman parliament.
The parliamentary record gathered for a later section supports one such delegate: Yusuf Diya al-Khalidi, elected in 1877 as the sole deputy for Jerusalem.
How that order worked in Palestine from 1799 is the subject of the next section.
The Papal States were lost in 1870, and Vatican City became a sovereign state only in 1929, as an earlier section showed.

The papacy's part in the later story of Israel arrives through absence: the Vatican did not recognize the State of Israel from its founding in 1948 until 30 December 1993, when the Vatican-Israel Fundamental Agreement was signed.

As of 2026 that recognition remains in force, and it has survived public criticism from Rome, including the description of Gaza as an "ongoing massacre" by the Vatican Secretary of State, Cardinal Parolin, reported by the Times of Israel in October 2025.
Why the Vatican waited 45 years is a question for later volumes.
There is also an interpretation of what the family's history means for Palestine, for the region and for today.
On that reading, the dynasty's direct role in Palestine ran through one branch only: one man, Edmond, in Paris, over four decades, 1882 to 1934.
The Frankfurt house had no role in Palestine, and the London house had no part in funding it; Walter received a letter.

The settlements Edmond paid for became part of the physical base of the Jewish community before the state, but the political order of the modern Middle East, from the Mandate to partition and the wars that followed, was made by states, not banking families.
Ferguson, on this account, is explicit that the Rothschilds took part in some financial episodes and did not design the geopolitical order.

To read the region as "Rothschild designed" is, on this reading, a category error that hides the documented actors: the British and American empires, the Israeli state, Palestinian resistance, the Arab states and Iran, intelligence services and arms makers.
Dynastic finance still exists: it cites a 2024 Deloitte report counting about 15,000 family offices in the United States managing more than $6 trillion.
Some of the families behind them are of Jewish origin and most are not.
The "Rothschild" of modern conspiracy content, it argues, is an imagined dynasty that ceased to exist in coherent form between 1901 and 1945, not the businesses that carry the name today.

The name survives in that content because it performs a substitution: it replaces an impersonal, documented pattern, concentrated capital passed down the generations, with a single Jewish family name.
Mayer Amschel Rothschild founded a banking family in Frankfurt in the late eighteenth century.
The family reached its peak in mid-nineteenth-century Europe as one of the largest private holders of capital in the world.
The Frankfurt house closed in 1901, the Austrian branch's property was seized by the Nazis in 1938, and by 1945 the dynasty as a cross-border force was gone.
The first holds that "the Rothschilds," as one undifferentiated collective, run world finance, started the world wars or engineered Israel.

That claim is antisemitic in structure, because it puts a Jewish family name in place of the documented forces at work, and it is false on the evidence, since the family's businesses today are not large enough to do what the legend assigns them.
The second is the defensive reply that the Rothschilds were "just another banking family" with nothing to examine.
That evades a dynastic pattern that did shape European capital in the nineteenth century.

The account used here points readers to Ferguson's two-volume The House of Rothschild (1998–1999), to the Rothschild Archive, and to Simon Schama's Two Rothschilds and the Land of Israel (1978) for the distinction between the branches.
The founding dates of the London and Paris houses differ across the sources, as noted above, and the Waterloo story is told two ways.

Several figures in this section, among them the capital estimate for 1875, the four causes of decline and the Nuremberg exhibits, reach this book through a single account summarizing Ferguson and the archive rather than through those works directly, and they are given here as that account gives them.

The shape of the board in 1815 is clear enough: a Frankfurt family lending across five capitals, a British state borrowing on a scale the Bank of England had made possible, a France that had emancipated its Jews, a Russia that confined them, an Ottoman Empire that ruled Palestine, and a papacy that still held its own territory.
The familiar account holds that Zionism is millennia old and that Jews always yearned for the land of Israel.
Zionism as a written political idea appears in the documents between the 1860s and the 1880s, in scattered proposals that answered a modern problem, modern European antisemitism.
When persecuted Jews in the Russian Empire could choose where to go, the great majority chose America.
And the largest Jewish religious movement in the United States formally rejected a return to Palestine in 1885.
Moses Hess (1812–1875) was a German-Jewish philosopher and an early, influential figure in socialist thought.
In the 1840s he collaborated and corresponded with Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, and some historians credit him with introducing Marx to communist ideas before Marx had fully formulated his own.
In 1862 Hess published Rome and Jerusalem: The Last National Question.
Its argument was that Jewish assimilation into European society had failed to end antisemitism, and that Jews therefore needed national self-determination.
It proposed, explicitly, a socialist Jewish commonwealth in Palestine, joining Hess's two commitments, socialism and Jewish nationalism, in a single dated text.
The book sold poorly and drew little serious engagement from socialist or Jewish intellectual circles.
Mainstream European Jewish thought in the 1860s and 1870s was moving toward emancipation and integration, not national separation, and Hess's socialist nationalism belonged to neither camp.

Only after the Zionist Congress of 1897 was he rediscovered and placed in the movement's own origin story as a founding intellectual, a common pattern in political movements, which canonize an ignored forerunner once a later effort succeeds.
There is no strong documented evidence that Herzl, who reached his own position chiefly through the Dreyfus Affair, was significantly influenced by Hess's book before writing his own.
Hess is best read as an early, isolated voice making a real proto-Zionist argument thirty-five years before the movement organized, not as the hidden origin of a plan that then unfolded on schedule.
The pressure that turned scattered ideas into a wider response came from Russia.
The Romanov Empire was home to roughly five million Jews, the largest Jewish population in the world, confined by law to the Pale of Settlement.
Waves of pogroms followed across the Pale: organized mob violence against Jewish communities, in many cases with the complicity of local officials.
Under his son Alexander III, who reigned from 1881 to 1894, the state then wrote the hostility into law.
The May Laws of 1882 formally restricted where Jews could live, what they could study and how they could earn a living.
Further decrees imposed quotas on Jewish admission to universities and barred Jews from rural areas.
The pogroms and the May Laws were separate pressures, and the record keeps them apart.
A second, from 1903 to 1906, included the Kishinev pogrom of April 1903, which killed 49 people, wounded hundreds and became an international scandal.
The third, during the Russian Civil War of 1917–1921, was by far the deadliest, with an estimated 100,000 to 250,000 Jews killed in Ukraine and the surrounding regions.
The first territorial answer came from Odessa.

Leon Pinsker (1821–1891) was a physician who had been decorated by the Tsarist state earlier in his life for public service and who had supported Jewish integration into Russian society: a model of the assimilated, patriotic Russian Jew.
The pogroms of 1881 and the May Laws of 1882 convinced him that integration offered no safety.
His pamphlet Auto-Emancipation, published in 1882, argued that antisemitism was a permanent, almost pathological feature of the nations among whom Jews lived as a perpetual minority.
Jews would never be granted true equality as guests; they needed a territory of their own, where they would be the hosts, and they should stop relying on the goodwill of host nations.
Pinsker did not specify Palestine.
One account documents him as open to alternatives including Argentina; another says he at points leaned toward a location in North America or Argentina rather than Palestine.

He and other early organizers of the Hovevei Zion societies discussed several possible territories before the movement's center of gravity settled on Palestine, a choice reinforced by the religious and historical resonance that a purely territorial safety argument did not by itself require.
At its written origin, then, political Zionism was territorially agnostic.
Herzl's Der Judenstaat would weigh Argentina and Palestine again in 1896, and the debates over a British offer of East African territory came later still.

Exactly when Palestine became fixed is itself given differently in the sources: one account places it with Herzl and his Congress, another, the account of Herzl's later negotiations, with the movement's Russian base in 1905.
Either way, the Palestine focus was a decision taken later, not the starting premise.
Its conclusion, that Jews could be safe only where they were not a minority, was a judgment about the future.
The conclusion is the political argument that the rest of this library follows, together with the costs it would carry for the people already living in the land Pinsker's successors chose.
Roughly two million Jews left Imperial Russia in the pogrom era.
Documented estimates put 90–95 percent of these emigrants in the United States and about 3 percent in Ottoman Palestine.
On the source's own reckoning, those who could choose chose America over Palestine by a factor of about thirty to one.
Jewish communities in New York, Chicago, Philadelphia and Boston grew from modest pre-1881 numbers into the multi-million American Jewish diaspora that exists today.
The Lower East Side, not the colonies of the First Aliyah, was where most of the exodus went.
It is the central evidentiary difficulty for any account that treats Palestine as the natural or inevitable destination of persecuted European Jews in this period.
It also explains why Zionism had to be built as a political movement: the ancient longing, whatever its place in prayer, did not by itself move populations toward Palestine.

One further consequence is a matter of interpretation rather than record, and is offered as such: the demographic and financial center of world Jewry moved to the United States in exactly these decades, and when the political-Zionist project needed a great-power patron in the twentieth century, the community that had chosen America became central to securing one.
The migration that bypassed Palestine helped, two generations later, to make the American relationship with Israel possible.
Opposition had a formal voice within three years of Pinsker's pamphlet.
In 1885 American Reform Judaism adopted the Pittsburgh Platform, which stated:
"We consider ourselves no longer a nation, but a religious community, and therefore expect neither a return to Palestine..."
The sentence continues, in the platform's text, to reject "the restoration of any of the laws concerning the Jewish state."

This was the founding-generation position of what was then the largest Jewish religious denomination in the United States, adopted three years after Auto-Emancipation and twelve years before the Basel Congress.
Nor was it permanent: Reform Judaism embraced Zionism only in the mid-twentieth century, a documented later reversal.

It was one of several Jewish objections to the national idea present from its beginning, alongside the Orthodox reading of the Three Oaths set out earlier in this chapter, and the socialist and cultural objections told in the section on Dreyfus and Herzl.
"Semitic" was coined in 1781 by the German scholar August Ludwig von Schlözer, from Shem, son of Noah in Genesis 10.
It named a language family, including Hebrew, Aramaic, Arabic and Amharic, and its speakers, and it carried no political charge.
That changed in 1879, when Wilhelm Marr coined "antisemitism", three years before Pinsker's pamphlet.
The modern political vocabulary that later arguments would turn on was being assembled in the same narrow window in which the earliest Zionist texts were written.
Palestine was not empty.
Its majority population in this period were Palestinian Arabs, speakers of a Semitic language.

Two peer-reviewed population-genetics studies, Nebel and colleagues in 2000 and Behar and colleagues in 2010, describe them as descended from populations continuously present in the region since antiquity.
The colonies of the First Aliyah were founded on land that was already inhabited.
It is often said that this population was named nowhere in the founding literature of political Zionism.
It holds for the earliest written texts as they are summarized here: neither Hess's argument nor Pinsker's, as the sources describe them, addresses the people already living on the land.
Ahad Ha'am proposed a cultural rather than a political Zionism.
He raised exactly this concern in writing in 1891, less than a decade after Pinsker.

And Herzl's own diary for 12 June 1895, published only after his death, contains a passage about spiriting "the penniless population" across the border, whose meaning and reference scholars dispute; it is examined, with both readings, in .

It does not quote Pinsker's pamphlet on the question of territory, so how far he leaned toward North America or Argentina, rather than simply leaving the question open, rests on two summaries that word it differently.
It records Ahad Ha'am's 1891 concern but not the text in which he raised it.

And it does not establish any line of influence from Hess to Pinsker or from either to Herzl: the ideas appeared one after another, in answer to the same pressures, but the documents do not show one man reading and building on the other.
Dreyfus, Herzl and Der Judenstaat, 1894–1896
Three years after Hirsch's company was incorporated in London, in December 1894, a French court-martial convicted Captain Alfred Dreyfus of treason.
Dreyfus was a Jewish officer of the French army, born in Alsace.
He was convicted on forged evidence; at its center was the bordereau, a note supposed to prove that he had been spying for Germany.
Among the journalists who covered the case was the Paris correspondent of the Neue Freie Presse of Vienna, Theodor Herzl.
Fourteen months after the conviction Herzl published Der Judenstaat, the pamphlet that became the founding text of political Zionism.
A familiar account holds that Zionism arose from ancient scripture.
As a hope, the return to Zion was much older than Herzl, and other sections of this book trace that hope and the rabbis who first argued for practical settlement.
As an organized political movement, though, Zionism took shape in response to a specific, documented modern antisemitism, and it was contested inside Jewish life from the moment it appeared.
The bordereau was later shown to have been written by another officer, Ferdinand Esterhazy.
Once his guilt became clear, the army's General Staff protected him rather than admit that it had convicted an innocent man.
Dreyfus was sent to Devil's Island.
The Affair divided France into Dreyfusards and anti-Dreyfusards, a rupture that shaped French politics into the twentieth century.

Its resolution came after this chapter closes: Émile Zola's open letter "J'accuse!", published in L'Aurore in January 1898, forced the frame-up into public view, and Dreyfus was fully rehabilitated in 1906, twelve years after his conviction.
It does not show that the whole French army or government was complicit.
Zola and many others who exposed the frame-up were French and not Jewish, and the correction came from inside France as well as from outside it.
Why France mattered.
France had emancipated its Jews in 1791, the first European state to do so.
A century later the same country produced the most publicized antisemitic trial of the nineteenth century, with crowds in the streets crying against the Jews while the case ran.
French Jews had built substantial civic and professional lives in the intervening century, and emancipation had not been meaningless.
That is exactly why the Affair felt like a rupture rather than a continuation.
Herzl drew the conclusion that if antisemitism could survive in emancipated, republican Paris, no Jewish community in Europe was structurally safe.
Herzl was born on 2 May 1860 in Pest, later part of Budapest, to an assimilated, German-speaking Jewish family; he was educated in German and was culturally German-Austrian.
The family moved to Vienna in 1878, where he entered the university to study law.
In 1891 the Neue Freie Presse, one of the most influential German-language papers in Europe, made him its Paris correspondent.
He did not receive Zionism ready-made from Jewish tradition.
The usual story says that Herzl saw Dreyfus publicly degraded, heard the crowd, and became a Zionist on the spot.
The short account says Herzl watched "Death to the Jews" chanted in the streets of Paris.
The fuller account, drawn from his diaries, says he heard the crowd shouting "À bas les Juifs!"
("Down with the Jews!"), which is a different phrase, and dates his attendance at the degradation ceremony to 22 December 1894.
What the accounts agree on is that Herzl was present and recorded the moment.
The diaries show that Herzl's thinking did not settle overnight.

During 1895 he considered mass conversion of Jews to Catholicism as a way to end antisemitism structurally; he considered social integration through political engagement; and, increasingly, he came to see territorial concentration as the only stable solution.
What the Affair did was fix a diagnosis.
In Herzl's reading, European antisemitism was not a leftover religious prejudice that modern life would wear away.
It survived assimilation and survived the successful entry of Jews into professional and cultural life.
Dreyfus was the very picture of that success, an officer of the French army who had married into the elite, and he had still been convicted on forged evidence, with his public humiliation cheered.
If safety could not be had inside European societies, Herzl concluded, it had to be had outside them, in a separate polity.
That was the argument of Der Judenstaat.
This is the strongest form of the case Herzl made, and it should be stated in its own terms.

It was an argument about physical and civic safety, made against a record that included the pogroms and May Laws in the Russian Empire and now a show trial in the first European state to emancipate its Jews.
Herzl's proposal answered a specific European failure of the 1890s and turned it into a permanent political program.
In an entry dated 12 June 1895, Herzl wrote:
The entry was not published in Herzl's lifetime.
It appeared in the Complete Diaries edited by Raphael Patai in 1960.

Benny Morris, in Righteous Victims, and Nur Masalha, in Expulsion of the Palestinians, treat it as evidence that Herzl was aware early on that the Zionist project would involve moving the existing population.
Other scholars have argued that the passage has been misread, or that it referred to a population other than the Arabs of Palestine.

Some accounts go further than the evidence allows: they state as undisputed that Herzl publicly assured Ottoman officials that Jewish settlement would benefit the local Arab population while privately entertaining plans for their displacement.
That conclusion depends on reading the 1895 entry as Morris and Masalha read it.
Der Judenstaat (The Jewish State, or The Jews' State) was published in Vienna on 14 February 1896.
Herzl proposed a "Society of Jews" to act as the political leadership and a "Jewish Company", a chartered economic-development corporation, to carry out the practical work.
He proposed an orderly transfer of population, a seven-hour working day, a flag and a bank: the administrative furniture of a nineteenth-century European nation-state, applied to the Jewish question.
He used "Jew" as a national category rather than a religious one and said that irreligious Jews would be included on equal terms.
Above all, the pamphlet did not treat Palestine as the only or obvious answer.
Herzl put the question directly: "Shall we choose Palestine or Argentine?
We shall take what is given us, and what is selected by Jewish public opinion."
Of Argentina he wrote that it was "by natural resources one of the richest countries on earth, comprising a vast extent of territory, a sparse population, and a mild climate."

The country was then recruiting European immigrants and offering wide, thinly settled land, and Baron de Hirsch's Jewish Colonization Association had already planted Jewish colonies there (see the preceding section).

One summary of the text adds that Herzl expected Argentina's government to "gladly provide" land, and that he later wrote that Palestine would give "the Jewish problem" a solution "not only just, but brilliant."
How much weight Herzl gave each country is itself read in two ways.
One account in the research holds that he treated Argentina and Palestine with roughly equal weight.

Another holds that he considered Argentina first and Palestine second, preferring Palestine for practical and political reasons, chiefly that it would move Jewish public opinion, rather than religious ones.

The Israeli writer and peace activist Uri Avnery went further: in his reading, Herzl "had obviously thought very little about Palestine as a concrete entity" and inserted Palestine into his blueprint as an afterthought.
Avnery's is an interpretation, not a fact about the text.
What the text plainly shows is that at its founding moment political Zionism was open about territory.
Part of the material behind this book says that Der Judenstaat weighed Uganda as a candidate.
The British offer of land in East Africa, known as the "Uganda" scheme, came in 1903, seven years later, and is told in .
The pamphlet's alternatives were Argentina and Palestine.
A program needs patrons, and in 1896 Herzl looked for two.

From that year he sought a charter from the Ottoman Sultan, offering help with the empire's public debt; his diary records a message relayed from Abdul Hamid II that the Sultan could not sell even a foot of the land, because it belonged not to him but to his people.
He did not meet the Sultan until May 1901, and then obtained no charter.
In July 1896 he asked Baron Edmond de Rothschild, the patron of the colonies in Palestine, to back a state secured by charter rather than colonies secured by purchase, and was refused.
His diary records his "rude telegram to Edmond Rothschild" and his resolve that "from Rothschild's negative attitude I must salvage everything."
Herzl turned instead to convening a congress.
The First Zionist Congress met at Basel on 29–31 August 1897, with 200 delegates from 17 countries, and founded the World Zionist Organization.
Herzl wrote in his diary afterwards: "At Basel I founded the Jewish State.
The State of Israel was declared fifty-one years later, in 1948.

Between 1901 and 1903 Herzl negotiated with Abdul Hamid II, Kaiser Wilhelm II, Pope Pius X and the British Colonial Secretary Joseph Chamberlain, and weighed Argentina, Cyprus, El-Arish in Sinai and East Africa.

By the account in the research, Cyprus was set aside in 1902 because of its existing Greek and Turkish population, El-Arish in 1903 for lack of water, and the Sultan refused any transfer of sovereignty over Palestine.
(Another source in this book dates Herzl's meeting with Pius X to January 1904, not to 1901–1903.)

In August 1903 Herzl provisionally accepted the British offer in East Africa as a refuge after the Kishinev pogrom; the Sixth Zionist Congress voted 295 to 177 to send an exploratory commission, and a minority, mainly delegates from the Russian Empire, walked out.
Herzl died of heart failure at Edlach, Austria, on 3 July 1904, aged 44.
His one visit to Palestine, in October 1898, had been made to lobby Kaiser Wilhelm II.
The Seventh Zionist Congress rejected the East Africa scheme in 1905.
When Palestine became fixed, and why.
One account in the research says the Palestine focus was settled through the negotiations at the Basel Congress of 1897.
Another says Palestine became the only acceptable territory in 1905, decided by the movement's Russian base rather than by Herzl or by the founding text.

The other holds that the Uganda debate was resolved by the religious and historical attachment of most Zionist supporters to the specific land: those who walked out in 1903 were not looking for any refuge but for a return to Zion, and "Zion Zionism" defeated "Territorial Zionism", sometimes called Ugandism.
As the research itself cautions, the pamphlet's openness does not make Palestine arbitrary or interchangeable with any other place.

Because the movement chose Palestine, it inherited a body of biblical texts tied to that land: Genesis 15:18, which speaks of a land "from the river of Egypt to the great river, the Euphrates river"; Deuteronomy 11:24; and the borders of Numbers 34.
In Argentina or East Africa, that argument runs, no such texts would apply, and the idea of a "Complete Land of Israel" (Eretz Yisrael HaShlema) could not have arisen.
Herzl's answer was one Jewish answer among several, and for decades it was not the majority's.

Reform Judaism had already rejected a return in its Pittsburgh Platform of 1885: "We consider ourselves no longer a nation, but a religious community, and therefore expect neither a return to Palestine... nor the restoration of any of the laws concerning the Jewish state."

The Jewish Labour Bund, founded in Vilna in October 1897, the same year as the Basel Congress, rejected Zionism in favor of doikayt ("hereness"): Jewish cultural and national autonomy within the multi-ethnic societies of Eastern Europe, pursued through socialist politics alongside non-Jewish workers.

It became the leading Jewish political movement in Eastern Europe, larger through the interwar years than the Zionist parties, and it was destroyed by Nazi and Soviet violence, not by losing the argument.
Ahad Ha'am proposed a cultural and spiritual center rather than a state, an alternative within Zionism rather than outright rejection.

Orthodox rabbis who opposed political Zionism held that return could come only through divine redemption, and that forcing it by human politics was a transgression; their line runs to today's Neturei Karta.

These four positions shared a rejection of political Zionism and little else: a socialist workers' movement, an American religious reform movement, a cultural essayist and Orthodox theologians often disagreed with one another.

Satmar and much of Haredi Jewry reject Zionism today; Jewish Voice for Peace and IfNotNow criticize it; Peter Beinart's The Crisis of Zionism (2012) and Judith Butler's Parting Ways (2012) are critiques written from within Jewish tradition.
To record that Herzl founded a modern political movement, distinct from Judaism as a religious tradition, is a matter of historical accuracy, and it is a distinction Herzl himself drew.

It holds that the modern State of Israel still works on Herzl's 1896 template: secular nationalism as the state's main framing; the split between a "Society of Jews" and a "Jewish Company" surviving in the division of labor between the state and the Jewish Agency; Herzl's vision of citizenship for Jews carried into statute by the Law of Return of 1950; and the question of the non-Jewish inhabitants left unresolved, from the Palestinian Arabs who made up 20% of Israel's pre-1967 population to the more than 5.3 million Palestinians under military occupation since 1967.

The same reading connects the 1895 diary's phrase about spiriting a population across the border with the displacement of 750,000 Palestinians in 1948, and lists later steps (the occupation from 1967, the annexation of East Jerusalem in 1980, the Nation-State Law of 2018 with its downgrading of Arabic and its declaration of Jewish settlement as a "national value", and the Gaza campaign from 2023) as the working-out of that framework.
It concedes that Herzl did not commit these acts and argues that he set the framework within which others did.

Against this reading stand the dispute over what the 1895 entry meant, the gap of half a century and more between Herzl and the events it lists, and the cautions already noted: the openness of the 1896 text does not make Palestine arbitrary, and a framework is not the same thing as a decision by the people who later acted.
The exact date of the degradation ceremony Herzl attended and the exact words the crowd used differ between the sources here and have not been checked against a primary document.
How much weight Herzl gave Argentina against Palestine depends on how one reads a short text, and the accounts used here read it differently.
The sources also disagree on when Palestine became the movement's fixed goal, at Basel in 1897 or with the rejection of East Africa in 1905.
Baron de Hirsch and the Argentine Alternative, 1889–1896
Edmond was not the only Jewish financier settling refugees on the land.

In September 1891, six years before the First Zionist Congress met at Basel, a company was incorporated in London to move persecuted Jews out of the Russian Empire and Romania and settle them as farmers.
Its founder was Baron Maurice de Hirsch, a German-Jewish financier and philanthropist.
Its destination was Argentina.
Its name was the Jewish Colonization Association, the JCA.
A common account holds that Zionism was the first and only organized plan to resettle persecuted European Jews somewhere new.
The first large, organized and capitalized attempt to answer what the century called "the Jewish Question" through mass resettlement was the JCA, and it was not a plan for a state.
That precedent was in front of Theodor Herzl when he wrote his own pamphlet five years later.
The JCA was incorporated under the English Companies Acts, a charitable body given the legal form of a company.
Hirsch subscribed 19,993 of the 20,000 himself.
According to Hadassah Magazine's review of Matthias Lehmann's history of the association, the JCA's budget was described as "the greatest charitable trust in the world at that time."

The association's purpose was written into its founding terms, and the Jewish Encyclopedia records it in these words: to "assist and promote the emigration of Jews...to any parts of the world, and to form and establish colonies in various parts of North and South America and other countries."
"Any parts of the world" is not a Palestine project under another name.
Argentina became the JCA's founding and primary field, but the charter did not confine it there.
The Argentine work began before the company existed.

Moisés Ville was founded in 1889 by Dr. Wilhelm Löwenthal with Hirsch's backing (one account calls the initiative Hirsch's, another Löwenthal's), and is described as the first large agricultural colony for Eastern European Jews in the JCA's network, although it predates the association's incorporation by two years.
Further colonies followed: Mauricio, Clara (also called Villa Clara) and San Antonio.
By 1896, the year Hirsch died, roughly 6,757 colonists lived across the Argentine settlements.
By 1939 the JCA held about 1,519,000 acres in Argentina.
Money came from one fortune, held in a London company.
The company bought land, brought families from the Russian Empire and Romania, and settled them on the land as farmers.
The Argentine government was the sovereign; the JCA was a landowner and a sponsor inside it.
Popular memory has often treated Moisés Ville as a bright counterpoint to European persecution, a place free of prejudice.
There is also a documented history of violence within the community, examined directly in Javier Sinay's book The Murders of Moisés Ville.
What separated the JCA from the political movement that followed was not its scale but its theory.

It was to "productivize" Jews: to move them out of urban trades, in which they were often persecuted, and into manual and agricultural labor, so that their social and economic position within existing nation-states would become normal.
Two answers were now on offer to the same nineteenth-century question of how persecuted European Jews could build a secure future.
They establish that the theory was held and acted on in Argentina.
The JCA aimed at agricultural resettlement and integration into Argentine society; there was no political program for Jewish national autonomy in Argentina.
That is why Argentina could appear in Herzl's pamphlet of 1896 as a candidate territory rather than as a competing national project already under way.
Had the JCA been building Jewish self-government on the Pampas, Argentina and Palestine would have been two national movements in competition.
That difference let Herzl weigh Argentina as an option, a choice examined in .
After Hirsch's death in 1896 the JCA also began to fund settlement in Palestine.
In the same year, Baron Edmond de Rothschild instructed the JCA to begin lending to the colonists he supported there.
The overlap matters here because it rules out a tidy picture of Argentina against Palestine.
Hirsch's death and its date.
Hirsch died in 1896, a year before the Basel Congress of 1897, and never saw it.
Because he died before Basel, his record cannot show what he would have made of political Zionism.
Organized, heavily funded planning for Jewish resettlement existed years before Herzl and decades before the Holocaust.
When the Zionist movement later fixed on Palestine, it was choosing among alternatives, one of which had already been tried on the ground at real scale.
The record does not show that Hirsch opposed the later Zionist project or saw himself as its competitor.
Nor do the sources here say how the colonists themselves weighed their choice, how many left the colonies, or how the Argentine settlements compared in cost per family with the colonies in Palestine.
A Newspaper Called Palestine: The Arab Public Sphere Before 1914
The governor who tried to stop the al-Fula sale was not a lone voice.
It is often said that "Palestinian" was an identity invented after 1948, or even after 1967.
The newspapers, parliamentary records and political programs of the years before the First World War answer that claim directly.

By 1914 the country had Arabic newspapers arguing about Zionism in print, elected deputies who had raised it in the Ottoman parliament, a governor who had tried to block a land sale, and a paper in Jaffa whose masthead carried the name Filastin, "Palestine."
One early statement came from outside Palestine, in French.

In 1905 Negib Azouri published Le Réveil de la nation arabe, and in it he set the Arab national awakening beside the Jewish one and wrote of the two movements: "Both these movements are destined to fight each other continually until one of them wins."
ents: Le Réveil de la nation arabe

sent: It was a prediction, not a program, written eight years after the Basel Congress and before any large Zionist purchase in the Jezreel Valley; but it framed the encounter as a contest between two national movements six years after Herzl had answered a Jerusalem notable's warning by writing that the existing population would be enriched by Jewish settlement (that exchange is told in ).
The same year Najib Nassar began the most sustained campaign.
From 1905 he wrote against Zionism in two Arabic papers, al-Muqattam in Cairo and Lisan al-Hal in Beirut.
In 1908 he founded his own paper, al-Karmil, in Haifa, appearing twice a week.
The authorities' tolerance of the new paper had limits: they closed al-Karmil for two months in June 1909.
In 1910 the Ministry of Justice ordered Nassar tried on a complaint from the Jewish community alleging incitement, and the court acquitted him.

It shows an Arab journalist prosecuted for his writing on Zionism; it shows a complaint brought in the name of the Jewish community through the Ottoman courts; and it shows those courts declining to convict.
Nassar did not stop.
In October 1911 he collected his articles as a book, Zionism: Its History, Objectives and Importance.
In 1913 he called for a non-Zionist national society based in Nablus.
In the summer of 1914 he urged Palestinian youth to press Arab landowners not to sell land to Jews.
That last appeal addressed the sellers in the mechanism described in : Arab landowners, many of them absentee, under a law that gave the tenants on their land no registered title.
The 1908 revolution also gave Palestine elected deputies in the Ottoman parliament.
Ruhi al-Khalidi was one of three deputies elected for Jerusalem that year.

In 1911, with his fellow Jerusalem deputy Sa'id al-Husayni, he raised Zionism in the Ottoman parliament, and he stressed that what he opposed was Jewish immigration, not the residence of Palestine's own Jews.

The distinction closely tracked the line the Ottoman government's own restrictions had drawn since the 1880s: between Jews who were already subjects of the empire and organized settlement from abroad.
In the same parliament Shukri al-Asali, now a deputy for Damascus, pressed the argument about dual citizenship and rural villages described in the previous section.
Ruhi al-Khalidi went further than speeches.
He left an unpublished manuscript, "Zionism and the Zionist Question," and died of typhoid in Istanbul in 1913, while serving as deputy to the head of parliament.
Into this setting came Filastin.
It was founded in Jaffa on 15 January 1911 by Issa El-Issa and his cousin Yousef El-Issa, Arab Orthodox Christians educated in Beirut.
It began as a twice-weekly paper, and its first cause was not Zionism at all but the dispute between the Arab Orthodox community and the Greek-led hierarchy of its church.
Between 1911 and 1914 its coverage of Zionism shifted.
The record also contains an event that complicates any account in which Arab politics before 1914 revolved around Zionism.
The Arab Congress met in Paris on 18–23 June 1913 with 25 official delegates.
It adopted ten resolutions, on Arab participation in the central government of the empire, on Arabic as an official language, and on administrative decentralization.
Its resolutions did not address Zionism.
Two Zionist representatives, Victor Jacobson and Sami Hochberg, attended unofficially.

The Congress's agenda was reform within the Ottoman Empire, framed in Arab rather than specifically Palestinian terms, and its silence on Zionism suggests that the subject that dominated al-Karmil and, by 1914, Filastin was not yet the first item for the wider Arab reform movement.
Why the Congress left it out, and what Jacobson and Hochberg sought there, the sources used here do not say.
Filastin outlived the empire in which it was founded.
Under the British Mandate it became one of the most influential Arabic dailies, known for its network of correspondents, and in 1927 Issa El-Issa helped found the Palestine Free Party.
The paper appeared in Jaffa until 7 April 1948, shortly before the city fell, and later moved to Jerusalem.
The National Library of Israel's Jrayed archive holds 6,692 issues, from 1911 to 1948.
A paper named "Palestine," carrying a public argument about land and immigration, was printed in Jaffa from 1911, sent to the villages of its district, and preserved in Israel's own national library.
That documents a Palestinian name in print and a Palestinian public sphere decades before 1948.

The fair statement of the other side is that this public sphere operated inside larger frames: its deputies sat in the Ottoman parliament and drew the Ottoman government's own line between subjects and immigrants, and its most ambitious political gathering, in Paris, spoke as Arabs seeking reform within the empire.

What the record does not settle is how widely, outside the press and the elected deputies, a distinctly Palestinian political identity was held before the war, how many people read these papers, and what weight the villagers who received Filastin gave it.
Any Power That Would Sign: Herzl's Search for a Charter, 1898–1904
When the delegates left Basel in 1897, the program they had adopted named an aim but no patron.
Theodor Herzl's answer to that gap was a charter.
By a charter he meant legal backing for Jewish settlement, granted by a great power that could make it stick.
The familiar telling of Zionist history has the movement looking to Britain from the start, as though 1917 had been the plan all along.
The diplomatic record of Herzl's own years shows something looser and more opportunistic.

Between 1898 and 1904 he approached the German Kaiser, the Ottoman Sultan, the British Colonial Secretary, the Russian Interior Minister and the Pope, and to each he brought whatever that power seemed most likely to want.
Herzl led an organization with a Congress and a program, but no territory, no army and no standing in international law.
Palestine belonged to the Ottoman Empire.
He tried Germany first.
The introduction came through William Hechler, a Christian restorationist, a believer in the return of the Jews to their ancient land.
Through him Herzl met Kaiser Wilhelm II three times in 1898: in Istanbul, at Mikveh Israel, an agricultural colony funded by the Rothschilds, and in Jerusalem itself.
The Kaiser did raise the matter with the Sultan.
The request failed, and the Kaiser's interest faded after it.
Herzl then went directly to the ruler of Palestine.
He had been pursuing a charter from Sultan Abdul Hamid II since 1896, and his offer had a consistent shape: help in consolidating the Ottoman public debt.
The empire's debts were chronic, and Herzl proposed to put Jewish finance to work on them in exchange for the right to settle.
On 17 May 1901 the Sultan finally received him.
Herzl made the offer in person.
The clearest statement of the Ottoman position comes from Herzl's own diary.
It records a message relayed to him from Abdul Hamid II: the Sultan could not sell even a foot of the land, because it belonged not to him but to his people.
It was not written by an opponent of Zionism to discredit Herzl; it was written down by Herzl himself.
It answers a claim still heard today, that the Ottoman Empire welcomed the Zionist movement or sold it Palestine.
From the 1880s the Ottoman government imposed restrictions on Jewish immigration to Palestine and on Jewish land purchase there.
A second Ottoman instrument worked in the opposite direction.
The Land Code of 1858 required land titles to be registered.

Many peasants avoided registering, and large tracts were registered instead to urban notables and absentee owners, whose later sales to the Jewish National Fund led to the eviction of the tenant farmers who worked the land.
The Ottoman state thus played two roles at once: the ruler who refused a charter, and the legal order under which land could change hands regardless.
With the Sultan's door closed, Herzl changed both his patron and his offer.
In October 1902 he proposed to the British Colonial Secretary, Joseph Chamberlain, a Jewish settlement at El-Arish in the Sinai.
He framed it as a buffer protecting British interests at the Suez Canal.
Britain tentatively agreed.
In 1903 Lord Cromer, Britain's man in Cairo, vetoed it.
The Nile water needed to irrigate a settlement in the Sinai, he said, could not be spared.
The inducement this time was strategic rather than financial, and the ground Cromer gave for refusing it was water.
In April 1903 came the pogrom at Kishinev, in the Russian Empire, told in .
In August 1903, months afterwards, Herzl twice met the Interior Minister, Vyacheslav von Plehve, a man widely regarded as responsible for the atmosphere that had produced the pogrom.
He did so without consulting Russia's own Zionists.
The meetings produced a letter in which the Tsar's government agreed to press the Sultan for a charter and to allow Zionist societies to operate in Russia.
Russian Zionists criticized the meetings sharply.
On one side stood what the meetings produced: a written commitment to press the Sultan, and legal room for Zionist societies inside Russia.
On the other stood the manner of them: the movement's leader had met the minister widely held responsible for the climate of Kishinev, without consulting Russia's Zionists.
The record shows the letter and the anger; it does not show that the letter ever moved the Sultan.
Weeks later Britain's offer of territory in East Africa split the Sixth Zionist Congress.
The last of these approaches went to Rome.
On 26 January 1904 Herzl had a private audience with Pope Pius X, Giuseppe Sarto, to ask for the Vatican's support for a Jewish homeland in Palestine.
Herzl's diary records the Pope's words: "We cannot give this movement our blessing...
We cannot prevent the Jews from going to Jerusalem — but we could never sanction it.
The ground of Jerusalem, if it were not always sacred, has been sanctified by the life of Jesus Christ.
As the head of the Church, I cannot tell you anything different."
Herzl also met the Vatican Secretary of State, Cardinal Rafael Merry del Val, who is described as similarly unreceptive.
One stresses doctrine: the Church could not support Jewish restoration to a land central to its own theology while the Jews denied Christ, a position later accounts call supersessionist.

The other stresses place: the Vatican's specific concern was Jerusalem and the status of the holy sites, which would be complicated by a non-Christian sovereign, rather than Jewish settlement as such.
The Pope's own words, as Herzl recorded them, contain both: he would not prevent Jews going to Jerusalem, but he would not sanction the movement, and he grounded that in the sanctity of the city.
Either way, the founder of the movement went to Rome and was refused.
The Vatican did not recognize the State of Israel until 30 December 1993, forty-five years after its independence; that longer story is told in .
Herzl did not carry one proposal from capital to capital.
He shaped each offer to its listener: finance for an indebted empire, a strategic buffer for a Britain anxious about Suez, and, in the Russian case, a movement that would draw Jews out of the empire.
Germany, the Ottoman Empire, Britain and Russia were all approached within five years.
On this reading, Britain's sponsorship in 1917 was the strategy finally succeeding with one power after failing with the others, not its point of departure.
The Kaiser lost interest, the Sultan granted nothing, Cairo vetoed El-Arish, the Russian letter yielded no charter and sharp criticism from Russian Zionists, and the Pope said no.
Herzl died in 1904.
It does not say what, if anything, Herzl offered the Kaiser in return for his intercession, nor exactly what the Kaiser asked of the Sultan.
The Sultan's refusal of land is known through Herzl's own diary, as a message relayed to him; the sources here do not give its date or its intermediary, or an Ottoman record of it.
Plehve's responsibility for Kishinev is a matter of how he was widely regarded, not a finding of a court.
And while the Pope's words survive in Herzl's account, the weight Pius X himself gave to doctrine and to the holy sites cannot be separated from that one record.
The People Already There: Herzl, al-Khalidi and the Arab Question, 1895–1905
A common belief holds that the founders of political Zionism imagined Palestine as empty, and that the existence of its Arab population came as a later surprise.
Herzl, his correspondents and his allies wrote about the people living in the land, sometimes privately and sometimes in print, from the movement's earliest days.
The question had been put to the movement before Herzl came to it.

In 1891 Asher Ginsberg, writing as Ahad Ha'am, published an account of his visit to Ottoman Palestine reporting that the land was farmed and lived on by a substantial Arab population, who would not simply acquiesce to displacement; his warning, and his wider quarrel with Herzl, are told in .

The historian Steven Beller, reviewing Derek Penslar's biography of Herzl, writes that Herzl, in Beller's words, "lacked a realistic view about the antagonistic effect" a Jewish settlement would have on the local Arab population, a point Ahad Ha'am raised at the time.
The phrase most often attached to this period has an older and non-Zionist origin.

The earliest published version of "a land without a people for a people without a land" appeared in an 1843 book by Alexander Keith, a Church of Scotland clergyman and an advocate of Jewish "restoration," who had himself traveled to Palestine in 1839 and knew it was populated.
The first use by a Zionist came in 1901, when Israel Zangwill wrote that Palestine was "a country without a people."
Whatever its authors meant, the Ottoman counts of the period, set out in , show a populated country.
Herzl's own first recorded thoughts on the matter came before the movement existed.

As the Israeli researcher Shaul Arieli quotes it, by way of Edward Said, it reads: "We shall try to spirit the penniless population across the border by procuring employment for it in the transit countries, while denying it any employment in our country."

Arieli, in a 2025 survey, places it at the head of a chronicle: in his account the idea of moving the Arab population out was a long-standing strand of Zionist strategic thinking, and this 1895 entry is where it begins.
Beller, drawing on Penslar, accepts that Herzl was "quite prepared to remove any local population," but adds two qualifications that matter.
Herzl preferred to do it peacefully.
And "the context in which he was discussing this was not Palestine": the passage concerned South America.

The strongest form of Arieli's case is continuity: whatever territory Herzl had in mind, the passage shows that the founder of the movement treated a resident population as something to be moved, and later Zionist thinkers returned to the same idea.
The strongest form of Beller's case is context: a private note about an unchosen territory, preferring economic pressure to coercion, is not the same thing as a plan for Palestine.
Neither the exact day of the entry nor its full surrounding text is given in the sources used here, so this book does not go beyond Arieli's quotation.
Four years later the question arrived at Herzl's desk from Jerusalem itself.
The writer was Yusuf Diya al-Khalidi.

According to the reference account of his career, he served as mayor of Jerusalem in 1870–76, 1878–79 and 1899–1906, sat for Jerusalem in the first Ottoman parliament, and had taught at the Oriental Academy in Vienna.
On 1 March 1899 he wrote to Zadoc Kahn, the chief rabbi of France, asking that the letter be passed to Herzl.
Al-Khalidi called the Zionist idea in itself "natural, beautiful and just."
But he set two facts against it: Palestine was part of the Ottoman Empire, and it was inhabited by others.
And he wrote: "in the name of God, let Palestine be left alone."
Herzl answered on 19 March 1899.
His argument was that Jewish immigration would benefit the people already there: "It is their well-being, their individual wealth, which we will increase by bringing in our own."
Taken on its own terms, it is a statement of good intent and a prediction: Jewish capital and labor would enrich the country, and no one proposed expulsion.
The historian Rashid Khalidi, a descendant of al-Khalidi's family, reads it otherwise.
He calls the reply condescending and argues that it did not answer al-Khalidi's central objection, that the people of Palestine would not accept being displaced.

One reading of the exchange, between the founder of political Zionism and a senior Jerusalem notable, is that the two men were writing past each other: one about sovereignty and consent, the other about prosperity.
Herzl returned to the argument in fiction.
His novel Altneuland, published in German in 1902, imagines Palestine in 1923, run by a cooperative "New Society" in which land is publicly owned.
The book has one Arab character, Reschid Bey.

According to the standard summary of the novel, Reschid Bey says that Arabs had no reason to oppose Jewish immigration, because the newcomers "developed the country and raised everybody's standard of living."
The character speaks almost the same argument Herzl had put to al-Khalidi three years earlier.
A reader sympathetic to Herzl can see in the novel a sincere vision of a shared, prosperous country without expulsion.
A reader persuaded by Rashid Khalidi can see the same objection unanswered: the only Arab voice in the book is one that agrees.
A blunter statement came from Zangwill, the writer who had first given the "country without a people" phrase a Zionist voice.

In 1905, as Arieli quotes him, Zangwill wrote that "Palestine itself is already occupied," and that Zionists must be prepared either "to drive out by the sword the tribes in possession as our forefathers did" or "to grapple with the problem of a large alien population, mostly Mohammedan and accustomed to despise us."
The quotation reaches this book through Arieli's survey; its original place of publication is not confirmed in the sources used here.
