That same year Zangwill broke with the Zionist Organization over the East Africa question and went looking for a territory elsewhere.
The founders knew Palestine was inhabited.
Keith had seen it in 1839;

Ahad Ha'am reported it in 1891; al-Khalidi told Herzl in writing in 1899, and Herzl answered him without denying it; Zangwill, the first Zionist to use the slogan, wrote in 1905 that the land was "already occupied."

What they said about it ranged widely: from Herzl's assurance that no one would send the inhabitants away, through Altneuland's picture of shared prosperity, to Zangwill's choice between the sword and the "problem" of a large population.
These are the words of individuals, in a diary, a letter, a novel and Zangwill's own statement, not resolutions of a Zionist Congress.
What the record does not settle is the question historians still divide on: what Herzl himself intended for the Arabs of Palestine.

The sources here give the passages on which Arieli, Beller and Rashid Khalidi build their readings, not Herzl's full diary entry or his letter in its entirety, and a reader should weigh those readings with that limit in mind.

What can be said plainly is that the warning al-Khalidi put to Herzl, that the people of Palestine would not accept displacement, was on paper in March 1899, and that the movement's founder answered it, in the passages quoted, with an economic argument.
For and Against: Jewish Currents, 1885–1914
The years between the Basel Congress and the First World War are easy to tell as the story of one movement gathering a people behind it.
Jewish opinion on Zionism in this period was plural, organized and argued in public, and several of its currents were founded expressly to oppose the movement or to contest what it should be.
The first wave of opposition, in 1897, came from the German rabbis of the Protestrabbiner declaration, from the Bund and from Ahad Ha'am, and is told in .
This section follows the currents that took shape around it, from a rabbinical platform in Pittsburgh in 1885 to a declaration in the Berliner Tageblatt in 1914.
Some stood outside Zionism and rejected it on principle.
Others stood inside the Zionist Organization and fought over its program.
The earliest of these positions predates Herzl.

In 1885 the Reform movement in the United States adopted the Pittsburgh Platform, which declared: "We consider ourselves no longer a nation but a religious community, and therefore expect neither a return to Palestine" nor the restoration of the laws of a Jewish state.
In 1897 the Central Conference of American Rabbis resolved: "We reaffirm that the object of Judaism is not political nor national, but spiritual."
ents: the Central Conference of American Rabbis

sent: Isaac Mayer Wise described Judaism as "not tied down to a piece of land here or there."
These words come to this book through a reference work quoting N. W. Cohen's study of the subject; the original text of the 1897 resolution has not been checked.
For these rabbis the Jews were a religious community whose object was spiritual, and a national program, in Palestine or anywhere, contradicted that self-definition.
It was to the idea that Jews were a nation needing one.
Within the Zionist Organization the argument was over what Zionism should do besides diplomacy.

At the Fifth Congress in Basel in 1901, the Congress that also founded the Jewish National Fund, a group known as the Democratic Faction, among them Leo Motzkin, Martin Buber and Chaim Weizmann, pressed for Hebrew culture and for more democracy inside the organization.
That December the Congress declared cultural work an essential part of Zionism.
Whether a national movement should take charge of Jewish culture at all was a question on which Zionists themselves divided, and the division soon had an organization of its own.
Three months later, on 4–5 March 1902, a convention in Vilna called by Rabbi Isaac Jacob Reines founded Mizrachi, the religious-Zionist faction within the Zionist Organization.
Tobias Grill counts 72 delegates at Vilna, 24 of them rabbis.
In its first year it built 210 branches in the Russian Empire, and its first world conference, held at Pressburg on 21–23 August 1904, drew about 100 delegates.
Its motto set out the synthesis it stood for: "The Land of Israel for the people of Israel according to the Torah of Israel."
Mizrachi worked inside the Zionist Organization, and its motto put the Torah at the center of the national program.
When the Tenth Zionist Congress, meeting in Basel in 1911, added cultural work to the organization's formal program, all the Mizrachi delegates walked out.
A later Mizrachi conference decided not to leave the Zionist Organization; some leaders who disagreed with that decision broke away.
In 1902–03 Orthodox leaders of the Free Association, based in Frankfurt, declared Mizrachi's principles incompatible with traditional Judaism.
A pamphlet by Raphael Breuer published in 1903 carried the title Nationaljudenthum ein Wahnjudenthum!
Here the objection ran opposite to Reform's.

Reform rejected Jewish nationhood in the name of a spiritual religious community; the Frankfurt Orthodox opposed it from within traditional religious observance, declaring Mizrachi's attempt to join Torah and nationalism incompatible with traditional Judaism.
Orthodox opposition acquired an international organization a decade later.
Agudat Israel was founded at Kattowitz in late May 1912 as a worldwide association of Torah-observant Jews.
Grill describes it as founded largely as a countermeasure to Mizrachi.

Another account in this library puts the emphasis more broadly: Agudat Israel was founded to strengthen Torah-observant Judaism as a separation from the emerging secular Jewish nationalist movement, which its founders regarded as a danger to Torah-observant Jewish life.
Either way, organized Orthodox opposition to political Zionism on religious grounds existed thirty-six years before the State of Israel did.
In the same year liberal German Jews organized against Zionism on political grounds.
In October 1912 they founded a league to combat Zionism, soon renamed the Antizionistisches Komitee.
About twelve days after the Balfour Declaration, in November 1917, anti-Zionist British Jews formed the League of British Jews.
Set side by side, these currents answer a common assumption: that Zionism in its first two decades spoke for the Jews of the world, and that its Jewish critics were a fringe.
American Reform rejected Jewish nationhood as such.
Liberal German Jews organized a committee against it.
Frankfurt Orthodoxy and then Agudat Israel rejected it as a departure from the faith.
And within the movement, secular nationalists and Mizrachi fought over whether culture or Torah would define it.
The strongest case on the Zionist side is also in the record.

Mizrachi's 210 branches in a single year show that religious Jews in the Russian Empire could be organized for the movement in large numbers, and the decision after 1911 to stay inside the Zionist Organization shows that the movement could absorb deep disagreement without losing the faction as a whole, though some of its leaders broke away.

The strongest case on the other side is that its opponents were not marginal cranks but the established rabbinical bodies of American Reform, leading Orthodox circles in Germany and an international Orthodox association, each stating a principled objection in public.
They do not measure what share of the world's Jews held each position.
The 1885 and 1897 Reform texts are quoted through a secondary source, and the Komitee's membership figure is reported rather than established.
The Country Before the Program: Ottoman Palestine, 1872–1914
When Theodor Herzl and his colleagues spoke of Palestine in the late 1890s, they were speaking of a place that had no border and no government of its own.
From 1516 to 1917, apart from a period of Egyptian rule in 1831–40, the land was governed as part of the Ottoman Empire.
It was administered chiefly as the district of Jerusalem and as parts of the provinces of Beirut and Damascus, and nothing separated it from the territories that are today Syria, Lebanon and Jordan.
Damascus, Baghdad, Jerusalem and Beirut were provincial cities of the same state, and people and goods moved between them without passports.
Syria, Iraq, Lebanon, Jordan and Israel were not states.
Almost every line that matters in the region's conflicts was drawn between 1916 and 1922, in a window of six years, by Britain and France.
Iran, a separate Persian state with its own dynasty, its own language and a Shia majority, was never Ottoman at all.
One holds that the Ottomans "occupied" Palestine in the way later settlers did.
The other holds that Palestine was an empty backwater of the empire, waiting to be filled.
Ottoman rule was imperial administration:
governors, garrisons and taxation imposed over a population that remained, for four centuries, largely Arabic-speaking Muslims and Christians, alongside long-established Jewish communities.
The Ottomans ruled the country; they did not replace its people.
A third misreading, that the Middle East has always been a set of hostile nations permanently at war, fails for a simpler reason.
The administrative shape that mattered in Herzl's lifetime dated from 1872.
In that year the Ottoman government created the Mutasarrifate, or Sanjak, of Jerusalem as an independent administrative unit.
It comprised the districts of Jerusalem, Jaffa, Hebron, Beersheba and Gaza.
To its north lay two further sanjaks, Nablus and Acre.
This arrangement lasted until Britain occupied Palestine in December 1917, when the Mutasarrifate was dissolved.
The country that Zionist delegates debated at Basel was therefore, in legal terms, one Ottoman unit centered on Jerusalem plus parts of two others.
When later writers speak of "Palestine" in this period, they are describing a region that the Ottoman state itself divided among several administrations.

Under the millet system the empire recognized religious communities, Muslims, Christians of several churches, and Jews, and allowed each to govern marriage, inheritance and schooling through its own religious law, its own courts and its own leaders.
Non-Muslims paid special taxes and held a lesser legal status, and revolts were suppressed.
The point is not that the Ottoman order was just.
The Jews already living in this country when the Zionist movement was founded had their own long history, and their own institutions, quite separate from the movement that would arise in Europe.
According to the National Library of Israel, the Jewish population of the land grew from about 7,000 in 1800 to about 27,000 in 1880.
It was concentrated in the four cities that Jewish tradition held holy, Jerusalem, Hebron, Safed and Tiberias, and in the nineteenth century most of it lived in Jerusalem.
The same four cities appear in the record of the wider Ottoman population as the places where Jewish communities lived among a mostly Arabic-speaking Muslim and Christian majority.
The Old Yishuv lived largely on money from abroad.

It depended almost completely on the halukka, funds collected from diaspora donors and distributed through kollels, which were organized by the donors' and recipients' country of origin and by Hasidic affiliation.
Before the Ottoman authorities, the Jews were represented by the Sephardi chief rabbi, the Hakham Bashi, a post later titled Rishon LeZion.
At the end of the nineteenth century the Ashkenazi kollels united under a single body, the General Committee of Knesset Israel.
ents: the General Committee of Knesset Israel

sent: These were the Jews of Ottoman Palestine as the empire knew them: a recognized religious community within the millet order, Sephardi and Ashkenazi, supported by charity.
That began to change before Herzl.

The National Library of Israel dates the beginning of a "New Yishuv" to the First Aliyah, the wave of immigration that began in 1881, and describes it as costing the Old Yishuv its leading position among the Jews of the country.
The Interactive Encyclopedia of the Palestine Question counts about 25,000 Jewish immigrants in 1882–1903, and more than 84,000 in 1850–1914, noting that not all of them stayed.
The Ottoman Land Code of 1858, which governed how land in the country was held, is examined in the previous stage of this book: .
Palestine's Jews were also one community among several in the Ottoman Middle East with deep roots.

Jewish life in Mesopotamia, modern Iraq, went back to the Babylonian conquest of Judah in 586 BCE, and the scholars of that community compiled the Babylonian Talmud, still the primary text of rabbinic study.
That continuous presence predated the Iraqi state of 1932 and the Israeli state of 1948 by millennia; its later history belongs to a different part of this library: .
How many people lived in Palestine on the eve of the First World War, and how many of them were Jews, is a question on which the sources disagree, and the disagreement is not a technicality.
The Ottoman census of 1914–15 recorded 722,000 people: 602,000 Muslims, 81,000 Christians and 39,000 Jews.
Roberto Bachi's reconstruction for 1914 gives a smaller total, 689,000, made up of 525,000 Muslims, 70,000 Christians and 94,000 Jews.
The gap between the two Jewish figures, 39,000 against 94,000, is larger than the whole Jewish population of 1880.
The Ottoman register recorded 38,754 Jews, and on the analysis of the historian Justin McCarthy it apparently counted only Ottoman subjects.
Many Jews in Palestine were foreign nationals and did not appear in it.
McCarthy, adjusting the Ottoman figures, gives a total of 722,143 for 1914–15 and puts the true Jewish figure, including foreign nationals, closer to 60,000.
Against this stands the figure long accepted in the literature, 85,000, as summarized by Roger Owen in his review of McCarthy's work.

The Interactive Encyclopedia of the Palestine Question agrees with McCarthy's order of magnitude: about 60,000 Jews at the start of the war in 1914, 39,000 of them Ottoman citizens, against more than 700,000 Muslim and Christian Ottoman subjects.
For about 1890, Bachi's reconstruction gives 532,000 people, 43,000 of them Jews; the Ottoman census of 1890–91 gives 516,000, with 18,000 Jews.
Here the reconstruction is higher on both counts, and its Jewish figure is more than double the census's.
The direction of McCarthy's corrections is also on record.

He adjusts Ottoman registers chiefly for the undercounting of young children, especially girls, and for categories of people the registers missed, and on the same reasoning he re-estimates the population of 1922 at 823,684, above the official British census total, arguing that modern methods correct the census undercount.
The lowest figure, 38,754, is a contemporary official register, but on McCarthy's reading it counted Ottoman subjects only.
McCarthy's estimate of about 60,000 adds back the foreign nationals the register left out, and his corrections are stated: young children, especially girls, and missing categories.
Those who hold to the higher figures rest on the figure long accepted in the literature, 85,000, and on Bachi's reconstruction, 94,000.
The sources available here do not set out Bachi's method in detail, so the case for his figure cannot be tested against the record in this book.
On every count, the Jewish population of Palestine in 1914 was a minority, living among a majority of Arabic-speaking Muslim and Christian Ottoman subjects.
On every count, too, it had grown several times over since 1800, first through the Old Yishuv's slow increase and then through immigration after 1881.

How far it fell during the war that began in 1914 is itself disputed, with one account holding that about a third left and McCarthy arguing the fall was much less than the commonly cited quarter, since many who fled to Alexandria returned; that story is told in .
British forces captured Jerusalem in December 1917, ending Ottoman rule in the city.
The Republic of Turkey, founded in 1923, renounced all rights over the former Arab provinces in the Treaty of Lausanne that same year.
Modern Turkey is thus the empire's successor state, not a claimant to Palestine.
The layers that followed, oil, the Anglo-French carve-up, installed rulers and revolts, were stacked on top of the Ottoman order, and later volumes take them up one at a time.

The record gives no single agreed figure for the Jewish population in 1914, and none of its figures can be treated as settled: the range runs from 38,754 to 94,000 depending on who was counted and how.
It does not say how many of the more than 84,000 Jewish immigrants of 1850–1914 stayed.
Nor does it measure how the Old Yishuv's members themselves regarded the newcomers of 1881 and after, beyond the National Library's judgment that the New Yishuv displaced them from leadership.
While the Zionist Organization argued in Basel and Hamburg, a second wave of immigrants was arriving in Jaffa.

The Second Aliyah, the immigration of 1904 to the outbreak of war in 1914, was small beside the more than 2.5 million Jews who left Eastern Europe between 1881 and 1914, about 2 million of them for the United States.
And about half of those who came to Palestine did not stay.
But the years of the wave produced the first collective farm, the first Jewish guards' commune, the first Hebrew high school, and the neighborhood that became Tel Aviv.
They also built, in the same years and through the same institutions, a principle of "Hebrew labor" that set Jewish and Arab workers apart.
The National Library of Israel puts it at about 35,000 immigrants, mostly from Eastern Europe, with a minority from Yemen; the Jewish Virtual Library gives 40,000.
At least half, by the National Library's estimate, and nearly half, by the Jewish Virtual Library's, left within a few years because of economic hardship.
By the end of the period the Jewish community numbered about 80,000.

That end-of-period total is itself one of several competing counts of the Jewish population in 1914, which range from under 40,000 Ottoman subjects to over 90,000; the reasons the counts differ are set out in .
The farming colonies of the First Aliyah, financed by Edmond de Rothschild, were by then under new management.
The Jewish Colonization Association, founded by Baron de Hirsch in September 1891 with a capital of £2,000,000, had taken over the administration of Rothschild's Palestine colonies.
The 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia dates that arrangement "since 1899."
On Gershon Shafir's account, discussed below, the First Aliyah colonies relied on cheap Arab labor.
David Ben-Gurion, born David Green in Płońsk on 16 October 1886, landed at Jaffa on 9 September 1906, according to Ben-Gurion House, and went that same evening to work in Petah Tikva.
Another educational source, the Center for Israel Education, gives his arrival as 7 September 1907; the two dates cannot both be right, and this book does not choose between them.
He joined the leadership of Poalei Zion; from 1912 he studied law in Istanbul with Yitzhak Ben-Zvi; and in 1915 the Ottoman authorities expelled him, and he went to Alexandria and then to New York.
The National Library of Israel notes that the ideal met friction in practice, because many Jewish farmers went on employing Arab workers.
In 1907 Bar-Giora was founded at Yitzhak Ben-Zvi's home in Neve Tzedek and set up the first Jewish guards' commune at Sejera.
In 1909 Hashomer grew out of it under the leadership of Yisrael Shohat.

Hashomer took over the guarding of Jewish settlements from Arab night watchmen, whom the Jewish Virtual Library's account describes as colluding with thieves; that characterization is the account's own, and the material here contains no Arab account of the same events.
Hashomer also made it a condition of guarding a settlement that only Jewish laborers be employed there.
Kinneret Farm, set up in 1908, was the first Zionist instructional farm.
At Umm Juni, on land owned by the Jewish National Fund, the first collective took root, though the sources date its founding differently.

According to the Center for Israel Education, Degania, counted as the first kibbutz, was founded on 28 October 1910, when the "Hadera Commune," ten men and two women, leased the land from the Jewish National Fund; an earlier group that Ruppin had placed there in 1909 had dispersed.
The Jewish Virtual Library dates Degania to 1909.
Ruppin's role came through the Zionist Organization's Palestine Office, whose work is told in .
Two other experiments followed in 1911: the Merhavia cooperative, which disbanded in 1918, and a women's training farm, which trained about 70 young women before it closed in 1917.
The arrangement at Degania shows the money's path: the land belonged to the Jewish National Fund and was leased to the workers who farmed it rather than sold to them.
The Hebrew Gymnasium, the first Hebrew high school, was founded in Jaffa in 1905; it later became the Herzliya Gymnasium.
The idea of a new neighborhood, Ahuzat Bayit, arose in summer 1906.
Its building plots were raffled at Passover 1909 among 60 founding families, and the neighborhood took the name Tel Aviv by majority vote.
The loan that helped finance it came from the Anglo-Palestine Company, as told in .
The Second Aliyah is usually told as a story of young Eastern European socialists.
A significant part of it came from Yemen, and that migration had begun long before.

From 1881 to 1882 a few hundred Jews left Sanaa and nearby settlements for Palestine, and migration from Yemen continued almost without interruption until 1914; in that period about 10% of Yemen's Jews left, according to a reference account.
In 1884 Yemenite families settled in a new neighborhood, Kfar Hashiloach, in Silwan, outside the walls of Jerusalem.
These early arrivals came independently of the Zionist Organization, which did not yet exist.
Shmuel Yavne'eli went to Yemen, at his own request, on behalf of the Palestine Office of the Zionist Organization, to encourage immigration; his journey lasted more than a year.
ents: the Palestine Office of the Zionist Organization

sent: About 1,000 Jews left central and southern Yemen as a result of his efforts, and several hundred more arrived before 1914, according to the 2003 study by Simon, Laskier and Reguer as summarized in the same reference account.

The National Library of Israel calls the Yemenite immigration of 1911–12 "the first planned immigration operation in the history of Zionism," and counts about 2,000 Yemenite immigrants in the Second Aliyah as a whole, about half of them sent to farming settlements.
Yavne'eli's own report, written in 1913, gives the scale from the inside: over the past year, he wrote, "some two hundred and fifty to three hundred Yemenite families have settled in the colonies."

On Gershon Shafir's reading, as summarized by Joel Beinin, the planters brought in Yemenite Jews "who were to be paid Arab wages": Jewish workers who would satisfy the national ideal of Hebrew labor at the price of Arab labor.
Yemenite families from Sharab reached the Kinneret area in spring 1912 and cleared and farmed land there.

According to the Yemenite heritage site Wysinfo, which reproduces the group's letters, their disputes with the neighboring Kvutzat Kinneret over land ended in 1930 with the Yemenites' removal to Marmorek, near Rehovot.

Gershon Shafir's study of 1989, as summarized by Joel Beinin, argues that the First Aliyah colonies relied on cheap Arab labor; that the Second Aliyah workers' "conquest of labor" failed to exclude Arab workers but did split the labor market in two; that the planters imported Yemenite Jews to be paid Arab wages; and that the kibbutz and Hashomer were forged in conflict over land and labor rather than mainly by prior ideology.

The record above gives this case its strongest evidence: the farmers' continued hiring of Arab workers, Hashomer's condition that only Jewish laborers be employed, and Yavne'eli's families settled in the colonies.
Against such readings, Anita Shapira argues, as summarized by Rebecca Stein, that the early socialist settlers became conquerors reluctantly, out of "good will and purity of faith."
Degania's founding date depends on which group counts as the founders, and Ben-Gurion's arrival is dated to two different years by two reputable sources.

The characterization of the Arab watchmen Hashomer replaced comes from one account, the Jewish Virtual Library's; the material gathered here holds no account from the watchmen, the Arab workers displaced by Hebrew labor, or the villages near the new settlements.
The Yemenite figures come partly from reference summaries, and the Kinneret group's later removal from a heritage site.
The war reached Palestine before it reached its battlefields.
When the Ottoman Empire entered the First World War, the country was still a set of Ottoman districts, centered on the Mutasarrifate of Jerusalem.
Its people were Ottoman subjects, but not all of them.
A large share of the Jewish community held foreign nationality.

The Ottoman register of 1914–15 recorded 38,754 Jews, apparently counting only Ottoman subjects, while other estimates run as high as 94,000; the counting dispute is set out in the opening section of this stage.
Over the next three years Palestine's people, Arab and Jewish, lived through expulsion, a plague of locusts, famine in the wider region, the hanging of Arab nationalists and the emptying of Jaffa.
The first blow fell on the Jews of Jaffa who held Russian citizenship.
In December 1914 up to 6,000 Russian citizens, all of them Jewish, were expelled from the city, according to a reference account of the period.
Many went to Egypt.
Contemporary reports in the New York Times, cited in a 2021 opinion column, put some 7,000 Jewish refugees from Palestine in British-held Alexandria by the end of January 1915.
In 1915 the Ottoman authorities went further.
Non-citizens, Jews included, were required to take Ottoman citizenship or leave.
In the same year the British Army formed the Zion Mule Corps from Jews exiled to Egypt, and it served at Gallipoli; that story, and the wider record of Jewish service to Britain, is told in .
From March to October 1915 swarms covered Palestine, Mount Lebanon and Syria.

The historian Zachary Foster estimates that they cut the 1915 winter harvest of wheat and barley by 10 to 15 percent, and destroyed between 60 and 100 percent of the summer and autumn fruit and vegetables.
The Ottoman response was a labor quota.
By 21 November 1915, the New York Times reported, 800 people had paid the fine rather than collect the eggs.
The locusts struck a region already under strain, and in Greater Syria, the wider territory of which Palestine was a part, the result was famine.
The American University of Beirut's documentary exhibit names four causes acting together.
The Allies blockaded the eastern Mediterranean in 1915.
And the exhibit names Ottoman paper money as a fourth cause.
The mortality figures given are for Mount Lebanon, and they are disputed.
The AUB exhibit says Mount Lebanon lost 20 to 30 percent of its population.
A higher figure, nearly half of the inhabitants of the Mount Lebanon Mutasarrifate, appears in the reference account of the locust plague, but without a source.
For Palestine itself the record used in this book gives no reliable death toll from the famine, and none is offered here.
The war also brought the state's hand down on Arab nationalists.
On Jamal Pasha's orders a group of them was hanged in Marjeh Square in Damascus.

One was Shukri al-Asali, the former governor of Nazareth who had tried to stop the al-Fula land sale of 1910 and had then argued against Zionist settlement in the Ottoman parliament; his part in that sale is told with .
The American University of Beirut's exhibit, however, dates the hangings in Damascus and Beirut to 1915.
Either way, an Ottoman official who had opposed a Zionist land purchase in public was put to death by the same Ottoman state, as one of a group of Arab nationalists.
In the spring of 1917 the war emptied Jaffa.
On 28 March 1917 Jamal Pasha ordered the evacuation of Jaffa.
One estimate puts those displaced at about 10,000, of whom 8,000 were Jews.
Another puts the number evacuated from Tel Aviv, the new Jewish neighborhood beside Jaffa, at up to 16,000.
A United States consular report of 1917 gave 8,000 Jews evicted.
The figures measure different things: the whole city or only its Jewish residents, Jaffa or Tel Aviv.
The lower Jewish figures agree with each other, and the highest figure applies only to Tel Aviv.
The order covered the city, but Jaffa's Muslim residents were able to return soon afterwards, while the Jewish deportees could not return until the summer of 1918.
A US consular report, published in the New York Times on 3 June 1917, described looting and killings of deportees; the report survives in that newspaper and is cited in the 2021 column.
The evidence here is a contemporary diplomatic report as carried by the press, not a court record, and no primary text of Jamal Pasha's orders is among the sources used here.
By the end of the war the Jewish community of Palestine was smaller than in 1914.
The Interactive Encyclopedia of the Palestine Question holds that about a third of the Jewish population left Palestine during 1914–18.
The demographer Justin McCarthy, as summarized by Roger Owen, argues that the fall was much less than the commonly cited quarter, because many of those who fled to Alexandria came back.
Return was also real: the Jaffa deportees were allowed back in the summer of 1918, and McCarthy's case rests on returns from Alexandria.
Ottoman rule in Palestine ended in December 1917, when Britain occupied the country, and the Mutasarrifate of Jerusalem was dissolved.
By then the British government had already made the commitments that would shape what followed, to the Zionist movement and to others in the region.
Those wartime undertakings, and the Balfour Declaration of November 1917 among them, are the subject of Stage Two and are told in .
The number of famine deaths inside Palestine itself is not established in the available sources.
The death toll in Mount Lebanon is given as a range, and its upper claim is unsourced.
The year of the Damascus and Beirut hangings differs between sources.
The size of the Jaffa deportation depends on what is counted, and the deaths it caused were never properly recorded.
How far the Jewish population fell between 1914 and 1918 remains disputed.
Basel, 1897: The Program and Its Opponents
The movement that set its sights on that Ottoman country has a precise birthplace and date.
Political Zionism was founded at the First Zionist Congress, which met in Basel, Switzerland, from 29 to 31 August 1897.
Its convener and chairman was Theodor Herzl, a journalist born in Budapest and a subject of Austria-Hungary, who had published Der Judenstaat the year before.
The Congress adopted a platform, the Basel Program, and founded the Zionist Organization with Herzl as its first president.
Its founding leadership was overwhelmingly European, and so were its funding and its location.
The familiar claim that the State of Israel grew from an ancient national presence with no meaningful break therefore needs a qualification at the start.
The movement that set out to build a state there was new, and it was organized in Europe in 1897.
A second familiar claim, that Jews embraced Zionism from the start, does not survive the record of that same summer.
The Congress was opposed before it opened, it was opposed by rabbis in Germany and Britain, and in the same season a rival Jewish movement was founded on the opposite premise.

The contest inside Jewish life over Herzl's project is one of the clearest pieces of evidence that Zionism and Judaism were not the same thing, and that Jewish opponents, religious and secular, were the first to insist on the difference.
Herzl had planned to hold the Congress in Munich.

On 5 June 1897 a notice in the Münchner Neueste Nachrichten rejected holding his congress in the city, and in mid-June, in letters dated 13 June, the board of the Munich Jewish congregation wrote to Herzl rejecting it as well.
The venue moved to neutral Switzerland.
In one account, the protest of local Orthodox and Reform rabbis helped push the Congress to Basel, and the German Rabbinical Association refused to support holding it in Munich.

On 6 July 1897 the board of the Allgemeiner Rabbiner-Verband, the Union of Rabbis in Germany, published a resolution protesting Zionism, on the grounds of loyalty to the state and of religious messianism.
Herzl gave its authors a name that stuck: the Protestrabbiner, the "protest rabbis".
The declaration appeared in English in the London Jewish Chronicle on 9 July 1897, on page 9.
It was signed by the Union's executive committee: Maybaum of Berlin, Horovitz of Frankfurt, Guttmann of Breslau, Auerbach of Halberstadt and Werner of Munich.
It called the Zionists' efforts toward a state "antagonistic to the messianic promises of Judaism", and it urged Jews to "hold aloof" from the movement and from its Congress.
The rabbis did not object to Jewish agricultural colonization of Palestine.
In Britain, the Orthodox Chief Rabbi Hermann Adler sided with the German rabbis and called Herzl's plan völlig unheilbringend, "completely disastrous".
The Congress met in the Basel Municipal Casino.
Herzl presided in top hat and morning coat, and a photograph of him leaning over the balcony of the Drei Könige hotel became one of the movement's most familiar images.
The Jewish Virtual Library gives "some 200 participants" without naming the number of countries.
The historian Tobias Grill writes that the delegates came from fourteen states.
The program that the Congress adopted unanimously on 30 August 1897 was short.
Zionism seeks to establish a home in Palestine for the Jewish people, secured under public law.
Another published translation renders the same sentence as "the establishment of a publicly and legally secured home in Palestine for the Jewish people".
The German original uses Heimstätte, a home or homestead, and not Staat, a state.
The wording was revised during the Congress itself.
The first was the promotion of settlement in Palestine by Jewish agriculturists, artisans and tradesmen.
The second was the organization of all Jews through local and general institutions "according to the laws of the various countries".
The third was the strengthening of Jewish national feeling and consciousness.
Der Judenstaat had framed it as secular nationalism, modeled on the nation-building of nineteenth-century Europe, and Herzl himself was religiously non-observant.
The First Congress's program, preserved in the Zionist Organization's own archives, deals with political organization, the mechanisms of land purchase and diplomatic outreach, not religious doctrine.
Religious authority was contested at the Congress and largely absent from its decisions.
None of this shows that no delegate had religious motives, or that Zionism never took on religious meaning for its adherents later.
The Congress's most durable product was an organization.
The Zionist Organization was built as a standing, congressional-style body of elected delegates with a governing executive, and from 1899 it had its own bank, the Jewish Colonial Trust.
Herzl was its first president; Chaim Weizmann would lead it in the period of the Balfour Declaration.
It ran the Congresses, managed land purchase through the Jewish National Fund from 1901, and conducted the great-power diplomacy that produced the Declaration in 1917.

In 1929 it created the expanded Jewish Agency for Palestine, which became the proto-government of the Jewish community under the British Mandate, running immigration, settlement, defense and diplomacy.
When the state was declared in 1948, the Agency's executive effectively became Israel's provisional government.
The organization continues today, and the Jewish Agency still administers immigration and diaspora relations with quasi-governmental status, formalized by an Israeli law of 1952.
The line from Basel to the state is an institutional one: a durable, public bureaucracy that outlived everyone who built it, and whose working is traced in .
Herzl understood that the members would have to be won.
At the Second Congress in 1898 his watchword was to "conquer the communities", meaning the established congregations.
Herzl's own verdict on the Congress has become part of its legend.
After Basel he wrote in his diary: "At Basel I founded the Jewish State.
He died in 1904 at the age of forty-four, exhausted by the diplomacy of offering his project to the Sultan, the Kaiser and the British.
Herzl foresaw an outcome, not the path to it; nothing in the entry anticipates the Balfour Declaration, the Mandate or the war of 1948 through which statehood actually came.
The General Jewish Labour Bund was founded in Vilna in October 1897, in the same season as the Basel Congress, and became Zionism's great rival for the loyalty of the Jews of Eastern Europe.

Against emigration to Palestine it set the idea of doikayt, "hereness": Jews should fight for their rights and build their culture where they already lived, as a national minority with autonomy inside democratic, multi-ethnic states, in solidarity with the non-Jewish working class.
It was socialist, Yiddishist and committed to the diaspora.

From the 1900s to the 1930s it was arguably the largest and most dynamic Jewish political movement in Poland and the Russian Empire, and in interwar Poland it regularly outpolled the Zionist parties in Jewish community elections.
The Bund did not lose its argument with Zionism; it was destroyed.

The Bolsheviks dissolved it in 1921, its leader Mark Liber was later executed in the Stalinist purges, its mass base in Polish and Soviet Jewry was murdered in the Holocaust or suppressed under Stalin, and the Polish Bund was suppressed a second time after the war.
For half a century the most popular Jewish political movement in the heartland of Zionist recruitment was explicitly anti-Zionist.

Orthodox anti-Zionist rabbis held that the return of the Jewish people to the land and the restoration of Zion were redemptive events reserved for divine action in the messianic age, not a political program to be forced by secular nationalists ahead of God's time.
To many Orthodox authorities, a secular state built in the Holy Land by non-observant socialists was closer to sacrilege than to fulfillment.
This was a different argument from the Bund's: the Bund wanted Jewish autonomy without a state, while these rabbis rejected human political action as the means of return.

The position has been held continuously since 1897, through Satmar Hasidism and, most visibly, the small Neturei Karta group, whose members still appear at Palestinian-solidarity demonstrations with signs distinguishing Judaism from Zionism.
It is a minority position within Orthodox Judaism; most Haredi Jews today are not Neturei Karta and have made various accommodations with the state.
Reform Judaism's opposition and the wider range of Jewish positions in these years are traced in .
Ahad Ha'am, "one of the people", was the pen name of Asher Ginsberg (1856–1927), the founder of what came to be called cultural Zionism and political Zionism's sharpest internal critic.
He had visited Ottoman Palestine, and in his essay of 1891, "Truth from the Land of Israel", he reported what much of the movement preferred not to see: the land was not empty.
It had a substantial Arab population, farming and living on it, who would not simply accept displacement, and he warned that treating them with contempt would poison the whole enterprise.
This is Zionist testimony, from 1891, that Palestine was inhabited.

Against Herzl he argued that a hurried political and diplomatic state would produce "a state of Jews" but not "a Jewish state": a polity Jewish in population but hollow in spirit, having skipped the slow cultural and ethical renewal he believed must come first.
Israelis across the political spectrum still invoke him.

Baron Edmond de Rothschild (1845–1934), of the Paris branch of the family, had privately funded the struggling agricultural colonies of the First Aliyah in Ottoman Palestine since the 1880s, among them Rishon LeZion and Zichron Ya'akov, which was named for his father.
His money, sums that would run to tens of millions in today's terms, effectively kept early Jewish settlement alive when it might otherwise have collapsed.
Yet Edmond personally opposed Herzl and political Zionism.

He distrusted Herzl's public, diplomatic, state-seeking approach and favored quiet, paternalistic philanthropic colonization that would not provoke the Ottoman authorities or make grand political claims, and for years he refused to place his settlements under the Zionist Organization.
The two men held incompatible theories of the project, as Simon Schama documents in Two Rothschilds and the Land of Israel.

Edmond must be kept distinct from Walter Rothschild of the London branch, who twenty years later was the ceremonial addressee of the Balfour letter and who neither funded the settlements nor wrote the policy.

The phrase "the Rothschilds created Israel" fuses two men with opposite roles and opposite views into one imaginary actor, the move by which a documented banking family is turned into an antisemitic hidden hand.
The record shows members of one family reaching their own, divergent judgments, not a coordinated plan; his colonies and his first refusal of Herzl are told in .
Two questions about Herzl himself remain open.

The usual account, repeated in many references, holds that his catalyst was the Dreyfus Affair: covering for a Vienna newspaper the 1894 degradation of a Jewish French officer, and watching a Paris crowd chant against Jews in the most emancipated society in Europe, he concluded that assimilation had failed as a strategy for Jewish safety and that a national home under public law was the only political answer.

The historian Steven Beller, reviewing Derek Penslar's 2020 biography of Herzl, points to a difficulty: Dreyfus "is not mentioned by name in the Zionist diary of 1895", and Beller uses this to question whether the Affair was the catalyst at all.
The strongest form of the traditional case is that Herzl was in Paris as a correspondent during the Affair and that its lesson about European antisemitism fits his program exactly.
The strongest form of the revision is that the diary in which he worked out his Zionism in 1895 is silent about the case.
The second question concerns a line often put in Herzl's mouth: that the Jewish state should run "from the Nile to the Euphrates".

Herzl's diary for 1898 records a plan to ask the Ottoman Sultan for territory "from the Brook of Egypt to the Euphrates"; Daniel Pipes, who is often cited as having debunked the line, confirms the diary entry and shows only that Herzl never made the request and that it never became the movement's programme.

The Herzl of the record was a secular nation-builder who weighed Argentina and entertained Britain's East Africa offer, not a man with a fixed scriptural map; the diary note is real, and it stayed a note.

It does not measure how many Jews in 1897 supported Herzl, opposed him or were indifferent; it records the institutions and named individuals who took positions, and on that evidence the movement began as one current among several in Jewish life, contested from its first summer.
The Jewish Colonial Trust: A Bank Owned a Pound at a Time
The Basel Program of 1897 named its means but not its money.
The Second Zionist Congress, meeting in 1898, decided to create one.
On 20 March 1899, the Jewish Colonial Trust, in Hebrew Otẓar Hityashvuth Hayehudim, was incorporated in London under the English Companies Acts.
Its stated aim was to acquire the capital, and the "charter," that would make large-scale settlement in Palestine possible.
Incorporated under English company law, the Trust was not a charity collecting gifts.
It was political Zionism's first financial institution.
A familiar account of Zionist finance holds that the movement was paid for by a few great patrons, with the name Rothschild usually standing in for all of them.
The design of the Trust points the other way.
The purpose was to let working-class Jews across Europe, and not only the wealthy, become shareholders in the national project.
Herzl set the example by buying the first 1,000 shares himself.
The Trust's founders each brought something different.
Herzl supplied the political leadership and the public name.

David Wolffsohn, a German-Jewish timber merchant and one of Herzl's closest associates, co-founded the Trust and would hold a remarkable run of offices: he chaired the Anglo-Palestine Company from its founding in 1902 and succeeded Herzl as president of the Zionist Organization in 1905.
Wolffsohn is also documented as the designer of the two-stripes-and-star flag adopted at Basel in 1897, the design that later became the state flag of Israel.
The third co-founder, Jacobus Kahn, was a Dutch-Jewish banker.
The record does not give Kahn a role in the wider movement comparable to Herzl's or Wolffsohn's, and none of the three acted alone; each institution they helped found had other named colleagues.
Measured against its own target, the Trust fell far short.
It continued for decades, and in time became a major shareholder of Bank Leumi, the bank that grew out of its Palestine subsidiary.
The Trust showed that a political movement could be financed by tens of thousands of ordinary owners, each holding a small stake, rather than by the goodwill of a handful of magnates.
The Jewish National Fund, founded two years later, turned it into a physical object, the blue collection box, and after 1920 Keren Hayesod made small-donor fundraising permanent.
By 1899 more than 100,000 people had subscribed for shares, yet lasting control of the Trust sat with a small founding bloc, through a block of "founders' shares" that carried super-voting rights.

The point here is the shape it gave the institution from the start: the cost of the project was spread across a mass of small shareholders, while its direction stayed with the founding leadership of the Zionist Organization.
A bank incorporated in London still had to reach Palestine.
On 27 February 1902, the Trust founded the Anglo-Palestine Company as its Palestine-facing banking subsidiary.

This was the point at which fundraising turned into settlement: the subsidiary would finance land purchases directly, run a network of credit cooperatives offering long-term agricultural loans to settlers, and in 1909 lend to the association that built the first neighborhood of Tel Aviv.
The parent company in London raised the capital; the subsidiary in Jaffa put it to work.
Its row for the Trust records it as £2,000,000 authorized and about £250,000 raised in £1 shares, the money that bought "the movement's own bank."

The ledger multiplies each amount by the ratio of the 2025 consumer price index to the index of the year in question, the method of the United States government's own inflation calculator, converting pounds into dollars at the period exchange rate first.
For years before 1913 it relies on estimates from the Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis, and it labels those conversions approximate.
By that measure the Trust's raise was modest beside what came later.
The ledger's own rows put Keren Hayesod's worldwide income for 1921–1929 at $20.1 million, about $370 million today, and the United Jewish Appeal's 1948 campaign at $150 million, about $2 billion.
The Trust's importance did not lie in its size.

The full map of the money behind the state, from the Trust through the land fund, Keren Hayesod and the wartime campaigns, shows where the Trust sits: first in time, and the base on which the later institutions were built.
The record leaves several questions about the Trust unanswered.
The Jewish National Fund: Land Bought and Never Resold

sent: The idea of a fund that would do exactly that was older than the Jewish Colonial Trust.
Hermann Schapira proposed a national land fund at the very first Zionist Congress, in Basel in 1897.
For four years the proposal sat on the Congress agenda, debated and deferred, Congress after Congress.
It came to a head at the Fifth Zionist Congress in Basel in December 1901.

With the delegates ready to disperse once more without a decision, Herzl stood before them and pushed the matter to a vote: "After striving for so many years to set up the fund, we do not want to disperse again without having done anything."
The motion passed, and the Jewish National Fund was founded on 29 December 1901.
Within a month it had its first director, Johann (Yona) Kremenetzky, who ran it from Vienna.

The sources describe repeated deferral, and the deferral appears to reflect ordinary institutional delay and competing priorities on a crowded Congress agenda, not organized opposition to a land fund as such.
As the sources give it: "The JNF shall be the eternal possession of the Jewish people.
Its funds shall not be used except for the purchase of lands in Palestine and Syria."
And whatever it bought became, in the resolution's language, the eternal possession of the Jewish people.
The JNF built a rule to prevent that.
The money that paid for the land came, as with the Trust, from many small givers.

Haim Kleinman, a bank clerk in Nadvorna, in Galicia, put a blue box labeled "Keren Le'umit" in his own office and wrote to the movement's newspaper, Die Welt, proposing that the idea be taken up more widely.
Kremenetzky adopted the suggestion, and the first mass-produced boxes were distributed in 1904.
By the interwar years roughly one million blue-and-white collection boxes sat in Jewish homes around the world.
The box made physical what the Trust's pound share had begun: a national project paid for in coins, household by household.
Kleinman himself was one of them.
In 1903 Isaac Leib Goldberg of Vilnius, a Russian Zionist leader, gave it 200 dunams east of Hadera, a parcel that later became an olive grove.
The units in that series shift: the 1935 figure is reported in acres and square kilometers, the others in dunams.
The record also places the fund within Jewish landholding as a whole.

At the moment of statehood, total Jewish holdings in Palestine came to roughly 2 million dunams, about 7 percent of Mandate Palestine's roughly 26 million dunams, and the sources describe the JNF's share as more than half of that total.
Taken at face value, the two rounded figures do not quite agree: 936,000 out of 2 million is a little under half.
A common account holds that Zionist land buying before 1948 was sporadic and small.
Even at the end, all Jewish-owned land together amounted to about 7 percent of the country.
The land fund was large within Jewish landholding and small within Palestine as a whole.
The legal framework of the purchases, the sellers, and the tenants who lived on land that changed hands are treated in , which carries this section's numbers into the Ottoman and Mandate land system.
The same JNF series appears again, with later figures beside it, in .

The record traces the fund's land but not, in these sources, its full annual income: how much the blue boxes collected in any given year is not documented here, and the library's funding ledger lists the JNF's income series among the totals still unavailable.
And the precise share of Jewish-held land the fund owned in 1947–48 depends on a total that is reported only as roughly 2 million dunams.
A Bank for Palestine, and an Offer for East Africa
In the eighteen months from early 1902 to the summer of 1903 the Zionist movement ran on two tracks at once.
On one, it built a bank inside Palestine.
On the other, under the pressure of a massacre in the Russian Empire, its own Congress voted to look seriously at land in East Africa.
The first track began in London.
On 27 February 1902, the Jewish Colonial Trust founded a subsidiary, the Anglo-Palestine Company, with initial capital of about £50,000.
Its chairman was David Wolffsohn, the Trust's co-founder and later Herzl's successor.
Its manager was Zalman David Levontin, one of the founders of Rishon LeZion in 1882, whom Herzl had recruited personally.
The parent company in London raised capital from small shareholders; the subsidiary was the arm that would put the capital to work on the ground, as  describes.
The company opened its first branch in Jaffa in 1903.
By 1914 it had branches in Jerusalem, Beirut, Hebron, Haifa, Safed, Tiberias and Gaza.
Its name later changed twice: it became the Anglo-Palestine Bank around 1930, and Bank Leumi in 1950–51.

The line runs unbroken from a £50,000 subsidiary of 1902 to one of the major banks of the State of Israel, though the bank's later operations are a different story from its founding years, and are not told here.
The Anglo-Palestine Company lent to the Ahuzat Bayit association, which used the money to build the first neighborhood of what became Tel Aviv in 1909, six years after the Jaffa branch opened.
The founding of the neighborhood itself, its lots and its first families, belongs to the story of the Second Aliyah and is told there.
At Easter, on 6–7 April 1903, a pogrom broke out in the town of Kishinev.

According to the Encyclopaedia Judaica, 49 Jews were killed and more than 500 injured; 700 houses were looted and destroyed and 600 businesses and shops looted; about 2,000 families were left homeless; and the losses were put at 2,500,000 gold rubles.
P. Krushevan's newspaper Bessarabets had incited the population with a steady stream of articles, among them a blood libel.
Local and central officials, it states, prepared the pogrom, "evidently with the backing of the minister of the interior, V. Plehve," and the town's garrison of 5,000 soldiers did not intervene.
The word "evidently" marks an inference from the evidence, not a document of instruction, and the role of Plehve rests in this book's sources on this one reference work.
Herzl's own meetings with Plehve that August are told with .
Protest meetings were held in London, Paris and New York.
In the United States a protest petition was handed to President Theodore Roosevelt for transmission to the tsar, and the tsar refused it.
The poet Bialik answered the pogrom with his poem "In the Town of Death."
Kishinev was not the end.
A second riot in the town in October 1905 killed 19 Jews and injured 56, and some Jewish youth formed self-defense units.
The pogrom fell inside a movement of people far larger than Zionism.
Between 1881 and 1914, according to the historian Shmuel Ettinger, more than 2.5 million Jews left Eastern Europe, about 80,000 a year.
About 2 million went to the United States, about 350,000 to Western Europe, and about 300,000 to other overseas countries, Palestine among them.
The great majority of Jews leaving Eastern Europe in this period chose America.
Palestine was one destination within a category of about 300,000.
After the Kishinev pogrom, Joseph Chamberlain, Britain's Colonial Secretary, offered Herzl the Guas Ngishu plateau in British East Africa for Jewish settlement.
The territory lay in what is now Kenya, not Uganda, but the plan has been remembered ever since, inaccurately, as "the Uganda Scheme."

It does not establish what longer-term purposes, if any, Chamberlain or the British government had in making it; the record documents the offer and its trigger, not Britain's wider calculations, which belong to the later story of British policy.
The Sixth Zionist Congress opened in Basel on 23 August 1903, with about 600 delegates, the largest Congress to that date.
It was the last Herzl would chair.
In his opening address he said of East Africa that "Zion this certainly is not and can never become," and described it as only an auxiliary colonizing measure.
He also called it a Nachtasyl, a night shelter: a temporary refuge from immediate danger, not a replacement for the Land of Israel.
They were not asked to accept East Africa as the national home.
The Congress voted 295 in favor and 178 against, with 98 abstentions.
Then members of the Russian delegation walked out, arguing that the plan violated the Basel Program.
The sources differ slightly on who left: one describes the Russian Zionist delegation walking out, another speaks of members of the delegation.
Herzl's, as his own framing of a night shelter implies, was a case about time.
People were being killed now; a great power was offering land; and a refuge, explicitly temporary and explicitly not Zion, could save lives while the political work for Palestine went on.
The Basel Program named Palestine.
The record does not show, however, that every Russian Zionist shared the walkout, nor that the rift was never repaired.
The familiar account has it that Palestine was always the only place Zionists were seriously prepared to build.

Six years after Basel, the movement's own Congress voted to examine a territory in East Africa, as a considered answer to escalating violence and not as a gesture, and the vote split its delegates badly enough that one delegation left the hall.
It was the nearest the movement came, after 1897, to turning away from Palestine.
Whether the 1903 vote would have led anywhere had Herzl lived is a question no document can answer.
How the matter ended, at the Seventh Congress of 1905, is told in .
They do not give the exact date of Chamberlain's offer, beyond placing it after the pogrom.
They rest the role of Plehve on a single reference work's inference.
East Africa Rejected:
Palestine Chosen by Elimination
The East Africa question did not end with the walkout of 1903.

It ended two years later, by a second Congress vote, and it ended at a price: a permanent split in the movement and the founding of a rival organization that spent twenty years looking for a homeland anywhere but Palestine.
Israel Zangwill, a British-Jewish writer and Zionist leader, led the "Territorialist Faction" at the Sixth Congress.
His argument was not that East Africa should replace Palestine.
It was that the British offer should be used as leverage in later negotiations with the Ottomans over Palestine.
Otto Warburg, a German botanist (1859–1938) from a wealthy Hamburg banking family, also supported the East Africa plan at the Sixth Congress.

He is a different man from the better-known twentieth-century biochemist of the same name, and his later career, traced below, shows that support for East Africa in 1903 did not rule out leading the movement's work in Palestine.
Herzl died in 1904.
The Seventh Zionist Congress met in Basel from 27 July to 2 August 1905.
It formally rejected the East Africa offer, closing the question the Sixth Congress had opened, and Britain withdrew the offer.
And it elected David Wolffsohn, co-founder of the Jewish Colonial Trust and designer of the movement's flag, as president of the Zionist Organization in Herzl's place.
One reference work states the decision in broader terms: the Seventh Congress rejected a national home outside Palestine and its vicinity.
The succession followed from Herzl's death and would have come whatever the Congress decided about Africa.
For Zangwill the rejection was final.

When the Congress turned the offer down outright, he led 28 delegates out of the hall and founded the Jewish Territorial Organization, the ITO, dedicated to finding land for Jewish settlement anywhere, no longer bound to Palestine.
The ITO had support at the time from two members of the Rothschild family, the brothers Leopold and Baron Nathan Mayer Rothschild, not to be confused with Baron Edmond de Rothschild.
The ITO's search was wide.
It sent exploratory expeditions to Canada, Australia, Mesopotamia (today's Iraq), Cyrenaica (in today's Libya) and Angola.
It also ran the Galveston Movement, which directed Jewish immigrants to the United States through the port of Galveston, Texas, instead of New York.
Zangwill himself, looking back, said that "there was not a land on earth that we did not think about."

Zangwill fought a case in the English courts against the Jewish Colonial Trust; as the sources describe it, the suit sought to restrain the Trust from colonizing anywhere outside Palestine, Syria, Asiatic Turkey, Sinai and Cyprus.
What it shows is that the boundaries of the movement's territory were contested in law as well as in Congress.

One calls the Galveston effort a failed attempt to settle Jewish refugees in Texas and says the ITO's search met with little success; another speaks of a single modest, temporary success without naming it.
They agree on the larger outcome: the ITO achieved little lasting settlement anywhere.
Zangwill rejoined the mainstream Zionist movement before his death in 1921.
The ITO officially disbanded around 1925, four years later.
Otto Warburg's path ran the other way.

Having backed East Africa in 1903, he became the Zionist Organization's third president, serving from 1911 to 1921, and with Arthur Ruppin founded the Palestine Land Development Company, which he named and led until his death, bringing the Jewish National Fund in as a shareholder.
A common view treats East Africa as a footnote and holds that no real alternative to Palestine ever existed.
It is in that sense that Palestine was confirmed by elimination.
Its place as the movement's target survived two organized internal challenges: the 1903 vote to examine East Africa, and the ITO's departure in 1905 to search elsewhere.
It does not mean the 1903 Congress chose East Africa: it voted to examine the offer, under a sponsor who said plainly it was not Zion.
Nor does it mean Palestine won only because everything else failed.
The Seventh Congress rejected East Africa in 1905, while the ITO's search had barely begun; the decision came first, and the failures came after.
It does not record a single rationale shared by the delegates who chose Palestine.
Some, like the Russian delegates of 1903, argued from the Basel Program, which named Palestine.
Others, like Warburg, backed East Africa in 1903 and later led the organization's work in Palestine.
A reading that ties the outcome to the Jewish masses' religious and historical attachment to the land is offered in , and it is a reading, not a documented finding.
The sources here say nothing about what the East Africa commission reported, or when exactly Britain withdrew its offer.
They do not give the vote at the Seventh Congress, only its result.
They do not name the 28 delegates who left with Zangwill, explain his suit against the Trust, or identify the "modest success" one of them mentions.
Suppose the Sixth Zionist Congress had gone the other way in 1903, and a Jewish state had been built in British East Africa or in Argentina.
What would it have been called, and would the structures later built on the name "Israel" still have worked?

The test is therefore built from documented pieces: what Theodor Herzl wrote in 1896, what the Congress did in 1903 and 1905, what Genesis 15:18 says, and what Cyrus Scofield's prophetic notes require.
In Der Judenstaat Herzl put the choice of territory as an open question: "Shall we choose Palestine or Argentine?
We shall take what is given us, and what is selected by Jewish public opinion."
He noted that Argentina's government would "gladly provide" Jews with land.
His framework was, in the first instance, a political answer to European antisemitism, and Herzl himself was a secular Jew.

One account of the text holds that he considered Argentina first and Palestine second, and that when he did prefer Palestine, it was because it would give "the Jewish problem" a solution "not only just, but brilliant," a practical and political reason (Palestine would mobilize Jewish public opinion) rather than a religious one.

The Israeli peace activist and writer Uri Avnery went further, judging that Herzl "had obviously thought very little about Palestine as a concrete entity" and had inserted it into his original blueprint as an afterthought.
Argentina offered practical advantages, fertile land and a sparse population.
Palestine was "our ever-memorable historic home... a force of marvelous potency."

Read this way, Herzl named, seven years before anyone offered him East Africa, the very difference the Uganda dispute would turn on: one territory had only practical merits, the other carried a weight no practical merit could replace.
They differ on emphasis: whether Palestine's pull, for Herzl, was mainly its power to rally Jewish opinion or its historic charge.
Neither reading claims that every later leader or delegate shared Herzl's reasons.
The Congress's own record bears on the same difference.
Herzl laid the British offer before the Sixth Congress in August 1903 as a temporary refuge for Jews fleeing persecution; the vote to send a commission and the walkout that followed are told in .

That account describes the minority as mainly Russian and Eastern European delegates who had lived through the worst of the pogroms, and reads their walkout as a statement that they were not looking for any land; they were returning to Zion.
Herzl died in 1904, and the Seventh Zionist Congress formally rejected the scheme in 1905.
Zionist historical scholarship describes two broad strands that the dispute brought into the open.
"Territorial Zionism," sometimes called Ugandism, held that any safe territory would serve: the purpose was refuge from persecution, and location came second to safety.
"Zion Zionism" held that only Palestine, the biblical Land of Israel, Eretz Yisrael, would serve, because the purpose was not refuge alone but national restoration to an ancestral homeland.
The debate of 1903–1905 settled the question in favor of Zion.

The conclusion this account draws is that even secular political Zionism could not override the religious and historical attachment of the Jewish masses to that land; for most supporters, location was not interchangeable.
"On that day the LORD made a covenant with Abram, saying, 'To your offspring I give this land, from the river of Egypt to the great river, the river Euphrates.'"
Another rendering has "I have given this land" and "the Euphrates river."

Deuteronomy 11:24 reads: "Every place on which the sole of your foot treads shall be yours; your territory shall be from the wilderness, from Lebanon, from the river, the Euphrates river, to the western sea."

Together these passages describe a territory in the Levant bounded by the Euphrates to the northeast, the Nile (or Wadi el-Arish) to the southwest, Lebanon to the north and the Mediterranean to the west.
The test concerns only the literal reading, because that is the reading on which Scofield's framework rests.
Scofield's dispensationalism, set out in the notes of his annotated Bible (told in ), arranges prophecy into an ordered sequence.
Every step after the second depends on the regathering happening at the place the earlier covenant named, Zion and Jerusalem.
A state in East Africa calling itself Israel would not satisfy "Israel regathered" in the sense the sequence's own logic requires.
It would not be a variant of the same prophecy but a different claim, one Scofield's notes never made.

On this argument, the 30 to 40 million Christian Zionists who later grew out of his framework exist because the state that formed stood where their theology pointed; move it, and there is a serious case that this constituency, and the sustained American political support it supplied, would never have formed.

It holds that the idea of Greater Israel, Eretz Yisrael HaShlema, the "Complete Land of Israel," is a biblical concept that can exist only because the state was established in the biblical Land of Israel.

In Argentina or East Africa, it reasons, five things would have been missing: the biblical land-promise framework, since Genesis 15:18 has no Argentine equivalent; the narrative of return to an ancestral homeland, since Jews had no historical claim to Argentina or East Africa; the concept of the Complete Land of Israel itself; the Revisionist Zionist claim to "both banks of the Jordan"; and the religious-nationalist settler ideology that draws explicitly on biblical texts about Levantine territory.

The argument's central step is that the same attachment to the land that made Argentina or Uganda unacceptable in 1903–1905 is the attachment that later generates territorial maximalism, so that the founding choice of Palestine already posed the question of the land's "completeness."
The opening of this library sets out one symbolic interpretation of the name, reading "Israel" as IS-RA-EL: a state of consciousness a person arrives at, rather than a bloodline or a border.
Put to the same counterfactual, even this reading draws its resonance from places named in the text: Jerusalem, the Temple, and Peniel, where Jacob wrestled.
A state in East Africa that borrowed the word would not carry that resonance by borrowing it.

The movement's financial and political institutions, among them the Jewish Colonial Trust and the Jewish National Fund, and later bodies such as AZEC, were built to fund and organize settlement, and nothing in their design tied them to one territory.
Before Herzl, real settlement infrastructure had in fact been built in Argentina under the JCA.
Palestine was not merely the sentimental favorite among roughly equal choices.

For at least one major source of the movement's eventual support, it was close to a structural requirement: the only site compatible with the theological and symbolic machinery that later supplied decades of American political and financial backing.

The familiar account holds that Zionism was first of all a response to European antisemitism, a movement for Jewish self-determination and safety; that the choice of Palestine was contested inside the movement, with some leaders open to other places; and that the eventual choice reflected the deep historical and religious attachment of most Jews to the biblical Land of Israel.

The East Africa offer was a real offer of refuge, debated and voted on; on the account cited above, those who walked out in 1903 were delegates from the communities that had suffered the worst pogroms, and what moved them was attachment to Zion, not a program of borders.

The same source that builds the Greater Israel argument says plainly that the internal debate "was resolved by religious and historical attachment to the specific land, not by territorial maximalism."
The Scofield test, likewise, bears on the support the state later received from Christians; it does not explain the choice the Zionist delegates themselves made.

No one knows what the founders would actually have named a state in East Africa, or how a Christian constituency would have responded to it, because those things never happened and cannot be documented.
The movement did seriously consider East Africa; that is on record.
Whether Herzl's own preference was chiefly political or chiefly historic remains a matter of reading the same pages two ways.
The Palestine Office: Settlement Gets a Bureaucracy
Behind the farms and guards of the Second Aliyah stood an office.
A familiar picture of Zionist settlement before the First World War shows lone pioneers improvising on the land, with no real organization behind them.
The decision came from the top of the Zionist Organization.
In 1907 its president, David Wolffsohn, sent Arthur Ruppin to Palestine.
In 1908 Ruppin opened the Palestine Office in Jaffa.
It became the organization's central operating agency in the country for buying land and coordinating settlement, and it worked directly with the funds of the Jewish National Fund.
Ruppin, a German-trained lawyer and economist, had first come on a pilot study of the prospects for colonization.
His fuller record, including the documented evidence that he believed Zionism required Jewish "racial purity," is set out in .
The Palestine Office had three jobs.
It coordinated land purchase with the Jewish National Fund, it assisted immigration, and it helped settle the people who arrived.
The Zionist Organization had founded a bank, the Jewish Colonial Trust, in 1899 and a land fund, the Jewish National Fund, in 1901.
The Palestine Office, added in 1908, was the body in the country itself through which money raised abroad was turned into specific purchases and specific settlements.
That is why a modest field office in Jaffa holds a central place in the institutional history.
The Palestine Land Development Company was founded beside the office.
Ruppin set it up with Otto Warburg, and the sources date its founding to 1908 or 1909.
The company bought land and prepared it physically for ownership by the Jewish National Fund and for use by settlers.
By the outbreak of the First World War it had handled approximately 50,000 dunams.
The Jewish National Fund was the owner, in whose name land was held.
Warburg, the German botanist who became the Zionist Organization's third president in 1911, had backed the East Africa offer in 1903; his path from that vote to Palestine is traced in .
He chose the company's name himself, led it until his death in 1938, and brought the Jewish National Fund in as a shareholder.
Nor does it give the Palestine Office's budget or staff.
It was raised by the Zionist Organization's own instruments, the Jewish Colonial Trust's shares and the Jewish National Fund's collections, which are described in their own sections.
In these prewar years Yehoshua Hankin, Arthur Ruppin and Jacob Thon negotiated and carried out land purchases.
Hankin was also the chief negotiator of the Sursock purchases, which are told in the section on how land was bought.
Warburg is said to have led the company until 1938, and the section on land purchase has Hankin becoming its head in 1932.
The Palestine Office is the institutional ancestor of the Jewish Agency, established in 1929.
The Jewish Agency became the institutional engine of state-building in Mandate Palestine.
It does not follow that every later Jewish Agency practice goes back directly to the methods of 1908.
Organizations change, and what runs from Jaffa to 1929 is an institutional line, not an unbroken set of procedures.
It begins with building a bank in 1899–1902 and buying land through the Jewish National Fund from 1901.
It moves through the permanent fundraising of the 1920s and the enlarged Jewish Agency to the war financing of 1948 and the step of 1948–49 that turned donors into state policy.
The Palestine Office does not have a step of its own in the panel.

The section on land purchase records that agents such as Hankin sometimes bought land first, at their own financial risk, and were reimbursed by the Jewish National Fund or the Jewish Agency only afterward.
The Federal Reserve, 1913: Structure, Need and a Coincidence of Dates
On 23 December 1913 the Federal Reserve Act was signed into law, creating the central banking system of the United States.

It falls sixteen years after the First Zionist Congress at Basel and seven years before the Keren Hayesod fund existed, and an often-repeated claim holds that the two stories are one: that the Federal Reserve was founded by, or to serve, the same financial network that was funding Zionism.
It sets out what the Federal Reserve actually was and why Congress created it, in the same plain terms this book uses for every other institution.
Most Americans learn the institution's name without learning its structure, and two simple accounts compete to fill the gap.
In one, the Federal Reserve is an ordinary federal agency like any other.
It consisted of twelve regional Federal Reserve Banks.
Each was owned by the commercial banks that were its members, and those member banks were required to hold stock in their district's Reserve Bank.
Each regional bank historically financed itself from its own earnings rather than from appropriations voted by Congress.

Above the regional banks sat a public body, the Board, known at first as the Federal Reserve Board and later as the Board of Governors, whose members are nominated by the President and confirmed by the Senate.
Presidential nomination and Senate confirmation of the Board are real mechanisms of democratic oversight.
Why Congress accepted so unusual a design begins with the decades before it.
Between 1865 and 1913 the United States suffered at least five major financial crises.

The Federal Reserve's own historical research states the pattern directly: nationwide banking panics came on average every fifteen years, each forcing financial institutions to suspend operations and each followed by a long, deep recession.
The Panic of 1907 is documented as among the most severe financial crises of the era before the Federal Reserve, and as the direct, immediate trigger for its creation.
With no central bank able to intervene, the nearest thing the country had to a backstop was the financier J.P. Morgan.
They do not settle Morgan's motives, and this book makes no claim about them.
In November 1910 Senator Nelson Aldrich gathered a party at the Jekyll Island Club, off the Georgia coast.

The Federal Reserve's historians describe the party as five bankers and a former Treasury official, and they give the reason for the secrecy plainly: "the plan was written in secrecy, as the public would never approve of a banking reform bill written by bankers, much less...a central bank."
The resulting Aldrich Plan gave private banks substantial control.
Aldrich chaired the National Monetary Commission, the body whose work produced the meeting.
Henry Davison was a senior partner at J.P. Morgan & Co.
Frank Vanderlip was president of National City Bank, documented as the flagship institution of the Rockefeller banking interests.
Paul Warburg was a partner at Kuhn, Loeb & Co.
A. Piatt Andrew, Assistant Treasury Secretary, is described as a technical bridge, on good terms with both the Morgan and the Rockefeller spheres but employed by neither.
Arthur Shelton was Aldrich's personal secretary, tied to Aldrich himself and with no banking connection of his own.
Aldrich's own link to the Rockefeller interests went beyond politics.
His daughter Abby married John D. Rockefeller Jr., which made Aldrich the younger Rockefeller's father-in-law; his grandson Nelson Rockefeller was named for him.
(The named list does not quite match the historians' summary: it holds three bankers from the great houses, a serving Treasury official and a secretary, besides Aldrich himself.)
The Federal Reserve's own historical researchers record it and explain it.
Nor was the Aldrich Plan simply handed to Congress and passed.
Public reaction to it was hostile, and historians are specific about why: "what people were really upset about was the political structure of Aldrich's plan."
Congress and President Wilson's administration rewrote that structure before anything became law.
In the Federal Reserve Act, private banks received considerably less control than Aldrich had designed.
Congress accepted the final structure because it had first forced the reduction of private banking control that the public and many legislators objected to.
Paul Warburg, the Kuhn, Loeb partner, was really present at Jekyll Island in 1910 and served on the first Federal Reserve Board, from 1914 to 1918.
The record shows no part for him in Zionist fundraising or planning.
Paul Warburg's brother, Felix Warburg, and his father-in-law, Jacob Schiff, were prominent non-Zionists and opponents of Zionism in exactly this period.
