Schiff put his position on record: "I cannot for a moment concede that one can be at the same time a true American and an honest adherent of the Zionist movement."
Felix Warburg held a similar, documented non-Zionist position at the same time.

If the claim is that a single family network was quietly coordinating American central banking and Zionist fundraising, a public, quoted rejection of Zionism by that family's most prominent members contradicts it about as directly as the historical record can.
Views on Zionism shifted over the following decades across the wider Warburg and Schiff families, and the sources here do not claim that every member held the same view for life.
Other named Jewish leaders and bodies also opposed Zionism in these years, set out in .

The Federal Reserve Act created a central banking system sixteen years after Basel, and there is no documented institutional or financial link between it and the Zionist Organization or its funds: neither the Jewish Colonial Trust, nor the Jewish National Fund, nor the Keren Hayesod, which did not yet exist.
A search of the founding documents of the Trust, the Fund and the Federal Reserve shows no connection between them.
It does not mean that no individual moved in both worlds; Paul Warburg's case shows exactly how far such overlap went in a small early-twentieth-century financial world.

The specific assertion of a connection between the Federal Reserve and Zionism goes back to Eustace Mullins's tract The Federal Reserve Conspiracy, promoted from the 1950s and recycled since by extremist groups and figures.
Mainstream fact-checking and civil-rights research organizations classify "Jewish control of the Federal Reserve" as a documented antisemitic myth, not a contested historical question.
It does not mean that everyone who repeats some version of the claim knows or endorses its origin; myths travel independently of their sources.
The one documented individual link runs to a man whose own family publicly opposed Zionism.
The sources document that Morgan's 1907 rescue happened and worked; they do not establish his motives.
They document the Warburg and Schiff positions in this period, not across the families' whole later history.
What it offers is the specific, checkable facts about the Federal Reserve's founding and the specific origin of the myth, so that any other version can be tested against the same documents.
The American Machine: Hadassah, Brandeis and the ZOA, 1912–1918
While Filastin was finding readers in the villages of the Jaffa district, a different public was being organized in the United States.
A familiar assumption holds that American support for Zionism became organized and significant only after 1948, or at the earliest after the Holocaust.

By 1918 the movement in the United States had a national women's organization raising money for medical work in Palestine, a Justice of the Supreme Court as its most influential advocate with direct access to the President, and a merged national political organization reporting more than 147,000 members.
None of this was built in Palestine.
It was domestic American institution-building, carried out years before there was a British Mandate to build under.
On 24 February 1912 Henrietta Szold founded Hadassah in New York.
In 1913 it sent the movement's first two nurses to Palestine, to provide maternity care and to treat trachoma.
Hadassah's significance for the architecture of the movement lies in the channel it created as much as in the clinics it funded.
Most of the financial and political machinery traced elsewhere in this stage, the Jewish Colonial Trust, the Jewish National Fund and, from 1918, the ZOA's own fundraising, was built and run by men.
Hadassah was a distinct American fundraising channel, financed specifically by American Jewish women and directed to medical and settlement infrastructure in Palestine.

It did not operate in isolation, however: in 1918 Hadassah became one of the founding member organizations of the Zionist Organization of America, so the two channels were joined institutionally while remaining distinct in organization and purpose.
Szold's own arc reached far beyond this period.

She later directed Youth Aliyah, founded in 1933, which the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum credits with bringing more than 14,000 unaccompanied children to Palestine and Britain between 1933 and 1945.

It is recorded here because it shows the scale an organization founded at a small New York meeting in 1912 would eventually reach, and with the caution that a child-rescue and resettlement operation of that size involved real hardships for the children, a fuller story than a founding-to-scale summary can tell.
In 1914 Louis Brandeis, who would join the United States Supreme Court in 1916, moved into active Zionist leadership after a meeting with Jacob de Haas, who had been Herzl's secretary.
The line from Herzl to Brandeis ran through one of Herzl's own staff.
From 1914 Brandeis led the American movement, and he remained its leader until 1921.
He worked with the Reverend William Blackstone on the Blackstone Memorial of 1916 to influence President Wilson.
In 1917 he met Balfour, and during the drafting of the Balfour Declaration he worked as a conduit between the British government and the President.
His direct line to Wilson in those months is documented by multiple historians; the channel itself is not in dispute.
How the Declaration was drafted, and what Brandeis's part in it was, is told with .
Nahum Goldmann later argued that without Brandeis "the Balfour Declaration would probably never have been issued."
It may be right, but no document can prove what Britain would have done without him, and it should be read as an argument, not as settled fact.
His personal motives for converting to Zionist leadership are contested among historians.
Some argue that the conversion was partly career-strategic, a reading that outlets such as Mondoweiss have cited in critical treatments of his role.

The distinction matters for how the American story is told: that a Supreme Court Justice had direct access to a sitting President is a documented, checkable fact about influence; why he chose to spend that access on this cause is a matter of interpretation on which historians can reasonably differ.
In 1918 the Federation of American Zionists, Young Judaea, Hadassah and other bodies merged into the Zionist Organization of America.
Brandeis became honorary president and Julian W. Mack president.

The size of the merged organization is the figure that the summary of the movement's whole build carries for these years: in the step-by-step account of how the state was built, 1912–18 is "the American machine," made up of Hadassah, Justice Brandeis and the ZOA at 147,000.
The American institutions were not a response to the Balfour Declaration; they were built before it, and one of their leaders was working the channel to the President while it was drafted.
Brandeis and his adherents favored private economic investment over the Zionist Organization's model of national fundraising, and at the Cleveland convention of 1921 they split away.
Louis Lipsky then became president of the ZOA.

The movement's most famous American member thus lost the argument over what kind of institution it should be within three years of its founding; the dispute and its consequences belong to the next stage.
The number of Hadassah's founders depends on which source is counted, from 38 to 122.
Brandeis's motives remain contested, and Goldmann's claim that the Declaration would probably not have been issued without him cannot be tested.
The Palestine Office and its land company existed to buy land, and that land had owners and occupants.
A common account holds that the British government sold Palestinian land to outside Zionist buyers, and that it did so with little scrutiny and little resistance.
The land was bought in private transactions, overwhelmingly from absentee landowners who had acquired large estates under Ottoman rule.
The British, when they came, regulated the process rather than selling into it.
And resistance was there from the first large purchase: an Ottoman governor tried to block it in 1910, and two decades later tenants fought an eviction through the courts for years.
The mechanism that did the work was assembled before 1917, and its first test came in the Jezreel Valley.
The chain of ownership began before Zionism existed as an organized movement.
In 1872 the Ottoman government itself sold the Jezreel Valley, Marj ibn Amir, to the Sursock family of Beirut, wealthy Greek Orthodox Christians.
Between 1901 and 1925, and mainly in the 1920s, the family sold roughly 60,000 to 75,000 dunams to Zionist purchasing organizations, for a fraction of the land's later value.
The Sursock Purchases alone represent approximately 22 percent of all Jewish land acquired in Palestine through 1948, and 58 percent of all land bought specifically from absentee landlords.
The chain ran through three parties and contained no government sale to Zionist buyers: the Ottoman state sold to a Beirut family, and the family later sold to Zionist purchasers.
Ottoman property law recognized two main categories of land.
Mulk was true private freehold.
Miri was state land held on a kind of lease, but treated in practice as owned by whoever held the registered rights to it.
It was a documented feature of Ottoman land tenure that predated Zionist land purchase entirely, and the record does not show that it was created for that purpose.
Starting in 1881–82 the Ottoman government issued a restriction specific to Palestine: foreign Jews could settle anywhere else in the empire, but not there.
By March 1883 only Ottoman Jewish citizens could buy land in Palestine at all; foreign citizens were barred outright.
In 1892 Sultan Abdul Hamid II went further, requiring imperial approval even for Ottoman Jewish citizens to buy.
The Ottoman authorities explained their reasoning to foreign diplomats, and the explanation survives in American correspondence from the 1890s.

American diplomats reported the Ottoman position that individual visitors of any background were welcome, but that the government "does not regard it to its interest to have too large a number of any race or nationality established there."
It was also an exact description of what Herzl's movement had been organized to achieve.
First, Ottoman Jewish citizens, who were still permitted to buy, purchased land and later transferred it to Zionist organizations.

Second, Jews holding British, French or German passports could sometimes invoke the capitulations, the extraterritorial privileges that European powers had negotiated with the Ottoman Empire, and claim consular protection that Ottoman domestic law could not easily override.

Third, and most directly documented, United States State Department correspondence from the 1890s records Russian Jewish emigrants who traveled to America, completed naturalization, and returned to Palestine as American citizens in order to claim American consular protection for residence and land purchase.
One named case, that of Simon Ben Nachman Lowenstein, was argued over directly between American and Ottoman diplomats.
After roughly four decades of organized purchasing against these laws, Jewish-held land in Palestine in 1918 came to approximately 418,000 dunams, around 2 percent of the territory.
The Jewish National Fund, founded in 1901, was the holding body: land went in and, by design, never came back out, held as inalienable Jewish national property.
The negotiating was done for the Palestine Land Development Company by Yehoshua Hankin, who personally negotiated the Sursock deal and most of the major Jezreel Valley acquisitions.

The third, the Palestine Jewish Colonization Association, or PICA, was founded in 1924 by Baron Edmond de Rothschild, a man who had opposed Herzl personally; it ran a separate, parallel operation on Rothschild money and became the single largest Jewish landowner in Palestine.
His working relationship with the Sursock family dated to 1891, and in 1932 he became head of the land development company.
In 1907 the Zionist Organization sent Arthur Ruppin, a German-trained lawyer and economist, to make a pilot study of colonization in Palestine.

In 1908 he opened the Palestine Office in Jaffa, and the same year, by this account, founded with Otto Warburg the Palestine Land Development Company as its operational purchasing arm; other sources date the company to 1909, a discrepancy taken up with the office's founding in .
Ruppin identified the strategic importance of the Jezreel Valley as early as 1907, years before the large Sursock sales closed.

His office coordinated directly with the Jewish National Fund, negotiated with Ottoman and later British authorities on behalf of Jewish immigrants, and, through the land company, handled the surveying, valuing and acquisition of land before settlers arrived.
It turned land purchase from an individual pursuit into a coordinated institutional program, and Ruppin became known as "the father of Jewish settlement in Palestine."
The same documented record contains a second fact about Ruppin, and it has to be stated with equal precision.

His Wikipedia biography says that early in his career he "accepted the crude racial views of his age, including the idea that Jews were an inferior race," and that he later "believed that realization of Zionism required 'racial purity' of Jews and was influenced by works of antisemitic thinkers, including some Nazis."
A peer-reviewed article in History of European Ideas examines these views at length.
Haaretz, in its own retrospective, states plainly: "Arthur Ruppin believed that the realization of Zionism demanded 'racial purity' among the Jews."

He is also documented as holding Ashkenazi Jews to be racially superior to Sephardi and Yemenite Jews, a view that, according to the same record, shaped in practice whom his office prioritized for settlement.
Three independent kinds of source, an encyclopedia entry, peer-reviewed scholarship and the mainstream Israeli press, agree on this.
It does not show that everyone involved in Zionist settlement shared his views, or that the purchase program as a whole was organized around them.
Both facts about Ruppin, the institutional achievement and the racial ideology, are part of the accurate account; neither cancels the other.
Ruppin recalled, in a memoir written in May 1929, that in February 1910 Hankin concluded an agreement for 9,500 dunams at Fule, al-Ful, the site that became Merhavia.
The Jewish National Fund took over 3,500 dunams and the land company the rest.
The seller was Elias Sursock, of the same Beirut family; one account describes the land as about 2,500 acres.
Ruppin's own account records the opposition.
The Turkish government, he wrote, refused to authorize the sale, and "the Governor in Nazareth, a rabid anti-Zionist," declared that he would fight it.
Permission was finally obtained through Hankin's friends in Constantinople.
The governor, according to the biographical record, was Shukri al-Asali, district governor (qaimaqam) of Nazareth from 1910, who tried and failed to stop the sale.

In 1911 he resigned to win a by-election to the Ottoman parliament for Damascus, and there he argued that Jewish settlers held Ottoman citizenship alongside foreign citizenship and were taking control of rural villages.
His argument about dual citizenship can be read as describing, from the other side, the evasion routes the American consuls had been documenting since the 1890s.

On 6 May 1916, by order of Jamal Pasha, al-Asali was hanged in Marjeh Square in Damascus with a group of Arab nationalists, a wartime story told with , where the dating of those executions is also discussed.
By 1929 about 290,000 dunams had been bought in the Emek and the Acre plain since 1910, for £970,000.
Elsewhere the record gives a broader benchmark: land sold by absentee landlords to Jewish buyers went for roughly six Palestine pounds a dunam by the early Mandate period.
That figure sits at the upper end of Ruppin's 1920 prices, and either way the scale explains why a dedicated financial system existed.
The Jewish Colonial Trust, founded in 1899, was the Zionist Organization's overall financial instrument.

Its subsidiary, the Anglo-Palestine Company (later the Anglo-Palestine Bank), established in 1902 with Jaffa as its base, did the work on the ground: financing land purchases directly and running a network of credit unions that gave long-term agricultural loans to Jewish colonists.
Herzl put the principle in one line: "Settlers in the Land of Israel need credit rather than charity."
On the philanthropic side, from 1920, Keren Hayesod raised donations specifically for settlement infrastructure.

The Trust was not the property of one family or a small circle of bankers: over 100,000 people had subscribed for shares by 1899, so many that London's Somerset House needed special accommodation for the shareholder register.
However widely the rest were held, the founding Zionist leadership kept permanent control.
The preparatory committee that launched the Trust was David Wolffsohn, the designer of what became the Israeli flag, Bodenheimer of Cologne, and Rudolf Schauer of Mainz.
Zalman David Levontin, whom Herzl personally summoned to a director's seat in 1901 and who had sold his own earlier land holdings to Edmond de Rothschild in 1883, ran the Jaffa branch from 1903.

As late as 1969 the Trust controlled 88.3 percent of the voting ordinary shares of Bank Leumi, the bank's descendant, while holding only 23.5 percent of its total share capital, a structure that lasted until the late 1980s, when it was sold to private investors.
Purchasing agents like Hankin sometimes bought land first, at personal financial risk, and secured reimbursement from the Jewish Agency or the Jewish National Fund only afterward.
How the sales looked depends heavily on who is describing them, and the two surviving accounts of al-Fula should be read side by side.
Ruppin's 1929 memoir presents willing sales by owners who wanted cash, through a buyer they trusted: Hankin, he wrote, "enjoyed the confidence of the Arabs."
Al-Asali's record describes a sale that the Ottoman district governor tried to block and later raised in parliament as a danger to rural villages.
Both can be true at once: the owners in Beirut may well have wanted cash and trusted Hankin, while the official responsible for the district saw the transaction as a threat to rural villages.
Ruppin's case, at its strongest, is that this was ordinary commerce, lawful and voluntary on both sides of the contract.

Selling land to Jewish purchasers was regarded by some in the Arab community as a serious betrayal, and in at least one documented case negotiations stalled for years because the selling landowners did not want to be seen to take responsibility for evacuating the tenants.

There is no documented record of a formal negotiation in which Zionist organizations sought the consent of the existing Arab political leadership, or of the Old Yishuv's leadership, before organized purchase began.

Within the movement the warning had been given early: Ahad Ha'am, a committed cultural Zionist, wrote in 1891, in "Truth from the Land of Israel," that the Arab population was being treated as effectively invisible in Zionist planning, years before political Zionism was formally organized (his critique is set out with ).
ents: Truth from the Land of Israel

sent: What took place was land acquisition and settlement building toward a territorial and political fact, not a negotiated agreement, which is precisely why the Ottoman restrictions existed.
The Jewish communities that had lived in Palestine before organized Zionist immigration were neither uniform supporters of the purchases nor absent from them.
The clearest documented window is Avraham Albert Antébi, a Sephardi Jew active in Jerusalem from 1897 to 1916.
He ran the Caisse de Prêts, a low-interest loan fund that served both the Old Yishuv, the Sephardi and Ashkenazi communities already in the country, and the settlers of the New Yishuv.
That role gave him working relationships with affluent Arab landowners and Ottoman officials as well as with the Zionist institutions.

Research on his surviving correspondence, published in Shofar: An Interdisciplinary Journal of Jewish Studies, examines Sephardi reaction to Zionist land purchases and the Arab-Jewish tension that followed, and finds a community financially and socially entangled with every side of the transaction.
ents: An Interdisciplinary Journal of Jewish Studies

sent: Antébi does not speak for every Old Yishuv resident; views varied by person, community and moment.
What his record establishes is that some of the Jews already in Palestine watched the displacement from inside the deals themselves.
The human cost of the Sursock purchases is documented in specific figures.
In the largest single group of Sursock-related purchases, 1,746 Arab farming families, 8,730 people, were evicted.
The main Sursock sales came in 1920–25, negotiated directly with Hankin.
Britain, as the Mandate power, enacted five separate laws between 1920 and 1940 meant to protect tenant cultivators from eviction after a sale.

Analysis of the period concludes that they "failed to provide the protection that Palestinian Arabs demanded, often due to loopholes, which allowed individuals and agencies to circumvent the legislation."
Wadi al-Hawarith became the case that tested the system.

In 1929 the Jewish National Fund bought 30,800 dunams there at auction from absentee landlords, which the historian Weldon Matthews counts as the third-largest single acquisition of the Fund in the whole Mandate period.
The Bedouin Palestinian tenants who lived on the land refused to leave, and the Fund began formal eviction proceedings.
Awni Abd al-Hadi, a significant Palestinian national political figure, represented the residents through a multi-year court battle.

The final eviction order was issued on 15 June 1933, and the response was immediate: the Istiqlal Party, the Palestine Communist Party and the Congress of Youth called strikes and issued public declarations of protest.
In 1938 the Mandate authorities moved in the opposite direction from their tenant laws.
They granted Zionist officials direct permission to copy land-registration and taxation records documenting Arab land ownership, explicitly to facilitate further Zionist acquisition.
Britain was neither seller nor bystander: it first attempted regulation that failed, then took a specific, dated step of facilitation.

That does not mean Britain orchestrated the purchase program from the start, or that 1938 was the whole of its policy; its immigration restrictions in the same years, the 1939 White Paper among them, cut sharply the other way.
The Mandate's record on land was inconsistent rather than a single coherent policy.
By 1947–48 total Jewish holdings came to roughly 2 million dunams, about 7 percent of Mandate Palestine's roughly 26 million dunams, of which the Jewish National Fund held approximately 936,000.

The Sursock land, around a fifth of everything acquired, was the single largest component of that total; and the restrictions, the evasions, the bank and the office that produced it were all in place before 1917.
Ruppin's memoir does not count the tenants at al-Fula, and the sources used here give no figure for them or for the price paid in 1910.
How the owners in Beirut weighed cash against the objections of officials like al-Asali survives only in the buyer's account.
And how far Ruppin's racial views shaped individual settlement decisions, beyond the documented fact that they shaped his office's priorities, is not set out case by case in the record this book has.
In 1909 Oxford University Press published a King James Bible with one man's notes printed beneath the text on every page.
A common view holds that Christian support for Israel comes straight from ancient scripture, read plainly.

The framework that links them to a modern political return of Jews to Palestine, and that made such a return a matter of prophecy for millions of American Protestants, has a more recent and more traceable origin.
Its main vehicle was this annotated Bible.
One line of scholarship argues that before Scofield the framework was "substantially absent" from American Protestant tradition, and that afterward it became a mainstream evangelical framework.

Over the following century, on this argument, it produced a political constituency of roughly 30 to 40 million Christian Zionists, which supported the Zionist project in America before American Jewish support consolidated.
The ideas did not begin with Scofield.
The more immediate source was John Nelson Darby (1800–1882), an Anglo-Irish minister who founded the Plymouth Brethren and developed dispensationalist premillennialism in the 1830s.
Darby made at least five journeys to North America between 1862 and 1877 and spread the framework among American Protestants decades before Scofield's Bible existed.
That qualifies the claim of absence, and the record goes further: the framework was not absent from America before 1909.

In 1878 the Niagara Bible Conference's creed looked for Christ's personal return "when Israel shall be restored to their own land", the first of a series of national prophetic conferences met in New York the same year, and the Bible institutes founded from the 1880s taught the new premillennialism almost without exception.

According to the research, standard nineteenth-century American Protestantism was largely amillennialist or postmillennialist, and did not treat the Church as a separate dispensation from Israel; the premillennial Bible-conference movement was a growing minority within it.
Nor did Darby himself make a Jewish return a precondition of Christ's return: his rapture could come at any moment, and the restoration of Israel belonged to the events that followed it.
The man who carried Darby's framework into the American mainstream had an unusual biography for the purpose.
Cyrus Scofield was born in Michigan in 1843 and was staying with relatives in Tennessee when the Civil War began.
He enlisted in the Confederate Army in 1861 and was discharged in September 1862 as a Michigan-born alien; ordered back to camp, he crossed to Union lines and took the federal oath.
In 1873 President Ulysses S. Grant appointed him United States Attorney for Kansas.
He held the post for about six months and, in the Justice Department's words, "was forced to resign" over "questionable financial transactions".

In October 1878 he was jailed in St. Louis on forgery charges and held awaiting trial for much of a year; on 6 November 1879 the prosecution dropped the charges by nolle prosequi, and he was never convicted or sentenced.
He began pastoral work in Dallas in 1882 and was ordained a Congregationalist minister in October 1883, without formal seminary training.
He was not a scholar of Hebrew or Greek.

The most cited critical biography is Joseph M. Canfield's The Incredible Scofield and His Book (1988), a hostile account; the legal record above rests on later work with court and newspaper sources, which shows no conviction.
Canfield is also the origin of a widely repeated claim: that Samuel Untermyer, a New York lawyer who later became a prominent Zionist, stood behind Scofield.

Scofield and Untermyer were both members of New York's Lotos Club, but Scofield's proposers were other men, no record shows the two ever met, and Canfield introduced Untermyer with the words "we assume".
The backers Scofield's contemporaries named were businessmen, among them Alwyn Ball Jr. and John T. Pirie, and a 2025 fact-check rated the later claim that the Rothschilds funded the Bible false.
The story's shape, Jewish money steering Christian belief, is an old antisemitic one, and it is examined, with its chain of sources, in .
The theology came largely from Darby, and Scofield's work would have found some readers in any case.

The research's own account of what produced the book's scale points elsewhere: Oxford's distribution, and what it calls the funding architecture that put the Bible "into every seminary, Sunday school, and pulpit in the American South and Midwest."
Scofield's personal history and the framework's later influence are separate facts, each to be checked on its own terms.
Each page carried the King James Version, the standard English Protestant translation of 1611, at the top.
Scofield's notes filled a substantial part of the bottom.
A reader did not open a Bible and then consult a separate commentary.
The commentary was already in place on the page, printed under Oxford's imprint and bound in the same covers as the text.
It dates its origin once to the eighteenth century and elsewhere to Darby in the 1830s.
Third, on the research's account, they presented the political return of Jews to Palestine as a prerequisite for the Second Coming of Christ.
Scofield's note on Deuteronomy 30:3 sets out Israel's future in order, and "The return of the Lord" comes before "Restoration to the land" and "National conversion".
Scofield had systematized Darby's framework and put it into the vocabulary of American Protestants.
The decisive step was placing it in the margins of the Bible ordinary readers already used.
Over years of daily reading, text and note merged in the reader's memory, until Scofield's reading became simply "what the Bible says."
The label on the book stayed the same, the Bible, while what the reader received under that label now included one man's interpretation.
The Reference Bible sold millions of copies through the twentieth century.
On the research's account, a mid-century American evangelical who studied the Bible seriously was likely to meet Scofield's notes as the frame for reading it.

It is often said to have added references to the Balfour Declaration, issued that November, but no source for this has been found, and the 1917 notes checked for this library contain no such reference; they still describe Israel as "now in the third dispersion".
Oxford's part is the step most easily misread.
Oxford University Press is one of the two oldest and most prestigious academic publishers in the English-speaking world; Cambridge University Press is the other.
Under Oxford's imprint, bound into the scriptural text, it reached millions.
The research calls this a transfer of legitimacy, not a conspiracy, and the Press's governance supports that reading.
Oxford University Press has never been privately owned.
It is a department of the University of Oxford.
Since the seventeenth century it has been governed by the Delegates of the Press, 15 sitting academics appointed by the university's Vice-Chancellor, who met fortnightly to approve every title.
Because the underlying text was technically just the King James Version with added footnotes, no special theological review was triggered.
It does not show that anyone used that gap deliberately, and it does not show any promotional strategy by the Press.
The Press did not set out to shape American policy in the Middle East, but its imprint gave the notes an authority its editors had not intended to confer.
The Press has never withdrawn the book.
Later editions, the New Scofield of 1967 and the Scofield Study Bible III of 2002, were revised but kept the core dispensationalist framework.
The research then sets out what the doctrines meant politically, as later Christian Zionist teaching drew them out.
Genesis 12:3 reads "I will bless those who bless you, and whoever curses you I will curse," and Genesis 15:18 gives the land promise.
The research's argument concerns how Scofield's framework applied them to a modern state.
On the research's reading, none of these doctrines had been part of mainstream American Protestant theology before Scofield placed them there.
It also argues that the framework leaves no theological role for the people already living in Palestine.
Palestinian Christians, members of a community older than most European churches, become an anomaly.
Palestinian Muslims become obstacles to the fulfillment of prophecy.
Evangelical Protestantism teaches salvation through Christ alone.
Scofield's scheme runs a separate track for national Israel, in which an ethnic nation and a literal grant of land carry weight of their own in the history of salvation, alongside the work of Christ.
Israel is dispersed.
Israel is regathered, in unbelief.
The regathered nation passes through the Tribulation.
Only then does Israel turn to Christ.
The Second Coming follows, Christ establishes a millennial kingdom, and Israel stands at its center.
Scofield's own summary at Deuteronomy 30:3 orders the end differently, placing the Lord's return before the restoration to the land and the national conversion.
One symbolic reading, put forward in this library's opening volume, holds that the confusion dissolves if "Israel" is read not as land but as IS-RA-EL, a "consciousness architecture."
In that reading IS stands for Isis, the receptive or lunar principle, RA for the solar or radiant principle, and EL for the unifying divine force.
Of the three, only EL is real Hebrew etymology.
On this reading "Israel" names a spiritual condition rather than a nation, and Scofield's notes performed a literalizing move, turning a symbol into a flag, a border and an ethnic deed.
Dallas Theological Seminary, founded in 1924, became an institutional home for training pastors in the framework.
Between the 1920s and the 1960s, according to the research, Scofield's theology became standard in Southern Baptist and other evangelical denominations and in Bible colleges of the South and Midwest.
Hal Lindsey's The Late Great Planet Earth (1970), the best-selling nonfiction book of the 1970s, carried it to a mass readership.
In 1979 Jerry Falwell founded the Moral Majority.
Tim LaHaye and Jerry Jenkins's Left Behind novels, published from 1995 to 2007, had sold over 50 million copies by one count and some 80 million by another at LaHaye's death in 2016.
In 2006 John Hagee, pastor of Cornerstone Church in San Antonio, published Jerusalem Countdown and founded Christians United for Israel (CUFI).
It holds an annual Washington Summit.
The alliance between these organizations and Israeli leaders is told in .

The research cites "Pew 2019" figures (42 percent of white evangelicals against 27 percent of American Jews, and 75 to 80 percent of white evangelicals backing Israel as a biblical requirement) for which no 2019 survey has been traced; they are not used here.
In a Pew Research Center survey published on 3 October 2013, 82 percent of white evangelical Protestants said God gave the land of Israel to the Jewish people, against 40 percent of American Jews.

In a LifeWay Research poll of 2,002 Americans with evangelical beliefs in September 2017, 80 percent said Israel's founding in 1948 fulfilled biblical prophecy, but only 23 percent favoured a treaty giving the Palestinians a state, 31 percent opposed one and 46 percent were unsure.
In Pew's survey of May 2026, white evangelical Protestants were the only religious group in which a majority, 57 percent, held a favourable view of the Israeli government.
The figure of 30 to 40 million Christian Zionist voters is a commonly cited estimate, not derived from any of these surveys.
Scofield published openly, Oxford's decisions were public, and Christian Zionist organizations argue their positions in public.
Scofield published in 1909, the Balfour Declaration came in 1917, and the state was declared in 1948.
He was one factor among many, and nothing here claims that he or Oxford brought the State of Israel about.
Second, this is a dispute within Christianity, not a case against Christianity.

Mainline Protestant denominations, including the United Methodist, Episcopal, Presbyterian (PC-USA), Evangelical Lutheran and United Church of Christ churches, largely do not embrace Christian Zionism.
Roman Catholic tradition does not endorse it.
The research describes Orthodox tradition as rejecting it explicitly in one passage, and speaks of "most Orthodox tradition" in another.

In 2006 the heads of four Jerusalem churches signed the Jerusalem Declaration on Christian Zionism, which calls it a "false teaching that corrupts the biblical message of love, justice, and reconciliation", and in 2009 Palestinian Christian leaders from across denominations issued the Kairos Palestine document.

The research names the Palestinian Christian Sami Awad, the mainline Protestant scholar Gary Burge and the evangelical Shane Claiborne as public figures whose positions show that the framework can be contested inside the tradition.
They show that holding it is not required of Christians.
The Christians who reject Scofield's framework do so on grounds within their own traditions.
It leaves open how far the Reference Bible itself, as distinct from Darby's earlier preaching, the Bible colleges and later popular writers, caused American Christian support for Zionism.
It also does not show what Oxford's Delegates discussed when they approved the book.
The research's account of later American policy, which it partly traces to this constituency, is examined in later volumes against the full record of who decided what.
A familiar account holds that the demand for a Jewish state grew out of the Holocaust, that "never again" was its direct cause.
Each comes at least a decade before Hitler took power in Germany in 1933, and at least sixteen years before the Holocaust itself.
The second half of this section then sets out what this stage actually built: the structure that stood in Palestine, Europe and America in 1917, and what stood against it.
That year Theodor Herzl published Der Judenstaat, The Jewish State, which openly weighed Palestine against Argentina as candidate territories for a political answer to European antisemitism.
This was a political program, dated and in print, thirty-seven years before Hitler took power.
That does not mean everything in Zionist history flowed in a straight line from one pamphlet.

The chapter that ends here has shown how much was contested: the Basel Program of 1897 spoke of a "home" (Heimstätte), not a state (Staat), and the movement argued for decades over culture, religion, territory and method.
The Sixth Zionist Congress voted in 1903 to investigate British East Africa; the Seventh Congress formally rejected it in 1905.
Palestine's place was confirmed by a contested decision in two stages, and the decision split the movement: the Territorialists who left founded the Jewish Territorial Organization.
In November that year Britain committed in writing to "the establishment in Palestine of a national home for the Jewish people."
The commitment came sixteen years before Hitler's rise and twenty-four years before the systematic phase of the Holocaust began.
Its drafting, its addressee and the opposition to it inside the British cabinet are told in .
At San Remo the Allied powers formally assigned Britain the Mandate for Palestine and wrote the Balfour language into an international agreement.
It does not follow that every Allied power shared the same enthusiasm or motive; the national interests behind the agreement varied.
The League of Nations approved the Mandate for Palestine in July 1922, and it came into force in September 1923.
Its Article 6 committed Britain to facilitate Jewish immigration and "close settlement by Jews on the land."
This was a binding international legal framework, eleven years before Hitler took power, complete before the word "Holocaust" described anything.
Within the same decade Britain's Churchill White Paper narrowed the same commitment, as Stage Two shows.

By the time Hitler took power, then, the movement had a political program thirty-seven years old, a territorial question it had settled twice in its own favor, a great-power commitment, the international ratification of that commitment and a binding legal mandate to build toward it.
The clearest evidence of that acceleration is the Biltmore Program of May 1942, the movement's first explicit, public demand for a state, in the form of a "Jewish Commonwealth."
But Biltmore was the culmination of forty-six years of institution-building and political commitment, not their origin.

The program of 1896 and the commitments of 1917–22 did not make a state inevitable, and for most of this period the movement was one current among many in Jewish life, opposed by Reform rabbis, the Bund, Orthodox opponents and, in 1917, the official bodies of British Jewry.
The Basel Program avoided the word "state."
At the top stood the Zionist Organization founded at Basel.
Any individual or group that accepted the Basel Program and paid the annual dues called the shekel could join.

Its 1899 constitution created a seven-member Smaller Actions Committee, chaired by the Congress president, and a 37-member Larger Actions Committee of national leaders; the Congress met every year until 1901 and every two years after.
Herzl, its first president, died in 1904; David Wolffsohn succeeded him in 1905, and the botanist Otto Warburg succeeded Wolffsohn in 1911.
National federations recruited members and raised money: the Federation of American Zionists from 1898 and the English Zionist Federation from 1899.

When war came the organization's head offices were in Germany and it declared itself neutral, while in London Chaim Weizmann, a Manchester chemist and president of the English Zionist Federation, and Nahum Sokolow became its de facto leaders.

The Jewish Colonial Trust, incorporated in London in 1899 with an authorized capital of £2,000,000 in £1 shares, had sold only about 250,000 shares, raising about £250,000, but it had proved that the project could be financed by many small shareholders.

Its subsidiary, the Anglo-Palestine Company, founded in 1902, opened its first branch in Jaffa in 1903 and by 1914 had branches in Jerusalem, Beirut, Hebron, Haifa, Safed, Tiberias and Gaza; its loan to the Ahuzat Bayit association financed the first neighborhood of what became Tel Aviv.
The Jewish National Fund, founded in 1901, held the land it bought as permanent national property, leased and never sold.
It began with 200 dunams east of Hadera in 1903, and its blue collection box appeared around 1904.

In Jaffa, the Palestine Office opened by Arthur Ruppin in 1908 coordinated purchase and settlement, and the Palestine Land Development Company had acquired and prepared roughly 50,000 dunams by the outbreak of war, through named agents including Yehoshua Hankin, Ruppin himself and Jacob Thon.

The Second Aliyah, from 1904 to the outbreak of war, brought about 35,000 immigrants by the National Library of Israel's count or 40,000 by the Jewish Virtual Library's, and at least half left within a few years by the first count, nearly half by the second; the Jewish community numbered about 80,000 at the end of the period.

It had a Hebrew high school in Jaffa from 1905, the lots of Tel Aviv raffled among 60 families at Passover 1909, and Degania, counted as the first kibbutz, founded on 28 October 1910 on land leased from the Jewish National Fund (another source dates it to 1909).
It had armed guards: Bar-Giora from 1907, and Hashomer, which grew out of it in 1909 and lasted until 1920.
In the United States, Henrietta Szold had founded Hadassah in 1912, and in 1914 Louis Brandeis took up Zionist leadership and became the movement's channel to President Wilson.
A year after this stage closes, those groups merged into the Zionist Organization of America with 147,551 members.
Separately, a Christian constituency had a text: the Scofield Reference Bible, published by Oxford University Press in 1909.
And in the war, NILI's intelligence and Jewish soldiers in British uniform had given the movement standing in London.
It departs from one source on one date: it places the Jewish Colonization Association's takeover of the Rothschild colonies in 1900, where the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia says "since 1899".
The Ottoman state had refused Herzl a charter, and from the 1880s it restricted Jewish immigration and land purchase, though unevenly.
An Arabic press, from Najib Nassar's al-Karmil to Filastin, argued against Zionism in print, and Jerusalem's deputies raised it in the Ottoman parliament in 1911.

Jewish dissent was organized too, from the Bund and American Reform to Agudat Israel and the Antizionistisches Komitee, and in May 1917 the Board of Deputies and the Anglo-Jewish Association declared against Zionism in The Times, which is why the Declaration was addressed to Lord Rothschild and not to them.
The war cut into all of it, from the expulsions of 1914–15 to the deportation from Jaffa in April 1917.
One claim often added to this picture, that the founding of the Federal Reserve in 1913 was tied to Zionist finance, finds no support in the record, as  shows.

It had an elected Congress and executive, federations in America and Britain, a bank with a Jaffa branch, a land fund with land, a professional land office, a labor movement with its own guards, an American constituency and now a British promise.
It did not have a majority of Palestine's people, the support of many organized Jewish bodies in the West, the official representatives of British Jewry among them, or any power of its own to govern.
Ottoman rule ended in December 1917, when Britain occupied the country.
What the record cannot settle is how much of what followed was set by this structure and how much by British policy, Arab resistance and the catastrophes of the next thirty years.
NILI, the Mule Corps and the Jewish Legion, 1915–1918
A common account treats the Balfour Declaration as a gift: a promise Britain handed over in November 1917 without receiving anything in return.

While the Declaration was being argued over in London, a ring of Jews in Palestine was spying on the Ottomans for British intelligence, and Jewish volunteers were serving in British uniform, first at Gallipoli and later in the campaign for Palestine itself.
Among those volunteers was David Ben-Gurion.
These services gave the Zionist movement standing with the British at the moment the cabinet was deciding.
A ring of about 40 members, based mainly in Zichron Ya'akov and Hadera, formed around the Aaronsohn siblings and Avshalom Feinberg.
It took the name NILI.
Its members gathered Ottoman military information and passed it to British intelligence, in part through a vessel run by the forerunner of MI6.
The CIA's own journal has reviewed its role.

NILI worked inside an Ottoman province at war, in a period when, as the previous section shows, the Ottoman authorities were expelling foreign nationals, hanging Arab nationalists and, in April 1917, emptying Jaffa; the risk to its members was real.
Among its members was Aaron Aaronsohn, a noted agronomist.
In 1916 he left Palestine to brief the British in person.
He influenced British officials including Sir Mark Sykes and William Ormsby-Gore, both of whom were later pivotal in persuading the cabinet to issue the Balfour Declaration.

This is the most direct documented line in this material between wartime service and the Declaration's authors: a man who had organized espionage for Britain inside Ottoman Palestine was talking, in person, to the officials who would press the cabinet.
The Ottomans broke the ring in October 1917, a month before the Declaration was issued.
Sarah Aaronsohn, one of the siblings at its center, took her own life after days of torture.
From Jews exiled to Egypt the British Army formed the Zion Mule Corps in 1915.
Its 737 volunteers, largely refugees expelled from Palestine, served at Gallipoli that year.
Five battalions of the Royal Fusiliers, numbered the 38th to the 42nd and known together as the Jewish Legion, fought in Allenby's Palestine campaign.
One battalion trained in Nova Scotia, and it included David Ben-Gurion.
He had been expelled by the Ottomans in 1915 and had gone to Alexandria and then New York.
That battalion's road back to Palestine therefore ran across the Atlantic.
Much of the British Zionist leadership opposed forming it.
Chaim Weizmann and Ze'ev Jabotinsky were the exceptions who supported it.
Weizmann was by then, with Nahum Sokolow, one of the movement's de facto leaders in London, because the Zionist Organization, whose head offices were in Germany, had declared itself neutral.
The organization as a body did not offer Britain its services.
Put together, intelligence from inside Ottoman Palestine and soldiers in British uniform gave the movement standing with Britain at the moment the cabinet was deciding on the Declaration.
The record places these services alongside other sources of British goodwill: Weizmann's wartime work as a chemist, and the restorationist sympathies documented in earlier chapters of this book.
The Declaration's drafting, its addressee, the opposition to it inside the cabinet, and Britain's other wartime undertakings in the region belong to Stage Two and are told in .

The familiar claim that the Declaration was given for nothing does not survive the record: a spy ring, a mule corps and five battalions were given to Britain's war effort, and one of the spies reached the officials who would argue the case in cabinet.

NILI collapsed in October 1917, before the Declaration was issued, and the Legion's battalions fought in 1917–18; the sources do not date that service closely enough against the cabinet's decision to weigh it.
The Machinery: How the Zionist Organization Worked, 1897–1917
The organization founded at Basel is sometimes remembered as a loose collection of enthusiasts without formal structure, a mood more than a movement.

Within two years of Basel the Zionist Organization had a written constitution, an elected parliament, a standing executive, a council of national leaders, national branches in the United States and Britain, and a bank.
By 1917 it had a land fund, an office in Palestine and a recognized channel to the British government.
Any individual or group that accepted the Basel Program and paid an annual due, called the "shekel", could join.
Authority flowed from the Congress.
Its constitution, adopted at the Third Congress in 1899, created two governing bodies.
The Smaller Actions Committee, with seven members, was the executive, and its chairman was the president of the Congress.
The Larger Actions Committee, with 37 members, was a council of national leaders.
The Congress itself met every year until 1901 and every two years after that; the Fifth Congress of 1901 made the change.
The Federation of American Zionists was founded in 1898 and later became the Zionist Organization of America.
The English Zionist Federation followed in 1899.
The Jewish Colonial Trust, its bank, was established in 1899; the Jewish National Fund, to buy land, in 1901; and the Palestine Office in Jaffa in 1908.
The Congress, a body of delegates, decided policy.
The federations supplied members and money, and the financial and land instruments turned that money into assets in Palestine.
It held no governing authority in Palestine, which remained Ottoman territory until 1917, and the consent of governments was still, as the Basel Program itself acknowledged, something to be obtained.
The Second Congress, at Basel in 1898, laid the groundwork for the Jewish Colonial Trust.

The Third, at Basel in 1899, resolved that the Trust's funds could be spent only in Palestine or Syria, an early decision that bound the movement's money to one region before any territorial alternative had been offered.
The Fourth Congress met in London in 1900; there religious Zionists led by Isaac Jacob Reines urged that the organization keep a purely political focus.
The Fifth, back at Basel in 1901, established the Jewish National Fund.
At the same Congress a group called the Democratic Faction, among them Leo Motzkin, Martin Buber and Chaim Weizmann, pressed for Hebrew culture and for more democracy inside the organization.
It was also this Congress that moved the meetings to every other year.
The Sixth Congress, at Basel in 1903, voted "295 in favor, 178 against and 98 abstentions" to send a commission to examine settlement in East Africa, a British offer told in full in .
Herzl died the next year.
The Seventh Congress, at Basel in 1905, voted against a national home outside Palestine and its vicinity.
Israel Zangwill's Territorialists walked out, and David Wolffsohn became president.
The decision settled that the organization's aim was Palestine, and it was taken by a vote of the Congress, not decreed by a leader.
At the Eighth Congress, held at The Hague in 1907, delegates debated "practical" against "political" Zionism.
The Congress supported practical work, including a Palestine branch of the organization under Arthur Ruppin, and Weizmann's "synthetic Zionism" gained ground.
That branch became the Palestine Office, whose work is traced in .
At the Ninth Congress, in Hamburg in 1909, the practical camp challenged Wolffsohn's leadership.
At the Tenth, at Basel in 1911, the first session was held in Hebrew, and the botanist Otto Warburg succeeded Wolffsohn as president.
The Eleventh Congress, in Vienna in 1913, backed the founding of a Hebrew University in Jerusalem, which opened twelve years later.

After Herzl's death and the East Africa split, it moved toward building in Palestine directly, while the Democratic Faction's push for Hebrew culture surfaced in the first Hebrew session of 1911 and the university resolution of 1913.
The movement's leadership changed in the same direction, from Herzl the diplomat, to Wolffsohn, whose leadership the practical camp challenged in 1909, to Warburg.
The First World War cut across this structure.
Before the war the organization's head offices were in Germany, and when war came it declared itself neutral.
Its effective leadership passed to London, where Chaim Weizmann, a Manchester chemist and president of the English Zionist Federation, and Nahum Sokolow became its de facto leaders.
The English Federation, founded in 1899 as one national branch among several, thus became in wartime the movement's channel to the British government.
That channel was contested within British Jewry itself.
In May 1917 the community's official representative bodies, the Board of Deputies and the Anglo-Jewish Association, published an anti-Zionist statement in The Times.
Days later the English Zionist Federation held a conference in London.
The episode explains a detail of the Balfour Declaration.
Because British Jewry's official bodies opposed Zionism, the declaration was not addressed to them.
It was instead addressed to Lord Rothschild, for transmission to the Zionist Federation.

It does not show how the 37 seats of the Larger Actions Committee were apportioned among countries, or how far the seven-member executive in practice controlled the Congress rather than answering to it.
It does not explain how the neutral organization's German headquarters and its London leaders divided authority during the war.
By What Right: How a British Letter Became International Law
The peace conference that set the King–Crane report aside also wrote the rule under which Palestine would be governed.
Any account of the Mandate for Palestine has to answer a prior question: by what authority did Britain act?
The familiar answer treats the Balfour Declaration as a lawful grant, made by the rightful authority over the country.
That instrument contained its own rule about the wishes of the people it governed, and whether the Palestine Mandate kept that rule is a question lawyers and historians still dispute.
On 2 November 1917, when Arthur Balfour signed his letter, Palestine was part of the Ottoman Empire.
British forces had taken Beersheba on 31 October.
They would take Jerusalem only on 9 December.
Britain was promising a territory that it neither held nor governed.
Its wording began with a draft formula that Lord Walter Rothschild sent to Balfour on 18 July 1917, after months of drafting with Zionist leaders; the final text was negotiated and drafted by others.

It was addressed to him, for passing on to the Zionist Federation, chiefly because of his standing as the most prominent figure in British Jewry; some accounts add that he presided over the Federation, a point the sources dispute.
The drafting and the choice of addressee are told in ; the occupation that followed in December 1917 belongs to the story of Allenby's entry into Jerusalem.
What turned the letter into law was a new piece of machinery: the mandate system of the League of Nations.
Its charter was Article 22 of the League's Covenant.

The League Commission's final report containing the article was approved on 28 April 1919, during the Paris Peace Conference, and the Covenant entered into force on 10 January 1920 together with the treaty of peace with Germany.
Article 22 set out its purpose in the language of trusteeship.
In the Covenant's own terms, the well-being of such peoples was a trust, and the Mandatory administered under supervision.
Paragraph 7 required each Mandatory to render "an annual report" to the League Council, and paragraph 9 created "a permanent Commission" to examine those reports.
The fourth paragraph dealt with the Arab provinces of the defeated empire, and it is the one on which the whole argument turns.

Communities formerly belonging to the Turkish Empire, it said, had reached a stage where "their existence as independent nations can be provisionally recognised subject to the rendering of administrative advice and assistance by a Mandatory."
These became known as the "A" mandates: communities whose existence as independent nations could, in the Covenant's words, be provisionally recognized, subject to a Mandatory's advice and assistance.
The "A" mandates were allocated by the Allied powers at San Remo on 25 April 1920.
They covered Palestine, Trans-Jordan, and Syria and Lebanon; Iraq was also designated an "A" mandate and was admitted to the League in 1932.
In all, 15 mandates were created over 3 former Ottoman and 7 former German territories.
Britannica lists Iraq, Syria, Lebanon and Palestine as Class A mandates and states that they all "achieved full independence by 1949."
The League Council then approved the text of the Mandate for Palestine, with Balfour's language set into its preamble, conditionally on 24 July 1922, pending a France–Italy agreement on Syria.
The League recorded the Mandate as in force on 29 September 1923, a date John Quigley disputes.
The articles of that text, and the dispute over its date, are examined in the section on the Mandate itself.
Here the point is the sequence: legal force came from the victors, through San Remo and through the League, and it came after the letter, not with it.
The Allied powers chose the Mandatory.
The League Council approved the terms and received the reports.
The Mandatory governed.

The communities whose wishes Article 22 called "a principal consideration" were not among the actors in these steps; according to the UN study discussed below, Palestinians were never consulted on the choice of Mandatory.
In a memorandum of 1919 Balfour wrote that "in Palestine we do not propose even to go through the form of consulting the wishes of the present inhabitants."
On Balfour's account, then, a mandate was a limitation the conquerors placed on themselves, and in Palestine consultation was not intended.

Palestinian Arab congresses opposed the policy from 1919 onward; an American commission sent by President Wilson recorded hostility to the Zionist program in the summer of 1919, and its report was shelved, as told in ; and Britain's own upper house objected.
On 21 February 1922 the Palestine Arab Delegation in London invoked Article 22 directly, demanding a "national independent Government."
The movement behind that delegation, and Britain's answers to it, are traced in the section on the Palestinian national movement.
The objection inside Parliament came in June 1922, on a date the sources give differently.
The House of Lords voted 60 to 29 for Lord Islington's motion that the Mandate in its present form was unacceptable.
A PalQuest biography of Musa Kazim al-Husseini dates the vote to 20 June 1922; The Spectator of 24 June places it on the Wednesday of that week, which was 21 June.
On 4 July 1922 the House of Commons voted to support its policy, by a margin reported as 292 to 35.
Across the Atlantic, Congress took up the Balfour policy after hearings that included anti-Zionist Jewish and Palestinian Arab witnesses.
The House passed a resolution endorsing it on 30 June 1922, the Senate passed it by unanimous consent on 13 July, and President Harding signed it on 21 September.
What that resolution did and did not commit the United States to belongs to the American side of this story.
Was the Palestine Mandate consistent with the Covenant that created it?

On this reading Palestine was an "A" community like its neighbors, whose provisional independence and whose wishes Article 22 protected, and the Mandate's national-home provisions, together with the absence of any consultation, departed from the article.

The United Nations study The Origins and Evolution of the Palestine Problem states that Palestine "was in no manner excluded" from the class "A" provisions and that Palestinians were never consulted on the choice of Mandatory.

John Quigley, in Britain and Its Mandate over Palestine (Anthem Press, 2022), goes further: he argues that Article 22 gave the League Council no power to distribute territory at all, and that the Mandate, drafted by Zionists, ignored the population's wishes in a manifest violation of the article.
The Palestine Arab Delegation made the same argument in 1922, from the text of the Covenant itself.
The second holds that the Palestine Mandate was meant to be different, and was lawfully so.
The League of Nations' own study of 1945 described the Palestine Mandate as "of a very special character": it followed the "A" framework but added provisions to carry out the Balfour Declaration.

The legal scholar Matthijs de Blois, writing in the Israel Law Review in 2016, argues that the Mandate was unique in naming the Jewish people, wherever they lived, as its beneficiaries, and that its specific obligations to them are its defining legal feature.
He also records that Palestinian Arab representatives rejected it as incompatible with self-determination.
On this view the Mandate was not a misreading of Article 22 but a deliberate special case, approved by the same Council that administered the article.
A third, middle position is attributed to Ralph Wilde: Palestine remained within the mandates system, and those provisions of the Mandate that purported to vary Article 22 had no legal effect.
On this reading the Covenant's protections for the inhabitants survived, whatever the Mandate's own text said.
The text of Article 22 is fixed, and it does say that the wishes of the former Ottoman communities "must be a principal consideration in the selection of the Mandatory."
Balfour's own words show that the British government did not intend to consult the inhabitants of Palestine.

And both sides agree that the Palestine Mandate differed from the other "A" mandates: the League itself said it added provisions to carry out the Balfour Declaration, and de Blois calls it unique in naming the Jewish people, wherever they lived, as beneficiaries.
One side calls that difference a violation; the other calls it the Mandate's defining purpose.
The sources gathered record no ruling, by a court or by the League Council, on whether the Palestine Mandate conformed to Article 22.
The answer depends on a prior judgment about where authority lay: in the Covenant's general rule, or in the Council's power to approve a special text.
The first reading makes the Mandate a breach of the trust it claimed to carry out.
It did so through the decisions of the victorious powers and the League, over the recorded objections of Palestinian Arab congresses, of an American commission and of Britain's own House of Lords.
Kings by Appointment: Cairo, 1921, and the Sharif Who Would Not Sign
By 1921 Britain had to decide who would rule the Arab lands it now held.
The wartime promises had been made: to Sharif Hussein of Mecca, to France and to the Zionist movement, as set out in .
Two of the new rulers were chosen at a single British conference in Cairo.
The third ruler in the story, Hussein, the father of both, refused the settlement that his sons accepted.
By one account, the refusal cost him British support when his kingdom was invaded.
Winston Churchill, the Colonial Secretary, met British officials at Cairo.
There they agreed to install Hussein's son Faisal as king of Iraq and another son, Abdullah, as emir of Transjordan.
Faisal came to Iraq after losing a kingdom elsewhere.
His Arab Kingdom of Syria, proclaimed in Damascus in March 1920, had been defeated by French forces at Maysalun on 24 July 1920.
Iraq itself had risen in revolt against Britain in 1920.
Abdullah's emirate, and the way Transjordan was separated from the rest of the Palestine Mandate, are the subject of .
A British minister and his officials agreed on names in Cairo, and the names became kings.
The populations of Iraq and Transjordan did not elect them.
When Iraq gained formal independence in 1932, it was under a treaty that preserved British bases.
Across the region, rulers whom Britain had chosen or backed now held most of the thrones.
The same pattern reached beyond the Arab lands.

In February 1921, a month before the Cairo meeting, an officer named Reza Khan led the Persian Cossack Brigade into Tehran in a coup that had the support of British officers, among them General Edmund Ironside.
He became prime minister, in 1925 was made Shah and founded the Pahlavi dynasty.
Iran's parliament survived, but with sharply reduced power.
Iran's later history belongs to another volume.
Set beside Cairo, the coup can be read as part of the same pattern: much of the region's leadership in these years was installed, not elected.
Faisal's reign in Iraq also opened a chapter in the history of Iraq's Jews that later volumes follow.
The mandate-era state founded in 1921 gave Iraq's Jews full citizenship, with the right to vote and to hold office.
Jews became prominent in commerce, law, journalism and government service.
Iraqi Jewish historians remember Faisal's reign as tolerant and call it a "Golden Age."
Iraq's Jewish community was the oldest and, at the time, one of the largest Jewish communities in the Middle East outside Palestine.
By the 1940s it numbered roughly 135,000, about 3 percent of Iraq's population, with 90,000 in Baghdad alone.
One says that Jews and Muslims in Iraq always lived in harmony.
After independence in 1932, Iraqi nationalist sentiment increasingly cast the country's Jews as pro-British and pro-Zionist, running together Jews, Zionism and British influence.
In 1919 Sharif Hussein declined to ratify the Treaty of Versailles.
He did so in protest at the mandates imposed on Syria, Palestine and Iraq.
Faisal had represented him in Paris.
According to the PBS account of his life, he refused to recognize the Paris settlements at all.
Britain then tried to bind him by a separate treaty.
The British India Office file that records the effort, IOR/L/PS/10/881, runs from 25 May 1921 to 25 August 1925.
It covers two linked questions: the subsidy Britain paid Hussein, and the negotiation of an Anglo-Hejazi treaty.
T. E. Lawrence negotiated for Britain.
On 28 November 1921 he telegraphed the Colonial Secretary with a proposal to revise draft Article 4 of the treaty.
The new wording would "clear away all agreements" that Hussein cited but could not produce.
In December 1921 Lawrence and Emir Abdullah signed a treaty text.
On 27 February 1922 Hussein threatened to abdicate.
The Foreign Office considered making two demands of him before he could be invited to Britain: that he ratify the Treaty of Versailles, and that he accept the British treaty.
On 19 April 1923 Curzon sent Jeddah a revised draft, initialled by himself and by Hussein's agent, Dr Naji al-Asil.
It differed from the earlier text chiefly in a new Article 2 and in Articles 3 to 5, which dealt with "the disputed land frontiers of the Hedjaz."
Britain also changed the money.
Instead of a continuing subsidy, it offered Hussein a single final payment of £50,000.
Why did Hussein refuse?
The British file shows that he refused and what was on the table.
Jordan's official Arab Revolt centennial site gives one.
It states that he refused the 1921 treaty because it required him to recognize the mandate over Palestine, and with it a Jewish national home.
That account comes from the Hashemite royal house's own heritage site.
No British document in these sources names Palestine as his reason, so the explanation rests on the Jordanian account alone.
According to PBS, his rejection of the Paris settlements and of the Anglo-Hashemite treaty cost him British support when Ibn Saud invaded.
In March 1924 Hussein proclaimed himself caliph.
In September 1924 an Ikhwan attack on Taif caught him unprepared.
After his abdication Britain declined to resume treaty talks with his son King Ali, "so long as present unsettled conditions in the Hejaz continue."
Hussein lived in exile in Cyprus until 1930 and died in Amman in 1931.
The Jordanian site gives the date as 3 June 1931 and says he was buried at the al-Aqsa compound.
Hussein's refusal bears directly on the old question of whether Britain kept its wartime promises to him.
Its strongest witness is Lawrence himself.
As Rick Richman has set out in the Jewish Review of Books, Lawrence wrote that the Cairo settlement was "fulfilling (I think) our promises in letter and spirit."
In January 1921 he told Churchill that Faisal had agreed to "abandon all claims of his father to Palestine."
On this reading Britain gave the thrones of Iraq and Transjordan to two of Hussein's sons, and, on Lawrence's account, a Hashemite prince had given up the claim to Palestine.
Faisal had also dealt directly with the Zionist movement in 1919, as told in .
The Hashemite account says plainly that "the Allies did not keep their promises," and it presents Hussein's refusal to sign a treaty recognizing the Palestine mandate as the expression of that view.
The Palestine Arab Delegation made the same case on the text of the correspondence.
In its reply to the British government in 1922, it argued that McMahon had written "districts," not "vilayet."
It argued that the area he reserved was Lebanon, and that "Palestine thus comes within the scope of the promise."
The third is the British government's official position, stated in the same 1922 parliamentary paper.
It held that "the whole of Palestine west of the Jordan was thus excluded from Sir H. McMahon's pledge."
Lawrence's case rests on what the Hashemites received.
Hussein's sons ruled two states, and one of them had, on Lawrence's account, agreed to give up the Palestine claim.
The Arab case rests on the wording of the letters and on what the Sharif himself refused to sign.
The British case rests on a reading of the wartime correspondence that the Arab Delegation disputed word by word in the same year.
Hussein's refusal does not settle what McMahon meant.
It does show that the man to whom the promise was made refused to recognize the Paris settlements and never ratified the treaty Britain offered him.
No British document in this material states Hussein's own reason for refusing, so the Palestine explanation rests on the Jordanian account.
The sources here do not give the final fate of Curzon's 1923 draft beyond Hussein's abdication the following year and Britain's refusal to negotiate with his son.
Lawrence's report that Faisal agreed to give up his father's claim is Lawrence's own account.
Nothing here records Faisal saying so himself.
And the meaning of McMahon's "districts" was argued in 1922 by the two sides that had most at stake, and it remains disputed.
Paris, 1919: A Conditional Signature and a Shelved Report
Faisal carried his case to Paris, where in 1919 the powers that had won the war met to settle the peace, and the future of the former Ottoman provinces was among the questions before them.
For Palestine, two records from that year cut against the story usually told about it.
Together they bear on a question that is still argued: did the governments that decided Palestine's future know what its inhabitants wanted?
At the peace conference, it is said, the Arabs accepted a Jewish homeland, and the powers acted on what the people of the country wanted.
The first record is the agreement signed in London on 3 January 1919 by Emir Faisal and Chaim Weizmann, in which Faisal accepted Jewish immigration into Palestine and the Balfour Declaration.
Beside his signature Faisal added a condition in Arabic: he would concur only if the Arabs obtained their independence as he had demanded in his memorandum.
According to two accounts, the Zionist Organization submitted the agreement to the peace conference without that caveat.
When the independence Faisal had named did not come, the condition failed.
For decades the document would be cited as evidence of Arab consent.
Palestinian Arabs were not only spoken for in Paris; they also spoke.
The First Palestine Arab Congress met in Jerusalem in January 1919, timed to coincide with the conference.
According to the Jewish Virtual Library, it opened on 27 January and cabled the conference to oppose the Balfour Declaration.
The second record came from the American delegation.
President Wilson sent a commission of his own, the King–Crane Commission, to find out what the people of the region wanted.
In that time it received about 1,875 petitions, 72 percent of them hostile to the Zionist plan.
Its findings on Palestine were blunt.
The non-Jewish population, the commission reported, made up nearly nine-tenths of the whole and was "emphatically against the entire Zionist program."
It was not a petition from one side or a protest from a congress.
The League of Nations Covenant, drafted that same year, made the wishes of such communities a principal consideration in the selection of the Mandatory, a story told in .
Its first appearance in print came in December 1922, in Editor & Publisher, by which time Britain and France had established their mandates.
Wilson himself may never have seen it.
Some members of the commission believed that the State Department and Zionists were responsible for suppressing it.
The first is that the commission's findings were a record of opinion, not a ruling; it recommended modification of the Zionist program, and the powers were free to disagree, as they did.
The Arab consent most often cited from 1919 was given on a condition, and by the accounts cited here the condition was missing from the copy the conference saw.
The population's opinion was measured by an American commission, and the measurement was kept out of public view until the decisions it might have affected had been made.
Whether the governments in Paris knew what the people of Palestine wanted is not, on this evidence, an open question.
The objections that Britain set aside in Paris and London came from somewhere.
A persistent claim holds that before Israel existed the Palestinians had no leaders, no national identity and no political demands.
The record of the first years of British rule says otherwise.

From the end of the war Palestinian Muslims and Christians organized together, held a series of national congresses, elected an executive, sent delegations to London and put a clear demand in writing: a government elected by the people of the country.
Britain answered in writing, and refused.
The movement's first organizations were the Muslim-Christian Associations, or Muslim-Christian Societies, local bodies that joined members of the two communities.
Their aims were plain from the start: they pressed the Peace Conference and Britain to repeal the Balfour Declaration, and they called for a united Syria.

One account, from a 2019 conference on a century of Palestinian nationalism, describes them as a Palestinian initiative, formed to counter British "divide and rule" and to present a united Palestinian front.

Another, from the Institute for Palestine Studies, records that the British military administration encouraged their establishment, and that Muslim leaders welcomed Christian participation as a sign of a united Arab opposition.
The first public test came on the first anniversary of the Balfour Declaration.
On 3 November the mayor of Jerusalem, Musa Kazim al-Husseini, led a demonstration that ended at government house with a written protest.
Musa Kazim would chair the movement's executive from 1920 until his death in 1934.
The First Palestine Arab Congress met in Jerusalem from 27 January to 10 February 1919, with 27 delegates from Muslim-Christian Associations across the country.
It was timed to coincide with the Paris Peace Conference, so that Palestinians could submit counter-claims to the Zionist claims being made there.
According to the Jewish Virtual Library's account, the congress resolved that Palestine was part of Arab Syria and cabled the Peace Conference opposing the Balfour Declaration.
What happened to Palestine's case in Paris is told in .
Between 1919 and 1928 seven congresses met, in Jerusalem, Jaffa, Haifa and Nablus.

They called for Palestine to be part of the promised independent Arab state, and for "a national government responsible to a representative assembly" chosen by the country's Arabic-speaking inhabitants.
They rejected the Balfour Declaration and mass Jewish immigration.
By the time the third congress met, the British had removed Musa Kazim from office.

After the April 1920 clashes in Jerusalem, the authorities accused him of inciting the violence, dismissed him as mayor and appointed Raghib al-Nashashibi, head of a rival leading family, in his place.
The Third Palestine Arab Congress met in Haifa in December 1920.

It declared the Balfour Declaration null and void, demanded an end to Jewish immigration, and created a nine-member Arab Executive Committee, with Musa Kazim al-Husseini as its chairman, a post he held until his death in 1934.
At the same congress the Muslim-Christian Association framework became the main organisational structure of the national movement.
Musa Kazim was its president, and its vice-presidents were two Christians: Ya'qub
Farraj of Jerusalem and Tawfiq Abdallah of Acre.
In 1921 the executive began to deal directly with the British government.
Musa Kazim led delegations to Winston Churchill, then Colonial Secretary, in Cairo and in Jerusalem.
According to the Jewish Virtual Library, Churchill met the Arab Executive in Jerusalem on 28 March 1921.
The Fourth Congress, meeting in Jerusalem in 1921, then sent a delegation led by Musa Kazim to London, to persuade Britain to abandon the Balfour Declaration policy.

The sources give three different dates for that congress: 29 May to 4 June 1921 in the PalQuest encyclopedia; simply May 1921 in a 2015 study of Musa Kazim by Naser and Abu Hilal; and 25 June 1921 in a Jewish Virtual Library article that credits Wikipedia.

A photograph in the Palestinian Museum Digital Archive identifies the members of the London delegation: Musa Kazim al-Husseini, Tawfiq Hammad, Ibrahim Shammas, Shibli al-Jamal, Amin al-Tamimi and Mu'in al-Madi.
The delegation's exchange with the Colonial Office was later published by the British government, and it shows both sides' positions in their own words.
