sent: The League of Nations, founded in 1920 under the Treaty of Versailles, was the authority in whose name the arrangement was made.
The mandate system was Woodrow Wilson's attempt to separate a temporary trusteeship, meant to lead toward self-government, from outright colonial annexation.
In practice, mandates were administered essentially as colonies.
That judgment concerns Palestine; the record summarized here does not show that every mandate across the world was run the same way.
The League itself did not survive the Second World War, and its successor, the United Nations, inherited its records.
Article 1 gave the Mandatory, Britain, "full powers of legislation and of administration."
Article 2 set out the Mandatory's core obligations, and it set out three of them in one sentence.

Britain was responsible for conditions that would secure the Jewish national home; for the development of self-governing institutions; and for "safeguarding the civil and religious rights of all the inhabitants of Palestine."

Article 4 provided that "an appropriate Jewish agency shall be recognized as a public body" to advise the Administration, and it recognized the Zionist Organization as that agency for as long as its constitution was deemed appropriate.
The League later recorded that in 1929 the Zionist Organization was replaced in this role by the "Jewish Agency for Palestine."
The articles summarized here name no equivalent public body for the Arab majority.

Britain's later offer of an "Arab Agency" analogous to the Jewish Agency, with members chosen by the High Commissioner, and its rejection in October 1923, belong to the story of the Legislative Council of 1922–23.
Article 6 turned the national home from a principle into a working instruction.

The Administration was to "facilitate Jewish immigration under suitable conditions" and to encourage close settlement by Jews on the land, while ensuring that other sections of the population are not prejudiced.
Article 7 provided the basis for a Palestinian citizenship, and part of it concerned the acquisition of Palestinian citizenship by Jews.
Three years later, that article became the legal ground of the Palestinian Citizenship Order, discussed below.
Article 11 dealt with the country's wealth.

It allowed the Administration to place natural resources and public works under public ownership or control, and to make arrangements with the Jewish agency for such works, with the profits that could be distributed capped.
The clause named the Jewish agency as a body that could be brought in to develop public resources, and it limited the profits that could be taken out of them.

Article 22 made English, Arabic and Hebrew the official languages of Palestine, and required that any Arabic inscription on stamps or money be repeated in Hebrew, and any Hebrew inscription in Arabic.
Article 25 concerned the lands east of the river.

It let the Mandatory, with the consent of the League Council, postpone or withhold the application of provisions of the Mandate in the territories between the Jordan and Palestine's eastern boundary, so long as nothing was done that conflicted with Articles 15, 16 and 18.
Britain used that power within two months of the text's approval.

The memorandum of September 1922 that removed the national-home provisions from Transjordan, one stage in a separation completed by 1923, is the subject of its own section, with the long political afterlife of that separation.
Set beside the letter it absorbed, the Mandate shows what changed in five years.

The 1922 text made the national home a legal responsibility of the governing power, added an immigration duty and a recognized Jewish public body, and widened the protected group from "existing non-Jewish communities" to "all the inhabitants."
When the Mandate took effect, and the dispute over it.
The League Council approved the terms of the Palestine and Syria mandates together, pending an agreement between France and Italy over Syria.

At its meeting in Geneva on 29 September 1923, the Council took note that the France–Italy agreement had been reported and that the two mandates had "automatically and simultaneously entered into force."
The United Nations later used that date.

John Quigley, writing in July 2026, argues that the Council only noted, in the future tense, that the mandates would enter into force, and that the Secretary-General, Drummond, changed the tense in the circular that reported the meeting.
Quigley adds a second argument: Britain lacked title to the territory at that point, because the Treaty of Lausanne, signed on 24 July 1923, entered into force only on 6 August 1924.

The case for the conventional date rests on the League's own record, circular C.L.101.1923.VI, which states that the mandates had "automatically and simultaneously entered into force," and on the United Nations' later reliance on it.
The case against rests on the minutes' wording and on the sequence of the Ottoman peace treaty.
The dispute is about the legal moment the Mandate began, not about whether Britain governed: British administration of Palestine was already in place, under a High Commissioner, from 1920.
Britain administered Palestine under the Mandate until 1948.

It issued passports, minted the currency, printed the stamps, ran the police and the courts, operated the railways and the ports, and staffed a civil service that employed Arabs and Jews alike, all under a High Commissioner headquartered in Jerusalem.
Beneath him sat a postal system and a customs and taxation apparatus that functioned for the whole of the Mandate's span.
The Mandate had a legal text, published borders and recognized standing in international law.
The first High Commissioner, appointed in 1920 by the Cabinet that had issued the Balfour Declaration, was Sir Herbert Samuel, a British Jew and a committed Zionist.

One reading holds that his appointment embedded the declaration's contradiction in the administration itself: a single government was charged at once with fostering a Jewish national home and safeguarding the rights of an existing Arab majority, two obligations that, on this reading, could not both be honored.
Citizens, passports, money.
The Palestinian Citizenship Order of 1925, which came into force on 1 August 1925, gave legal form to a Palestinian citizenship under Article 7.
Under it, about 70,000 brown passports were issued over the years of the Mandate, each stamped "BRITISH PASSPORT / PALESTINE."
The word "British" on the cover is what later led casual observers to misremember them.
The holders were citizens of Palestine, Arab and Jewish.
The Palestine pound was minted from 1927 and circulated as legal tender; Palestine issued its own postage stamps, ran its own courts, and registered its own births, deaths, marriages and land titles.
The historian Lauren Banko's study The Invention of Palestinian Citizenship, 1918–1947 traces how this status was built.
It was not an informal identity but a specific legal status created by British administrative order, with its own bureaucratic history, population records, and legal disputes over who qualified.

They are held today by the descendants of Palestinian families in Ramallah and Haifa, in the refugee camps of Lebanon and Jordan, and across the diaspora, as evidence that their grandparents were citizens of a recognized polity.
By one general account of the Mandate, its population at the start was roughly 90 percent Arab and 10 percent Jewish, about 600,000 Arabs and 60,000 Jews.
An account of the 1922 White Paper puts the Jewish population at about 80,000 in 1922.
The one count from these years is the British census of October 1922, which recorded 757,182 people: 590,890 Muslims, 83,794 Jews and 73,024 Christians.
The census total is well above the first estimate, and its Jewish count is close to the second.
By 1947, the last full year of the Mandate, the figures had moved to roughly 1.3 million Arabs and 600,000 Jews.
Jewish growth came substantially through waves of immigration from Europe between the wars, heaviest in the 1930s as antisemitism in Europe intensified.
The Jewish National Fund, founded in 1901, and the other Zionist institutions had acquired about 9.8 percent of Mandate Palestine by purchase by 1948.
The two measures are taken against different wholes, Mandate Palestine in one case and the territory of the new state in the other, so they should not be read as a single sum.
What the comparison does establish is that fifty years of organized, funded purchase left Jewish institutions owning under a tenth of the country's land on the eve of statehood.
A familiar line holds that Palestine was an empty desert until Jewish pioneers made it bloom.
The administrative record of the Mandate answers the first half of that sentence directly.

The territory Britain governed had a High Commissioner, a treasury, a passport office, courts, a postal service, a registry of births and land titles, a currency, and a population numbering in the hundreds of thousands.

The Mandate text itself legislated for "all the inhabitants of Palestine" and for "other sections of the population" whose rights were not to be prejudiced, wording that presupposes people already living there.
It establishes something narrower: that a functioning civic polity called Palestine, with a documented citizenry, existed for a quarter-century before 1948.
The record also supports the strongest form of the Zionist reading of the same document.
The Mandate was not a British favor that could be quietly withdrawn.

It was an instrument approved by the Council of the League of Nations that wrote the national home into binding articles: Britain was responsible for securing it, was obliged to facilitate Jewish immigration and close settlement, and was required to work with a recognized Jewish public body.

The Arab leadership's reading pointed to what the framework did not give: in February 1922 the Palestine Arab Delegation demanded a "national independent Government" and said the Balfour Declaration could not be a basis for discussion, and the Colonial Office replied that "the creation at this stage of a national Government would preclude the fulfilment of the pledge."
On one reading, the disagreement is over which of Article 2's obligations governed when they could not all be met at once.
It does not resolve present arguments about citizenship, return or statehood; it shows only that a formal, legal Palestinian citizenship existed under British administration decades before 1948.
The two estimates of the Jewish population at the Mandate's start, 60,000 and about 80,000, are not reconciled with each other or with the census count of 83,794.
Whether the Mandate entered into force on 29 September 1923 remains, as of the scholarship cited, contested.
It bound Britain to a national home, to self-governing institutions and to the rights of all inhabitants, and it named no rule for choosing among them.
The documents of 1922 that tried to supply such a rule, the Churchill White Paper and the Transjordan memorandum, are where the next sections turn.
The council's failure left one office at the center of Palestine's government.
The Mandate is often written about as though "the British government" ran Palestine as a single, faceless machine.
Herbert Samuel opened the office in 1920.

His successors, Plumer, Chancellor, Wauchope, MacMichael, Gort and Cunningham, presided in turn over the riots of 1929, the Arab Revolt, the years of the 1939 White Paper, the Jewish armed campaign against British rule, and the withdrawal of 1948.
The office drew its power from the Mandate itself.
Article 1 gave the Mandatory "full powers of legislation and of administration."

Britain exercised those powers through a High Commissioner based in Jerusalem, at the head of a civil government that ran everything from passports and currency to police, courts and railways, and that employed Arabs and Jews alike.
Above him stood London and, more distantly, the League of Nations.
The Colonial Office conducted the negotiations over Palestine's constitution in 1922, and the Mandatory reported to the League on its administration.
Beside the administration, Article 4 of the Mandate recognized the Zionist Organization as the "appropriate Jewish agency," a public body to advise it.
The constitution of 1922 placed the High Commissioner at the head of a Legislative Council of twenty-two members, ten of them officials and twelve elected.

After the boycott of the 1923 elections, Britain governed with an advisory council of British officials only, and the High Commissioner ruled without an elected legislature for the rest of the Mandate.

Its effect on the office was lasting: for the rest of the Mandate, the "full powers of legislation and of administration" that Article 1 gave the Mandatory were exercised in Palestine through the High Commissioner without any elected body beside him.
The first man to hold this office had a direct link to the Balfour Declaration.
Herbert Samuel was a British Cabinet minister and an advocate of Zionism, and a memorandum he wrote in 1915 influenced the Balfour Declaration itself.
He was appointed in 1920 by the same British Cabinet that had issued the declaration, and by many accounts he was the first Jewish governor of the land since Roman times.

It sharpened Arab suspicion that the Mandate was built to deliver the Balfour promise, and it placed inside a single administration the double charge of fostering a Jewish national home while safeguarding the rights of the Arab majority.
Samuel's record in office does not fit either of the simple portraits drawn of him.

According to J. B. Schechtman's account in the Encyclopaedia Judaica, one of his first acts, in July 1920, was an amnesty for those imprisoned over the Jerusalem riots of that April, Jews and Arabs alike.
He also pardoned Amin al-Husseini, whom a British military tribunal had convicted in his absence after the same violence.
What became of Jabotinsky's sentence under the amnesty is disputed, as told with .
Samuel lent his name, as Honorary President, to the Pro-Jerusalem Society of Ronald Storrs, Jerusalem's military governor until 1920 and its civil governor from that year.
In 1921 he made Amin al-Husseini Mufti of Jerusalem, after recording Amin's pledge to keep the city calm and after Storrs, at his request, secured a rival candidate's withdrawal.
On 20 December 1921 the Supreme Moslem Sharia Council Order created the council over which Amin would preside.

After the Jaffa riots, on 15 May 1921, Samuel temporarily prohibited Jewish immigration, and on 3 June he tied future immigration to the country's economic capacity, the principle the 1922 White Paper would write down.
He created a mixed Arab-Jewish militia, which the last 400 Palestinian Legionnaires of the Jewish Legion joined.
On 1 September 1922 he proclaimed the Palestine Order in Council in force, the constitution under which the Mandate was to be governed.
When the Legislative Council it created failed in 1923, the office he handed on governed with officials alone.
A Zionist by conviction, chosen by the Cabinet that issued the Balfour Declaration, Samuel suspended Jewish immigration after Jaffa and backed as Mufti a man he had pardoned.
Field Marshal Herbert Plumer, who came to the post from command of the British Expeditionary Force's Second Army, served from 1925 to 1928.
He was named without consultation with the World Zionist Organization, yet he was regarded as committed to fairness toward Zionist aspirations.
When he died in 1932, a Jewish Telegraphic Agency obituary described his tenure as "the only period when complete tranquility existed in Palestine."
Sir John Chancellor served from December 1928 to September 1931, a period of what has been described as "tremendous tension."
It began with a dispute at the Western Wall on Yom Kippur 1928 and culminated in the Hebron Massacre of 24 August 1929.
He was on home leave in England through the critical period of July and August 1929.
Harry Luke served as acting High Commissioner throughout, and Chancellor returned to Jerusalem only on 29 August 1929, five days after the killings.
Arthur Wauchope held the office from 1931 to 1938, through years of rising Jewish immigration and the outbreak of the Arab Revolt of 1936–39.
Historians generally regard him as more sympathetic to Zionist settlement than his successors, and his approach has been called relatively conciliatory.
Harold MacMichael, from 1938 to 1944, administered Palestine as the 1939 White Paper was put into effect and through the early years of Jewish paramilitary resistance.
In 1944 Lehi, also known as the Stern Gang, attempted to assassinate him in an ambush on his motorcade.
The shortest tenure, and the one most often left out of popular accounts, belonged to Field Marshal John Vereker, 6th Viscount Gort.
The last was Alan Cunningham, from 1945 to 1948.
He presided over the most violent period of Jewish paramilitary resistance, including the bombing of the King David Hotel, and over the chaotic British withdrawal from Palestine in May 1948.
Treating the period as one undifferentiated British policy erases a calm three years under one man, an absence during a massacre under another, and an assassination survived under a third.
No one High Commissioner's character explains the Mandate's outcome.
Each worked inside a much larger structure: a Mandate held by Britain under the League, directed from London, and from 1923 governed without an elected chamber in Palestine.
It does not name every acting commissioner who filled the gaps between tenures, beyond Harry Luke in 1929.
It does not show, for any of the seven, how much of what he did was his own decision and how much followed instructions from the Colonial Office.
It does not give the content of Samuel's 1915 memorandum, only that it influenced the Balfour Declaration.

And for Wauchope, MacMichael, Gort and Cunningham it gives a reputation and a few dated events rather than a full account of their administrations; those belong to the later chapters in which their crises fall.
The First American Campaigns: Weizmann, Einstein and the Fight Over the Money
The Mandate's text was settled in London and Geneva, but much of the money and some of the political backing for the national home were being sought in the United States.
American support for a Jewish homeland is usually dated to the years after the Second World War, as a response to the Holocaust.
The organized American campaign began a generation earlier.
By the spring of 1921 the Zionist movement was running national fundraising tours across the United States, and by January 1922 one of its leaders was sitting with the President.
American Jewish opinion was not yet its own: much of the established community still kept its distance.
The United States had figured in Zionist and British calculations from the start.

Among the motives the British War Cabinet weighed in 1917, when it approved the Balfour Declaration, was the hope of winning sympathy in Russian and American Jewish communities, to help keep Russia in the war and bring America into it.

At a London conference on 24 December 1920 the Zionist Organization founded the Keren Hayesod, the Palestine Foundation Fund, as its central and permanent fundraising arm, open to non-Zionist donors as well, with an original five-year target of £25,000,000.
America was where a large part of that money would have to come from.
In March 1921 Chaim Weizmann invited Albert Einstein to accompany him to the United States.
The two toured the country for two months that spring, raising money for the new Keren Hayesod and for the Hebrew University.
The Einstein Papers document it.
Weizmann wanted the Keren Hayesod centralized under the Zionist Executive.
The American faction led by Supreme Court Justice Louis Brandeis and Judge Julian Mack wanted American control of the money and businesslike management of how it was spent.
At stake was who would decide how American donations were spent: the world movement's executive, or the American organization that raised them.
The dispute came to a head at the 1921 convention of the Zionist Organization of America in Cleveland.
Weizmann's side won, and the Brandeis group withdrew from the leadership of American Zionism.
Weizmann's centralized model for the fund had prevailed.
In November 1921 a second delegation arrived for a Keren Hayesod tour: Nahum Sokolow, who with Weizmann had drafted the Balfour Declaration, Otto Warburg and Jabotinsky.
On 13 January 1922 Sokolow met President Warren Harding for nearly an hour.
Within months, Congress would take up a resolution endorsing the Balfour Declaration, the subject of .
None of this meant that American Jewry as a whole had embraced Zionism.
Much of the established community remained non-Zionist.
Paul Warburg avoided the cause, and when Einstein invited about fifty non-Zionist notables to take part, few responded.

The campaign of 1921 and 1922 was the work of an organized movement within American Jewish life, not the voice of that community entire, and the distance kept by many of its leading figures is as much a part of the record as the money raised.

American support for a Jewish national home did not begin after 1945: by 1921, twenty-seven years before statehood, the movement had a national fundraising operation in the United States, a public figure of Einstein's standing on tour, a fight over control of the proceeds, and an audience with the President.
But that support was not yet broad, even among American Jews.
It does not say what Sokolow and Harding discussed, or whether the meeting bore on the congressional resolution that followed.
And it records the outcome of the Cleveland convention, not the vote or the arguments made on its floor.
Congress Endorses Balfour: The Lodge–Fish Resolution of 1922
Official American support for a Jewish homeland is usually dated to 1948 and President Truman's recognition of the new state.
The first formal endorsement by the United States government came twenty-six years earlier.
On 21 September 1922 President Warren Harding signed a joint resolution of Congress favouring a national home for the Jewish people in Palestine.
It had been requested by American Zionist leaders, opposed by the State Department, and passed by the House and, by unanimous consent, the Senate.
The initiative came from the American Zionist movement, then in the middle of the fundraising campaigns described in .

American Zionist leaders approached two Republicans, Senator Henry Cabot Lodge of Massachusetts and Representative Hamilton Fish III of New York, and asked them to introduce a resolution endorsing the Balfour Declaration of 1917.
The Jewish Virtual Library credits a significant lobbying effort by the American Zionist community, and in particular the work of Rabbi Simon Glazer.
Nahum Sokolow had met Harding for nearly an hour on 13 January 1922, during the Keren Hayesod tour that raised nearly $5 million.
The State Department opposed it, and so did the New York Times.
The House approved it on 30 June 1922, and the Senate followed by unanimous consent on 13 July.
The Senate's passage came eleven days before the Mandate for Palestine, which wrote the Balfour Declaration into an instrument of the League of Nations, was done at London on 24 July 1922.
The Mandate itself is examined in .
Harding signed the measure on 21 September 1922 as Public Resolution 67-73.
Its text favoured "the establishment in Palestine of a national home for the Jewish people," repeating the phrase the Balfour Declaration had used in 1917.
It also carried a condition: that nothing should be done which might prejudice "the civil and religious rights of Christian and all other non-Jewish communities in Palestine."

Congress, like the British government before it, favoured a national home for one people and stated in the same text that the rights of the communities already living in the country were not to be prejudiced.
Inside American Jewish life the resolution mattered too.
The World Jewish Congress notes that it helped legitimize Zionism within American Jewry by giving it a "stamp of approval" from the non-Jewish world.

That carries weight against the background of the previous year, when much of the established American Jewish community still kept its distance from the cause, and when Einstein's invitation to about fifty non-Zionist notables drew few replies.
The initiative did not come from the State Department, the arm of government responsible for foreign policy, which opposed it.
It came from an organized domestic movement that approached members of Congress directly and won passage in both houses, after which the President signed.
What it committed the United States to is a narrower question than its importance might suggest, and the record used here answers it only in part.
The text says what Congress favoured and on what condition.
Nor do they give the grounds on which the State Department and the New York Times objected, or the House vote count.
What is documented is the sequence, the words of the text with their condition, and the fact that the first official American endorsement of a Jewish national home came in 1922, not 1948.
Rutenberg's grid followed the map of Jewish settlement; the census showed how small that map still was.
Every later argument about Palestine, about immigration, land and partition, rests on numbers, and the most important of them were gathered by the British administration in these years.
The first says Palestine was "a land without a people."
The second says Palestinian Arabs owned 94 percent of the land.
Neither survives the Mandate's own statistics.
Britain's first census of Palestine, taken in 1922, counted 757,182 people.
Of these, 83,794 were Jews, about 11 percent of the population .
The second census, in 1931, found Jews at 17 percent of the population, Muslims at 73 percent and Christians at 9 percent .
In nine years the Jewish population had doubled.
Yet the growth of the non-Jewish population over the same years was larger than the entire Jewish population .
The 1931 census also asked where people were born: 42 percent of Jews had been born in Palestine and 58 percent abroad .
The Yishuv of 1931 was, by a clear majority, a community of immigrants, though a substantial share was native-born.
The line above traces the Jewish share of the population across three counts: about 11 percent in 1922, 17 percent in 1931 and about 33 percent at the end of 1946  .
The first two points are British census results.
The third is an estimate, made by the United Nations Special Committee on Palestine (UNSCOP).
UNSCOP put the population at the end of 1946 at about 1,846,000: roughly 1,203,000 Arabs (65 percent) and 608,000 Jews (33 percent) .
Over almost the same span, British records count 376,415 Jewish immigrants between 1920 and 1946 .

The 757,182 people of 1922 are the country as Britain found it when the Mandate began; the 376,415 recorded Jewish immigrants of 1920–1946 are the arrivals that changed its composition; and the roughly 1.85 million of late 1946 are the country UNSCOP had in front of it when it made its recommendation   .
Even at the end of 1946, after a quarter-century of immigration, about two in three of the inhabitants were Arabs.
The Jewish Agency's economic case to the Peel Commission in 1937 put the Jewish population of 1922 at 84,000, or 13 percent, on a non-Jewish base of only 565,000 .
The Village Statistics of 1945 was compiled for the Anglo-American Committee of Inquiry and later used by UNSCOP.

In 1947, the United Nations partition plan allotted about 56 percent of the territory to the proposed Jewish state, at a time when Jews owned under 7 percent of the land; the proposed Jewish state would also have contained a large Arab minority .
How the Jewish share of land was assembled in these years, through the purchases of the Jewish National Fund and others, is told in ; the partition plan itself belongs to a later chapter.
"A land without a people" is refuted by every census the British took.
The 1922 count found three-quarters of a million people, and the 1931 and 1946 figures found the Arab majority still growing  .
The country was inhabited, and mostly by Arabs.
The claim that Palestinian Arabs privately owned 94 percent of the land counts large areas of state and public land as Arab-owned .
Jewish ownership of under 7 percent does not mean Arab private ownership of the remainder.

They do not tell us how the land not privately owned by Jews or Arabs was divided between state land and other public categories in any given year; the sources here give the distinction, not the totals.
And the gap between the census and the Jewish Agency's 1937 figures for 1922 is not explained in the material used here.
Jacob de Haan and the Orthodox Opposition, 1919–1924
The Revisionists challenged the Zionist leadership from inside the movement.
Jacob de Haan challenged it from outside, and paid with his life.
On the evening of 30 June 1924, Jacob Israël de Haan left evening prayers at a synagogue on Jaffa Road in Jerusalem and was shot three times.
The killing is widely described by historians as the first political assassination inside the Jewish community of Palestine, and its victim was neither a British official nor an Arab leader.

He was a Jew, a former Zionist sympathizer, and in the years before his death the most effective political voice, in English, of the Jewish community that rejected the Zionist movement's claim to speak for it .
A common account of these years holds that Jewish opposition to Zionism before 1948 was marginal, peaceful, and faded away on its own.
De Haan's career does not fit that account.
The opposition he represented was organized, it had a leadership, it took its case to the British authorities and to Arab rulers, and it was met, at least once, with a bullet.
De Haan was born in the Netherlands in 1881 and was a poet and a lawyer by training.
He arrived in Palestine in 1919 as a newspaper correspondent, and he taught law in Jerusalem at the Mandate government's law classes .
He came with some sympathy for Zionism.
He moved from that sympathy to the other side of the question entirely, into the Haredi camp, the strictly Orthodox community of the old Yishuv .
The "old Yishuv" was the name for the Orthodox Jewish communities of Jerusalem, Safed, Hebron and Tiberias, which had lived in the country for generations before political Zionism existed .
Its leadership, including Rabbi Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld, rejected a secular Jewish state on religious grounds, and objected to the Zionist Organization speaking in its name.

Agudath Israel was founded in 1912 as a worldwide movement to strengthen Torah-observant Judaism, and specifically to separate it from the emerging secular Jewish nationalist movement, which its founders regarded as a danger to Torah-observant Jewish life   .
Its opposition to political Zionism on religious grounds was thus organized thirty-six years before the State of Israel was founded.
He wrote for British newspapers and lobbied Mandate officials directly .
De Haan's case was narrow and precise.
The Zionist Organization, he argued, was one political movement among Jews.
It was not the representative of all the Jews in Palestine .

For the old Orthodox community, whose presence in Jerusalem long predated the Zionist movement, that distinction was the whole point: a secular national movement should not speak in the name of religious Jews who rejected its aims.
It was the argument he pressed on British officials .

It was, in method, a claim about representation, and de Haan carried it to two audiences: the Mandatory power, whose officials he lobbied, and Arab leaders, with whom he sought a separate understanding .
He sought a separate understanding between Orthodox Jews and Arab leaders, on the premise that Jews who did not seek a state need not be in conflict with the Arab majority .
In 1924 this led him to meetings with the Hashemite leadership in Transjordan .
He was then preparing to travel to London with an anti-Zionist Orthodox delegation .
The sources in this book do not record what was said at the Transjordan meetings, what, if anything, was agreed, or what the London delegation intended to ask for.
After the shooting on Jaffa Road, each side looked to the other.
The Zionist leadership publicly condemned the killing.
Orthodox leaders blamed Zionist circles .
Avraham Tehomi, by then elderly, said on Israeli television that he had shot de Haan, and that he had done so on the orders of the Haganah, the underground defense force of the Jewish community .

He was the Haganah's Jerusalem district commander from 1929 to 1931, and he then led a group that seceded from it and, together with Revisionist groups, formed the Irgun Zvai Leumi; he returned to the Haganah in 1937  .
Tehomi went further than naming the Haganah.
He named Yitzhak Ben-Zvi, later Israel's second president, as the man from whom the order had come .
The first part, that the shooting was a Haganah operation, carried out by the man who was speaking, is the documented core of the case.
It is a confession by the gunman himself, and it is what allows historians to treat the killing as an act of the Haganah rather than a private crime .
The second part rests on Tehomi alone.
Ben-Zvi had died in 1963, twenty-two years before the interview, and could not answer.

Tehomi's account of his own act and of the organization behind it is a confession; his account of who stood above him is an accusation against a man who could no longer reply, given six decades after the event, with nothing else in the sources to support it.
Organized Jewish opposition to Zionism existed inside Palestine in the early Mandate years, with a leadership, an international organization behind it and a public spokesman.
It was argued openly, to the British and to Arab leaders.
And the Zionist movement's own armed wing, by its gunman's admission, killed its most effective spokesman .
This opposition was also distinct from the other Jewish dissent of these years.
The binationalists of Brit Shalom, founded in 1925, argued from inside Zionism about the form a national home should take; the old Yishuv rejected the national project itself on religious grounds.
Orthodox opposition did not end with de Haan's death.

Its later history lies outside this chapter, but its next turn is documented: in 1938 Neturei Karta split from Agudath Israel to preserve a more uncompromising anti-Zionist position, after Agudath Israel began making practical accommodations with Zionist institutions .
The split itself shows that Agudath Israel, which had organized the old Yishuv's refusal, had by then begun to accommodate the institutions it once opposed.
The sources do not say who, if anyone, above Tehomi gave the order, if Ben-Zvi did not.
They do not record why no one was charged in 1924, what the British authorities established about the crime, or what the Hashemite leadership said to de Haan.
They do not show whether his London delegation would have changed anything.
The decision behind the shot stays where Tehomi left it, resting on his word alone.
The Histadrut and "Hebrew Labour"

In December 1920, in Haifa, the two labor Zionist parties of the day, Ahdut HaAvoda and Hapoel Hatzair, joined forces to found the General Federation of Hebrew Workers in the Land of Israel, known by its Hebrew short name, the Histadrut .
ents: the General Federation of Hebrew Workers

sent: Membership stood at about 4,400 in 1920 and about 8,400 in 1922, in a country where, by a Zionist historian's estimate, there were roughly 50,000 Arab workers  .
Those workers were outside the federation by rule, not by accident: from its founding, membership was restricted to Jews .
Labour Zionism is often remembered as a socialist workers' movement, committed to class solidarity across national lines.
The Histadrut, however, was not a union of the country's workers.
The decisive figure was David Ben-Gurion, elected secretary of the federation at the end of 1921 .
In the account of the historian Zeev Sternhell, Ben-Gurion turned the Histadrut into a national instrument for realizing Zionism rather than a conventional class union .
The Histadrut pressed Jewish employers, especially citrus growers and builders, to hire only Jewish workers .
The demand was made of Jewish employers; the workers it was meant to exclude were Arab.
From December 1920 it also took responsibility for defense, and the Haganah was placed under its direct control; through the 1920s the Haganah had only "a few hundred" volunteer members .
The Histadrut also owned the places where its members worked.
It built the construction and public-works company Solel Boneh.
In association with the World Zionist Organization it founded the Workers' Bank, Bank Hapoalim.
It ran the Kupat Holim health fund, on which many Israelis later depended for their health insurance, and it gathered industrial holdings that later became Koor Industries .
The scale it eventually reached shows what this structure made possible: by 1989 the Histadrut employed about 280,000 workers .
The Jewish National Fund held land that could not be resold to non-Jews and leased it on terms requiring Jewish labor; that clause is set out in .

Taken together, the land fund and the labor federation meant that the Yishuv had separate economic institutions decades before 1948: land that stayed in Jewish hands, a labor market organized for Jewish workers, its own bank and its own health system.
Pinhas Lavon, the Histadrut's secretary-general in 1960, described its founders as young people seeking work in a country "which rejected its inhabitants."
On this reading the Histadrut was what young immigrants built in order to find work at all, and its enterprises were a means of employing them.

On Sternhell's account, under Ben-Gurion the Histadrut became a national instrument for realizing Zionism rather than a conventional union; its socialism served the national project, not the other way round .

Critics including the BDS movement go further, describing the pre-state Histadrut as a national-exclusivist rather than a socialist body, and "Hebrew labour" as national exclusivism in place of worker solidarity .
The Histadrut was also a school for government.
Ben-Gurion went on to chair the Jewish Agency from 1935 and became prime minister in 1948.
He was followed by two Histadrut veterans, Levi Eshkol and Golda Meir  .
Arab workers were admitted to full membership only in 1959, eleven years after the state was founded.
By 1983 about 170,000 of the federation's 1.6 million members were Arab  .

Nor do they measure how far "Hebrew labour" actually succeeded: how many Jewish employers complied, how many Arab workers lost work in Jewish-owned groves and building sites, or what the policy cost employers in wages.
The German emigration that reached Palestine from 1933, and the Transfer Agreement that moved part of its capital there, began with the collapse of a democracy in Berlin.

The documented record supports a narrower and more specific account: an economic catastrophe, a real but already declining surge of support for the Nazi Party, a decision taken by a small number of conservative politicians who believed they could control Hitler, and then a fire, an emergency decree, and a legislature that voted away its own authority.
The Weimar Republic's recovery in the mid-1920s had been built in large part on a steady flow of American loans.
The Wall Street Crash of October 1929 led to the recall of those loans and plunged Germany back into economic catastrophe and mass unemployment  .

The money ran in one direction and then reversed: American lenders supplied the capital that carried the stabilization, and when they withdrew it, the cost came due in Germany as mass unemployment, borne by a republic that had depended on that capital.
The timing of Nazi support matches that sequence.

According to the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum's Holocaust Encyclopedia, genuine popular support for Hitler and his party began to accumulate from late 1929 onward, not before, while the economy still functioned .
Economic hardship does not by itself explain Nazi support.
Millions of Germans lived through the same conditions and did not become Nazis, and the more immediate causes of what followed were political decisions, not economic forces acting alone.
The Nazi Party's electoral high point came in July 1932.
By November 1932, three months before Hitler became Chancellor, its vote share had fallen to roughly 33 percent .
Hitler did not come to power at the crest of a rising wave.
Franz von Papen, an aristocrat and former chancellor, brokered the arrangement that made Hitler Chancellor.

According to the accounts cited here, Papen assured his associates that he had Hitler's measure and could control him from within the cabinet, using him, in the phrase historians use, as a "battering ram" against the political left  .
Hitler was appointed Chancellor on 30 January 1933 .
It does not show that Papen or his circle intended, or foresaw, what came after.
In March 1933 Hitler introduced the Enabling Act, which allowed him to pass laws without the approval of Parliament or the President.
To secure its passage he forcibly prevented the Communist members of Parliament from voting  .
With its enactment the Weimar Republic's twelve-year democratic experiment ended, not by a street coup but by a legislature voting away its own constitutional authority .

The instrument was a statute passed through the legislature's own procedure; the members who could have opposed it were, in the Communists' case, physically kept from the vote, and the remaining members voted under the climate of intimidation that followed the February decree.

One emphasizes the depth of the economic collapse and the real popular support the Nazi Party won from late 1929; on that reading the Republic was gravely weakened from below, and the support was genuine.
It does not settle who set the Reichstag fire.
It cannot show that the Republic would have survived had Hitler not been appointed when he was; the decline of late 1932 makes that possible, not certain.
And it does not show what Papen and his allies expected beyond their belief that they could control the man they empowered.
The Nuremberg Laws, 1935:
A month after the Lucerne Congress upheld Haavara, the regime it had dealt with turned its persecution into statute.
On 15 September 1935 the Reichstag met in special session at Nuremberg, where the Nazi Party was holding its annual rally.

The parliament that voted had already surrendered its own authority two and a half years earlier, when the Enabling Act of March 1933 allowed Hitler to make law without the approval of the Reichstag or the President, a measure carried after Communist deputies had been forcibly kept from voting .

They did something that came first and made the rest administrable: they wrote antisemitism into the law of the German state, defining Jews as a separate category of person by descent and removing them from the body of citizens.
By the autumn of 1935 Germany had a complete legal framework that defined who was a Jew, stripped Jews of citizenship and made marriage between Jews and other Germans a crime.
That framework stood three years before the mass violence of Kristallnacht, told in .
Law came before the pogrom, not after it.
The first of the two statutes, the Reich Citizenship Law, turned on a single definition.
A citizen of the Reich was a person "of German or related blood" who proved through conduct a willingness to serve the German people and Reich  .
German Jews were reduced from citizens to "subjects" of the state, without full political rights .
The second statute, the Law for the Protection of German Blood and Honor, passed the same day, reached into private life.

It banned marriage between Jews and "subjects of the state of German or related blood," and it declared such marriages void even when they had been concluded abroad for the specific purpose of evading the law.
It made "extramarital intercourse" between Jews and non-Jewish Germans a crime.
It barred Jews from employing non-Jewish German women under the age of 45 in their households.
The regime had its own name for the new offense: Rassenschande, "race defilement" .
It presented ordinary love, marriage and domestic employment between Jews and other Germans as a contamination that the state was entitled to punish.
Both laws depended on knowing who was a Jew, and here the regime made its most consequential choice.
It did not define a Jew by religion.
Under the Nuremberg Race Laws a person with three or four Jewish grandparents was a Jew, whatever that person believed or practised .
Germans who had not practised Judaism in decades fell within the definition.
So did people who had formally converted to Christianity.

On 14 November 1935 the First Supplementary Decree to the Reich Citizenship Law created the category of Mischling, "mixed blood," for people with one or two Jewish grandparents, and attached its own separate legal restrictions to it .
The decree distinguished degrees of Jewish ancestry, each carrying its own legal consequences.

The arithmetic was the mechanism: once ancestry could be counted, a clerk could place any German in a category, and the category decided whom that person could marry, whom he or she could employ, and whether he or she was a citizen at all.
The decision was made inside the Nazi state and ratified unanimously by a parliament that had already given up its law-making authority.
The burden fell on German Jews, including converts and the non-observant whom the ancestry test caught, and, through the Mischling decree, on people with one or two Jewish grandparents.
What the 1935 laws meant for Palestine can be stated only as far as the sources go, and they do not go far.
Jewish immigration to Palestine reached its highest recorded level of the Mandate years in 1935.

The figures compiled by the US State Department from British returns give 61,854 Jewish immigrants that year, against 42,359 in 1934 and 29,727 in 1936 ; a second series, printed by the Jewish Virtual Library after Yehoshua Porath, gives 66,472 for 1935 .

The research does not break the year's arrivals down by country of origin or by month, so it cannot show how many German Jews came, or whether any of the rise followed September rather than preceding it.

The surge had begun in 1933, two years before Nuremberg, when the same series records 30,327 arrivals ; and the British labor schedule, which governed one channel of entry, was cut from 8,000 places for April–September 1935 to 3,250 for October 1935–March 1936 .

The most that can be said is that the laws were passed in the year of the peak, while the transfer agreement through which German Jews had been moving to Palestine since 1933 remained in force , as told in .

The documentation here establishes the provisions and the penalties, not a count of prosecutions for Rassenschande, which varied in intensity across regions and years; it establishes that the Mischling system existed and how it worked, not the full detail of the distinctions it drew between its categories.
In Baghdad a German diplomat placed Nazi propaganda in the press.
With the Zionist movement the same regime made a commercial deal.
On 25 August 1933 Zionist bodies signed an agreement with the government of Nazi Germany.
It let German Jews who were emigrating to Palestine take part of their assets with them, not as money but as German goods.
Over the following six years it helped roughly 60,000 people reach Palestine.
It also undercut the worldwide boycott of Nazi Germany that had begun in 1933, and it divided the Jewish world more sharply than any other financial arrangement of the pre-state period.
It was called the Haavara, Hebrew for "transfer."
A common assumption holds that the Zionist movement and Nazi Germany were simply adversaries from 1933 onward.
One calls Haavara a straightforward rescue; the other calls it collaboration.

The documents support both halves at once: a mechanism that moved some 60,000 people out of Nazi reach, and a commercial accommodation that the Nazi state wanted for reasons of its own, chosen by the Zionist movement's own Congress over the objections of some of its own leaders .
The agreement had three parties: the Zionist Federation of Germany; the Anglo-Palestine Bank, acting for the Jewish Agency; and the Reich Economics Ministry  .
An emigrating German Jew deposited assets in an account in Germany.
Those funds were used to buy German export goods, which were shipped to Palestine.
When the goods were sold there, the emigrant was repaid in Palestine from the proceeds  .
For the emigrant, it was a way to move part of a lifetime's assets out of Germany.
For the Zionist bodies, it brought immigrants and goods to Palestine.
For the Nazi state, according to the record, it served two aims.
The regime wanted Germany Judenrein, emptied of Jews, and it wanted to break the anti-Nazi boycott of 1933, which had mass Jewish support and which German officials regarded as an economic threat .
Haavara did both.
Jews left, and German goods found a market abroad at the very moment a boycott was trying to close markets to them.
The rise of that regime and the destruction of the Weimar Republic are told in .
The agreement was a major factor in the emigration of approximately 60,000 German Jews to Palestine between 1933 and 1939 .
By the end of 1937, goods worth 77.8 million Reichsmarks had moved; by the outbreak of war, about 105 million  .
The Jewish Virtual Library records the total transfer as £8.1 million in Palestine pounds, roughly $40.4 million at the time, and states that this included £2.6 million provided by the Reichsbank .
How these German arrivals fit into the immigration of the 1930s as a whole, including the peak year of 1935, is set out in .

The Center for Israel Education ties the German trip that Chaim Arlosoroff, head of the Jewish Agency's political department, made shortly before his murder in June 1933 to the Haavara agreement ; that claim is weighed in .
A chart of US-dollar flows in the record from 1921 to 1949 shows Haavara at about $40 million for 1933–39, one of the largest bars on it, converted from the 105 million Reichsmarks.
The chart's own note warns that its figures are nominal dollars of the year reported, not adjusted for inflation, and that Haavara has been converted at the period estimate .

The smallest bars matter too: the reported $0.15 million that sustained the American Christian committees founded by Emanuel Neumann, discussed in the section on the American Palestine Committee, appears near the foot of the same chart .
The Revisionist leader Ze'ev Jabotinsky, Rabbi Stephen Wise of the American Jewish Congress, and Abba Hillel Silver all opposed the agreement, on the ground that it sabotaged the boycott  .

Their case at its strongest was that the boycott had mass Jewish support and was regarded by German officials themselves as an economic threat, so that a Zionist agreement moving German goods abroad weakened pressure the regime actually felt.

The defenders' case at its strongest was the one the numbers make: people were leaving Germany, they could take something with them only by this route, and tens of thousands reached Palestine through it.
The Nineteenth Zionist Congress, meeting at Lucerne in August 1935, voted by a large majority to continue the agreement and placed Haavara under the supervision of the Jewish Agency  .
The decision was taken knowingly, two years into the agreement's operation and a month before Germany enacted the Nuremberg Laws.
The historian Edwin Black wrote that the agreement "tore the Jewish world apart" .
Haavara also served as the model for a smaller arrangement with Czechoslovakia on the eve of the war .
The Haavara transfer appears as one stream among many on the map of how the pre-state build was financed, between the American donors of the 1920s and the fundraising and arms purchases of 1948.
It does not measure how much damage Haavara did to the boycott, only that it undercut it.
While the Weimar Republic was failing, London was reconsidering Palestine.
British policy there is often described as moving in one steady direction from the Balfour Declaration to the White Paper of 1939.
After the violence of August 1929, two official inquiries concluded that Jewish immigration and land purchase were feeding Arab fears and creating a landless Arab class.
In October 1930 London published a policy built on those findings.
Four months later the Prime Minister, in a letter to the leader of the Zionist movement, explained it in terms that removed its restrictions.

It is the clearest case before 1939 of a British decision on Palestine reversed within months under political pressure, and the immigration figures of the following years show what the reversal allowed.
The first inquiry was the Shaw Commission, sent to investigate the 1929 violence.

It found the fundamental cause in Arab hostility rooted in disappointed political aspirations and fear for their economic future, a fear of displacement through Jewish immigration and land purchase, and it recommended that Britain clarify its policy on both  .
Its findings on the Mufti and on the riots themselves are told in .
Sir John Hope Simpson surveyed land and agriculture across the country; his report was published in October 1930 .

He found that a large share of rural Arab families had too little land to live on, that evictions after land sales were producing a landless class, and that without development there was no margin for further Jewish agricultural settlement .
His full figures, and the Jewish Agency's challenge to them, are set out in .
On the basis of these two reports, the Colonial Secretary, Lord Passfield, issued a White Paper in October 1930.
It made immigration depend on Arab as well as Jewish unemployment, and it tightened control of land transfers .
It was the first serious attempt to slow the machinery of settlement the Mandate had set running.
The mechanism lay in two levers the Mandatory already held: the rate at which immigration certificates were issued, and the approval of land transfers.
The White Paper proposed to tie the first to the condition of the whole labor market, Arab included, and to hold the second more tightly.
Chaim Weizmann resigned as president of the Jewish Agency in protest.
Senior Conservative and Liberal politicians attacked the policy in Parliament and the press as a breach of the Mandate, and the press campaign was intense.
In a closely watched by-election at Whitechapel, a constituency with a large Jewish electorate, Labour's majority shrank .
The pressure fell on a minority Labour government .
On 13 February 1931 Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald sent Weizmann a letter, which was read into the record of the House of Commons .

On immigration, it stated that the government did not contemplate "any stoppage or prohibition of Jewish immigration", and tied any limits to the principle of absorptive capacity, described as "purely economic considerations".

On land, it said the 1930 policy did not bar further Jewish land purchase and referred only to "temporary control of land disposition and transfers"; the duty to settle landless Arabs applied to those displaced by land passing into Jewish hands.

On labor, it accepted the Jewish Agency's right to affirm the preferential employment of Jewish labor, while saying that the Mandatory must take account of any resulting displacement of Arab labor or rise in unemployment .
And it restated the Mandate itself: "an undertaking to the Jewish people and not only to the Jewish population of Palestine", a double undertaking to which equal weight was to be given .

The Zionist reading, which leading opposition politicians had also put in Parliament before the letter was written, was that the White Paper had breached the Mandate, and that the letter corrected the breach .

If the Mandate was an undertaking to the Jewish people as a whole, not only to the Jews already in Palestine, then a policy that measured immigration by the local labor market alone weighed only one side of a double obligation.
The Arab reading was summed up in the name Arab leaders gave the document: the "Black Letter" .

A policy founded on two official inquiries was withdrawn within four months, through a letter to the head of one party to the dispute, after a campaign waged in Parliament, the press and a by-election.
The letter's effect on Arab trust is documented by Arab officials of the Mandate government itself.
On 30 June 1936, 137 Arab senior government officials told the High Commissioner that the Arabs had lost faith in official pledges.
They cited the 1931 letter, issued as an interpretation of the 1930 White Paper, as a cause, and recommended that immigration be stopped .
Five years after it was written, men who served the Mandate administration still cited the letter when they explained their loss of faith in British commitments.
Recorded Jewish immigration, as compiled by the United States State Department from British returns, was 4,075 in 1931, 9,553 in 1932, 30,327 in 1933, 42,359 in 1934 and 61,854 in 1935 .
A second series, printed from the historian Yehoshua Porath, gives higher figures for most of these years; both are set out in .
The 1935 figure was the highest of the Mandate years.
From 1933 the Nazi takeover in Germany drove Jewish emigration on a new scale.
What the letter did was keep in place the rules under which that emigration could enter Palestine.
The Arab Revolt began the following year.
The sources do not show which pressure weighed most with MacDonald: the parliamentary attack, the press, the Whitechapel result, or Weizmann's resignation.
They do not separate the letter's effect on immigration from the effect of events in Germany; the two arrived together, and any attempt to apportion the rise between them goes beyond the evidence.
De Haan's community had lived in the country for generations.
Between 1923 and 1936 the number of Jews entering Palestine each year rose and fell steeply.

They followed pressures and decisions outside Palestine, in Poland and in Washington among them, and they passed through a British administration that counted the arrivals and set an allotment for those who came as workers.
Two great waves came in these years, the Fourth Aliyah of the mid-1920s and the Fifth Aliyah of the 1930s, and the official figures for them do not always agree.
The Jewish Virtual Library puts the Fourth Aliyah at 82,000 Jews who came to Palestine between 1924 and 1929, of whom 23,000 left again .
One was in Poland: an economic crisis and anti-Jewish policies there pushed Jews to leave .
The other was in the United States.

The Jewish Virtual Library points to stiff American immigration quotas, and the Center for Israel Education ties the rise in immigration to Palestine directly to the US Immigration Act of 1924, which limited annual immigration from each country to 2 percent of its residents in the 1890 census  .
Most of the Fourth Aliyah's immigrants were middle class, with modest capital .
The town whose growth tracks the wave most visibly is Tel Aviv.
The Yishuv, the Jewish community in Palestine, suffered an economic crisis in 1926–1928 .
Recorded Jewish immigration, which stood at 33,801 in 1925, fell to 13,081 in 1926, 2,713 in 1927 and 2,178 in 1928 .
Many of those who had arrived left: the 23,000 departures are part of the Fourth Aliyah's own total .
The British inquiry that followed the violence of August 1929 drew a lesson from those years.

The Shaw Commission, reporting in March 1930, criticized what it called "excessive" immigration in 1925–26, and quoted Sir John Campbell's view that the crisis of 1927–28 had come from immigrants arriving "in excess of the economic absorbing power of the country" .
The argument that followed Shaw, through Hope Simpson and the White Paper of 1930, is told in .
Out of that low point came the Fifth Aliyah.
The Jewish Virtual Library dates the Fifth Aliyah from 1929 to 1939.
It states that nearly 250,000 Jews arrived in that wave by 1940, of whom 20,000 later left; that 174,000 settled in the four years 1933–1936 alone; and that the Yishuv reached 450,000 by 1940 .
The emigration of Jews from Nazi Germany in these years, and the Transfer Agreement that let some of them bring capital, are told with their own numbers in .
The sources used here do not break down the annual totals by country of origin, so they cannot say what share of the 1933–1936 arrivals came from Germany and what share from Poland and elsewhere.
Tel Aviv again shows the effect most plainly.
A State Department memorandum of 6 November 1936, written by Paul Alling for Assistant Secretary Moore, cites Palestine Government statistics for that year.
Of the 61,854 Jews who entered in 1935, 14,653 came under the labor schedule and 13,076 were their dependants.

What the breakdown does show clearly is that in the peak year fewer than one immigrant in four entered as a worker on the schedule; the rest came as dependants or, on Alling's estimate, in categories defined by means or occupation.
The memorandum by J. Rives Childs of the State Department's Division of Near Eastern Affairs, dated 3 June 1939, gives recorded Jewish immigration year by year, compiled from the British returns .
A second series, printed by the Jewish Virtual Library from the historian Yehoshua Porath, gives higher figures for most years .
For the mid-1920s the Porath figures are a few hundred to about a thousand higher each year.
In 1936 the order reverses, and the Porath figure is slightly lower  .
This book uses the State Department figures as the recorded series and gives the Porath figures beside them where the difference matters.

The Jewish Virtual Library's total of 82,000 for the Fourth Aliyah is higher than the sum of either annual series for 1924–1929, while its 174,000 settlers for 1933–1936 falls between the two series' totals for those years    .
The same 1939 memorandum carries a finding that bears on one of the most argued questions of the Mandate.

It cites a Consul General's report dated 10 January 1939, that the Jewish population had risen sixfold since 1920, almost entirely through immigration, while the Arab population had risen by about 57 percent, almost entirely through natural increase .

Read this way, the finding helps explain why the level of Jewish immigration, and the Shaw Commission's test of the country's "absorbing power," carried so much weight: on the consul's account, immigration was the means by which the Jewish share of the population changed.
The question of Arab immigration into Palestine in the 1930s, its scale and its sources, lies outside this account, and the prose here makes no claim about it beyond what the consul wrote.
And the 44,000 in Alling's memorandum does not square with the numbers it is drawn from.
Palestinian Politics, 1928–1935:
From Congress to Parties
The riots of August 1929 came a year after the Palestinian national movement had briefly reunited.
A familiar claim holds that the Palestinians had no leaders, no national organization and no political demands before 1948.
By 1928 they had already held seven national congresses, and their central demand to Britain was an elected government.

From 1919, Muslims and Christians organized together through Muslim–Christian Associations; the congresses chose an Arab Executive under Musa Kazim al-Husseini, called for "a national government responsible to a representative assembly", and rejected the Balfour Declaration and mass Jewish immigration  .
That earlier history, from the first congress of 1919 to the delegations of 1921–22, is told in .
It is a story of choices made by Palestinians, among themselves and against one another, under a mandatory power that never recognized their Executive  .
Raghib al-Nashashibi's opposition bloc took part, and Nashashibi himself joined the Arab Executive that emerged from it .

Rivalry between the factions aligned with the Husseini family and those aligned with the Nashashibis had divided Palestinian politics since the British dismissed Musa Kazim al-Husseini as mayor of Jerusalem in 1920 and appointed Raghib al-Nashashibi in his place  .
The 1928 congress briefly brought the two camps into one front .
Nashashibi held the mayoralty throughout: re-elected in 1927, he served until 1934, when Hussein Fakhri al-Khalidi was elected .
Two months after the violence of August 1929, Palestinian organization widened.
On 26 October 1929 the first Palestine Arab Women's Congress met in Jerusalem, with about 300 delegates.
Salma al-Husseini led it; Wahida al-Khalidi and Amina al-Husseini organized it.
The congress called for repeal of the Balfour Declaration and an end to Jewish immigration, and it elected a fourteen-member executive .
The Executive's next move was diplomatic.
In 1930, while London weighed the findings of its inquiries into 1929, an Arab Executive delegation went to London.
Nashashibi traveled with it in March 1930, and Jamal al-Husseini sat on the delegation that negotiated there in April and May  .
The policy London published that autumn, and its withdrawal in February 1931, are told in the section on the Passfield White Paper.

The General Islamic Congress opened in Jerusalem on 7 December 1931 with 130 delegates from 22 countries, according to an account in Middle East Eye, and Hajj Amin al-Husseini, the Mufti, was among its main organizers.
It resolved to defend the holy places, to boycott Zionist goods, to found an Islamic university in Jerusalem and to form a company to buy Palestinian land .

The same account records Britain's response: High Commissioner Wauchope questioned the Mufti about the delegates' political speeches; Britain deported Abd al-Rahman Azzam and refused entry to the former caliph Abdulmecid II; and the university project stalled for lack of funds in 1935 .
The Mufti's congress did not speak for all Palestinians.
In the same month Nashashibi held a rival conference in Jerusalem to counter it .
In 1932 the Executive launched a "Piaster Project", a fund to keep land in Arab hands .
Like the Islamic Congress's land company, it answered the purchases described in .
The sharpest challenge to the Executive came from inside the national movement.
In August 1932 eleven founders, among them Rashid al-Haj Ibrahim, Awni Abd al-Hadi and Muhammad Izzat Darwaza, officially announced the Istiqlal (Independence) Party.
It called for full Arab independence and Arab unity, and named British imperialism as the main enemy  .
The congresses had petitioned Britain; Istiqlal treated Britain itself as the adversary, and it attacked the established leadership for inaction in 1932–33 .

According to a reference account drawing on Porath, Khalidi, Kedourie and others, the party never built a large membership; its influence peaked among young educated Palestinians in early 1933 and then fell, partly through Husseini hostility and partly for lack of funds .
Its founders remained active: until June 1933 Awni Abd al-Hadi was representing the tenants of Wadi al-Hawarith in court, and Istiqlal joined the protests when the eviction order came .
Open confrontation with the government came in October 1933, called not by Istiqlal but by the Arab Executive.
Following its call for protest demonstrations, disturbances broke out in Jerusalem on 13 October, in Jaffa, Haifa and Nablus on 27–28 October, and in Jerusalem again on 28–29 October.
The Murison Commission, which investigated them, found that they were "aimed against the Government and not against the Jews" .
All the public deaths were by gunfire, 15 of them at Jaffa, where police fired 102 rifle and 43 revolver rounds .
Musa Kazim al-Husseini, the Executive's president, was injured by British forces at the Jaffa protest  .
In Murison's own judgment, the police acted "with restraint and forbearance" and no officer departed from regulations.
Musa Kazim al-Husseini died in March 1934, and the Arab Executive dissolved that year  .

Over fifteen years the congresses and their Executive had sent petitions and delegations asking for an elected government; Britain recognized the Zionist Organization's Jewish Agency but never recognized the Palestinians' own Executive .
Nashashibi moved first.
Having lost the mayoralty of Jerusalem to Hussein Fakhri al-Khalidi in 1934, he founded the National Defense Party in early December 1934.
Its program rejected the Balfour Declaration, Jewish immigration and land sales, and called for parliamentary government; Nashashibi was close to Emir Abdullah .
The Palestine Arab Party was officially established on 27 March 1935, and Jamal al-Husseini, close to the Mufti, was unanimously chosen as its leader .
By the end of 1935, five Arab parties stood where one Executive had been.
Late that year they formed a united front, which the American consul general Leland Morris described in April 1936 as a response to a "national emergency" .
The Husseini pole ran through the Mufti, who held religious office and had organized the Islamic Congress, and through the Palestine Arab Party under Jamal al-Husseini, who was close to him.
The Nashashibi pole ran through the National Defense Party, which held to the same rejection of the Balfour Declaration but looked toward parliamentary government and stood close to Emir Abdullah.
Istiqlal, small and short of money, named British imperialism as the main enemy.
The Palestinian leaders had no recognized channel to government.
The Islamic Congress shows both sides of that balance.

It could gather 130 delegates and pass resolutions on land, boycott and a university; the High Commissioner could question its organizer and Britain could expel a delegate, and the university project stalled in 1935 for lack of funds .
The sources do not say what the 1930 London delegation won or lost in its negotiations.
The figures for the Islamic Congress and for Istiqlal's decline come from secondary accounts and are attributed as such.
The sources do not name the two smaller parties of the 1935 front, or show how far the front reconciled the Husseini and Nashashibi camps rather than suspending their rivalry.

And the Murison report leaves open the question at the center of October 1933: whether a police force that fired 145 rounds at Jaffa and killed 15 people there acted with restraint, as the commission found, or whether the toll itself is the better measure.
The Haavara agreement was signed inside a movement already at war with itself.
On the night of 16 June 1933, Chaim Arlosoroff was walking on the beach at Tel Aviv with his wife, Sima, when he was shot.
Arlosoroff was the head of the Jewish Agency's political department.

His killing opened two years of open conflict between that leadership and the Revisionist movement led by Ze'ev Jabotinsky, a conflict that ran through a murder trial, a Zionist Congress, an attempt at reconciliation and a vote of the labor federation's members, and ended with the Revisionists leaving the Zionist Organization altogether.
Arlosoroff had come back from Germany about two days before he was shot.
The Center for Israel Education links that trip to the Haavara transfer agreement with Nazi Germany, which was formally signed on 25 August 1933, some ten weeks after his death .
Three Revisionists were charged.
Abba Ahimeir was accused of plotting the killing, and Avraham Stavsky and Zvi Rosenblatt of carrying it out as the gunmen.
Sima Arlosoroff identified Stavsky and Rosenblatt .
Only Stavsky was convicted, and in 1934 he was cleared on appeal for lack of corroborating evidence.
Jabotinsky, who believed the accused innocent, campaigned on their behalf for more than a year .
The labor movement's leaders accused Revisionist extremists of the killing.
At the Eighteenth Zionist Congress, which met in Prague from 21 August to 3 September 1933, the Revisionists were accused of the murder in the movement's own parliament .
The Revisionists, for their part, charged that the accusation against them was a "blood libel" .
Labour's account was that Revisionist extremists, the three accused, had killed Arlosoroff, and it could point to his widow's identification of two of the men.
The Revisionists' account was that the accused were innocent and that the accusation was a defamation of their movement; the acquittal on appeal, for want of corroborating evidence, supported them.
The sources gathered here record the accusation, the identification, the acquittal and Jabotinsky's campaign.
In March 1982 the government of Menachem Begin appointed a three-member commission chaired by David Bechor, a former Supreme Court justice.
It cleared Ahimeir, Stavsky and Rosenblatt.
It could not determine who had killed Arlosoroff, or whether the killing was a political act at all.
And it cleared the labor movement of the Revisionist charge that the accusation had been a "blood libel" .
Each side was thus partly vindicated: the Revisionists in the innocence of the accused, labor in being cleared of the charge of a "blood libel."
In 1934 Ben-Gurion and Jabotinsky, the leaders of the two camps, signed three agreements in London  .
The labor agreement was put to the members of the Histadrut, the labor federation, who rejected it in a referendum  .
The Jewish Telegraphic Agency's report the next day gave early returns: about 12,000 votes against the agreement and about 9,000 for it.
In Tel Aviv the count was 3,983 against and 3,296 for; in Haifa, 3,785 against and 1,555 for .
The newspaper Haaretz called the result "a grave mishap for the entire Zionist movement" .
In Tel Aviv the vote was close; in Haifa it was more than two to one against.

Later in 1935 the Zionist General Council adopted a "discipline clause" barring independent political action, the Revisionists voted to secede, and in September 1935 Jabotinsky's New Zionist Organization held its constituent assembly in Vienna .
That story, and the growth of the Revisionist movement that preceded it, is told in .

On the reading offered here, the murder, and the accusation that followed it, hardened a division between the labor leadership and the Revisionists that the London agreements tried and failed to close.
The secession that followed left the Zionist movement, by the end of 1935, with two rival organizations and two rival armed lines.
No court and no commission has established who killed Arlosoroff or why.
The Bechor commission, half a century later, could not say whether the killing was political.
The link between his German trip and Haavara rests on one source.
The exact dates and full terms of the London agreements, and the final count of the 1935 referendum, are not in the sources gathered here.
The Hebrew University and Brit Shalom
Four years before Zurich, the movement had marked a different kind of building.
On 1 April 1925 Arthur Balfour stood on Mount Scopus above Jerusalem and opened the Hebrew University.
Chaim Weizmann presided, as chairman of the university's board .

In the same year, and prompted by a lecture given at that same opening, a small group in Jerusalem founded an association around a question the rest of the movement answered differently: if Jews and Arabs were both to live in Palestine, on what terms would they share its government?
The association was Brit Shalom, and its answer was a binational country in which neither people ruled the other .
Twelve foundation stones were laid on Mount Scopus on 24 July 1918, and Albert Einstein gave the first lecture there in 1923 .
At the opening in 1925, Balfour performed the ceremony and Weizmann presided.
Judah Magnes became the university's chancellor, and later its president.
Balfour's presence was itself an event in Jerusalem.
A report in the Detroit Jewish Chronicle of 10 April 1925 described "excitement" among the city's Arabs at a rumor that he would visit the Omar Mosque, and stated that no incidents occurred .
That is the extent of what the sources used here record about the Arab response to his visit.
Brit Shalom was founded in Jerusalem in 1925 on the initiative of Arthur Ruppin.
According to the Encyclopaedia Judaica, the immediate prompt was a lecture by Professor Joseph Horowitz at the university's opening .
Its early members included Ruppin, Jacob Thon, Joseph Lurie, Yitzhak Epstein, Haim Margolis-Kalvaryski and Rabbi Binyamin .
Brit Shalom sought a binational arrangement in which Jews and Arabs would share the administration of the country equally, regardless of their numbers .
Brit Shalom proposed to separate political power from population: parity of government whichever people was the larger.
For Jews, then a minority in the country, it meant giving up any claim to rule by majority should they become one.
For Arabs, then the majority, it meant sharing power equally with a minority.
Its best-known figures, Buber and Magnes among them, are described as Zionists who rejected the model of sovereignty and partition specifically, not as anti-Zionists.

In that they were a different current from the Orthodox opposition of the old Yishuv, which rejected the national project itself on religious grounds and whose spokesman was killed in Jerusalem the year before Brit Shalom was founded; that story is told in    .
Brit Shalom never had more than 200 members .
It functioned more as a small study circle of academics and intellectuals than as a political party, and it never grew into a mass constituency among either Jews or Arabs  .

According to the Encyclopaedia Judaica, after 1929 Central European intellectuals influenced by Martin Buber predominated, among them Hugo Bergmann, Hans Kohn, Gershom Scholem, Ernst Simon and Robert Weltsch .
Albert Einstein, who had given the university's first lecture, publicly backed it, a fact rarely mentioned alongside his name  .

One account used elsewhere in this library calls Martin Buber and Judah Magnes "both founders of Brit Shalom (1925)," and names Gershom Scholem and Henrietta Szold among the colleagues who founded it with them   .
The Encyclopaedia Judaica gives a different picture.

It credits the initiative to Ruppin and lists different early members; it places Scholem among those who predominated after 1929; it describes the later members as influenced by Buber rather than naming him as a founder; and it states that Magnes, though he advocated binationalism in this period and his name was often linked to the association, was never a member of it .
Buber's influence on its later members is common to both accounts.
Brit Shalom drew open hostility from the rest of the movement.
Most Zionist parties attacked it .
The opposition came from both of the dominant currents, Labour and the Revisionists, and some of its opponents explicitly called its members traitors  .
The violence of August 1929, in Hebron above all, undermined the premise on which the association was founded: that Arab political leadership would accept binational equality  .
The killings in Hebron and Safed, told in , came in the same year, and the sources here record no Arab political body that took up the offer.
The association carried on for a few more years, with the Buber circle now predominant.
By 1933 Brit Shalom had virtually ceased to exist , about eight years after its founding .
The sources record the hostility to Brit Shalom more fully than the reasoning behind it.
The case against it, as historians reconstruct it, is that it depended on an Arab political partner willing to accept binational equality, and that 1929 showed none in view  .
