On the record here it was never put to the test, and the association never grew into a mass constituency, among Jews or among Arabs.

Buber and Magnes went on to found Ihud in 1942, Hannah Arendt warned against an exclusively Jewish sovereign state in 1944, and Buber and Magnes testified against partition before the United Nations commission in 1947.
The sources do not settle who founded Brit Shalom or whether Magnes ever joined it.
They do not record any formal Arab response to its proposals, or name an Arab group with which it negotiated.
They give no membership figures beyond the ceiling of 200, and they do not say what Joseph Horowitz argued in the lecture that prompted its founding.
The Last Offer Before the Revolt: Wauchope's Council, 1935–1936
ents: The Last Offer Before the Revolt: Wauchope's Council

sent: Five weeks after al-Qassam's death, Britain made the last political offer of the stage.
On 23 December 1935 the High Commissioner for Palestine, Sir Arthur Wauchope, called in the leaders of the Jewish community and laid before them a plan for a legislative council.
It would have 28 members: 14 Arabs, 7 Jews and 7 Britons.
Who would have a voice in governing Palestine, in what proportion, and over which questions?
The demand for an elected body had come, from the beginning, from the Arab side.
From 1919 the Palestine Arab congresses had asked Britain for a national government responsible to a representative assembly chosen by the country's inhabitants .
As recently as December 1934 Raghib al-Nashashibi's new National Defense Party had called for parliamentary government .
The Zionist Congress, meeting at Lucerne in 1935, had taken the opposite view, resolving against any council that would fix the Jews as a minority .
Wauchope's offer therefore tested both sides at once, and the way each answered it is the best single view of where Palestinian and Zionist politics stood at the end of 1935.

As reported at the time, the basis of representation was to be fixed for five years; one of the elected Arab members was to be a Bedouin; the High Commissioner could nominate members to fill the seats of any community that boycotted the elections; and the council could not deal with the labor immigration schedule .

A council barred from the labor schedule would have had no hand on the immigration of workers, a question the Arab congresses had raised since 1919, when they rejected mass Jewish immigration ; and the High Commissioner's power to fill a boycotting community's seats meant that refusing to take part would not stop the council from sitting.
The Zionist answer was reported the next day.
Chaim Weizmann rejected the plan as contrary to the Mandate, citing the resolution of the Zionist Congress at Lucerne that such a council would fix the Jews as a minority.
Yitzhak Ben-Zvi, speaking for the Vaad Leumi, concurred, and so did A. L. Maleh for the Sephardi community .

The Zionist reading of the Mandate held that Britain's obligation ran not only to the Jews already in Palestine but to the Jewish people as a whole; the British government itself had put it that way in 1931, calling the Mandate "an undertaking to the Jewish people and not only to the Jewish population of Palestine" .

On that reading, a legislature apportioned by the population of the moment and frozen for five years would hand a permanent majority a veto over the growth that the Mandate was meant to permit, at the very time that growth was fastest.

The Jewish Agency's own figures, prepared for its case to the Peel Commission and so to be read as advocacy, put the Jewish population at 84,000, or 13 percent, in 1922 (the census put that year's share at about 11 percent) and 375,000, or 28 percent, in 1935  .
Not every Jewish voice gave the same answer.
Rabbi Moshe Blau, speaking for Agudath Israel, said only that the time was "not yet ripe" .
Agudath Israel had been founded in 1912 as a movement of Torah-observant Jews that held itself apart from secular Jewish nationalism .
Its answer was a postponement, not a rejection on the Zionist ground of minority status.
The Arab answer was slower and less unanimous.
Arab leaders withheld their reply and objected to women voting; the Mufti of Jerusalem, Hajj Amin al-Husseini, was reported to be still opposed .
The arithmetic of the offer allows the Arab objection to be reconstructed in outline, though the sources here do not record it in the leaders' own words.

By the Jewish Agency's figures for 1935, the non-Jewish population was 975,000 against 375,000 Jews , roughly seven in ten of the inhabitants; the council would have given Arabs half its seats, with British officials holding a quarter and the High Commissioner able to fill boycotted seats, and it would have had no say over immigration under the labor schedule.
To the Zionist leadership, the same body offered the majority too much.
The record held here does not give the detailed arguments of the Arab parties, and it should not be assumed that all of them shared the Mufti's position.
The decision did not rest in Jerusalem.
On 24 March 1936 the Prime Minister, Stanley Baldwin, announced a debate on the council in the House of Commons, and the Colonial Secretary, J. H. Thomas, said that final action would wait for it.
The Jewish Telegraphic Agency reported that day that Jewish organizations were "unitedly opposed" and that some Arab groups were accepting .
The chain of authority is plain in the record: the High Commissioner proposed, the Colonial Secretary held final action, and a Commons debate could hold it up.
The available record does not establish what the Commons debate concluded, and this account does not guess.
The offer's most lasting effect was on Palestinian unity.
By late 1935 the five Arab parties had formed a united front, which the American Consul General described as a response to a "national emergency" .
In April 1936 the same consul reported that the council proposals had broken that front, and that "all thought of united Arab action" on the council had been abandoned .
On 5 May 1936, according to the Center for Israel Education, the Mufti and other Arab leaders declined to attend a conference in London on the proposal .
By then events in Palestine had overtaken the council entirely; what followed belongs to .

The offer was put to Jewish leaders in a fixed form; the Zionist leadership rejected it in principle; Agudath Israel deferred; the Arab leadership hesitated and divided, and the Mufti was reported opposed; and the decision was in any case held in London.

Several things remain unsettled by the sources available here: what the Commons debate decided, what reasons the Arab parties that accepted gave, how the women's-suffrage objection weighed against the others, and whether the council would ever have sat had the country not moved into revolt.
At the top stood the British state.

The Mandate had been in force, by the League Council's own minutes, since 29 September 1923, a date that Professor John Quigley argues had no legal force, so that Britain held Palestine without title  .
Under it the High Commissioner proposed policy, allotted the labor schedule in half-year periods, and answered to the Colonial Secretary and, through him, to Parliament.
Beside the Mandate government, the Jewish community had built the institutions of a state in all but sovereignty.
The Jewish Agency, enlarged in 1929 to give half the seats on its Council to non-Zionists, with Keren Hayesod as its main financial instrument , was chaired from 1935 by David Ben-Gurion .
The Histadrut, founded in 1920 and restricted to Jews, ran its own construction company, bank and health fund .

The Haganah, placed under the Histadrut's direct control in December 1920, had since 1931 been led by a six-member national command with parity between three Histadrut members and three non-labor members; its urban branches had memberships "in the hundreds," and it ran workshops producing hand grenades .
Outside this structure, and against it, stood the Revisionists.

Their New Zionist Organization had met in Vienna in September 1935, said to have been "elected by 713,000 voters," with Ze'ev Jabotinsky as president , and the Irgun had existed since 1931, formed by Avraham Tehomi's group with Revisionist groups after their secession from the Haganah .
The Jewish population, by the Agency's count, had grown from 84,000 to 375,000 in thirteen years ; Tel Aviv alone had about 120,000 people in 1935 .
The Palestinian Arab side had no comparable apparatus and no recognized representative body.
The Arab Executive, never recognized by Britain, had dissolved in 1934, the year Musa Kazim al-Husseini died .

In its place stood parties built around rival families and rival programs: Nashashibi's National Defense Party, founded in December 1934 and close to Emir Abdullah ; the Palestine Arab Party, established on 27 March 1935 under Jamal al-Husseini, close to the Mufti ; and the Istiqlal, announced in August 1932, which named British imperialism as the main enemy but never built a large membership  .
In late 1935 the five parties stood briefly together, and outside all of them a Haifa preacher had taken a band to the hills and died there, as told in .

The Revisionist line runs through it from Betar in 1923  to the Paris founding of 1925 ; the Hebrew University opened on 1 April 1925 ; the 1929 row pairs the violence of August with the enlarged Jewish Agency ; the 1930 and 1931 rows record the Shaw and Hope Simpson inquiries, the Passfield White Paper and MacDonald's letter of February 1931, which Arab leaders called the "Black Letter" and which withdrew the White Paper's restrictions within four months  ; and 1933 carries the Haavara Agreement with about 105 million Reichsmarks of goods moved by the outbreak of war .
The 1934 row marks the dissolution of the Arab Executive .

The 1935 row gathers the stage's ending in a single line: the peak of immigration, recorded as 61,854 in the State Department series and 66,472 in the Porath series  , the Nuremberg Laws , and al-Qassam's death .

The other had a national movement of long standing, a demand for representative government it had pressed since 1919, five parties that could unite only briefly, and no institution that Britain recognized as speaking for it.
Britain held the decisions, and had just offered one that neither side would take on its terms.
The findings London adopted and then explained away in 1930–31 were findings about land.
Two opposite simplifications surround the land of Mandate Palestine.
One holds that the British government sold the country's land to Zionist buyers with little scrutiny or resistance.
The other holds that Jewish land purchase was small and sporadic before 1948.
The land was not, in the main, sold by Britain.

It was bought, privately and lawfully, from landowners, most of them absentees, by Zionist institutions that held it permanently and leased it under terms, in the Jewish National Fund's draft lease, that required Jewish labor.
The Mandate tried to protect the tenants who lost their land and failed, and its own inquiries of 1930 measured the result.

Under Ottoman law, tenant farmers who had worked land for generations usually held no registered title; when the registered owner sold, the tenant had no ownership claim to assert, so a lawful sale and a lawful eviction could be the same transaction  .
How that law worked, how the Ottoman restrictions on Jewish purchase were met and circumvented, and how the purchasing institutions were built before 1914 are told in .
The Sursocks of Beirut, a wealthy Greek Orthodox Christian family, had acquired great tracts of the Jezreel Valley under Ottoman rule; the Ottoman government itself sold them Marj ibn Amir in 1872.
Between 1901 and 1925, and mainly in the 1920s, the family sold roughly 60,000 to 75,000 dunams to Zionist purchasing organizations, for a fraction of the land's later value  .
The Sursock purchases alone account for about 22 percent of all the land Jews acquired in Palestine up to 1948, and 58 percent of all the land bought from absentee landlords .
The Jewish National Fund held purchased land as the inalienable property of the Jewish people.

The Palestine Land Development Company did the actual purchasing, led by Yehoshua Hankin, who had worked with the Sursock family since 1891, personally negotiated the Sursock deal and most of the major Jezreel Valley acquisitions, and became head of the company in 1932.
The Palestine Jewish Colonization Association, PICA, founded in 1924 by Edmond de Rothschild, became through parallel acquisitions the largest single Jewish landowner in Palestine .
By the early Mandate years land sold by absentee owners to Jewish buyers went for roughly six Palestine pounds a dunam.
Purchasing agents such as Hankin sometimes bought first, at their own financial risk, and were reimbursed by the Jewish Agency or the Fund afterward  .
The banks and campaigns that supplied the capital are described in the section on the Mandate economy.
In the largest single group of Sursock-related purchases, 1,746 Arab farming families, 8,730 people, were evicted.
Selling land to Jewish buyers was seen by some Arabs as a serious betrayal.
The Jewish National Fund turned each purchase into a permanent holding.
Its land was leased long-term rather than sold, so that no later transaction could reverse an acquisition; its founding resolution called the land "the eternal possession of the Jewish people" .
The Mandate's role was that of regulator, not seller, and as regulator it failed.
Between 1920 and 1940 Britain enacted five separate laws meant to protect tenant cultivators from eviction after a sale.

A documented analysis of the period concludes that they "failed to provide the protection that Palestinian Arabs demanded, often due to loopholes, which allowed individuals and agencies to circumvent the legislation"  .

The Shaw Commission said the same in 1930 about the laws then in force: the Land Transfer Ordinances of 1920 and 1921 had failed, the Protection of Cultivators Ordinance of 1929 did not stop evictions, and the evictions were creating a landless class, "a potential danger to the country" .

Later in the decade British policy moved the other way: in 1938 the Mandate authorities allowed Zionist officials to copy land-registration and tax records of Arab ownership in order to facilitate further purchases  .
Britain's record on land was inconsistent rather than a single policy, and its restrictions on immigration in 1939 cut in the opposite direction.

In 1929 the Jewish National Fund bought 30,800 dunams at Wadi al-Hawarith at auction from absentee landlords; the historian Weldon Matthews counts it as the third-largest single acquisition the Fund made in the whole Mandate period.
The Bedouin Palestinian tenants who lived there refused to leave, and the Fund began legal proceedings to evict them.
Awni Abd al-Hadi, a leading Palestinian national figure, represented the residents through a court battle that lasted several years.
The response was organized and crossed party lines: the Istiqlal Party, the Palestine Communist Party and the Congress of Youth called strikes and issued public declarations of protest .
The case was decided in the Mandate's own courts, under its own law.
The fullest measurement of all this came from Sir John Hope Simpson.
It is the most detailed British land study of the Mandate period .

He adopted the Director of Surveys' estimate of 8,044,000 metric dunams of cultivable land, including 1,500,000 in the Beersheba region, and found that only 40 percent of the hill country was cultivable, not the 66.6 percent that had been assumed.
He put Jewish-held land in June 1930 at about 1,250,000 Turkish dunams.
Deducting about 900,000 metric dunams of Jewish holdings, he left 5,644,000 metric dunams for non-Jewish cultivators .
The two Jewish figures are in different units, Turkish and metric dunams, and the report as summarized here does not reconcile them further.
His own enquiry into 688 Arab families displaced by land sales found that only 379 were cultivating land again; the other 309 had joined the landless.
Without development, he concluded, there was no margin for further Jewish agricultural settlement .
Hope Simpson also examined labor, and here he quoted the movement's own documents.

The Jewish National Fund's draft lease required the lessee to cultivate "only with Jewish labour", on penalty of ten Palestinian pounds for each breach and repossession of the land after three breaches.
The Jewish Agency's constitution of 1920 committed it to colonization "based on Jewish labour".
Read against the purchase chain, the clause meant that, on the draft lease's terms, a tenant evicted from land the Fund bought could not be hired back to work it.

Shaw had added two further findings: the allocation of labor-schedule immigration certificates by political creed was indefensible, and Jewish immigration within the country's absorptive capacity had brought material benefits .
The labor movement's own doctrine of "Hebrew labour" is described in the section on the Histadrut.
The Jewish Agency contested Hope Simpson's numbers.
In 1931 it published a memorandum, The Statistical Bases of Sir John Hope Simpson's Report, to challenge the report's figures .
Hope Simpson held that without development there was no margin for settlement, that at most 100,000 dunams were available, and that a landless class was forming .
The Agency held that his statistical foundation was unsound .

On the Agency's side, the strongest evidence in the record used here comes from a British inquiry: Shaw's finding that Jewish immigration within the country's absorptive capacity had brought material benefits.
What London did with these findings is told in .

The total number of Arab families displaced by land sales in these years is not established; Hope Simpson's 688 families were those his own enquiry traced, and the 1,746 Sursock-linked families are one group of sales.
Whether there was room for more settlement in 1930 is a question on which Hope Simpson and the Jewish Agency disagreed, and the Agency's arguments have not been examined here.
The full Jewish holding in 1930 is given in two units that the summarized report does not reconcile.
By the summer of 1922 Britain had governed Palestine for nearly five years.
Its forces had taken Jerusalem in December 1917, and the text of the Mandate had been approved by the Council of the League of Nations.
ents: the Council of the League of Nations

sent: The state that had ruled the country for four centuries had not yet given it up, and the Mandate had not yet formally entered into force.
Between 1923 and 1925 both gaps were closed, or so the standard account holds, and the Mandate government then defined, for the first time, who was a citizen of Palestine.
The first step was taken at Lausanne.
The peace treaty between the Allies and Turkey was signed there on 24 July 1923 .
In it the new Republic of Turkey, founded that year, renounced all rights over the former Arab provinces of the Ottoman Empire .
The treaty made modern Turkey the empire's successor state, not a claimant to Palestine .
Professor John Quigley stresses a further point about the wording: the renunciation was not made in favor of Britain or of the Allies .
Turkey gave up its rights; it did not hand them to anyone.
The second step was the Mandate's entry into force, and here the record holds two accounts.
The League Council had approved the mandates for Palestine and Syria on 24 July 1922, on a condition: they would take effect once France and Italy reached a final agreement over Syria .
One scholarly source gives a different date for that approval, 12 August 1922 ; the UN's document gives 24 July .

At the Council's meeting of 29 September 1923, according to the minutes as reproduced by the United Nations, the mandates for Syria and Palestine "had thereby automatically and simultaneously entered into force," and the British representative, Sir Rennell Rodd, said the question was "finally settled" .
On this account, 29 September 1923 is the date the Mandate became law.
Britain, the League Secretariat and, in 1947, the United Nations all treated it as such .
Quigley disputes it.
He argues that the Council minutes used future-tense wording and that the Council took no resolution.
In his reading, the past-tense formula, that the mandates had entered into force, was supplied afterwards by the League's Secretary-General, Eric Drummond, in his Circular Letter 101.

If that is right, the 29 September 1923 date has no legal force, and since Lausanne did not take effect until 6 August 1924 and gave Britain no title in any case, Britain held Palestine without title .
Quigley's argument was published in July 2026; it is a challenge to the standard date, not yet a settled finding.

The standard date rests on a primary document, the minutes, and on the conduct of the bodies involved: Britain administered the Mandate, the League supervised it, and the UN in 1947 started from that date.
Quigley's case rests on the same kind of evidence read more closely: the tense of a verb, the absence of a resolution, and the question of who changed the wording.
The practical history of the Mandate did not wait on the answer; the legal question remains open in the sense that the argument has been made and not, in the sources used here, answered.
The Palestinian Citizenship Order was issued on 24 July 1925 and took effect on 1 August 1925.
It made Palestinian citizens of Ottoman subjects habitually resident in Palestine on that date .
The first were Arabs who had emigrated abroad: the Order, Lauren Banko notes, denied them citizenship .
According to Nadia Abu Alia and Asem Khalil, the Government of Palestine reportedly accepted about 100 of some 9,000 naturalization applications in one period, using an "absolute discretion" clause.
By 1946, on their figures, about 130,000 foreigners had acquired Palestinian citizenship by naturalization, 99 percent of them Jews .
The historian Lauren Banko reads the Order as a first step and as a contrast at once.
It was, she notes, the first Mandate legislation to treat the Arab population as citizens rather than as "ex-enemy Ottoman subjects" .

But it treated Jewish citizenship and the naturalization of immigrants in sharp contrast to Arab citizenship, in Banko's account, and Palestinian Arabs answered it by invoking Ottoman-era principles of descent and birthplace .
Descent and birthplace would have reached the emigrants abroad, whom the Order excluded.

Read beside Banko's argument, the naturalization figures reported by Abu Alia and Khalil, in which 99 percent of those naturalized by 1946 were Jews, suggest which way the contrast ran in practice; that is a reading of the two sources together, not a finding stated in either  .
Whether the Mandate ever validly entered into force is argued, not decided.

The sources do not give the number of Arab emigrants who lost a claim to citizenship under the 1925 Order, nor the year-by-year breakdown of naturalizations, nor, for the reported period when about 100 of 9,000 applications were accepted, who the applicants were.
The Jews of the Arab World, 1929–1936: Baghdad and Constantine
While American Zionists organized at a distance, Jewish communities elsewhere in the Arab world were living through crises of their own.
Two places show how differently the early 1930s could run for Jewish communities outside Palestine, and how much turned on the decisions of states and of named individuals.
In Iraq, a Jewish community that had taken part in building the new state's institutions found itself, after independence, under a series of restrictions.
In French Algeria, Jews of one city were killed in a riot whose causes a recent historian argues lay partly in the politics of the colonial state.
Neither case is evidence about Arabs or Muslims as a whole, and neither should be read that way.
Iraq first.
Under the British Mandate there, according to Sephardi Voices UK, Jews held government posts, Hebrew could be taught, and several Zionist organizations were permitted to operate until 1929 .
Iraq became independent in 1932.
In the years that followed, the same source reports, prominent Jews helped build the Iraqi civil service, and several sat in the first independent parliament .
The Mandate-era history of Iraq, and how its independence came about, is told in .
According to Sephardi Voices UK, Iraqi Jews from that year had to pay a deposit of £50 to travel abroad.
In 1935 the teaching of Hebrew was barred, and state secondary schools set quotas on the number of Jewish pupils.
In 1936 Jews were dismissed from the civil service .

These measures, if accurately reported, amounted to discrimination by the state against its Jewish citizens in movement, education and employment, within four years of a period in which Jews had helped staff that same state.
The 1936 dismissals in particular are stated in that source in sweeping terms, and the source does not say how many people were affected or whether every Jewish official was removed.
The same source records an episode from 1933 that connects Iraq to the events in Germany described in .
During the first premiership of Rashid Ali al-Gaylani, in 1933, the German chargé d'affaires, Fritz Grobba, was allowed to publish Mein Kampf in Iraqi newspapers .
That was antisemitic propaganda, placed in the Iraqi press by a German diplomat with the permission of an Iraqi government.
What these years led to in Baghdad, the Farhud of 1941, belongs to a later chapter.
Algeria second.
In Constantine, in French Algeria, in August 1934, over a few days of violence, 25 Jews and 3 Muslims were killed .
Those figures come from the historian Joshua Cole, whose book Lethal Provocation: The Constantine Murders and the Politics of French Algeria (Cornell University Press, 2019) is the study used here.

He argues that the French colonial state had an interest in "provoking and nurturing" tension between Jews and Muslims, because that tension helped it resist demands to extend citizenship rights to Algerian Muslims .
Cole also identifies Mohamed El Maadi, a veteran with ties to the extreme right, as a key participant in the violence .
His account therefore names both a structure, the colonial state's interest, and a specific person with extreme-right ties, rather than attributing the killings to Muslims in general.

What can be said is that Cole's reading rests on the colonial context of citizenship and on a named participant, and that the killings themselves, 25 Jews and 3 Muslims, are not in question in the sources used here.

Antisemitism in these years reached Jewish communities in the Arab world through more than one channel: in Iraq, through state measures and through Nazi propaganda placed by a German diplomat; in Algeria, according to Cole, through violence that a European colonial state had reasons to tolerate or encourage, with a veteran tied to the extreme right among its key participants.
Neither source used here ties these events to Palestine.

The Iraqi measures of 1934 to 1936 rest on a single source, and their scale is not recorded: how many travellers paid the deposit, how many pupils the quotas excluded, how many officials lost their posts.
The record gathered here says nothing about the Jews of Syria, Lebanon, Egypt, Yemen or Morocco in these years.
For Constantine it gives the toll and Cole's argument, but not the course of the riot day by day, or what the French authorities did afterwards.
Shaykh 'Izz al-Din al-Qassam:
From Jabla to Ya'bad, 1882–1935
Two months after Nuremberg, in Palestine, a Haifa preacher took a small band to the hills.
On 20 November 1935, in the hills near Ya'bad, close to Jenin, a British police force fought a small armed band for six hours.
When it was over the band's leader, a preacher from Haifa in his fifties, was dead .

Shaykh 'Izz al-Din al-Qassam had spent fifteen years in Palestine as a teacher, imam and official of the Muslim religious courts, and the last several of them, by the accounts that survive, organizing in secret for armed struggle.
His death drew the largest funeral Haifa had held, and the argument over what to call him has not ended.
He was not born in Palestine.
Al-Qassam was born in 1882 in Jabla, on the Syrian coast south of Latakia, and studied at al-Azhar in Cairo .
He joined the revolt of 1919–20 against the French there, and the French sentenced him to death .
He reached Haifa in late 1920, or in December 1920 in another account, taught at the Burj school, and became imam and preacher at the Istiqlal Mosque  .
The preacher who settled in Haifa already carried a death sentence from one European mandatory power for fighting it.
Through the 1920s his career ran through the ordinary institutions of Muslim public life under the Mandate.

In July 1928 he was elected president of the Haifa branch of the Young Men's Muslim Association, and in 1930 the Haifa Shari'a court appointed him a ma'dhun, an official post conferred by the religious court .

Those accounts describe cells of no more than five men, organized into units for preaching, for intelligence and for military training, and guerrilla attacks on Jewish settlements beginning in 1931 that soon paused after leaks reached the British .

What is reported is the structure: a small, compartmented organization that kept religious teaching, intelligence and arms in separate hands, and that chose Jewish settlements as well as the British as targets.
The decision to go to the hills came in the autumn of 1935, and, by one account, the Mufti did not support it.
Al-Qassam wrote to Rashid al-Haj Ibrahim of his plan to take to the hills .
Al-Haj Ibrahim was one of the eleven founders of the Istiqlal party, which had named British imperialism as the main enemy .
According to Al Majalla, the Mufti of Jerusalem, Hajj Amin al-Husseini, declined to back a revolt, saying the time was not right .
That account is reported, from one outlet; the research does not hold the Mufti's own words.
If it is accurate, al-Qassam went to the hills without the backing of the Mufti, whose place among the rival leaderships and parties of these years is described in .

In October or November 1935 (the sources disagree on the date) the British seized 537 barrels at Jaffa port that had been shipped from Belgium with rifles and ammunition hidden in cement, and the discovery caused significant unrest among Palestinian Arabs; one account dates a protest general strike to 26 October 1935  .
That shipment and the armed bodies of the Yishuv belong to .
The sources used here do not say whether the seizure bore on al-Qassam's decision, and this book does not assume it did.
On 12 November 1935 al-Qassam declared jihad in Haifa and left for the forests of Ya'bad, near Jenin, with about eleven companions .
Eight days later, on 20 November, he was killed in a six-hour fight with a larger British police force near Ya'bad .
The nearest thing to a contemporary official account is an American one.

Leland Morris, the US Consul General, reporting to Washington in April 1936, wrote that al-Qassam's bands had caused the death of one British constable, and that four of his men died and five were captured .
Al Majalla, drawing on British archives, puts his fighters at between 50 and 200 and calls a claim of 800 "grossly exaggerated"; it says he died with two colleagues .
The Interactive Encyclopedia of the Palestine Question says al-Qassam and four of his men were killed, and the US consul's despatch likewise reports four of his men killed and five captured  .
The consul's figure is the only one here written at the time by an outside official; it agrees with the Palestinian encyclopedia and not with Al Majalla on the dead.
Haifa declared a general strike on 21 November 1935 and held the largest funeral procession the city had seen; he was buried at Balad al-Shaykh .
It came at a moment of unusual Palestinian unity.
By late 1935 the five Arab parties had formed a united front, which the same American consul described as a response to a "national emergency" .
The established leaders had not followed al-Qassam into the hills; a crowd of Haifa's people followed his coffin.
Palestinian accounts present al-Qassam as a leader of resistance to British occupation whose death helped ignite the revolt of 1936–39  .
In that reading he was a man who had already fought one European mandatory power in Syria and chose arms against a second; the fight in which he died was a fight with British police.
His group's attacks were directed at Jewish settlers as well as at the British, and he called for confronting Jewish settlers "as enemies and not as immigrants or guests" .
The documented record supports both halves: an armed campaign against the Mandate power, and attacks on Jewish settlements, with civilians among the targets.
In 1991 Hamas named its military wing the 'Izz al-Din al-Qassam Brigades, according to Al Majalla .
Much about al-Qassam remains unsettled by the sources available here.
The Mufti's refusal rests on a single reported account.
The Electricity Concession and the Grid
Land, labor and arms are the usual measures of how the Yishuv was built.
On 12 September 1921 the Mandate government signed the Auja (Yarkon) Concession.

It granted the Jaffa Electric Company of Pinhas Rutenberg the exclusive right, for 70 years, to generate, distribute and sell electricity in the Jaffa district, using hydroelectric turbines on the Auja .
ents: the Jaffa Electric Company of Pinhas Rutenberg

sent: The common view of the Mandate's public works is that they were neutral economic modernization, of benefit to everyone in the country.

Its terms, the politics of its approval and, above all, the shape of the network it produced show something more particular: infrastructure that followed Jewish settlement and helped bind it together.
The concession had a legal footing in the Mandate itself.
Article 11 allowed the administration to arrange with the Jewish Agency to construct or operate public works .
Rutenberg also had backing at the top.
The High Commissioner, Herbert Samuel, and the Colonial Secretary, Winston Churchill, both supported him .

The point of the arrangement, in mechanical terms, was that the British administration did not have to build or run a power system itself; it could grant the right to a concessionaire, and the Mandate named the body with which such arrangements could be made.
In 1922 the House of Lords passed an amendment to stop the concession.
The House of Commons then overturned the Lords by a large majority, in a vote led by Churchill .
The Lords had tried to stop the monopoly; the elected chamber chose to keep it.
Euripides Mavromatis, a rival Greek concessionaire, contested the monopoly before the Permanent Court of International Justice.
ents: the Permanent Court of International Justice

sent: The hydroelectric plant on the Auja was never built.
When the grid switched on in 1923, it ran on diesel, in Tel Aviv  .
The concession had also brought Rutenberg irrigation rights in the Auja valley, and those rights ended up benefiting only Jewish settlers  .
A concession framed around hydroelectric power from the Auja produced a diesel network in the Jewish city and water for Jewish farms.
In 1923 Rutenberg founded the Palestine Electric Corporation.
It built the country's only hydroelectric plant, not on the Auja but at Naharayim, on the Jordan.
In 1961 the corporation was renamed the Israel Electric Corporation .
The company founded under the Mandate thus carried on, under a new name, in the state.
The Mandate government granted a monopoly over a whole district's electricity for 70 years; the concessionaire gained a protected market and, with it, the irrigation rights in the valley.
The fullest study of where the power went is the historian Fredrik Meiton's prize-winning work on electrification in Palestine.
Meiton finds that the centralized grid knit Jewish settlements together while marginalizing and bypassing most Palestinian Arab communities  .
Another historian writes that the Yishuv's economic separatism "was given a tremendous push" by the 1921 monopoly.
On this reading, electricity was statecraft: a network laid along the lines of Jewish settlement drew a map of a future state in copper and diesel, decades before any partition line was proposed.

The familiar account holds that the Mandate's development of Palestine was neutral economic modernization that benefited everyone, carried out by the means the Mandate text itself provided, a concession under Article 11.
The Commons approved the concession by a large majority.
Nothing in the sources shows that Arab communities were barred from connection by rule.
The findings of Meiton and the second historian concern the shape and effect of the network, not a written policy of exclusion.

The sources here do not say how many Arab towns or villages were connected by 1936, or on what terms; whether the bypassing Meiton describes was planned or followed from where the company chose to build; or how the Mavromatis case ended.
The Revisionist Line, 1923–1935
While Britain's title was being settled at Lausanne and Geneva, the movement it had promised to help was dividing.
Zionism is often described as a single political movement that divided into parties only after the state was founded.

Its foundational split, between the movement led by Chaim Weizmann and the one led by Ze'ev (Vladimir) Jabotinsky, opened in the years of this chapter and was documented step by step: a youth movement in 1923, a secession in 1925, a second and final break in 1935.
The organization Jabotinsky built is the direct ancestor of Herut and then Likud.
It also produced the armed groups, the Irgun and later Lehi, that operated alongside and often against the Haganah and the Jewish Agency  .
Jabotinsky was a Russian-Jewish writer and Zionist leader .
In 1923 he founded Betar, a youth movement built on discipline and military training.
Its watchwords were hadar, pride or dignity, and armed self-defense, and it spread through Poland, the Baltic states, Palestine and the Americas .
The same year he set out the argument on which his politics rested, in an essay called "The Iron Wall."
Its claim was that the Arabs of Palestine would never voluntarily accept a Jewish majority, and that Zionism could therefore proceed only from a position of overwhelming military strength  .
Zionist colonization, even the most restricted, must either be terminated or carried out in defiance of the will of the native population.
A follow-up essay, "The Ethics of the Iron Wall," argued that this approach was itself moral  .
ents: The Ethics of the Iron Wall

sent: Among the young men drawn to the movement was Benzion Netanyahu, born Mileikowsky in Warsaw in 1910, who had emigrated to Palestine in 1920.
In the 1930s he edited the Revisionist newspaper Ha'Yarden   .

His later role belongs to a later chapter: in 1940 Jabotinsky sent him to the United States, where he served as Jabotinsky's personal secretary until Jabotinsky's death that year and then ran the movement's American operations for eight years   .

His son, Benjamin Netanyahu, told a Jabotinsky memorial audience in 2023 that one hundred years after the "iron wall" was set down in Jabotinsky's writings, Israel was "continuing to successfully implement these principles" .
He has also, separately, dismissed the idea that his father's formation under Jabotinsky shaped his own views as "psychobabble" .
In April 1925, in Paris, Jabotinsky founded the World Union of Zionist-Revisionists, known by its Hebrew acronym Hatzohar  .
Its first president was Vladimir Tiomkin .

The founding is described as a secession from the World Zionist Organization that Weizmann led ; yet the Revisionists went on sending delegates to Zionist Congresses for the next decade, so in practice the break of 1925 created a rival faction rather than a separate body .
Its founding platform called for transforming Palestine and Transjordan into a Jewish commonwealth within the British Commonwealth, in direct opposition to the mainstream's gradualist strategy .
The heart of that platform was the claim to "both banks of the Jordan," a Jewish majority on both sides of the river, covering what is now Israel, the West Bank, Gaza and the whole of Jordan .

Jabotinsky argued that Britain's separation of Transjordan from the Palestine Mandate in 1922 was an arbitrary partition, which denied Jews the territory they would need to absorb millions of future immigrants .
What does the word Palestine mean?
Palestine is a territory whose chief geographical feature is this: that the River Jordan does not delineate its frontier, but flows through its center.
The movement's anthem made the same point in a line: "Two Banks has the Jordan — This is ours and, that is as well" .

This is one of three documented versions of what is called "Greater Israel," and the narrowest in territory: a claim to the whole of the original Mandate area, territorial rather than primarily religious.
In 1925 the Revisionists were a small faction.
They had four delegates at the Fourteenth Zionist Congress that year .
In 1931 they won 17 percent of the vote for the Yishuv's elected assembly, the Asefat ha-Nivharim, and became its second-largest party.
At the Seventeenth Zionist Congress in Basel the same year they had 52 delegates, and proposed a resolution for a Jewish state on both sides of the Jordan .
In 1933, at Katowice, Jabotinsky suspended the party's executive.
A plebiscite of the membership backed him, and his opponents, led by Meir Grossman, seceded to form the Jewish State Party.
At the Eighteenth Congress the Jewish State Party had seven delegates to the Revisionists' 46 .

The Revisionists' quarrel with Labour Zionism grew sharper the same year, when Revisionists were accused of the murder of Chaim Arlosoroff (the accused were later cleared), and of the three agreements Ben-Gurion and Jabotinsky signed in London in 1934, the labor agreement was rejected in a Histadrut referendum; that story is told in .
According to the Encyclopaedia Judaica, more than 600,000 Jews in 24 countries signed a Revisionist petition addressed to the British king and Parliament in 1934 .
Other accounts present the same figure as the membership the broader Revisionist movement claimed by 1934 .
A smaller figure, for Betar alone, is given as over 70,000 by the mid-1930s in the account of the "two banks" claim cited above.
That year the Zionist General Council adopted a "discipline clause" that barred independent political action by member parties .
The Zionist Executive formally rejected Jabotinsky's platform .

A Revisionist plebiscite chose secession, and the constituent assembly of the New Zionist Organization met in Vienna in September 1935, said to have been "elected by 713,000 voters," with Jabotinsky as its president .
He resigned from the World Zionist Organization altogether  .
The New Zionist Organization ran its own political and fundraising work, parallel to and in competition with the Jewish Agency and, later, the American Zionist Emergency Council  .
The Revisionist case, in its own terms, was argued openly.

Its premise was that the Arab population would never consent to a Jewish majority, so that any plan built on consent would fail; better to say so, and to build the strength on which the project could proceed without that consent.
Its territorial claim held that Britain had cut the Mandate in two in 1922 arbitrarily, and that a state confined to the western bank could not take in the millions of Jews who would need it.

The Zionist leadership's answer is on record in what it did: the General Council's discipline clause barred exactly the independent political action the Revisionists practiced, and the Executive rejected their platform.
Within the movement itself, Grossman's followers broke away in 1933 over Jabotinsky's suspension of the executive.
Both readings start from Jabotinsky's own words.
In 1937 he testified before the Peel Commission against any partition of Palestine, insisting on Jewish rights to the entire Mandate territory, Transjordan included.
He died of a heart attack in 1940 while visiting Betar in the United States .
Herut was founded on 15 June 1948 by Menachem Begin, a former Irgun commander, as a challenge to Hatzohar, which was then succeeded by and merged into Herut after the state was established.

Herut joined the Liberal Party in 1965 to form Gahal, which in 1973 became the founding core of Likud, the party that has led or co-led Israeli governments for most of the past five decades, including under Netanyahu    .
It is not a claim that Likud's platform today is Jabotinsky's; parties change over a century.

The sources do not give a verified membership figure for the Revisionist movement or for Betar in any year; the 600,000 and the 713,000 are a petition count and a claimed electorate, and the 70,000 for Betar comes from a single account.
They do not set out the specific policy disputes behind the Executive's rejection of the platform in 1935 beyond the discipline clause.
And they do not show how much money the New Zionist Organization raised in its parallel campaigns.
What they do show is that by September 1935 organized Zionism had two rival centers, each with its own leader, program and electorate, thirteen years before the state.
The Wall and August 1929: Jerusalem, Hebron, Safed
A common account of Mandate Palestine dates organized violence between Arabs and Jews to the Arab Revolt that began in 1936.
In the last week of August 1929, violence that began in Jerusalem over the Western Wall, which Muslims call al-Buraq, spread to Hebron and Safed.

It left a precise death toll, ended one of the oldest continuous Jewish communities in the country for nearly four decades, led to a British commission of inquiry, and, in the judgment of historians, made the political reputation of the Mufti of Jerusalem, Hajj Amin al-Husseini  .
In September 1928, on Yom Kippur, Jewish worshippers set up a portable screen at the Wall to separate men from women, and its removal opened the conflict .
The Wall belonged to Muslim religious authorities, and Jews prayed there.
A documented Arab campaign asserted Muslim rights over the site, and documented Jewish activity pressed for prayer arrangements there; each side treated the dispute as central to its larger claim .
Hajj Amin al-Husseini is documented as leading the 1928 campaign asserting Muslim rights over the Wall .
On 15 August 1929 a few hundred Jewish youths, Betar members among them, marched to the Wall and raised a flag.
On 16 August a Muslim demonstration went to the Wall, beat Jews who were there and burned prayer notes   .
In the days that followed, according to the historians cited here, rumor and organized propaganda inflamed the city, and the Mufti's activists distributed inflammatory material  .
The outbreak came on 23 August in Jerusalem.

The Shaw Commission, which investigated it the following year, found that it began there as an attack by Arabs on Jews, that it "was not premeditated", and that it was not a revolt against British authority .
Only about 150 British police and 1,500 local police served the whole of Palestine  .
The British command at the time is part of the story of the High Commissioners in .
The worst of the killing was in Hebron.
Eight American students of the Slobodka Yeshiva were among the dead .
Sixty-seven Jews were killed in the city .

Human Rights Watch gives 67 Jews killed and dates the massacre to 23 August; the EBSCO reference account records one yeshiva student killed on 23 August and 64 killed at the Heichal residence on 24 August  .
Those two EBSCO figures add to 65, not 67, and the sources used here do not reconcile the difference.
Hebron also produced a documented account of rescue.
According to Human Rights Watch, the Zionist Archives list 435 Hebron Jews who found refuge in 28 Arab homes.
Norman Bentwich wrote that many Jews were saved by their Arab neighbors  .
The figure of 435 rests on that one archival list as reported by Human Rights Watch; it is not, in the sources here, independently counted.
After the killing the British authorities evacuated Hebron's surviving Jews.
A community present in the city for centuries was removed within days, and organized Jewish life there did not resume until 1968, thirty-nine years later .
The violence reached Safed on 29 August 1929.
Between 18 and 20 Jews were killed there and about 80 wounded, and some 200 Jewish homes were burned  .
By the end of the week the dead numbered 133 Jews and 116 Arabs, according to the EBSCO reference account and the Jewish Virtual Library.
Most of the Arab deaths were caused by British police and military fire during the suppression  .
The Jewish toll is itself disputed.
The Jerusalem Story lexicon of the Institute for Palestine Studies gives 113 Jews and 116 Arabs, and adds that the Mandate probably under-reported Palestinian casualties .
The two accounts agree on the Arab figure and differ by twenty on the Jewish one; neither source, as used here, explains the gap.
The reckoning took several forms, and Britain's own report to the League of Nations for 1929 records the first of them.
Collective punishments were imposed on towns and villages that took part in attacks on Jews at Hebron, Safed, Motza, Artuf and Beer Tuvia, with fines totalling £P17,840.
By the end of December 1929, 791 Arabs and 66 Jews had been tried summarily; 17 Arabs and 1 Jew had received capital sentences, and 7 death sentences had been confirmed on appeal .
These were measures of the Mandate administration, and Britain reported them to the League as the mandatory power answerable to it.
On 17 June 1930 three Arab men were hanged in Acre for their part in the riots.
Twenty-five other death sentences, two of them on Jews, were commuted.
Palestinians remember the day as "Red Tuesday" .
The Shaw Commission reported in March 1930.
On the question that has divided accounts ever since, the Mufti's role, it was precise.
It found no evidence that Hajj Amin al-Husseini had incited the outbreak, but held that he "must accept a share in the responsibility".
It found premeditation not proved against the Arab Executive .
On causes, Shaw distinguished two levels.
The fundamental cause was Arab hostility rooted in disappointed political aspirations and fear for their economic future.

The immediate causes included the incidents at the Wall from September 1928 to 16 August 1929, the Jewish demonstration of 15 August, an inflammatory press, and the enlargement of the Jewish Agency in 1929 , whose making is told in .
What London did with Shaw's findings, and with the land inquiry that followed, is the subject of .

A commission of three members, none of them British, sat in Jerusalem from 19 June to 19 July 1930 under the approval of the League Council: Eliel Löfgren of Sweden, Charles Barde of Geneva and J. van Kempen of the Netherlands.
It found that the Wall and the pavement before it are Muslim property, and that the Wall is "sacred to both Parties".
Jews were to have free access for their devotions, but could bring only the appurtenances permitted under the Turkish regime, and screens separating men and women were barred .
It confirmed Muslim ownership and Jewish access together, and held Jewish worship there to the arrangements of the Ottoman years.

In the Palestinian account, preserved in the Jerusalem Story lexicon under the name "al-Buraq Uprising", the trigger was a provocation: Betar-led demonstrators raised the Zionist flag at a site under Muslim authority, and the response grew from a real fear that the holy places would be taken over .

The march of 15 August appears in each of the accounts cited here, and Shaw named it among the immediate causes, so this reading draws support from the inquiry's findings as well as from Palestinian memory.
In the Jewish account, the cause was a Muslim campaign over the Wall led by the Mufti, and incitement that ended in massacres of unarmed communities  .

Its evidence is equally concrete: the Mufti's documented 1928 campaign, the inflammatory material his activists distributed, and the fact that the dead of Hebron, eight American yeshiva students among them, were killed in another town, a day after the outbreak in Jerusalem.
The British inquiry stood between the two.
It found no premeditation, a share of responsibility on the Mufti, and the 15 August demonstration among the immediate causes, while naming an Arab attack on Jews as the form the outbreak took .
Behind the question of the Mufti's role in the riots lies a larger one about what the riots did for him.

Historians, among them Oren Kessler in a 2024 account, describe 1929 as the event that made al-Husseini's political reputation among Palestinians, the platform on which his leadership of the 1936–39 revolt was later built .
The first is the Mufti's direct part.

Whether he organized the violence itself, or capitalized on tensions that moved beyond his control, is a question historians still debate; Shaw's "share in the responsibility" was a judgment, not a finding of organization  .

The Jewish dead of the week are given as 133 or 113, the Hebron dead as 67 or, by one day-by-day account, 65, and the Arab dead, most of them killed by the forces of order, may have been under-recorded   .
The third is the rescue: the 435 sheltered in Hebron rest on one archival list as reported by one organization.
The Armed Line: The Haganah, the Irgun and the Jaffa Barrels, 1920–1935
Alongside land and labor, the Yishuv was building a force of its own.
A familiar picture of the Mandate years shows one Jewish defense force, the Haganah, acting under a single political direction until it became the army of the new state in 1948.
By the end of 1931 there were already two Jewish armed organizations in Palestine, the Haganah and the Irgun, and by 1940 there would be three.
When the Histadrut, the Jewish labor federation, was founded in December 1920, it took responsibility for defense, and the Haganah was placed under its direct control.
Through the 1920s the Haganah had only "a few hundred" volunteer members .
In 1924 its senior commanders drew up a "Constitution of the Haganah," a first attempt to give the organization written rules.
In 1926 former members of Ha-Shomer formed a separate underground of their own inside the Gedud ha-Avodah .
Even before the Revisionist split that is the usual subject of this story, the Yishuv's armed structure was divided.
The violence of August 1929 changed the Haganah's position.
In that month its volunteers helped defend the Jewish communities of Jerusalem, Tel Aviv and Haifa.
The massacres of that August happened where the Haganah was absent or weak: in Hebron, in Safed and at Motza .

A national command of six members was set up, with parity between the labor movement and everyone else: three members came from the Histadrut, Eliyahu Golomb, Dov Hos and Meir Rutberg, and three were non-labor members .
A group led by Avraham Tehomi, who had been the Haganah's Jerusalem district commander from 1929 to 1931, seceded.
Together with Revisionist groups it formed the Irgun Zvai Leumi, also known as Etzel  .
Tehomi is the same man whose 1985 account of the 1924 killing of Jacob de Haan is weighed in .
He did not stay with the organization he founded: he returned to the Haganah in 1937  .

The Irgun's founders were officers aligned with Ze'ev Jabotinsky's Revisionist movement, and the point of principle on which they broke was havlagah, the Haganah's policy of restraint in the face of Arab attacks, which they rejected .
Through the 1930s and 1940s the Irgun conducted an armed campaign against British rule and against Arab civilian targets.
From 1943 it was commanded by Menachem Begin, who later became Israel's sixth Prime Minister .
The source establishes the founding rationale and the line of command; it does not, on its own, give a full operational history of the Irgun, and this section does not attempt one.
The Haganah's leadership held to restraint and, after 1931, to a command shared equally between labor and non-labor members, removing the commander who opposed that public control.
The Irgun's founders rejected restraint in the face of Arab attacks and left the Haganah.
Between 1931 and 1935 the Haganah built itself into something more permanent.
It had urban branches in Jerusalem, Tel Aviv and Haifa, each with memberships "in the hundreds," it ran annual officers' courses, and it had workshops producing hand grenades .
The clearest single episode of these years came at the port of Jaffa in 1935.
Rifles and ammunition had been shipped from Belgium hidden in barrels of cement.
British authorities seized 537 barrels at Jaffa, and the discovery caused significant unrest among Palestinian Arabs  .

One account, drawing on the Palestine Post and the Peel report among other sources, gives the contents as 25 Lewis machine guns, 800 rifles and 400,000 rounds, found in 359 of the drums, and says they were consigned to a merchant in Tel Aviv who was never identified.
The account just cited, relying on Palestine Post reports and the Peel report, dates the discovery to 16 October 1935 .
The Encyclopaedia Judaica's entry on the Haganah dates it to 18 November 1935 .
Neither source, as gathered here, names who in the Yishuv ordered the shipment.

A compiled account of Zionist intelligence before 1948, drawn on elsewhere in this library, says that the first Jewish intelligence organization in Palestine was established under the Haganah in 1929.
The same account also dates the founding of the Shai, the Sherut Yediot or Information Service, the Haganah's intelligence and counter-espionage arm, to 1940 .
ents: the Sherut Yediot or Information Service

sent: The two statements may describe different bodies, an informal service in 1929 and a formal one in 1940, but the account does not say so, and this book has not been able to confirm a founding date for any Haganah intelligence body in 1929.
The Shai's wartime and American story belongs to a later period and is not told here.
In 1940 the Irgun split in turn.

Avraham Stern led a faction out to form Lehi, Lohamei Herut Israel, "Fighters for the Freedom of Israel," often called the Stern Gang, rejecting the Irgun's decision to suspend operations against the British during the Second World War .
ents: Fighters for the Freedom of Israel

sent: Stern's group is documented as having explored contact with Fascist Italy and, most controversially, Nazi Germany, in search of any power willing to oppose British rule in Palestine.
The episode was widely condemned at the time, including within the broader Zionist movement.

In 1944 and 1945, in what became known as the "Hunting Season," the Haganah, under Jewish Agency direction, moved against members of the Irgun and Lehi through surveillance, exposure to the British authorities and detentions, in an attempt to suppress their independent operations and keep political control unified .
And at independence, when the Haganah became the core of the Israel Defense Forces and the Irgun and Lehi were formally absorbed, the merger was contested.

In June 1948 the Altalena affair, an armed confrontation between the new army and Irgun forces over a weapons shipment, left sixteen Irgun members and three soldiers dead; the ship was shelled and burned off Tel Aviv on Ben-Gurion's direct order.
Begin's refusal to let the clash become a civil war, in his words "there will be no civil war with the enemy at our gates," is documented as decisive in preventing a wider fight .
According to a 2026 report in the Jerusalem Post, the wreck was found intact on the Mediterranean seafloor that year, 78 years later .
This library gives full weight to the internal divisions on the political side: the Bund, Reform Judaism's early ambivalence, Neturei Karta.

The record of 1920 to 1935 shows the armed side divided almost from the start: between the labor federation and the old Ha-Shomer men in 1926, between labor and non-labor in the command of 1931, and between restraint and its rejection in the secession of the same year.
It gives no membership figures for the Irgun in its first years and no count of the Haganah beyond "a few hundred" and "in the hundreds."
It does not establish who arranged the Belgian shipment, or the date it was found.
And it does not support the claim of a Haganah intelligence service founded in 1929.
Bringing In the Non-Zionists: The Enlarged Jewish Agency, 1924–1929
American quotas, by one account, turned Jewish emigrants toward Palestine in the mid-1920s.
American Jewish money was harder to steer.
It is often assumed that American Jewish leadership was Zionist from the start, and that the money which built the Jewish national home flowed from a settled consensus.
Much of the wealthiest American Jewish leadership was non-Zionist, and a non-Zionist relief body ran its own appeals in competition with the Zionist fund .
Bringing those leaders and their money inside the movement's institutions took Chaim Weizmann the better part of five years.

When it was done, in Zurich in August 1929, the Jewish Agency had become a body in which Zionists and non-Zionists sat in equal numbers, and the institution that would govern the Yishuv until 1948 rested on a funding base that reached well beyond committed Zionists.
The American Jewish Joint Distribution Committee, a non-Zionist relief body chaired by the banker Felix Warburg, ran its own campaigns.
The Zionist Organization of America saw them as a rival to the Keren Hayesod, the movement's permanent fund, and the two clashed.
To protect the Keren Hayesod, the ZOA created a United Palestine Appeal under Rabbi Stephen Wise .
Two appeals were now asking the same American Jewish public for money, one Zionist and one not.
The stakes were large, because the United States had already become the movement's main source of funds.
From April 1921 to December 1929 the Keren Hayesod raised $20.1 million worldwide, about $370 million in today's dollars.
More than half of it, $11.0 million, came from the United States  .
Over the fund's first twelve years, the United States gave about half of the £4.82 million raised .
The money paid for the core of the movement's work in Palestine: before 1948 the fund's mandate covered immigration, settlement, defense, water and public works .
After the United States came South Africa with $1.5 million, Germany with $0.98 million, Romania and Britain with $0.88 million each, Poland with $0.82 million and Canada with $0.74 million .
No other country gave even a seventh of the American total.
And this was the Zionist fund alone; the non-Zionist Joint Distribution Committee under Warburg raised its money separately .
Weizmann's answer was to stop competing with the non-Zionists and bring them in.

From December 1924 to February 1925 he was in the United States, launching the annual Keren Hayesod campaign and negotiating an expanded Jewish Agency with Louis Marshall, president of the American Jewish Committee .
The offer was institutional: the non-Zionists were to be brought inside the Jewish Agency itself, as partners in its governance, rather than courted as donors to a rival appeal.
It ended at Zurich in August 1929.
There the Sixteenth Zionist Congress ratified the agreement, and the Council of the enlarged Jewish Agency met, with Albert Einstein, Léon Blum and Herbert Samuel present  .
The Council's membership was split equally between Zionists and non-Zionists.
Louis Marshall became chairman of the Council and Lord Melchett its associate chairman.
Felix Warburg, who had chaired the rival relief appeal, became chairman of the Administrative Committee.
And the Keren Hayesod was recognized as the Agency's main financial instrument  .
The man who had chaired the rival relief body now held a chair inside the Agency, beside the Zionist fund.
Marshall and Warburg assured him that his "financial troubles are over"  .
Whether they were is another matter, and the sources here do not show how much non-Zionist money actually flowed through the enlarged Agency in the years that followed.
Marshall died weeks after Zurich, in September 1929.

One summary of these events places his death in the same month that the riots in Palestine began; the violence in Jerusalem, Hebron and Safed in fact began in August 1929, weeks before he died, and is told in .
The enlargement was not only an internal Jewish matter.
The Shaw Commission, sent to investigate the August violence, listed the enlargement of the Jewish Agency among the immediate causes of the outbreak, beside the incidents at the Wall .
The two descriptions of Zurich sit uneasily together.
For Weizmann, by his papers' account, it brought the assurance that his financial troubles were over.
The Commission, by contrast, placed it beside the Wall incidents among the immediate causes of the violence.
The record supports both: it was an act of Jewish communal organization, and a British inquiry judged it to have helped bring on the outbreak of 1929.
The sources here do not record the Arab leadership's own statements about Zurich.
The importance of 1929 lies in what the Agency became afterward.

By that year the body that would run the pre-state Yishuv had brought wealthy American non-Zionists inside its governance, widening its funding base well beyond committed Zionists, nineteen years before 1948.

In the sequence of institutions shown below, from the Basel Congress to the State of Israel, the Jewish Agency stands between the British Mandate and the American political effort of the 1940s, enlarged in 1929.
It does not say how much non-Zionist money the enlarged Agency actually received, or how Warburg's Administrative Committee used it.
It does not show how far the non-Zionist half of the Council shaped the Agency's political decisions, as distinct from its finances.
And the structure was tested at once: within weeks of Zurich, the Agency faced the crisis of August 1929 and lost the chairman around whom the partnership had been built.
The American Palestine Committee, 1932

In 1932, while the Zionist movement in Palestine was building its labor federation, its banks and its defense force, one of its executives in the United States began building something of a different kind: a committee of prominent Americans who were mostly not Jewish.
Emanuel Neumann, a member of the Zionist Executive, founded the American Palestine Committee that year to organize prominent, mainly non-Jewish Americans in support of a Jewish homeland .
The committee's existence and its founder are documented in the records of the American Jewish Archives .
A common account of the 1940s holds that the wave of Christian and elite American support for a Jewish state arose on its own.
The record shows that the most visible bodies expressing that support were founded and later revived by one Zionist official, working from inside the movement's political office.
What they do record is what happened when Neumann returned to it.

In January 1941 he joined the Emergency Committee for Zionist Affairs as head of public relations and political action, and from that post he revived the American Palestine Committee, with Senator Robert Wagner as its chairman .
ents: the Emergency Committee for Zionist Affairs

sent: The person charged with the Zionist emergency body's public relations and political action was the same person who rebuilt the committee through which prominent non-Jewish Americans would speak.
In December 1942 Neumann organized a second, parallel body for clergy, the Christian Council on Palestine .
Its founding minutes describe it as an "autonomous committee working in cooperation with the American Palestine Committee" .

By the end of the war the American Palestine Committee claimed some 6,500 members, among them senators, congressmen, cabinet members and governors, and by one description mayors; the Christian Council claimed about 3,000 clergy  .
In 1946 the two merged into the American Christian Palestine Committee, which disbanded after 1948 .
How these committees fitted into the wider American campaign of the 1940s is told in .
The Christian Council's founding minutes call it "autonomous" .
The historian Peter Grose described the committees' operations as "hardly autonomous" .
Reporting that draws on Grose's work states that Zionist funds, reaching up to $150,000 by 1946, sustained them .

The strongest case for "hardly autonomous" is structural: both committees were founded by the same Zionist official, the larger one was revived from the Emergency Committee's political office, and, according to reporting on Grose's work, the money that kept them running came from Zionist funds.
The same arrangement, organized support presented as independent, appears again in later decades, and this library documents it for the predecessors of AIPAC in its own place.
And it does not show how much direction Neumann's office gave the committees day to day, which is the real substance of Grose's phrase.
Money, Currency and the Mandate Economy, 1922–1936
Brit Shalom argued about who would govern; the economy was being built regardless.
When Israel declared independence in 1948 it did not start from nothing.
It inherited a currency managed by the Mandate, and a banking network that the Zionist movement had built and run for half a century before the state existed.
In 1926 the British Colonial Secretary appointed a Palestine Currency Board, and from 1 November 1927 the board issued the Palestine pound  .
The board was appointed by the Colonial Secretary, and the currency it issued was tied one for one to the British pound.
It was a currency managed from London.
No body in Palestine, Jewish or Arab, issued the country's money or set its value.
The Palestine Currency Board's notes stayed in circulation until 18 August 1948  .
Alongside the Mandate's currency ran a separate financial structure, owned by the Zionist movement.
The Jewish Colonial Trust was chartered in London in 1899.
Its operating subsidiary, the Anglo-Palestine Bank, was founded in 1902, was London-based, and was owned through the Jewish Agency  .

Their founding belongs to an earlier volume of this library; what matters here is that by the 1920s the Yishuv, the Jewish community in Palestine, had a bank of its own that operated in the Mandate's currency but answered to the movement's institutions.
The movement's own banking ran through institutions chartered in London, in a currency pegged to sterling.
The figures for that investment come mainly from the Jewish Agency itself, and they have to be read as what they are.
In 1937 David Horowitz of the Jewish Agency's Economics Department prepared Economic and Social Transformation of Palestine for the Agency's case before the Peel Commission .
ents: Economics Department prepared Economic and Social Transformation of Palestine

sent: It is an advocacy document, written to persuade a British commission, and its figures are the Agency's own.
They are reported here as Horowitz gave them.
According to Horowitz, "LP 80,000,000 have been invested by Jews in economic enterprise" over sixteen years.
Annual Jewish investment in building, he wrote, rose from LP 900,000 in 1924 to LP 7,000,000 in 1935 .
Industrial output, in his figures, rose from under LP 1,000,000 in 1921 to over LP 8,000,000 in 1935 .
In his account there were 84,000 Jews in 1922, 13 percent of the population, and 375,000 in 1935, 28 percent; the non-Jewish population was 565,000 in 1922 and 975,000 in 1935 .
His Jewish figure for 1922 is close to the census count of 83,794.
The 1922 census counted 757,182 people in all and put Jews at about 11 percent .
Horowitz's 13 percent rests on a smaller non-Jewish base of 565,000, and the source does not explain how that base was drawn.
The Mandate government grew along with the economy.
Horowitz gave government revenue as LP 2,371,000 in 1922–23 and LP 5,452,000 in 1934–35, and expenditure rising over the same years from LP 1,900,000 to LP 3,200,000 .
The British garrison cost £1.5 million in 1923–24 , more than three-quarters of the civil spending of 1922–23, and it was paid by Britain.
The full ledger of what the Mandate cost Britain, to its end in 1948, is told in .

The rows of that table for these years tell the story in brief: Mandate civil spending of £P1.9 million in 1922–23 and £P3.2 million in 1934–35 ; the garrison's £1.5 million in 1923–24 ; and, set beside them, the Agency's estimate of £P80 million of Jewish capital invested between 1921 and 1937 .
Horowitz went further than investment totals.

He argued that Arabs gained directly from Jewish economic activity: from Jewish contributions to government revenue, from land prices that had risen 400 to 500 percent, and from falling death rates in the districts of Jewish immigration.
He set daily wages of 10–15 piastres in Palestine against 2–3 in Iraq and Egypt .
This is the strongest form of the Zionist economic case, and it was made in the movement's own words, to a British commission, for a political purpose.
A British official had reached a different conclusion seven years earlier.

Sir John Hope Simpson, reporting in October 1930, found that Jewish National Fund leases required Jewish labor only, that a landless Arab class was forming, and that families displaced by land sales had not been resettled .

On his account the benefits of Jewish investment did not flow freely across the population; the institutions that directed it were built to employ Jews, and some of the cost fell on Arab cultivators who lost their land.
His figures, and the Agency's rebuttal of them, are set out in .
But the sources used here do not measure how gains and losses were distributed among Arabs, and neither Horowitz's figures nor Hope Simpson's settle that question.
Each was produced for a purpose, the first to argue for the national home before Peel, the second to advise the British government on land and immigration.
The record supports neither the claim that Jewish investment benefited everyone nor the claim that it benefited no one.
One more flow of these years ran through Palestine without passing through either the Mandate's budget or the movement's banks.
The Iraq Petroleum Company built a pipeline from Iraq to the Mediterranean between 1932 and 1934.
At Haditha it split into two branches, one to Tripoli and one to Haifa .
The transit agreements with Palestine, Transjordan, Lebanon and Syria had been signed between 5 January and 25 March 1931 .
The first oil reached Haifa on 16 October 1934, and official opening ceremonies were held in January 1935.
Palestine had become a transit country for the oil of a neighbouring state, with a terminal on its coast.
The arrangement lasted until 1948, when Iraq stopped sending oil to Haifa .
Before independence the Anglo-Palestine Bank's chairman, Eliezer Hoofien, persuaded the American Bank Note Company in New York to print new notes.

According to Israel's state mint, the notes were not marked "legal tender," and the printer's name was left off, to get around the need for the US Secretary of State's approval to print foreign currency  .
They reached the country secretly in July 1948 and became legal tender by law on 17 August 1948, the day before the Mandate's notes went out of circulation   .
On 1 May 1951 the bank's assets passed to Bank Leumi le-Israel, and the currency became the Israeli pound .
One already existed: a London-chartered bank that had operated for decades, inside a currency system the British had set up in 1926–27.
On this reading, what 1948 required was a change of name and of sovereign, and the first notes for that change were printed in New York.
The sources do not give the Anglo-Palestine Bank's own balance sheets, its lending, or how much of the £P80 million Horowitz reported passed through it.
They do not say how the Currency Board's reserves were held, or what the peg to sterling cost or gained the country.

And they do not measure how the gains of the Mandate economy were divided between Jews and Arabs, or among Arabs themselves, which is the question on which Horowitz and Hope Simpson most sharply disagree.
The Haganah that Britain trained and jailed by turns had a second task besides defense: bringing people in.
Postwar Jewish immigration to Palestine is often pictured as a flight of desperate refugees acting on their own.
From 1938 to 1948 they were organized and routed by a network built for the purpose, run from within the institutions of the Jewish community in Palestine.
Both things are true, and the history of Aliyah Bet only makes sense when they are held together.
Aliyah Bet means "immigration B." It was the name for the clandestine immigration of Jews to Palestine against the limits Britain set on legal entry.
In 1938, the year of Évian, the Jewish leadership created the Mossad LeAliyah Bet as a branch of the Haganah to coordinate it.
It was founded in the same year that 32 countries met at  and almost all declined to take more Jewish refugees, while Britain kept Palestine off the agenda.
The Mossad LeAliyah Bet was an arm of the Haganah, the defense organization of the Jewish community, not an independent charity.
It organized ships from Europe's ports, against a British limit on entry that the Royal Navy enforced at sea.
Two of the wartime ships, the Patria in 1940 and the Struma in 1942, ended in mass death and are told in .
With Britain's quota at about 18,000 a year, the clandestine route became the main one.

The Brihah ("flight") network, run with Mossad emissaries, partisans and youth movements, moved nearly 200,000 survivors out of displaced-persons camps in Germany, Austria and Italy to ports in Italy, France, Yugoslavia and Greece.
Zionist youth movements inside the camps supplied the passengers.
Ships, including a fleet bought and crewed largely by American volunteers, made about 142 voyages in all.
More than 90 percent of them were intercepted by the Royal Navy.
Interception did not end the journey, and Britain needed somewhere to put the people it stopped.
In July 1947 the Exodus 1947, carrying about 4,500 people, was boarded in international waters, and its passengers were sent back not to Cyprus but to camps in Germany.
The US Holocaust Memorial Museum reads that decision as an admission that the Cyprus deterrent had failed.

What the Exodus did to international opinion, and whether it moved the United Nations vote, belongs to the next stage and is set out, with both sides of the argument, in the account of the ships linked above.
By 1948 well over 100,000 people had come to Palestine this way, including more than 70,000 Holocaust survivors.
Set against the whole of Jewish immigration under the Mandate, that is a large share.
Britain's own records count 376,415 Jewish immigrants between 1920 and 1946.
A separate estimate puts total Mandate-era immigration, legal and illegal together, at about 480,000.
The British count stops in 1946 and records the entries Britain registered.
The larger estimate runs to the end of the Mandate and includes people who entered without Britain's leave.
In Britain's 1922 census, 757,182 people were counted in Palestine.
By the United Nations committee's estimate in late 1946, the population was about 1.85 million.
The question of what Aliyah Bet was has two answers, and both have evidence behind them.
They were survivors with nowhere else to go after the doors closed at Évian.
