The movement that carried them was an organized state-in-waiting, with its own intelligence service, logistics, fleet and recruitment, and every intercepted ship became a public argument against the Mandate.
The youth movements that supplied the passengers in the camps and the Haganah branch that organized the ships were part of the same operation as the people on board.
It does not say how the fleet was paid for, beyond noting that American volunteers bought and crewed much of it.
It does not break down how many voyages or passengers fall before 1945 and how many after, or how many of the people who took the route were stopped and how many reached Palestine directly.
It does not give the Revisionist voyages separately.
The Bergson Group: Rescue by Advertisement
In 1940 a member of the Irgun arrived in the United States and began to work under another man's name.
Hillel Kook was a nephew of Palestine's first Ashkenazi chief rabbi.
In America he called himself "Peter Bergson," and over the next four years he ran a public campaign on behalf of Europe's Jews.
He was Lithuanian-born, and he did not represent the established Zionist organizations.
He came from the Irgun, and he built his operation outside the mainstream bodies and against their opposition.
A common assumption holds that American opinion about Palestine and about the destruction of European Jewry formed on its own, from the news alone.
Opinion was worked on, by paid advertising, staged events, celebrity sponsors and lobbying on Capitol Hill.
Another emissary crossed the Atlantic the same year.
Benzion Netanyahu, born Mileikowsky in Warsaw in 1910, had emigrated to Palestine in 1920 and edited the Revisionist newspaper Ha'Yarden in the 1930s.
In 1940 Vladimir Jabotinsky, the Revisionist leader, sent him to the United States.

Netanyahu served as Jabotinsky's personal secretary until Jabotinsky's death later that year, and then ran the Revisionist movement's American operations as executive director for the following eight years.
Kook's vehicle was a succession of committees, each built around a single demand and each carrying long lists of prominent sponsors drawn from Hollywood, Congress and the press.
The first, the Committee for a Jewish Army, appeared in 1941.
ents: the Committee for a Jewish Army

sent: In 1943 came the Emergency Committee to Save the Jewish People of Europe.
ents: the Emergency Committee to Save the Jewish People of Europe

sent: Later the group created the Hebrew Committee of National Liberation.
ents: the Hebrew Committee of National Liberation

sent: The names tracked the shifting goal: first a Jewish fighting force, then rescue, then a claim to speak for a nation.
The committees bought full-page advertisements in major newspapers, with stark headlines about the destruction of European Jewry and demands that the government act.
The sponsor lists can be read as doing similar work: a demand carrying names from Hollywood and Congress was harder to wave away as the view of a fringe group.
"We Will Never Die" was a memorial pageant written by Ben Hecht, produced by Billy Rose and directed by Moss Hart, with music by Kurt Weill.
It played twice in one night at Madison Square Garden, to about 40,000 people in all.
Among its stops was Washington, where the audience included Eleanor Roosevelt, justices and members of Congress.
The pageant brought the campaign's two instruments together: mass public feeling in New York, and an audience of officials in the capital.
It turned the killing of Europe's Jews into a public occasion that people attended in person and that the powerful were seen to attend.
On 6 October 1943, about 400 Orthodox rabbis, in an action organized with the Bergson group, marched to the Capitol and then to the White House to plead for rescue.
President Roosevelt did not receive them.
What it shows is the limit of the campaign's reach at that moment: it could fill an arena and bring rabbis to the Capitol steps, but it could not open the President's door.
The campaign's pressure on Congress took the form of a rescue resolution the Bergson group promoted.
A Treasury Department report charged the State Department with obstructing rescue.
In January 1944, President Roosevelt created the War Refugee Board by Executive Order 9417.
How much credit belongs to the Bergson campaign is a fair question, and the record does not settle it.
The documented sequence is clear: congressional pressure from the resolution the group promoted, together with the Treasury report, came before the executive order.
A reader who credits the Bergson group with forcing the Board's creation has the timing on his side.
A reader who credits the Treasury report, an internal charge from one department against another, has the same timing.
Some of the Bergson group's firmest opponents were fellow Zionists.
Mainstream Zionist leaders, including Rabbi Stephen Wise, opposed it, and fought it as a rival: an Irgun delegation operating outside the organizations that spoke for the movement in Washington.
The contest was not between Jews and their critics.
It ran inside the Zionist movement and inside American Jewish organized life, between a disciplined establishment and an insurgent wing that had come from Palestine's armed underground.
For the mainstream leaders, the Bergson group was a rival from the Irgun, outside the movement's institutions and answerable to none of them, competing for the same officials' attention.
For the group's defenders, its loud methods were what preceded a government rescue agency, and the timing of the War Refugee Board is their evidence.
From 1944, the same machinery turned to a new target: a campaign for a Hebrew state and for the Irgun's revolt against Britain.

In 1944 the Hebrew Committee of National Liberation opened a "Hebrew Embassy" in Washington and registered with the Justice Department as the agent of a foreign principal, a step the next section follows.
ents: the Hebrew Committee of National Liberation

sent: A critic could take it as a sign that rescue had been a vehicle for the Irgun's politics all along.

A defender could answer that the rescue campaign was real, that it achieved a real result in the War Refugee Board, and that turning to statehood after 1944 was a change of target, not a confession about the past.
The Bergson committees were one of two machines working on American opinion and on Congress in these years.
The other was the mainstream one: the American Zionist Emergency Council, founded in 1943, which built a disciplined lobby of local committees, letters and telegrams directed at Washington.
The Bergson group worked through paid media and spectacle, aimed at the public and at officials at once; its line of pressure ran through the advertisements and the pageant to the War Refugee Board.
The mainstream council worked through organized constituents, aimed at members of Congress and at the party platforms.
They do not establish how much of American sympathy in these years was created by these campaigns and how much they merely organized and directed a concern that would have existed anyway.
Nor do the sources used here say how the Bergson campaign was financed, or give a single estimate of the lives the War Refugee Board saved.
Britain Trained the Army That Would Fight It
In the same summer of 1938 that the powers met at Évian, Britain was arming and training Jewish fighters in Palestine.
The Jewish fighting force of 1948 is often remembered as self-made, built in defiance of Britain.
Defiance is part of the record, and from 1945 it became the larger part.
Between 1938 and 1945, much of that force's training, its fighting method and its future officers came through British channels.
Britain opened those channels when it needed Jewish fighters, first against the Arab Revolt and then against the Axis, and closed them, sometimes with arrests, when the need passed.
Three episodes show the pattern: Wingate's Special Night Squads in 1938, the Palmach in 1941 and the Jewish Brigade Group in 1944–45.
Running beside them was a second story, of the money the Jewish community in Palestine raised to pay for its own defense.
The first channel opened in 1938, at the height of the Arab Revolt ().
Captain Orde Wingate was a British intelligence officer and a devout Christian restorationist who embraced the prophetic vision of a Jewish return to the land.
He proposed a joint unit of British soldiers and Jewish supernumerary police drawn from the Haganah, the Jewish defense organization that Britain never officially recognized.
The Jewish Agency eventually agreed.
The Special Night Squads operated from Kibbutz Ein Harod from June to October 1938.
About 75 Haganah volunteers served in them.
Among them were Moshe Dayan and Yigal Allon, both future generals, and Pinchas Kopel, who later founded the Border Police.
What Wingate taught was a method: small units moving at night and raiding into Arab villages.
The Israeli writer Uri Avnery traced a line of retaliation-raid doctrine from Wingate through the Palmach to the Israel Defense Forces.
The men Wingate trained went on to command.
And the squads were a British instrument against the Arab Revolt, staffed partly by Haganah volunteers, whose targets were Arab villages.
The same administration that sponsored the squads also prosecuted Haganah members caught training with arms.
Dayan, one of Wingate's trainees, was imprisoned in 1939.
One reading fits the two facts into a single policy: training under British command served British aims, and training outside it led to arrest.
Facing a possible Axis breakthrough in North Africa, Britain cooperated with the Haganah in forming the Palmach in May 1941.
After El Alamein, when the danger receded, so did British support.
The third channel came after long negotiation: the British Army announced a Jewish Brigade Group, formed in 1944.
It fought the Germans in northern Italy in March 1945.
The record here says nothing more about the Brigade: not its strength, its casualties or the negotiations that produced it.
Nor does it say how many Jews and Arabs from Palestine volunteered for the British forces during the war.
British training was one input.
The other was money raised inside the Jewish community.
By 1939 the Jewish Agency's budget carried an £80,000 line for "security service (defense)" within a total of £720,000, about one-ninth of the whole.
In 1938, the year of the Night Squads, the community created the Kofer HaYishuv, a levy on cigarettes, restaurant bills and luxuries, to fund the Haganah.
These are the first two steps of a funding chain that later ran through American donors and charity channels, a story told in full in .
The Agency's budget and the levy paid for an organization that Britain did not recognize.
Britain trained parts of it when British interests required, and it jailed members caught training with arms.
The result by 1947 was a force the Mandate had never legalized: about 10,000 mobilized men and 40,000 reservists, under officers many of whom had learned their trade in British service.
From 1945 those cadres would turn against Britain itself.
How much the British contribution mattered, compared with what the Haganah built for itself, is a question of weight that the record here does not settle.
It documents the channels, the dates and the men, but not a measure of how far the 1948 army's effectiveness came from Ein Harod, the Palmach or Italy rather than from its own training.
No audited total of the Haganah's budget is publicly available.
"No One Wants Them": Évian, Bermuda and the Closing Doors
In the summer of 1938, while Woodhead's commission was in Palestine testing whether partition could work, the question of where Europe's Jews could go was put to the world.
A common belief about the years before the Holocaust is that the world did what it could for Europe's Jewish refugees.
The first met in the summer of 1938, about Jewish refugees fleeing the Nazis.
And at both, opening Palestine was kept off the table.
President Roosevelt called the first meeting after Germany annexed Austria.
Delegates of 32 countries met at Évian from 6 to 15 July 1938.
Britain's delegate, Lord Winterton, said that the United Kingdom "is not a country of immigration."
France said it had reached saturation.
Brazil asked for certificates of Christian baptism.
Canada wanted only experienced farmers.
The United States offered only to fill its existing German–Austrian quota, which had gone unfilled in earlier years.
The American offer opened no new places.
One country made a large offer: the Dominican Republic, under the dictator Rafael Trujillo.
The offer came from a regime whose soldiers had massacred thousands of Haitians the year before, in 1937.
The record here gives no figure for how many refugees the Dominican Republic proposed to take or how many it eventually received, and it does not set out Trujillo's reasons.
It records only that the most generous answer at Évian came from a government that had just carried out a massacre.
Palestine was not discussed.
At Britain's insistence, any mention of Palestine as a destination was excluded from the agenda.
Golda Meir attended as the Jewish observer from Palestine.
Britain held the Mandate and therefore controlled entry to Palestine.
The sources here do not give Britain's stated reasons for the exclusion.
What they show is the result: the conference was free to discuss any door except the one the Zionist movement was trying to open, and the power that held that door kept it shut.
The conference's failure was noticed in Germany.
The Nazi party's newspaper summed it up in three words: "No one wants them."
Chaim Weizmann gave the Jewish side of the same conclusion.
He told the Manchester Guardian that the world was now divided into two kinds of places for Jews: places where they could not live, and places they could not enter.
Five years later the Western powers met again, under far worse conditions.
In April 1943, with the extermination of Europe's Jews under way, the United States and Britain held a conference on refugees in Bermuda.
A program proposing that Britain open Palestine to refugees was put forward and was not considered.
Palestine had been kept off the agenda at Évian in peacetime.
At Bermuda, in the middle of the killing, it stayed off.
It does not list the positions of the other 26 countries at Évian.
It does not give the Dominican offer in numbers or say how much of it was carried out.
It does not say why Britain insisted on excluding Palestine, or who proposed opening Palestine at Bermuda and on what terms.
The first is the argument they handed the Zionist movement.
When nearly every country refused, the argument that Jews needed a place of their own gained force.
Much of what came after in this chapter can be read against that background, among it the clandestine ships () and the American campaign for a Jewish commonwealth.
Britain, which kept Palestine off the agenda at Évian and off the table at Bermuda, held the one door the movement was pushing against.
Ten months after Évian, Britain set that policy out in , and the clandestine ships of the following years sailed against its limits.
Who Washington Watched, 1938–1945
In 1938 Congress passed the Foreign Agents Registration Act.
The law did not forbid anyone from working in the United States for a foreign cause.
It required disclosure: a person acting in America as the agent of a foreign principal had to register with the Justice Department and say whom he served.
Through the war years, foreign-born organizers and Palestine-based movements worked on American soil to shape American policy, and the question is what the government did about them, and how evenly.
A familiar claim holds that the United States government simply never noticed or questioned foreign-directed Zionist operations in America.
Washington noticed.
The State Department noticed, the FBI investigated, British officials sent warnings, and the wartime intelligence service kept a desk devoted to the subject.
What the record shows is not blindness but selection: scrutiny fell hard on one wing of the movement, the Irgun-aligned fringe, while the main political apparatus operated in the open.
The wing that drew the heat was the Bergson group, whose campaigns are told in .
Its leader, Hillel Kook, was a Lithuanian-born member of the Irgun who had worked in the United States since 1940 under the name "Peter Bergson."
He built a network of committees, and in 1944 he opened a "Hebrew Embassy" in Washington.
In June 1944 his Hebrew Committee of National Liberation registered with the Justice Department's foreign agents section.
At the same time deportation proceedings were opened against Kook himself.
British officials had already warned the State Department that he was a "bomb-thrower."
FBI files obtained under the Freedom of Information Act by the Wyman Institute show that the investigation began at the State Department's instigation.
Agents planted informants inside the Bergson group, opened its leaders' mail and searched their trash.
One internal memo noted that Bergson had "been in the hair of" Secretary of State Cordell Hull.
Leaders of established Jewish organizations urged officials to deport Kook or to draft him into the army.
They included Morris Waldman of the American Jewish Committee and Nahum Goldmann.
The rivalry between the Bergson group and the mainstream Zionist leadership was not only a matter of competing advertisements and rival rallies.
The Jewish Agency and the American Zionist Emergency Council operated openly through the 1940s.
Their successor body, the American Zionist Council, received such an order only in November 1962, and the order was later withdrawn.
That episode belongs to the Cold War, and this library tells it there.

The Office of Strategic Services, the wartime predecessor of the Central Intelligence Agency, ran a Foreign Nationalities Branch, and within it a Palestine desk that tracked Zionist movement activity during the Second World War.
Its intelligence came largely from Jewish officials who volunteered information.
Its list of people tracked reportedly included Moshe Shertok, later Moshe Sharett, Israel's second Prime Minister.

A 2016 review of declassified documents by the Forward described a wide surveillance effort aimed at Jewish organizations and Zionist political activity, with some informants highly placed in Jewish agencies, building a picture of which American Jewish leaders aligned with which Zionist faction.
The OSS had a wartime foreign-intelligence interest; the FBI's interest was domestic security.
A reader who imagines one coordinated American operation watching Zionist activity in these years is reading more unity into the record than it holds.
Meanwhile the Yishuv was building intelligence of its own.
In 1940 the Haganah established the Shai (Sherut Yediot, the Information Service) as its intelligence and counter-espionage arm.

It holds that the Shai had American branches, Zionist networks in New York and Detroit serving as nodes for procurement and intelligence, that these were not registered under the 1938 Act, that the FBI knew, and that the Justice Department, asked repeatedly to prosecute or to compel registration, declined every time.

The same account describes the Haganah's arms-buying branch, Rekhesh ("Acquisitions"), as an illegal procurement network in the United States, funded by American Jewish donors and buying surplus military equipment from demobilized American stocks and from black-market dealers, with smuggling routes that often relied on organized crime to get past export controls and the arms embargo on the region.

It calls the Justice Department's restraint "deliberate," a political decision dressed as prosecutorial discretion, made because the Truman administration was moving toward support for a Jewish state.

First, Rekhesh's main activity in the United States came in the mid-1940s and after the war, and the account ties the restraint to the Truman administration's later policy; the bulk of the story it tells belongs to the next stage of this library, told in .

Second, the account's own evidentiary note marks one question as contested: whether the Justice Department's decisions reflected explicit political direction from the White House or independent prosecutorial judgment.
Third, it marks the full extent of Zionist intelligence operations on American soil in the 1940s as only partly documented and partly still classified.
The documented core is narrower: a wartime OSS desk that watched, an FBI that investigated the Bergson group, and a mainstream apparatus that was not asked to register.
The arms operation was taken to court after the war, under the Neutrality Act.
Charles Winters was convicted in 1949 and served 18 months.
Herman "Hank" Greenspun and Al Schwimmer were convicted and served no prison time.

Greenspun by President Kennedy in 1961, Schwimmer by President Clinton in 2000, and Winters posthumously by President George W. Bush in 2008, after an appeal campaign that included a letter from Steven Spielberg.
Those convictions sit uneasily with the claim that the Justice Department declined every case, and the two parts of the record should be read side by side.

A later chapter sets the federal court order compelling an Irish republican fund-raising group to register as an agent of the Provisional IRA against a Justice Department inquiry into a pro-Israel lobby that closed without public explanation: .
The State Department, the FBI and British officials noticed, and the wartime intelligence service kept its own file.

But the scrutiny fell on the Irgun-aligned fringe, often at the urging of mainstream organizations themselves, while the main state-building apparatus operated openly for nearly two decades; and the later convictions of individual smugglers were erased by pardon.

It is possible to read the pattern as political favor toward the mainstream movement, as an establishment using the state against a rival, as a department settling a score with a lobbyist who had irritated its Secretary, or as ordinary security worry about a man the British called a bomb-thrower.
Kristallnacht: The Turn to Open Violence
Four months after the Évian conference ended with almost no country willing to take more Jewish refugees (), the German state turned to open violence.
Over the night of 9–10 November 1938, synagogues burned and Jewish shops were smashed across Germany, Austria and the Sudetenland.
More than 30,000 Jewish men were sent to concentration camps.
The event marked the turn in Nazi policy from mainly legal persecution toward open, state-organized mass violence.
The familiar account holds that Kristallnacht was spontaneous popular outrage, a crowd reacting to the assassination of a diplomat.
Germany forcibly expelled Polish Jews living in the country to the Polish border town of Zbąszyń, where thousands of them were held in harsh conditions.
Among them were the parents of Herschel Grynszpan, a 17-year-old German-born Polish Jew living in Paris.
On 7 November 1938, after learning what had happened to his family, Grynszpan shot the German diplomat Ernst vom Rath at the German embassy in Paris.
Vom Rath died of his wounds two days later, on 9 November.
Grynszpan's motive was personal and is documented: his own parents had just been deported and held at the border.
It records why the shots were fired, which is a different matter from what the German state then did with them.
Historians identify the propaganda minister, Josef Goebbels, as seeing in vom Rath's death the moment to unleash violence he had long advocated, and as using it to call for exactly that.
The pogrom that followed was coordinated across Germany, Austria and the Sudetenland within a 48-hour window.
Over that night rioters destroyed more than 1,400 synagogues and prayer rooms across the three territories, burning or desecrating Torah scrolls and religious objects.
About 7,500 Jewish-owned businesses were looted and destroyed.
The glass that littered the streets afterward, from Berlin to Vienna, gave the night its German name, Kristallnacht, the Night of Broken Glass.
More than 30,000 Jewish men were arrested and sent to concentration camps in Germany, Austria and the Sudetenland.
The historian Nikolaus Wachsmann calls this "the first mass imprisonment of Jews in concentration camps solely because they were Jews."
Anti-Jewish persecution under the Nazi regime had come earlier, on a smaller scale.
What was new in November 1938 was mass imprisonment in the camps of Jews as Jews.
At least 91 Jews were murdered during the pogrom itself.
The regime held the German-Jewish community collectively responsible for the destruction and imposed a fine of $400 million at 1938 rates.
By the end of 1938 Jews were barred from schools and most public places in Germany.
On 15 November 1938, President Franklin Roosevelt recalled the US ambassador to Germany in protest.
Kristallnacht belongs in a history of Palestine because of where it falls.

It came four months after Évian had shown that almost no country would take Germany's Jews, and six months before Britain's White Paper of May 1939 set new limits on Jewish immigration to Palestine ().
In that half-year the danger to Jews in the Reich became open and violent, while the places they might go stayed closed or were narrowed.
The pogrom also marks a stage in the Nazi record that runs from legal exclusion through open violence to the bureaucratic planning of murder, the next step of which was taken at  in January 1942.
The Wannsee Conference is often remembered as the meeting at which Hitler's regime decided to murder the Jews of Europe.

What happened at a villa in the Berlin suburb of Wannsee on 20 January 1942 was the coordination of that decision: fifteen officials from across the German state and the Nazi Party, agreeing on how to carry out a policy already made, with no recorded objection from any of them.
Its own document, the Wannsee Protocol, shows exactly what the meeting was and what it was not.

On 31 July 1941, shortly after Germany invaded the Soviet Union, Reichsmarschall Hermann Göring ordered Reinhard Heydrich, head of the RSHA, the Reich Security Main Office, "to make all the necessary preparations... for the Final Solution of the Jewish problem in the German sphere of influence in Europe" .
The order is dated and documented, and it predates Wannsee by nearly six months.
This is the single most important correction to the common account, and it does not shrink Wannsee's significance.
It explains what Wannsee was for.
On 20 January 1942 fifteen high-ranking officials of the Nazi Party and the German government met at the Wannsee villa for about ninety minutes.
Heydrich chaired  .
He opened by announcing his own appointment as Plenipotentiary for the Preparation of the Final Solution.
ents: Plenipotentiary for the Preparation of the Final Solution

sent: He then indicated that approximately 11 million Jews across Europe would fall under its provisions, a figure that included Jewish populations in countries not yet under Axis control  .
Its frame was not the territory Germany held in January 1942 but the whole of Europe, including states Germany had not conquered.
Göring's order gave Heydrich the authority; Heydrich's new title made him the plenipotentiary for the task.
The fifteen men around the table represented the SS, the Nazi Party and several ministries of the Reich government  .
Their presence turned an order from the top of the regime into the shared business of the German civil state.
The Protocol, the surviving record of the meeting, was compiled and heavily edited by Adolf Eichmann from notes taken during it.
Because Eichmann compiled and edited the Protocol after the event, it records the meeting's substance, its outcome and the positions taken.
The absence of a recorded objection is a documented fact; whether any attendee held private reservations that went unrecorded is something the Protocol cannot show either way.
The Protocol was reproduced and distributed at the time to leading officials of the Party and the government .

After the war the Protocol became key documentary evidence in the Subsequent Nuremberg Proceedings, and it was cited again in 1961 at the trial of Adolf Eichmann in Jerusalem, the man who had compiled it .
The sources here establish those two uses in court; they do not give a full legal history of every case in which the Protocol was cited.
Wannsee's significance, then, is not that it originated the decision to murder the Jews of Europe.
Göring's order to Heydrich had already done that.

Its significance is that it formally brought the machinery of the German civil government into direct, coordinated participation in carrying out the decision, through named ministries and named officials, none of whom is recorded as objecting  .
They do not list the fifteen attendees by name beyond Heydrich, who chaired, and Eichmann, who kept the record, or set out which ministry each of the others represented.
They do not reproduce the Protocol's text beyond the passages quoted, and the Protocol itself, being edited, cannot settle what was said in the room word for word.
The number most often given for the Jewish dead is six million, and a common objection holds that it is a round figure that cannot be checked, one that historians simply accept.
The Holocaust is, in the words of the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, the best-documented case of genocide in history .

Its scale has been established by several independent methods, using different kinds of evidence: demographic reconstruction, captured German administrative records, and a name-by-name documentation project that has so far identified about 4.8 million victims individually and is still continuing   .
The historian Raul Hilberg built a detailed demographic breakdown of the Jewish dead and arrived at an estimate of 5.1 million .
The historian Lucy Dawidowicz, working separately in 1975 from birth and death records across the cities of prewar Europe, arrived at 5,933,900 .
Yad Vashem's Book of Names project records victims one by one, through survivor testimony and archival research.
The Holocaust Memorial Museum's own position is that research continues to refine the estimates as more records come to light .
Auschwitz: the largest single site.
Nazi Germany and its allies established more than 44,000 camps and other sites of incarceration between 1933 and 1945 .
Auschwitz operated from May 1940 to January 1945.
At least 1.3 million people were deported there, and at least 1.1 million of them were murdered there, the largest death toll at any single site of the Holocaust  .
They apply to Auschwitz specifically.
Other sites left different kinds of surviving records, and the Auschwitz figures are not a template applied across the other 44,000.
As the Red Army approached in January 1945, the SS forced most of the remaining prisoners at Auschwitz onto death marches toward camps inside Germany and Austria.
Soviet troops liberated the camp on 27 January 1945 .
Since 2005 the date has been commemorated as International Holocaust Remembrance Day .
Documented accounts describe the Soviet soldiers, battle-hardened men already accustomed to the deaths of war, as shocked by what they found .

The Holocaust Memorial Museum documents Holocaust denial directly, and it names its core false claims: that six million deaths never occurred, that Nazi Germany had no official policy of extermination, and that the gas chambers of Auschwitz-Birkenau never existed .
Against each of these the record converges: captured German administrative records, demographic reconstruction, and individually verified named victims all lead to the same conclusion .

Wannsee's own document, the Protocol, answers the second claim on its own: an extermination policy that was ordered in July 1941 and coordinated across the ministries in January 1942 was an official one.

It runs from a democracy's collapse through specific and avoidable decisions by its elites; to a legal architecture of exclusion built before any mass violence; to the open, state-coordinated pogrom of  in November 1938; to the formal bureaucratic coordination, at Wannsee, of an extermination decision already taken; and finally to a verified, independently documented scale of six million Jewish dead, established by converging methods and not accepted on faith.
How the Jewish community of Palestine learned of the killing, when, and what it did in response is not documented here, and nothing about it is asserted.
The sources gathered here also do not reproduce the country-by-country tables behind Hilberg's or Dawidowicz's totals, and they do not give the number of victims of the death marches.
The Uncomfortable Record: Lehi's Offer to Germany and the Killing of Lord Moyne
A familiar account of the war years holds that every Zionist faction stood with the Allies against Nazism and set itself against terrorism.

For its militant fringe it is not, and two episodes in particular are often left out of the story: an offer made to Nazi Germany in January 1941, and the assassination of a British minister in Cairo in November 1944.
So, too, is what the State of Israel later did with the memory of the men involved.
The group at the center of both episodes was Lehi.
Avraham Stern led it out of the Irgun so that it could keep fighting Britain during the war .
The armed organizations of the Yishuv before the war, and the Haganah's later campaign against the Irgun and Lehi, are told in ; this section takes up the two wartime episodes themselves.
The Ankara document, 11 January 1941.
A document dated 11 January 1941, found after the war in the files of the German embassy in Ankara, records Lehi's offer to Germany.
Naftali Lubenchik carried it to the German diplomat Werner Otto von Hentig in Beirut, then under Vichy control.
In it Lehi proposed to "actively take part in the war on Germany's side" in exchange for German support for a Jewish state  .
What the German files do not contain matters as much as what they do.
There is no record of any German response  .
Nothing in the sources gathered here shows that Berlin took the offer up, that any arms or money changed hands, or that Lehi acted on the proposal in any way.
Nor does it speak for the Zionist movement as a whole, whose leaders, as shown below, disowned the fringe.
Cairo, 6 November 1944.
On 6 November 1944 two Lehi members, Eliyahu Hakim and Eliyahu Bet-Zuri, shot Lord Moyne outside his residence in Cairo  .
Moyne was Britain's Minister Resident in the Middle East and a close friend of Winston Churchill.
The ships that the immigration limit turned away, and the deaths aboard two of them, are described in ; the sources here do not say which ships Lehi had in mind.
Hakim and Bet-Zuri were hanged in March 1945  .
Churchill's papers show its effect in London.
When a request came for a 70th-birthday greeting to Chaim Weizmann, Churchill wrote "no message" on it.
He also warned against pressure from Zionists and American Jews for clemency for the two men, according to the Churchill Archives Center .
The rebuff fell on Weizmann, and nothing in these sources connects him to the shooting.
The leadership of the movement did not treat Lehi as its own.
The Zionist Executive and the mainstream youth movements denounced the Irgun and Lehi as "traitors"  .
The Haganah had already acted against them, in the campaign of 1944 and 1945 known as the "Hunting Season," which is told in .
Yitzhak Shamir, one of Lehi's leaders, later became prime minister of Israel, and he had Hakim and Bet-Zuri reburied on Mount Herzl, the national cemetery  .

The sources here do not date Lehi's break from the Irgun (the earlier account does), and they do not give the terms of the debate inside Lehi over the Ankara offer, or whether any further contact with German officials followed it.
And they do not show how far Churchill’s response to Cairo changed British policy on Palestine, as distinct from his personal stance toward Weizmann.
Peel's "Exchange of Population": Transfer Enters the Record
The Peel report of July 1937 is remembered for its partition map.
The model was explicit: the exchange of populations between Greece and Turkey in 1923.
Approximately 225,000 Arabs would be moved out of the territory allotted to the Jewish state, and about 1,250 Jews out of the Arab state.
It was the first official British document to put population transfer in writing.
Ori Yehudai gives about 200,000 Arabs and about 1,000 Jews.
Middle East Eye gives about 225,000 Palestinians against 1,250 Jews, matching the figures above.
The movement the report envisaged was overwhelmingly of Arabs out of the proposed Jewish state.
A widely held view is that the idea of removing the Arab population from a future Jewish state was invented by Israeli extremists after 1948.
Compulsory transfer entered the official record in a British royal commission report in 1937.
It was then discussed, and not rejected, at the top of the Zionist movement more than a decade before the displacement of 1948.
The concept itself was on the table well before the Nakba.
The recommendation was Britain's, made by a royal commission of the Mandatory power.
The Arab response was a plain rejection.
The Zionist response is the disputed part of the record.
In October 1937 David Ben-Gurion wrote to his son Amos.
The letter welcomes partition as a stage toward a larger state and discusses the Arab population.
One sentence in the Amos letter has become the center of a dispute over its wording.
It has been quoted as support for expelling Arabs.
Historians have not only disagreed about the sentence; some have changed their own positions on it, Benny Morris among them.

Those who read the sentence as support for expulsion can point to its context: a letter welcoming partition as a stage, written in the same months in which Ben-Gurion's diary and letters weighed compulsory transfer as a possibility.
The Twentieth Zionist Congress met in Zurich in August 1937.
On the transfer clause the record is plain: the Congress did not reject it.
Transfer was therefore a live subject at the highest level of the movement eleven years before 1948.
The Arab Higher Committee rejected the Peel report outright, the transfer recommendation with the rest.
The word did not leave British politics either.
In December 1944 the Labour Party's conference adopted a resolution on Palestine that again spoke of Arabs moving out as Jews moved in.
That resolution, and what was expected of Labour once in office, is told in .
The exact wording, and so the meaning, of Ben-Gurion's sentence to Amos remains disputed between historians.
The sources here do not show how the Congress debated the transfer clause, only that it did not reject it.
And the figures themselves differ slightly by source: about 225,000 and 1,250 in the report as cited here, about 200,000 and 1,000 in Yehudai.
They were captured by the Allies in 1945, entered into evidence at Nuremberg, and in some cases surfaced only decades later.

According to the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, the European rail network played a crucial role in the Final Solution: the Transport Ministry organized the train schedules, and millions of people were transported by rail to killing centers between autumn 1941 and autumn 1944 .
The Einsatzgruppen reports, 1941–1942.
Their reports survive in a series called the Operational Situation Reports USSR, the Ereignismeldungen.
A set of 195 of them, covering June 1941 to 1 May 1942, was circulated across branches of the German government, the Wehrmacht among them .
On 3 September 1945 the 6889th Berlin Document Group found the set on the fourth floor of Gestapo headquarters in Berlin .

At the Einsatzgruppen trial, the prosecution read from Operational Situation Report No. 128, which stated that "approximately 80,000 persons were liquidated until now by the Kommandos," and from Report No. 106, which stated that approximately 35,000 Jews of Kiev were killed on 29–30 September 1941.
The Jäger Report is a local tally of the same kind.
It was signed at Kovno on 1 December 1941 by SS-Standartenführer Karl Jäger, commander of Einsatzkommando 3.
It states that there are no more Jews in Lithuania apart from working Jews and their families.
Yad Vashem holds it under the reference YVA O-18/245 .

According to the English translation published by the University of South Florida's Florida Center for Instructional Technology, and to Holocaust Denial on Trial, the report's running tally ends with the line "Total 137,346," covering 21 June to 1 December 1941 across 113 operations in 71 locations, and the original is held in the Central Lithuanian Archives in Vilnius  .
These reports were the basis of the prosecution in the ninth of the Subsequent Nuremberg Proceedings, the Einsatzgruppen Case.
Twenty-four defendants were indicted, led by Otto Ohlendorf; 22 were tried.
The trial ran from 29 September 1947 to 12 February 1948, and the prosecutor, Benjamin Ferencz, relied on the wartime SS reports rather than on witnesses  .
Only four of the death sentences were carried out, those of Ohlendorf, Naumann, Blobel and Braune, on 7 June 1951  .
The United States Holocaust Memorial Museum gives the indictment's figure as between 723,661 and one million .
Harvard Law School's Nuremberg Trials Project gives the prosecution's estimate as more than one million .
The meeting of 20 January 1942 is told in : fifteen officials, about ninety minutes, Reinhard Heydrich in the chair, nearly six months after Hermann Göring's documented order of 31 July 1941  .
The minutes were compiled and heavily edited by Adolf Eichmann from notes taken at the meeting; they are not a word-for-word transcript .

Each American document received a trial identification number in one of five letter series that indicated how it had been acquired, among them L, R, C and EC; documents such as 2903-PS carry the PS suffix.

The Nuremberg records are in the United States National Archives as Record Group 238.

The captured-document series were microfilmed, among them NG (publication T1139, 70 rolls), NI (T301, 164 rolls) and NOKW (T1119, 47 rolls), and the Tribunal's proceedings were published in 42 volumes .

In the early 1950s the Department of the Army, working with the American Historical Association, microfilmed captured records before the originals were returned; by March 1968 the Army had returned 35 shipments to Germany .
On 12 April 1945 General Eisenhower visited the camp at Ohrdruf with Generals Patton and Bradley.

On 19 April he asked Marshall to bring members of Congress and editors to the camps, so that the evidence could not be dismissed as propaganda .

On 29 November 1945, introduced by the American prosecutor Thomas Dodd, the prosecution at the International Military Tribunal showed an hour-long film, The Nazi Concentration Camps, compiled from footage shot as Allied troops liberated the camps, with clips credited to George Stevens  .

The commandant of Auschwitz, Rudolf Höss, signed affidavit 3868-PS at Nuremberg on 5 April 1946.

In it he estimated that "at least 2,500,000 victims were executed and exterminated" at Auschwitz by gassing and burning, and that "at least another half million succumbed to starvation and disease making a total dead of about 3,000,000"  .
Testifying before the Tribunal on 15 April 1946, he confirmed the affidavit's contents as true and agreed that Eichmann had told him more than 2 million Jews had been destroyed at Auschwitz.
He stated that he had commanded Auschwitz from May 1940 until December 1943 .
In a further affidavit, dated 14 May 1946, he gave 2 million Jews gassed and 500,000 killed by other means .
The Auschwitz-Birkenau State Museum states that Höss's figures were "highly overinflated," as Höss himself later said while in Polish custody.
The Museum likewise treats as overinflated the Soviet figure of 4 million.

The research of Franciszek Piper, published in 1990, gave 1.1 million as the most probable number of victims, and the Museum's present figures are that about 1.3 million people were deported to Auschwitz, of whom about 1.1 million were murdered .
Höss's total of about 3,000,000 is nearly three times the Museum's figure of about 1.1 million.

Labour and Palestine, 1939–1945
In July 1945 Clement Attlee became Prime Minister at the head of a Labour government.
On Palestine, Labour came to office with a record, going back six years, of opposing the policy it now inherited, and with a conference resolution on Palestine adopted seven months earlier.
Whether that record would become policy was a question American diplomats were already weighing by the end of the month.
In the House of Commons debate of 22–23 May on the White Paper, whose terms and reception are set out in , Attlee voted against the policy, and so did Hugh Dalton.
Herbert Morrison told the House that the government should not adopt a policy "as to which grave doubt exists as to its consistency with the Balfour Declaration and the Mandate."
Labour members argued in 1939 that the White Paper's limits on immigration and on land transfers were "contrary to the terms of the Mandate."
This was a legal argument as well as a political one: the objection was not only that the policy was unwise but that Britain, as the mandatory power, had no right under the Mandate to adopt it.
In December 1944, with the war not yet over, the party's annual conference adopted a resolution on Palestine.
It held that there was no case for a Jewish national home "unless we are prepared to let Jews, if they wish, enter this tiny land in such numbers as to become a majority."
It went on: "Let the Arabs be encouraged to move out, as the Jews move in."
And it proposed re-examining "the possibility of extending the present Palestinian boundaries."
The White Paper had capped Jewish immigration and made further entry after five years depend on Arab acquiescence; the resolution called for immigration on a scale to produce a Jewish majority.
The White Paper had promised an independent Palestine state within ten years; the resolution spoke of moving the existing population and redrawing the frontier.
The phrase about Arabs moving out did not appear from nowhere.

Seven years earlier, in July 1937, the Peel Commission's report had recommended an "exchange of population" on the model of the 1923 Greek–Turkish exchange, compulsory in the last resort, the first official British document to put transfer in writing; that proposal and the Zionist movement's response to it are told in .

The Labour resolution differed in its language: it spoke of Arabs being "encouraged" to move, not compelled, and it was a party conference's statement, not a royal commission's recommendation to the government.

But it shows that the idea of moving Palestine's Arab population, first put on paper by a British commission in 1937, was still being written into the program of a major British party in 1944, now as a call from a party whose leaders, by the State Department's account, had consistently supported the Balfour Declaration.
The sources here record the resolution's words as quoted in an American diplomatic memorandum.
They do not include its full text from Labour's own records, the debate that preceded it, who moved it, or how Zionist, Arab or British officials responded to it at the time.
What the resolution meant to those who voted for it, and how seriously its authors intended the passage on the Arab population, therefore cannot be settled from this record.
What the new government was likely to do was assessed in Washington by the end of July.

A memorandum signed by William Yale of the State Department's Division of Near Eastern Affairs, dated 30 July 1945 and prepared for the Potsdam conference, set out the Labour government's probable Palestine policy.

Yale recorded that Labour leaders, Labour members of Parliament and the major trade unions "have consistently given their support to the Balfour Declaration," and he recalled the party's arguments of 1939 that the White Paper's limits were contrary to the Mandate.

His forecast was that the Labour government would not try to implement it, and would instead "modify or repeal the White Paper policy of 1939," above all on immigration, since the remaining quota would soon be exhausted.
He also expected the government to consult the Soviet and American governments before deciding Palestine's future status.

Yale's reading was that the Labour government would act on the part of its record that was narrow and legal, its objection to the White Paper's immigration limits, and would leave aside the part that called for moving a population and redrawing borders.
He also read the decision as one Britain would no longer take alone: the future status of Palestine, in his forecast, would be settled only after consulting the Soviet and American governments.

Whether the Labour government modified the White Paper, how it handled immigration once the quota ran out, and how its relations with Washington over Palestine developed belong to the postwar period and are told in the next stage of this history.

What this record establishes is the starting point: a party pledged by its own words in 1939 and 1944 against the White Paper, and an American diplomat predicting in July 1945 that it would keep the first pledge in a modified form and not the second.
Much of the British side of these years is not documented in the sources used here.

They do not name the Colonial Secretaries who served during the war, the High Commissioners who governed Palestine on Britain's behalf, or the deliberations of the wartime cabinet on Palestine's future, and they do not cover the appointment of the Labour government's Foreign Secretary.
Who governed Palestine for Britain during the war, and how that government's thinking moved between 1939 and 1945, is therefore a question this chapter cannot yet answer.
Al-Husseini's War: Exile, Iraq and Berlin, 1937–1945
The Arab Revolt left its leader outside Palestine.

Hajj Amin al-Husseini had held the office of Mufti of Jerusalem since 1921 and in April 1936 became president of the Arab Higher Committee, the body that united the leaders of the rival Palestinian parties  .
By 1941 he was in Berlin.

The path between those two points is one man's documented choices, and this section follows them in order: flight in 1937, Iraq and the collapse of the pro-Axis coup there in 1941, and the war years in Germany.
Some accounts use his record to indict Palestinians as a people; others minimize it.
One account has al-Husseini taking sanctuary in the Dome of the Rock on 17 July 1937 to avoid arrest by the British .

After gunmen killed Lewis Andrews, the District Commissioner for Galilee, in Nazareth on 26 September, Britain outlawed the Arab Higher Committee, stripped al-Husseini of his official positions and deported several of the committee's members to the Seychelles  .
He escaped in the autumn of 1937, to Lebanon according to Unpacked and to Syria according to the Jewish Virtual Library, a disagreement set out with the rest of the revolt in   .
From there he moved on to Iraq .
By Unpacked's account he authorized attacks from abroad on Britons, on Jews, and on Palestinians considered collaborators .
His rivalry with the Nashashibi family followed him abroad.
Fakhri Nashashibi, who had organized the British-paid "peace bands" against the rebels, was killed in Iraq in 1941 by gunmen backed by al-Husseini, according to Matthew Hughes's study of the bands.
Fakhri 'Abd al-Hadi, a former rebel commander who had turned to the bands, was murdered in 1943; Hughes's account as summarized here does not name his killers .
Iraq, 1941: the coup and the Farhud.
In Iraq, Rashid Ali al-Gailani led a pro-Axis coup.
Its government collapsed when British forces defeated it, days before the beginning of June 1941.
The sources here place al-Husseini in Iraq in this period but do not document his part in the coup itself, and this section does not supply one  .
On 1–2 June 1941, during the Shavuot holiday, mobs in Baghdad turned on the city's Jewish community.

Iraqi soldiers and police who had backed the coup, together with the pro-Axis Futuwwa youth militias, incited and led two days of killing, rape and looting, joined by civilian mobs and by Bedouin from the outskirts of the city.
British forces, victorious just outside Baghdad, did not intervene  .
The power vacuum left by Rashid Ali's fall, and the nationalist and pro-Axis feeling it had inflamed, produced the violence .

The United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, the most rigorous single source used here, counts between 150 and 180 Jews killed, 600 injured, an undetermined number of women raped, and roughly 1,500 stores and homes looted .
On the consequence the Museum's account is plain: the Farhud marked the turning point after which Iraq's ancient Jewish community began its decline toward near-total emigration within a decade .
The sources drawn on here do not document a direct role for al-Husseini in the Farhud.
After his period in Iraq, al-Husseini relocated to Berlin in 1941 .
There he met Hitler in person.
He asked for German support for Arab independence and for German opposition to a Jewish national home in Palestine .
Throughout the war he broadcast Nazi propaganda to the Arab world over German radio.
He personally recruited and inspected Muslim volunteer units for the Waffen-SS, primarily in the Balkans; the scale given is thousands of volunteers for Waffen-SS divisions .
These facts rest on German diplomatic records, wartime broadcast archives and postwar historical research, and they are not contested .
Al-Husseini escaped prosecution.
He was in French custody, escaped in 1946, avoided the Nuremberg proceedings, and eventually settled in Egypt.
Yugoslavia sought his extradition for war crimes connected with the SS recruitment, and it was never carried out.
He went on to play a diminished but real political role among Palestinian factions into the 1960s .
One version treats al-Husseini's alliance with Nazi Germany as the wartime stance of Palestinian Arabs.

The overwhelming majority of Palestinian Arabs were not involved in his wartime activities, had no vote in his exile-era decisions, and had no means of removing him from a religious appointment he had held since 1921 .
The killing of Fakhri Nashashibi in Iraq shows, too, that Palestinian politics was itself divided over his leadership.
This section covers only the documented core of al-Husseini's war.

They include the details of his meeting with Hitler, the particular Waffen-SS formations he recruited for, his wartime correspondence about the emigration of Jewish children, and the historians' dispute over his role in the Holocaust.

The sources gathered here also do not document what he did in Iraq during the coup, whether he had any part in the Farhud, or where exactly he went when he left Palestine in 1937, on which they disagree.
Partition had been proposed in 1937 and abandoned by the end of 1938, and the London conference of early 1939 had ended without agreement (see ).
Britain then set its own course.
Parliament approved the policy on 23 May.
The familiar account treats Israel's founding as the gradual fulfillment of the Balfour Declaration's promise, unfolding step by step from 1917 to 1948.

In 1939 the power that had issued the Balfour Declaration and held the Mandate wrote down, in its own words, a policy that pointed in the other direction, and the men who led the Zionist movement read it as Britain reneging on Balfour entirely.
It declared that "it is not part of their policy that Palestine should become a Jewish State."
Its stated objective was "the establishment within ten years of an independent Palestine State," bound to the United Kingdom by treaty, after a transitional period.

It provided for "some 75,000 immigrants over the next five years": a quota of 10,000 Jewish immigrants a year for five years, plus 25,000 refugees to be admitted when the High Commissioner was satisfied that provision could be made for them.
After the five years, "no further Jewish immigration will be permitted unless the Arabs of Palestine are prepared to acquiesce in it."
The effect, as Churchill quoted the paper back to the Commons, was to bring the Jewish population to approximately one-third of the total.
Most levers in the paper sat with the British administration.
After five years the decision passed, on immigration alone, to the Arabs of Palestine, whose acquiescence was now the condition for any further Jewish entry.

Issued in May 1939, months before the war that would make Palestine one of the few remaining escape routes for European Jews, it arrived, as Zionist leaders saw it, at the exact moment the need to leave was most urgent.
Six months earlier, Kristallnacht had shown what that need meant inside Germany.

The sources for this account document the restriction and its reception; they do not set out Britain's full stated rationale for it, which this book treats in its account of the Mandate's strategic and administrative considerations elsewhere.
The paper was debated in the House of Commons on 22 and 23 May 1939, and it met sharp criticism in the House.
Leo Amery called the policy a repudiation of Britain's pledges.
Winston Churchill called it "an act of repudiation" and said he would vote against it.

For Labour, Herbert Morrison called it "a cynical breach of pledges given to the Jews and the world, including America," and urged that it be referred to the Permanent Mandates Commission of the League of Nations.
The government nonetheless carried the House, and the policy was approved on 23 May.
(Labour's later record against the paper, and what was expected of it once in power, is followed in .)
The Jewish Agency answered in its own terms, as a legal case.
On 31 May 1939 Chaim Weizmann wrote to the High Commissioner that the White Paper meant "denying to the Jewish people the right to reconstitute their National Home in Palestine."

The Agency's memorandum to the Permanent Mandates Commission, published in London in June as The Jewish Case against the Palestine White Paper, argued that the paper breached Articles 2, 6 and 15 of the Mandate, and that an Arab veto on immigration could not be squared with the Mandate's duty to "facilitate Jewish immigration."
In its strongest form, the case was that the Mandate bound Britain, and that a duty to facilitate immigration could not be turned into a power to end it.
The Arab reception is harder to state in one line, and the sources here pull in two directions.

The United States consul general in Jerusalem, George Wadsworth, reported to Washington in early June 1939 that the promise of an independent state within ten years was broadly acceptable to Arabs and strongly opposed by Zionists.
Jews, he wrote, responded with bitterness and "a sullen determination to continue" building the national home.
Arabs showed "very obvious relief," but distrusted British intentions and resented the indefinite ban on the return of the Mufti of Jerusalem, Hajj Amin al-Husseini.
The Arab Higher Committee nevertheless rejected the White Paper.
It demanded a complete prohibition of Jewish immigration and, by one account, dismissed the promised independence as illusory.

According to a secondary summary of Benny Morris's work, Morris attributes al-Husseini's rejection in part to the fact that the plan did not place him at the head of the future state; Morris's own text has not been read, and the attribution should be treated as his interpretation, reported at second hand.
The other reading takes the committee at its own word: it wanted a complete halt to Jewish immigration, which the paper did not give, and it did not trust the independence the paper promised.

Either reading can stand alongside Wadsworth's report, which describes relief at the paper's provisions together with distrust of British intentions; the formal rejection came from the committee, the relief from the wider Arab public he observed.
The Permanent Mandates Commission took up the paper at its 36th session, from 8 to 29 June 1939.
Its members held unanimously that the policy was not in accordance with the interpretation the Commission had always placed on the Mandate.
On the harder question, whether the policy nevertheless conformed to the Mandate, they split.
By a majority of one, four members to three, the Commission found that it could not say the policy conformed.
The minority of three held that existing circumstances could justify the policy, provided the League Council did not object.
Against the paper's conformity with the Mandate stood the Jewish Agency, Morrison and Churchill in the Commons, and four of the Commission's seven members.
For it, or for its justification in the circumstances, stood the British government, which carried Parliament, and the Commission's minority of three.
The body that could have decided the matter for the League never did.
War broke out before the League Council could act, and the White Paper never came before it.
Britain had meanwhile begun to apply the paper's terms.
In July 1939, citing illegal immigration, it suspended the next six-month quota of controlled Jewish immigration.
In the Commons debate of 20 July Malcolm MacDonald said it "would have been a breach of that policy" not to suspend it.
Once the war began, the Jewish leadership in Palestine faced a Britain that was enforcing the White Paper and fighting Germany at the same time.
David Ben-Gurion's answer, as it is usually given, was to help the British army "as if there were no White Paper" and to fight the White Paper "as if there were no war."
Three years later, in a New York hotel, the movement's answer to the White Paper took the form of an explicit demand for a Jewish commonwealth (see ).

On the figures compiled for this library's account of the censuses, Jews made up about 11 percent of Palestine's population in 1922 and 17 percent in 1931; by the United Nations committee's estimate of late 1946 the share was 33 percent.

They do not give the Commons division on 23 May, the number of the 75,000 places actually used by the end of the five years, or the text and zones of the land-transfer regulations Britain issued under the paper's land clause; each of these is reported elsewhere but has not been verified, and the account above does not rely on them.
Nor do they settle what moved the Arab Higher Committee to reject a paper that, by Wadsworth's report, many Arabs received with relief.
And the legal question was left open by history itself: the only body empowered to rule on the paper's conformity with the Mandate never met to do so.
Woodhead and St James's Palace, 1938–1939
The Peel plan did not survive its first two years.

Its publication in July 1937 had been followed by the restart of the revolt that autumn and by refusals from both sides, told in ; a United Nations paper later summed up the outcome as rejection by both.
London's next step was not to impose the plan but to test whether it could be carried out at all.
For that purpose Britain sent a technical commission under Sir John Woodhead.
It had four members: Woodhead, Sir Alison Russell, Percival Waterfield and Thomas Reid.
It investigated in Palestine from April to early August 1938.
The difference from Peel was one of mandate.
Peel had been asked to investigate the causes of the revolt.
Woodhead's commission, formally the Palestine Partition Commission, was asked a narrower practical question: whether partition could be made to work.
Its conclusion was that no practical partition plan could be devised, because both Jews and Arabs refused partition.
The British government accepted its conclusion that partition was politically, administratively and financially impossible.
Having dropped partition, Britain tried negotiation.
It invited the Palestinian Arabs, the neighbouring Arab states and the Jewish Agency to a conference in London in early 1939, known as the St James's Palace conference.

The Palestinian delegation was led by Jamal al-Husseini, a founding member of the Arab Higher Committee in 1936, and included Awni Abd al-Hadi, Musa al-Alami and others, with George Antonius as a secretary.
Raghib al-Nashashibi joined two days after the opening.
Egypt sent a delegation, as did Iraq, under its Prime Minister Nuri al-Said, and Saudi Arabia, under Prince Faisal.
The Jewish Agency's delegation was led by Chaim Weizmann, with Ben-Gurion dominant in its decisions.
It included non-Zionists and Rabbi Stephen Wise.
The Arab side came as a regional coalition, with three states represented alongside the Palestinians, which suggests that Palestine had become a question for the surrounding governments as well.
And the Palestinian delegation brought Husseini and Nashashibi figures together in one delegation, after the split described in the revolt section.
The Arab Higher Committee's delegation refused to sit with the Zionist delegation, so the British held separate meetings with each side.
Britain was the only party that sat with both.
One strand of the talks went back to the First World War.
An Anglo-Arab committee under the Lord Chancellor, Lord Maugham, examined the Hussein–McMahon correspondence of 1915–16.
It found that the Arab case had been given too little weight.
But the two sides on the committee could not agree on the central point: whether Palestine had been included in the British pledge of Arab independence.
The finding carried weight because of who chaired it, Britain's own Lord Chancellor.
It did not settle the question on which the Arab case rested.
The conference failed, and the British government said so in its own words.

In the White Paper that followed, it recorded that after talks lasting several weeks, "Neither the Arab nor the Jewish delegation felt able to accept these proposals, and the conferences failed to reach an agreement."
Britain then issued its own policy.
One reading stresses British retreat: having proposed partition, London dropped it within sixteen months, once the revolt reached its height and both communities had refused the plan.
Another stresses that the refusals were real and mutual, as Woodhead's own conclusion and the 1949 United Nations paper both record.
Britain's stated reason for abandoning partition was the refusal of both peoples, and the timing places that decision at the peak of the Arab revolt.
The sources here do not name the British ministers who ran the London talks, nor give the conference's exact dates or the populations of the Woodhead plans.
They do not record what the separate meetings with the Arab states' delegations discussed.
The Arab Revolt, 1936–1939
In November 1935 British forces killed Izz al-Din al-Qassam, and historians name his death as part of the background to what followed.
The uprising of 1936 followed the sharpest rise in Jewish immigration under the Mandate, and it came in the same decade that produced the Irgun (1931) and, later, Lehi (1940).
Each of these movements, Arab and Jewish, formed in reaction to the other side and to British policy.
Palestinian Arabs killed two Jews near Tulkarm, Jewish retaliation followed, and riots broke out in Jaffa and Tel Aviv.
The Jewish Virtual Library describes it as an attack on a Jewish bus and gives three Jewish dead, not two.
On 19 April a newly formed Arab National Committee in Nablus called for a general strike, the withholding of taxes and a boycott of Jewish products.
Local national committees across the country then united on 25 April as the Arab Higher Committee.
The new committee was led by Hajj Amin al-Husseini, Mufti of Jerusalem.
It declared a general strike with three demands: an end to Jewish immigration, an end to land sales to Jews, and an independent national government.
Another account dates al-Husseini's own strike call, as the committee's president, to 16 May 1936.
According to the list drawn from the Peel report, it brought together the leaders of rival clans and parties.
Amin al-Husseini was president.

Raghib al-Nashashibi represented the National Defense Party, Jamal al-Husseini the Palestine Arab Party, Yaqub al-Ghusayn the Youth Congress, Abd al-Latif Salah the National Bloc and Husayn al-Khalidi the Reform Party.
Awni Abd al-Hadi of the Istiqlal was general secretary and Ahmed Hilmi Pasha treasurer.
The coalition did not last long: Raghib al-Nashashibi left soon after it was formed.
It does not mean that every participant in three years of fighting took orders from al-Husseini, and the sources do not make that claim.
Its end is recorded in a British document.
On 12 October 1936 the General Officer Commanding issued a Special Order announcing that the strike and armed rebellion had been "called off unconditionally by the Higher Arab Committee."
The rulers of neighbouring Arab states had mediated its end.
Different sources name them as the rulers of Transjordan, Iraq, Saudi Arabia and Yemen.
Some sources stress the rulers' appeal, together with British concessions and the threat of martial law.
The same Special Order gave the British army's own count of the cost of the strike period.
It recorded 25 British soldiers killed and 120 wounded, 7 British police killed and 40 wounded, and 9 Palestine police killed and 64 wounded.
London's political answer was already in motion.
Peel's proposal was followed by the revolt's second phase.
On 26 September 1937, four gunmen described as followers of al-Qassam killed Lewis Andrews, District Commissioner for Galilee, as he left a service at Christ Church in Nazareth.
Within 24 hours police had detained about 100 Palestinian Arabs.
Britain then moved against the political leadership.
It outlawed the Arab Higher Committee, around 30 September 1937, stripped al-Husseini of his offices, arrested members of the committee and deported several of them to the Seychelles.
The sequence of al-Husseini's flight is told slightly differently in different sources.
Other sources place his refuge in the Haram al-Sharif and his escape in the autumn of 1937.
They disagree on where he went: Lebanon, according to Unpacked, or Syria, according to the Jewish Virtual Library.
The account that sends him to Lebanon continues to Iraq, and historians document that he went on directing the revolt from exile.
By Unpacked's account, he authorized attacks from abroad on Britons, on Jews, and on Palestinians considered collaborators.
Britain sent about 20,000 troops.

Its measures included house demolitions, executions, the outlawing of the Arab Higher Committee, arrests and expulsions of activists, indefinite detention, collective fines on whole neighborhoods, and the disarming of Palestinians.
Matthew Hughes's 2019 study of the campaign groups these methods into eight categories.
Between 108 and 122 Palestinian Arabs were hanged in the 1930s.
The reviewer of Hughes's study compares this with the 1,090 Kenyans hanged during the Mau Mau emergency of the 1950s.
Two Jews were hanged.
Raghib al-Nashashibi, a former mayor of Jerusalem, favoured compromise with the British; the Mufti opposed it.
Their rivalry produced hundreds of killings of Palestinians by Palestinians.
The Nashashibi-aligned "peace bands" were raised with British and Jewish military and financial help to fight the rebels.
Hughes's study of the peace bands supplies the detail.
By March 1938 Fakhri Nashashibi was organizing them from Lebanon.
Fakhri 'Abd al-Hadi, a former rebel commander, returned to Palestine on 21 September 1938 with backing from the British consul in Damascus, Gilbert MacKereth.
Britain paid band members £P6 a month.
Both men were later killed: Husseini-backed gunmen killed Fakhri Nashashibi in Iraq in 1941, and 'Abd al-Hadi was murdered in 1943.
The 1941 killing belongs to al-Husseini's exile, which continued into an alliance with Nazi Germany from 1941: he met Hitler and recruited for the Waffen-SS, a record set out in .
The overwhelming majority of Palestinian Arabs had no part in it and no say over it.
Britain paid the bands that fought them.
And the general strike itself pushed the Yishuv toward a more self-reliant economy.
Jewish attacks on Arab civilians are part of the same record.
In November 1937 the Irgun abandoned the policy of restraint and killed ten Arab civilians on the day later called "Black Sunday."
After an attack on an Arab bus in April 1938, the British hanged Shlomo Ben-Yosef in June 1938.
He was one of the two Jews hanged during the revolt.
By Unpacked's count, at least 250 Palestinian Arabs had died at Irgun hands by the summer of 1939.
The Irgun was formed in 1931, and its turn to reprisal belongs to the pattern the opening of this section described.
Like the rebels' attacks on Jewish civilians, it is named here for what it was.
For Arab deaths, the most detailed figure comes from Walid Khalidi's analysis of British statistics.
He counts 3,832 Palestinian Arabs killed by the British and 1,200 killed in internal strife, 5,032 in all, with 14,760 wounded.
Official British figures are lower and divided differently.
They give over 2,000 Arabs killed in combat, 108 hanged and 961 killed by "gang and terrorist activities."
The Jewish Virtual Library estimates roughly 5,000 dead, 15,000 wounded and 5,600 imprisoned.
Middle East Eye gives about 5,000 killed, 15,000–20,000 wounded and 5,600 imprisoned.
At the high end, Unpacked (Noam Weissman, 2024), drawing on Oren Kessler, gives 5,000–8,000 Palestinian Arab dead and says about 20 percent of Palestinian Arab men were jailed at some point.
The summary published by the Palestinian church committee states that over 10 percent of Palestinian Arab men aged 20 to 60 were killed, wounded, imprisoned or exiled.
For Jewish and British deaths, the scholarly and reference figures cluster closely, and they are the record: roughly 400 to 415 Jews and 100 to 200 British.
Ori Yehudai gives about 415 Jews and 100 British.
The Jewish Virtual Library gives 415 Jewish deaths for 1936–39.
Fred Strickert gives nearly 400 Jews and 200 Britons.
Hughes's reviewer writes of "hundreds" of Jews.
Much higher Jewish and British figures, attributed to the US Holocaust Memorial Museum, also circulate.
According to the review of Hughes's study, about 40,000 Christian Arabs and others left for Syria and Lebanon during the revolt.
In the Palestinian national reading, as Middle East Eye puts it, the revolt was "the most sustained armed resistance" against the Mandate, a national uprising crushed by brutal British repression.
A critical reading, given by Unpacked, stresses that the rebels also turned on Palestinians, extorting and killing those they deemed disloyal, with leaders encouraging it.
Its evidence is the intra-Palestinian killing and al-Husseini's reported authorization of attacks on supposed collaborators.
Hughes's scholarship takes both seriously.
He concludes that the peace bands "never won the war for the British."
Collaboration, he finds, was driven more by survival, personal gain and feuds than by political conviction, and "Palestinian collaboration in the 1930s was too partial to damn the Arab revolt."
The Palestinian leadership was left weak, divided and in exile.
Military cooperation between Britain and the Zionist movement deepened, a story taken up in .
And the general strike pushed the Yishuv toward a more self-reliant economy.

The ledger of these years shows the sequence at a glance: the revolt in 1936, Peel's partition and transfer proposal in 1937 with the Arab Higher Committee objecting, and in 1939 the White Paper's limit on immigration, which the Zionist movement opposed.

The death toll is the clearest gap: the Arab figures range from British official counts to 8,000, and the sourced Jewish and British figures run from about 400 to 415 and from 100 to 200, beside much higher figures that could not be verified.
The sources do not settle the exact date of al-Husseini's flight or its first destination, or how much of the second phase he actually directed from abroad.
The leadership that had called the strike in 1936 ended the revolt divided and in exile, just as London turned from partition to a policy of its own.
The Peel Commission: Partition's First Draft
Britain's political answer to the revolt was a royal commission.
The Palestine Royal Commission, known after its chairman as the Peel Commission, had six members.
In its place there would be an independent Arab state, formed by joining part of Palestine to Transjordan, and an independent Jewish state in another part of the country.
Jerusalem and some other places would stay under British mandate, in a British-administered corridor that included the city.
The Jewish state would be small.
The sources give its size differently: 17 percent of the country according to Ori Yehudai, about 20 percent according to Fred Strickert.
That recommendation, the first time population transfer appeared in an official British document, is the subject of the next section, .
A common belief holds that partition was the United Nations' original idea in 1947, reached through a neutral international process.
A British royal commission proposed partition a decade earlier, and both sides had already responded to it, in different ways, before the United Nations took up the question.
The UN committee's 1947 map bore a documented resemblance to this earlier partition thinking, which is examined in .
The two maps were not identical line for line, and the claim here is only that the idea came first from London.
The first came from the Twentieth Zionist Congress, which met in 1937.
The movement was deeply divided over the plan, and the Congress produced a carefully balanced position.
It accepted partition in principle, or at least did not reject it, and it authorized continued negotiation with Britain.
Some write that the Congress "accepted" the principle of partition; others that it "did not reject it outright."
A United Nations working paper of 1949 put it more starkly than either: it summarized the outcome as rejection of the plan by both Jews and Arabs.
The strongest form of the "acceptance" reading is that the movement's leadership accepted the idea of a Jewish state in part of the country and wanted to bargain over its size.
The strongest form of the "rejection" reading is that the Congress refused the plan actually on the table, since the boundaries were the plan.
The second response was the Arab Higher Committee's, and it was unambiguous.
The committee, led by al-Husseini, rejected the plan outright, with no conditional language.
It does not show that every person in the Arab population held identical views on partition, and the sources do not measure what others thought.
The third response came from the Revisionist movement.
Ze'ev (Vladimir) Jabotinsky had founded the Union of Revisionist Zionists, Hatzohar, in 1925.
Its core territorial claim was that the Jewish state must cover both banks of the Jordan River: what later became Israel, the West Bank and Gaza, and the whole of Transjordan.
In 1929–1930 Jabotinsky put the argument in geographical terms:
"What does the word Palestine mean?
Palestine is a territory whose chief geographical feature is this: that the River Jordan does not delineate its frontier, but flows through its center."
The movement's anthem made the same claim in verse: "Two Banks has the Jordan — This is ours and, that is as well."
The claim was territorial and historical rather than primarily religious; Jabotinsky was not himself religious.
He argued that Britain's 1922 separation of Transjordan from the Palestine Mandate had been an arbitrary partition, one that denied Jews the land needed to absorb millions of future immigrants.
