Testifying before the Peel Commission, he argued forcefully against any partition and for Jewish rights to the whole of Mandate Palestine, Transjordan included.
It was not the mainstream Zionist position of 1937, which, as the Congress's resolution shows, was far more ambiguous.
The later history of this claim, through Herut and Likud, is traced in .
According to Unpacked and the Jewish Virtual Library, Peel's partition proposal prompted rebel groups to restart the revolt in the autumn of 1937.
The 1937 rejection is often used as evidence for a later slogan: that the Arabs "rejected every offer."
Arab leaders did reject the 1937 Peel plan, and later the 1947 partition plan.
Israel's 1949 refugee offer at Lausanne was made only within a full peace and was later withdrawn.
The 2000 Camp David offer is disputed by participants, and some on the American side say it was never written down.
Peel, in particular, was refused by both: outright by the Arab Higher Committee, and in its actual boundaries by the Zionist Congress.
The precise share of the country allotted to the Jewish state differs between sources, and the boundaries of the plan are not set out in the material here.
The documents do not say how the Congress's delegates divided, beyond the description of the movement as deeply divided.
Within sixteen months, London would abandon the plan altogether.
Biltmore: From National Home to Commonwealth
Less than four months after Wannsee, in May 1942, the Zionist movement met in New York and changed its stated goal.
The founding of Israel is often told as the gradual, natural fulfillment of the Balfour Declaration, unfolding step by step from 1917 to 1948.
Balfour's 1917 language was deliberately ambiguous.
It ended in May 1942, in a New York hotel, when an authoritative Zionist body for the first time demanded in so many words a sovereign Jewish Commonwealth covering all of Mandatory Palestine.
The road to that hotel began with a British document.
In May 1939 the British government issued a White Paper that capped Jewish immigration to Palestine at 75,000 over five years, with any further immigration subject to Arab consent.
In effect it would have frozen the Jewish population of Palestine as a permanent minority.
Zionist leaders read it as a direct abandonment of the promise of 1917, and it arrived at the moment when Europe's Jews had the most urgent need to leave.
The White Paper's full terms and the debate it caused in London and Geneva are set out in .
What matters here is the line the sources draw from it: Biltmore was triggered directly by the White Paper, which Zionist leaders took as Britain reneging on Balfour entirely.
A regular Zionist Congress could not be convened in wartime, yet the pressure to act was mounting fast.

The White Paper had closed most of the door to Palestine just as the Holocaust was accelerating, and reports of the scale of Nazi atrocities were reaching American Jewish leaders through 1941 and early 1942.
The conference at the Biltmore Hotel was called to fill the gap a cancelled Congress had left, and it was treated as the functional equivalent of one.
Among them were Chaim Weizmann, president of the World Zionist Organization, and David Ben-Gurion, who led the Jewish Agency's leadership in Palestine.
Weizmann favored continued diplomatic engagement with Britain, the approach that had defined the movement for 25 years.
Ben-Gurion, speaking for the Jewish population of Palestine directly, argued that explicit, uncompromising statehood was the only path that could work.
Biltmore is documented as the moment Ben-Gurion's approach prevailed.
That outcome should not be stretched further than the record allows: it does not show that Weizmann's diplomacy was abandoned altogether, or that he opposed the final resolution.
It shows that the strategic tension between the two men was settled, for the moment, in Ben-Gurion's direction.
The resolution's key sentence urged that Palestine be established as a Jewish Commonwealth, integrated into the structure of the postwar democratic world.
It also demanded that the Jewish Agency, not the British Mandatory administration, be vested with control over immigration.
Both parts answered the White Paper directly.
Britain had made future immigration depend on Arab consent; Biltmore asked that it depend on a Jewish body instead.
The historian Rafael Medoff's research on the conference addresses the point directly.
"Commonwealth" was not meant to suggest anything less than a sovereign state.
The delegates had in mind a status like that of Australia or Canada: fully sovereign in practice.
But measured against Balfour's undefined "national home," the change was an escalation, and it was meant as one.
In October 1942 the Zionist General Council formally adopted the program as official policy.

That step converted it from the position of the delegates who happened to attend into the platform of the whole organized Zionist movement, and it remained the movement's operative goal until late 1946.
The record here documents the top-level decision; it does not trace how each national Zionist body adopted the program in turn.
In America that work ran through the American Zionist Emergency Council, which took the Biltmore position into Congress and the party conventions.

By 1944, two years after the hotel conference, according to Silver's own biographical record, Abba Hillel Silver had lobbied for a Palestine resolution and both major American parties had put Palestine into their platforms.
It came from two directions: from those who preferred to continue the diplomatic course, and from those who wanted an explicitly binational state instead of a Jewish one.

Other Jewish dissent from the program, including the American Council for Judaism and the American Jewish Conference of 1943, is not documented here, and this book leaves it undescribed rather than describe it without sources.
The fair summary is the one the record supports: Biltmore marks the moment the demand for a state became explicit and dominant in the Zionist movement.
It is not evidence that every Zionist voice agreed.
Two readings of Biltmore follow from the same facts.

In one, it was a response to emergency: a movement that had worked within British promises for a generation watched Britain close the door in 1939, learned of mass murder in Europe, and concluded that only sovereignty, with control of its own immigration, could guarantee a refuge.

In the other, it was a claim to sovereignty over the whole of Mandatory Palestine and its Arab population, made by reversing the very condition, Arab consent, that the White Paper had set on further immigration.
The documents support the facts both readings rest on: the White Paper as trigger, the demand for all of Mandatory Palestine, the Jewish Agency's control of immigration.
It does not give the vote at Biltmore or the size of any dissent inside the hall.
It does not record how the program's claim to all of Mandatory Palestine was squared, by those who voted for it, with the Arab population living there.
And it does not trace the program's reception among Palestine's Arab leaders.
What is not in doubt is the change itself: in May 1942, in New York, the movement's stated goal changed from a national home to a state, and in October 1942 that change became binding policy.
The Ships: What the Immigration Limit Cost, 1940–1947

The White Paper of May 1939, whose text and reception are set out in , allowed some 75,000 Jewish immigrants over five years and provided that illegal immigrants would be deducted from the yearly quotas .
In July 1939, citing illegal immigration, Britain suspended the next six-month quota altogether .

Over seven years, three vessels marked the stages of the policy's enforcement: the Patria in Haifa harbor in November 1940, the Struma in the Black Sea in February 1942, and the Exodus 1947 in July 1947.
Under the White Paper, entry to Palestine came through the quota, and illegal arrivals counted against it.
The decision about what happened to refugees who reached the coast without permits lay with the British authorities, who in these cases chose deportation or refused entry outright.
The Haganah, as the first case shows, tried to stop one deportation by force.
The Patria, Haifa, November 1940.

In the autumn of 1940 British authorities decided to deport roughly 1,800 Jewish refugees, who had reached Palestine without valid entry permits, to Mauritius, a British colony in the Indian Ocean, for the duration of the war.
They were to be carried there aboard the Patria .
The Haganah's plan to prevent this was narrow and specific.
It would place a limited explosive charge below the waterline, damage the ship just enough to delay its departure and force a change in British policy, and do so without endangering the passengers .
By most documented counts 267 to 268 people died, most of them the refugees the operation had been meant to keep in Palestine .

The Haganah's own postwar historical accounts describe the sinking as a serious operational failure with a devastating and unintended human cost; the organization that carried it out did not conceal or deny it .

Every documented account, the Haganah's included, describes a catastrophic accident inside an operation meant to help the people who died, and nothing in the record shows any intent to harm the passengers.
To describe it as anything else would misstate the record, and to omit it, or to blame the deaths on Britain alone, would misstate it in the other direction.
The policy created the deportation order; the bomb that sank the ship was the Haganah's.
The Struma, the Black Sea, February 1942.
The Struma carried Jewish refugees from Romania.
It was denied entry to Palestine under the White Paper's immigration limit and spent weeks stranded at Istanbul before it was forced back out into the Black Sea .
On 24 February 1942 it was torpedoed, most likely by a Soviet submarine operating under standing orders to sink any vessel in the area.
Two questions about the Struma need to be kept apart.
Saying that the submarine did not target refugees does not clear the policy that left them there, and saying the policy left them there does not make the British government the author of the torpedo.
Taken together, the Patria and the Struma killed more than 1,000 people, refugees trying to reach the one place whose doors the White Paper was narrowing  .
The Patria's dead died because of a Haganah miscalculation; the Struma's because of a third party's mistaken attack.
When Lehi gunmen killed Lord Moyne in Cairo in November 1944, the group blamed him for turning back refugee ships, as  describes .
The sources do not tie Moyne to either of these two ships by name, and this book does not.
In July 1947 the Royal Navy intercepted the Exodus 1947, which carried roughly 4,500 Holocaust survivors, and forcibly returned its passengers to displaced-persons camps in Germany .
Its significance lay less in its immediate human cost, which was real but not comparable to the death tolls of the Patria and the Struma, than in what followed.

International press coverage of the interception became a major, documented turning point in Western public sympathy for the Zionist cause, a few months before the United Nations partition vote of November 1947 .

On one side, historians credit the Exodus coverage as a genuine contributor to the shift in Western opinion ahead of November 1947: the sight of Holocaust survivors being returned to camps in Germany reached a world audience through the press .

On the other side, the documented record of the American decision, told in a later volume of this library through the Henderson memorandum, the Joint Chiefs' warnings and Clifford's electoral calculus, shows that the United States' vote turned mainly on domestic political pressure, not international sympathy .

They do not name the passengers of either wartime ship or give a full manifest for the Struma; they describe the Soviet submarine's role as likely, not certain; and they do not record what the Mandatory government itself concluded about either sinking.
Nor do they measure the Exodus coverage's effect on any particular government's vote, which is why the weighing above stays a weighing and not a verdict.
Roosevelt's Position: Warm in Public, Cautious in Private
Britain set its Palestine policy down in a numbered command paper.
Washington's position in the war years was harder to pin down.

A common account of Franklin Roosevelt holds that he was a committed supporter of Jewish statehood, and that his successor simply failed to honor the one specific promise he had made to the Saudi king, Ibn Saud, before he died.

It shows two Roosevelts, each documented: one who sent warm, friendly messages to American Jewish organizations, and one who, in private meetings and in writing to Arab governments, held a cooler and more cautious line.

Rabbi Stephen Wise, a leader of Reform Judaism who co-chaired the American Zionist Emergency Council, met Roosevelt several times during the war, as did Chaim Weizmann, both seeking firmer support for a Jewish state.

Wise left at least one of these private meetings, by his own account, "surprised and shocked" by the president's actual position, which was considerably cooler than the messages Roosevelt sent to Jewish audiences.
Its limit is equally plain: it records Wise's characterization of his own reaction, not a transcript of what Roosevelt said.
Roosevelt approved a State Department plan to suppress public discussion of the Palestine question for the duration of the war.
The approval is documented in declassified records examined by historians studying the gap between Roosevelt's stated and actual policy.
The third is the State Department's own later description of its correspondence.
On 5 April 1945 Roosevelt wrote to Ibn Saud, following their meeting aboard the USS Quincy in February, which is told in full in .

When the department confirmed the text of that letter in a press release of 18 October 1945, it described it as one of "several letters addressed by President Roosevelt to Arab leaders," each carrying the same assurance that the United States would consult before acting.
It is the government's own contemporary statement that the promise went to more than one Arab leader.
The release does not name every recipient government beyond Ibn Saud, and the sources here do not supply the list.

Historians working on this period, including work cited in the Brandeis Center's review of newly available documents, note that Roosevelt's warm, boilerplate pro-Zionist messages to Jewish organizational events served political narratives better than his actual Palestine policy did, which was more cautious and committed to consultation.
That changes how the Ibn Saud letter should be read without changing anything about the letter itself.
The meeting, the letter and the later departure from its terms under Truman remain as documented.
What the wider record adds is that the commitment to Ibn Saud was not an exceptional promise from an otherwise pro-Zionist president.

It was consistent with a repeated, more cautious position that Roosevelt held throughout the war, expressed privately and in writing to several governments, and distinct from his warmer public rhetoric.
There are two ways to read Roosevelt, and each has a serious case.

The first reads him as an instrumentalist on Palestine: a president who gave Jewish audiences the language they wanted, gave Arab rulers written assurances of consultation, and approved silence on the question at home while the war lasted.
Its evidence is the evidence above, two pieces of it in Roosevelt's own government's records and one in the words of a Zionist leader who had expected better.
They do not establish which motive produced it, and the sources here make no claim about why Roosevelt chose to speak in two voices.
What the record leaves open, then, is Roosevelt's purpose rather than his conduct.

It is clear that he approved the suppression plan, that a leading Zionist came away from a private meeting shocked by his position, and that he sent the consultation assurance to more than one Arab leader.

It is not clear what was said in the meetings that shocked Wise, how the suppression plan worked in practice, which governments received the other letters, or what Roosevelt himself intended the future of Palestine to be.
Roosevelt's Hidden Decline and the Choice of Truman, 1944
On 28 March 1944, seven months before the presidential election, a Navy cardiologist examined Franklin Roosevelt and found serious heart disease.
Roosevelt's official physician told the public the opposite of what the cardiologist had found.
And the man chosen that year as Roosevelt's running mate, who would inherit the presidency and with it the American decisions on Palestine, was kept as uninformed as the voters.
The story belongs in a history of Palestine for one reason.
The American commitments of these years, Roosevelt's private assurances to Arab leaders and the public promises of the 1944 platforms, would be carried out or broken by his successor.
The examination took place at Bethesda.
The cardiologist, Dr. Howard Bruenn, found acute congestive heart failure, an enlarged heart, hypertension and hypertensive heart disease.
He did not volunteer a prognosis even to Roosevelt himself, who, by the available account, asked no questions .
One historian later wrote that the findings were guarded "on a level with the Manhattan Project."
What the record does not show is Roosevelt's own state of mind: that he asked no questions is documented; what he privately understood or suspected is not.
Roosevelt's official physician since 1933 was Ross McIntire, an ear, nose and throat specialist with no training in cardiology.
It does not establish McIntire's motive, or exactly how much of Bruenn's findings he knew at the moment he spoke.
The Lahey memorandum.
Frank Lahey, a Boston surgeon, set down his conclusion in a written memo dated 10 July 1944:
Roosevelt was unlikely to survive a full fourth term.
The memo was placed in a Boston law firm's vault.
It was not found and made public until decades after Roosevelt's death, more than sixty years after it was written .
The 1944 Democratic convention replaced the sitting vice-president, Henry Wallace, with Senator Harry Truman of Missouri  .
The reasons for Wallace's removal, and the question of whether Palestine had anything to do with it, are examined in .

Set beside what Roosevelt's doctors knew, the choice of a running mate was in practice, though not in public understanding, the choice of the next president, and the voters who ratified it in November did not know that.
It does not show that every party leader involved in replacing Wallace knew the specifics of Bruenn's or Lahey's findings.
Why Truman.
The documented reasons for choosing Truman were political.

As chairman of the wartime Truman Committee, which investigated profiteering by defense contractors, he had earned real credibility and was ranked by 1944 among the most respected officials in Washington.
But he had also opposed Roosevelt's earlier bid for a third term, which made him tolerable to the conservative Southern Democrats who distrusted Wallace's leftward tilt.
Contemporary observers mocked the choice as "the Missouri Compromise," because Truman was no faction's first choice, only a candidate enough factions could accept   .
Truman's career had been launched by Tom Pendergast, the corrupt political boss of Kansas City, and party leaders had to work to establish that Truman was not "a Pendergast lackey"  .
A different theory is sometimes offered: that Truman was chosen because his personal finances or tax affairs left him open to pressure.
On the record, Truman won the nomination by being broadly tolerable, not because anyone held something over him.
Several historical accounts describe the new vice-president as kept "entirely in the dark" about how ill Roosevelt was .
The man about to inherit the presidency, and with it the American side of every decision on Palestine that this library follows through 1948, had no more medical information than the public.
Public speculation about Roosevelt's appearance and vigor was itself widespread and documented, and the accounts do not say Truman had no sense at all that the president was failing.
What they say is that he lacked the specific findings Bruenn and Lahey had made.
Roosevelt died on 12 April 1945, two months after his meeting with King Ibn Saud aboard the USS Quincy and a week after his written assurance to the king .
The documents establish the diagnosis, the public statements that contradicted it, the hidden memo and Truman's exclusion from the medical facts.
They do not establish what Roosevelt himself believed about his prognosis, what McIntire knew when he spoke, or which party leaders, if any, knew the specific findings when they chose Truman.
Whether the course of American policy on Palestine would have differed under a healthier Roosevelt is a question this record cannot answer, and this book does not speculate on it.
Henry Wallace and Zionism

In 1944 the Democratic Party replaced Vice President Henry Wallace on its ticket with Senator Harry Truman, the man who would become president within a year and who, in 1948, would recognize the state of Israel.
Seen backwards from 1948, the swap invites a suspicion: that Wallace's views on Palestine had something to do with his removal.
A version of the story circulates in which Zionist-aligned donors and organizations preferred Truman after Wallace said something unfavorable about Palestine or about Jews.
Start with Wallace himself.
His interest in Zionism began in the 1930s, while he was serving as Roosevelt's Secretary of Agriculture, and it came through a working relationship rather than a political one.
The soil scientist Walter Clay Lowdermilk had examined agricultural conditions in British Mandatory Palestine, and Wallace absorbed his enthusiasm.
Wallace later recalled of Lowdermilk: "I don't think he has any Jewish blood, but he was the most complete Zionist convert anyone could ask for."
Through that influence Wallace came to see the Jewish settlers in Palestine as frontiersmen on the American pattern.
Wallace's sympathy was a personal conviction that he described in his own later recollection, and it predated the convention fight by roughly a decade.
It does not prove that every later public statement he made on Palestine was free of political calculation, and the sources do not claim that it was.

Historical accounts state plainly that Roosevelt grew wary of Wallace's left-wing, pro-Soviet political tilt, and that this broader concern, not any statement about Palestine, Jews or Zionism, drove the push to replace him.
Wallace kept real support to the end.

Labor organizations, including the CIO and the UAW, campaigned for him at the convention itself, and a Gallup poll taken on the day of the convention showed 65% of delegates still favoring Wallace over Truman.
The same section sets out the documented reasons Truman was chosen in Wallace's place.
The sources identify the general pattern historians treat as the main driver of Wallace's removal, and that pattern has no documented connection to Palestine or Zionism.
What they do show is that the Palestine explanation has no documentary basis, while the ideological one does.
Wallace did not leave the story in 1944.
Four years later, running for president as the candidate of the Progressive Party, he returned to the Palestine question from the side opposite to the one the common assumption gives him.

His campaign literature included a booklet, Meet Henry Wallace, written by James Waterman Wise, the son of Rabbi Stephen Wise, the Zionist leader whose wartime dealings with Roosevelt run through this chapter.
The booklet carried a half-page photograph of Wallace "helping the Jewish settlers in Galilee harvest their fields."
At rallies Wallace accused Truman of "playing politics with the lives of the people of Israel," aiming directly at Truman's arms embargo on the newly declared state.
That attack was the center of his appeal to Jewish voters.
It was not the center of his campaign as a whole, which was built mainly on opposition to Cold War policy and support for continued engagement with the Soviet Union.
Israel was one real, deliberate element of a broader platform, not its foundation.

New York newspapers reported widespread talk of Jewish voters leaving Truman for Wallace out of dissatisfaction with Truman's Palestine record, and the result was documented as the lowest share of the New York Jewish vote for any Democratic presidential candidate in modern history, except Jimmy Carter's.
The sources credit Truman's Palestine record as a contributing factor in that decline, not its only cause.
Other parts of Wallace's campaign, and general dissatisfaction with Truman, likely contributed as well.
In 1944 Wallace was removed for reasons that had nothing documented to do with Palestine, and he was himself a long-standing sympathizer of the Zionist project.
In 1948 he became one of Truman's most direct critics from the pro-Israel side, and that criticism cost Truman votes in New York.

If the episode points to any electoral incentive, it points the opposite way from the one usually assumed: in the 1948 record it is being seen as insufficiently pro-Israel, not too closely tied to the cause, that carried a cost.
The sources give the New York result only as a ranking, not as a percentage, so the size of the shift cannot be stated from them.
They do not separate how much of it came from the Palestine issue and how much from Wallace's wider campaign.
And while they find no Palestine dimension to the 1944 decision, they do not record what, if anything, Wallace said in public about Palestine during his vice presidency.
The belief that Wallace was pushed aside over Zionism has no documentary support, and the documents that exist point in the other direction.
Roosevelt and Ibn Saud at Great Bitter Lake
On 14 February 1945, on his way home from the Yalta Conference, Franklin Roosevelt received King Abdulaziz Ibn Saud of Saudi Arabia aboard the USS Quincy in the Great Bitter Lake on the Suez Canal.
Roosevelt arranged it himself, two months before his death and visibly declining.
Ibn Saud, the founding monarch of Saudi Arabia, who reigned from 1932 to 1953, rarely left Arabia and had deep reservations about the journey, yet he traveled by ship specifically for the encounter.
Both men went to real, documented lengths to sit in the same room, and the principal subject between them was the future of Palestine.
Why an American president would make that effort has a plain answer in the record.
By 1945 the Arabian American Oil Company, ARAMCO, had already established the core of the American–Saudi oil relationship.
The meeting reflected an existing, high-stakes strategic partnership that the United States government understood clearly, and the Palestine question was becoming entangled with it.

The sources establish that the relationship existed and mattered; they do not set out the full scope of ARAMCO's operations or the specific terms of the oil relationship at this date, and nothing here should be read as a claim about them.
The meeting ran for roughly five hours by one account and five and a half by another, longer than most of Roosevelt's wartime sessions with other heads of state.
Roosevelt, a habitual chain-smoker, did not smoke throughout it, out of respect for the king's preference.
Its official record is a memorandum of conversation drafted by William Eddy, the United States Minister to Saudi Arabia, and Yusuf Yassin, the Saudi Deputy Foreign Minister.
Both leaders signed it, and the State Department later published it in its own documentary series, Foreign Relations of the United States.
ents: Foreign Relations of the United States

sent: Roosevelt argued the case for Jewish settlement in Palestine: one account describes him arguing for a Jewish state, the memorandum-based account for a Jewish national home.
By multiple accounts, Ibn Saud pressed back directly and forcefully, describing continued large-scale Jewish immigration as an existential threat to Arab interests in the region.

When Roosevelt raised the question of Jewish immigration, the king answered that Jews displaced by Nazi persecution should be given land in Germany, "in the country of their enemies," as he reportedly put it, rather than in Palestine at the expense of its existing Arab population.
In another rendering of the same exchange he proposed that the Jews be given a state in Bavaria.
What Roosevelt gave the king was a specific assurance.

The United States government, he said, would make no decision altering the basic situation in Palestine without full, prior consultation with both Arabs and Jews, and would take no action hostile to the Arab people.

He later called the meeting "so outstanding a success," and told his daughter Anna that he had "learned more about the whole problem of Palestine and the Middle East by talking with Ibn Saud for five minutes than I could have learned in an exchange of two or three dozen letters."
About three weeks after the meeting he wrote formally to Roosevelt, asking him to oppose continued Jewish settlement in Palestine.
Roosevelt answered on 5 April 1945, one week before his death.
In that letter he affirmed that he would "take no action, in my capacity as Chief of the Executive Branch of this Government, which might prove hostile to the Arab people."
The letter reaffirmed in writing the commitment made aboard the Quincy, which closes any gap between an informal verbal impression and a deliberate written undertaking by the president himself.

One account describes Roosevelt as taking the king's concerns seriously enough to respond in writing more than once in the weeks after the meeting; the letter of 5 April is the one whose words the sources quote.
The wording also limits the promise: it is given in Roosevelt's own capacity as head of the executive branch.

Whether such a letter was an isolated gesture or part of a pattern is taken up in , which shows that the State Department, when it confirmed the letter in October 1945, described it as one of several such letters to Arab leaders.
Roosevelt died on 12 April 1945.
On 14 May 1948 his successor, Harry Truman, recognized the state of Israel eleven minutes after its declaration, without the prior consultation with Arab leaders that Roosevelt had promised.

One account traces the recognition decision through Clark Clifford's domestic electoral calculation rather than through consultation with Arab heads of state; that process belongs to the next stage of this history and is told there.
What the documents do not show is Truman's own state of mind about Roosevelt's specific commitment: whether he was personally aware of it, considered himself bound by it, or set out to break it.
The first is that American support for a Jewish state ran consistently and without a break from Roosevelt to Truman.

The record shows a president who, two months before his death, gave the Arab head of state most affected a direct assurance, spoken and then written, that the United States would not act on Palestine without consulting the Arabs, and a successor who acted without that consultation three years later.
The second is that Saudi opposition to a Jewish state in Palestine is a modern political position with no deep roots.

The second reading has the stronger documentary footing on one point: the promise was Roosevelt's, made "in my capacity as Chief of the Executive Branch," and nothing in these sources shows that it bound his successor.
What the record cannot settle is what Roosevelt himself would have done.

He died before the partition vote or the recognition decision came before him, and no evidence exists of how he would have weighed his promise to Ibn Saud against the domestic pressures his successor faced.
The American Zionist Emergency Council, 1943–1945

In August 1943, five years before there was a state to lobby for, the leading American Zionist organizations placed their political work under a single body: the American Zionist Emergency Council (AZEC).
A familiar account holds that American political support for Israel grew up after 1948, a natural response to the founding of a new democracy.
Before 1943 the major American Zionist organizations had operated under separate leaderships and sometimes pursued competing priorities.
Rabbi Abba Hillel Silver and Rabbi Stephen Wise were its first co-chairs .
Its importance outlasted its own years: through a documented line of succession, the council became the direct institutional predecessor of AIPAC .

It came into being a little more than a year after the Biltmore conference of May 1942 had committed the movement to a "Jewish Commonwealth" in Palestine, and as another, rival campaign was already filling American newspapers with full-page advertisements: the Bergson group's committees, whose story is told in .
Where the Bergson committees bought space and staged pageants, the council built a standing national network that could be pointed at Congress on a given week.
Earlier Zionist leaders had preferred a more cautious diplomatic approach, and Silver's course was an explicit and named departure from it, not a continuation of established practice .
The same period saw a comparable contest over method between Chaim Weizmann and David Ben-Gurion, told in the section on .

Inside the council the disagreement was serious enough that Silver resigned as co-chairman during a controversy in 1944–45 over how hard the organization should confront the American government; his own archived papers document the episode.
The fullest account of how the council worked comes from its internal correspondence, preserved among the Abba Hillel Silver Papers at the American Jewish Archives.
These are the organizers' own memos, and they describe a national method run from a New York headquarters at 342 Madison Avenue.
Instructions went out to "Chairmen of Local Emergency Committees" in cities across the country .

When Senators Robert Wagner and Robert Taft introduced their Palestine resolution in January 1944, a memo told the local chairmen that they would be sent sample letters, so that within a concentrated period letters from all over the country would "pour into Washington."
Telegram campaigns were aimed at particular members by name.
Among them was Representative Sol Bloom, chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee .
The council also published a book, America and Palestine, and sent it to every member of Congress.
It printed the pro-Zionist statements of nearly 400 members of the 78th Congress, so that each legislator could see in print the public commitments his own colleagues had already made .
The same machinery carried on after the war ended in Europe.
In 1945, with Harry Truman now president, local councils mobilized thousands of telegrams to the White House.
In Detroit alone, 150 Zionist and community leaders organized the appeal .

In 1948, after Bloom remarked that Truman was "on the right track" during the administration's retreat toward a trusteeship for Palestine, an AZEC staff memo called the remark "horrible" and urged that people in Bloom's district take it up with him .
According to that account, mail addressed to Senator Wagner in his capacity as chairman of the American Palestine Committee was opened and kept at Zionist headquarters, and Wagner was sent a copy .
Silver's biographical record credits his lobbying in 1944 with securing a Palestine resolution in Congress, and in the same year both major parties wrote Palestine into their platforms .
The House Foreign Affairs Committee approved the resolution on 30 November 1944; the full Congress deferred it that December, and a version was adopted only in December 1945  .

Both accounts agree on the substance: within roughly a year of its founding, the council had moved Palestine into the language of both parties and through a congressional committee, four years before there was a state.
They show organization: memos, sample letters, a book mailed to Congress, telegrams.
The money in the American movement during these years flowed through a different channel: philanthropic giving through the United Jewish Appeal.
The scale of that giving is set out in the library's funding ledger, drawing on Marc Lee Raphael's history of the United Jewish Appeal.
The campaign split its money three ways: relief for Jews in Europe, the Palestine program, and the resettlement of refugees in the United States.
Counting the whole sum as "funding Israel" would overstate what went to Palestine.

The ledger's precise split is documented for 1948, when about half of the year's $150 million went to the Palestine arm, about 43% to relief in Europe and the rest to resettlement in the United States; for the war years the record here gives the three destinations but not the shares.
The appeal's money went to relief, the Palestine program and resettlement; the council's work in Congress ran on letters, visits and telegrams.
They settle that American political support for a Jewish commonwealth did not simply arise of its own accord.
The map of the two American machines, the Bergson committees and the council, appears with the account of the Bergson group earlier in this chapter.

The map below places the council in the longer structure, the half-century from the Basel Congress to the State of Israel, where it stands as the "US political machine" between the Jewish Agency and the United Nations.
They do not prove that the council alone set American policy toward Palestine.

Truman's eventual decision to recognize Israel in 1948 had several causes, among them domestic electoral calculation and the competing objections of the State Department, and the council's five years of pressure were one factor among them, not the sole or sufficient explanation .
Citizens, Ships and a Law of 1938
The clandestine ships ran from Europe to Palestine; the movement's political turn in these years ran across the Atlantic, to the United States, and a practical question comes with it.
Who were the people running the American side of the movement, how did leaders from Palestine and Europe reach them, and under what law did any of it operate?
The leaders of American Zionism were Americans.
Louis Brandeis, Rabbi Stephen Wise and Rabbi Abba Hillel Silver were United States citizens, and their advocacy was the legal political activity of citizens.
Some of the movement's figures from Palestine had American lives of their own.
Golda Meir, then Golda Meyerson, grew up in Milwaukee and emigrated in 1921.
She later became Israel's prime minister.
David Ben-Gurion, expelled from Ottoman Palestine, lived in New York from 1915 to 1918.
There he recruited volunteers for the Jewish Legion, and there he married.
Visiting leaders such as Chaim Weizmann crossed the Atlantic by ocean liner, as most travelers did.
Regular transatlantic passenger flights began only in 1939, with Pan Am's flying boats.
Before that year no American law required people working for foreign principals to register at all.
Congress passed the Foreign Agents Registration Act in 1938.
The Bergson group was watched by the FBI, and that story is told in .
The first test of the act against the movement's main American apparatus came in 1962, with a Justice Department order to the American Zionist Council ().
Palestine in Congress and the Party Platforms, 1944–1945
It is often assumed that Congress and the two American parties took up Palestine only after the war, and then on its merits.

In that election year a resolution for a Jewish commonwealth went before both houses, the Army and the War Department asked Congress to shelve it, both parties wrote Palestine into their platforms, for the first time by the council's own appraisal, and the War Department dropped its objection days before the November vote.
The State Department then held the resolution back again.
The story turns as much on the timing of these moves as on their content, and much of it can be read in the American Zionist Emergency Council's own records.
Congress had spoken on Palestine before.
After President Wilson endorsed the Balfour Declaration in 1918, Congress passed the Lodge–Fish resolution unanimously in 1922, an episode told in an earlier chapter of this library.
Congress passed or pushed resolutions of support.
It never voted to create a Jewish state or to recognize one: partition and recognition, when they came, were acts of the executive  .
Congress shaped the climate; the executive made the decisions.
Early in 1944 two matching resolutions were introduced, each with one Democratic and one Republican sponsor.
In the House they were Representatives James Wright, a Democrat of Pennsylvania, and Ranulf Compton, a Republican of Connecticut.
In the Senate they were Robert Wagner, a Democrat of New York, and Robert Taft, a Republican of Ohio.
Both called for unrestricted Jewish immigration to Palestine and for a "free and democratic Jewish commonwealth"  .
Both demands ran against the British policy of the day, set out in .
The House Foreign Affairs Committee held hearings.
Not every Jewish witness supported the resolution.
Among the opponents was Rabbi Morris Lazaron, who told the committee that Zionism was an internal Jewish matter and not a question for Congress .
His testimony is a reminder that American Jewish opinion in 1944 was not unanimous, and that some of the resistance came from inside the community the council claimed to speak for.
In March 1944 the Army Chief of Staff, General George Marshall, and the Secretary of War, Henry Stimson, asked Congress to postpone action for military reasons.
The council's records describe the same step: Stimson opposed the Wagner–Taft resolution on military grounds, and it was put aside  .
The War Department's case was about the conduct of a war still being fought.

The State Department, for its part, had its own plan, approved by Roosevelt, to suppress public discussion of the Palestine question for the duration of the war; that plan and Roosevelt's two registers on Palestine are examined in .
"The first time in American history."
Blocked in Congress, the issue moved to the parties.
That summer both party conventions adopted Palestine planks.
The council's own appraisal of the year called it "the first time in American history that Palestine was included in the party platforms" .
It meant that in a presidential election year Palestine had become a matter on which both parties had taken a public position, and on which their candidates could be held to account.
In October Stimson wrote to Senator Taft.
According to the record of that letter, he told Taft that political considerations now outweighed military ones .
Days before the November election, the War Department had in effect withdrawn its objection  .
On 30 November, after the election, the House Foreign Affairs Committee approved the resolution .
The council's records attribute the deferral to the insistence of the State Department; another account describes it as a deferral at the administration's request  .
The resolution came back after the war, with Truman in the White House.
It had the support of the American Palestine Committee and the Christian Council on Palestine .
Its wording had changed, and the State Department noticed.

A department memorandum observed that the resolution called not for a "Jewish commonwealth" but for a "democratic commonwealth in which all men, regardless of race or creed, shall have equal rights" .
The champions in Congress were named members of both parties.
Wagner and Taft led in the Senate.
In the House, Representative Emanuel Celler of Brooklyn and Sol Bloom, chairman of the Foreign Affairs Committee, were among the leading supporters  .

Members of Congress could introduce and approve resolutions, and the party conventions could adopt planks; both were open to organized constituent pressure, which is where the council concentrated its work.
The War Department and the State Department could not vote, but they could ask committees to wait, and in 1944 they did so twice.
By 1944 Palestine had become a party-platform and election-timing issue, with the military and diplomatic bureaucracies on the other side.
It is the same alignment the record shows again in Truman's decisions of 1947–48.

One reads the year as the work of electoral politics: a resolution shelved on military grounds in March was cleared by the Secretary of War in a letter to a Republican senator days before a presidential election, after both parties had written the issue into their platforms.
Stimson's own reported words, that political considerations now outweighed military ones, give this reading its strongest support .

The resolution came while the war was still being fought; Marshall and Stimson asked only for postponement, not rejection; and after the election the executive branch, through the State Department, again asked Congress to wait, which an administration acting only on electoral motives had no reason to do.
The sources here do not show who asked Stimson to write to Taft, or what he weighed beyond the one sentence the record preserves.
They do not give the vote counts of December 1945, or explain who changed the resolution's wording from "Jewish commonwealth" to "equal rights," and why.

What they do show is that by the end of 1944, four years before statehood, Palestine had been placed inside American electoral politics by an organized campaign, and that the War and State Departments were already its main opponents inside the government.
What the Vatican's Authority Covered
Kristallnacht raised a question that ran through the years that followed: who outside the Reich would speak against what the German state was doing, and with what authority.
The wartime record of the Catholic Church, taken up in the next section, is often argued over with a loose idea of what the Church could and could not do.
A common assumption holds that the Vatican has, or claims, authority over Christian scripture and doctrine in general, Catholic and Protestant alike.
Its binding authority reaches Catholics only, and Protestants have rejected it since the sixteenth century.
Discussed elsewhere in this library for its role in American Christian Zionism, it was never submitted to Rome for approval, and Rome was never in a position to demand its retraction.
That was not an oversight on Rome's part.
It follows from the structure of Church authority itself.
That authority is called the magisterium: the Church's teaching office, exercised through the Pope and the bishops.
It binds Catholics, which in practice means Catholic doctrine, Catholic clergy and Catholic religious publications.
It has never claimed, and has no mechanism to exercise, binding authority over people or institutions outside the Catholic Church.
The instrument through which it governs what Catholics print is the imprimatur, Latin for "let it be printed."
It is an approval process applied to Catholic religious publications specifically: catechisms, devotional works, and translations of scripture intended for Catholic use.
Among them was Oxford University Press, which published the Scofield Bible.
The reason for the boundary lies in the Reformation.
Its founding premise was the rejection of Rome's authority to bind the conscience of believers.
The principle of sola scriptura held that scripture, not the Church hierarchy, was the final authority.
Evangelical Protestants who read the Scofield Bible stood, by their own tradition's founding principle, entirely outside any claim Rome could make on their beliefs.
To ask why the Vatican did not stop Scofield is a little like asking why one country's supreme court did not strike down another country's law.

The Vatican has routinely issued prominent public statements on subjects entirely outside its binding jurisdiction: climate policy, nuclear weapons, immigration law, and the birth-control policies of secular states.
So the fair question about Scofield is not why Rome failed to force a retraction; it never could have.

It is why the Church, which by the account in this library's sources had already ruled against premillennial dispensationalism internally in the 1940s, did not use its considerable public voice to say so loudly, as it has on other questions equally outside its jurisdiction.
The same distinction, between what the Church could command and what it could say, runs through the far graver wartime question of .
It establishes the reach of the Church's formal authority and nothing more.
It does not settle why the Church spoke on some subjects and kept quiet on others; the sources here state the distinction, not the motives behind any particular silence.
Pius XII and the Holocaust: The Wartime Record
Eugenio Pacelli became Pope Pius XII in March 1939, six months before the war began, and he led the Catholic Church through the whole of the Holocaust.
He had served as the Vatican's Secretary of State and, before that, as nuncio to Germany, which gave him direct, personal experience of the Nazi state before the war began.
One holds that historians agree the Vatican did essentially nothing to help Jews.
The other holds that Pius XII was a quiet hero whose actions saved hundreds of thousands.
Pius XII never issued a public statement during the war that directly and explicitly condemned the Holocaust, or Nazi genocide, by name.
The address did not mention Jews.
It did not mention Germany or Nazism.
Historians working in the Vatican archives have documented that Vatican diplomatic staff at the time privately acknowledged that the address was intentionally indirect.
It was understood inside the Vatican as a coded reference that informed listeners would recognize, while staying vague enough to avoid direct confrontation with Germany.
Pius XII never issued a more direct statement at any later point in the war, even as details of the systematic genocide were more thoroughly confirmed through Allied and other channels.
Substantial documented evidence shows Jews sheltered in convents, monasteries and Vatican-connected properties in Rome and elsewhere during the German occupation.

Some historians, drawing on Vatican archives opened in 2020, argue that this reflected a real, if quiet, rescue effort, carried out with degrees of papal awareness and tacit approval, and some later archival researchers credit coordinated Church rescue networks with saving substantial numbers of lives.
The first is fear: that an explicit condemnation would worsen the persecution, or provoke Nazi retaliation against Catholics and Church institutions.
The second is diplomacy: a strategy of preserving the Vatican's neutrality so that it could help broker an eventual peace.
The case from fear rests on the possibility that a direct condemnation would have been answered by harsher persecution and by reprisals against the Church.

The case for moral failure rests on the plain fact that the Pope's voice, which the Church used freely on other subjects, was never raised by name against the murder of the Jews, even as the evidence mounted.
A related claim holds that ancient noble families secretly controlled Vatican policy in this period and that hidden financial incentives drove the Church's silence.

Vatican finances had been close to bankruptcy before they were bolstered by the 1929 Lateran settlement with Mussolini's government, which compensated the Holy See for the loss of the Papal States in 1870.
The settlement came to $92.1 million: 750 million lire in cash plus 1 billion lire in Italian government bonds.

The treaty was negotiated between Cardinal Secretary of State Pietro Gasparri and Mussolini's government, and Pope Pius XI was reportedly so pleased with it that he called Mussolini "the man sent by providence."
The Pope's chosen envoy for the negotiations was Francesco Pacelli, the brother of Eugenio Pacelli, who ten years later became Pius XII.
Bernardino Nogara served as the Vatican's financial adviser from 1929 to 1954.
Pius XI appointed him the first Director of the Special Administration of the Holy See, and Pius XII kept him in that post through the whole of the Holocaust period.
ents: the Special Administration of the Holy See

sent: The Vatican had recently received a large financial settlement from the same Italian state that later allied with Nazi Germany.
The settlement was administered by an adviser kept on across the change of popes, and it had been negotiated in part by the future Pope's own brother.
What they do not establish is a proven causal link between that financial history and Pius XII's public silence during the war.

The question belongs in a history of the road to 1948 because, on the reading this library takes, it is one instance of a recurring pattern in the Vatican's dealings with this story: real, documented concern paired with limited direct public confrontation.
The same shape appears later in the Holy See's long withholding of recognition of Israel, which ended in 1993, and in its response to Gaza in 2023–25.
Whatever a reader concludes about Pius XII himself, the wartime record is that pattern tested at the highest possible stakes.
What the record does not settle is why Pius XII chose as he did, and how far the rescue in Rome was his own work.
The Anglo-American Committee of Inquiry, 1945–1946
It is sometimes said that no international body heard the Arab case, or the case for a shared state, before the United Nations voted to partition Palestine in November 1947.

More than a year and a half before the vote, a joint British and American committee heard the Jewish Agency, Arab spokesmen, Jewish advocates of a binational state, Christian and Jewish organizations, and the refugees themselves.
It then produced a unanimous report that rejected both a Jewish state and an Arab state.
Washington took the one recommendation it wanted and left the rest; London attached a condition to even that one; and the follow-up plan pleased no one.

The committee was announced in November 1945 by the Foreign Secretary, Ernest Bevin, as a "joint Anglo-American Committee of Inquiry, under a rotating chairmanship" (the announcement and its context are told in ).
It was created as Washington pressed London to admit Jewish displaced persons to Palestine, and it was built to share the question between the two governments.
It had six American and six British members.
The Americans included Bartley Crum and James McDonald; the British included Richard Crossman.
Between January and March 1946 the committee held hearings in Washington, London, the displaced-persons camps of Europe, Cairo and Jerusalem.
It took evidence from governments, the Jewish Agency, Arab states and the Arab Office, Christian and Jewish organizations, and refugees in the camps.
The Jewish Agency's leaders presented the Zionist case.
Arab representatives presented theirs, among them the Arab Office, where the historian Albert Hourani gave testimony that the record describes as notable.
The sources used here do not give the substance of what Hourani said, so this book does not paraphrase it.
The third case came from Jews who opposed a Jewish state.
Judah Magnes, president of the Hebrew University, and the Ihud association argued that Arabs and Jews should share one state with political parity.
Their testimony shows that a Jewish alternative to partition was argued, in person, before an official body.
First, the immediate issue of 100,000 immigration certificates for Jewish refugees.
Third, the continuation of the Mandate toward a United Nations trusteeship.
And fourth, as a principle of the future constitution, that Palestine should be neither a Jewish state nor an Arab state, with neither people dominating the other.

The 100,000 certificates answered the plight of the survivors in Europe; the repeal of the 1940 land regulations lifted restrictions on land transfers; trusteeship and the "neither Jewish nor Arab state" principle expressed the report's principle that neither people should dominate the other.
Unanimity mattered: the six Americans and six Britons had agreed on all of it together.
What Washington kept, and what London required.
President Truman publicly endorsed the 100,000 and was silent on the rest.
The admission of refugees was popular with American voters.
The constitutional recommendation against a Jewish state was not something he endorsed.
Prime Minister Attlee answered by tying any admissions to the disarmament of the Jewish and Arab armed groups in Palestine.
The British condition was not abstract.
At the time, the Haganah, the Irgun and Lehi were acting together against British rule, as told in .
By making the 100,000 depend on disarmament, London made the one recommendation Washington wanted depend, in part, on the surrender of arms by Jewish groups then in open revolt against British rule.
Morrison–Grady.
In July 1946 a follow-up Anglo-American plan, known as Morrison–Grady, proposed provincial autonomy for Palestine.
Zionist and Arab leaders both rejected it, and Truman declined to back it.
With that, the joint Anglo-American attempt to settle Palestine was finished.
The question went to the United Nations the following year.
Washington, which did not govern Palestine, could press on the one point that cost it nothing at home and had public support.
London, which governed Palestine, could attach conditions.
The people heard by the committee, whether the Jewish Agency, the Arab Office, Magnes and Ihud, or the refugees in the camps, had a hearing but no hand in what followed.
The binational option that Magnes argued, and that the report's "neither Jewish nor Arab state" principle partly echoed, had no government willing to carry it.
Another reading puts it more sharply: what survived into American policy was the part with domestic political value.
They differ on how much weight to give Truman's own reasons, a question taken up in .
What neither reading supports is the claim that the Arab and binationalist cases went unheard before 1947.
They do not give the content of Hourani's testimony or of the Jewish Agency's.

They do not say what, if anything, London said about the land regulations, trusteeship or the "neither Jewish nor Arab state" principle once the report was published, beyond its disarmament condition on the 100,000.
The American network was one source of the Haganah's arms.
A familiar belief holds that the United States armed Israel from its founding.
Washington kept its arms embargo in place, and the government that sold the Jewish side the fighters and rifles it used in the war was communist Czechoslovakia, acting with Soviet consent.
Some of the money that paid for them was raised in the United States, but the weapons came from the East.
The American military relationship with Israel that later defined its arms supply did not exist in 1948.
On 14 January 1948 the Jewish Agency signed its first arms contract with Czechoslovakia, coordinated through "Secretariat D" of the state engineering-works holding.
It came four months before independence, at a time when the purchaser was not a state but the Agency that represented the Jewish community of Palestine.
And it came three months before the United Nations Security Council imposed its own arms embargo on 17 April 1948, in Resolution 46.
Czechoslovakia became communist in the coup of February 1948, a month after the first contract, and sold with Stalin's consent.
The sources record Soviet consent for the sales; they do not explain how Moscow's position related to a contract signed before the coup.
Operation Balak.
From May to August 1948 a secret airlift, Operation Balak, ran from the Žatec airfield west of Prague, code-named "Zebra," to Ekron.

It carried arms, ammunition and personnel, and it carried fighters: the Avia S-199, a Czech-built derivative of the German Messerschmitt Bf 109, dismantled and crated inside C-46 and C-54 transport aircraft.
A defector exposed the Zebra base, the United States pressed the United Nations to have it closed, and operations moved to Nikšić in Yugoslavia.
The episode shows Washington's posture plainly: it did not supply arms, and it acted to shut down the supply that was reaching the new state.
The deliveries included some 35,000 German-pattern Karabiner 98k rifles and heavy weapons, many of them originally produced for the Wehrmacht.
Many of the rifles of the new state's first war were German-pattern army rifles sold by a Soviet-bloc government.
Czechoslovakia was not the only outside power arming a party to the war.
Britain, according to the same sources, supplied aircraft and training to the Arab air forces, while the United States maintained its embargo.
And the Soviet bloc's choice was not lasting.
Within months, the record notes, it began shipping the same kind of weapons toward the Arab side.
The Soviet diplomacy behind the bloc's position in 1947–48 is told in ; what the arms record shows is a convergence of interest for a period, not an alliance.
In a 1952 report, the Czechoslovak Foreign Minister, Viliam Široký, put the receipts from the sales at almost $14.5 million.
It gives a range for the Czechoslovak arms from $14.5 million to about $90 million, about $0.19 billion to $1.2 billion in today's dollars, and notes that estimates vary up to six-fold.

It sets this beside the reported $50 million from Golda Meyerson's American tour, spent mostly on arms, $3 million in letters of credit from Nicaragua's Somoza for arms buying, and Al Schwimmer's roughly 30 aircraft, whose cost the record does not total.
The two ends of the Czechoslovak range each have a case.
The higher estimates in the ledger are not attributed in the sources used here to a named document, and this book cannot say what they include that Široký's figure leaves out.
The reported $50 million that Golda Meyerson brought back from the United States financed weapons purchases, including those from Czechoslovakia, as told in .
American private money paid, in part, for Soviet-bloc arms.

The library's summary of the money behind the state sets these sums side by side: the reported $50 million from the 1948 tour; about $14.5 million paid for Czechoslovak arms, with Stalin's approval; and a $100 million US Export-Import Bank loan earmarked for Israel after recognition.
Only the last came from the American government, and it was a loan for building the state, not weapons.
When American arms came.
The aid ledger's timeline fixes the American side.
From 1948 to 1961 US aid to Israel consisted of economic aid and loans only; Washington avoided selling arms for fear of alienating the Arab oil states.
The first American military aid came in 1962, and then as loans.
Ben-Gurion's verdict.
Ben-Gurion left no doubt about how he weighed the shipments.
In 1968 he said: "Czechoslovak arms saved the State of Israel, really and absolutely."
It sits beside his tribute to Meyerson's fundraising as "the money which made the state possible," and the two are not in conflict: the money, in part, paid for the arms.
The sources establish the first contract's date, the airlift's route and months, the number of fighters and rifles, and Široký's figure.
They do not show how the January contract, signed before the communist coup, related to the Soviet consent recorded afterwards.

And Ben-Gurion's verdict, however weighty, is an assessment rather than a measurement of how much the Czechoslovak weapons, as against other factors, decided the war; the balance of forces is examined in .
Deir Yassin, the Hadassah Convoy and Tantura: The Massacres of 1948 and How the Record Changed
In the spring of 1948 Jewish forces killed Arab villagers, and Arab forces killed Jews, sometimes within days of each other and sometimes in answer to each other.

What has changed over the decades is not whether these events happened but how much is known about them, and much of that knowledge came from Israeli archives, an Israeli student and Israeli veterans.
Deir Yassin was a village west of Jerusalem.
On 9 April 1948 it was attacked by the Irgun and Lehi, two right-wing Zionist militias, supported by the Haganah and the Palmach.

The attack came on the day after Abd al-Qadir al-Husayni, commander of the Palestinian Army of the Holy War, was killed leading the counter-attack at al-Qastal, which overlooks the road from Jerusalem to Jaffa.

sent: For decades the number killed at Deir Yassin was given as 254.
A Red Cross representative reported seeing some 150 bodies in a cave.

The letter to the New York Times of 4 December 1948, signed by Albert Einstein, Hannah Arendt and 26 others against Menachem Begin's visit, said the attackers had "killed most of its inhabitants (240 men, women, and children)."
Arendt had already condemned the Irgun's attacks, Deir Yassin among them, in May 1948.
Benny Morris wrote that Deir Yassin was followed by mass Arab flight.

An account drawn from Israeli historians adds two details: that the attackers announced the killings by radio to nearby villages, which the official Haganah history by Yehuda Slutsky records, and that Ben-Gurion later noted in his diary that Deir Yassin "had a decisive effect" on Arab flight.
Material on Deir Yassin in Israeli military archives remains classified.
On 13 April 1948 Arab forces attacked a convoy travelling to Hadassah Hospital on Mount Scopus and killed 78 Jews, most of them doctors and nurses.
The attack was a reprisal for Deir Yassin.
The Hadassah convoy was not the only such killing of Jews in these weeks.
Before the Mandate ended, the Arab Legion attacked the Gush Etzion bloc of Jewish settlements; its defenders surrendered, and some of them were massacred, according to Avi Shlaim's account.
During Abd al-Qadir al-Husayni's command, the Army of the Holy War's explosives unit blew up the Jewish Agency building in Jerusalem; the source does not give the date or the toll.

sent: Tantura shows most clearly how the record has grown.
It was a coastal village captured by the Alexandroni Brigade on 22–23 May 1948, about a week after the state was proclaimed.
A master's thesis by Theodore Katz later recorded testimony that villagers had been killed after the village surrendered.
Veterans of the brigade sued him for libel, and he retracted.
In the 2022 Israeli documentary Tantura, veterans then in their nineties described on camera killings and a mass grave near what is now Dor Beach, a popular resort.
The Deir Yassin numbers show how a toll can move in both directions.
The Red Cross representative's 150 bodies is a count of what one witness saw in one place, not a total.
Much of what is known came from Israelis: historians working in Israeli archives, a student who gathered veterans' testimony, and veterans who decided late in life to speak.
Atrocities against Jews in the same weeks, at the Hadassah convoy and at Gush Etzion, are equally part of the record.
The later expulsions at Lydda and Ramla in July 1948, with their own disputed tolls, are told with the Arab states' war in .
Israeli military archives on Deir Yassin are still partly closed, so the exact toll and the full chain of command cannot yet be documented.
The number killed at Tantura cannot be established, and the veterans who were there disagree about what happened.
The sources used here give no date for Katz's thesis or for the libel case, and no toll for the bombing of the Jewish Agency building.
For Gush Etzion it says that some defenders were massacred but gives no number.
It is often assumed that Israel's army was a single national force from the day of independence.
On 14 May 1948 three armed bodies claimed to fight for the new state: the Haganah; the Irgun, commanded by Menachem Begin; and Lehi, led by three men.
Making them one army took four months, an order, a confrontation on a Tel Aviv beach in which Jews killed Jews, and an assassination that the new government itself called terrorism.
Twelve days after the declaration of independence, the provisional government headed by David Ben-Gurion issued an order establishing the Israel Defense Forces.
It outlawed any other armed force and required the Haganah, the Irgun and Lehi to merge into the new army.
The war with the Arab states, told in , was then in its second week, and the new army was being formed while it fought.
The Altalena, June 1948.
In June 1948 the Irgun brought an arms ship, the Altalena, to the coast, carrying weapons that it intended partly for its own units.
Ben-Gurion refused to let the cargo bypass the army.
The two positions could not both stand: an Irgun that kept its own weapons was an army beside the army, which the order of 26 May had outlawed.
On 22 June IDF units under the command of Yitzhak Rabin shelled the ship off the Tel Aviv beach.
The Irgun's separate units were then disbanded.
The episode fell during the first truce of the war, which ran from 11 June to 9 July, when arms were reaching the Israeli army from Europe.
The dispute over the Altalena was therefore not about whether weapons should come in, but about who would hold them once they arrived.
The same commander, Rabin, would sign the order to expel the inhabitants of Lydda three weeks later.
The killing of Bernadotte, September 1948.
The second test came from Lehi.

Count Folke Bernadotte had been appointed United Nations mediator on 21 May 1948; he had supervised the first truce and proposed a settlement giving the Galilee to Israel, the Negev to the Arabs and Jerusalem to the United Nations, which both sides rejected.
On 17 September 1948 members of Lehi assassinated him in Jerusalem.
The government declared Lehi a terrorist organization and arrested its members.
The word matters: the government of the new state applied it, in its own name, to a Jewish underground.
In February 1949 the Lehi members were released under a general amnesty.
Menachem Begin, whose ship the army had shelled, became prime minister in 1977.
Yitzhak Shamir, one of Lehi's three leaders, became prime minister in 1983.
Begin's new party drew a public protest in a letter signed by Albert Einstein and Hannah Arendt in December 1948, discussed in .

One stresses the state's resolve: a provisional government, at war, fired on its own citizens rather than tolerate a private army, and named a Jewish underground's assassination of a UN mediator for what it was.
The other stresses how quickly the line was redrawn: the arrests ended in an amnesty within five months of the killing, and the men who had led the Irgun and Lehi later became prime ministers.
The sources gathered give the dead of the Altalena but not the fate of its cargo.
They name Lehi's members as the assassins of Bernadotte but not the individuals who planned or carried out the killing, and they record the amnesty without its terms or its reasons.
They do not say how the Haganah's own structure was carried into the new army.
The New CIA's First Warning: ORE-55
When the State Department and the Joint Chiefs of Staff warned against partition in September and October 1947, the Central Intelligence Agency was only weeks old.
Ten weeks after it came into being, it delivered a formal estimate of its own, dated the day before the General Assembly vote.
It predicted war if partition passed, and it warned that American backing for partition was already costing the United States prestige and would endanger its interests.
A common assumption holds that American intelligence either never assessed partition or supported it.
Who ran American intelligence.
Before 1947, American foreign intelligence ran through the wartime Office of Strategic Services, which operated from 1942 and led by William J. Donovan, whom Roosevelt appointed.
The OSS was dissolved in October 1945, and its analysts and operatives fed the agencies that followed.
In 1946 an interim body, the Central Intelligence Group, carried the work forward.

The OSS also had a Palestine desk during the war; that history, and the Zionist intelligence service that operated on American soil in the same years, are told with the July 1945 Sonneborn meeting in .
The National Security Act of 1947 put the system on a permanent footing.
It created the Central Intelligence Agency, the National Security Council, and the structure that became the Department of Defense; the CIA came into existence on 18 September 1947.
Its first Director of Central Intelligence was Rear Admiral Roscoe Hillenkoetter, appointed by Truman.

James Forrestal, the first Secretary of Defense, oversaw the department that grew from the same Act, so his warning on oil and the agency's estimate on partition came from two parts of one newly built national-security structure.
The CIA was born four days before Loy Henderson sent his "not workable" memorandum to Secretary of State Marshall.
The agency's Office of Reports and Estimates issued ORE-55, titled "The Consequences of the Partition of Palestine," dated 28 November 1947, one day before the General Assembly voted on partition.
