sent: The declassified document is held in the CIA's own reading room.
Armed hostilities between Jews and Arabs would break out if the General Assembly adopted partition.
The United Nations would be morally bound to enforce its decision.
Jewish forces would at first prevail, because of superior organization and equipment.
The United States, by backing partition, had already lost much of its prestige in the Arab world.
And imposed partition would place American commercial and strategic interests in serious danger.

The first prediction was borne out quickly: sustained fighting began as a two-sided civil war inside Palestine within days of the 29 November vote, five and a half months before the armies of neighbouring Arab states crossed any border.
The prediction of early Jewish advantage through organization and equipment belongs to the long argument over the balance of forces taken up later in this chapter.

The estimate's concern for American standing in the Arab world restated, in the language of intelligence, what Henderson had put to Marshall and the Joint Chiefs had put in "The Problem of Palestine."

Within ten weeks, four separate parts of the American government warned in writing against American sponsorship of partition: the State Department's Near East office, the Joint Chiefs of Staff, the Secretary of Defense, and the new CIA.

The President's domestic political advisers, led by Clark Clifford and David Niles, argued the opposite case, and their view prevailed, first in the partition vote and then in the recognition of Israel eleven minutes after its independence was proclaimed on 14 May 1948.

It states that declassified CIA and State Department documents from 1947 and 1948 warned consistently against recognizing Israel on strategic grounds; that CIA assessments noted Zionist arms-procurement networks operating across Europe and the United States and predicted that recognition would at once produce armed conflict with Arab states; that the State Department under Marshall opposed recognition on the same grounds; and that Truman's recognition came at 6:11 p.m. on 14 May 1948, eleven minutes after the declaration, the fastest diplomatic recognition in American history, so fast that his own State Department was caught unprepared.
It goes on to describe the intelligence relationship with Israel that grew out of 1948, a later story told in .
It states that a CIA report predicted that an arms embargo would lead to "peaceful coexistence."
American intelligence assessed partition, did so in writing, and predicted war and damage to American interests; the decision was taken anyway.
What the record does not establish is how much weight the President gave the estimate, which arrived on the eve of a vote whose American position had been announced seven weeks earlier.
Nor does the summary say what Hillenkoetter or Truman did with it once it was delivered.
On 10 March 1948 the general staff of the Haganah issued the operational plan that would govern its conduct in the weeks before and after the British withdrawal.
In Hebrew it was Tochnit Dalet; in English it is usually called Plan D or Plan Dalet.
A long-standing popular account holds that Palestinians left their homes in 1948 of their own accord, at the urging of Arab leaders, before Jewish forces did anything to them.
Walid Khalidi, the Palestinian historian whose 1961 essay set out the argument that it was a master plan, dates the earlier Plan B to September 1945 and Plan C, or Gimmel, to May 1946.
Plan C, he writes, was put into practice from 1 December 1947, the first day of the fighting that followed the United Nations vote.
Plan D was issued nine days before the United States told the Security Council that partition could not be carried out peacefully (), and its operations began three weeks later.
Khalidi first made his case in a 1961 essay titled "Plan Dalet: Master Plan for the Conquest of Palestine."
When the Journal of Palestine Studies republished it in its Autumn 1988 issue (volume 18, number 1), it printed the text of Plan D, dated 10 March 1948, as an appendix.
The plan opens with its purpose: "The objective of this plan is to gain control of the areas of the Hebrew state and defend its borders."
Its scope reached past those borders, to "areas of Jewish settlement and concentration which are located outside the borders."
Khalidi also listed the operations that, in his account, carried the plan out between 1 April and 14 May 1948.
They are his translations and his characterizations, not an Israeli official list.
The list covers the weeks in which the mixed towns fell: Haifa, Jaffa, Safed and others, with the depopulation of several hundred villages.
What happened in Tiberias and Haifa, and the separate argument over why Haifa's Arab population left, are told in .
In this list Khalidi assigns Haifa to Misparayim and the Jaffa villages to Chametz.
In his separate study of Haifa he writes that the operation planned as Misparayim was renamed Chametz.
The two accounts by the same historian do not line up, and the material gathered does not resolve which name the Haifa operation finally carried.
Khalidi's own text contains a correction that is easy to miss.
He wrote that "Up to 1 March not one single Arab village had been vacated by its inhabitants."
The first treats Plan Dalet as a master plan.
Khalidi's 1961 essay and Ilan Pappé's 2006 book The Ethnic Cleansing of Palestine read it as the blueprint for deliberately removing the Arab population from the territory of the Jewish state.
In his 1988 restatement Khalidi argued that Plan D created "the military fait accompli upon which the state of Israel was to be based," and that the exodus was its product.
He called the claim that Arab leaders had ordered an evacuation "a piece of mythmaking," citing the radio monitoring records of the BBC and of FBIS.
And he faulted Benny Morris for treating the exodus in "an historical vacuum."
Pappé went further on the question of terms, arguing that the plan meets the United Nations definition of ethnic cleansing.

The strongest form of this case rests on the document's own words: destruction and expulsion were written into an order issued before the Arab states invaded, and the operations Khalidi lists began within three weeks of it.
The second reading is Benny Morris's.
He reads Plan Dalet as a military plan to secure territory and lines of communication before the Arab states' invasion.

The strongest form of this case rests on the same text read differently: the plan states a military objective, makes expulsion conditional on resistance, and, in Morris's reading, the record of 1948 shows villages treated in different ways under the same orders.
The text of Plan Dalet is settled, and so is the depopulation that followed.
None of the three positions supports the claim that Palestinians left before any Jewish forces acted.
Khalidi's own footnote records villages captured before March.
Morris, whose reading is the less sweeping, is also the historian whose research documented the expulsions.
How large a part Arab leaders' orders played is a separate question, and an estimate from an Israeli army intelligence report of June 1948 is taken up in .
The operation list rests on Khalidi's translations and characterizations, and his two accounts of the Haifa operation's name do not agree.
Abdullah Between the Jewish Agency, Britain and the Arab League, 1947–1948
Of the Arab rulers who sent armies into Palestine in May 1948, one had been talking to the Jewish Agency for months beforehand.
King Abdullah of Transjordan commanded the Arab Legion, a force trained and commanded by British officers, and he had territorial aims of his own.
A familiar account holds that Jordan went to war in 1948 solely to destroy the new Jewish state alongside its allies, with no separate interest of its own.
Abdullah's separate position was visible before the partition vote.
When the United Nations Special Committee on Palestine toured the region in the summer of 1947, Transjordan declined to send a representative to testify outside the country.
Instead the committee's chairman and seven of its members visited the king in Amman on 25 July 1947.
In early November 1947, at Naharayim on the Jordan, Abdullah met Golda Meyerson, later Golda Meir, of the Jewish Agency.

According to the Center for Israel Education's account, he told her that he intended to annex the Arab areas of Palestine, and she replied that the Zionist leaders would not oppose this if there were no clashes between Jewish and Transjordanian forces.
The historian Avi Shlaim calls the understanding reached
What existed, on this account, was a shared expectation: the king would take the Arab part of Palestine, and the Jewish state would not fight him for it.
The British side of the triangle came into view in February 1948.
That month Britain's Foreign Secretary, an office Ernest Bevin had held since July 1945 , met the prime minister of Transjordan and John Glubb, the British officer who commanded the Arab Legion.

After that meeting, according to Graham Jevon's study of Glubb and the Legion (Cambridge University Press, 2017), Glubb "actively sought to thwart the efforts of the Arab irregular forces" in Palestine and sought a military accord with the Zionists.
Jevon writes that his findings corroborate Shlaim's disputed claim that Britain gave Abdullah a "green light" to occupy the areas allotted to the Arab state.
He also concludes that Glubb was not the architect of this Greater Transjordan scheme but the man who carried it out.
The abstract of Jevon's chapter, which is what this book has drawn on, does not give the date of the meeting or record what was said.
Shlaim states the British policy plainly.
Britain, he writes, "was resigned to the emergence of a Jewish state but supported her client, King Abdullah," and in doing so "helped to abort the birth of a Palestinian state."
The Arab League pulled Abdullah the other way.
The League's anti-Hashemite members suspected him of collaborating with the Zionists.
He, for his part, opposed every move toward Palestinian independence and refused to deal with Hajj Amin al-Husayni, the Mufti, who led the Arab Higher Committee.
The quarrel over who would speak for the Palestinians is told in .
On 30 April 1948 the League's Political Committee decided that "all the Arab states must prepare their armies for the invasion of Palestine on 15 May."
Under pressure from Transjordan and Iraq, Abdullah was named commander-in-chief.
The man suspected of a private arrangement with the Jewish Agency was now the nominal head of the Arab war against it.
On 10 May 1948, four days before the end of the Mandate, Meyerson crossed to Amman with Ezra Danin.
The two traveled disguised as an Arab couple.
According to the Center for Israel Education, Abdullah told her that he was now "one of five" and asked: "why don't you wait a few years?
Drop your demands for free immigration."

Meyerson's own report at the time, as summarized in Shlaim's notes, records that the king did not deny their earlier understanding, said he had no choice but to join the invasion, and that they did not part as enemies.
On 13 May Yaacov Shimoni of the Jewish Agency weighed it up: the king "has not entirely betrayed the agreement, nor is he entirely loyal to it."
On 15 May, as the armies moved, Syria's president, Shukri al-Quwwatli, urged a halt to the advance.
Abdullah refused.
What the Arab Legion then did can be set against those meetings.
Even before the Mandate ended, the Legion attacked the Gush Etzion bloc of Jewish settlements; its defenders surrendered and some were massacred, according to Shlaim's notes.

Once the war between states began, the State Department's Office of the Historian records, Transjordanian forces intervened only in areas designated for the Arab state or for the Jerusalem corpus separatum, the separate Jerusalem zone of the partition plan.

sent: Within those limits the Legion fought hard.

In the first round, according to Shlaim's notes, the Jewish Quarter of Jerusalem surrendered on 28 May, and three frontal Israeli attacks on Latrun, on 25 and 30 May and 9 June, were repelled by the Arab Legion.

After the second truce began on 18 July, the Legion continued shelling West Jerusalem through October and on 12 August demolished the Latrun pumping station, which the United Nations held, according to an Israeli army account.
The Legion's commander was also the source of many of the most-quoted figures on the balance of forces, which historians treat with caution because he commanded one of the sides.
By the end of the war the Legion held East Jerusalem's Old City and the West Bank.
It was Jordan's most consequential military action of the war, and the territory remained under its administration for the next nineteen years.
Under the armistice agreements of 1949, Jordan kept the West Bank.

Abdullah opposed the Arab League's All-Palestine Government in Gaza and answered it, on 1 December 1948, with the Jericho congress that proclaimed the union of Palestine and Transjordan under his crown, as told in the section on Arab leadership.
In brief: on 24 April 1950 Jordan's parliament annexed the West Bank, declaring support for "complete unity between the two sides of the Jordan and their union into one State."
Only Britain, Iraq and Pakistan recognized it, and Britain's recognition excluded Jerusalem.

The strongest regional opposition came from Jordan's fellow Arab League states, whose Political Committee ruled in Cairo that the annexation violated the League's earlier resolution and considered expelling Jordan.

During the nineteen years of Jordanian rule that followed, Jewish access to the Western Wall and other religious sites in the Old City was denied, contrary to the 1949 armistice terms, and dozens of historic synagogues were damaged or destroyed.

One reading notes that the 1950 resolution's "two banks" language mirrors the Revisionist Zionist claim, associated with Jabotinsky, that both banks of the Jordan belong together, used here in the opposite direction; it is a structural parallel, and the record does not show that either side was answering the other.
Was there collusion across the Jordan?
The case that there was, in substance, is Shlaim's, and on the British side Jevon's study says its findings corroborate it.

On this view there was a tacit understanding between Abdullah and the Jewish Agency to divide the territory the United Nations had allotted to an Arab state, Britain gave the king a green light to take his share, and Glubb restrained the Arab irregulars and sought an accord with the Zionists.
The Legion's conduct fits: it stayed out of the territory allotted to the Jewish state, and the Palestinian state that the partition plan foresaw was never born.
In Amman on 10 May Abdullah called himself "one of five," asked the Jews to defer statehood and drop their demand for free immigration, and joined the invasion.
The Jewish Agency's own Shimoni judged him neither loyal to the understanding nor in full breach of it.
And the Legion fought Israeli forces hard where their aims met, in Jerusalem and at Latrun.
Both accept that Abdullah and the Jewish Agency talked, that he wanted the Arab part of Palestine, and that he went to war as part of the Arab coalition.
The Naharayim and Amman exchanges come largely through the Center for Israel Education's account and Meyerson's own report, not through a Jordanian record.
The February 1948 meeting is known from the abstract of Jevon's study, without its date or the words spoken.
And the Legion's restraint toward the Jewish state's territory can be read as the keeping of an understanding or as the pursuit of the king's own aims, which happened to coincide with it.
Who Spoke for the Palestinian Arabs, 1945–1948
In the years when the Jewish Agency was building a diplomatic case, an arms network and a government in waiting, the Arab side of Palestine's politics was being reorganized from outside the country.

On one reading of the record, set out below, the central fact of the period is institutional: the decisions that shaped the Palestinian Arab response to partition were taken, for the most part, not in Jerusalem or Jaffa but in the council chambers of the Arab League, in Cairo, Bludan, Aley and Alexandria.
The Palestinian leadership had a voice in those rooms, and a record of its own choices.

From its founding in March 1945 until Britain's decision to withdraw in the autumn of 1947, the Arab League consistently supported, in the historian Avi Shlaim's words, a "unitary and independent Palestinian state."
It was the position the Arab case to the Anglo-American Committee had set out in 1946, when it promised that Jews "will be full citizens" of a Palestinian state.
The League also rebuilt the Palestinians' own leadership body.
The Arab Higher Committee had first been formed in 1936, by the Palestinian parties themselves.
After a nine-year hiatus it was re-established in 1946, and this time, Shlaim notes, not by the Palestinian parties but "by a decision of the Arab League."
The difference in origin would define the committee's position for the rest of the period: it spoke for the Palestinian Arabs, but it held its mandate from the League.
Its chairman was Hajj Amin al-Husayni, the Mufti of Jerusalem.
Al-Husayni had spent the Second World War allied with the Axis powers, a record told in .
After the war he was refused asylum in Switzerland and held by France, which declined a British proposal to deport him to the Seychelles.
In May 1946 he escaped from his residence near Paris to Cairo, where King Faruq of Egypt gave him asylum, and the Arab League made him chairman of the new Arab Higher Committee.
The man who led the Palestinian Arabs through 1947 and 1948 therefore did so from exile in Egypt, under the protection of an Arab king, at the head of a body the League had created.
The League's own decisions on Palestine can be followed session by session.
The list compiled by the Jewish Virtual Library from League records gives the following.
In December 1945 the Council set up a committee to enforce a boycott of Zionist goods (Resolution 16) and provided for up to three Palestinian representatives to sit on the Council (Resolution 17).
In March 1946 it approved a company with £E1 million to buy Arab land in Palestine.

In June 1946, at Bludan, it made the boycott part of the "creed of the Arab nations," called for land sales to Zionists to be made a crime (Resolution 72), and created a Higher Arab Executive for Palestine (Resolutions 80 and 82).
In December 1946 it rejected partition (Resolution 142).

In October 1947, at Aley, it adopted a resolution titled "Defending Palestine" (the League's own Resolution 181, not to be confused with the UN resolution of the same number a month later), calling for military preparations along the Arab borders.
The League's chosen instruments in 1945 and 1946 were economic: a boycott of Zionist goods, a land fund of £E1 million to keep Arab land from being sold, and a call to criminalize sales to Zionists.
They were aimed at the mechanism by which the Jewish community had been acquiring land.
When, in February 1948, the Arab Higher Committee asked the League for a loan to meet its administrative costs, the League refused.
The Arab Higher Committee chose to boycott the United Nations special committee that visited Palestine that summer, a decision told in .
The UN partition vote of 29 November then moved the question from argument to war.
For the Cairo session of December 1947, the list records no public announcement, and a decision against formal military intervention unless the United States and Britain intervened militarily.
In February 1948 the Council approved political, military and economic measures, including the withholding of petroleum concessions and sanctions on states aiding the Zionists.
The Mufti wanted something the League would not give.

At the Council sessions in Aley in October 1947 and Cairo in December 1947, Shlaim writes, al-Husayni "pleaded passionately for the establishment of a shadow government" under the Arab Higher Committee.
In the months when the Jewish Agency was preparing the institutions of a state, the Palestinian leadership was refused both a government and the money to run its own committee.

The fighting forces reflected the same division: the League's own Arab Liberation Army under Fawzi al-Qawuqji and the Husayni family's Army of the Holy War acted without cooperating, as the account of the civil war below shows.

The Dictionary of the Israeli-Palestinian Conflict describes the League as divided: King Abdullah of Transjordan "opposed every move toward Palestinian independence" and refused to deal with al-Husayni.
Abdullah's separate course, and his contacts with the Jewish Agency, are told in .
The League changed course only after the state of Israel had been proclaimed and the Arab armies had entered the war.
On 8 July 1948 the League's Political Committee agreed on a "temporary civil administration" for Palestine, responsible to the League.
On 20 September 1948, at Alexandria, the Political Committee announced an All-Palestine Government with its seat in Gaza, headed by Ahmad Hilmi Abdul Baqi.
On 22 September the Arab Higher Committee proclaimed Palestine independent, and on 30 September a Palestinian National Council met in Gaza under the Mufti's chairmanship.
Egypt recognized the new government first, in mid-October 1948, followed by Iraq, and then Syria, Lebanon and Saudi Arabia.
Britain refused.
Abdullah opposed it and said it would not operate in the areas held by his Arab Legion.
Abdullah answered with an assembly of his own.
On 1 December 1948, according to Shlaim, a congress of about 3,000 delegates at Jericho proclaimed the union of Palestine and Transjordan and acknowledged Abdullah as king.
Abdullah afterwards stripped al-Husayni of the title of Mufti of Jerusalem.

By the end of 1948, then, two rival claims to speak for the Palestinian Arabs existed: a government in Gaza recognized by five Arab states and chaired in council by the Mufti, and a congress at Jericho that had placed the Arab parts of Palestine under the Transjordanian crown.
Historians weigh this record differently, and the difference is a question about Palestinian agency itself.

Shlaim reads it as a story of control: the League reconstituted the Arab Higher Committee, refused it a government-in-exile until September 1948, and armed the Arab Liberation Army under its own command.
On this reading the Palestinian leadership's instruments were in other hands, and decisions about Palestine were made by states with their own interests.
The Dictionary of the Israeli-Palestinian Conflict gives more weight to Palestinian choices, and is harder on them.

The Mufti and the Arab Higher Committee pursued their own line, boycotting the UN special committee, pressing for a shadow government and forming the Army of the Holy War; but the 1946 committee was ineffective, its paramilitary forces were uncoordinated, and the League around it was divided.

sent: One explains what the Palestinian leadership could not do; the other records what it chose to do, and how weakly it was able to do it.

The League's session list comes from a compilation of League records rather than from the full minutes, and for the Cairo session of December 1947 it records a decision without any public announcement; what was said in that room is not in the material here.
The date and attendance of the Jericho Congress rest on Shlaim's account alone.

And the counterfactual that hangs over the period, whether a Palestinian government formed in early 1948, when the Mufti asked for one, would have changed the course of the war, is one the documents cannot answer.

What they do establish is the sequence: a League committed to a single Palestinian state, a Palestinian leadership reconstituted by the League and refused a loan, a refusal of government in February 1948, and a government granted in September 1948, four months after the Mandate had ended.
Ernest Bevin and the Palestine Question, 1945–1946
In the same month that the network took shape in New York, the power that actually governed Palestine changed hands.
Clement Attlee formed his Labour government on 26 July 1945 and chose Ernest Bevin as Foreign Secretary.
Bevin had been born on 9 March 1881; he would die on 14 April 1951.

Over the next eighteen months his statements set the terms of British policy on Palestine, and his name became attached to it, by the Zionist leaders who fought him, by the Americans who pressed him, and by the historians who have tried to explain him.
To Chaim Weizmann and to Christopher Mayhew, who dealt with him, he was a man who disliked Jews.
To the historian Alan Bullock, to Ben-Gurion and to Attlee, he was an opponent of a Jewish state, not an enemy of Jews.
To a third school, his policy followed from what the Foreign Office took to be Britain's interests in the Middle East, and his personal feelings mattered little.
Before weighing them, it helps to set out what Bevin actually said and did in his first eighteen months.

Britannica's entry on Bevin offers only one judgment on Palestine: that his plans of 1947–48 "for a federal Jewish-Arab nation or other partition of Palestine collapsed" in the face of the Arab-Israeli conflict.
The detail lies in his own statements, in American diplomatic reports, and in the scholarship that has tried to explain him.
Bevin's first major act on Palestine came on 13 November 1945.
He announced a "joint Anglo-American Committee of Inquiry, under a rotating chairmanship."
Until it reported, he said, there would be "no interruption of Jewish immigration at the present monthly rate."
The statement also set out the terms in which London saw the problem.
Bevin referred to the Palestinian Arabs' "90,000,000 co-religionists in India," and he said that Palestine "does not by itself provide sufficient opportunity" for solving the Jewish problem.

Read together, the two phrases framed Palestine as one part of an answer for Europe's Jews, not the whole of it, and placed the Arabs of Palestine within a far larger population whose opinion London had to weigh.
What matters here is that the inquiry was Bevin's chosen instrument.
It brought Washington into the question, and in the interim it left immigration where it stood.
The same day, Bevin spoke privately to the American ambassador in London, John Winant.

Winant's telegram, received in Washington on 14 November 1945, reported that Bevin said he would be willing to "stake his political future on finding solution for Palestine problem," and that he "made a plea against approaching this subject in spirit of racial antagonism."

The telegram is a primary American record, not Bevin's own text, but it shows how he wished to be understood by the government he most needed to persuade: as a minister who had staked his career on a settlement and who wanted the question kept out of racial politics.
According to the historian Raphael Langham, Bevin told the House of Commons on 13 November, "We cannot accept the view that the Jews should be driven out of Europe."
At a press conference the same day, he warned that if Jews "want to get too much at the head of the queue" there was a danger of an antisemitic reaction.
The first sentence stated a principle: the survivors had a future in Europe and should not be treated as people to be removed from it.
Langham calls the remark "unfortunate."
"Too many Jews in New York."
The pressure Bevin resisted came above all from the United States, where President Truman was pressing for the admission of Jewish refugees to Palestine.
At the Labour Party conference in June 1946, Bevin said of that pressure that "They did not want too many Jews in New York."
Langham calls it "a gratuitous sneer."
It angered Truman and provoked protests in the United States.
It suggested that American support for Jewish immigration to Palestine was a way of keeping Jews out of America, and it was made at a party conference, in public.
Whatever conclusion one reaches about Bevin's policy, the sentence itself needs no softening.
The London conference and the American visit.
In September 1946 Britain convened a conference at Lancaster House in London.
According to Langham, Bevin told the Arab delegation there that no solution could ignore Jewish claims.

This sits awkwardly beside the remarks above, and that is part of what makes him hard to read: the same minister who sneered at American motives told the Arab states that Jewish claims had to be part of any settlement.
Two months later he traveled to the United States, in November and December 1946.
During that visit, Langham writes, Bevin reportedly came to the view that Britain would have to give up the Mandate.
In these months Bevin held the levers that mattered for Palestine: the rate of Jewish immigration, the choice of forum, and the timing of any settlement.

It kept immigration at the existing rate rather than opening the gates or closing them, it moved the question into a joint inquiry with the United States, and it pointed toward trusteeship rather than either a Jewish or an Arab state.
The Jewish Agency and the Arab representatives could put their cases to the inquiry but could not decide; and Washington, though it pressed hard on immigration, did not govern Palestine.
What Bevin could not control was the American response, and his June 1946 remark shows how much that pressure grated.
Why did Bevin oppose a Jewish state?
Historians have given three answers, and Langham sets them out side by side.
Christopher Mayhew said that "Ernest detests Jews," and Chaim Weizmann said Bevin was "blinded by his hatred of the Jews."
The historian Peter Weiler takes a more careful line: he finds that Bevin "held antisemitic views" but sees "no evidence that they shaped his policy."
Its weakness, as Weiler's own wording shows, is the step from a man's prejudices to the reasons for his decisions.
The second answer is that Bevin was an anti-Zionist, not an antisemite.
The historian Alan Bullock wrote that he "was not moved by hatred of the Jews."
David Ben-Gurion, who had every reason to think the worst of him, said, "I prefer to consider Bevin simply as an anti-Zionist."
Attlee defended him in the same terms in the House of Commons in 1949.
The strength of this case is that it comes in part from Bevin's opponents, Ben-Gurion above all, and that it fits his statement to the Arab delegation in September 1946.
Its weakness is that the remarks of November 1945 and June 1946 are hard to describe as political opposition to Zionism alone.

A Foreign Office briefing attributed to Harold Beeley stressed Middle East oil, communications and the Suez route as Britain's interests in the region, and Langham cites the historian W. Roger Louis on Britain's Middle East position.

On this reading, Bevin's policy was the Foreign Office's policy: Britain needed the goodwill of the Arab states and of Muslim opinion, the "90,000,000 co-religionists in India" whom Bevin himself had invoked, and a Jewish state imposed against that opinion would put those interests at risk.
The strength of this case is that it explains the policy without needing to explain the man, and that it rests on the Foreign Office's own statement of British interests.
Langham's own conclusion leans toward the third answer.
Bevin, he writes, was probably not motivated by antisemitism when he made policy, and "genuinely thought it was in the best interests of Britain."
But his opposition hardened over time into anti-Zionism, and Langham leaves open whether, in that later stage, Bevin crossed into antisemitism.

That conclusion keeps two things apart that are often run together: what a man said about Jews, which in Bevin's case included antisemitic remarks stated in public, and why his government did what it did, which Langham ties to what Bevin judged to be Britain's interests.
The sources used here do not show what "the present monthly rate" of immigration was in November 1945, since Bevin's text gave no figure.
They do not show what Bevin said to American officials during his visit in late 1946, only Langham's report that he came to think the Mandate would have to be given up.
Nor can any document settle what Bevin felt, as against what he said and did.
Britain Lets Go, February–September 1947
While Washington argued over the President's motives, London was deciding to give the problem up.
In the space of eight months in 1947, Britain went from governing Palestine to announcing that it would leave.
The steps were formal and dated: a Cabinet decision in February, a letter to the United Nations in April, and a statement to the General Assembly's Ad Hoc Committee in September.
Between them came hangings, kidnappings, riots in British cities and a refugee ship turned back to Europe.
The question historians still argue over is how these events related to one another, and in particular how far the Jewish armed campaign drove Britain out.

By the start of 1947 the policy that Ernest Bevin had staked his name on in November 1945 had run out of road; that earlier course, from the Anglo-American Committee to the London conference, is traced in .

On 14 February 1947 Bevin told the Arab delegates in London that the Cabinet had agreed the question should go to the United Nations without British recommendations, "inasmuch as plan offered by British Delegation had met with no acceptance from either Arabs or Jews".
Britain, he said, would present the matter "as impartially as possible" .
The words survive in a telegram from the American embassy in London to the Secretary of State.
Four days later, on 18 February 1947, Bevin explained the decision in the House of Commons.
In the text reproduced by the Center for Online Judaic Studies, which gives no archival citation, he described "an irreconcilable conflict of principles".
ents: the Center for Online Judaic Studies

sent: For the Jews, the essential principle was a sovereign Jewish state.
For the Arabs, it was to resist Jewish sovereignty anywhere in Palestine.
He called the Mandate "unworkable in practice", and he put the country's population at about 1,200,000 Arabs and 600,000 Jews .
Because that text could not be checked against Hansard, its wording should be read as reported rather than verified.
The historian Raphael Langham adds that in the Commons Bevin blamed the Jews and the United States for the failure .

On 2 April 1947 Sir Alexander Cadogan, for the United Kingdom, asked the United Nations to "place the question of Palestine on the Agenda of the General Assembly at its next regular Annual Session", and to "summon, as soon as possible, a special Session" to constitute a special committee .
Britain did not surrender the Mandate in April.
It asked the Assembly to take up the question and to set up a committee, while it went on governing.
The committee that resulted, UNSCOP, spent the summer in Palestine and the region; its work is told in .
On 16 April 1947 Britain executed four members of the Irgun: Dov Gruner, Yehiel Dresner, Mordechai Alkahi and Eliezer Kashani.
On 4 May the Irgun broke into Acre prison.
Three of the attackers who were captured, Avshalom Haviv, Yaakov Weiss and Meir Nakar, were sentenced to death and hanged on 29 July 1947 .
By then the Irgun held two British hostages.
On the night of 11 to 12 July 1947 it kidnapped two Intelligence Corps sergeants, Clifford Martin and Mervyn Paice, in Netanya.
On 30 July, the day after the Acre men were hanged, it hanged the sergeants, and booby-trapped their bodies .
The killings provoked a reaction in Britain itself.
From 1 August 1947 anti-Jewish rioting broke out, beginning in Liverpool and spreading to other cities .
It should be named for what it was: antisemitic violence in British cities, aimed at Jews in Britain in response to killings carried out by the Irgun in Palestine.
The same month brought an episode that, in the Holocaust Memorial Museum's account, helped shift diplomatic sympathy.

In July 1947 a ship formerly called the President Warfield, renamed Exodus 1947, sailed from Sète in France with more than 4,500 Jewish passengers, most of them displaced persons and Holocaust survivors  .
When the Royal Navy boarded it, three Jews were killed, one crew member and two passengers according to the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, and dozens were wounded  .
Yad Vashem states that the ship was attacked on 17 July in international waters, that three people were killed, and that it reached Haifa on 18 July .
The Holocaust Memorial Museum dates the clash to 18 July 1947 and specifies one crew member and two passengers among the dead .
What Britain did next made the ship a symbol.
The passengers were moved onto three navy transports and taken back to Port-de-Bouc in France.
France declined to remove them by force.
After a hunger strike of 24 days and about three weeks in the summer heat, they were carried to Hamburg and interned in camps in the British zone of Germany .
Langham records that Bevin insisted the passengers be returned to their port of embarkation, and suggests that prejudice may have played a part .
That is Langham's suggestion, and he frames it as a possibility rather than a finding.

Yad Vashem states that the voyage was meant to draw the attention of the UNSCOP members then working in the country; the Holocaust Memorial Museum says the "public embarrassment for Britain" helped shift diplomatic sympathy  .
The decision to leave outright, rather than to hand over a question for advice, was announced at the United Nations.

On 26 September 1947 Arthur Creech Jones, the Colonial Secretary, told the Ad Hoc Committee that "in the absence of a settlement" Britain had to plan for "an early withdrawal of British forces and of the British administration".
Britain, he said, "was not prepared to undertake the task of imposing a policy in Palestine by force of arms" .
The Assembly could recommend what it liked; Britain would not enforce it.
When the Assembly voted on partition on 29 November 1947, Britain abstained .

The funding ledger compiled for this library puts the cost of the forces in Palestine in 1945–47 at about £100 million, with some 100,000 troops deployed and about 750 British killed over the period; in today's money the cost is roughly $6.7 billion.
The ledger's sources are listed with the panel below, and the full account of Britain's bill appears in the next stage of this book.

Britain's military bill for 1945–47 is the second-largest item on it, behind only the Jewish capital invested in Palestine between 1921 and 1937, and well above the United Jewish Appeal's wartime giving of 1939–45.
The sources used here do not say how much weight the Cabinet gave to that cost when it decided to leave; they show only that the cost was being paid.
How much did the Jewish insurgency, and the sergeants affair in particular, cause the withdrawal?

The historian J. Bowyer Bell called the sergeants affair the "straw that broke the Mandate's back", and Creech Jones himself, writing in 1961, listed the sergeants affair as one of four major factors behind the Cabinet's September 1947 decision to evacuate .

The strength of this case is the testimony of the minister who announced the withdrawal, and the timing: the sergeants were hanged on 30 July, riots broke out in Britain on 1 August, and the withdrawal was announced eight weeks later.

Britain's own stated reason, in February, was the irreconcilable Arab and Jewish positions and the failure of its own plan; the Cabinet had agreed to hand the question to the United Nations before the executions, the Acre break-in, the kidnapping or the Exodus .
Langham points to strategic considerations and Britain's relations with the Arab states .
February's decision referred the question; September's decision ended the Mandate; the events between may explain why the second followed the first so fast, even if they did not cause the first.
Britain's departure did not end Bevin's part in the story.
In May 1948 he told the Commons, "there are, after all, no Arabs in the House", and Britain recognized Israel only in January 1949, with Bevin's acceptance, in Langham's word, "grudging" .

The Cabinet's own minutes for February and September 1947 are not among the sources used, so the weight the ministers themselves gave to cost, to the insurgency, to American pressure or to Arab opinion cannot be measured from them.
Creech Jones's four factors are known from a later account, written in 1961, and only one of the four is named in the source.
The exact date of the Exodus boarding differs between two reputable institutions.
And whether prejudice shaped Bevin's handling of the Exodus is, in the one historian's account that raises it, a possibility and not a demonstrated fact.

What the documents do show is the order of events: Britain referred the question because its plan had failed with both sides, endured a summer of executions, reprisals and a refugee ship that embarrassed it before the world, and then announced that it would not stay to enforce whatever the world decided.
The Fall of the Mixed Towns, April–May 1948
ents: The Fall of the Mixed Towns

sent: For four months after the partition vote, the fighting in Palestine was a civil war, with attacks in both directions.
The Palestinian historian Walid Khalidi writes that the Zionist forces "did not begin to seize and hold on to Arab territory" until the offensive that began on 1 April 1948.
That offensive opened under Plan Dalet, issued three weeks earlier ().
Within six weeks the towns in which Arabs and Jews had lived side by side, and the Arab towns near them, had changed hands one after another.

Khalidi's phrasing is precise, and it should be read beside his own correction elsewhere: a footnote in his study of Plan Dalet records that at least ten Arab villages had been captured by 1 March 1948.
Villages were taken before April; the systematic seizing and holding of Arab territory, in his account, began with the April offensive.
Its Arab population, about 4,500 to 5,000 people and swollen by refugees from nearby villages, was evacuated.
Haifa followed within the week, and its fall is the best documented and the most argued over.
Early on 21 April 1948 the Haganah's Carmeli Brigade, under Moshe Carmel, attacked as British forces withdrew from their dividing positions in the city.
That same day Major-General Hugh Stockwell, the British commander, had told Arab representatives that his forces would redeploy.
The cost is known from British figures, which Khalidi cites: about 100 Arabs killed and 200 wounded, and about 20 Jews killed and 40 wounded.
On 22 April about 50,000 Arabs were crowded into the Old Town.
On 22 April the Arab delegates met Stockwell at the Town Hall over the terms of a truce; Haifa's Jewish mayor was there too, according to one account.
What was said there, and what it meant, is the heart of the dispute over why Haifa's Arabs left.
Khalidi's account, which draws on an account by Koussa, runs as follows.
Stockwell warned the Arab delegates that if they did not sign the truce he would not be responsible if "three or four hundred more" were killed.
The delegates had asked Damascus for instructions and had no reply.
Their request for transport out of the city, according to Koussa's account, was made "on the spur of the moment," not under orders from the Arab states.
Khalidi concludes: "Within a week, some 50,000 Arab inhabitants had been expelled."
Khalidi goes further on the British role.
He argues that the Haganah had advance knowledge of the British redeployment, and he calls Stockwell "an accomplice in the fall of Haifa."

The strongest form of his case is that the timing of the attack, the redeployment and the ultimatum at the Town Hall fit together too closely to be chance, and that the evacuation request was the improvised act of men without instructions under military pressure, not a plan from outside.
A sharply different account appears in an opinion article in the Jewish Chronicle by Florit Shoihet, published on 12 August 2026.
According to that article, Haifa's Jewish mayor, Shabtai Levy, pleaded with the Arab delegates at the same meeting: "Stay in the city and be equal citizens."
The Haganah, it says, broadcast assurances of safety and civil rights, and about 60,000 Arabs left.

The strongest form of this case is that Haifa's Arabs were offered terms of equal citizenship by the Jewish mayor and urged to stay by the British commander, and that their own delegation chose to leave.
The third position is the historian Benny Morris's, as Khalidi reports it, and it has shifted.
Morris first acknowledged, in 1987, that there were no Arab evacuation orders.
Khalidi disputes the later position.
The broader question of evacuation orders, and the June 1948 Israeli intelligence estimate that attributed no more than 5 percent of departures to them, is set out in .

Even the Haifa operation's name is unsettled: Khalidi's Haifa study says the operation planned as Misparayim was renamed Chametz, while his list of Plan D operations keeps the two apart, a discrepancy set out with the Plan Dalet record.
After Haifa the other towns followed in the last three weeks of the Mandate.

Khalidi's operation list gives the frame: Chametz against the villages around Jaffa from 27 April; Yiftach in eastern Galilee from 28 April; Matateh in the Tiberias area from 3 May; Gideon at Beisan from 11 May; and Ben Ami at Acre on 14 May, the day the state was proclaimed.
Jaffa and Safed fell in these weeks.
During the war an estimated 100,000 to 110,000 Palestinian Arabs fled or were displaced into Lebanon, the large majority from northern Palestine, including the Acre area.

Tiberias and Haifa are documented in detail; Jaffa, Safed, Beisan and Acre appear here only through Khalidi's list of operations, and the exact dates on which Jaffa, Safed and Acre fell are not established in the sources used here.
For Haifa, the British casualty figures and the timing of the redeployment are documented.
Whether the Haganah knew of the redeployment in advance rests on Khalidi's argument.
What was said at the Town Hall rests on two accounts that cannot both be complete: Khalidi's, from the Arab side, and an opinion article that cites no archive.
And Morris's own changing view shows that the question of evacuation orders in Haifa has not been settled even by a historian whose archival work documented the expulsions in detail.
The Arab States' War, May 1948 – 1949
The British Mandate ended at midnight on 14 May 1948.
Within hours the fighting already under way inside Palestine became a war between the new State of Israel and the armies of its neighbors.
In one, five Arab armies set out to destroy a newborn state on the day of its birth.
In the other, the Arab states sent their armies to protect the Palestinian Arabs from a Jewish force already on the offensive.
On 15 May 1948 the Secretary-General of the Arab League sent a cablegram to the Secretary-General of the United Nations, registered as document S/745.
It is the Arab states' own statement of why they were going to war, and it deserves to be read as such.

The Mandate, it said, had ended "leaving no legally constituted authority behind," and the Arab states were therefore intervening "to restore law and order and to prevent disturbances prevailing in Palestine from spreading" into their own territories.

It stated that "approximately over a quarter of a million of the Arab population have been compelled to leave their homes," and it declared support for "the creation of United State of Palestine based upon the democratic principles."

The first was a statement about displacement that had already taken place before the invasion; the second was a political aim, a single state in place of the partition the General Assembly had voted for six months earlier.
The US State Department's Office of the Historian records that the war began with an Arab air attack on Tel Aviv on the eve of 14 May.
ents: The US State Department's Office of the Historian

sent: Armies from Lebanon, Syria, Iraq and Egypt invaded; a Saudi formation fought under Egyptian command; and Transjordanian forces intervened only in the areas designated for the Arab state or for the Jerusalem corpus separatum, the international zone the partition plan had drawn around the city.
Through all of it the United States kept an arms embargo on all belligerents.

The record on Lebanon says that on 15 May Lebanon "joined Egypt, Syria, Jordan, and Iraq in declaring war and invading the new state," and the record on Egypt likewise counts Jordan among the invaders.

Whether Transjordan's Arab Legion invaded Israel or entered the parts of Palestine the United Nations had assigned to the Arabs is the heart of a long argument about King Abdullah's intentions, told in the section on his dealings with the Jewish Agency.
Lebanon's is often passed over.
It fielded the smallest of the five Arab armies, and its choice to fight was its own.

According to Makram Rabah, a history lecturer at the American University of Beirut, the country's founding leaders, Riad al-Solh and Bechara el-Khoury, who had led Lebanon to independence from France in 1943, had debated and rejected an alliance with the Zionist movement before 1948, concluding that they could not keep relations with the neighbouring Arab states while holding one.
Lebanon's posture was thus a deliberated political choice, not simply a reaction imposed from outside.
Egypt joined the invasion in May 1948 after the end of the Mandate.
Saudi Arabia did not launch an invasion of its own.
Its part was a small contingent of troops placed under Egyptian command.
Accounts of the kingdom's role explain the modest scale by its greater distance from Palestine.

The Arab League's boycott of Israel, formalized in 1948, barred member states from any direct economic relationship with the new state; a secondary boycott added in 1950 extended the bar to foreign companies doing business with Israel, and a tertiary boycott later reached companies dealing with those on the secondary list.

According to the account of the kingdom's role, Saudi Arabia was among its most consistent enforcers and kept it in some form for over seven decades, and it has never established diplomatic relations with Israel.

Avi Shlaim gives the forces on 15 May 1948 as 35,000 Israeli troops against 20,000–25,000 Arab troops, and argues that "illicit arms-imports decisively tipped the military balance in favour of Israel."

His seminar notes add that the forces the Arab states actually sent were "well below the level demanded by the Military Committee of the Arab League," and that the Israeli army had more men but weaker firepower.
A US assessment of July 1948, discussed in , counted about 90,000 Israeli forces by then.
Shlaim's notes give the outline of the first four weeks.
The Egyptian advance stalled at Ramat Rahel on 24 May and at Ashdod on 29 May.
The Syrians were stopped at Degania but held Mishmar Hayarden.
The Iraqis held the triangle of Jenin, Nablus and Tulkarem.
In Jerusalem the Jewish Quarter surrendered on 28 May, and three frontal Israeli attacks on the Arab Legion's position at Latrun, on 25 and 30 May and on 9 June, were repelled.
Syria's army fought on the northern front and ended the war holding small areas west of the international border.
Lebanon's invasion was repelled, and Israeli forces for a time occupied part of southern Lebanon.
The first round thus ended with the Egyptian and Syrian advances stopped, the Iraqis holding their triangle, the Jewish Quarter lost and Latrun still in the Legion's hands.
The United Nations mediator, Count Folke Bernadotte, had been appointed on 21 May.
The truce he supervised ran 28 days, from 11 June to 9 July 1948, with observers from Belgium, France, Sweden and the United States.
According to the Israel Defense Forces' own account, published by the Jewish Virtual Library, materiel reached the Israeli army during the truce from Europe, "particularly Czechoslovakia."
Bernadotte used the pause to propose a settlement: the Galilee to Israel, the Negev to the Arabs, and Jerusalem under the United Nations.

The arms that crossed during those four weeks are the subject of the section on the Czechoslovak pipeline; Bernadotte's own fate, at the hands of Lehi in September, is told in the section on the founding of the army.
Lydda and Ramla, July 1948.
Operation Dani was launched from Ben Shemen on the night of 9–10 July.
The assault on Lydda began on 11 July, and by 12 July the town was under full Israeli control, without a formal surrender.
According to Sana Hammoudi's account in the Interactive Encyclopedia of the Palestine Question, between 80 and 176 people were killed at the Dahmash mosque and more than 400 in the town.
Both that account and Zachary Lockman, each citing the Israeli historian Benny Morris, report that on 12 July David Ben-Gurion answered a question about the inhabitants with the words "Expel them."
Yitzhak Rabin then signed an order to expel Lydda's inhabitants quickly.
Israeli censors later made Rabin remove the episode from his memoir.
Lockman, summarizing Morris, puts the combined population of Lydda and Ramla at 50,000–70,000, about 15,000 of them refugees, with 250–400 Palestinian civilians and four Israeli soldiers killed.
The Palestinian encyclopedia estimates that about 70,000 people were forced out on 13 July and that close to 1,000 died in the towns and on the march that followed.
The second truce and Jerusalem.
It did not bring quiet to Jerusalem.
According to the IDF account, the Arab Legion continued to shell West Jerusalem through October and on 12 August demolished the pumping station at Latrun, then held by the United Nations.
The war ended in separate armistice agreements between Israel and Egypt, Lebanon, Transjordan and Syria; Egypt kept the Gaza Strip and Jordan the West Bank.
The Office of the Historian dates them, collectively, to "February 1949."

The agreements with Egypt were negotiated on the Greek island of Rhodes; they set a ceasefire line, not a peace, which served as the de facto border along the edge of the Gaza Strip for the next two decades.
From 1948 to 1967 Egypt governed Gaza directly as a military protectorate, and its officials maintained throughout that it had not annexed the territory.
Why Cairo avoided annexation is not settled by the record: some accounts stress an Arab League consensus against it, others Egyptian strategic caution.
Lebanon's armistice, signed on 23 March 1949, restored the internationally recognized border.
Syria's took longer, and the delay holds one of the war's least-known episodes.

After Husni al-Za'im seized power in Damascus in March 1949, armistice talks opened on 5 April; Za'im offered a peace treaty and military cooperation, proposed meeting Ben-Gurion or Moshe Sharett, and offered to resettle 250,000–300,000 Palestinian refugees in Syria, with the border drawn through the middle of Lake Hula and the Sea of Galilee.
Ben-Gurion would not stake policy on him, partly from distrust of his ties to Washington.

The armistice signed on 20 July 1949 turned the areas Syria evacuated into demilitarized zones, which became the fault line of the frontier; in August Za'im was deposed and executed in Syria's second coup of the year, and the offer died with him ().
More than 6,000 Israelis were killed in the war, about 1% of the roughly 650,000 Jews then in the country, according to a Reuters figure published by Ynet in 2005.
The war's other costs fell on the Palestinian Arabs: the quarter of a million already displaced by 15 May on the League's own count, and many more after it, as told in .
In Lebanon alone an estimated 100,000–110,000 arrived from northern Palestine.
The number of Arab soldiers and civilians killed in the war has not been established here, and no figure is offered.
The fighting of the autumn and winter of 1948–49, between the second truce and the armistices, is not covered by the sources used here beyond the Jerusalem front.
The sources disagree on whether Transjordan invaded Israel or entered only the areas assigned to the Arab state, and on the date of the armistices.
The tolls at Lydda and Ramla rest on estimates that differ by a factor of two or more.

And the deepest question, whether the armies came to save the Palestinian Arabs, to prevent a Jewish state, or to take territory for themselves, has no single answer: the League's cablegram, Lebanon's deliberated choice, Saudi Arabia's distant contingent, the Legion's entry, on the Office of the Historian's account, only into the areas assigned to the Arab state or the international zone, and Egypt's nineteen-year administration of Gaza without annexation point in different directions, because the states that went to war in May 1948 were pursuing different ends.
After the Vote: Jews of the Arab World, 1947–1948
The war of 1948 is usually told as a war inside Palestine, and its refugees as one people's loss.
The record of the same months shows a second set of events running in parallel, outside Palestine.

From the day after the partition vote, Jewish communities in Syria, Egypt, Lebanon, Aden, Bahrain, Iraq and Libya came under attack from mobs, under arrest and sequestration by governments, and in Iraq under a law that made Zionism a crime.
In Yemen, by the end of 1948, the ruler permitted the Jews to leave.
These were not acts of "the Arabs" in general.
Together they began the decline of these communities, a story that runs well past 1948 and is set beside the Palestinian displacement in .
On 30 November 1947, the day after the General Assembly voted for partition, anti-Jewish riots broke out in Damascus, Aleppo, Cairo, Beirut and Aden, according to the Center for Israel Education.
In Cairo, the same account reports, leaders of al-Azhar declared a holy war against the Zionists.
The worst damage that the sources record in Syria was in Aleppo.
A mob broke into the Great Synagogue, destroyed Torah scrolls and damaged the Aleppo Codex; most of the Codex was saved and smuggled to Jerusalem in 1958.
Across the city, according to the same account, 150 Jewish homes, 50 shops, five schools and 18 synagogues were destroyed.
On 5 December 1947, in Bahrain, Jewish homes and shops were looted, the synagogue was destroyed and one Jewish woman was killed.
The deadliest of these riots took place in Aden, then a British colony.
The Center for Israel Education lists Aden among the cities where violence broke out after the vote; the accounts of Aden itself date the riots there from 2 December 1947.
The Center for Israel Education gives 82 Jews killed and 76 wounded.
The Jewish Virtual Library, which credits Wikipedia for its entry, gives between 76 and 82 Jews killed, and also 38 others killed: 33 Arabs, four Indian Muslims and one Somali.
It records that 106 of the 170 Jewish-owned shops in Crater were looted.
The sources agree on the order of magnitude, between 76 and 82 Jewish dead, and differ on the exact count.
It is "The Situation of Jews in Moslem Countries," by H. Dewey Anderson, chapter XIV of The Arab Refugee Problem, a set of proposals submitted to the United Nations General Assembly in December 1951.
It is available today through the Center for Israel Education, which presents it as a UN report.
It is a contemporary compilation by a named author, written three years after the events and placed inside a work about the Arab refugees.
It is not a resolution or a finding of the General Assembly.
Its dates and figures are specific, and they are used below as Anderson's, attributed to him, because the sources gathered do not test them against the governments' own records.
Egypt: arrests, sequestration and bombings.
When the Arab armies entered Palestine in May 1948, the Egyptian government turned against the Jews of its own cities.
According to Anderson, more than 1,000 Jews were arrested in Cairo on 15 May 1948.
Proclamation No. 26, issued on 29 May, sequestered the property of internees; of the 68 sequestration orders issued up to 30 September, 67 involved Jews.
Proclamation No. 30, of 6 June, allowed Jews to be searched without a warrant.
Violence followed in Cairo's Jewish quarters.
Anderson records 12 houses destroyed and 20 people killed; Wikipedia, citing the historian Beinin, gives 22 killed and 41 wounded.
The Cicurel department store was bombed on 19 July, and a bombing on 22 September killed 19 people.

In November 1948 the government arrested 32 leaders of the Muslim Brotherhood and banned the organization, and in a trial in 1950 members of the Brotherhood were charged with the bombings of June to November.
Iraq: a law, a hanging and an armistice never signed.
Iraq took part in the war from the start.

It joined the invasion on 15 May 1948, the day after Israel declared independence, and when the fighting ended it was the only Arab state that had fought which refused to sign an armistice with Israel, leaving a formal state of war that, in the Israeli government's account, has never ended.
The invasion itself is told in the section on the Arab states' war.

At home, according to accounts of the Iraqi Jewish community, the measures escalated after the partition vote from mob violence to the confiscation of property and prosecutions those accounts call trumped-up.
Anderson writes that it made Zionist activity punishable by death or by at least seven years' imprisonment.
An account in Yated Ne'eman dates the law to 19 July 1948 and gives the penalty as up to seven years in prison.

It adds that every Jew was presumed to be a Zionist under the law, so that it worked as a blanket criminalization of the community, and that the testimony of two Muslim witnesses was enough to convict, with little means of appeal.
On 28 August 1948 Jews were barred from banking and from dealing in foreign currency, and on 19 October they were ordered discharged from government departments, according to Anderson.
On 23 September 1948 Shafiq Ades, a prominent and well-connected Jewish businessman, was publicly hanged in Basra on charges of selling weapons to Israel and to the Iraqi Communist Party.

That is a judgment about how Iraqi Jews read the hanging, recorded by those who wrote their history; the sources do not describe the proceedings against him, and the charges cannot be tested from them.
Syria, Libya and Yemen.

Anderson records that on 15 May 1948, the same day as the Cairo arrests, 250 Jews were imprisoned in Aleppo; that a "second wave of violence" struck the Jews of Tripoli, in Libya, on 14 June 1948; and that in December 1948 the ruler of Yemen permitted the country's Jews to leave.
Over the following decades the large Jewish communities of Iraq, Yemen, Libya, Egypt, Syria and North Africa shrank dramatically.

Estimates of the total who left the Arab countries and Iran between 1948 and the 1970s commonly fall between 800,000 and 900,000 people, and the causes varied by country: emigration, pressure, expulsion and state persecution in different proportions.
Morocco shows the variety.

Its Jewish community, rooted there for some two thousand years, numbered in the hundreds of thousands in the 1940s and largely emigrated after 1948, mostly to Israel; between 1961 and 1964 about 97,000 left in Operation Yachin, with payments to the Moroccan government that historians record.
The later exodus from Iraq is told in .
The war of 1948 is often described simply as a war between Israel and its neighbors, and Iraq's part in it as one army among several.
Iraq's war had a domestic side, a law and a public hanging aimed at its own Jewish citizens, and it ended without the armistice every other Arab combatant signed.

And the same pattern, in different degrees, appears in Egypt, Syria, Aden, Bahrain and Libya: riots on the day after the vote, the destruction of synagogues, killings, and proclamations and laws aimed at Jews by the governments of Egypt and Iraq.

It names mobs in particular cities, particular governments issuing particular orders, the leaders of a particular institution, al-Azhar, declaring holy war, and, in Cairo, a particular organization whose members were charged in court.
The exact death tolls in Aden and in the Cairo bombings remain in dispute, as the figures above show.
The penalty in Iraq's July 1948 law is given differently by the two sources.

Much of the official record of 1948 reaches this book through a single compilation, Anderson's, made in 1951 for a debate about refugees, and the governments' own archives are not among the sources used here.
The outcome of the 1950 trial in Cairo is not recorded in them.
Nor do they give the number of Jews who left the Arab countries in 1948 itself, as distinct from the totals for the decades that followed.
What is established is the pattern of the first thirteen months: violence by mobs, arrests and sequestration by governments, and a law in Iraq that put a whole community under suspicion.
The war of 1948 produced two outcomes that have shaped everything since: a Jewish state, and a Palestinian Arab population largely displaced from the territory that state came to hold.
Palestinians call the second the Nakba, Arabic for "catastrophe."
The displacement began before the Arab armies entered.
In its cablegram of 15 May 1948 the Arab League told the United Nations that "approximately over a quarter of a million of the Arab population have been compelled to leave their homes."
One figure for the whole war comes from the United Nations itself.

In a report dated at Lausanne on 19 August 1949 (document A/AC.25/Com.Tech/9), the Technical Committee of the UN Conciliation Commission for Palestine adopted an estimate made by P. J. Loftus of the UN Statistical Office: about 711,000 refugees from the territory under Israeli control, a figure the committee described as "as accurate as circumstances permit."
The warning matters, because UNRWA's later figure drew on relief rolls.
Rex Brynen's Palestinian Refugee ResearchNet at McGill University set out the range in 1996.

It gives the Conciliation Commission's figure as 726,000; UNRWA's 1950 figure as 957,000; the Israeli government's past figure as "as low as 520,000"; and Palestinian researchers' upper estimate as 850,000.
The two figures attributed to the Conciliation Commission, 711,000 in its own technical report and 726,000 in Brynen's summary, do not match, and this book gives both.
The panel above sets that figure, about 700,000 with the UN estimate of about 711,000, beside the land and immigration numbers of the Mandate years.
According to Brynen, about a third of the refugees went to the West Bank, a third to Gaza, and the rest to Jordan, Syria, Lebanon and beyond.
Gaza was then under Egyptian administration and the West Bank under Jordanian.
Lebanon received an estimated 100,000–110,000, the large majority from northern Palestine, including the Acre area, in a country of about 1.3 million people.
The International Committee of the Red Cross, and from 1950 UNRWA, ran the camps that resulted.
ents: The International Committee of the Red Cross

sent: Jordan later gave citizenship to most Palestinians who had come after 1948, under its 1954 nationality law; Lebanon restricted their work and, much later, their right to own property; and the Arab League instructed its members not to grant citizenship, in its words "to avoid dissolution of their identity and protect their right of return."
The displacement became, in the words of one account, the foundational political fact around which every later Palestinian political movement organized.
A central document is an intelligence report of the Israel Defense Forces from June 1948, known through the work of the Israeli historian Benny Morris and summarized by Zachary Lockman.
It estimated that by 1 June 1948 about 240,000 Arabs had fled the areas of the Jewish state and about 150,000 had fled other areas.

It attributed about 70% of the flight to direct Jewish military operations, 2% to psychological warfare and 2% to expulsion orders, a figure Morris considers an underestimate, and no more than 5% to evacuation orders from Arab leaders.
The claim that Palestinians left on the orders of their own leaders, broadcast by Arab radio, corresponds to that last category, and the IDF's own estimate put it at 5% or less.
The investigation of the radio claim itself is told in the section on independence and the Nakba.
Morris concludes, according to Lockman, that deliberate expulsions helped create about 300,000 further refugees, but that there was no explicit, general Israeli decision to expel.

The expulsion from Lydda and Ramla in July, after Ben-Gurion's reported words "Expel them" and Yitzhak Rabin's signed order, is the best-known case; its tolls are disputed and are set out in the section on the Arab states' war.
Morris, as Avi Shlaim summarizes him, "rejected both the 'Arab order' and the 'Jewish robber-state' explanations" and treated the refugee problem as "a by-product of the war."
Shlaim holds that the evidence "suggests a far higher degree of Israeli responsibility."
Walid Khalidi's reading goes further: that the flight was produced by design, under Plan Dalet, the plan discussed earlier in this chapter.
The strongest form of Morris's case is that the flight came in waves with different causes, that most of it followed fighting rather than orders, and that no general order to expel has been found.
"As early as June 1948," Lockman writes, "the cabinet had reached a consensus against allowing the refugees to return to their homes."
The decision came while the war was still being fought, and before the expulsions from Lydda and Ramla in July.
Lockman also writes that a report by Yosef Weitz in October 1948 falsely blamed Arab leaders for organizing the flight.
That is Lockman's judgment of Weitz's report; the point it carries is that the "Arab leaders' orders" explanation was being put forward in an Israeli report within months.

One offer to settle part of the question came from an Arab government: in 1949 Syria's new military ruler, Husni al-Za'im, offered to resettle 250,000–300,000 refugees in Syria as part of a peace treaty, an offer Ben-Gurion declined and which ended with Za'im's overthrow and execution that August.
The United Nations' response, and the negotiations that followed, belong to the next stage: see  and .
How many Arab villages were emptied depends on what is counted.
Morris, in 1987, counted 369.
Walid Khalidi's All That Remains (1992) counted 418, excluding towns and 151 places found on other lists.
Aref al-Aref counted 399; Nijm and Muammer 443; Saleh 472; and the Palestine Land Society 531 localities, counting tribal lands and towns.
No single count of the refugees commands agreement; the sources range from 520,000 to 957,000, and even the Conciliation Commission's figure is reported two ways.

The share of the flight caused by deliberate expulsion, as against fighting, fear and the collapse of Palestinian society, is estimated from an army report that its own principal interpreter considers incomplete on expulsions.
The number of Arabs who remained inside Israel in 1948–49 has not been established in the sources gathered.

What is not in dispute is the outcome: by the summer of 1949 several hundred thousand Palestinian Arabs were outside the territory Israel held, and its cabinet had reached a consensus, a year earlier, against their return.
The Jewish Resistance Movement, 1945–1946
For fourteen months after the Second World War, the three Jewish armed organizations in Palestine fought the British together.
The Haganah and the two other organizations, the Irgun and Lehi, whose origins are told in , had been separate commands.
The arrangement they made has a name, the Jewish Resistance Movement, and a beginning and an end that can be dated.
The account of the movement used in this section comes from the Lehi heritage association, which keeps the memory of one of the three organizations.
It is written from Lehi's own perspective, and it gives no casualty totals for the movement's operations.
Every operational detail below is therefore Lehi's account of events, reported as such.
British records, Haganah records and independent scholarship on these operations are not part of the material available here for this period.

In early September 1945, according to the heritage account, four men agreed to form a united Jewish Resistance Movement: Moshe Sneh and Yisrael Galili for the Haganah, Natan Yellin-Mor for Lehi, and Menachem Begin for the Irgun.
The Haganah took part through its Palmach.
Three separate commands kept their own organizations and their own leaders; what they agreed was to act against the British in concert.
As the ending of the movement would show, the Haganah's part in it could be switched off by the Jewish Agency and the Zionist Congress; the Irgun's and Lehi's could not.
The agreement came in the weeks after a new Labour government took office in London on 26 July 1945.

Its Foreign Secretary, Ernest Bevin, did not set out his policy on Palestine until 13 November 1945, when he announced a joint Anglo-American inquiry and said that Jewish immigration would continue only "at the present monthly rate" in the meantime.
The Night of the Trains, 1 November 1945.
Operations began on the night of 1 November 1945, remembered as the "Night of the Trains."
At the railway station at Lydda, Lehi and Irgun fighters destroyed three engines and damaged a train and a signal box; some police and railway workers were killed or injured.
The same night, a Lehi bomb at the Haifa refinery went off early and killed the operation's commander, Moshe Bar-Giora.
The source that records the deaths and injuries of police and railway workers at Lydda does not count them.
The Night of the Bridges, 17 June 1946.

Between the two nights, the Anglo-American Committee of Inquiry heard evidence and reported, in April 1946, and the British Prime Minister, Clement Attlee, tied the admission of the 100,000 refugees it recommended to the disarmament of the Jewish and Arab armed groups (see ).
The resistance movement's answer, in the sense that it was the next major operation the heritage account records, came on 17 June 1946, the "Night of the Bridges."
The Palmach attacked eleven bridges across Palestine.
Where the first night had been carried out by Lehi and the Irgun, this one was the Haganah's own operation, through the Palmach.
Britain's answer and the summer of 1946.

Twelve days later, on 29 June 1946, Britain launched Operation Agatha, a raid by roughly 17,000 troops and police that arrested more than 2,700 people, including senior Jewish Agency officials, and seized documents from the Agency's Jerusalem headquarters.
On 22 July 1946 the Irgun, commanded by Begin, bombed the King David Hotel in Jerusalem, killing 91 people.
In early August 1946 the Jewish Agency's leadership met in Paris, and there, according to the heritage account, the decision was taken to halt armed action until the Zionist Congress met.
The Congress, meeting in Basel, decided on 9 December 1946 to halt the armed struggle.
After that, in the Lehi account's words, the fight "fell to Lehi and IZL", that is, to Lehi and the Irgun.
The movement had been an alliance of three commands, but only one of them, the Haganah, answered to the Jewish Agency and the Zionist Congress.
When those bodies decided to stop, the fight, in the Lehi account, passed to Lehi and the Irgun; their decisions were not the Congress's to make.
The decision in Paris was a political one, taken by the leadership that also had a diplomatic course to pursue that same August (see ).
The decision in Basel confirmed it.
The united movement thus ended by a political decision on the Jewish side, not by British arms, and the armed campaign against Britain went on without the Haganah.
In the Lehi account, it was a "united armed offensive against the British," and the decisions in Paris and Basel left the fighting to Lehi and the Irgun.
Read from the British side and from the side of those killed or injured at Lydda, the same operations were attacks on railways, a refinery and bridges in which police and workers died.

The heritage account gives no casualty totals for the movement's operations, no number for the police and railway workers killed or injured at Lydda, and no casualty figure for the Night of the Bridges.
It does not say whether the King David Hotel bombing was carried out under the united movement's coordination or by the Irgun alone, and the available material does not settle that question.

It does not record the reasons given in Paris for the halt, or whether the bombing of 22 July weighed in that decision; the sequence is plain, with the bombing coming about two weeks before the Paris meeting, but the source draws no causal line, and neither does this book.
A full account of the movement would need British military and police records and the Haganah's own papers, set against the Lehi account.
Washington Retreats: The Trusteeship Proposal of March 1948
On 18 March 1948 Harry Truman received Chaim Weizmann at the White House.
He had refused to see the Zionist leader officially, and the meeting happened only because Eddie Jacobson, his former partner in a Kansas City clothing store, asked him to.
The meeting is widely credited with securing Truman's commitment to recognition.
The next day, 19 March, the American ambassador to the United Nations stood up in the Security Council and announced that the United States was stepping back from partition.
Warren Austin told the Council that the partition plan "cannot now be implemented by peaceful means."
In its place, he said, "a temporary trusteeship for Palestine should be established under the Trusteeship Council."

He asked the Council to request a special session of the General Assembly, under Article 20 of the Charter, and to instruct the United Nations Palestine Commission to "suspend its efforts to implement the proposed partition plan."
A common shorthand holds that the United States backed the Jewish state steadily from the partition vote to recognition.

The record of these four months shows something else: a government that voted for partition in November, proposed to suspend it in March, and recognized the new state in May, with its own delegation at the United Nations still arguing for trusteeship when the recognition was announced.
The scale of the retreat is clearest set against what the United States had voted for.

On 29 November 1947 it was among the 33 states that adopted the partition resolution, whose timetable ended the Mandate by 1 August 1948, required provisional councils of government by 1 April and two states by 1 October, and gave the work to a five-state Palestine Commission ().
Austin's statement asked that commission to stop, less than two weeks before the date set for the provisional councils.
Trusteeship was not a new idea, and it had not belonged to one side.
In 1944 the American Jewish Committee had proposed an international trusteeship instead of a Jewish commonwealth.
In April 1946 the Anglo-American Committee of Inquiry recommended continuing the Mandate toward a United Nations trusteeship, and declared that Palestine should be neither a Jewish nor an Arab state.
In May 1948 Hannah Arendt would argue in print for a binational federation under United Nations trusteeship, and Judah Magnes would meet Truman to press the same case.
The reasons the State Department gave for caution were on record well before Austin spoke.
