Loy Henderson, director of Near Eastern Affairs, Under Secretary Robert Lovett and Secretary of State George Marshall opposed early recognition of a Jewish state, arguing that it would damage American relations with the Arab world and endanger the oil supply.
Austin's own stated ground was narrower and practical: partition could not be carried out without force.

By then fighting between Palestine's Jewish and Arab communities had gone on since 1 December 1947 , and nine days before Austin spoke the Haganah had issued Plan Dalet, its plan for the period of the British withdrawal ().
The meeting with Weizmann ran through a personal channel, an old friend reaching a tired president, while the professional foreign service was strongly advising the other way.
The statement at the Security Council came from the diplomatic machinery that Henderson, Lovett and Marshall directed.
The material gathered does not show whether Truman knew that Austin would speak on 19 March, what he had told Weizmann in detail, or who drafted the statement and cleared its timing.
The Secretary-General, Trygve Lie, saw the new American position as "a rebuff to the United Nations."
According to his memoir, as footnoted in the State Department's documentary history, he suggested that he and Austin should both resign; Austin declined.
An American memorandum recorded that the Arab representatives "were pleased with this latest turn of events, but they did not gloat."
For the Jewish Agency, Abba Hillel Silver answered in the Council the same day.
He called the proposal "a shocking reversal" of the American position and warned that it was likely "to lead to increased violence in Palestine."
On 20 March David Ben-Gurion went further, and his answer amounted to a refusal:
He called the reversal "a surrender to the terrorism of the Arab gangs" and said it would not "prevent the establishment of the Jewish State."
The two characterizations of what had moved Washington could hardly be further apart.
Austin spoke of the impossibility of a peaceful partition.
Ben-Gurion spoke of surrender to force.
The Soviet Union took the opposite course from Washington.

When the United States moved toward trusteeship, Andrei Gromyko told the Security Council that the rapid creation of two states was the only way to reduce bloodshed, and Moscow stood behind partition.
The Soviet calculation is taken up in the section on Moscow's course; here it matters that in March 1948 the two powers that had voted together in November were on opposite sides of the question.
Austin's proposal did not stop the Jewish Agency from preparing for statehood, as Ben-Gurion had said it would not.
On the same day Austin spoke, Golda Meyerson returned from her American fundraising tour with a reported $50 million, spent largely on weapons.

Eight weeks later the United States extended de facto recognition to Israel eleven minutes after its proclamation, while the American delegation at the United Nations was still working for trusteeship.
It holds Austin's statement and the first reactions to it, but not the proceedings of the special session he requested or what became of the trusteeship draft there.

It does not document the internal deliberations that produced the statement, and it cannot say how far Truman's private meeting with Weizmann and his ambassador's public retreat were known to each other at the time.
What it does establish is that in the spring of 1948 the United States held two positions at once, and that both were visible to everyone watching.
The United States recognized Israel on the day it was declared.
The decision is sometimes remembered as an act of Congress, as if the House and Senate had voted the new state into American favor.
Recognition came in a short press release from the White House, issued on the authority of one office, and Congress had no vote on it.
How that power came to rest with one office, how Truman used it, and how other governments answered the same question in 1948 and 1949 together show what recognition did and did not decide.
Article II, Section 3 provides that the President "shall receive Ambassadors and other public Ministers."
In Zivotofsky v. Kerry (2015)
the Supreme Court held that the clause gives the President the exclusive power to recognize foreign sovereigns.
It states the law as it now stands, and it confirms that the power Truman used was his alone.
Eleven minutes after Israel's proclamation, he announced de facto recognition in a short press release.
In one account in this library, the second step came only after Truman's election victory.
Two accounts in this library give the time of the first announcement as 6:11 p.m. Washington time.
The Declaration had been read in Tel Aviv at four in the afternoon, and the Mandate expired at midnight.
Clark Clifford, the President's counsel, managed the timing against the objection of the State Department, which was not told in advance.

The American delegation at the United Nations was caught out too: at that moment it was still pressing the trusteeship proposal that Washington had put forward in March as an alternative to partition.
The decision came after Eddie Jacobson, Truman's old business partner, had brought Chaim Weizmann to see him, and after a November 1947 memorandum had analyzed "The Politics of 1948 and the Jews."
Recognition went against the written advice of the Secretary of State, the Joint Chiefs of Staff, the Secretary of Defense and the CIA.

The CIA's estimate ORE-55, dated 28 November 1947, the day before the partition vote, had predicted armed hostilities if partition passed and warned that American commercial and strategic interests would be put in danger.

It describes declassified CIA assessments predicting that recognition would immediately produce war with the Arab states, and calls the eleven minutes the fastest diplomatic recognition in American history.
Why Truman acted as he did is argued in the opening sections of this chapter.
One reading stresses the domestic calculation that Clifford's memorandum set out.
Another stresses Truman's own repeated statements of humanitarian conviction.
The State Department, the Pentagon and the new intelligence agency could advise.
Congress's part was real but indirect.
It could pass resolutions of support, it controlled appropriations, and the Senate confirmed ambassadors, including the first American ambassador to Israel.
None of these powers decided whether the United States would recognize Israel.
The Soviet Union went further than Washington, and almost as fast.
On 17 May 1948, three days after independence, it became the first state to recognize Israel de jure, while the American recognition was still de facto.

It was the same course Moscow had followed since Andrei Gromyko's speech at the United Nations in May 1947, and analysts at the time and since have read its motive as removing British influence from the region.
That is their reading, not a stated Soviet aim.
In December 1948 the Soviet bloc voted against Resolution 194 on the return of refugees.
The fuller Soviet story is told in .
Britain, the outgoing Mandatory power, came slowly.
In May 1948 Ernest Bevin told the House of Commons that "there are, after all, no Arabs in the House."
Britain recognized Israel in January 1949; the historian Raphael Langham describes Bevin's acceptance as "grudging."
The government that had issued the Balfour Declaration and held the Mandate accepted the state that emerged from it only after eight months.

In 1947, according to secondary reports, Ben-Gurion sent a secret telegram or telephone message to Muhammad Ali Jinnah, the founder of Pakistan, proposing that Pakistan recognize the Jewish state when it was established.
Jinnah's reply was reportedly negative.
According to the sources used here, Pakistan has never recognized Israel and has no diplomatic relations with it.

Its documented reasons were three: Catholic doctrine on the place of the Jewish people in salvation history, the unresolved status of the holy sites of Jerusalem, and concern for the Christian and Muslim communities of Palestine under the new state.

In 1949 the Vatican pressed at the United Nations to make Israel's admission conditional on two commitments: a return of Palestinian refugees and formal guarantees for the Christian and Muslim holy sites, above all in Jerusalem.
Ben-Gurion is recorded as saying that year: "There is a major religion in the world, which has to settle with us a historical reckoning."
Israel was admitted to the United Nations in May 1949 without the guarantees the Vatican had sought.
The Holy See did not establish diplomatic relations until the Fundamental Agreement of 30 December 1993, forty-five years after independence.
In Washington that office was the presidency, and the reasons were contested inside the government itself.
In Moscow, on the analysts' reading, the reason was Britain.
In London it was reluctant acceptance of a settled fact, and in Rome theology and the holy places.
The approach to Jinnah is known only from secondary accounts.
The details of the Vatican's 1949 campaign at the United Nations, beyond its two demands and its failure, are not documented in this book's sources.
How much any single adviser or argument weighed with Truman remains, as the earlier sections show, a matter of interpretation.
Who Objected at the Time
It is sometimes said that no one in the United States questioned the campaign for a Jewish state, or the money raised for it, until much later.

Objections were raised while the decisions were being made, by an anti-Zionist Jewish organization, by a mainstream Jewish body, by a future intelligence officer and a former college dean, by a foreign parliament, and in 1948 by Hannah Arendt, Albert Einstein and others who signed their names to public protest.
The American Council for Judaism.
The most direct objection came from Jews who rejected Zionism on religious grounds.
The American Council for Judaism was founded in 1942 and led by Lessing Rosenwald, with Rabbi Elmer Berger.
It argued that Judaism was a religion, not a nationality, and it opposed partition.
In 1948 it went further and objected to funds raised by the United Jewish Appeal being used "for political and foreign governmental purposes."

The complaint touched the same charitable campaigns whose 1948 proceeds are traced in this chapter's account of Golda Meyerson's American tour: in the Council's view, charity was being put to political ends abroad.
The Council's own historian documents it as a small minority that the mainstream Jewish organizations opposed, and Zionist sources describe it as a fringe group.
Its argument mattered less for its numbers than for its content: it showed that the claim to speak for American Jews as a whole on Palestine was contested from inside the community.
The American Jewish Committee.
At the congressional hearings of 1944, the American Jewish Committee, a mainstream organization, proposed an international trusteeship for Palestine instead of a Jewish commonwealth.
This was not anti-Zionism of the Council's kind.

It was an alternative arrangement offered by a leading Jewish organization, and it shows that support for a Jewish state was not yet a settled position among American Jewish institutions in the middle of the war.
The same 1944 congressional resolutions drew protest abroad: Iraq's parliament formally objected to them.
Judah Magnes, president of the Hebrew University, had argued before the Anglo-American Committee in 1946 for a single binational state shared by Arabs and Jews, an argument told in .
In May 1948, the month of independence, Magnes met Truman to press for a federation under trusteeship.
Kermit Roosevelt and the Gildersleeve committee.
In 1948 Kermit Roosevelt Jr. published a 24-page pamphlet, "The Partition of Palestine: A Lesson in Pressure Politics."
ents: The Partition of Palestine: A Lesson in Pressure Politics

sent: Roosevelt was later the CIA's field commander in Iran's 1953 coup.

With Virginia Gildersleeve, the former dean of Barnard College, he formed the Committee for Justice and Peace in the Holy Land, which warned that "extreme Zionist pressure" risked disrupting national unity.
These objections echoed, from outside government, the warnings that the State Department, the Joint Chiefs and the Defense Secretary had made from inside it the year before.
Arendt: "There Is Still Time."
Hannah Arendt's essay "To Save the Jewish Homeland: There Is Still Time" appeared in Commentary that month, on pages 398 to 406.

In the historian Robert Manne's account, Arendt argued that Jewish near-unanimity for a state, reached before any settlement with the Arabs, would bring war, and that even a victorious Jewish state would remain small, surrounded by hostile neighbors and absorbed in its own defense.

She proposed instead a gradual binational federation, built on mixed Jewish-Arab local councils under United Nations trusteeship with American and British support, and wrote that "It is still not too late."
She condemned the Irgun's attacks, including Deir Yassin.
Arendt worked closely with Magnes, and their proposals ran in parallel: a federation, under trusteeship, in place of partition.
In 1952 she called Magnes "the conscience of the Jewish people."
Manne also reports that she later estimated the Arab "evacuation" of 1948 at 500,000, a figure that sits among the many estimates of the refugee exodus discussed elsewhere in this chapter.
As her title said, her aim was to save the Jewish homeland; her case was that a state won by war against its neighbors would leave it small, besieged and absorbed in self-defense.

A letter dated 2 December 1948 and published in the New York Times on 4 December, signed by 28 people including Albert Einstein, Hannah Arendt and Sidney Hook, protested Menachem Begin's visit to the United States.
It described his Tnuat Haherut, the Freedom Party, which had grown out of the Irgun, as bearing "the unmistakable stamp of a Fascist party."
The Irgun's own path from underground army to political party, after the Altalena and the absorption of the militias into one army, is told in .
The letter named Deir Yassin directly.
Later research has revised the count of the dead at Deir Yassin, and the current state of that evidence is set out in .

The Council for Judaism objected in principle to Jewish nationhood; the American Jewish Committee to the form a solution should take; Roosevelt and Gildersleeve to the political pressure behind the decision; Arendt and Magnes to partition by war rather than federation by agreement; and the signers of December 1948 to a specific party and its record.
Partition was voted, the state was proclaimed and recognized, and the fundraising the Council objected to continued.
Formal action on foreign-agent questions came only much later, with the 1962 order under the Foreign Agents Registration Act and the Fulbright hearings of 1963, told in a later volume.
The sources measure the Council for Judaism only in words, a small minority in its own historian's account and a fringe in Zionist accounts, and give no membership figures.
They say nothing about how many Americans read Roosevelt's pamphlet or Arendt's essay.
What they do establish is that the objections existed, in print, in the years the decisions were made, and that several of the most pointed came from Jewish organizations and Jewish writers.
A common account of Israel's founding war holds that its weapons arrived only after May 1948, once the state existed and could ask the world for help.
The documents place the start of the supply effort almost three years earlier, in a private apartment in Manhattan, in the summer that the war in Europe ended.
By July 1945 the fighting in Europe was over, and the full scale of the Holocaust was becoming documented and public.
David Ben-Gurion, chairman of the Jewish Agency Executive and the de facto head of the Yishuv, the Jewish community of Palestine, had traveled from Palestine to New York with a specific purpose.

His assessment, made three years before independence and not in response to any declared war, was that the Arab states would go to war against the Jews of Palestine, and that the Haganah, the Yishuv's underground defense force, had neither the weapons nor the money to survive such a war.
He needed a supply and financing pipeline in America, and it was a task he could not ask the Jewish Agency to carry out openly.

The meeting took place in the Manhattan apartment of Rudolf Sonneborn, a wealthy New York industrialist and scion of an oil-and-chemical business, who had traveled to Palestine himself and formed a friendship with Ben-Gurion.
One account has Ben-Gurion convening the meeting; another has Sonneborn convening it at Ben-Gurion's request.
The two are compatible: the request was Ben-Gurion's, the room
Sonneborn's.

The man who gathered the guests was Henry Montor, who by 1948 was executive vice-chairman of the United Jewish Appeal, a connection that would matter again in 1948 when the same Montor arranged Golda Meyerson's appeal to the American federations, told in .
Accounts describe roughly seventeen prominent Jewish businessmen in the room.
One account gives seventeen American businessmen in one place and seventeen Americans and one Canadian in another.

Ben-Gurion warned them of the coming war and of the Haganah's poverty, and the men in the room, moved, by later accounts, by the warning together with the recent revelation of the Holocaust's scale, agreed that same afternoon to build what became a Jewish-American arms underground.

Firsthand descriptions of the meeting, including Leonard Slater's 1970 book The Pledge, were written decades afterwards, sympathetically, by an author who interviewed participants long after the fact.
What emerged from the meeting was the Sonneborn Institute, a network that became the financial and logistical backbone of the Haganah's transatlantic supply effort.
Ben-Gurion directed its formation; the day-to-day American procurement work was run by Sonneborn and a small operational circle.
Sonneborn received no formal recognition for his part beyond a private letter of thanks from Ben-Gurion after Israel was founded.
One historical account calls it Materials for Palestine; another calls it Materials for Israel.

In one account it operated under the guise of an ordinary commercial and charitable enterprise, providing cover for buying and shipping machinery, tools and industrial materials, legally purchasable surplus, destined for Ta'as, the Yishuv's clandestine arms-production effort.

In the other, the network operated under the legal cover of a charity for European Jewish relief, raising funds and moving industrial equipment, machine tools and eventually munitions toward Haganah forces in Palestine.

The two descriptions are not contradictory so much as describing different stages: the first stresses the legal machinery bought for production inside Palestine, the second the move toward finished munitions as the war drew closer.

Shipments moved under falsified manifests and disguised invoices, routed through Panama, Mexico, Czechoslovakia, Canada and France to evade American export controls, and arrived with Haganah forces in Palestine.
By the time the United States formally tightened arms-export enforcement under the Neutrality Act in December 1947, the network already had two years of working tradecraft in place.
What the network did was, under American law, illegal arms export, and the people who built it arranged matters so that the official Jewish Agency would not be directly exposed.
Historians who have documented the network note that it was kept deliberately separate from the Agency, and that this compartmentalization was a choice, not an accident of organization.
Abba Hillel Silver, chairman of the Jewish Agency's American section, served as a liaison between the two.
The record therefore shows both things at once: a structure built to insulate the Agency, and a named senior figure connecting it to the Agency anyway.
It does not show that the Agency was unaware of what the network did, nor does it give an account of what each Agency official individually knew.
The sources give no total for what the Sonneborn circle raised or spent, and no ledger of individual shipments or transactions.

The panel below places the network in the longer sequence of channels that paid for the Yishuv's defense, from the Jewish Agency's own budget and a community levy of the 1930s to the American appeals of 1948.
That sequence matters because the Sonneborn network sat in the middle of it, and because the same people moved along it.
Montor's role in both the 1945 meeting and the 1948 appeal shows that the arms network and the open federation-and-appeal fundraising overlapped directly through named individuals.
Among the network's key financiers was Abraham Feinberg, who met repeatedly with Sonneborn and later founded Americans for Haganah.
In 1952 the United States government would order him to register as a foreign agent, a later chapter of his story told in .

The first Jewish intelligence organization in Palestine had been established under the Haganah in 1929, and the Shai (Sherut Yediot, the Information Service) was set up in 1940 as the Haganah's intelligence and counter-espionage arm.
By 1948, according to one account, the Shai had 68 staff, 60 British and Jewish agents and 80 Arab agents, and spent nearly $700,000 a year.

Its stated objectives were to promote an independent Israeli state, to infiltrate British Mandate offices, to collect intelligence for propaganda, to penetrate Arab factions, and to secure the Rekhesh arms-smuggling operations.
It had American branches, Zionist networks in New York and Detroit that served as procurement and intelligence points, and these were not registered under the Foreign Agents Registration Act.
After 1948 the Shai became the seed from which Israeli military intelligence grew, and its American networks formed the early North American foundation of the Mossad.
Rekhesh, Hebrew for "acquisitions," was the Haganah's arms and munitions procurement branch in the United States in the mid-1940s.
It built an extensive illegal procurement network despite the arms embargo on the Palestine region.

Its operations were funded by American Jewish donors and involved buying surplus military equipment from demobilized United States Army stocks and from black-market dealers, then smuggling it out through covert shipping routes, often with the help of organized crime to get around export controls.
One account describes the networks as violating both American export law and the British arms embargo.
The FBI documented these operations and repeatedly recommended that key figures be prosecuted or required to register as foreign agents; the Justice Department declined each time.

The attorney William Bernstein, according to the FBI, trained Mossad agents, incorporated companies that smuggled arms for Zionist groups, and conducted surveillance of Arab delegates at the United Nations; the Bureau linked him to sophisticated technical surveillance of Arab officials and to break-ins at consular offices.
The Justice Department declined every FBI recommendation that Bernstein be prosecuted or made to register.
Federal agencies, the FBI and Customs among them, were aware of the network while it operated.
No prosecution of its top organizers, Sonneborn or Feinberg, is documented.

At least one participant, Charlie Winters, was convicted and sentenced to eighteen months; one account adds a $5,000 fine, a detail on which the sources differ, as the account of the network's trials shows.
During the war the Office of Strategic Services, the predecessor of the CIA, ran a Palestinian Desk in its Foreign Nationalities Branch that tracked Zionist activity in the United States.

A 2016 review of declassified documents by the Forward found that much of its information came from Jewish officials, some highly placed in Jewish organizations, who volunteered it as a wartime patriotic duty and not under coercion.
Its target list reportedly included Moshe Shertok, later Moshe Sharett, Israel's second prime minister.
The desk built a picture of which American Jewish leaders were aligned with which Zionist factions; it took no action against the Rekhesh procurement networks.
The OSS's wartime foreign-intelligence interest and the FBI's domestic-security interest had separate rationales and separate reporting chains, and they are documented independently.
Why the Justice Department declined is the question on which the sources divide.

One account, built on FBI records reported by the Forward and on later analysis, argues that the non-enforcement was deliberate and political: the Truman administration was moving toward support for Jewish statehood, and prosecuting the future state's arms networks, or requiring its American political organizations to register as foreign agents, would have been incompatible with that course.

On this reading the decision not to enforce was a foreign-policy decision in the form of prosecutorial discretion, and it set a precedent, never reversed, that later shaped pro-Israel lobbying in the United States; the same account traces it to 1963, when Isaiah Kenen, himself formerly registered as a foreign agent, moved the lobbying function from the American Zionist Council to the newly created AIPAC.
That the FBI recommended prosecution or registration, that the Justice Department declined, and that the procurement operations broke American law are, in their judgment, documented.
Whether the Justice Department acted on explicit direction from the Truman White House, or exercised its own discretion, is not established.

The reading of a fixed political will also has to account for the rest of the record of these years: the same administration's State Department opposed early recognition of a Jewish state, as the opening section of this chapter shows, so "the government" did not speak with one voice on Palestine.
In July 1945 Ben-Gurion expected a war that he believed the Haganah could not survive without weapons it did not have, and a British arms embargo stood between it and the means to get them.
On that view the procurement effort was the preparation of a community's defense, organized by American donors who had just learned the full scale of the Holocaust.

The case against it, as stated in the sources critical of it, is that it was a foreign-directed intelligence and arms operation on American soil that broke American law and was allowed to continue because of whom it served.
Both cases rest on the same documented facts: the meeting, the front company, the deliberate separation from the Agency, the false paperwork, and the decisions not to prosecute.
It does not show whether the Justice Department's restraint came from the White House or from its own discretion.
And by the sources' own account, the full extent of Zionist intelligence operations on American soil in the 1940s is only partly documented, with part of the record still classified.
What it does establish is the starting point: a working, financed, deliberately compartmented supply network on American soil from 1945, three years before the state it was built to arm.
The Arms Network in Operation, 1945–1948
The network founded at Rudolf Sonneborn's apartment in 1945, described in , was not a fund or a statement of intent.
For three years it bought real weapons, aircraft and machinery in the United States and moved them, through a set of named front operations and transit countries, to the Haganah in Palestine.
One is that American law enforcement knew nothing of an organized effort to arm the Haganah before 1948.
The documents show federal agencies watching parts of the operation while it ran, and a large share of the material reaching Palestine from private American buyers through third countries.
Both the United States and Britain maintained embargoes on arms for Palestine, and the network's purchases were designed to defeat them.

Academic research on the operation documents purchases of trucks, radios, aircraft parts and weapons components, funnelled through countries that were neutral in the conflict: Czechoslovakia, Panama, Mexico, Canada and France.
Mexico was one of the named and documented transit points, not an incidental stop.
Goods left the United States for a country that was not at war, and were re-shipped from there to Haganah operatives.

The weapons that the new state carried into 1948 were bought in part by American citizens, with American donations, and moved through other countries' ports; the Czechoslovak supply that began in January 1948 is the other half of that story, told in .
Al Schwimmer's airline.

Al Schwimmer, a veteran of the US Army's Air Transport Command, bought roughly 30 surplus American warplanes and moved them toward Palestine via Panama, Brazil and Casablanca, evading the FBI and the State Department for months.
One describes a fictitious Panamanian airline, Lineas Aereas de Panama, created to carry the aircraft.
The other describes a near-bankrupt charter airline, Service Airways Inc., used as commercial cover to fly aircraft and parts out of the United States.
The crate on the New Jersey dock.
By the end of January 1948, a crate marked "used industrial machinery" broke apart while it was being loaded onto a freighter in New Jersey, spilling explosives onto the dock.
It was one of 76 identical crates bound for Palestine.
In one, the accidental spill, not investigative work, gave US authorities their first concrete evidence that the network existed.

In the other, the FBI, the Customs Service and other federal authorities had already been uncovering parts of the network while it operated, and the spill accelerated their work into open prosecution.

Later scholarship and reporting from the era of declassification confirm that the FBI, the Customs Service and the intelligence units descended from the wartime OSS each uncovered parts of the smuggling operation while it was running, not after the fact.
A National Security Council memorandum of the period referred to the operation directly.
One thing the FBI was doing in the same months is easily confused with this case, and the record keeps them apart.

Records obtained decades later under the Freedom of Information Act by the Cato Institute show that the FBI maintained an investigative focus on the Zionist Organization of America, founded in 1897, in 1947–48.
The Bureau believed, incorrectly on the evidence of what it overheard, that the organization had been infiltrated or influenced by Communists.

Between September 1947 and May 1948 the FBI also wiretapped Sol Rotenberg, a Jewish political activist tied to the International Workers Order, on the theory that the Order was a Communist Party front.
These were two distinct concerns running at the same time: a Neutrality Act investigation of the arms network, and a counter-subversion inquiry into suspected Communist influence.
Nine men involved in the network were tried in a federal courthouse in Los Angeles in 1950.
Schwimmer was convicted under the Neutrality Act and lost his American citizenship.
He later moved to Israel and led its aircraft industry; one account says he founded Israel Aerospace Industries, the other that he became head of Israel Aircraft Industries.
Charlie Winters was charged with conspiracy to export military aircraft in violation of the Neutrality Act, pleaded guilty and served 18 months in prison.
On every version, both men were eventually pardoned by an American president, decades after the trial.
A man convicted of breaking the Neutrality Act went on to lead the new state's aircraft industry, and the United States later formally forgave both him and Winters.
The documents establish the routes, the scale of some 800 shipments and roughly 2,400 tons, the Los Angeles trial and the pardons.
They do not provide a full ledger of what moved by which route, or a total cost; the library's funding ledger records Schwimmer's roughly 30 aircraft without a price.
Relations between Britain and the Jewish community of Palestine are often described as having worn down slowly after the war, with no single moment at which they broke.

The slow wearing-down is real: from September 1945 the Haganah, the Irgun and Lehi had acted together against British targets, from the railways at Lydda in November 1945 to eleven bridges on the night of 17 June 1946 (see ).
Twelve days after the Night of the Bridges, on Saturday 29 June 1946, Britain launched Operation Agatha.
Roughly 17,000 British troops and police searched Jewish settlements, kibbutzim and offices across Mandate Palestine at the same time.
The operation was a direct response to the escalating operations of the Haganah, the Irgun and Lehi against British installations.
Those arrested included senior officials of the Jewish Agency.
Agatha was not a narrow sweep for known fighters of the two underground groups.
One reading of that choice of target ties it to what the united resistance had become.
The Night of the Bridges had been carried out not by Lehi or the Irgun but by the Haganah, acting through its Palmach.
The campaign Britain was answering was no longer only the work of the two underground groups, and the raid reached past them to the political leadership.
What they establish is the scale, the simultaneity and the reach of the operation into the Agency's leadership.
British forces also seized a substantial cache of documents from the Jewish Agency's headquarters in Jerusalem.
The material was believed to include evidence linking the Agency's leadership to Haganah operations.
The Jewish Agency had kept a deliberate legal and organizational separation between the political leadership and armed resistance.
"Agatha" was the official British codename.
"Black Sabbath" was the name given by the Jewish community whose institutions were raided, because the raid fell on a Saturday, the Jewish Sabbath.
There is no evidence that the British name carried any hidden meaning; codenames of the period were, as a rule, assigned without symbolic intent.
The documents did not stay at the Agency.
They were taken to be processed and stored in the Secretariat wing of the King David Hotel in Jerusalem.
Its southern wing housed the Mandate Secretariat, the central administrative offices of the Mandate government, and served as the regional British military headquarters.
It was not a hotel that happened to contain a few government offices; it was, in effect, the center of British administration in Palestine.
In the Irgun's planning, the hotel was at once a symbol of British authority and the physical place where the evidence against the Jewish Agency's leadership was held.

Irgun intelligence assessed that the documents seized in Agatha, including the material believed to implicate the Agency's leadership in coordinating with the Haganah, were being processed and stored in the Secretariat wing specifically.
The Irgun's planning for what became the King David Hotel bombing began in direct response to Black Sabbath.
The first is that it does not establish that retaliation for Black Sabbath was the bombing's only motive; the bombing's planning and its stated objectives are taken up in .
The bombing killed 91 people, many of whom had no connection to the administrative work the Irgun meant to strike.
Setting out the chain from Agatha explains how the hotel came to be chosen.
The armed campaign of 1945–46 and the British response to it built up over months.

Within that build-up, Agatha stands out as a single dated operation of a different order, with a troop count, an arrest total, a seizure of the Agency's own papers and a direct line to the deadliest single attack on the British of the whole Mandate period.
They do not give the contents of the seized documents, so the belief that they tied the Agency's leadership to the Haganah cannot be tested here.
They do not record what the British government said, at the time, to justify the decision to arrest the Agency's senior officials.
And they do not show how the raid bore on the decisions the Agency's leadership took a few weeks later, in early August 1946, to halt armed action.
Those questions need the British and Jewish Agency archives, which are not part of the material verified.
The King David Hotel Bombing, 22 July 1946
The bombing of the King David Hotel is sometimes passed over as an incident in a British office building, one act of violence among many in the last years of the Mandate.
On 22 July 1946 an explosion in the hotel's southern wing in Jerusalem killed 91 people, British, Arab and Jewish.
It was the deadliest single attack against the British in the whole Mandate period.

It was carried out by an organization whose commander would later lead the government of Israel, it drew a public condemnation from the Jewish Agency, and it hardened British opinion toward leaving Palestine.
From Agatha to the hotel.
The attack came twenty-three days after Operation Agatha.

On 29 June 1946 British forces had arrested more than 2,700 people, including senior Jewish Agency officials, and seized documents from the Agency's Jerusalem headquarters; the documents were believed to link the Agency's leadership to Haganah operations, and they were taken to the Secretariat wing of the King David Hotel to be processed and stored (see ).

The hotel's southern wing housed the Mandate Secretariat, the central administrative offices of the Mandate government, and the British military command; hotel business carried on in the rest of the building.

The Irgun, assessing that the seized papers were held there, planned the attack in direct response to the raid, with the documented aims of destroying that evidence and striking the administration that had carried out the arrests.
The Irgun was commanded at the time by Menachem Begin.
Its fighters placed explosives, reportedly concealed in milk churns, in the basement of the southern wing, beneath the Secretariat and the military command, and detonated them.
They were a mix of British, Arab and Jewish civilians and administrative personnel.
Many had no connection to the administrative functions the Irgun meant to strike.

The Irgun's own account holds that warning calls were placed about 25 minutes before the detonation to three places: the hotel switchboard, the French consulate and the office of the Palestine Post newspaper, each urging evacuation.
British investigators, and later historians, have disputed whether any warning actually reached the hotel's management in time to act on it, or whether a call that did arrive was dismissed as a hoax.

The Irgun's account is specific: it names the time, the three recipients and the purpose of the calls, and, taken on its own terms, it presents an intention to empty the building rather than to kill those in it.

The British case rests on the outcome and on the investigation: 91 people did not leave, and the investigators doubted that any usable warning had reached the people who could have ordered an evacuation.
Even on the Irgun's own account, the question of whether a warning of about 25 minutes, sent partly to outside offices, was adequate remains open.
The Jewish Agency's condemnation.
The Jewish Agency publicly condemned the bombing.
It was the Agency's own documents, seized in Agatha, that the attack was meant to destroy.

And the Haganah, whose ties to the Agency's leadership the seized documents were believed to show, had itself been part of the united Jewish Resistance Movement with the Irgun and Lehi since September 1945, carrying out the Night of the Bridges only five weeks earlier through its Palmach.
The sources record the public condemnation; they do not record the internal debate behind its wording or the private views of individual Agency officials.

The sequence is suggestive: about two weeks later, in early August 1946, the Jewish Agency's leadership, meeting in Paris, decided to halt armed action until the Zionist Congress met, and the Congress confirmed the halt in December.
But the only source for those decisions, the Lehi heritage association, does not say that the bombing caused them, and no other source verified does either (see ).
What it changed in London.
The bombing is documented as having significantly hardened British public and parliamentary opinion toward disengaging from Palestine altogether.
It contributed directly to Britain's decision, the next year, to hand the whole question to the United Nations.

The same record that ties the bombing to Britain's change of mind does not claim that the attack alone caused the referral of 1947; other pressures were at work, and how much weight the armed campaign carried in Britain's withdrawal is itself disputed, as the section on  sets out.
Menachem Begin personally commanded the Irgun at the time of the bombing.
He later served as Israel's sixth Prime Minister, from 1977 to 1983.

What the sources used here do not provide is Begin's own account: his justification for the attack and what he said about it in later years are not part of this material, and they are not supplied here.
Ninety-one people from three communities were killed in a single attack, the largest such toll against the British in the Mandate.
Its commander went on to lead the government of Israel.
It drew a public condemnation from the Jewish Agency, and it moved British opinion toward leaving.
The first is the warning: whether the calls the Irgun describes were made as it says, whether any reached someone able to order an evacuation, and whether they were treated as a hoax.

The third is cause and effect after the attack: how far the bombing drove the Jewish Agency's August decision to halt armed action, and how far it, rather than the other pressures on Britain, drove the decision to go to the United Nations.
The Jewish Agency Prepares: Partition as Policy, 1946

The partition plan voted on in November 1947 is usually described as the product of the United Nations' own process: an eleven-member committee that investigated the problem from scratch and reached its recommendation independently.
The Jewish Agency had prepared its own partition proposal more than a year before the committee reported, and by then had made partition its declared aim.
Two separate diplomatic tracks lay ahead: recognition by the United States, and a decision at the United Nations.
The Agency worked both, and the groundwork for the second was laid early.
In August 1946 it submitted its own detailed partition proposal, with boundaries drawn for a Palestinian rump state .
Those boundaries bear a documented resemblance to the area that became the West Bank after 1948 .
The source records a likeness between two maps, not a line of descent: it does not show that the United Nations committee, or anyone after it, adopted the Agency's exact lines.
Historical accounts of the United Nations process note that by 1946 partition had become the Jewish Agency's avowed, public policy .
The Agency did not arrive at partition in reaction to the United Nations.
It came to the United Nations with partition already as its stated goal, and with a prepared case for it.
August 1946 was also a turning point in the Agency's other policy, the armed one.

According to the heritage association of Lehi, one of the underground groups then allied with the Haganah, the Agency's meeting in Paris in early August 1946 decided to halt armed action until the Zionist Congress met, and the Congress, in Basel, confirmed the halt on 9 December 1946 .
That account, written from Lehi's own perspective, is the only source here for the Paris decision.
The sources do not say whether the partition proposal was discussed or adopted at the same Paris meeting, and this book does not join the two.
What can be said is that in the same month the record shows the Agency submitting a partition plan, the Lehi account has it standing down from armed struggle until its Congress could meet.
The Agency's proposal came roughly nine months before the United Nations created its committee, and more than a year before that committee's report.

When the committee did hear the Agency in 1947, its head, David Ben-Gurion, told it that an independent Jewish state was the only acceptable outcome, and the Agency presented a prepared map and a large body of supporting material .
That hearing, and the Arab Higher Committee's decision to boycott it, are the subject of .
None of this makes the committee's recommendation a copy of the Agency's plan, and the evidence here does not support saying so.
It does correct the impression that the United Nations faced a blank page.
UNSCOP and the Empty Chair

The plan that the General Assembly voted on in November 1947 began as the report of an eleven-nation committee that spent the summer of 1947 between Lake Success, Jerusalem, Beirut, Amman, Geneva and the displaced-persons camps of Munich, Salzburg, Vienna, Berlin, Hamburg and Hanover.
The United Nations Special Committee on Palestine, known as UNSCOP, is usually remembered as a neutral fact-finding body that heard both sides equally and reached its own conclusion.
But it did not weigh two prepared Palestinian cases against each other.
One party, the Jewish Agency, came with a map, witnesses and a proposed itinerary.
The other, the Arab Higher Committee, chose to stay away.
The Arab case was put to the committee instead by the governments of six Arab states, in Beirut, and members also called on Transjordan's king in Amman.
The committee was Britain's doing.

On 2 April 1947 Sir Alexander Cadogan, for the United Kingdom, asked the United Nations to put Palestine on the agenda of the next regular Assembly and to summon a special session as soon as possible to constitute a special committee .
(How London reached that point is told in .)
The special session convened at Flushing Meadow on 28 April 1947.
On 15 May it adopted Resolution 106 (S-1), which created the Special Committee on Palestine with "the widest powers to ascertain and record facts" and told it to report by 1 September 1947  .
Australia proposed eleven members, none of them permanent members of the Security Council.
The Assembly adopted that proposal by 13 votes to 11, with 29 abstentions .
The members chosen were Australia, Canada, Czechoslovakia, Guatemala, India, Iran, the Netherlands, Peru, Sweden, Uruguay and Yugoslavia  .
On its face this was a multi-continent body, not a proxy for Washington or London.
It held its first meeting at Lake Success on 26 May 1947, and on 2 June elected Justice Emil Sandström of Sweden as chairman and Alberto Ulloa of Peru as vice-chairman  .
Its members arrived in Palestine on 14 and 15 June and first met in Jerusalem on 16 June .
The day before the members landed, the Arab Higher Committee had informed the Secretary-General that it would abstain from cooperating with the committee.
On 10 July 1947 its vice-chairman, Jamal Husseini, wrote again to say that it would not reverse that decision .

The Arab Higher Committee regarded the whole framework as illegitimate: in its view any United Nations body that set out to decide Palestine's future without first affirming the self-determination rights of the country's existing majority was biased before it began .
The Jewish Agency took the opposite course.
The consequence inside Palestine was a hearing room in which only one of the two Palestinian communities' organized leaderships made a formal case.
For the Jewish Agency the committee heard Moshe Shertok and David Horowitz, and it heard Chaim Weizmann in a personal capacity .
David Ben-Gurion, testifying as head of the Jewish Agency, told the committee plainly that an independent Jewish state was the only acceptable outcome.
The map presented on the Zionist side was substantially the Peel Commission's map of 1937, with the Galilee, the Negev and West Jerusalem added .
One historical account describes the Agency's presentation as forthright and exhaustive, overwhelming the committee "with data, logic, and cogent analyses of every central and tangential issue" .
The imbalance it describes did not come from the Arab argument being weak.
It came from the Arab Higher Committee's argument never being formally put before the committee in Palestine at all.
Nor was the Agency improvising.
By 1946 partition had already become its avowed policy, and in August 1946 it had drawn up its own partition proposal, more than a year before UNSCOP existed  .
It is here that the familiar charge against UNSCOP, and the committee's own record, have to be read side by side.
The charge, as it is often put, is that the committee heard testimony "almost exclusively" from the Zionist side .
No Palestinian Arab body testified, because the Arab Higher Committee boycotted the proceedings .
But the Arab states did put their case.

After an informal visit to Damascus on 21 July 1947, the committee heard the governments of Egypt, Iraq, Lebanon, Saudi Arabia, Syria and Yemen in Beirut on 22 July, with the Lebanese Foreign Minister, Hamid Frangié, among them.
Transjordan declined to send a representative outside the country, so on 25 July the chairman and seven members went to Amman to see King Abdullah  .
The committee also traveled through the region and could observe conditions directly; it did not hear literally nothing of Arab objections .
"One side only" is accurate for the Palestinian parties: the Jewish Agency was heard at length and the Arab Higher Committee by its own decision not at all.
It is not accurate for the Arab case as a whole, which six governments presented in Beirut; members also met Transjordan's king in Amman.
What the record establishes is that no prepared Palestinian Arab case, with its own witnesses and its own maps, stood in the committee's record beside the Agency's.
The committee also looked beyond Palestine.
After a vote of six to four, with one abstention, a subcommittee visited displaced-persons camps in Munich, Salzburg, Vienna, Berlin, Hamburg and Hanover between 8 and 14 August 1947 .
The drafting began in Geneva on 28 July.

A majority of seven, Canada, Czechoslovakia, Guatemala, the Netherlands, Peru, Sweden and Uruguay, recommended partition into a Jewish state and an Arab state joined in an economic union, with an international regime for Jerusalem.
A minority of three, India, Iran and Yugoslavia, recommended a single federal state with Jerusalem as its capital.
Australia abstained on both votes, which were recorded as 7 to 3 and 3 to 7   .
The Center for Israel Education states that eight of the eleven members endorsed partition, and that the Jewish Agency accepted the plan while the Arab Higher Committee rejected it .
The committee's own report records seven, with Australia abstaining .
The Assembly's Ad Hoc Committee revised it in the autumn, and the revised plan went to the General Assembly vote of 29 November 1947 .
The documents used here do not say what the Arab governments argued in Beirut, beyond the fact that they were heard, nor what King Abdullah told the members in Amman.

They do not record how individual members weighed the Jewish Agency's testimony against the Arab governments' statements, or whether the Arab Higher Committee's absence changed any member's vote; the account of the Agency "overwhelming" the committee is one historian's characterization, not a record of members' private responses.
And while the boycott is documented as a choice, with its reasons, whether a Palestinian presence would have altered the outcome is a counterfactual that no document can settle.

What the record does show is how the recommendation was built: by a committee chosen in a close vote, that heard one Palestinian party in full, heard the Arab case only through Arab governments, visited the displaced-persons camps after a divided vote, and ended seven to three.
State, the Pentagon and Oil
On 22 September 1947 the State Department's senior official for the Middle East put a blunt judgment on paper: the partition of Palestine was "not workable."
Eighteen days later the Joint Chiefs of Staff said much the same in a memorandum of their own, and the Secretary of Defense made the argument in public, before a committee of Congress.
The oil company that held America's concession in Saudi Arabia, meanwhile, was lobbying the White House directly.

A familiar explanation of American policy holds that the strategic costs of backing partition were not understood until much later, and that the gap was one of limited information or the slow communications of the era.
The question the record raises is not whether Washington knew, but why what it knew did not decide the outcome.

It is a government divided against itself: career diplomats, the military command and the Defense Secretary on one side, the President's political advisers on the other, with an oil company pressing from outside and a President who had to choose.
The State Department's regional expert.
Loy Henderson directed the State Department's Office of Near Eastern and African Affairs, the office whose job was to understand the practical consequences of American policy in the region.
ents: the State Department's Office of Near Eastern

sent: He had served as American ambassador to Iraq in the mid-1940s and had watched at first hand how Arab governments were reacting as the Palestine question took shape.
On 22 September 1947 Henderson sent Secretary of State George Marshall a memorandum warning that partition was "not workable" and would lead to "untold troubles" in the future.
His views, he wrote, were shared by "nearly every member of the Foreign Service or of the department who has worked to any appreciable extent on Near Eastern problems."
On Henderson's own account, then, the memo stated the shared view of the government's regional specialists, not one official's dissent.
Under Secretary of State Robert Lovett was impressed enough by its substance to read it aloud to President Truman himself.
What the record does not show is that every one of Henderson's predictions proved right in every detail.
The Joint Chiefs of Staff.
On 10 October 1947 the Joint Chiefs of Staff filed a memorandum titled "The Problem of Palestine."

It warned that dividing Palestine into Jewish and Arab states would open the way for the Soviet Union to displace American and British influence in the region, and that it would endanger American access to Middle East oil.
These were the two concerns, regional alignment and access to resources, that drove American policy in the Middle East generally in these years.
On 11 October 1947, one day after the Joint Chiefs filed it, the United States announced its support for the UN partition plan.
The Secretary of Defense, in public.

James Forrestal had been Secretary of the Navy and became the first Secretary of Defense, overseeing the consolidation of the armed forces under the new Department of Defense created by the National Security Act of 1947, the same year as his warning.
He was the Cabinet official most directly responsible for whether the American military could function.

Testifying before a House committee, he said that oil was "the life blood of a war machine," and warned that the Arab world's response to partition would threaten the pipelines carrying oil out of the Persian Gulf, the physical infrastructure on which American forces and the American economy relied.
Forrestal's testimony and the Joint Chiefs' memorandum made the same argument through two different routes, one public and political, the other internal and military.
It shows it as one voice in a chorus of institutional warning, alongside Henderson and the Joint Chiefs, that was set aside together.
Forrestal's diary entries decrying the "bullying" that preceded the final vote belong to the story of the vote itself, told in .

A 1947 memorandum submitted to President Truman was published under the title "Oil and the State Department policy on Palestine: the documentary evidence of how ARAMCO attempts to destroy the partition resolution of the United Nations."
Its title states its thesis: that it presents documentary evidence of an active lobbying campaign by the Arabian American Oil Company against partition.
ARAMCO held the core American oil concession in Saudi Arabia, the same relationship that lay behind Franklin Roosevelt's meeting with King Ibn Saud two years earlier.
A Middle East turned against the United States by partition threatened that concession's value and its security.
ARAMCO's interest was commercial; the Joint Chiefs' was strategic; Henderson's was diplomatic.
Nor does the published memorandum reproduce ARAMCO's internal communications or give a full account of its methods.
What the record establishes is that a documented lobbying campaign existed and that it failed: the company with the most money at stake in Arab goodwill did not move the decision.
Truman had heard Henderson's memo directly.

According to several historical accounts, he was worried about his prospects in the 1948 election, and his adviser Clark Clifford urged him to endorse partition in order to secure Jewish-American votes in key swing states.

Clifford's memorandum to Truman of November 1947 made the electoral case, naming New York, Pennsylvania and Illinois, and his later memoirs acknowledged both the political framework and Marshall's opposition to it.
One of the sources says the United States voted for partition at the General Assembly
"five days" after Henderson's memo.
The memo is dated 22 September; the American announcement of support came on 11 October; the General Assembly vote came on 29 November 1947.
In the months after the vote, Palestine descended into serious violence.

By 24 February 1948 George Kennan, the State Department's Director of Policy Planning, was warning that only the introduction of foreign troops could now stop it, an escalation of exactly the "untold troubles" Henderson had forecast five months earlier.
A month later Washington itself would retreat from partition at the United Nations, a reversal told in .

Its first node is the Anglo-American Committee, whose unanimous report of April 1946 recommended that Palestine be neither a Jewish nor an Arab state; Washington kept only one of its recommendations, the immediate admission of 100,000 Jewish refugees.
Henderson at State, the Joint Chiefs, and Forrestal at Defense.
A fifth, the Central Intelligence Agency's estimate ORE-55 of 28 November 1947, came the day before the vote and is the subject of the next section.
All five lines run into Truman; the four warnings are marked as overruled, and the committee's line as one recommendation kept.

On the other side of the scale sit Clifford and David Niles, who made the domestic political case, and Eddie Jacobson, Truman's former business partner, whose personal channel brought Chaim Weizmann to the President on 18 March 1948.
The final node is the outcome: American support for Resolution 181 in November 1947, and recognition of Israel in May 1948.

Every warning came through an established institution doing the work it existed to do: the regional desk assessing the region, the military assessing strategic risk, the Defense Secretary speaking for readiness, the oil company protecting its concession.
The counterweight came through the White House's own political staff and through a personal friendship.

Second, the surviving documents show the warnings and the decision but do not contain a written internal rationale connecting the two, so the weight Truman gave to the 1948 election, against his own stated convictions, rests on the accounts of his advisers and on historians' readings rather than on a single decisive document.

The State Department's regional director, the Joint Chiefs of Staff and the Secretary of Defense reached the same conclusion independently, in writing, within a few weeks of each other, and the President heard it.
FDR Dies, Truman Chooses
The American decision on Israel was made by a president whom almost no one, three years earlier, had expected to be making it.
The story of that decision therefore begins not in 1948, and not even in 1945, but at the Democratic convention in Chicago in 1944.
Henry Wallace had served as Franklin Roosevelt's Vice President since 1941.

He was a progressive in the full sense of the word in his time: pro-labor, anti-imperialist and anti-colonial, an early and forceful advocate of civil rights well ahead of the American political mainstream, and a supporter of accommodation rather than confrontation with the Soviet Union.
To the Democratic Party's conservative and machine wings he was unacceptable.

At the 1944 convention, with an ailing Roosevelt unlikely to survive another term, the party bosses maneuvered Wallace off the ticket and replaced him with a compromise choice, the little-known senator from Missouri, Harry Truman.
Wallace went on to run for president on the Progressive Party ticket in 1948, lost badly, and died in 1965.

The fuller account of his removal, including the reasons behind it and Wallace's own Zionist sympathies, belongs to an earlier part of this book; what matters here is the single substitution and its timing.
Roosevelt himself had one more Middle Eastern act left.
In February 1945, aboard the USS Quincy in the Suez Canal, he met King Ibn Saud of Saudi Arabia and gave assurances that no action would be taken hostile to the Arab people without consultation.
One week later, on 12 April 1945, Roosevelt, born in 1882, died at Warm Springs, Georgia, less than three months into his new term and before any of the postwar decisions on Palestine had to be made.
What Roosevelt would have done had he lived cannot be known, and this book does not pretend to know it.

On this reading, but for the convention maneuver, Henry Wallace and not Harry Truman would have become president in April 1945, and the 1948 recognition of Israel, along with the opening of the Cold War, might have unfolded very differently.

The reading uses Wallace to mark the contingency of the whole story: an American commitment to Israel that is often narrated as destiny turned, at its origin, on a party back-room and a single substitution, so that "FDR dies, Truman chooses" became the operative sequence only because the machine had already chosen Truman over Wallace four years before recognition.
Wallace's dated removal is documented; what Wallace would have decided about recognition had he been president is not, and no record can supply it.
Truman, born in 1884, a Missouri Democrat and a former haberdasher turned senator, had been Vice President for eighty-two days when Roosevelt died.
Over the next three years he would make the single decision on which this chapter's American story turns, and he would make it with a recurring cast around him.
That cast is set out here, because its members reappear, in one combination or another, at each American turning point between 1945 and 1948.
The first is Clark Clifford (1906–1998), White House Special Counsel.

In November 1947 Clifford sent Truman a memo arguing that the Jewish-American vote was likely decisive in several key swing states, New York, Pennsylvania and Illinois, for Truman's uncertain reelection prospects in 1948, and framing early and unambiguous recognition of a Jewish state as electorally advantageous.

Clifford's own memoir, Counsel to the President, published in 1991, openly describes this domestic-political framework as part of the advice he actually gave Truman, and acknowledges both Marshall's opposition and the argument between the two men.
A related document appears in another source: a November 1947 memo to Truman titled "The Politics of 1948 and the Jews," which analyzed the Jewish vote for the coming election.
The sources used here do not say whether that title and Clifford's memo are one document or two.
The second figure is the man who objected to Clifford most strongly.
George Marshall, Secretary of State, architect of the strategy that won the war in Europe and of the Marshall Plan, was one of the most prestigious figures in postwar American public life.
He told Truman directly: "If you follow Clifford's advice and if I were to vote in the election, I would vote against you."
Truman recognized Israel anyway, and Marshall did not resign.
Marshall's decision not to carry out the threat is itself part of the documented record; it does not show that his broader relationship with Truman was permanently damaged.
Behind Marshall stood the third element of the cast, the professional State Department.
Loy Henderson, director of Near Eastern Affairs, Under Secretary Robert Lovett and Marshall himself opposed early recognition.

Their argument was cold strategic realism: recognizing a Jewish state would damage American relations with the Arab world, jeopardize access to Middle Eastern oil at the opening of the Cold War, and possibly require American troops to enforce partition.

The pattern they form is the point here, and it is a pattern this book meets again: the permanent foreign-service establishment judged support for the Zionist program to be against American strategic interest, and the elected political leadership overruled it.

Eddie Jacobson, an American Jew from Kansas City, was Truman's old army comrade and his former partner in a men's clothing store, Truman & Jacobson, which went bankrupt in the early 1920s; Jacobson had been best man at Truman's wedding and remained one of his most trusted friends.
By March 1948 Truman, worn down by Zionist lobbying, had refused to see Chaim Weizmann through official channels.
Jacobson went to the Oval Office and, invoking their friendship and Truman's admiration for the aging Zionist leader, persuaded the President to receive Weizmann privately.
That meeting, on 18 March 1948, is documented in multiple biographies and in Truman's own recollections, and historians widely credit it with securing Truman's commitment to recognition.
Jacobson's documented contribution is that one meeting; the record does not give him a broader coordinating role in the recognition decision.
The meeting with Weizmann had an immediate and awkward sequel.

The very next day the American delegation at the United Nations announced a retreat from partition toward a temporary trusteeship, and the collision between what the President had told Weizmann in private and what his diplomats said in public is the subject of .
The end of this American arc can be stated briefly here.

On 14 May 1948, at 6:11 p.m. Washington time, eleven minutes after David Ben-Gurion declared the State of Israel in Tel Aviv, the United States extended de facto recognition, with Clifford arranging the timing and Marshall's professionals, and the American delegation still arguing for trusteeship at the United Nations, left uninformed.
De jure recognition followed in January 1949, after Truman's election victory; the Soviet Union had extended full de jure recognition first, in May 1948.
Why did Truman do it?

On its reading, the recognition was primarily a domestic political calculation for the 1948 election, orchestrated by Clifford: Marshall threatened to resign, the State Department opposed, and the President's personal channel to Zionist leadership ran through his former business partner.
Truman's own memoir later presented the recognition as principled, and Clifford's memoir and Marshall's documented opposition tell a different story.
The case is strengthened by Clifford's own admission, which is first-person evidence and not inference.
The familiar account holds the opposite: that Truman recognized Israel out of moral conviction.
That account has evidence too, and the strongest form of it rests on Truman's own words.
As a senator in 1943, years before any recognition question or any campaign money, he spoke at a mass rally for Europe's Jews, as the next section shows.

In February 1947 he publicly called the impression that partisan and local politics motivated American policy on Palestine "most unfortunate and misleading," and said his position had been consistent since 1945.

The same documents that show Clifford's arithmetic also show that Truman was pressed by Zionist lobbying to the point of refusing to see Weizmann, and that it took a friend's personal appeal, not a political operative's, to change his mind about that meeting.

Clifford's memo documents one real and significant thread in the decision; it does not show that electoral calculation was the only factor, or that humanitarian and strategic considerations played no part.

What the record does show, specifically, is a president with little foreign-policy grounding moving faster than his own government's formal machinery, guided partly through a personal relationship outside normal channels, against the explicit, documented objection of his Secretary of State.
Accounts of 1948 as a hidden-hand operation, in which an organized interest secretly controlled American policy, cannot accommodate the documents.

A plot that controls a government does not have that government's Secretary of State, its Near Eastern division and its oil-strategic establishment fighting it openly in signed memoranda, as Marshall and Henderson did.
Nor was Jacobson a secret agent; he was the opposite.

To readers inclined to conspiracy he looks like proof of hidden influence; on the record he is proof of something more ordinary, that a haberdasher's personal loyalty could move a president when the State Department could not, and that the channel was a friendship documented in biographies, not a secret.
What remains open is the weight of each motive in Truman's own mind.
The record establishes the sequence: the 1944 substitution, the April 1945 death, the November 1947 memo, Marshall's threat, the 18 March meeting, the eleven minutes.
Nor can it say what Roosevelt, or Wallace, would have done in Truman's place; those questions are counterfactuals, and they stay open by their nature.
Resolution 181: The Vote, the Pause and the Numbers
By the autumn of 1947 the question of Palestine had passed from Britain to the United Nations.
It now fell to the General Assembly, the body that had replaced the League of Nations as the forum of the world's states, to decide what to do with that recommendation.

The Assembly did so in two stages: first in an Ad Hoc Committee on Palestine, where the plan was debated and alternatives were voted down, and then in plenary session, where a two-thirds majority was required.
The familiar account compresses all of this into one image: the nations of the world, gathered peacefully, created Israel by democratic consensus.
The first count came in the Ad Hoc Committee on 25 November 1947.
On the same occasion the committee rejected the alternative: a draft for a single, unitary state, known as Draft Resolution III, failed by 29 votes to 12, with 14 abstentions.
A Pakistani amendment that would have capped land ownership at 10% for each community was also rejected, by 22 votes to 8.
So by 25 November the Assembly had, in committee, turned down both a unitary state and a limit on land holding, and had approved partition.
Published accounts describe the initial tally of 25 in favor as short of that threshold, and record that the Assembly's president, Aranha, arranged a three-day postponement before the decisive vote.
The Yearbook excerpt dates the committee vote to 25 November and the plenary vote to 29 November; the material does not record the exact day on which the postponement was called.

It does not explain every delegation's reasoning, and it was never meant to; what it does document is several of the forces at work inside it, and the plainest of them was the government of the United States.
The Truman administration's executive branch pushed for a yes vote.
Its own foreign-policy and military establishment pushed the other way: the State Department and the Pentagon opposed the push, citing Arab anger and the Cold War stakes of Middle Eastern oil.
The most senior internal objection on record came from James Forrestal.
Forrestal had been a Wall Street financier before entering government, had served as Secretary of the Navy, and had become the first Secretary of Defense.
He approached Palestine through strategy and petroleum, and believed that alienating the Arab world would endanger American access to Middle Eastern oil and hand an advantage to the Soviet Union.

His diaries, published after his death as The Forrestal Diaries (1951), record his distaste for what he called the "bullying" and "coercion" of small, dependent states to secure their votes, and his conviction that American policy in the Middle East was being driven by domestic political calculation rather than national interest.
Forrestal's diary records his characterization and his objection; it is not an operational record of which tactics were used on which country by which official.
He left office early in 1949 and, weeks later, died in a fall from a high window at Bethesda Naval Hospital, where he was being treated for depression and exhaustion.
The pressure Forrestal deplored had named targets.
Haiti, Liberia and the Philippines.

The historian Michael Cohen, in Palestine and the Great Powers (1982), documents the shift and connects it to a broader pattern of pressure on smaller, economically dependent states in exactly this window.
Liberia is the best-documented case, because its dependency was so large and so visible.

The Firestone Tire and Rubber Company held a rubber concession in Liberia that the sources put at about 1.1 million acres; the company was the country's dominant employer, its largest source of foreign exchange, and, in effect, its economy.
