Liberia's own ambassador complained that the American delegation had threatened aid cuts to several countries in the same period.
Firestone had no stake in Palestine.
The Philippines, a recent American possession bound to Washington by aid and security ties, came under American pressure through those economic ties.
According to one account, the Philippine delegation reversed a speech critical of partition and voted yes after American intervention.

General Carlos Romulo, the Philippines' own representative, later wrote of being recalled and overruled by his own president: "This particular chapter in history had been exceedingly unpleasant to me."
Haiti changed its position after direct communication from the American executive.

Reports at the time and since describe private approaches to these delegations in the crucial days by influential Americans inside and outside the government; those reports do not name the individuals in the material available here.
The Liberian link is documented by a serious historian; the exact mechanism behind the Haitian and Philippine shifts is less fully documented, and should be held at that lower confidence.
Cuba's delegate announced that Cuba would vote against partition "in spite of the pressure that has been brought to bear upon us."
Cuba appears in the final list of those voting against.
The Soviet Union voted yes, and its motive, as the sources describe it, was not sympathy for Zionism, which Soviet doctrine regarded as bourgeois nationalism.

Partition would end British rule in Palestine and weaken Britain's position in the Middle East; many of the Jewish community's leaders were socialists who had grown up in the Russian Empire; and a new state looked, in 1947, like a way to reduce a rival empire and gain influence.
The same logic would bring arms to the new state through Czechoslovakia in 1948.
Soviet-Israeli relations cooled within a few years, which fits a vote driven by strategy rather than lasting alignment.
(The Soviet record is told in .)
Washington and Moscow, already rivals, pushed the same way for opposite reasons.
On 29 November 1947 the Assembly adopted the plan by 33 votes to 13, with 10 abstentions.
The thirteen against were Afghanistan, Cuba, Egypt, Greece, India, Iran, Iraq, Lebanon, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, Syria, Turkey and Yemen.
The ten abstaining were Argentina, Chile, China, Colombia, El Salvador, Ethiopia, Honduras, Mexico, the United Kingdom and Yugoslavia.
Those in favor included Australia, Canada, France, Poland, Sweden, the Soviet Union, the United States and Uruguay.
Britain, the Mandatory power that would have to hand over the country, abstained.
The Mandate was to end "as soon as possible but in any case not later than 1 August 1948."
An area with a seaport in the Jewish state was to be evacuated "not later than 1 February 1948."
A Palestine Commission of five states, Bolivia, Czechoslovakia, Denmark, Panama and the Philippines, was to carry it out.
The two cases presented to the Assembly deserve to be heard in their strongest form.
The Jewish Agency's argument, as the UN Yearbook records it, set the plan against the map of the region.
The Arab states held about 17,000,000 Arabs in roughly 1,290,000 square miles.
Palestine, after the separation of Transjordan, was about 10,000 square miles.
On that reckoning the plan gave the Jewish National Home less than one-eighth of the territory originally set aside for it.
The Agency accepted the plan, though it disliked the borders and the separation of Jerusalem.
The Jewish Virtual Library, a pro-Israel reference source, states that the Jews of Palestine were dissatisfied on both counts but "welcomed the compromise."

It also reports, citing the writers Avneri and Horowitz, that Arab League Secretary-General Azzam Pasha told David Horowitz and Abba Eban on 16 September 1947: "The Arab world is not in a compromising mood."
The Arab delegations argued on law as well as justice.

Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, Iraq, Syria and Yemen denounced the plan as contrary to the Charter, illegal and immoral, said they regarded it as a recommendation, and declared that they would not feel bound by it.

The historian Muhsin Yusuf, of Birzeit University, sets out the reasons for rejection as he reads them: fear of later expulsion and of land confiscation; the injustice of granting statehood to a largely immigrant minority while the majority was denied self-determination; and a view of Zionism as a European imperial project.
He recalls that the Arab case to the Anglo-American Committee in 1946 had promised that Jews "will be full citizens" of a Palestinian state.
The Arab majority of Mandate Palestine had no vote in the General Assembly and no direct representation in the decision that partitioned the territory.
Arab member states voted against; the people most affected were an object of the resolution, not a participant in it.

The 1947 British Mandatory census, as summarized in the sources used here, counted about 1.3 million Arabs and 630,000 Jews in Palestine, which is the reason the familiar claim that the land was largely empty before 1948 does not survive contact with the record.
On the overall shares, the sources agree in outline: Jews were roughly a third of the population (one account gives about 30%), Arabs roughly two-thirds (about 70%).
One account in the sources used here gives the Jewish state 55% of the territory and the Arab state 45%, with Jerusalem as an international zone.
Another, and Yusuf, give the Jewish state 56%; Yusuf gives the Arab state 43%, the other account 44%.
On population inside the proposed Jewish state, the gap is wider.
Yusuf counts about 498,000 Jews and about 494,000 Arabs, a near-even split; the Arab state about 725,000 Arabs and 11,000 Jews; and the Jerusalem district about 105,000 Arabs and 100,000 Jews.

The Jewish Virtual Library, citing the historian Howard Sachar, gives the Jewish state about 5,500 square miles with 538,000 Jews and 397,000 Arabs, and the Arab state 4,500 square miles with 804,000 Arabs and 10,000 Jews; citing Aharon Cohen, it adds that about 60% of the Jewish state was Negev desert.

Yusuf's figure supports the argument that the Jewish state would have had barely a Jewish majority; Sachar's supports the argument that it would have had a clear one, on land much of which was desert.
One account in the sources used here says the Jewish population legally owned under a tenth of the land.
The summary of the pre-1948 record puts Jewish ownership at approximately 7% of the country's land in 1947.
Yusuf gives about 6% of Palestine overall, and about 10% of the land inside the proposed Jewish state.
The dashboard panel above sets the two ratios side by side: about 7% of the land in Jewish ownership in 1947, and 56% of the territory allotted to the Jewish state by the plan.

Resolution 181 stands at the point where two lines meet, the special committee's recommendation of partition and the votes lobbied by the American Zionist political machine, and from it runs the line marked "legal basis claimed" to the state proclaimed in May 1948.
This section has added a second American line, as it appears in the record of the three days: an executive pressing for votes, over the objection of its own professionals.
Those voting against, and several of those abstaining, regarded the resolution as a recommendation; Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, Iraq, Syria and Yemen said so in terms.

The territorial and demographic shares would soon be overtaken: the war of 1948 produced roughly 700,000 Palestinian Arab refugees, a figure documented by Israeli, Palestinian and international historians, including Israeli scholars working in declassified military archives from the 1980s, and Israel's lines in 1949 lay far beyond those of the plan.

The record establishes the three-day window, the three changed votes and the leverage on Liberia; it does not establish the full mechanism behind the Haitian and Philippine changes, or which American officials made which approaches.

The population of the proposed Jewish state is given differently by serious sources, from a near-even split to a clear Jewish majority, and the land shares vary by a point or two depending on the account.
And Forrestal's death, ruled a suicide, remains questioned at the margins without any documented link to his politics.
Acceptance, Rejection and the Two Escalations
One sentence has long served as the summary of what followed the partition vote: Israel accepted, the Arabs rejected and started the war.
In its fuller form the familiar account holds that the Arab side rejected a peaceful UN compromise and at once launched a war against a state that had only accepted it.
The first is who accepted and who rejected Resolution 181.
The Jewish Agency accepted Resolution 181, reluctantly, with real misgivings about the plan's narrow borders.
The Arab Higher Committee and the Arab League rejected the plan in its entirety.
Jamal Husseini, speaking for the Arab Higher Committee, told the United Nations that the partition line would be "nothing but a line of fire and blood."
It was a civil war inside Mandate Palestine, between the Jewish and Arab communities and their paramilitary forces, fought while Britain still formally governed the country.
The neighbouring Arab states' armies did not cross a border until 15 May 1948.
The forces on the Arab side were of two kinds, and they did not work together.
The Arab Liberation Army was created by the Arab League and led by Fawzi al-Qawuqji.
Its forces were volunteers, in the historian Magdalena Pogońska-Pol's description "few in number, and poorly armed."
The Army of the Holy War (Jaysh al-Jihad al-Muqaddas) was made up of Palestinian volunteers and was subordinate to the Husayni family.

The American government's own historians describe the fighting of these months in terms that favor the familiar account.

The State Department's Office of the Historian describes irregular Palestinian Arab bands, attached to Arab Liberation Army units, attacking Jewish cities, settlements and forces, with the Haganah, the Irgun and Lehi fighting back.

In early January 1948 a car bomb at the former Ottoman government house in Jaffa killed 26 people; the material available here gives the toll but does not name who planted the bomb.
On 15 February 1948 Haganah and Palmach forces attacked the village of Qisarya near Haifa.

The sources place Qisarya within a documented pattern of Jewish paramilitary attacks on Palestinian towns and villages in the war's first months, well before the massacre at Deir Yassin, which is told in .
The decisive struggle of the spring was over the road to Jerusalem.
At the end of March 1948 Abd al-Qadir al-Husayni went to Damascus to seek arms from the Arab League's Military Committee.
Jewish forces took al-Qastal, the village overlooking the Jerusalem–Jaffa road.

Read one way, the episode compresses the Palestinian predicament of these months: a local commander who had to travel to the League's Military Committee in Damascus to ask for weapons, and who died on the road he was trying to hold.
The Arab Legion of Transjordan attacked the Gush Etzion bloc of Jewish settlements; its defenders surrendered, and some were massacred.
The source, the historian Avi Shlaim's seminar notes, does not give the date or the number killed, and this book does not supply them.
The second escalation came on 15 May 1948, the day after Israel's declaration of independence, when the armies of neighbouring Arab states invaded.
The war they entered ended in 1949 with Israel's territory extending far beyond the lines of the UN plan.
The invasion is real, documented and significant; its course, the Arab League's own stated reasons for it and the forces on each side are told in .

The reading that "the Arabs rejected and attacked" is supported on the vote, which was a clean Arab rejection backed by a public threat of "fire and blood," and it has support on the fighting: the Office of the Historian describes Arab bands attacking and Jewish forces fighting back, Abd al-Qadir's men bombed the Jewish Agency building, and the Arab Legion attacked Gush Etzion before the Mandate ended.
By then the country had been at war for five and a half months, with documented Jewish paramilitary attacks on Arab villages and towns among the events of those months.
The reading that "a two-sided war began at once" is supported by the dates: violence from 1 December, attacks documented in both directions, Qisarya in February, the Jerusalem road in April.
What it cannot carry is any suggestion that the rejection was incidental, or that Arab forces were merely reactive.
The Arab Higher Committee had promised resistance in advance, and the Army of the Holy War and the Arab Liberation Army were organized to fight.

Nor does it deliver a verdict on responsibility: it does not argue that the Arab League's rejection was justified, or that the later invasion was unprovoked.
Independence and the Nakba, 1948
On Friday 14 May 1948, at four in the afternoon, David Ben-Gurion stood in a hall of the Tel Aviv Museum and read out the Declaration of the Establishment of the State of Israel.
ents: the Declaration of the Establishment of the State of Israel

sent: The British Mandate was due to expire at midnight, a few hours later.
The signing line reads "5th day of Iyar, 5708 – 14th May 1948," while the body of the text, referring to the end of the Mandate, gives "6th Iyar, 5708 (15th May, 1948)."
Ben-Gurion, born in 1886 and dead in 1973, was a Polish-born organizer of the labor Zionist movement.
Palestinians call what followed the Nakba, Arabic for "catastrophe."
The founding of the state and the displacement of much of the Arab population from the territory it came to hold took place in the same months, and this section follows both.
The first is that the Palestinians left of their own accord, on instructions broadcast by Arab radio.
The second is that America created and armed Israel.
The Declaration began with its grounds.

It based the state on "our natural and historic right," on the Balfour Declaration of 2 November 1917, on the Mandate of the League of Nations, and on the General Assembly resolution of 29 November 1947.
ents: the Mandate of the League of Nations

sent: The other three were international instruments: a British pledge, a League mandate and a United Nations vote.
It appealed to the Arab inhabitants of the state "to preserve peace" and to take part in building it on the basis of "full and equal citizenship."
They promised a state for the Jewish people in which its Arab citizens would be full citizens, and they offered peace to its neighbors.
Whether and how the first promise was kept is a question for the later volumes of this library, because the record of the Arabs who stayed inside Israel begins after 1948.
The answer to the second came within hours: armies from Lebanon, Syria, Iraq and Egypt invaded, and Transjordanian forces entered the areas designated for the Arab state and Jerusalem.
It referred to Eretz-Israel, the Land of Israel, and it pledged steps toward "the economic union of the whole of Eretz-Israel."
Economic union between the two states was what the UNSCOP majority had recommended in 1947.
The People's Council became the Provisional Council of State, and a constitution was to be adopted by an elected Constituent Assembly "not later than the 1st October 1948."
When the First Knesset met, it deadlocked over what a constitution should contain, above all over the place of religion in public life.
Instead it resolved to enact Basic Laws one at a time.

There are now fourteen, covering the Knesset, the government, the military, the judiciary and civil rights, and the Supreme Court treats them as having constitutional weight, though a simple Knesset majority can amend them.
The institutions the Jewish Agency had built under the Mandate became, almost overnight, the institutions of a sovereign government.
The Haganah, the pre-state militia, became the Israel Defense Forces; a state intelligence service, the Mossad, was established in 1949.
The United States extended de facto recognition within eleven minutes, a timing arranged by Clark Clifford over the State Department's objection.
Recognition is examined in the next section.
Recognition was a political act.
The United States imposed an arms embargo on all parties to the 1948 war.
The Truman administration recognized Israel within minutes, but it did not lift the embargo.
The weapons that reached the new army in the decisive months came instead from communist Czechoslovakia, flown in by C-54 transports from Žatec airfield in an airlift code-named Operation Balak.
One account describes them as former German arms: Mauser rifles, Messerschmitt Bf 109G fighters and ZK 383 submachine guns.

The fuller record of  is more precise about the fighters, Avia S-199s, a Czech-built derivative of the Bf 109, about 25 of them, and adds some 35,000 Karabiner 98k rifles sent by sea and a 1952 Czechoslovak figure of almost $14.5 million in receipts.
Israeli military historians have documented the operation, and so has Zeev Sternhell in his work on the founding.
Ben-Gurion's verdict survives in two forms: "Czech arms saved the State of Israel," in his memoir,  and, in 1968, "Czechoslovak arms saved the State of Israel, really and absolutely."
The shorter statement has the United States, Britain and the United Nations all embargoing; the pipeline record has Britain supplying aircraft and training to the Arab air forces.

Nor was Czechoslovakia the only source: the clandestine American procurement network, and the money Golda Meyerson raised in the United States early in 1948, are described in earlier sections of this chapter.
Czechoslovakia did not act alone.
It lay inside the Soviet sphere, and the sales went ahead with Moscow's permission.

The motive usually given is the same one read into the Soviet vote for partition in November 1947: anything that hastened the end of the British Mandate weakened Britain's position in the eastern Mediterranean.
On that reading, Soviet interest and the new state's survival ran in the same direction for a few years and then parted.
The first is that the state later regarded as America's closest ally was armed at birth by the Soviet bloc while Washington held back.
That is accurate for 1948, but it was a dated episode, and Soviet-Israeli relations changed markedly in the years that followed.
The second is that Israel was a Western implant.
The arms record is the strongest evidence against that view: at the decisive moment, the Western power most often credited with Israel's birth was withholding weapons from it.
The same months produced the Nakba.
The figures given in the main account in this book's sources are between 700,000 and 750,000 Palestinians displaced, with about 500 villages depopulated or destroyed.
Benny Morris estimates 700,000.
Walid Khalidi gives 750,000, and Rashid Khalidi accepts the higher figure.
Walid Khalidi's All That Remains (1992) documents the villages one by one.
Much of the sustained documentation comes from Israeli historians writing from inside the country's own archives: Morris's 1948:
A History of the First Arab-Israeli War, Ilan Pappé's The Ethnic Cleansing of Palestine, Tom Segev's 1949: The First Israelis and Avi Shlaim's The Iron Wall.
The UN Conciliation Commission's technical estimate of 1949 was about 711,000; a later summary gives the same commission's figure as 726,000.
Other figures run from a past Israeli government estimate "as low as 520,000" up to 850,000 from Palestinian researchers.
UNRWA's rolls of 1950 held 957,000, but the commission had already warned that relief rolls were inflated by duplicate ration cards and by people who were not refugees.

Counts of depopulated villages also vary with method, from 369 in Morris's 1987 count to 418 in Khalidi's and 531 localities in the Palestine Land Society's list, which includes towns and tribal lands.
By 1948, land in Jewish ownership, bought parcel by parcel over decades, amounted to roughly seven percent of Mandate Palestine.
Resolution 181 had allotted about 55 percent of the country to the Jewish state (56 percent in other sources used in this chapter).
By the 1949 armistice, about 78 percent of Mandate Palestine was under Israeli control.
How the departure happened is the core of the dispute, and Plan Dalet is the central document in it.

The Haganah finalized it on 10 March 1948; according to the account in the sources used here it was released from the Israeli archives in the 1980s, and Walid Khalidi published its text as an appendix to his article "Plan Dalet: Master Plan for the Conquest of Palestine," republished in 1988.
Its text, its village clause and the operations carried out under it are set out in the section on Plan Dalet.

One account in this book's sources summarizes the plan as authorizing three things: securing the areas assigned to the Jewish state by expelling villages that resisted; taking Arab-majority cities in those areas; and a stated vocabulary of destruction (haricha) and expulsion (gerush).
Walid Khalidi argues that it created "the military fait accompli upon which the state of Israel was to be based," and that the exodus was its product.
Pappé argues in The Ethnic Cleansing of Palestine (2006) that Plan Dalet meets the UN definition of ethnic cleansing.

Morris, who stands politically to Pappé's right and does not use that term, documents many of the same operations but reads the plan differently: as a military plan whose village provisions gave local commanders discretion, used in some places and not others, rather than a central order to expel.
His wider conclusions on the causes of flight, and Avi Shlaim's reply, are set out with the refugees at the end of this chapter.

One summary in this book's sources holds that "the debate is over the term, not the facts," and that the Haganah carried out a plan to secure and expel which produced the outcome of 750,000 displaced.
Was there a central decision to remove the Arab population, or a military plan whose village clause left expulsion to local commanders and the course of battle?

On 9 April 1948, Irgun and Lehi forces, the two right-wing militias later folded into the Israel Defense Forces, attacked the village of Deir Yassin west of Jerusalem, with Haganah and Palmach support.

Current scholarship puts the toll at about 110, generally between 107 and 120, against the 254 cited for decades and the 240 of the letter signed by Albert Einstein, Hannah Arendt and others in December 1948; one account in this book's sources gives about 107.
The figures and their sources are weighed in the section on the massacres of 1948, and Israeli military archives on the attack remain partly classified.

According to Yehuda Slutsky's official history of the Haganah, the attackers announced the killings by radio to nearby villages in order to spread panic, and in the following weeks many families in those villages fled.
Ben-Gurion later wrote in his diary that Deir Yassin "had a decisive effect" on Arab flight.
That is an inference from Slutsky's record and from the flight that followed, and it is presented here as such.
Four days after Deir Yassin, on 13 April, Arab forces attacked a convoy to the Hadassah Hospital on Mount Scopus and killed 78 Jews, most of them doctors and nurses, in reprisal.
The same account argues that the mechanism did not depend on any one militia, and points to Lydda and Ramla in July 1948.
There, it says, about 50,000 civilians were expelled by the Haganah on written orders signed by Yitzhak Rabin, with no Irgun or Lehi involvement.
By July, however, the Haganah had been merged into the Israel Defense Forces under the provisional government's order of 26 May.

The two main accounts of the episode give wider numbers: 50,000 to 70,000 inhabitants and 250 to 400 Palestinian civilians killed in Lockman's summary of Morris; about 70,000 driven out and close to 1,000 dead, counting the march that followed, in the Palestinian encyclopedia Palquest.
Citing Morris, both report that on 12 July Ben-Gurion answered a question about the inhabitants with the words "Expel them," and that Rabin then signed the expulsion order.
The operation is told in full in the section on the Arab states' war.
Ben-Gurion appears on both sides of this record.
He led a community that included Holocaust survivors and refugees from the Middle East to statehood against invading armies.
Whether his authority amounted to a general policy of expulsion is the point on which Morris and his critics differ.

For years after the war, it was widely said that Arab governments had broadcast instructions telling Palestinians to leave their homes for a short time, with the promise that they could return once the Arab armies had won.
If true, the claim placed the cause of the refugee problem with Arab leaders, not with events on the ground.
The Irish journalist Erskine Childers went to the monitoring records.
The BBC Monitoring Service had recorded and transcribed Middle Eastern radio throughout the period for British intelligence, and American monitors had done the same.
Childers searched them for the evacuation orders and published his findings in The Spectator:
There was not a single order, or appeal, or suggestion about evacuation from Palestine from any Arab radio station, inside or outside Palestine, in 1948.
There is a repeated monitored record of Arab appeals, even flat orders, to the civilians of Palestine to stay put.
Walid Khalidi, citing the BBC monitoring and its American counterpart, the FBIS, called the evacuation-order claim "a piece of mythmaking."
One summary in this book's sources says that Morris, working in the archives in the 1980s, found no evidence of the broadcasts in Israeli, Arab or British records either.
The Israeli archival record Morris used points the same way.

An IDF intelligence report of June 1948, in Lockman's summary, attributed about 70 percent of the flight up to that date to direct Jewish military operations and no more than 5 percent to evacuation orders from Arab leaders; its full breakdown is given with the refugees.
So some local evacuation orders were given; the Israeli army's own estimate at the time counted them as a small cause, and they were not the blanket radio campaign of the later story.
Lockman also writes that Yosef Weitz's report of October 1948 falsely blamed Arab leaders for organizing the flight.
Jewish need for safety after the Holocaust was real.
The Zionist claim that Europe's Jews needed a place of refuge after 1945 was not false.
That need was met in a land whose Arab inhabitants bore no responsibility for the crimes committed in Europe, and the cost of meeting it fell on them.

Jewish communities had lived among Arab populations across the Muslim world for more than a millennium: in Andalusia's Golden Age, under the Ottoman millet system, in Baghdad, with a community of 140,000, and in Damascus, Cairo, Sana'a and Fez.
The claim that this coexistence was "substantial" and of a kind "Europe never matched" is a reading of a long and varied history, and is offered as one.
The exodus of roughly 850,000 Jews from Arab lands between 1948 and 1972 had several documented causes, including active recruitment by Israeli and Jewish Agency operations.
The violence against Jews in Arab cities after the partition vote, which was among those causes, is set out in its own section of this chapter.
On 28 October 1948 the Provisional Council adopted the state flag.
It chose the design of the First Zionist Congress at Basel in 1897, a Magen David between blue stripes, and placed the ancient Menorah on the state seal.
One symbolic reading holds that the choice shows which lineage the new state saw itself as continuing: the political project of 1897 rather than the ancient Temple.
Placing the Menorah on the seal did not mean it was disregarded.
It shows only the order of precedence the Council set between two available symbols.
On 11 December 1948 the General Assembly's Resolution 194 affirmed a right of return for the refugees.
Israel has refused it on the ground that a return would end the Jewish majority in the state.
According to the same account, the Palestinians registered with UNRWA as descendants of the displaced numbered some 6 million as of 2026, most of them stateless.
Resolution 194 and the negotiations that followed it belong to the next stage of this volume.
The account of the Nakba in this book's sources goes further, and its argument should be stated in full and labelled for what it is.
It holds that the Nakba was not a single event but a structure that has continued for 78 years.
Among them are the occupation of the West Bank since 1967 and the blockade of Gaza since 2007, with some 2 million people in 365 square kilometres.
West Bank settlers numbered 110,000 in 1993 and more than 500,000 in 2025, plus 250,000 in East Jerusalem, according to Peace Now and Israel's Central Bureau of Statistics.

The list includes the war in Gaza since October 2023, South Africa's genocide case at the International Court of Justice, filed on 29 December 2023, and the International Criminal Court's arrest warrants for Benjamin Netanyahu and Yoav Gallant, issued on 21 November 2024.

It also cites the conclusions of Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch and B'Tselem that the two legal systems in the West Bank meet the international-law definition of apartheid, and Israel's unilateral annexation of East Jerusalem in 1980 under Basic Law: Jerusalem.
In Jordan, more than 2 million Palestinians hold citizenship, about 40 percent of the population.
Lebanon hosts about 500,000 refugees in 12 UNRWA camps, barred from most professions and from owning property.
Syria hosts about 500,000, many displaced again since 2011.
Egypt administered Gaza from 1948 to 1967.

In Egypt's 1979 treaty, Jordan's of 1994 and the Abraham Accords of 2020 with the UAE, Bahrain, Morocco and Sudan, Arab states normalized relations with Israel without resolving the Palestinian question.

In 1946 and 1947 the entries are the Anglo-American Committee, the King David Hotel bombing, UNSCOP, the CIA's estimate ORE-55 and Resolution 181, a sequence of pressure, inquiry and warnings overruled.
The entry for 1948 lists Deir Yassin, Plan Dalet, independence, the eleven-minute recognition, the Czech arms and the Nakba under a single heading: execution.
The first is about $50 million reported raised on Golda Meyerson's American tour, spent largely on weapons.
The second is almost $14.5 million in Czechoslovak arms receipts.

The objectors' column for the year names the letter of December 1948, signed by 28 people including Albert Einstein and Hannah Arendt, which protested Menachem Begin's visit to the United States and described his new party, which had grown out of the Irgun, as bearing "the unmistakable stamp of a Fascist party."
Money raised in America paid in part for weapons sold by the Soviet bloc, under an American embargo.

Whether the expulsions followed a central decision or accumulated from local orders under a plan that allowed them is still the main point of disagreement between Morris and his critics, and the documents do not close it.
The death toll at Deir Yassin is now put at about 110, but part of the Israeli military record remains classified.
The tolls at Lydda and Ramla vary by source.
This book has not yet compiled the Arab military and civilian dead of the war.
The radio claim is settled in its broad form and not in every local detail: the Israeli army's own estimate allowed a small share for Arab evacuation orders.
On the arms, the scale of Czechoslovak supply is clear, but the sources differ on the aircraft, on Britain's role and on whether any other supplier mattered.
Both facts are documented, and much of the documentation is Israeli.
The Military Balance of 1948
In the first, Israel was a tiny nation, vastly outnumbered, that defeated overwhelming Arab armies through will and endurance, a story often told as a near-miracle.
In the second, Israel won not through real capability but because international sympathy, born of the Holocaust, tipped the scales.
The most valuable single document is a US government assessment dated 1 July 1948, written while the outcome was still unknown.
It put Israeli forces at roughly 90,000 in total, with about 35,000 of them used in active operations.
It also found that the Arab armies were, at that moment, stronger than Israel in artillery and tanks, while carrying a wide variety of small arms.
One account calls it, in one place, a contemporaneous CIA assessment and, in another, a US State Department report.
This book has not resolved which office produced it, and refers to it here simply as the July 1948 US assessment.
From the invasion of 15 May until the first truce in June 1948, accounts describe the Israeli forces as initially inferior in both numbers and armament.
After the truce, new enlistments and arms deliveries, among them the Czechoslovak shipments traced in , allowed Israel to seize the initiative.
One historical anthology states that for most of the war, excluding that first period, "the Jews were superior in personnel, equipment, logistics and organization."
Avi Shlaim gives the forces on 15 May 1948 as 35,000 Israeli troops against 20,000–25,000 Arab troops.

His seminar notes put it more precisely: the Israeli army had more men but weaker firepower, and the forces the Arab states actually sent were "well below the level demanded by the Military Committee of the Arab League."
On Shlaim's figures, then, Israel was not outnumbered even in May; it was outgunned.
The anthology's "inferior in both numbers and armament" and Shlaim's "more men but weaker firepower" cannot both be right about numbers, though they agree about weapons.
Shlaim's 35,000 describes 15 May.
The US assessment's 90,000 describes 1 July, and its own figure of about 35,000 refers to the troops in active operations at that later date, not to the army's size at the invasion.
Shlaim calls the June truce "a turning-point," and he argues that "illicit arms-imports decisively tipped the military balance in favour of Israel."
That judgment places the turn where the anthology places it: in the weeks of the first truce, when arms reached the Israeli army and the Arab states did not match them.
Much of the popular "tiny, outnumbered Israel" arithmetic traces back to estimates by John Glubb, commander of Jordan's Arab Legion during the war.

Historians who have worked on the order of battle note that, as the commander of one of the fighting armies, Glubb had a direct and plausible incentive to exaggerate Israeli numbers and play down Arab ones.
It does not show that Glubb falsified anything; it shows that a widely repeated figure comes from an interested party, a fact rarely mentioned when his numbers are cited as neutral.
By the later stages of the war, accounts state that Israel's army outnumbered the combined Arab armies by roughly two to one.
The Arab states reinforced their forces over the course of the war, but they never matched the pace of Israeli growth in men and arms.
On this record they did not: the advantage had passed decisively to Israel well before the fighting stopped.
The difficulty of the first weeks, when the Arab armies held real advantages in heavy weapons, stands in the record beside the reversal.

The underdog story holds, at most, for the opening weeks, and even there it leans on one commander's disputed figures and on a count of men that Shlaim's figures contradict; what the record does support is an Arab advantage in firepower, in artillery and tanks, which the US assessment still found on 1 July.
The record gathered here does not settle the size of the Israeli force on 15 May: one account says it was inferior in numbers, Shlaim says it was larger.
It does not say which office of the US government wrote the July 1948 assessment.
And it offers no independent figures for the Arab armies' strength after May against which Glubb's estimates could be checked.
What it does establish is the shape of the war's balance: a real early disadvantage in firepower, a turn at the first truce, and a decisive Israeli superiority by the end.
Moscow Said Yes
The popular memory of 1948 has two superpowers in fixed places: the United States as Israel's sponsor, and the Soviet bloc hostile from the start.
Between May 1947 and May 1948 the Soviet Union backed a Jewish state earlier, and held to it more steadily, than Washington did.

Its satellites voted for partition, it stood firm at the Security Council when the Americans retreated, it was the first government in the world to recognize Israel in law, and arms from a Soviet-bloc country reached the new state while an American embargo was in force.
In December 1948 the bloc voted against the UN resolution on refugee return, and only in the 1950s did Moscow turn toward the Arab states.
The first move came at the special session of the General Assembly that Britain had requested.
On 14 May 1947, the day before the Assembly created the Special Committee on Palestine , the Soviet representative Andrei Gromyko addressed the session.
He said the Soviet Union preferred a single Arab–Jewish state in which both peoples would have equal rights.
Coming from Moscow, that was a reversal.
For decades the Soviet state had opposed Zionism .
Gromyko's speech did not endorse partition outright; it ranked it second.
But it put the Soviet Union on record, before Washington had committed, as willing to accept a Jewish state.
Why Moscow changed course is not stated in any Soviet document among the sources used here.
Analysts at the time and since have read the motive as a wish to remove British influence from the region .
It remains an interpretation of Soviet interest, drawn from what Moscow did, rather than a finding from Moscow's own records.
What it does explain is why the Soviet Union and the Zionist movement could find themselves on the same side without sharing any larger aim.
When the Assembly voted in November 1947, the Soviet Union and its satellites voted for partition .
In March 1948 the United States moved to retreat from partition toward a temporary United Nations trusteeship, a shift told in .
The Soviet Union did not follow.
At the Security Council it stood behind partition, and Gromyko told the Council that the rapid creation of two states was the only way to reduce the bloodshed  .
On 14 May 1948 Israel declared its independence, and Truman's recognition followed the same day, but it was de facto recognition.
On 17 May 1948, three days after independence, the Soviet Union became the first state to grant Israel full legal, or de jure, recognition  .
The Soviet recognition was thus the fuller of the two.
The wider story of who recognized Israel, when and on what legal basis, is told in this chapter's section on recognition.
Recognition was not the only support that came from the Soviet side.
Arms reached the new state from Czechoslovakia, a Soviet-bloc country, at a time when an American embargo was in force .

The contracts, the airlift and their price are documented in ; the point here is that the first great power to recognize Israel in law and the government behind its Czechoslovak arms both stood on the same side of the Cold War line.
In December 1948 the Soviet bloc voted against United Nations Resolution 194, the resolution on the return of refugees .
From the 1950s, Moscow turned toward the Arab states .
The common account holds that Israel was created by American support while the Soviet bloc was hostile from the start.
American support mattered, but it wavered in March 1948.
Soviet support came first, held through that wavering, and produced the first full recognition.
In 1947 and 1948 both superpowers backed the new state, for different reasons, Moscow earlier and more firmly, apparently to push Britain out.
Gromyko's speech, the votes, the Security Council statement and the recognition are all documented acts.
The reasoning behind them inside the Soviet leadership is not documented in the sources used here; the "remove Britain" explanation is the reading analysts have drawn from those acts.
Nor do these sources show how far Soviet diplomacy and the Czechoslovak arms sales were coordinated as a single policy, rather than running in parallel.
Truman in His Own Words, 1943–1948
Harry Truman is often remembered as a lifelong and uncomplicated champion of a Jewish state.
The first item comes from Truman's years in the Senate.
In April 1943, before he was Vice President and long before any decision about Palestine was his to make, Senator Truman spoke at a mass rally in Chicago Stadium urging help for Europe's Jews.
According to David McCullough's biography, he said that under "mad Hitler" they were being "herded like animals" into camps.

Whatever weight one gives later political motives, this was said by a senator with no Palestine policy of his own to defend, and it is the earliest documented evidence for the humanitarian side of his outlook.
On 10 November 1945, seven months into his presidency, Truman met his chiefs of mission from the Arab world.
The meeting itself is in the State Department's official record.

They come from William Eddy, the American minister to Saudi Arabia, who attended and who wrote, in a pamphlet published in 1954, that Truman had told the diplomats: "I'm sorry, gentlemen, but I have to answer to hundreds of thousands who are anxious for the success of Zionism; I do not have hundreds of thousands of Arabs among my constituents."
The historian John Judis has quoted Eddy's account.
And Eddy was himself a State Department opponent of Zionism, so his account comes from a witness with a settled view of the policy under discussion.
None of that proves the quotation false; Eddy was in the room.

On 4 October 1946, the eve of Yom Kippur and a month before the midterm elections, Truman issued a statement urging immediate large-scale immigration to Palestine and saying the United States could support a viable Jewish state "in an adequate area of Palestine."
On 21 July 1947, after Henry Morgenthau telephoned him about the refugees aboard the ship Exodus, Truman wrote in his private diary: "The Jews, I find are very, very selfish."
He added that once underdogs gain power, "neither Hitler nor Stalin has anything on them for cruelty."
The diary was found at the Truman Library and released by the National Archives in 2003.
It is a sweeping judgment about Jews as a people, written by a sitting president in anger at a particular telephone call, and it is antisemitic in the plain sense of the word.
It is also private, written by the same man who had spoken at the Chicago rally four years earlier and who would recognize Israel ten months later.
The entry is evidence of how the pressure felt to him; it is not, by itself, evidence of what his policy would be, and ten months later he recognized the Jewish state.
In November 1947 a memo to Truman titled "The Politics of 1948 and the Jews" analyzed the Jewish vote for the coming election.
In March 1948, after refusing to see Zionist leaders, he met Chaim Weizmann at the urging of his old business partner Eddie Jacobson.
On 14 May 1948 he granted de facto recognition to Israel eleven minutes after its proclamation, against the opposition of Secretary of State George Marshall.
Four days later, on 18 May 1948, he described American Jews as "very emotional."
The people around those decisions, Clifford, Marshall and Jacobson among them, are introduced in .

Those who see Truman as a man of principle can point to the 1943 rally, given years before any Palestine decision was his, and to a recognition decision he took against the most respected member of his own cabinet.
Those who see electoral calculation can point to Eddy's account, to the Yom Kippur timing and to the November 1947 memo on the Jewish vote.
Those who see reluctance can point to the diary, to his refusal to see Zionist leaders until a friend intervened, and to the "very emotional" remark days after recognition.
Golda Meyerson's Tour: The Money of Early 1948
In the first weeks of the civil war, the Jewish Agency's most pressing shortage was money.
When David Ben-Gurion looked back on the winter of 1948, he credited a single fundraising campaign in the United States, and the woman who ran it, with making the state possible.

It was run by Golda Meyerson, later Golda Meir, and it depended on an American fundraising network that had been built over a quarter of a century and that, through one man, reached directly into the arms network of the same years.
After the partition vote of November 1947, the Jewish Agency needed money quickly.
Its treasurer, Eliezer Kaplan, traveled to the United States to raise $7 million and failed.
Ben-Gurion proposed going himself; the Agency's executive sent Meyerson instead.
She was then acting head of the Jewish Agency's political department, and she left for America in January 1948.
Her opening came through Henry Montor, executive vice-chairman of the United Jewish Appeal.
Montor pressed the Council of Jewish Federations to give her a speaking slot at its assembly in Chicago, and it did.
Three years earlier, in 1945, Montor had gathered seventeen wealthy businessmen to meet Ben-Gurion at Rudolf Sonneborn's apartment, the meeting that founded the arms-buying network described in .
Chicago's Jewish federation took out a $5 million loan and handed the proceeds to her.
By one comparison, that was several times Saudi Arabia's oil revenue for 1947.
The money went largely to weapons, including the arms bought from Czechoslovakia.
Ben-Gurion's response is on record in his own words.
He wrote in his diary that her success was "the only ray of light," and he said that history would record that "there was a Jewish woman who got the money which made the state possible."
She came home on 19 March 1948, the same day the United States told the Security Council that partition could not be carried out by peaceful means, a retreat told in .
The American government was stepping back from partition in the week that private American money arrived to pay for its defense.

Ben-Gurion's tribute, in the record's own summary, credits American donors' money raised through a federation-and-appeal network that had been built since the 1920s and that, through Montor, overlapped directly with the arms network.
Meyerson did not have to build an audience.
The federations already existed in the cities she visited, and the Chicago assembly brought their leaders into one room.
Kaplan had failed to raise $7 million; Meyerson, speaking through that apparatus, was reported to have raised about seven times as much in about two months.
The library's funding ledgers set the tour inside the larger flow of American money that year.
The reported $50 million is the second-largest sum shown, behind only the $100 million Export-Import Bank loan of 1949, and well ahead of the $14.5 million paid for Czechoslovak arms in 1948.
The tour also overlapped with the United Jewish Appeal's regular campaign, so its sum cannot simply be added to the appeal's.
The ledger, compiled from the JTA archive's year-end report on the 1948 campaign, records a record $150 million for the United Jewish Appeal that year, about $2.0 billion in today's dollars.

Of that, $74.7 million went to the United Palestine Appeal, the share for Palestine and then Israel; $64.9 million to the Joint Distribution Committee for relief in Europe; and $10.4 million to resettlement in the United States.
The Palestine share was just under half.
The ledger notes that Keren Hayesod's own history lists defense among the things its money financed before statehood, and that in 1948 Meyerson's campaign money went largely to weapons.
Kaplan's attempt failed; Meyerson's succeeded on a scale far beyond his target; and the money paid largely for arms, including the Czechoslovak arms told in .

They also support the point Ben-Gurion made himself: the claim that the state was built chiefly on its own resources does not survive his own account of where its money came from in the months before independence.
What they do not support is any reading of the money as American government money.
It came from private donors through private institutions, and in the same weeks the American government was retreating from partition.

The $25 million and $50 million figures are reported totals, not audited accounts, and the sources do not say how much of the $50 million was new money and how much came through the United Jewish Appeal's own campaign.
They do not break down what the money bought item by item, or how much of it reached Czechoslovakia.
The comparison with Saudi oil revenue is given without its underlying figure.

Ben-Gurion's verdict is a judgment, by the person best placed to make it, and not a measurement; other parts of this chapter show that weapons, diplomacy and the state's own forces each have a claim on the outcome of 1948.
Inside the White House, 1945–1948
The Agency's other diplomatic track ran to Washington, and there it met a peculiarity of the Truman presidency.
American policy on Palestine is often described as a State Department product, made on the merits by career diplomats.

Inside the White House a small number of aides and friends gave the President views and visitors that the State Department did not, and at least one of his most consequential statements was issued a month before a national election.
The longest-serving of those aides was David K. Niles.
He served in the White House from 1942 to 1951, first under Franklin Roosevelt and then under Harry Truman, and he was one of only two Roosevelt aides whom Truman kept on  .
Niles was a committed Zionist, and he became an important channel through which American Zionists reached the White House  .
That is a documented role, not an accusation: he had been entrusted with minority affairs, and his own commitment was to the Zionist cause.
Max Lowenthal advised the President's special counsel, Clark Clifford, on Palestine .

And outside the staff altogether there was Eddie Jacobson, Truman's personal friend and former business partner, who provided a separate, private channel to the President; his role, including the March 1948 meeting he arranged, is told in .
The clearest test of that influence came in the autumn of 1946, after a conference on Palestine in London had adjourned; the conference and Britain's part in it are set out in .
On 4 October 1946, the eve of Yom Kippur and a month before the congressional midterm elections, Truman issued a statement on Palestine  .
He regretted the adjournment of the London conference.
He urged immediate, large-scale Jewish immigration into Palestine.
And he said that the United States could support a solution along the lines of a viable Jewish state "in an adequate area of Palestine"  .
The statement landed hard in London.
The British Prime Minister, Clement Attlee, was furious, and Truman wrote to him that he "very much" regretted any embarrassment it had caused .
The timing invited an explanation, and the New York Times printed one within three days.

On 7 October 1946 James Reston wrote in that paper that the President "went against his advisers' foreign policy and chose to follow the promptings of those who were primarily interested in retaining Democratic majorities in Congress" .
On Reston's reading, the statement was electoral, and its date, a month before the midterms, was part of the evidence.
Truman rejected that reading publicly.

In February 1947 he issued a statement calling the impression that partisan and local politics motivated American policy on Palestine "most unfortunate and misleading", and insisting that his position had been consistent since 1945 .
Reston's case rests on the calendar, which no one disputes, and on his reporting that the statement went against the foreign-policy advice the President had received.

Truman's case rests on consistency: the October statement's call for immediate, large-scale immigration was, on his account, the position he had held since 1945, and a statement that restates an existing position is not by itself proof of a new electoral calculation.
The White House channel was the last link in a longer chain, told in the previous stage of this book.

Two American Zionist campaigns of the 1940s, a rival and aggressive one led by the Irgun's delegation in the United States and a disciplined mainstream lobby, moved American opinion through advertising, local committees and Christian supporters into Congress and both parties' platforms.

From there the pressure reached the White House, where Niles provided access and the Yom Kippur statement of 1946 put the President on record, and finally the United Nations, where the United States lobbied for the partition vote of November 1947.
The sources here document Niles's access but not the content of his advice on any given day, nor whether he drafted or proposed the October statement.
They record Lowenthal's role as an adviser to Clifford without detailing what he advised.
And no document in this section records Truman saying, in private, that the midterms were or were not on his mind when he spoke on 4 October 1946.
The accounts of motive therefore remain what they are: Reston's reporting on one side, the President's own public denial on the other.
The Absentees' Property Law: From Flight to State Title, 1948–1953
The war of 1948 left hundreds of Palestinian localities empty of their inhabitants.
Together they moved the property of the refugees first into the custody of the state, then into its ownership and that of the Jewish National Fund, and finally into retroactive legal validation.
It is widely believed that the Palestinian Arabs who stayed inside Israel in 1948 kept their homes and land as full citizens.

But tens of thousands who had moved from one village to another inside the lines Israel held were classed in law as "absentees," and their property was taken on the same terms as that of refugees across the border.
In December 1948 the government issued Emergency Regulations on absentees' property, which transferred control to a new Custodian of Absentee Property.
The historian Michael Fischbach, working from Israeli sources, gives 2 December 1948; an American document he cites refers to an "Israeli ordinance of December 12, 1948."
In April 1949 the United Nations Conciliation Commission for Palestine proposed, as a preliminary measure, "suspension of the application of the Absentee law until the final peace settlement."
Arab delegations argued that the law treated nationals of Palestine as enemy aliens.
Israel did not suspend it.
On 14 March 1950 the Knesset passed the Absentees' Property Law, an expanded version of the 1948 regulations, and it remained the main law governing refugee property for decades.
All absentees' property is vested in the Custodian.
Every right an absentee had passes automatically to the Custodian.
The law reached anyone who, during the war, had left his usual place of residence for areas outside Israeli control, or for anywhere else.

It captured not only the refugees beyond the armistice lines but also Arabs who had moved between villages inside Israel and had then been registered as citizens, issued identity numbers, and allowed to vote and to stand for the Knesset.

By 2001 the present absentees were estimated at about 200,000 people, nearly 17 percent of Israel's Arab citizens, and half the populations of the two largest Arab towns in Israel are internally displaced.

Their flight, too, has been confused with something else: two Palestinian migrations are often run together, and the confusion costs both of them their history.
The first began under the Ottoman Empire, some seventy years before the state of Israel existed, and carried families from a handful of towns around Bethlehem to the Americas.

The second was the flight and expulsion of 1948, which carried some 700,000 people across the new armistice lines into the neighbouring Arab states and into the parts of Palestine that Israel did not hold.
A common assumption holds that the Palestinian communities of Latin America are made up of 1948 refugees who found open doors there.

Palestinian emigration to the Americas began in the 1870s.
Most of the early migrants were Christian families from Bethlehem, Beit Jala and Beit Sahour.
They traveled on Ottoman papers, and so in their new countries they were long called "Turcos", Turks.
Its scale, relative to the towns that sent it, was large: El Salvador's population of Bethlehem descent is described today as several times larger than Bethlehem's own.
Chile became the largest center.

Charity for an Army: The Operating Budgets and Britain's Bill
Two assumptions often sit beneath accounts of the Mandate's last decades.
The first is that the Jewish community's underground army was paid for secretly, by means no one can now trace.
The second is that Britain held Palestine cheaply.
Britain's own accounts, meanwhile, record a bill that by the end ran to about £100 million in three years.
The clearest early view of the operating budget comes from an American diplomat.
After the Zionist Congress of 1939, the United States consul in Jerusalem reported that the Jewish Agency's budget had been set at £720,000, about $74 million in today's money.
Of that, £100,000 was earmarked for refugee settlement and £80,000 for what the budget itself called "the Jewish security service (defense)."
The line is small, about one-ninth of the whole, but it is explicit: defense sat inside the Agency's budget, under its own heading, nine years before the state.
The budgets grew quickly during and after the Second World War.
In 1944 the Jewish National Fund spent $10.8 million and the Jewish Agency and Keren Hayesod together $14.9 million of money raised in the United States, some $25.7 million in all.
The United Palestine Appeal's budget for 1945 was $35.3 million.

Inside Palestine, the community taxed itself for defense.

It was run by the community's own council, not by the Mandate government, and it gave the Haganah a revenue stream raised inside the country alongside the money that came from abroad.

The same campaign that fed survivors in Europe and resettled refugees in America was, in its own words, the official channel for the Haganah.
It shows the mainstream campaign separating the Haganah from the armed groups outside it in what it told American donors, and naming one channel as the only legitimate one.

The other side of the ledger is Britain's.
The cost of governing Palestine rose steadily under the Mandate.
Civil government spending grew from £P1.9 million in 1922–23 to £P3.2 million in 1934–35, a rise of about two-thirds in twelve years; the Palestine pound was then at par with sterling.
The garrison was a separate charge, paid by Britain: £1.5 million in 1923–24.

Parliament debated keeping 80,000 to 100,000 soldiers in the country, and some 100,000 troops were deployed.
The human cost was about 750 British military and police killed over the period.
Measured in today's dollars, Britain's three-year military bill was larger than any single year of American giving, and larger than the whole of the wartime appeals of 1939–45.

The Jewish community's defense was financed through documented channels: a budget line, a community levy, an arms network funded by American donors and, at the end, a national charity that called itself the Haganah's official American agency.
Britain, for its part, did not hold Palestine cheaply.

Lausanne, 1949: Two Sequences That Never Met
Za'im's offer was made in the same months as the conference that was meant to settle the refugee question for all the parties at once.
Two opposite accounts of that conference, at Lausanne, are still repeated.
One says that Israel never offered anything on the refugees.
The other says that the Arab states refused every offer.
The United Nations' own report on the talks supports neither.

It records an Israeli offer, a number, and the conditions attached to it; it records an Arab position with conditions of its own; and it shows that each side's conditions came in an order the other would not accept.
The forum was the UN Conciliation Commission for Palestine, created by Resolution 194 of December 1948.
That resolution named France, Turkey and the United States to the Commission ; its full text, and the competing readings of its refugee paragraph, are set out in .
The Commission convened talks at Lausanne from 27 April to 12 September 1949.
The Arab delegations refused to negotiate directly with Israel, so the Commission shuttled between the parties.
The Commission had begun to press on the refugee question before the conference opened.
In April 1949 it asked Israel to suspend its absentee regulations until the final peace settlement, and Israel declined.
On 12 May 1949 the parties signed the Lausanne Protocol, which took the 1947 partition map as a basis for discussion.
The Arab states wanted the 1947 partition lines, and demanded that Israel first accept the return of the refugees under Resolution 194.
Israel held that the partition plan had been nullified by the Arab invasion, and that the refugees could be dealt with only within a final peace.
Israel first floated a proposal to annex the Gaza Strip together with its refugee population.
Egypt refused.
Washington intervened while the talks were under way.
On 28 May 1949 Truman's secret note to Ben-Gurion warned that if Israel kept rejecting the December 1948 resolution, "a revision of its attitude toward Israel has become unavoidable."
Israel rejected the demands in June, and the revision never came.
The note is set in the sequence of Truman's decisions in .
Israel's offer came on 3 August.
According to the Commission's own progress report, Israel offered to accept the return of 100,000 refugees, which would have brought its Arab population to a maximum of 250,000.
The Arab delegations called it contrary to Resolution 194 and to the Protocol.
Israel later withdrew it.
The same report records that Israel blocked a committee on orange groves owned by refugees.
The conference ended on 12 September without agreement, and the United States warned Israel that it might revise its relations over the impasse.
The positions on Jerusalem at Lausanne are not recorded in the sources used here, which is why the comparison leaves them out.

Israel's rested on three points: the partition plan the Arab delegations now invoked had, in its view, been nullified by the Arab invasion; Resolution 194 itself spoke of refugees who wished to return "and live at peace with their neighbours," which
Ben-Gurion read as making return contingent on peace with the Arab states  ; and an offer of 100,000 within a final peace was a concrete figure, not a refusal.

The Arab case rested on three points as well: paragraph 11 of the resolution said that refugees wishing to return "should be permitted to do so at the earliest practicable date"  , which on their reading made return something owed rather than something to be traded for peace; the Protocol Israel had signed took the 1947 map as its basis; and an offer conditional on a final peace, later withdrawn altogether, returned no one.
Israel would discuss return only after peace.
The Arab states would discuss peace only after return.
The offer of 100,000 shows that Israel was prepared to put a number on the table; the conditions attached to it, and the Arab rejection of those conditions, show why the number never became policy.
In the same months Israel was declining Husni al-Za'im's offer to resettle 250,000–300,000 refugees in Syria as part of a peace, an episode told in the section on Syria in 1949.

The Commission's report shows the positions as stated; it does not show what either side would have accepted under sustained pressure, and the one external power that threatened such pressure, the United States, did not apply it.
Whether a larger Israeli offer, or Arab acceptance of the 100,000 as a first step, would have led to a settlement is a matter of judgment, not of documents.
Behind the arguments put to the public lies a harder question: what money did to American policy on Palestine before and during 1948.
In one version, Zionist money bought Congress and the White House.

The American Zionist Emergency Council, the movement's national lobbying body in the 1940s, built local committees across the country and ran letter and telegram campaigns aimed at members of Congress.
It compiled legislators' statements of support into a book, America and Palestine, and used it to press for more.
The same files document the campaign around both parties' 1944 platforms and the Wagner–Taft resolution in Congress.

The historian John Judis records that in mid-1948 Truman wanted Israel to stop taking territory beyond the United Nations partition lines and was disturbed by its refugee policy, but backed away from pressing either objection, in part because his nearly broke campaign needed $100,000 from Abraham Feinberg and Ed Kaufmann for a whistle-stop tour.

Among the dollar flows the record documents between 1921 and 1949, the Feinberg–Kaufmann money is the smallest, about a tenth of a million dollars beside a $100 million Export-Import Bank loan of 1949 and tens of millions raised for arms.
The third claim is that members of Congress were paid, systematically, before 1948.
Until the Federal Election Campaign Act of 1971, the governing law was the Federal Corrupt Practices Act of 1925.
It left enforcement to Congress itself, and it was rarely enforced.
Jewish voters were concentrated in electorally important states such as New York.
Christian restorationist conviction, the belief that the Jews would be restored to their ancient land, was sincere and had a history going back to 1839.
Henry Wallace held Zionist views of his own.
And the 1922 Lodge–Fish resolution, by which Congress endorsed the Balfour Declaration, is credited to lobbying with no payment documented.
The State Department, the Joint Chiefs of Staff and the Secretary of Defense opposed the policy in writing, and they were overruled.
"Money bought Congress and the White House" stretches one documented episode, involving one decision and one campaign, into a general claim about legislators for whom no payment record exists.

Whether any member of Congress received money in connection with a vote on Palestine before 1948 cannot be known from the records that exist, and this book does not supply an answer the documents cannot.

Nor does the Judis account, by itself, measure how much weight the campaign's need carried against the other pressures on Truman in the summer of 1948; it records the need as one reason among others, and that is how it is reported here.

For many of the Jews who came from Arab and Muslim countries after 1948, the record is different, and its most painful chapter is the disappearance of children from the camps.
The setting was the transit camps, the ma'abarot described in .

Among those placed there were the Yemeni Jews flown in by Operation Magic Carpet between June 1949 and September 1950, about 49,000 people, many of whom had walked for weeks to reach the airlift at Aden; their journey is told in .

It is part of the record that many readers raised in Israel come to late.

Once the war ended, the question of why so many Palestinian Arabs had left their homes became a political argument as much as a historical one, because the answer seemed to settle who was responsible for the refugees.
For more than a decade the account that prevailed in the West was that they had left voluntarily, on the orders of Arab leaders, and that this had been established at the time.

The record shows a slower and more complicated history: some of the war's events were reported within days, the explanation for the mass flight that took hold was not the one the documents supported, and the correction came in stages, the last and weightiest of them from Israel's own archives forty years later.
The killings at Deir Yassin in April 1948 were reported in Western newspapers within days, and they were documented by the delegate of the Red Cross who entered the village.
News of the massacre spread through Arab Palestine.
The Israeli historian Benny Morris, writing four decades later, records it as a major accelerant of flight.
The Red Cross's place in that moment, before any international human-rights treaty existed, is part of .

On 4 December 1948 a group that included Albert Einstein, Hannah Arendt and Sidney Hook published a letter in The New York Times warning against Menachem Begin's new Herut party.

Arab leaders, it held, had broadcast orders by radio telling civilians to leave.

Its political effect was clear: it placed responsibility for the refugee problem on the Arab states.

In 1959 the Palestinian historian Walid Khalidi argued from Arab sources that no such general order had been given.
