The Network of the American Build-Up, 1897–1948
A common picture of American support for Zionism before 1948 is of a loose and scattered sympathy: individuals of goodwill, a few friendly senators, some generous donors, acting each on their own.
Laid out by distance from the center, they form a network with a clear structure and two loops that fed themselves.
At the apex stood the Jewish Agency and the World Zionist Organization, led in these years by Weizmann and Ben-Gurion.

In November 1962 the Justice Department ordered the American Zionist Council to register as a foreign agent, alleging that it had received more than $5 million from the Jewish Agency over the preceding eight years.

The 1962 finding concerned the American Zionist Council, the body into which the wartime emergency council was renamed in 1949, and the years it covered; it was not a finding about the emergency council of the 1940s, and the record here does not document Agency funding of that earlier body.
At the first degree, bound to the apex by direct organizational ties, stood three American bodies.
The American Zionist Emergency Council, co-chaired by Abba Hillel Silver and Stephen Wise, ran the national political campaign of the 1940s.
The Zionist Organization of America was the mass-membership body; it had reached 147,000 members by 1918.
Hadassah completed the first ring.
The American Palestine Committee and the Christian Council on Palestine presented themselves as independent voices of American and Christian opinion.
Both were organized by the Zionist executive Emanuel Neumann, and one historian has described them as "hardly autonomous."
The United Jewish Appeal, under its executive Henry Montor, was the fundraising engine described in .
The Sonneborn Institute and its front company, Materials for Palestine, were set up at Ben-Gurion's 1945 meeting with American donors, to buy arms.
Abraham Feinberg, who appears again at the third degree, was one of the original seventeen members of the Sonneborn Institute.
In Congress, Senator Robert Wagner chaired the American Palestine Committee, and Senator Robert Taft co-sponsored the 1944 Palestine resolution.
Senator Henry Cabot Lodge and Representative Hamilton Fish III gave their names to the 1922 resolution endorsing the Balfour Declaration.
Sol Bloom, chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, was a target of the telegram campaigns.
In the White House, the aides David Niles, Clark Clifford and Max Lowenthal, and Truman's friend Eddie Jacobson, carried the Zionist case to the President.

Among donors, Abraham Feinberg and Ed Kaufmann raised the $100,000 that Truman's 1948 campaign needed, and Golda Meyerson's tour of 1948 raised about $50 million through Montor's network, largely for arms.

The White House channel, Niles, Clifford, Lowenthal and Jacobson, sat at the third degree but did not hang beneath any one second-degree body; it connected to the legislators on one side and, through the 1948 campaign money, to the donors on the other.

The emergency council collected statements of support from legislators; printed them in its book America and Palestine; mailed the book to every member of Congress; used it to press for votes and platform planks; and so gathered new statements, which went into the next round.
The second was the Montor loop, and it ran through one fundraiser.

Henry Montor gathered the donors for the 1945 Sonneborn meeting; that meeting produced the arms network; Montor then secured Golda Meyerson's platform before American audiences in 1948; and her tour raised about $50 million, largely for arms, which returned the money to the purpose the 1945 meeting had set.

Feinberg's place inside it is documented further: the FBI file released decades later documents his ongoing meetings with Sonneborn, and in 1952 he was ordered to register as a foreign agent over a publication he ran, a story told in .

Two of them belong to it directly: the Zionist Organization of America's 147,000 members by 1918, the mass base of the first degree, and the roughly $50 million of Golda Meyerson's 1948 tour, the largest single return of the Montor loop.

The land and population figures in the same panel, the share of land in Jewish ownership in 1947 and the share the 1947 partition plan allotted, are taken up in the chapter's closing account of the founding narratives.

The money panel sets four documented sums side by side: Golda Meyerson's tour at about $50 million, the transfer of German Jewish capital in the 1930s, about $14.5 million for Czechoslovak arms in 1948, and the $5 million raised by the American delegation of 1921–22 that met President Harding.
Two of them, the tour and the Czechoslovak purchases, are the financial output of the second-degree arms and fundraising network in its final year.

It shows a movement that built its own institutions, created allied committees that presented themselves as independent, organized the money and the arms channel through a small number of named people, and reached Congress and the White House through named legislators, aides and a friend of the President.

Against it stood the State Department, the Joint Chiefs and the Defense Secretary, who opposed the policy in writing; the network's success was political, and it was contested inside the government it sought to move.

It records that Niles and Clifford carried the case to Truman, not how far they changed his mind; that legislators made statements, not what moved each of them to make one; and that the Agency funded the American Zionist Council in the decade before 1962, not whether or how it funded the wartime council before 1949.
The Mechanism, in Plain Terms: A State Set Running Before It Was Declared
The familiar statement is that Israel was created in 1948.
The kitchen is the financial base: the Jewish Colonial Trust and the Anglo-Palestine Bank, founded between 1899 and 1902.
The land is the permanent holdings of the Jewish National Fund, which began buying in 1901 and did not resell.
The permit is Article 4 of the Mandate of 1922, which recognized a "Jewish agency" and so gave the movement's agency legal standing.
The marketing team is the American political machine of the 1940s, the American Zionist Emergency Council, whose local committees and letter campaigns worked Congress district by district .
Its institutions were founded by different people in different decades, in London, Palestine and the United States.
Edmond de Rothschild, who funded the early colonies, opposed Herzl.
In Washington the State Department, the Joint Chiefs of Staff and the Secretary of Defense opposed American support in writing, the CIA warned against it, and all were overruled.
Britain spent about £100 million on its forces in Palestine in 1945–47 before it gave up the Mandate .
Seven Founding Narratives, Checked Against the Record
The founding of Israel acquired a story, and much of that story was taught in American schools and repeated in the press as settled history.
The seventh comes from the opposite direction: the claim that the Rothschilds, or a few Jewish bankers, paid for it all.
Britain's own census, taken in 1922, two years into the Mandate, counted 757,182 people, about 11 percent of them Jewish.

The figures that followed show how quickly the balance then changed: Britain recorded 376,415 Jewish immigrants between 1920 and 1946, and the UN Special Committee on Palestine put the population at about 1.85 million in late 1946, by which time the Jewish share was about a third.
Its population was counted, and the count was British.
"They left because Arab leaders told them to."
This was the standard Western and Israeli official explanation of the refugee exodus through the 1950s, and it placed responsibility on the Arab states.
Its strongest form rests on something real: some local Arab commanders did order evacuations of women and children in particular places.

But in 1959 the Palestinian historian Walid Khalidi argued from Arab sources that no general order had been given, and in May 1961 the Irish writer Erskine Childers reported in The Spectator that he had examined the British and American monitoring records of Arab broadcasts in 1948 and found no evacuation orders, but rather appeals to stay .

In 1988 the Israeli historian Benny Morris, working from Israeli military and state archives, concluded that the main causes of flight were military attack, expulsion and fear, with local evacuation orders in some places and no general Arab order .
A contemporary CIA assessment from 1948, and research since, describe a war in two phases that Israel ended with roughly a two-to-one advantage in manpower.
"Israel was born of the Holocaust."

The genocide in Europe transformed the urgency of the Zionist case, the politics around it and the moral argument for a state, and in 1945–48 the plight of some 250,000 Jewish displaced persons in Europe was the central argument made to the American public.
The program, the British pledge and the Mandate all predate Hitler, by between 11 and 37 years; the record dates them to 1896, 1917, 1920 and 1922.
"Israel accepted partition; the Arabs rejected it and started the war."
The fighting began as a two-sided civil war inside Palestine months before the Arab armies entered in May 1948.
The claim that the war simply began with the Arab invasion leaves out the months of fighting that came before it.

But in 1947 only about 7 percent of Mandate Palestine's land was in Jewish ownership, roughly 2 million of some 26 million dunams, while the UN plan of that year allotted 56 percent of the territory to the Jewish state.
Purchases from absentee landlords under Ottoman land law displaced the tenant farmers who worked the land, and those evictions are documented.

The Absentees' Property Law of 14 March 1950, building on regulations of 1948, vested the property of those who had left in a state Custodian , and the chain by which that property passed to the Development Authority and the Jewish National Fund is set out in .

Inside the 1949 armistice lines, which Israel's Foreign Ministry describes as enclosing about 78 percent of the Mandate area, the land that had been bought was a small part of the land that was held .
The opposite myth: "the Rothschilds paid for it all."
Edmond de Rothschild in Paris did fund early colonies, and the Balfour Declaration of 1917 was addressed to Lord Rothschild.
But the Paris Rothschild who funded colonies opposed Herzl, and the documented money came overwhelmingly from mass giving.
Keren Hayesod raised $20.1 million worldwide between April 1921 and December 1929, $11.0 million of it from the United States .
In 1948 alone the United Jewish Appeal raised a record $150 million from more than a million contributors in 4,950 American communities .

Even that figure cannot simply be counted as "funding Israel": $74.7 million went to the United Palestine Appeal, $64.9 million to the Joint Distribution Committee for relief in Europe, and $10.4 million to resettling refugees in the United States .
A founding paid for by very large numbers of ordinary donors, much of whose money fed survivors in Europe, is.
The census that undoes the empty-land slogan, the archives that undo the orders-to-flee story and the campaign ledgers that undo the Rothschild myth are the same kind of evidence, read the same way.
Most of the refugees barred from return were in territory held by Arab armies.

By the late summer of 1948 the question of who would govern the parts of Palestine that Israel did not hold had become a contest among Arab governments as much as a matter for Palestinians themselves.
Three answers were offered within a few months of one another: an Arab League administration, a Palestinian government proclaimed in Gaza, and union with the Hashemite kingdom across the Jordan.
By April 1950 the third had prevailed on the West Bank, Egypt held the Gaza Strip under military administration, and the Gaza government had become, in one historian's word, a phantom.
This section follows that contest from September 1948 to the assassination of King Abdullah in July 1951.
A common account holds that Jordan went to war in 1948 purely to destroy the new Jewish state alongside its Arab allies, with no territorial interest of its own.
Jordan's army took and kept territory, and its parliament annexed it.
Egypt took and governed another strip of land for nineteen years.
Their rivalry over what would become of Arab Palestine was itself one of the forces that shaped the outcome.
Egypt joined Jordan, Syria, Lebanon and Iraq in invading the newly declared State of Israel in May 1948, after the end of the British Mandate.
Jordan's Arab Legion, trained and commanded by British officers, took the Old City of Jerusalem and the West Bank.
It was Jordan's most consequential and successful action of the war, and the territory it held afterward would stay under Jordanian administration for the next nineteen years.
Egypt's forces ended the war holding the Gaza Strip.
Where the armies stood when the fighting stopped decided, in practice, which Arab government would have the power to act in each part of the country.
The Arab League tried to set the terms first.
On 8 July 1948 it created a temporary civil administration for Palestine, and in September it agreed to an Arab government seated in Gaza, announced on 20 September.
Two days later, on 22 September, a communiqué of the Arab Higher Committee declared Palestine independent under the All-Palestine Government, headed by Ahmad Hilmi Abdul Baqi.
On 30 September a Palestinian National Council met in Gaza under the presidency of Hajj Amin al-Husayni.
It adopted a provisional constitution and declared independence over the whole of Palestine.
These were acts of Palestinian political leaders, taken in their own name, and they claimed the whole country, not a partition share of it.
Five Arab states recognized it.
Egypt recognized the new government first, then Iraq, then Syria, Lebanon and Saudi Arabia in the middle of October.
King Abdullah of Transjordan refused.
On the same day the National Council met in Gaza, 30 September 1948, a rival congress in Amman pledged loyalty to Abdullah.
On 1 December 1948 the Jericho Congress went further: it proclaimed the union of Palestine and Transjordan and acknowledged Abdullah as king.
The contest thus ran through rival assemblies: one proclaimed independence in Gaza; others, in Amman and Jericho, pledged loyalty to Abdullah and proclaimed union with his kingdom.
Why did the Arab states back a government in Gaza at all?

The historian Avi Shlaim, in a study of the All-Palestine Government published in 1990, argues that Egypt sponsored it as a "focal point of opposition to Abdullah," to frustrate the king's plan to join Arab Palestine to Transjordan.
His verdict is severe: the government was "a phantom deliberately created by the Arab states, with Egypt at their head."
After Israel's October 1948 offensive its ministers were moved to Cairo.
Gamal Abdel Nasser closed its offices in 1959.
Shlaim's judgment and the Palestinian initiative are both part of the record, and they do not cancel each other.
The declaration of 22 September and the Council of 30 September were real political acts by Palestinian leaders who claimed a state in the whole of their country.
The government in Gaza depended on Egypt's sponsorship, and its fate followed Egypt's purposes.
Egypt's own position in Gaza took a form that set it apart from Jordan's.
From 1948 to 1967 Egypt administered the Gaza Strip as a military protectorate.
It governed the territory directly but never annexed it as Egyptian territory, and Egyptian officials kept to that distinction throughout.
Some accounts stress the Arab League's political consensus against formal annexation; others stress Egyptian strategic caution.

After the revolution of 1952, Nasser's rise made Egypt the leading voice of pan-Arabism through the 1950s, and in 1956 his nationalization of the Suez Canal brought an invasion by Israel, Britain and France that was reversed under American and Soviet pressure.

The common belief that Egypt never had any administrative role in Gaza is mistaken: for nineteen years it was the governing power there, a history that still shapes Egypt's relationship with the territory's border.
On the West Bank, Abdullah moved step by step.
He took the title of king in December 1948, and in April 1949 he ordered the country renamed the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan.
About 500,000 Palestinian Arabs had taken refuge in Transjordan or the West Bank.
The West Bank itself had about 500,000 indigenous residents.
Transjordan's prewar population had been about 340,000.
By these estimates the Palestinians brought under the crown, residents and refugees together, outnumbered the kingdom's original subjects by roughly three to one.
Elections were held on both banks in April 1950, and after them Abdullah formally annexed the West Bank.
The ceasefire lines on which this rested were fixed in the Jordanian–Israeli armistice of April 1949, which is told in .
On 24 April 1950 Jordan's parliament passed the resolution of union.

One gives it as support for "complete unity between the two sides of the Jordan and their union into one State," grounded in what the resolution called the "national, physical and geographical unity" of both banks.
Martin Kramer, writing in 2020, quotes it as "complete unity between the two banks of the Jordan, the eastern and western, and their union in one single state."

The idea that the two banks of the Jordan belong together as one political unit had appeared earlier in this history in Ze'ev Jabotinsky's Revisionist Zionist program, which claimed both banks for a Jewish state.
In 1950 the Hashemite Kingdom used the same territorial reasoning in the opposite direction, to bring the West Bank under the crown in Amman.
The next day, 25 April 1950, the British cabinet agreed to recognize the union of Arab Palestine and Jordan together with the State of Israel.
The decision paired two recognitions: Britain accepted Jordan's annexation and Israel in the same act.
The Library of Congress country study of Jordan says it was recognized only by Britain and Pakistan.
Kramer notes that Israelis customarily say either that only Britain recognized it or that Britain and Pakistan did.
Another account, used elsewhere in this library, names three states, Britain, Iraq and Pakistan, and adds that even Britain's recognition excluded Jerusalem.
All agree that the list was very short and that Britain was on it.
The strongest contemporary regional opposition to the annexation came not primarily from Israel or the Western powers but from Jordan's partners in the Arab League.
The Library of Congress study records that the annexation was condemned within the League as advancing Hashemite dynastic ambitions.

Weeks after the vote, the League's Political Committee met in Cairo, with Jordan absent, and ruled that the annexation violated the League's own earlier resolution, which had declared that annexation of Arab Palestine by any single Arab state would be treated as a breach of the Charter and subject to sanctions.
The committee went so far as to consider expelling Jordan from the League.
Later scholarship links this rejection partly to competing Arab state ambitions over Palestine's future, a thread the sources here do not fully unpack.
The same rivalry that produced the Gaza government in September 1948 shaped the reaction to Jordan's union in 1950.
Jordan's rule over the Old City had another side, which the record documents plainly.

During the nineteen years of Jordanian administration, Jewish access to the Western Wall and the other Jewish religious sites of the Old City was denied, contrary to the terms of the 1949 armistice agreement,  and dozens of historic synagogues were damaged or destroyed.
On 20 July 1951 Abdullah was assassinated as he entered al-Aqsa Mosque in Jerusalem for Friday prayers, with his grandson Hussein at his side.
The assassin was a Palestinian, reportedly hired by relatives of Hajj Amin al-Husayni,  the man who had presided over the National Council in Gaza less than three years before.
Jordan held and had annexed the West Bank and East Jerusalem.
Egypt administered Gaza without annexing it.
The All-Palestine Government survived only as offices in Cairo.
It does not establish how much support each side commanded among Palestinians in 1948–1950, whether the Gaza government or the Jericho union.
The reasons Egypt chose administration over annexation in Gaza are disputed.
The list of states that recognized Jordan's annexation is given three ways, and the assassin's sponsors are named only on the strength of report.

What the record does settle is that no independent Arab government came to rule any part of Palestine in these years, and, on Shlaim's reading, the rivalry between Egypt and Jordan, as well as the war with Israel, had much to do with it.
The Rhodes Armistices, 1949: Lines That Were Not Borders
Resolution 194 urged a final settlement.
The lines they drew lasted until 1967 and became known as the Green Line.
The man who brought the parties to the table was Ralph Bunche, who had succeeded the assassinated UN mediator, Count Bernadotte.
In January 1949 he brought Israeli and Egyptian delegations to negotiate on the island of Rhodes.

The mediation he inherited had already cost lives: in July 1949 he reported to the Security Council that ten members of the UN mission, the Mediator among them, had died over fourteen months, and that about twice as many had been wounded.
The plans Bernadotte had put forward, and the killing that ended his mission, are told in .
Bunche's task was narrower than Bernadotte's had been.
The first agreement, between Egypt and Israel, was signed at Rhodes on 24 February 1949.
Mahmed Seif El Dine and M. K. El Raliniany signed for Egypt; Walter Eytan, Yigael Yadin and Elias Sasson signed for Israel.
Egyptian forces encircled in the Al Faluja pocket were to withdraw beyond the Egypt–Palestine frontier under UN supervision, a movement that Annex I set to begin at 0500 GMT on 26 February 1949.
The village of El Auja and its surroundings were demilitarized under Article VIII.
In the Gaza–Rafah area, Article VI froze Egyptian forces at the positions they held.
The Gaza Strip, which Egypt held under the armistice, became the territory whose administration is described in the section on Arab Palestine after the war.
The Egyptian text is also the clearest statement of what an armistice was meant to be.
Article IV(3) says that its provisions are "dictated exclusively by military considerations" and are valid only for the period of the armistice.

Article V says that the demarcation line "is not to be construed in any sense as a political or territorial boundary," and that it is drawn without prejudice to the rights of either party in the ultimate settlement.

Supervision was given to a seven-member Mixed Armistice Commission: three members appointed by each party, with the Chief of Staff of the UN Truce Supervision Organization in the chair, and its headquarters at El Auja.
The agreement was to remain in force "until a peaceful settlement between the Parties is achieved" (Article XII).

Neither side could change the line by itself without breaking a signed agreement; neither side gave up its claims by signing; and the body set up to supervise the agreement was a commission on which the two parties had equal numbers and a UN officer held the chair.
Lebanon had entered the war by its own government's decision.
On 15 May 1948, the day after Israel declared independence, Lebanon joined Egypt, Syria, Jordan and Iraq in declaring war and invading the new state, fielding the smallest of the five Arab armies.
Israeli forces repelled the invasion and temporarily occupied part of southern Lebanon.
The decision to fight was not simply imposed on Lebanon from outside.

According to Makram Rabah, a historian at the American University of Beirut, the country's founding leaders, chiefly Riad al-Solh and Bechara el-Khoury, who had led it to independence from France in 1943, had debated and rejected an alliance with the Zionist movement before 1948, concluding that they could not keep relations with the neighbouring Arab states if they made one.

During the war an estimated 100,000–110,000 Palestinian Arabs, the large majority from northern Palestine, including the Acre area, fled or were displaced into Lebanon, a country of about 1.3 million people at the time.
The International Committee of the Red Cross, and from 1950 UNRWA, ran the camps that received them.
ents: The International Committee of the Red Cross

sent: The agreement with the Hashemite Jordan Kingdom was signed at Rhodes on 3 April 1949.
Colonel Ahmed Sudki El-Jundi and Lieutenant-Colonel Mohamed Maayte signed for Jordan; Reuven Shiloah and Lieutenant-Colonel Moshe Dayan signed for Israel.
Article II(2) repeats the reservation of the Egyptian text: no provision shall prejudice the rights, claims and positions of either party in the final settlement.
The first was Jerusalem.

Article VIII set up a Special Committee whose agreed agenda included free access to the Holy Places and cultural institutions, use of the cemetery on the Mount of Olives, the resumption of the institutions on Mount Scopus, and free movement on the Bethlehem road and the Latrun–Jerusalem road.

Whether it was carried out is another matter: according to Germany's Federal Agency for Civic Education, Jews were denied access to their holy sites in the eastern part of the city that Jordan held after the war.
The fate of the city at the United Nations is taken up in the section on Israel's admission and Jerusalem.
The second feature was the Iraqi front.
Iraq's army had fought in 1948 and held a sector of the line.
Under Article VI, Jordanian forces replaced the Iraqi forces on that front, and the Wadi Ara area passed to Israel.
How those guarantees fared under the regime later imposed on Arab citizens is a question for the section on military government.
The last agreement, with Syria, was signed on 20 July 1949 and completed the Rhodes armistice negotiations.

It was negotiated under a new regime: Syria's talks with Israel opened on 5 April 1949, days after Husni al-Za'im seized power in a coup, and the agreement turned the areas Syria evacuated into demilitarized zones that became the setting of two decades of clashes.
The next day, 21 July 1949, Bunche wrote to the Security Council.
He listed the four agreements by their UN document numbers: S/1264 (Egypt), S/1296 (Lebanon), S/1302 (Transjordan) and S/1353 (Syria).
He noted that the Transjordan agreement also covered the Iraqi front, so that separate negotiations between Iraq and Israel were unnecessary.
Bunche received the Nobel Peace Prize for 1950 and accepted it in Oslo on 10 December 1950.
Two Arab states that had taken part in the war signed nothing.
Iraq never signed an armistice with Israel; its front was handed over to Jordan under the Jordanian agreement, which Bunche judged sufficient.
Iraq's policies toward its own Jewish citizens in the same months, including the law of July 1948, are told in .
Saudi Arabia never signed either.

It did not launch a direct invasion in 1948; it sent a limited contingent of troops placed under Egyptian command, a modest commitment that the record attributes to its greater distance from Palestine.
Saudi Arabia never established diplomatic relations with Israel, and for decades it barred entry to anyone holding an Israeli passport or a passport with an Israeli stamp.
The Arab League's boycott of Israel was formalized in 1948 and barred member states from any direct economic relationship with Israel.

A secondary boycott, added in 1950, extended the ban to foreign companies doing business with Israel, and a tertiary boycott later targeted companies that did business with firms on the secondary list.
Saudi Arabia was among the boycott's most consistent participants and maintained it in some form for over seven decades.
The new lines enclosed far more territory than the United Nations had proposed for the Jewish state.
Israel's Foreign Ministry describes the territory inside the 1949 armistice demarcation lines as "about 78% of the Mandate area."
The same Foreign Ministry page states the limits of that territory as plainly as the treaties do.
The lines became known as the Green Line.
Jordan held the West Bank and Egypt the Gaza Strip, and Iraq and Saudi Arabia never signed agreements with Israel.
The texts of 1949 are the measure of what it did not change in law: by their own words, nothing in them settled where Israel's borders lay.
The year-by-year ledger of this period sets the armistices beside the other events of 1949: Israel's admission to the United Nations, the Lausanne conference and the creation of UNRWA.
The common belief that the Green Line was Israel's agreed border in 1949 does not survive a reading of the texts.
Article V of the Egyptian agreement and Article II(2) of the Jordanian one deny it in terms.

At Lausanne a few months later, Israel held that the 1947 partition plan had been nullified by the Arab invasion; the Arab delegations, for their part, wanted the 1947 lines and demanded that Israel first accept the return of the refugees.
Bunche's own description is more modest than either: a set of voluntary agreements amounting to non-aggression pacts, nothing more and nothing less.

The sources used here describe the Egyptian Mixed Armistice Commission in detail but not the commissions on the other fronts, and they do not give the commissions' rulings or the number of complaints they heard.

Whether the Special Committee for Jerusalem ever met to any effect on its agenda is not documented here either; the only evidence on that point is the report that access to the holy sites in the eastern city was denied.
The Mediator: Count Bernadotte's Two Plans, May–September 1948
The first outsider to try to turn the war's facts into a settlement was the United Nations' mediator.
Yet his last report outlived him, and two of its proposals reappeared in the General Assembly's Resolution 194 three months later.
Folke Bernadotte came to the post with a reputation made in the last months of the Second World War.
As head of the Swedish Red Cross he is credited with saving some 20,000 inmates of German concentration camps.
He was appointed United Nations mediator in Palestine on 20 May 1948.

The UN's own press release of 17 September 1948 records that he was chosen by the five permanent members of the Security Council, sitting as a committee of the General Assembly under a General Assembly resolution of 14 May 1948.
Encyclopaedia Britannica says more simply that the Security Council named him.
On the UN's account his mandate flowed from a General Assembly resolution, with the five permanent members acting as its committee.
On the shorter account it came from the Council.
The UN's own contemporary record is the more detailed of the two, but this book records both.
On 15 July the Security Council ordered a second truce, which was to last "until a peaceful adjustment of the future situation of Palestine is reached."
The second was ordered by the Council and had no end date at all: it was meant to hold until there was a settlement.
It was inside that open-ended truce that Bernadotte wrote his final report.
During the first truce, on 28 June 1948, Bernadotte presented the parties with a set of written suggestions at Rhodes.
The American government's published diplomatic record preserves their text.
They proposed that Palestine, including Transjordan, might form a union of "one Arab and one Jewish" member.
Within that union, the Negev, in whole or in part, would go to Arab territory, and Western Galilee, in whole or in part, to Jewish territory.
The City of Jerusalem would be included in Arab territory, with municipal autonomy for its Jewish community.
Two shared facilities would serve the whole union: a free port at Haifa, including the refineries and terminals, and a free airport at Lydda.

The Jewish side was asked to accept a union rather than an independent state with its own frontiers, and to see Jerusalem, with its Jewish community, placed in Arab territory with only municipal autonomy.
The Arab side was asked to accept a Jewish member of a joint union, with its own control of immigration.
The Progress Report of 16 September 1948.
The report Bernadotte completed in September, dated 16 September 1948, began from a premise the June suggestions had avoided: "A Jewish State called Israel exists in Palestine."
The union with Transjordan was gone.
In its place the report drew a territorial settlement between a recognized Jewish state and the Arab territory around it.
The Negev should be Arab territory and Galilee should be Jewish territory.
Ramleh and Lydda should be in Arab territory.
The precise frontiers would be set by a UN technical boundaries commission.
Jerusalem would no longer be placed in Arab territory; it would be under "effective United Nations control."
Haifa would be a free port and Lydda a free airport, as in June.
On the refugees, the report urged that Arab refugees be allowed to return to Jewish-controlled areas "at the earliest possible date," with adequate compensation for those choosing not to return.
It proposed a Palestine conciliation commission to carry the settlement forward.
And on the Arab territory, it saw "compelling reasons for merging the Arab territory of Palestine with the territory of Transjordan."
The idea of joining Arab Palestine to Transjordan survived from June, but now as a merger of the Arab part alone, not a union that took in the Jewish state as well.
The June suggestions treated Palestine and Transjordan as one framework to be divided into two members.

The September report accepted Israel as a state, gave it Galilee, assigned the Negev, Ramleh and Lydda to Arab territory, removed Jerusalem from either side's control, and turned the right of return "without restriction" into return "at the earliest possible date," paired for the first time with compensation as the alternative.
Bernadotte was killed in Jerusalem on 17 September 1948, the day after the report was dated, by members of the Stern Gang (Lehi).
A French air force colonel serving as a UN observer, André-Pierre Sérot, was killed with him.
The UN noted that the completed report reached Paris almost simultaneously with the news of his death.
The government's response to the killing, including the dissolution of Lehi and the amnesty that followed, belongs to .
The first was Washington.

Four days after the killing, on 21 September 1948, Secretary of State George Marshall endorsed the plan, including its award of the Negev to the Arab side, and the endorsement became an issue in an American presidential campaign; how President Truman then backed away from it is told in .
The second was the General Assembly.

Two of the report's central proposals, a conciliation commission and the return of refugees with compensation for those who chose not to return, reappeared in the Assembly's Resolution 194 of December 1948, whose full text and competing readings are set out in .
Britannica also credits Bernadotte's work with laying the groundwork for the UN Truce Supervision Organization and for UNRWA, the relief agency for Palestinian refugees.
The documents here establish what Bernadotte proposed, when, and that both sides rejected his first plan.
Nor do they settle the narrower question of which UN body appointed him; the UN's contemporary account and Britannica's summary differ, and both are recorded above.

A mediator who had begun by trying to fold the new state into a union with Transjordan ended by taking its existence as the starting point, and by proposing the refugees' return, with compensation as its alternative, in terms the General Assembly took up in Resolution 194.
The Constitution That Was Deferred, 1948–1950
The armistices left Israel's borders unsettled.
Most readers assume that Israel, like most democracies, has a written constitution.
The Declaration of Independence of May 1948 committed the new state to a constitution "adopted by the Elected Constituent Assembly not later than the 1st October 1948."
Two days later it renamed itself the Knesset.
The body elected to draft the founding charter thus became the First Knesset, the state's ordinary legislature, and the constitution became one item on its agenda among many.
The man most responsible for what followed was David Ben-Gurion, the prime minister.
He opposed a written constitution, and the account by Michael Dickerman gives two reasons.

The second was a fear that a fight over religion, which a constitution would force into the open, would deepen the divide between religious and secular Israelis while the conflict with the Arab states was still unresolved.
On 13 June 1950 the Knesset adopted a compromise moved by Yizhar Harari of the Progressive Party, known since as the Harari Resolution.

The First Knesset, in the summary of a later account, deadlocked over what the constitution would contain, above all over the place of religion in public life, and chose to enact Basic Laws one at a time instead.

All members of the Knesset are elected in a single nationwide district by proportional representation, so that the whole country forms one constituency and parties win seats in proportion to their share of the vote; under today's rules a party must clear a threshold of 3.25% to win any seats.
Israel's president is elected by the Knesset, not by the public, and under the present rules serves a single, non-renewable term of seven years.
The office's formal powers are limited to granting pardons, tasking a member of the Knesset with forming a government, and representing the country abroad.
If that member fails, the president may task another, or the Knesset can name a candidate with a 21-day window if 61 members support it; if every attempt fails, the country goes to new elections.
The first Basic Law, on the Knesset itself and its elections, was not passed until 1958.

Others followed: on the military and its subordination to civilian government in 1968, on Jerusalem as the united capital in 1980, on human dignity and liberty in 1992, a partial bill of rights that the Supreme Court later used to justify judicial review, and in 2018 on Israel as the nation-state of the Jewish people, which enshrined Jewish self-determination as a national right without parallel language for Arab citizens.
As the sources used here count them, there are 14 Basic Laws, covering the Knesset, the government, the military, the judiciary, land, Jerusalem and civil rights.

The Supreme Court treats them as having constitutional weight, but most can be amended by a simple majority of the Knesset; only a few clauses are entrenched, Freedom of Occupation and the Knesset's electoral clause needing 61 of the 120 members and the Referendum law requiring 80 members or a referendum before territory under Israeli law is given up, unlike the United States Constitution, which needs two-thirds of Congress and three-quarters of the states, or Germany's Basic Law, some provisions of which cannot be amended at all.
The Nation-State Law passed by 62 votes to 55; the 2023 law on the "reasonableness" standard passed 64 to 0 because the opposition walked out.

The coalition arithmetic described above produced five national elections between April 2019 and November 2022 , and in July 2023 the Biden administration invited President Isaac Herzog, rather than Prime Minister Netanyahu, to address a joint session of Congress and visit the White House, a choice TIME described as honouring "a largely ceremonial role with no executive authority" in place of "the man who runs the country."
Dickerman's account gives Ben-Gurion two reasons: fear of deepening the religious–secular divide in wartime, and reluctance to bind the government by courts.

Nor does it settle how much of Israel's later instability belongs to the structure set up in these years and how much to the choices of individual leaders; political scientists contest that attribution, and this book treats the structure as a documented contributor, not a sole cause.
The Jews of the Arab World After 1948
About 700,000 Palestinians were displaced and not allowed to return.

In the years that followed, the large Jewish communities of Iraq, Yemen, Libya, Egypt, Syria and North Africa shrank dramatically, through emigration, pressure, expulsion and state persecution in proportions that varied from country to country.
Estimates of the total who left Arab countries and Iran between 1948 and the 1970s commonly fall in the range of 800,000 to 900,000 people.
The historian Philip Mendes counts nearly one million Jews, Mizrahim, who left Arab countries in the decade or so after 1947–48, most of them for Israel.
The governments that lost the war were discredited, as armies and publics blamed their rulers: Syria's government fell to a military coup in March 1949, Egypt's monarchy in 1952, and Iraq's in 1958.
For the Jewish communities living under those governments, the years after 1948 were the years in which a long presence came to an end.
Iraq.
Iraq's Jewish community was a community of some 2,800 years' standing.
After the United Nations voted for partition in November 1947, anti-Jewish measures in Iraq escalated, and pogroms gave way to systematic confiscation of property and trumped-up prosecutions.
On 15 May 1948, the day after Israel declared independence, Iraq joined the invasion.

When the fighting ended, Iraq refused to sign an armistice with Israel; Israeli government sources describe it as the only Arab combatant to refuse, leaving a formal state of war that, by their account, has technically never ended.
Saudi Arabia, whose limited contingent had fought under Egyptian command, signed no armistice either.
On 19 July 1948 Iraq made "Zionism" a crime punishable by up to seven years in prison.
Since every Jew was presumed to be a Zionist, the law worked as a criminalization of the whole community.
The testimony of two Muslim witnesses was enough to convict, and there was little avenue for appeal.
On 23 September 1948 Shafiq Ades, a prominent and well-connected Jewish businessman, was hanged in public in Basra on charges of selling weapons to Israel and to the Iraqi Communist Party.
In March 1950 Iraq passed a law allowing Jews to emigrate if they renounced their citizenship.
In practice it worked as a mechanism to strip Jewish citizens of nationality and then of property once they had registered: those who signed up were denaturalized and their assets taken.
Israel and the Near East Transport Company flew the community out, first by way of Cyprus and later on direct flights from Baghdad to Lod.

The airlift, named Operation Ezra and Nehemiah after the biblical leaders of the return from Babylonian exile, was largely funded by the American Jewish Joint Distribution Committee, at a cost of about $4 million.
By 1952, according to Israeli government sources, a community of roughly 135,000 had been reduced to about 6,000.

Other sources count differently: the Jewish Agency gives 121,512 of Iraq's 130,000 Jews as arriving in Israel, and a table drawn from the Israel State Archives gives 124,226 immigrants from Iraq between 1948 and the end of 1952.

Between April 1950 and June 1951, during exactly the months when the denaturalization law was driving mass registration, at least five bombing incidents struck Jewish institutions and gathering points in Baghdad, including the Masuda Shemtov synagogue.
At least four Jews were killed and others were injured.
The Iraqi government of the time, and later some historians, attributed them to Zionist underground agents trying to panic the community into leaving faster.

Israeli officials have consistently and firmly denied any involvement, calling the accusation an antisemitic fabrication meant to shift the blame for a persecution the Iraqi state had itself created through pogroms, denaturalization and criminalization.
Iraq tried and executed men for the bombings: two, Basri and Shalom, were hanged in January 1952.
The fairness of those trials, held amid intense anti-Zionist fervour, and the evidence on which they rested are themselves disputed.

Independent historical work, drawing on newly released Israeli, British and American archives as reviewed by the Middle East Forum, finds insufficient evidence to confirm Israeli involvement, without fully closing the question.
Both the Iraqi government's accusation and Israel's denial are documented positions, and the evidence does not decide between them.

What is not in dispute is the legal sequence that preceded them: the 1948 law that made the community presumptively criminal, the hanging of Ades, and the 1950 law that turned emigration into the loss of citizenship and property.
Yemen.
The Jews of Yemen had lived there for well over a thousand years, one of the oldest Jewish communities in the world.
Between June 1949 and September 1950, Operation Magic Carpet, also called "On Wings of Eagles", airlifted about 49,000 of them to Israel.
It was organized with the American Jewish Joint Distribution Committee and flown by Alaska Airlines and other carriers.
Many reached the airlift only after walking for weeks to the British colony of Aden.
The Jewish Agency says that nearly all of Yemen's 45,000 Jews came, and the State Archives table gives 48,375 immigrants from Yemen and Aden together between 1948 and 1952.
In Israel many of the newcomers were placed in transit camps, where hundreds of children were reported dead or vanished, the subject of .
Morocco.
Morocco's Jewish community was rooted over two millennia and numbered in the hundreds of thousands in the 1940s, one of the largest in the Arab world.
On 7 and 8 June 1948, three weeks after Israel's founding, riots against Jews broke out in Oujda and Jérada, killing 5 Jews in Oujda and 38 people in Jérada, with more than a hundred wounded.
According to the record compiled by JewishGen, the riots are linked to young Jews crossing the border near Oujda on their way to France and Israel.
Most of the community emigrated after 1948, mostly to Israel.

The largest single movement came later and lies outside this chapter: between 1961 and 1964 the secret Operation Yachin brought about 97,000 Moroccan Jews to Israel with the Moroccan government's quiet consent, and historians record that Israel, together with American Jewish organizations, made payments to that government to allow the departures.

Israelis of Moroccan descent became one of Israel's largest communities, and a human link between the two countries long before Morocco and Israel opened liaison offices in 1994, after Oslo, and closed them in 2000 during the second intifada.
Egypt.
Egypt's Jewish population was about 75,000 in 1948.

Between June and November of that year, bombs set off in the Jewish quarter of Cairo killed more than 70 Jews and wounded nearly 200, according to the historian Howard Sachar as cited by the Jewish Virtual Library.
The State Archives table counts 17,114 immigrants from Egypt to Israel between 1948 and 1952, a much smaller share of the community than left Iraq or Yemen in those years.
Mendes notes that many Egyptian Jews appear to have left for economic reasons rather than because of specific persecution.
After the Sinai campaign of 1956 the Egyptian government expelled almost 25,000 Jews and confiscated their property, and about 1,000 more were detained.

A proclamation read in mosques on 23 November 1956 declared that "all Jews are Zionists and enemies of the state", according to contemporary reports by the Associated Press and the New York World-Telegram cited by the Jewish Virtual Library.
Libya.
The Jewish Agency records that 30,500 of Libya's 35,000 Jews came to Israel in the first years of the state; the State Archives table gives 32,129 immigrants from Libya between 1948 and 1952.
One, which he associates with Zionist and Israeli accounts, attributes the exodus almost solely to Arab violence or the threat of it.
The other, which he associates with Arab and anti-Zionist accounts, attributes it to Zionist activity and agitation, in its strongest form "a malicious Zionist conspiracy".

The first can cite the Iraqi law of July 1948, the hanging of Ades, the denaturalization and confiscation of 1950, the dead of Oujda, Jérada and the Cairo Jewish quarter, and the Egyptian expulsions and mosque proclamation of 1956.
The second can cite the Iraqi government's accusation over the Baghdad bombings, which independent historians have not been able to confirm but have not fully closed either.

Mendes's own conclusion is the third answer: the exodus is best explained as "a complex combination of push and pull factors", with harassment, discrimination and, in Iraq, expulsion on one side, and the pull of Zionism and of life in Israel on the other.
In Iraq the state criminalized and then denaturalized a community; in Yemen people walked for weeks to reach an airlift; in Egypt, before 1956, many appear to have left for economic reasons.

The antisemitism in this record is named here because it is documented: a law that presumed every Jew a criminal, a public hanging staged as a warning, bombs in a Jewish quarter, a state proclamation that all Jews were enemies.
They do not describe Arabs or Muslims as peoples, and the same record shows Jewish communities that had lived among their neighbors for one, two and nearly three thousand years.
The bombers of Baghdad have not been identified beyond dispute.

The totals differ from source to source, for Iraq (about 135,000 reduced to about 6,000; 121,512 of 130,000; 124,226), for Yemen (about 49,000; nearly all of 45,000; 48,375 with Aden) and for the region as a whole (800,000 to 900,000 across three decades including Iran; nearly one million in about a decade), and no one figure can be preferred on the evidence given here.
How the newcomers were received in Israel is the subject of .
Paying for the New State, 1949–1953
While the American organization was reorganizing itself, the state it supported had bills to pay.

The money for that effort came from three outside channels that opened in quick succession: loans and grants from the United States government, bonds sold to buyers abroad, and reparations from West Germany.
Each worked differently, each was paid for by different people, and one of them divided Israel's own public.
A common assumption is that American military support flowed to Israel from the beginning.
The documents of the period show something else: American help in these years was economic, modest and uneven, and the largest single agreement of the early 1950s was made with West Germany.
The first channel was the American government.
After Truman's re-election an Export-Import Bank loan of $100 million was earmarked for Israel, a decision placed in its political sequence in .

The Congressional Research Service's table of US aid to Israel, compiled by the Jewish Virtual Library, records the year-by-year sums in millions of dollars: 100.0 in 1949, from the Export-Import Bank and other sources; nothing in 1950; 35.1 in 1951; 86.4 in 1952; 73.6 in 1953; 74.7 in 1954; 52.7 in 1955; 50.8 in 1956; 40.9 in 1957; 85.4 in 1958; and 53.3 in 1959, the last including a first military loan of 0.4.
From Israel's founding through the early 1960s, US assistance was economic aid and loans only.
According to one study of the aid relationship, Washington avoided direct arms sales because it did not want to alienate the Arab oil-producing states.

Among the American-dollar flows in the record from 1921 to 1949, the $100 million loan of 1949 is the largest single sum, double the $50 million of Golda Meyerson's 1948 American tour and a thousand times the $100,000 that Abraham Feinberg and Ed Kaufmann provided for Truman's whistle-stop campaign, as the chart in the section on Truman shows.
When American military aid began is a point on which the sources differ, and both versions should be stated.
The CRS table shows a military loan of $0.4 million in 1959.
The study of the aid relationship cited above dates the first US military aid, itself in the form of loans rather than grants, to 1962.
Congress first designated a dedicated earmark for Israel in 1971.
The 1973 war was the turning point: President Nixon ordered an emergency military airlift and requested $2.2 billion in emergency aid, a rise of roughly 800 percent over prior annual levels.

Economic aid became all grants in 1981, and military aid in 1985, the year of a separate $1.5 billion supplemental economic package, the largest aid package for a single country since the Vietnam War era.

The often-quoted cumulative total of $300 billion is the Council on Foreign Relations' inflation-adjusted estimate; the Congressional Research Service, in its most recent tally, using the same appropriations data without adjusting for inflation, places cumulative bilateral assistance and missile defense funding at about $174 billion.
According to the Jewish Virtual Library's history of the program, David Ben-Gurion conceived an overseas bond issue in 1950, amid economic crisis and mass immigration.
In September 1950 he convened American Jewish leaders at the King David Hotel in Jerusalem, and sales were launched in the United States the following spring with a rally at Madison Square Garden.

Within six years, the same source reports, bond sales accounted for 35% of Israel's special development budget, financing the National Water Carrier, the Dead Sea Works, power plants, ports and immigrant towns.
The 1951 issue paid its buyers interest rather than asking for a gift, it was sold in the United States, and its proceeds went to the state's special development budget and the projects named above.
On 12 March 1951 Moshe Sharett presented a claim of $1.5 billion against Germany.
It was calculated as the cost of absorbing 500,000 victims of the Nazis at $3,000 each.
On 9 January 1952 the Knesset voted 61–50 to negotiate directly with West Germany, while thousands demonstrated outside and police used tear gas.
The opposition was led by Menachem Begin, who spoke at mass demonstrations in the spring of 1952.
The dispute was not between Israel and its adversaries but within Israel.
The case for the agreement, in the government's own terms, was that the new state was bearing the cost of absorbing hundreds of thousands of the Nazis' victims and that Germany should meet it.
The narrow vote, 61 to 50, shows how evenly the Knesset was divided.
The agreement was signed in Luxembourg on 10 September 1952 by Sharett, Nahum Goldmann and Konrad Adenauer, and took effect on 21 March 1953.
They came not as cash transfers but in kind: 30% for crude oil bought in Britain and 70% for German goods.
Over the decade they made up 12–14% of Israel's annual imports.

The Jewish Virtual Library, citing Israeli Foreign Ministry documents of 1953 and the Encyclopaedia Judaica, gives a total of $845 million, of which $100 million went to the Claims Conference, paid over 14 years from 1953 to 1966.
The National Library of Israel gives goods and services valued at 3.5 billion marks over 12 years, plus 450 million marks more.
The American government lent and granted modest sums, without arms, for reasons tied to its relations with Arab oil producers.
West Germany paid in oil and goods, over the objections of a large part of Israel's own public.

What the record cited here does not settle is the whole: it gives no single account of the state's budget in these years, no measure of how much of the cost of absorption fell on Israel's own taxpayers and on the immigrants themselves, and no agreed figure for the largest of the three transfers.
The month the first bonds were sold, and the reason the two sources date the first American military loan three years apart, also remain open.
Most of the Jews who left Iraq, Yemen and Libya came to Israel, and they arrived in a state already absorbing survivors from Europe.
In its first three and a half years the new state took in more Jewish immigrants than its entire Jewish population at independence.

According to the Jewish Agency, 203,000 Jews from 42 countries arrived in Israel's first year alone, and 684,201 immigrants arrived between May 1948 and the end of 1951, "more than the entire Jewish population when independence was declared".
This section sets out who came, in what order, how they were housed and fed, and when the flow slowed.

According to the Jewish Agency, the first to come were the former illegal immigrants whom the British had held in detention camps on Cyprus, and Holocaust survivors from the displaced-persons camps in Germany, Austria and Italy.
The Jewish Agency records 121,512 of Iraq's 130,000 Jews, more than 37,000 of Bulgaria's 45,000, 30,500 of Libya's 35,000, and nearly all of Yemen's 45,000.
Why the communities of the Arab world left when they did is told in .
A table drawn from the Israel State Archives gives a fuller count, through the end of 1952.
Of these, 377,251 came from Muslim countries and 307,082 from Communist states.
Of the countries it names, the largest were Iraq, with 124,226, and Romania, with 121,537, followed by Poland, with 106,751.

From the Muslim countries the table lists Iraq; Yemen and Aden, 48,375; Tunisia, Morocco and Algeria together, 52,584; Turkey, 35,025; Syria and Lebanon, 34,608; Libya, 32,129; Iran, 25,593; and Egypt, 17,114.
For Iraq, the Jewish Agency's 121,512 sits beside the State Archives' 124,226, and Israeli government sources describe the community as reduced from about 135,000 to roughly 6,000 by 1952.

For Yemen, the Jewish Agency's "nearly all of Yemen's 45,000" sits beside the archive figure of 48,375 for Yemen and Aden together, and the commonly cited count of about 49,000 flown out in Operation Magic Carpet.

Part of the difference is in the categories (Yemen alone, or Yemen with Aden; arrivals counted by year of immigration, or by community before and after), and part cannot be explained from the sources given here.
In 1950 the state introduced a second kind of settlement, the ma'abara, or transitional camp, where newcomers could work while they waited for permanent homes.
The ma'abarot multiplied fast.
Jews arriving from Arab and Muslim countries were often placed in these camps and, according to the Times of Israel, largely sidelined by the European-born leadership of the ruling Labor party.
In the Knesset election of 1951, the General Zionists, who campaigned against rationing, won 20 seats.
Who paid for the absorption and the state around it, through American aid, the sale of bonds and German reparations, is told in .
One is that the immigration of these years came mainly from Europe.
Survivors from the displaced-persons camps came first, but by the end of 1952 more immigrants had come from Muslim countries, 377,251, than from the Communist states, 307,082.
What these sources do not settle is how the burdens of absorption were shared among the newcomers: who was sent to the ma'abarot and who to permanent housing, for how long, and on what criteria.
Who Belongs: The Law of Return and the Nationality Law
While the camps filled, the Knesset wrote down who had the right to come.
The Law of Return of 1950 said who had the right to come.
The Nationality Law of 1952 said who became a national, and how.

Read together, they set up two routes into citizenship, one for Jews from anywhere and one for the Arabs who had lived in Palestine and remained, and the conditions on the two routes were not the same.
Section 1 states: "Every Jew has the right to come to this country as an oleh", that is, as an immigrant who comes to settle.
Section 2 makes the right operational.

Every Jew who wishes to settle in Israel receives an oleh's visa, unless the minister finds that the applicant is acting against the Jewish people, or is likely to endanger public health or the security of the state.
Section 4 closes the circle backward: Jews already in the country, and Jews born there, are deemed to have come as olim.
The law was signed by Prime Minister David Ben-Gurion, by the Minister of Immigration, Moshe Shapira, and by Yosef Sprinzak as Acting President and Chairman of the Knesset.

The law itself is dated 20 Tammuz 5710, which is 5 July 1950, and the Encyclopedia of the Modern Middle East gives the same day; the Palestinian jurist Anis Kassim says the bills were submitted on 3 July and the law adopted on 5 July.
The Encyclopaedia Judaica gives 3 July 1950, the anniversary of Herzl's death.
Kassim's account, in which the bills were submitted on 3 July, would explain how the earlier date arose, but none of the sources says so directly, and the discrepancy stands.
Ben-Gurion's case for the law was stated in its own terms when he presented the bill.
The right it recognized, he said, "is inherent in every Jew by virtue of his being a Jew", and "This right preceded the State of Israel".
The Encyclopaedia Judaica places it in a line of documents running back half a century: the Basel Program of 1897, Article 6 of the Mandate of 1922, and the Declaration of Independence.

A definition of who was a Jew entered the law only twenty years later, when an amendment in 1970 extended the law's rights to a Jew's child and grandchild and to their spouses, and defined a Jew as one "born of a Jewish mother or has become converted to Judaism and who is not a member of another religion".
That amendment, and the long dispute over "who is a Jew" that produced it, belong to a later volume.
The first was nationality "by return": every oleh under the Law of Return became an Israeli national by that fact alone.
The second was nationality "by residence", for former Palestinian citizens.

They could become nationals only if they met three conditions together: that they had been registered as inhabitants on 1 March 1952; that they were inhabitants on the day the law took effect; and that they had been in Israel continuously from the establishment of the state, or had entered it legally in the meantime.
The same law repealed the Palestinian Citizenship Orders retroactively to the day the state was established.
A Jew came into nationality by coming; the only bars were the minister's grounds for refusal.
A former Palestinian citizen came into it only by passing a test of registration and continuous presence.
And because the Mandate's citizenship had been repealed retroactively, those who failed it were left, in Kassim's argument, without a nationality at all.
How the Arabs who remained were governed in the same years is told in .
The case against the law is made here by Kassim.

In his reading, the Law of Return amounts to "legally-authorized racial discrimination": it grants Jews from anywhere what it denies to Palestinians who lived on the land, so that "an indigenous Palestinian has no such inherent right even if he used to live on the land".
He argues that the Palestinians who stayed were left stateless for about thirty years.
To Ben-Gurion and the Encyclopaedia Judaica, the law was one of return, recognizing a right older than the state.
To Kassim it was one of discrimination, granting to Jews from anywhere what it denied to Palestinians who had lived there.
The word "return" itself carries the dispute, because the same word stands at the center of the United Nations' resolution on the Palestinian refugees, read in .
The debate was not only between Jews and Palestinians.
Within Jewish life the law drew argument from several directions.

According to the Encyclopedia of the Modern Middle East, some Orthodox leaders wanted the definition of "Jew" narrowed; the Reform and Conservative movements opposed that; and some non-Zionists called for the law's repeal as discriminatory.
It does not give the number of Arab inhabitants who met the residence test in 1952, or the number who failed it.
Kassim's figure of about thirty years of statelessness is his own, and the sources cited here do not show how many people it describes or how their status was later resolved.
And the date on which the Knesset passed the Law of Return, 3 or 5 July 1950, remains in conflict between the law's own text and the Encyclopaedia Judaica.
The Arabs Who Stayed, and the Military Government
On the other side of the lines, not every Palestinian Arab inside the territory Israel held in 1949 had left.
According to Israel's Central Bureau of Statistics, as compiled by the Jewish Virtual Library, the state's population at the end of 1948 was 716,700 Jews and 156,000 non-Jews.
By 1950 it was 1,203,000 Jews and 167,100 non-Jews.
For the next eighteen years most of the Arabs who remained lived under a separate regime that applied to them as one category of citizens.
It is often said that the Arab citizens of Israel have enjoyed equal civil rights since 1948.
In the first Knesset election, in 1949, the Democratic List of Nazareth, an Arab party described as a satellite list of Mapai, won 7,387 votes, 1.7 percent of the total, and 2 seats.
Arab citizens could vote and stand for parliament.
The terms on which former Palestinian citizens became Israeli nationals, including the residence test of the 1952 Nationality Law, are told in .

The historian Alina Korn dates its official establishment to October 1948, with five military governors, and notes that when the fighting ended the regime was "neither cancelled nor was it legally regularized."
Its legal tools were mostly British.
The Defense (Emergency) Regulations of 1945, issued by the Mandate government, were absorbed into Israeli law by Article 11 of the Law and Administration Ordinance of 1948.

The Arab citizen could apply for a permit but could not compel one.
According to Korn, the travel-permit requirement had no legal foundation at all for its first 18 months, until January 1950.
In 1958, Korn reports, only one in three Arabs in the areas under military government held a travel permit.

Korn reports that between 1948 and 1967 about a third of all convictions of Arab citizens were for violations of the Defense Regulations, and that about 95 percent of these were administrative offenses, such as lacking a permit.
In 1955, 2,714 of the 2,888 people convicted under the regulations were Arab.
In practice, more than nine in ten of those convicted under them that year were Arab citizens.
Israel had signed armistices with its neighbors, not peace treaties.
The Rattner Commission, which reviewed the regime in February 1956, concluded that it should not end until "true peace" existed.
Korn argues that the regime's main purposes were different: to control the movement of Arab residents and to prevent their access to land that had been confiscated.

Both readings rest on documented material: the security rationale on the government's own statements and the Rattner Commission's finding, the control reading on the conviction figures and the regime's link to the land.
The regime's worst single event came on 29 October 1956, the eve of the Sinai War.
Brigadier Issachar Shadmi moved up a dusk curfew on villages near the Jordanian border, without adequate notice to the villagers.
When Major Shmuel Malinki asked how to treat villagers returning from work who did not know of it, Shadmi's reply, according to the court record, was that anyone who left his house would be shot.
The Border Police unit at Kafr Qasim, about a kilometre from the Green Line, did not.
Shadmi, tried separately, was fined one-hundredth of an Israeli lira, a sum Palestinian citizens remember as "Shadmi's penny."
The same trial established the doctrine that a soldier must refuse a "manifestly illegal" order, one over which "a black flag flies," a standard the Israeli army still teaches.
The Sinai War that began that week, and Egypt's part in it, belong to a later volume.
The Knesset eased it in 1962 and rejected bills to abolish it in 1963.

Six months later, on 4 April 1967, the Prime Minister's adviser on Arab affairs, Shmuel Toledano, wrote to Levi Eshkol that "in practice, hardly any restrictions have been loosened," since closed areas and travel passes remained.

Some accounts draw a further conclusion: that before Israel governed a single Palestinian in the West Bank or Gaza, it had already run an eighteen-year separate administration for Palestinian citizens inside its own borders, and that the occupation after 1967 inherited a model rather than inventing one.
They do not give a source-backed count of Israeli casualties from cross-border attacks in these years, a figure that would bear directly on the weight of the security case.

What they do establish is the structure: a population with the vote, held for eighteen years under British emergency law, through a permit system that for its first eighteen months had no legal basis at all.
Truman's discomfort in the summer of 1948 had two objects, territory and refugees.
On the second, the question most often asked about the Palestinian refugees of 1948 is why they did not go home when the fighting stopped.
The first was a decision taken by Israel's government in the middle of the war, and the facts that grew up around it.
The decision is known through the research of the historian Benny Morris.
As Arthur Hertzberg summarized Morris's research in 1988, Israel's cabinet decided on 16 June 1948 that "there could be no return during the war," leaving the question to be reconsidered later.

It fell during the first truce, twelve days before the UN mediator, Count Bernadotte, proposed at Rhodes that displaced people be allowed "to return to their homes without restriction and to regain possession of their property."
Israel's government had decided against return during the war before the international proposal for return was put on the table.

Hertzberg, summarizing Morris, wrote that from the summer of 1948 abandoned houses and property were quickly occupied by Jews, and that by the time of the 1949 armistices Israel was both unwilling and unable to allow substantial return.
The legal machinery that converted this occupation into state ownership, from the Custodian of Abandoned Property to the Absentees' Property Law of 1950, is set out in .
Morris's research also bore on the older and more charged question of how the refugees came to leave.
According to Hertzberg's account, Morris found no formal decision to expel taken by the highest leaders, while the authority of commanders in the field shaped what happened.
Morris's own finding contains both: no order from the top, and a war in which those on the ground had wide latitude.
Israel called them infiltrators.
The most detailed study is Morris's Israel's Border Wars.
As Avi Shlaim reported in his review of it in 1994, Morris estimated that "90 per cent or more" of the infiltrations of 1949–56 were driven by economic and social concerns rather than political aims:
Morris estimated that between 2,700 and 5,000 infiltrators were killed in 1949–56, "the great majority of them unarmed."
Israel's army, border guard and police adopted a policy of shooting suspects on sight.
The 90 percent is Morris's judgment of motive across thousands of crossings, not a count.
Both come to this book through Shlaim's review, not from Morris's text directly.
Retaliation and Qibya.
Israel answered cross-border attacks with retaliation across the line.
One instance came in October 1953 at Qibya.
Unit 101, under Ariel Sharon, blew up 45 houses and killed 69 Jordanian villagers, "the majority of them women and children."
Israel's leadership was divided over this policy.
Morris divided them into "activists," led by David Ben-Gurion and including Dayan and Lavon, and "moderates," led by Moshe Sharett.
Shlaim, reviewing the book, faulted Morris for underplaying Sharett's secret contacts with Nasser.
The Israeli case rests above all on what the border became by 1955.
The Jewish Virtual Library, presenting the Israeli account, records that on 31 August 1955 Nasser announced that Egypt would dispatch "her heroes" to Israel's borders.
It describes the fedayeen as fighters trained and equipped by Egyptian intelligence to carry out attacks inside Israel, in breach of the armistice agreements' ban on paramilitary hostilities.
On this account, whatever most crossings had been in 1949, by 1955 a hostile state was organizing armed attacks across the line, which Israel answered with retaliation.
The first reading, Morris's, holds that the crossings were overwhelmingly economic and social, the movement of refugees toward homes, crops and relatives, and that most of those killed were unarmed.

The second reading, presented by the Jewish Virtual Library, holds that the border was a security threat that, by 1955, included fedayeen organized by a hostile government's intelligence service, which Israel answered with retaliation.
Its strongest evidence is Nasser's own public announcement and the fact that the attacks breached signed agreements.
Morris's estimate covers the whole period of 1949–56; the fedayeen belong chiefly to its last two years.
On 29 October 1956, the eve of the Sinai war, a Border Police unit enforcing a curfew killed 49 Arab citizens of Israel returning home to Kafr Qasim, a village about a kilometre from the Green Line.

The cabinet decision of 16 June 1948 is known here through Hertzberg's summary of Morris, not from the cabinet record itself, and it is described as deferring the question, not closing it; the sources here do not say when, or whether, the government formally reconsidered it.
And the number of Israelis, civilian and military, killed in cross-border attacks between 1949 and 1956 is not established in the sources gathered.
Syria in 1949: The Offer, the Coups and the Demilitarized Zones
The last of the four armistices was negotiated with a Syrian ruler who had seized power days before the talks opened.
A familiar account holds that Syria rejected every chance at peace with Israel from 1948 onward.
For a few months that year Syria's ruler offered Israel a peace treaty, a meeting at the highest level, and the resettlement of a large share of the Palestinian refugees inside Syria.

Israel's prime minister declined, the ruler was overthrown and executed, and the armistice frontier the two states left behind, the border for the next 18 years, became the setting of two decades of clashes.
Syria's army had entered the war in May 1948 and fought on the northern front.
When the fighting stopped, Syrian forces held small areas west of the international border.
On 30 March 1949 Syria's elected government was overthrown by an army officer, Husni al-Za'im, in the first of three coups that year.
Declassified records and historians document contacts between US officials and Za'im before the coup; how far the United States directed it is debated.
Armistice talks between Syria and Israel opened on 5 April 1949.

In the course of them, Za'im offered a peace treaty and military cooperation, proposed a meeting with Ben-Gurion or with Moshe Sharett, and offered to resettle 250,000–300,000 Palestinian refugees in Syria.
The border he proposed would have run through the middle of Lake Hula and the Sea of Galilee.
The offer is documented in Israeli archives and by historians.

Its scale is clearest against the numbers at Lausanne a few months later, where Israel offered to take back 100,000 refugees as part of a final peace: Za'im was offering to absorb two and a half to three times as many himself.
Ben-Gurion was unwilling to stake policy on him, in part from distrust of Za'im's ties to Washington.

A wider argument for caution can be built from documented facts: Za'im had seized power by force less than a week before the talks opened, his contacts with American officials before the coup are on the record, and the border he asked for ran through the middle of both lakes.

The offer included a treaty, a summit and a resettlement figure larger than anything Israel itself put forward on refugees that year, and it addressed, for a large number of refugees, the question on which the Lausanne conference failed.
In August 1949 Za'im was deposed and executed in Syria's second coup of the year, and the offer died with him.
The armistice had already been signed on 20 July 1949, the last of the four agreements negotiated under Ralph Bunche.
Under its terms, the areas Syria evacuated west of the international border became demilitarized zones.

In a meeting in 1953–54, recorded by the State Department, Moshe Dayan told American officials that Israel claimed sovereignty over Jewish-owned lands inside the zones, that "someone must keep the area alive," and that Israel did not want Syria to have direct access to the Jordan River.
Syrian forces fired from the heights on Israeli farmers and fishermen.
Israel sent armoured tractors to cultivate disputed land in the zones and carried out reprisal raids.
The map traces the line from Za'im's offer forward.

In the 1960s the dispute turned to water: Israel built its National Water Carrier, the Arab League backed a plan in 1964 to divert the headwaters of the Jordan, and Israeli strikes hit the diversion works between 1965 and 1967.
And in an interview given in 1976 and published in 1997, Dayan said that at least 80 percent of the clashes had been provoked by Israel, which sent tractors into the zones until the Syrians fired.
That account is his own, given long after the events; others contest it, and it does not cancel the documented Syrian fire on farmers and fishermen.
It does show that the familiar picture of clashes caused entirely by shelling from the Golan is incomplete.
Syria's three coups of 1949 opened a decade in which the region's old order gave way.
Egypt's Free Officers, the movement Nasser led, overthrew King Farouk in July 1952.
In August 1953 the CIA and MI6 removed Iran's elected prime minister.
After Egypt nationalized the Suez Canal in 1956, Britain, France and Israel invaded, and US and Soviet pressure forced them to withdraw.
Iraq's monarchy was overthrown on 14 July 1958.
By the end of the decade, military or royal autocrats, Cold War alignments and outside intervention had become the pattern of the region's politics.
The record ties that pattern to the coups of named officers and, in Iran, to the CIA and MI6, not to local culture or religion alone.
Za'im's coup was the first of the decade.
