Admission to the United Nations and the Question of Jerusalem, 1949–1950
The General Assembly voted on Israel's membership while the Lausanne talks were still in session.
In the year after the war Israel sought two kinds of acceptance: recognition by other states, and membership of the United Nations.

The terms on which it won the second, and the argument over Jerusalem that followed within the year, show how much of the 1947 plan the new state's admission left formally in place, and how little of it was carried out.
Recognition came from an unexpected direction in March 1949, when Turkey established diplomatic relations with Israel, the first Muslim-majority state to do so.
The relationship that grew from it, including a secret intelligence pact with Israel and Iran in 1958 and military-cooperation agreements in 1996, belongs to later volumes and is followed in .
In 1949 its significance was simpler: a Muslim-majority state had recognized Israel.
Membership was a harder question, because the United Nations had already set out terms for the territory in two resolutions.
Before voting, the General Assembly's Ad Hoc Political Committee met on 6 May 1949 to take up Israel's attitude to Resolution 181 of November 1947 and Resolution 194 of December 1948.

It named three issues: the internationalization of Jerusalem, the repatriation of the refugees, and the investigation of the assassination of Count Bernadotte and Colonel Sérot, the UN mediator and the French officer serving as a UN observer who was killed with him in September 1948.
Egypt had opposed inviting Israel's representative to explain.

Alongside it, the Holy See ran a diplomatic campaign at the United Nations to make Israel's admission conditional on two commitments: allowing the return of the Palestinian refugees, and formal guarantees protecting Christian and Muslim holy sites, particularly in Jerusalem.
In that context Ben-Gurion is documented as saying in 1949: "There is a major religion in the world, which has to settle with us a historical reckoning."
The Vatican's position had a long history.

In January 1904 Theodor Herzl had sought Pope Pius X's support for a Jewish homeland in Palestine and been refused, on the ground that the Church could not support the restoration of the Jews to a land central to its own theology while they denied Christ.
That refusal held as official Vatican policy for 89 years.
On 11 May 1949 the General Assembly adopted Resolution 273 (III), admitting Israel to membership of the United Nations, by 37 votes to 12, with 9 abstentions.
It noted Israel's declaration that it "unreservedly accepts the obligations of the United Nations Charter."
It recalled the resolutions of 29 November 1947 and 11 December 1948, the partition resolution and Resolution 194.
And it took note of "the declarations and explanations made by the representative of the Government of Israel" before the Ad Hoc Political Committee.
Israel was admitted without the guarantees the Vatican had sought, a documented diplomatic defeat for the Holy See at that moment.

Palestinians and their supporters, who treat Resolution 194 as establishing a right of return, note that Israel's admission came with a pledge to honor it; one reference account names Israel's representative, Abba Eban, as giving an assurance that Israel would honor Resolutions 181 and 194.
The committee's summary record consulted documents the agenda of 6 May, not the content of Israel's answers, and the resolution itself only "takes note" of them.
The wording of any assurance, and how binding it was meant to be, cannot be stated here from the primary record; the competing readings of Resolution 194 are set out in .
Jerusalem was the issue on which the gap between the resolutions and the ground was widest.
Resolution 181 had made Jerusalem and Bethlehem a corpus separatum, a separate entity under UN administration.

After the war, according to Germany's Federal Agency for Civic Education, Israel held West Jerusalem and Jordan held East Jerusalem, including the Old City, the Temple Mount and the Western Wall, and Jews were denied access to their holy sites there.
The armistice with Jordan had put free access to the holy places on the agenda of a special committee.
On 9 December 1949 the General Assembly, in Resolution 303, again called for international status for Jerusalem.
Ben-Gurion spoke against the resolution in the Knesset on 13 December.
On 26 December the Knesset moved from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem.
On 23 January 1950 it declared Jerusalem the capital of Israel by 60 votes to 2; the two votes against were cast by Communists who supported international status.
The same source reports that the declaration was not internationally recognized, and that no state opened an embassy in West Jerusalem until 1967.

On the other, the internationalization of Jerusalem had already been overtaken by a war that left the eastern city, and the holy sites in it, under Jordanian rule with Jewish access denied, and Israel's admission resolution had recorded the UN's resolutions without making membership conditional on carrying them out.
The Vatican's own reckoning took decades.
It maintained non-recognition for 45 years after Israel's founding.

The precondition for change was doctrinal: the Second Vatican Council's declaration Nostra Aetate of 1965 revised Catholic teaching on Judaism, stating that God "holds the Jews most dear for the sake of their Fathers."

The Fundamental Agreement of 30 December 1993, signed in Jerusalem, established diplomatic relations, and ambassadors were exchanged in 1994; property rights, tax exemptions and the status of Jerusalem were left for continuing negotiation.

After the General Assembly's vote of November 2012, the Vatican recognized the State of Palestine in 2013 and in 2015 signed an accord governing the Church's activity in Palestinian-controlled territory, which drew a formal Israeli protest.
The first is the content of Israel's statements to the Ad Hoc Political Committee, which this book has not been able to read in the primary record.
The second is the Vatican campaign's reach: the sources used here document the campaign and its aims, but not which governments, if any, it moved among the twelve that voted against admission.
The last of that week's three texts, Resolution 194, is usually remembered for one paragraph, the eleventh, on the return of the refugees.
It is a longer document than that: it also set up a conciliation commission, called for an international regime for Jerusalem and protection for the Holy Places, and urged a final settlement.

Abraham Feinberg: One Donor, One Decision, 1945–1958
The one decision in that sequence that a historian ties to money runs through Abraham Feinberg, a name absent from most popular accounts of 1948.
He is the person through whom the documented record comes closest to showing a campaign contribution changing a particular decision of the American president.
Abraham "Abe" Feinberg was born in 1908 and died in 1998.
He was born and raised in the Bronx and built his fortune in the hosiery business.
From 1945 he played a significant role behind the scenes in the relationship between the United States and Israel, a role that lasted until 1968.
Across those years he served as a confidant and a key financier to three presidents: Truman, Kennedy and Johnson.
He was also one of the original seventeen members of the Sonneborn Institute, the arms-procurement network founded in 1945, whose place in the wider American structure is mapped in .
Feinberg was not a donor who appears once in the record and then disappears.
He links two structures that are often told separately: the private arms-procurement network that operated on American soil from 1945, and the presidential campaign of 1948.
In mid-1948 Truman's campaign was broke, and Thomas Dewey was widely expected to make him a one-term president.
Truman needed $100,000, a large sum in 1948, to pay for a whistle-stop tour by train through the Midwest.
Feinberg and the jewelry magnate Ed Kaufmann led the fundraising that produced that amount, at that moment.
Feinberg later described his own method plainly.
The link between the money and a decision comes from the historian John Judis.
In mid-1948, by Judis's account, Truman wanted Israel to stop seizing territory by military force beyond the UN partition lines, and he was personally "disgusted" by Israel's refugee policy.
He is reported to have said that Jews had turned their own narrative on its head by denying Palestinians the right of return.
Judis documents that Truman folded on these impulses in part because he needed the $100,000 from Feinberg and Kaufmann for the whistle-stop tour at that moment.
The dated sequence of what Truman did and did not do on territory and refugees, from the Bernadotte plan to the threat he sent Ben-Gurion in May 1949, is set out in .

The familiar account holds that Truman's support for Israel was a matter of personal conviction and of a broad political calculation about Jewish voters, with no instance in which financial dependence changed a specific decision.
Judis's account is such an instance.
It is also a limited one, and the limits are in Judis's own words.
He says Truman folded "in part" because of the financial need.
It does not show that Feinberg's money bought American policy toward Israel in general, and it does not show what Truman thought he was giving in return.
When Truman later threatened Israel over the same two questions, territory and refugees, the money of 1948 did not prevent him.
Some accounts go further and place the recognition of Israel, eleven minutes after its declaration of independence, inside the same financial relationship.
On the chart of dollar flows in the previous section, the $100,000 is the smallest bar, one-thousandth of the $100 million Export-Import Bank loan of 1949.
Yet it is the only sum in that record that a historian ties to a specific policy decision, because, by Judis's account, it was raised at the moment a decision was being made.
The federal government did eventually reach Feinberg, not for arms but for publishing.
In 1952 he was formally ordered to register as an agent of a foreign principal under the Foreign Agents Registration Act.
The order concerned Israel Speaks, a bimonthly publication he ran on behalf of Israeli interests, the successor to an earlier publication aligned with the Haganah.
Feinberg briefly considered selling the publication to the Jerusalem Post.
The order corrects a claim sometimes made about the Sonneborn network, that none of its figures was ever required to register as a foreign agent and that the network enjoyed complete legal immunity.
The same FBI file, released decades later, shows more.

It documents Feinberg's continuing meetings with Sonneborn, and it shows that the Israeli government tasked him with intervening in the criminal prosecutions of members of the arms-smuggling network who had been caught.
"Call Abe," 1958.
Feinberg's role did not end with the 1948 campaign.

According to Avner Cohen's history Israel and the Bomb, David Ben-Gurion secretly named Feinberg his chief coordinator for raising private American funds for Israel's clandestine nuclear weapons program, beginning in 1958.
Ben-Gurion is said to have told his staff simply to "call Abe."
On that account, the man who helped fund a whistle-stop tour in 1948 became, a decade later, the coordinator of private American funds for a clandestine nuclear program.
The account is Cohen's.
It establishes Feinberg's role and the instruction; it does not give the program's finances or the sums he raised, and that story belongs to a later volume.
Feinberg's career runs from the arms network of 1945 through a presidential campaign, a foreign-agent order and, by 1958, a nuclear fundraising role.

Over those years he is documented as a channel: for money into a campaign, for a publication on Israel's behalf, for Israel's government into an American prosecution, and for private funds into a secret program.
The one point at which the record ties his money to a specific American decision is the summer of 1948, and it does so through one historian's account, qualified by the words "in part."
The record does not show how much weight Truman gave that need against votes, conviction or advice.
It does not show any later president changing a decision because of Feinberg's money.

How the Case Was Made to Americans: Refuge, Bible and Democracy
The flight was explained to Western readers; so, from the start, was the case for the state itself.
A familiar explanation for American support of Israel runs backward from the present.

Because the two countries later became close strategic partners, it is assumed that Americans backed the new state in 1948 for the same reason: that Israel was already a proven ally whose value to Washington was plain.

The case put to the American public in the founding years rested on three different arguments, none of them strategic, and the men responsible for American strategy in that period made the opposite case in writing.
In Europe after the war some 250,000 Jewish displaced persons were still waiting in camps, and the destruction of European Jewry in the Holocaust was recent.
America's own door was part of the same argument: Truman signed the Displaced Persons Act of June 1948 while condemning it as discriminatory against Jewish displaced persons, a story told in .
Christian restorationist belief, the conviction that the Jews would be restored to the land of the Bible, had a history going back to 1839.
For Christian supporters the new state could be read as a biblical fulfillment.
The third argument was political in the plainest sense: the new state was presented to Americans as a democracy.
Against all three stood the American national-security establishment.
The State Department, the Joint Chiefs of Staff, the Secretary of Defense and the Central Intelligence Agency each warned that American backing for a Jewish state would harm American interests.
Declassified CIA documents from 1948 predicted that recognition would produce armed conflict and damage American access to oil.
Truman overruled them.
He recognized Israel eleven minutes after its declaration of independence on 14 May 1948, so quickly that his own State Department was caught unaware.
The White House aides who argued the domestic political case, Clark Clifford and David Niles among them, and the personal channel that reached him through his friend Eddie Jacobson, carried the day.
Whatever moved American policy in 1948, it was not a consensus inside the government that Israel served American strategy.
The publicity of the period also had a hostile side, aimed at the Arab opponents of partition.
Pro-Zionist publicity drew heavily on the wartime collaboration of the Grand Mufti of Jerusalem with Hitler.
A single leader's alliance with the Axis was used as a broad brush to color Arab opposition as a whole, which the documented episode does not support.
The first is the organized anti-Islam network in the United States.
The organized, well-funded anti-Islam network is documented mainly from the 2000s, building on currents that formed after 1967 and after 1979.
The anti-Arab framing of 1948 leaned on a specific wartime episode, not on an industry.

The claim that Israel was a strategic asset to the United States grew after Israel's victory in 1967, a generation after the founding, and was formalized under President Reagan, who called Israel a strategic asset and signed a strategic-cooperation agreement with it in 1981.

Until then American aid was cautious: from 1948 into the early 1960s it consisted of economic aid and loans, with Washington avoiding direct arms sales for fear of alienating Arab oil-producing states, a pattern taken up in .
In 1948 Americans were asked to support Israel as a refuge for survivors, as the fulfillment of a promise that some Christians read in scripture, and as a new democracy.
The strategic argument was then being made by the other side of the debate, inside the American government, and it pointed against support.

The documents establish which arguments were made and which officials opposed the policy; they do not measure how many Americans were moved by the survivors, how many by scripture and how many by the language of democracy, or how far the hostile portrait of Arab opposition shaped opinion.
Truman After Recognition: A Retreat, a Pledge, and a Threat Not Kept, 1948–1950
Bernadotte's September plan was one of several moments at which Washington had to decide how far to back the new state.
American recognition in May 1948 had not settled that question.
It opened a two-year sequence in which Harry Truman's decisions moved sometimes toward Israel's position and sometimes against it.
One holds that once the donors had paid, Truman did whatever Israel wanted.
The other holds that money had nothing to do with it, and that his policy followed from conviction and from the interests of the United States.
The second can point to a president who signed legislation he called discriminatory against Jewish refugees and later threatened Israel in writing.
Recognition itself had been made against the advice of the government's own specialists.
Declassified CIA and State Department documents from 1947 and 1948 record consistent warnings against recognizing Israel on strategic grounds.

The CIA's assessments noted the Zionist arms-procurement networks operating across Europe and the United States, predicted that recognition would immediately produce armed conflict with the Arab states, and warned of damage to American access to oil.
One CIA report held that an arms embargo would lead to peaceful coexistence, the opposite of what followed.
The State Department under George Marshall opposed recognition on strategic grounds as well.
Truman overruled both.
He recognized Israel at 6:11 pm on 14 May 1948, eleven minutes after its declaration of independence, a recognition so fast that his own State Department was caught unprepared.
It has been called the fastest diplomatic recognition in American history.
The familiar explanation is that Truman acted from moral conviction about Jewish statehood after the Holocaust, and that the CIA's concerns were one input among many.

One reading, made with the advantage of hindsight, holds that this set a pattern in which political decisions overrode intelligence assessments, and that the intelligence relationship which followed began on terms Israel could shape.

That is an interpretation of later history, not a finding about 1948, and the later relationship, from the start of James Jesus Angleton's tenure as the CIA's counterintelligence chief in 1954 to the Khrushchev speech of 1956, is told in .
25 June 1948: the Displaced Persons Act.
The first decision of the summer concerned Jewish refugees in Europe rather than the new state itself.
On 25 June 1948 Truman signed the Displaced Persons Act "with very great reluctance," saying that it "discriminates in callous fashion against displaced persons of the Jewish faith."
He pressed Congress for two years, until the act was amended in 1950.
The episode does not fit a president acting on donors' instructions, nor one indifferent to Jewish refugees: he signed a law he condemned and then spent two years trying to change it.
Summer 1948: what Truman wanted and did not press.
Through the summer, Truman privately wanted Israel to stop taking territory beyond the partition lines, and he was disturbed by its refugee policy.

The historian John Judis documents that his nearly broke whistle-stop campaign needed $100,000 from two donors, Abraham Feinberg and Ed Kaufmann, at that moment, and that this need was part of the reason he stopped pushing.
The donors, the sum and the way Judis frames it are the subject of .
21–28 September 1948: the Bernadotte plan.
On 16 September the UN mediator, Count Folke Bernadotte, completed a report that would have given the Negev to the Arab side; the next day he was murdered in Jerusalem.
On 21 September 1948 Secretary of State Marshall endorsed the plan.

On 28 September the White House aide Clark Clifford was upset that Marshall had approved it without the President's endorsement, and the camp of Truman's opponent, Thomas Dewey, sought to exploit the episode.
Truman backed away from the plan.
The American government was not of one mind: the Secretary of State had endorsed what the President's aide opposed.
Ten days before the election, and two days after a statement by Dewey, Truman went further.

He quoted the Democratic platform, which pledged full recognition of Israel and revision of the arms embargo "to accord to the State of Israel the right of self-defense," and he directed government agencies to expedite Israel's applications for loans.
29 November 1948: the Negev.
After winning, on 29 November, Truman reassured Weizmann that Israel would keep the Negev.
Two months earlier his Secretary of State had endorsed a plan that would have taken it away.
An Export-Import Bank loan of $100 million was earmarked for Israel, and on 31 January 1949 the United States granted de jure recognition, full legal recognition of the state.
The $100,000 that Feinberg and Kaufmann raised for the campaign train is the smallest, one-thousandth of the loan.

Those who argue that money played no role point to the scale: a government loan of $100 million was a decision of the United States made through the Export-Import Bank after an election had been won, not a return on a campaign contribution.
On 28 May 1949, while the Lausanne talks were under way, Truman had a secret note delivered to David Ben-Gurion.
It said the United States was "seriously disturbed" by Israel's position on territory and refugees.
It said Israel should offer territorial compensation for the land it held beyond the partition lines.
And it warned that if Israel continued to reject the UN resolution of December 1948, "a revision of its attitude toward Israel has become unavoidable."
The note took up exactly the two questions, territory and refugees, on which Truman had stopped pressing in the summer of 1948.
Israel rejected the demands in June.
The documents gathered here do not explain why Washington did not follow its warning with action.
What came at Lausanne after the note is told in .
May 1950: the Tripartite Declaration.
In May 1950 the United States joined Britain and France in the Tripartite Declaration on the region.
Laid out in order, the decisions have a clear shape.
Two moves favorable to Israel in 1948, the retreat from the Bernadotte plan and the October pledges, came when money and votes were most needed.
After the election Truman both delivered and pushed back: he delivered recognition and the loan, and then, six months later, threatened a revision of policy over the very issues he had set aside.
It is not the record of a president who did whatever Israel's supporters asked, since in May 1949 he sent a note threatening a revision of policy over territory and refugees.
The documents establish timing, not motive: they show when Truman moved, not how much weight he gave to money, votes, conviction or advice at each step.
Judis's account attributes the summer retreat to financial need "in part," and no source here measures that part.

And the record gathered does not say why the threatened revision of May 1949 was never carried out, which is perhaps the most consequential question of the sequence, since it was the moment at which Washington had stated its terms and then let them go.

Israel has argued that neither creates a binding right of return for descendants.
The text of Article 13(2) itself is not disputed.
The General Assembly created the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees, UNRWA, in December 1949, and it began work in May 1950.
ents: the United Nations Relief and Works Agency

sent: It provides schools, health care and relief to registered Palestine refugees.
The Refugee Convention adopted that year defined who was a refugee and what protection states owed.
Its Article 1D excluded people already receiving protection or assistance from another United Nations agency.

Because the Palestinian refugees had UNRWA, the clause left them outside the protection system that covers every other refugee population, and outside the durable-solutions mandate of the UN High Commissioner for Refugees.

In practice, this meant that through the 1950s the Palestinian refugees had an agency that gave them relief, schooling and health care, but no international body whose task was to protect their legal status or to find them a permanent solution, whether return, settlement where they were, or settlement elsewhere.
The one body with a political mandate, the Conciliation Commission created by Resolution 194, was a commission of three member states, not a protection agency.
The Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court was adopted in 1998 and entered into force in July 2002, without retroactive reach.
Palestine acceded in 2015, which is why the Court's jurisdiction in Palestinian matters begins in that era.
The common claim that the international human-rights system examined the Palestinian displacement and judged it in 1948 therefore runs ahead of the record.
What followed was relief through UNRWA and a refugee convention that, by its own text, did not apply to the Palestinians.
The record leaves open why the drafters of the 1951 Convention wrote Article 1D as they did, and the sources used here do not give the debates.
Nor do they settle the legal weight of Article 13(2) for the 1948 refugees and their descendants, which remains the subject of the opposing positions set out above.
Fifty-One Years From a Bank to a State: The Whole Sequence, Step by Step
A familiar account treats Israel's creation as a sudden event: a response to the Holocaust, ratified by a postwar decision at the United Nations and completed in a single war.
The genocide in Europe did change the politics of the question; the General Assembly did vote in November 1947; the war of 1948 did decide where the lines would run.
Laid end to end, the documents of Volume II show a sequence built over five decades and across two continents, each step resting on the one before.
In 1897 the Basel Congress set the goal.
Two years later, in 1899, the movement founded the Jewish Colonial Trust, a bank chartered in London and capitalized by small shareholders.
In 1901 the Jewish National Fund began buying land on a principle that defined it for the next half-century: land it bought was held permanently and never resold.
In 1902 came the Anglo-Palestine Bank.
Between 1912 and 1918 an American organization took shape: Hadassah; Justice Brandeis with access to President Wilson; and the Zionist Organization of America, which reached 147,000 members by 1918 .
In 1917 Britain issued the Balfour Declaration, addressed to Lord Rothschild.
In 1920 the movement created Keren Hayesod, its permanent fund, whose mandate before 1948 covered immigration, settlement, defense, water and public works .
1921–1933: tours, Congress, a currency and a wider money base.
In 1921 Weizmann and Einstein toured the United States, and a $5 million delegation tour of 1921–22 met President Harding.

Keren Hayesod's worldwide receipts from April 1921 to December 1929 came to $20.1 million, of which $11.0 million came from the United States, followed by South Africa, Germany, Romania, Britain, Poland and Canada .
In 1922 Congress endorsed the Balfour Declaration through the resolution sponsored by Senator Henry Cabot Lodge and Representative Hamilton Fish III .
In 1927 came a Palestine pound managed from London.
In 1929 non-Zionist American money joined an enlarged Jewish Agency, widening the base beyond the movement's own members.
Christian committees were organized from the Zionist political office in 1932, when the American Palestine Committee was formed, and again in 1941–42.
The American Palestine Committee and the Christian Council on Palestine were both organized by the Zionist executive Emanuel Neumann, and one historian has described them as "hardly autonomous" .
In 1933 came the Haavara transfer agreement, valued at 105 million Reichsmarks, about $40 million at the time, over 1933–39.
In 1938 the Jewish National Council in Palestine created Kofer HaYishuv, a levy on cigarettes, restaurant bills and luxuries, to fund the Haganah .
In 1939 the Jewish Agency's budget was set at £720,000, of which £80,000 was for "the Jewish security service (defense)," as the American consulate reported .
In 1942 the Biltmore program committed the movement to a Jewish commonwealth.

In 1943 the American Zionist Emergency Council, co-chaired by Abba Hillel Silver and Stephen Wise, built a national lobbying machine of local committees, letter and telegram campaigns and a published record of legislators' statements .

In 1944 both American party platforms adopted the movement's aims, and US-raised spending that year reached $10.8 million through the Jewish National Fund and $14.9 million through the Jewish Agency and Keren Hayesod .

In 1945 a secret meeting convened by Ben-Gurion, with donors gathered by the United Jewish Appeal's Henry Montor, set up the Sonneborn Institute and its front company, Materials for Palestine, which linked American fundraising to arms .
In 1946 the Agency sought a $56 million budget .

In 1948 the United Jewish Appeal raised a record $150 million from more than a million contributors ; a June 1948 campaign advertisement called it "the official American agency for aid to Haganah" ; Golda Meyerson's American tour raised about $50 million, largely for arms; arms were bought in Czechoslovakia; and banknotes for the new state were printed in New York.
In the same year Abraham Feinberg and Ed Kaufmann raised the $100,000 that, in one historian's account, weighed on a single presidential decision.

Beneath all of this lay older foundations: the Ottoman and British layers of administration, a Christian restorationist lobby dating from 1839, and the Rothschild colonies in Palestine dating from 1882.

What the Holocaust changed, and what it did not.
In 1945–48 the argument made to Americans rested first on refuge for some 250,000 Jewish displaced persons in Europe.

The money changed in scale: the United Jewish Appeal, formed in 1939, raised more than $124 million across all of 1939–45, then $100 million in 1946 alone , about $110 million in 1947  and $150 million in 1948.
Much of that money was for the survivors themselves: $64.9 million of the 1948 campaign went to the Joint Distribution Committee for relief in Europe .
What the record does not support is the step from "the Holocaust changed everything" to "the Holocaust created the state."
The bank, the land fund, the recognized agency, the American fundraising and lobbying machinery, the congressional endorsement and the defense levy all existed before 1939.
Edmond de Rothschild, who funded the early colonies, opposed Herzl.

In Washington the State Department, the Joint Chiefs of Staff and the Secretary of Defense opposed the policy in writing, the CIA warned that American backing would harm American interests, and all were overruled.
Britain spent about £100 million on its forces in Palestine in 1945–47 alone, with some 100,000 troops deployed, before giving up the Mandate .
They were not borders by their own terms: Article V of the Egyptian agreement says the demarcation line "is not to be construed in any sense as a political or territorial boundary" .
But they enclosed what Israel's Foreign Ministry describes as about 78 percent of the Mandate area , against the 56 percent the 1947 plan had allotted.

A Custodian of Abandoned Property was appointed on 15 July 1948; emergency regulations in December 1948 transferred control to a Custodian of Absentee Property; and on 14 March 1950 the Knesset passed the Absentees' Property Law .
A Development Authority established in 1950 became, in the words of a 2016 study, both a major land allocator and the body that set "the rules of the game" .

According to an analysis published by BADIL, the 1950 law let the Custodian pass absentee land to the Development Authority and on to the Jewish National Fund; nearly 2.4 million dunams were transferred, "more than trebling the JNF's holdings as of 1941," and by 1951 the government and the Fund together held 92 percent of the land within the state .
Those are BADIL's figures, and the scholarly sources in this chapter do not give a settled total of their own.
According to the same analysis, the Land Acquisition Law of 1953 then retroactively validated seizures made during and after the war .
Section 1 of the Law of Return, dated 5 July 1950, states that "Every Jew has the right to come to this country as an oleh" .

sent: Presenting it, Ben-Gurion said the right "preceded the State of Israel," and the Encyclopaedia Judaica links the law to the Basel Program of 1897, Article 6 of the Mandate of 1922 and the Declaration of Independence .

The Nationality Law, in force from 14 July 1952, made every immigrant under the Law of Return a national "by return," while former Palestinian citizens could become nationals "by residence" only if they met a registration test tied to 1 March 1952 .

In the same years, Arab citizens lived under a military government, dated by Alina Korn to October 1948  and by other accounts to 1949 , and administered through the British Defense (Emergency) Regulations of 1945 .
Private American giving remained, but now beside it came a state's own instruments.

The United States government gave $100.0 million in 1949, through the Export-Import Bank and other channels, then nothing in 1950, $35.1 million in 1951 and $86.4 million in 1952, all of it economic .
Israel Bonds, launched in the United States in 1951, sold more than $52 million in their first year and within six years were financing 35 percent of the state's special development budget .

And the reparations agreement with West Germany, signed in Luxembourg on 10 September 1952, paid in oil and German goods that made up 12 to 14 percent of Israel's annual imports over the following decade .
Here the Holocaust entered the architecture directly: Sharett's claim of $1.5 billion was calculated as the cost of absorbing 500,000 Nazi victims at $3,000 each .

The agreement's total value is given differently in two sources, and the Knesset vote to negotiate, 61 to 50 on 9 January 1952 with protesters outside, shows how divided the new state's own public was .

On the American side, the lobbying council of 1943 was renamed the American Zionist Council in 1949 , and in 1953–54 Isaiah Kenen founded a separate American Zionist Committee for Public Affairs, renamed AIPAC in 1959 by one account, while another dates AIPAC's emergence to a restructuring in 1963 .

Israel was not improvised in two years.

The bank, the land fund, the recognized agency, the American fundraising and lobbying machinery, the congressional endorsement and the arms channels were assembled over five decades, and the state's first laws on land and immigration were built on them.
